papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) perform strongly in face recognition (FR), yet their fixed-depth inference limits deployment in resource-constrained settings. We propose SD-ViT, a training framework that gives a usable exit at every block depth by making every depth produce discriminative embeddings, for budget-selected fixed-depth exits. Standard ViTs supervise intermediate layers only through backpropagation, so their intermediate representations are not directly optimized to form usable identity embeddings. SD-ViT adds a stochastic auxiliary signal: at each iteration a randomly selected intermediate block is passed through the same embedding head as the final layer and trained with a weighted margin-penalty softmax loss. The objective is thus stochastically sampled deep supervision through a shared classifier. Because both loss terms share that head and classifier, intermediate tokens are trained to map into the same embedding space as final-layer tokens. This matters for FR, where matching is by similarity: a probe processed at an early exit can be compared directly against full-depth gallery embeddings, with no gallery recomputation or adaptation layers. On established benchmarks, SD-ViT stays within 0.4 IJB-C points of the same backbone trained conventionally at full depth, while its early-exit probes recover over 96% of their own full-depth performance at 50% of the computational cost without modifying the reference gallery. A single verification threshold calibrated at full depth remains usable from quarter depth onward.
bullets: Fixed-depth ViTs are inefficient for resource-constrained face-recognition deployment because intermediate layers lack directly optimized identity embeddings.
At each iteration, a randomly selected intermediate block is trained through the final embedding head and shared classifier with a weighted margin-penalty softmax loss.
Shared supervision aligns early-exit and final-layer embeddings, allowing early probes to match unchanged full-depth gallery embeddings without adaptation layers or gallery recomputation.

On established benchmarks, the method remains within 0.4 IJB-C points of conventional full-depth training; at half the computational cost, early exits retain over 96% of their own full-depth performance.
A single threshold calibrated at full depth remains usable from quarter depth onward.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of SD-ViT. A face image is tokenized and processed by L blocks. The full-depth tokens z(L) form the primary exit. At each iteration a secondary exit is read out at a uniformly sampled block z(k), k ∼ U{1, . . . , L−1}. Both are decoded by the same head H and scored against the same prototypes W under a margin-penalty loss, combined with weight ω (Eq. 4). Sharing H and W across depths places all embeddings in one space, so at inference a probe may exit at any depth k (Eq. 5) and match a gallery enrolled once at full depth.

Figure 2. Per-exit accuracy under both protocols. Top (a-c): self-evaluation, with probe and gallery embedded at the same exit, for three configurations. Color denotes the configuration and line style the method (see the legend panel). Baseline early exits collapse while SD-ViT degrades far less, on every backbone and both training sets. Bottom (e-g): the gallery-fixed protocol of Sec. 4.4, an exit-k probe against a gallery enrolled once at the final block, for ViT-S/12. Here the Baseline is near zero on the harder benchmarks below half depth, and Feature-MSE lies between it and SD-ViT. (h): mean cosine similarity between each exit and the final-block embedding, averaged over the test sets. SD-ViT aligns intermediate embeddings more than the explicit feature-matching variant.

Figure 3. Ablations on ViT-S/12, WebFace4M (IJB-C TAR@FAR= 10−4 top, TinyFace Rank-1 bottom). (a) Weight ω: full depth (solid) is nearly constant for ω ≥ 0.5, mid-depth (dashed) stable for ω ≤ 0.9 and collapsing at ω=1, dotted marks ω=0.7. (b) Loss: comparable early-exit accuracy under AdaFace and ArcFace. (c) Depth: the gains hold at L=15. (d) Where to supervise: sampling degrades smoothly toward exit 1, while fixed exits collapse below the chosen depths. (e) Auxiliary objective: teacher KD and feature-MSE raise early exits above the baseline yet collapse at shallow depths, while SD-ViT stays far above them at early exits.

Reading its intermediate blocks through the shared head is the training-free ViT-FREE [12] protocol. ViT-FREEFT trains one projection and one prototype set per exit on that frozen Baseline. ViTFREEFT was not designed for this protocol (Sec. 2).

papers.selection_reason: Early-exit ViT for computational efficiency in face recognition.
papers.title: Stochastic Deep Supervision for Gallery-Consistent Early-Exit Face Recognition
papers.tldr: SD-ViT enables ViTs to perform gallery-consistent early-exit face recognition by stochastically supervising intermediate depths in a shared embedding space.

papers.abstract: Inference-time steering in vision-language models often entangles query-relevant reasoning dynamics with low-level perceptual noise, causing collateral degradation on correct predictions. We propose Question-Contrastive Visual Steering (QCVS) to isolate task-specific intervention directions via double-differential activation probing. By contrasting spatial layout perturbations under the target query against a generic description reference, QCVS cancels task-agnostic visual artifacts without ground-truth supervision. A dual-threshold gating mechanism then evaluates relative interaction strength and signal amplitude, selectively applying a single bounded hidden-state update only when necessary. Empirical evaluations across multiple scales of Qwen3.5 (2B to 9B) and DeepSeek-VL2 on DynaMath and We-Math demonstrate that QCVS achieves state-of-the-art accuracy gains under sparse coverage (approximately 22%-30%). Crucially, QCVS yields repair rates up to 13.98% while suppressing collateral damage down to 0.41%, proving high intervention precision and computational efficiency.
bullets: Targets task-relevant reasoning signals while filtering out low-level visual perturbation noise.
Uses double-differential activation probing with spatial-layout contrasts and a generic-description reference, requiring no ground-truth supervision.
Applies a single bounded hidden-state update through dual-threshold gating only when intervention is warranted.
Evaluated on Qwen3.5 and DeepSeek-VL2 across DynaMath and We-Math, with sparse coverage of approximately 22%–30%.
Reports repair rates up to 13.98% and collateral damage as low as 0.41%, alongside state-of-the-art accuracy gains.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Motivation and computation of QCVS. (a) Describing a scene and counting water-filled glasses require different evidence. The BLINK [19] example has dataset label 3; the crops are human-selected illustrations, not model outputs. (b) One visual encoding feeds a frozen Qwen3.5 model: two questions and three visual conditions give six prefix readouts. (c) Paired clean–control differences at each final assistant-prefix token ta yield the interaction µ. Its direction defines a bounded edit; R and A determine selection. A selected input receives one update at (ℓ∗, ta) in a fresh clean-prefix replay; otherwise, decoding uses the retained clean hybrid state.
Fig. 2. Fixed-action coverage sweep on Qwen3.5-4B/DynaMath. Curves show repairs, harm and net change as percentages of all inputs; net change equals accuracy gain (pp).

papers.selection_reason: Inference-time steering of vision-language model reasoning via activation probing; directly relevant to multimodal LLM methods.
papers.title: QCVS: Question-Contrastive Visual Steering for Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: QCVS improves multimodal reasoning at inference time by selectively steering hidden states to correct errors while minimizing harm to correct predictions.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models produce large KV caches during multi-round video generation. Keeping all these KV chunks would consume substantial memory, while rebuilding discarded caches would significantly delay video chunk generation. This paper presents ReelCache, a KV cache compression system for efficient multi-round, long video generation. ReelCache combines an intra-chunk compressor with an inter-chunk cache manager. The compressor applies low-rank decomposition across channels and video coding to the resulting coefficients, predicting the decomposition rank per transformer layer online to meet retained-energy targets. The cache manager shares basis directions across consecutive chunks and organizes chunk states in a tree, allowing generation branches to share historical state while supporting restoration for resume, rewind, and fork. Experiments across five video generation models show that ReelCache reduces KV storage by 14.46-21.13x relative to baselines and accelerates next-chunk generation by 1.25-3.36x, with less than 1% drop in six representative VBench metrics. GitHub: https://github.com/Tianyu9748/ReelCache
bullets: Addresses the large memory cost and regeneration delay of KV caches in autoregressive video diffusion.
Combines online low-rank, video-coded intra-chunk compression with inter-chunk basis sharing and tree-based cache management.
Supports efficient cache restoration for resume, rewind, and fork generation branches.
Across five video generation models, reduces KV storage by 14.46–21.13× and accelerates next-chunk generation by 1.25–3.36×.
Reports less than a 1% drop in six representative VBench metrics.

(b) Session pointer and user operations: resume, rewind, and fork. shown in Figure 12(b). The multi-round video generation then becomes tree operations: resume continues from this node; rewind selects an ancestor; and fork starts a new branch whose first chunk is a child of any existing node and leaves the parent’s branch untouched. Existing nodes remain unchanged, allowing branches to share their common history without copying it. The detailed algorithm for determining if a node can share the basis of its parent node is in §H.

papers.abstract: General-purpose mobile manipulation requires a combination of capable robot hardware, scalable demonstration collection, expressive whole-body control, and effective policy learning. Yet these components are often developed independently, creating mismatches that limit the capabilities of the complete system. We present Pixel, a co-designed full-stack system for learning general-purpose mobile manipulation. Pixel combines a low-cost wheeled humanoid with human-aligned kinematics and compliant grippers, multiple teleoperation and robot-free human data-collection interfaces, a unified whole-body controller, and a common policy learning pipeline across human and robot demonstrations. A hierarchical learning stack further enables language-conditioned visuomotor control and long-horizon task execution. We evaluate the system across hardware, data collection, and policy learning, and demonstrate mobile-manipulation behaviors requiring dexterity, active perception, navigation, and whole-body coordination. We hope that Pixel provides an integrated and extensible foundation for studying how robot hardware, data, control, and learning can be designed together for robot learning. More results at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel
bullets: Combines a low-cost wheeled humanoid with human-aligned kinematics and compliant grippers.
Supports multiple teleoperation and robot-free interfaces for scalable human demonstration collection.
Uses a unified whole-body controller and shared policy-learning pipeline across human and robot demonstrations.
Adds hierarchical, language-conditioned visuomotor control for long-horizon tasks.
Demonstrates behaviors involving dexterity, active perception, navigation, and whole-body coordination.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a full-stack mobile manipulation system integrating human demonstration collection, whole-body control, and language-conditioned visuomotor policies.
papers.title: Pixel: A Co-Designed Full-Stack Robot System for Learning General-Purpose Mobile Manipulation
papers.tldr: Pixel is a co-designed, full-stack robot system that integrates hardware, demonstration collection, whole-body control, and policy learning for general-purpose mobile manipulation.

papers.abstract: Sensorized human demonstrations offer scalable data for mobile manipulation, but embodiment differences complicate policy learning. We present Pixel-UMI, a pipeline for learning environment-aware whole-body policies from human data. We first introduce Environment-Aware Retargeting (EAR), which combines reconstructed scene geometry with demonstrated head and gripper trajectories to determine robot posture and generate collision-aware joint and base targets. Delay-calibrated action assignment converts these trajectories into actions. However, kinematic differences can leave residual pose errors, creating viewpoint mismatches between human demonstrations and robot observations. We therefore introduce Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking (REAM), which uses these errors during training to reduce reliance on mismatched views at deployment. Finally, because estimated actions cannot fully capture contact-rich interactions, we collect on-policy human corrections through DAgger to improve performance. We evaluate Pixel-UMI on five challenging tasks spanning articulated-object manipulation, deformable-object handling, constrained-space reaching, whole-body collision avoidance, and contact-rich bimanual coordination, achieving 87.0% average task progress. Video results are available at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel-umi
bullets: Addresses embodiment differences between human demonstrations and mobile manipulation robots.
Uses Environment-Aware Retargeting to convert scene geometry and human head/gripper trajectories into collision-aware robot joint and base targets.
Applies Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking to reduce reliance on observation views mismatched by residual retargeting errors.
Uses delay-calibrated action assignment and on-policy human corrections via DAgger to handle imperfect, contact-rich actions.
Evaluated across five challenging manipulation tasks, achieving 87.0% average task progress.

papers.abstract: Learning from human data offers a scalable path toward embodied intelligence, yet it requires models to accurately understand fine-grained human actions from egocentric observations. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association. We introduce EgoActionBench, a benchmark that represents continuous human manipulation as temporally localized atomic actions associated with the left hand, right hand, or both hands. EgoActionBench contains 1,407 episodes with 41,132 human-refined action annotations. To evaluate such dense predictions, we propose an evaluation protocol that retrieves temporally eligible candidates, selects a prediction by content agreement, and scores semantic fidelity and temporal overlap alongside action precision and recall, jointly capturing what happens, when it happens, and which hand performs it. We benchmark 20 baseline models and systems on EgoActionBench and further adapt two backbones, Qwen3-VL-4B and LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B, through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning on automatically annotated training episodes. EgoAction improves EgoActionScore by 15.9 and 23.2 points on the two backbones, and both adapted models outperform all open-source baselines. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations of current models in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association, highlighting the gap between general video understanding and the action understanding required for embodied intelligence.
bullets: Introduces 1,407 episodes with 41,132 human-refined annotations of temporally localized atomic actions linked to the left hand, right hand, or both.
Proposes an evaluation protocol measuring semantic fidelity, temporal overlap, action precision, and recall.
Benchmarks 20 models and systems, including adapted Qwen3-VL-4B and LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B backbones.
Supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning improves EgoActionScore by 15.9 and 23.2 points on the two adapted backbones.
Finds persistent limitations in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association.

papers.abstract: We present Isekai3D Synthetic Data Generation (SDG), a platform for simulating and capturing synthetic 3D gameplay for research in vision and world models, neural graphics, gameplay agents, and other applications. The platform combines reusable environment and character assets with Unreal Engine plugins in a two-stage workflow. First, world simulation generates gameplay while recording the world state, character movements, actions, and camera tracks needed for replay. Second, the recorded simulation is replayed to capture selected outputs, such as rendered video, images, and depth maps, at a specified resolution and frame rate under selected rendering and camera configurations. Separating simulation from capture allows the same recorded gameplay to produce multiple output variants without repeating the original simulation. Visual outputs are accompanied by frame-aligned camera, character, and action metadata. The platform uploads generated data directly in a training-friendly format, reducing intermediate storage, preparation time, and manual processing. This report describes the design of our overall system, including the platform's assets, plugins, and their functionality, explaining how they work together to generate diverse synthetic gameplay data.
bullets: Targets research in computer vision, world models, neural graphics, gameplay agents, and related areas.
Simulates gameplay once while recording world state, movements, actions, and camera tracks.
Replays recorded simulations to produce configurable videos, images, and depth maps.
Provides frame-aligned camera, character, and action metadata with training-ready uploads.
Separating simulation from capture enables multiple output variants without rerunning gameplay simulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) hold promise for zero-shot video task-progress estimation in robot learning, yet existing frameworks frequently suffer from confirmation bias, hallucinating progress in failed executions due to implicit success assumptions or relative temporal ranking designs. Naive prompting of frontier models collapses into a binary success detector that fails to capture nuanced, non-linear progress and failures. While post-training approaches can mitigate this through explicit training, they demand expensive real-world robotics data and require computationally intensive post-training for every individual base model. To resolve these limitations, we introduce D&A (Describe & Assess): our approach decouples progress estimation into an objective, task-grounded textual description of scene dynamics followed by an assessment phase using explicit rubrics. By compelling the VLM to synthesize an explicit, text-based definition of absolute success before scoring, the framework anchors evaluations to an external, global criterion rather than the video's internal timeline. Empirical results demonstrate that our method calibrates zero-shot estimates and mitigates confirmation bias, providing fine-grained, partial progress metrics that accurately penalize failed executions while correctly interpolating successful runs. Being purely prompt-based, D&A generalizes across tasks, embodiments, and benchmarks---matching or surpassing post-trained reward models---and its reward estimates enable efficient downstream reinforcement learning.
bullets: Addresses confirmation bias, hallucinated progress, and binary success judgments in video-based robot task evaluation.
First prompts the VLM to define task-grounded absolute success through textual scene descriptions, then scores progress against explicit rubrics.
Produces fine-grained, non-linear progress estimates that penalize failures and interpolate successful executions.
Uses only prompting, enabling generalization across tasks, embodiments, and benchmarks without per-model post-training.
The resulting reward estimates support efficient downstream reinforcement learning and match or surpass post-trained reward models.

papers.abstract: Neural operators provide efficient surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD), but most are designed for static geometries and are not equipped to model unsteady flows induced by continuously moving boundaries. We study dynamic-boundary 4D CFD prediction for articulated moving geometries and introduce RoboCFD-4D, a temporally resolved robotic CFD benchmark spanning diverse morphologies and flow conditions. To address the computational and autoregressive challenges of this setting, we propose DynaSolver, a neural operator that explicitly conditions on boundary evolution and causal flow history. DynaSolver employs an efficient physical-token formulation that amortizes point-to-token projection across the operator stack, substantially reducing repeated point-space spatio-temporal computation while retaining accurate point-level reconstruction. We further introduce Replay-Augmented Parallel Training, which exposes the model to autoregressively generated histories while preserving parallel dense supervision, narrowing the gap between ground-truth-conditioned training and autoregressive rollout. Experiments on RoboCFD-4D show that DynaSolver achieves the best full-rollout accuracy among a broad range of learned CFD surrogates, with its advantage increasing as rollout proceeds, indicating substantially reduced autoregressive error accumulation. Project page: https://made-gpt.github.io/DynaSolver-ProjectPage.
bullets: Addresses CFD surrogate modeling for articulated geometries with unsteady, continuously changing boundaries.
Introduces RoboCFD-4D, a temporally resolved benchmark covering varied morphologies and flow conditions.
Uses physical tokens to reduce repeated point-space spatio-temporal computation while retaining point-level reconstruction.
Replay-Augmented Parallel Training exposes the model to its own autoregressive histories during training.
Experiments report the best full-rollout accuracy among evaluated learned CFD surrogates, with growing benefits over longer rollouts.

figures.caption: Figure 7 | Overview of the RoboCFD-4D data generation pipeline. Public robot assets are standardized and repaired at the link level, followed by prescribed motion synthesis and reusable link-local SDF construction. The transformed link-local fields define the prescribed moving immersed boundary for multi-condition CFD simulations. Aligned volumetric fields and tracked near-surface observations are then extracted and subjected to geometric, numerical, and dataset-level validation before inclusion in the final published dataset.

Figure 2 | Overview of DynaSolver. Given the spatial condition, boundary evolution, and previous CFD states over a causal window, DynaSolver lifts and fuses the point-wise inputs before mapping them into separate surface and volume physical tokens. A single Fast Slice/Deslice pair encloses the spatio-temporal operator stack, where self-attention, cross-attention, and causal attention jointly model spatial and temporal flow interactions. The reconstructed point features are decoded into a residual flow field and added to the previous CFD state to predict the current velocity and pressure.

Figure 3 | Comparison of training strategies for autoregressive flow prediction. Dense Unrolled Training (a) and Dense Pushforward Training (b) construct autoregressive histories sequentially, whereas Parallel Teacher-Forcing Training (c) predicts all transitions in a clip simultaneously from ground-truth histories. Our Replay-Augmented Parallel Training (d) decouples autoregressive history generation from student optimization: a frozen model first rolls out replay inputs (d.1), which are then used for parallel dense supervision of the current model (d.2). Red solid arrows→ denote feedforward computation, while green dashed arrows d denote backpropagation.

In contrast, RoboCFD-4D requires joint modeling of articulated three-dimensional boundary motion and the resulting time-evolving flow field across diverse robot morphologies.

papers.abstract: In the near future language model pretraining will become bound by total data rather than total compute. Such a regime requires revisiting scaling laws and scaling law theory. Motivated by prior works that have found utility in ensembling, we study how the number of training epochs and ensemble size jointly shape generalization when training data are fixed. In language-model experiments on FineWeb, logit averaging reduces late-training deterioration, delays optimal stopping, and can outperform wider or deeper single models at matched parameter-token budgets over a common training horizon. To analyze this interaction between data reuse and ensembling, we derive a dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for multi-epoch stochastic gradient descent in power-law random-feature ensembles, tracking error correlations across epochs and models. Ensembling reduces the prediction variance responsible for late-time growth in expected test error, changing the optimal stopping time. We use these stopping times to derive compute-allocation laws at fixed data and individual model sizes. Under this allocation, ensemble size grows with compute at least as fast as training time per member, while excess test loss above the limiting loss decreases as a power of compute.
bullets: Studies how training epochs and ensemble size jointly affect generalization in the data-limited regime.
FineWeb experiments show logit averaging reduces late-training deterioration and delays optimal stopping.
Ensembles can outperform wider or deeper single models at matched parameter-token budgets over a shared training horizon.
Develops a dynamical mean-field theory for multi-epoch SGD that tracks cross-epoch and cross-model error correlations.
Derives compute-allocation laws: ensemble size should grow at least as quickly as each member’s training time, with excess loss decreasing as a power of compute.

papers.abstract: Robust 3D point-cloud recognition is critical for robotics, mapping, and urban sensing, yet point-cloud classifiers often suffer performance drops under domain shifts caused by sensor changes, environmental variation, and acquisition artifacts. Many existing adaptation methods are difficult to deploy in practice because they require access to source data or the internal parameters of the source model, which may be restricted by privacy, licensing, or security constraints. We present 3D-BBDA, a backpropagation-free black-box domain adaptation framework that adapts a source-trained predictor to unlabeled target data using only black-box outputs. Our method performs pseudo-label guided prototype-based alignment and employs a weighted prediction module to fuse source logits with alignment logits, reducing sensitivity to noisy pseudo-labels. To stabilize prototype memory when pseudo-label coverage is incomplete, we construct a Gaussian-perturbed prototype prior from unlabeled target predictions and use it as a fallback for missing or unreliable class prototypes during alignment. Experiments on four corrupted 3D benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines. On ModelNet-40C, 3D-BBDA achieves mean errors of 32.08% (PointNet) and 29.62% (GDANet), outperforming Source-only (35.88% / 34.03%) and BFTT3D (33.78% / 32.36%). 3D-BBDA requires only a single forward pass with no gradient updates making it suitable for real-time, privacy-preserving deployment in transferable 3D recognition pipelines. Project page is available at https://visdomlab.github.io/3D_BBDA
bullets: Addresses domain-shift degradation from sensor changes, environmental variation, and acquisition artifacts.
Uses pseudo-label-guided prototype alignment and weighted fusion of source and alignment logits.
Builds a Gaussian-perturbed prototype prior to handle missing or unreliable class prototypes.
Experiments on four corrupted 3D benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines.
Requires a single forward pass, supporting real-time and privacy-preserving deployment.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly generate actions and imagined futures, but a plausible prediction need not be realized by its co-generated action. We introduce WISE (\emph{World Action Inference Scaling through Evaluation}), a pre-execution selector that scores each sampled rollout on action validity and temporal regularity, inverse-dynamics consistency between the proposed action and the imagined motion, and instruction-conditioned task progress, and executes the highest-scoring candidate while keeping the WAM frozen. With four candidates per decision, WISE raises closed-loop success from 6.0\% to 24.0\% on RoboLab with Cosmos~3 Edge and from 75.1\% to 78.3\% mean success on LIBERO with DreamZero, and exceeds the best existing selector in aggregate by 4.0 and 0.9 points. Component ablations and agreement analyses show that the three scores rank candidates differently and that task progress carries the largest weight in the fused decision.
bullets: Addresses the gap between plausible imagined futures and actions that actually succeed.
Scores sampled rollouts using action validity and temporal regularity, inverse-dynamics consistency, and instruction-conditioned task progress.
Executes the highest-scoring candidate without updating the underlying world action model.
With four candidates, success increases from 6.0% to 24.0% on RoboLab and from 75.1% to 78.3% on LIBERO.
Task progress contributes the largest weight, while the three scoring components rank candidates differently.

Figure 2: WISE at each control decision. A frozen WAM samples B paired action–future candidates (B = 4 in our evaluations). Each candidate receives three scores in [0, 1]. The IDM maps imagined frames back to actions for comparison with the candidate’s proposed controls; the task evaluator scores progress at the final imagined frame. WISE sums the scores, executes the selected action chunk, and observes the resulting state before replanning.

papers.tldr: WISE improves frozen world action models by selecting the most consistent and task-progressing rollout before execution.

papers.abstract: Open-world robotic mobile manipulation requires acting in physical environments with only partial information. While recent Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) agents show strong open-world reasoning capabilities, existing architectures that rely on direct tool calling struggle with geometric uncertainty and thus are limited to fully-observable tabletop environments. In contrast, Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) systems can solve long-horizon tasks under partial observability but incur high computational costs and require closed worlds. We propose \textbf{TAMPAgent}, an agentic planning framework that unifies the reasoning of LVLMs with the structured constraint satisfaction of TAMP systems. We endow an LVLM agent with a belief-space planning model operating over an extensible API of perception, planning, and control tools. The agent formulates a partial task plan composed of parameterized observation and execution actions, which is subsequently completed using classical search algorithms. After extracting the plan's geometric constraints, the agent leverages its tool API to bind valid parameter values, satisfying feasibility requirements and producing an executable motion plan. Upon execution, the agent continuously updates its belief history and repeats this closed-loop process by interleaving observation and manipulation actions. Evaluated across complex household mobile manipulation tasks on Rainbow Y1 and Unitree G1 platforms, TAMPAgent significantly outperforms direct tool-calling agentic baselines, demonstrating that integrating TAMP constraint satisfaction into agentic planning loops is essential for unstructured, partially observable environments.
bullets: Targets open-world mobile manipulation, where geometric uncertainty challenges direct tool-calling agents.
Uses an LVLM to create partial plans with parameterized observation and execution actions.
Completes plans through classical search, geometric constraint extraction, and tool-based parameter binding.
Continuously updates belief history by interleaving perception and manipulation in a closed loop.
Evaluated on Rainbow Y1 and Unitree G1 household tasks, it outperforms direct tool-calling baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Integrating agents with planning. We compare four systems that maps a history of observations to whole body control for long-horizon mobile-manipulation tasks: (a) TAMP [14, 7] solves hand-authored problems with a task planner that orchestrates tools. (b) VLM-TAMP [9, 10] uses the agent to write the problem from open-world understanding but keeps the planning pipeline fixed. (c) CaP [3, 15, 5, 6] lets the agent write programs that orchestrate tools directly to find solutions. (d) TAMPAgent (ours) lets the agent orchestrate both the task planner and the tools to find certified solutions that satisfy the planner derived constraints.

Figure 4 | TAMPAgent planning loop. We show how the agent orchestrates the planner and tools to solve the task “put the apple on the black table (hidden behind a toy penguin) in a bowl”. (1-3) The agent observes, hypothesizes where the apple is, and writes the problem and a plan, (4) the planner compiles the plan into a CSP, and (5) the agent writes a computation graph that calls tools to find an assignment 𝛽𝑡 satisfying the CSP. (6) The tools certify the first action’s constraints and the planner accepts 𝛽𝑡, allowing (7) the robot to execute the first action. (8) The loop repeats until (9-10) the placement is planned and the goal is achieved.

In the mobile manipulation (MM) tasks T1 and T2, the apple is in plain view, next to the plate or on the countertop. The MM + non-prehensile tasks add an object the robot must move first. In T4 to T6, a cup, an open drawer, or both block the direct pick, in T10, a mustard bottle stands in front of the apple, and in T8, a cracker box stands in front of the plate. The MM + occlusion tasks hide the apple, inside the fridge in T3 and behind a cracker box in T7, so the agent must hypothesize where to search. T9 is MM + non-prehensile + occlusion: the apple is inside the fridge behind a cup, which the robot must move before it can pick the apple. In the close-ups of T3 and T9, we draw the refrigerator doors translucent so that the shelf is visible. In the simulation the doors are closed.
Figure 8 | Failure attribution for RBY1 simulation experiments. Failed episodes out of 20 per task, in which an object fell or the scene was destroyed (solid), or which timed out (hatched).

Figure 3 | Hybrid beliefs over perception and manipulation variables. Left: The belief over the apple’s location moves from Unif, a uniform prior over the room, to a Lang hypothesis written by the agent, “... on the visible counter / dining table / inside the refrigerator ...”. The agent then chooses a viewpoint and calls SAM 3 to represent apple’s location as a Mask, and then as a RGBD estimate when its close enough. Finally, the agent chooses a valid option based on implicitly represented planning objectives.

Figure 2 | Plan skeleton as a factor graph. The skeleton ?⃗? = ⟨detect[𝐴], pick[𝐴], place[𝐴, 𝐵]⟩ unrolled over states 𝑠0, . . . , 𝑠3 (columns) becomes factor graph with: (i) nodes 𝑉 as the planning variables (rows), such as the configurations 𝑞1, 𝑞2, 𝑞3, the apple’s pose, the grasp 𝑔2, and the placement 𝑥3 and (ii) factors 𝐹 as the constraints between them, such as RGBD, Grasp, Kin, Motion, and Stable visualized in boxes. In T11, the robot must move a bowl from the living-room table to the kitchen table, and in T12, it must throw a used sponge from the laundry machine in the washroom into the kitchen trash can. T13 has the same goal as T11, but a chair blocks the living-room doorway. We show the layout of the home at the start of T11 (ceiling hidden), followed by close-ups of the bowl on the living-room table (T11), the sponge on the laundry machine (T12), and the chair in the living-room doorway, seen from the kitchen (T13).

papers.tldr: TAMPAgent combines LVLM reasoning with belief-space task-and-motion planning to enable closed-loop mobile manipulation in partially observable household environments.

papers.abstract: Most parameters of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model belong to its experts, and standard training keeps every expert gradient in GPU memory until the optimizer step. This memory grows with the number and size of the experts, so it rises as MoE models scale. We introduce Sonar-MoE, which updates each expert tensor during the backward pass and frees its gradient right away. It brings optimizer-in-backward from dense models to batched MoE expert tensors, so the GPU never holds more than one layer of expert gradients. When we fine-tune OLMoE-1B-7B and Granite-3.1-3B-A800M in bf16 with two expert-kernel backends, Sonar-MoE lowers peak memory by 19% to 22%. Its updates are bitwise identical to standard training without expert gradient clipping, and held-out loss stays within 0.003 of all baselines. Each step also takes 17% to 23% less time than standard training with global-norm clipping. Updating whole batched tensors rather than individual experts is what keeps Sonar-MoE fast, as it avoids a 20% to 72% slowdown while using the same memory. Sonar-MoE matches optimizer-in-backward over all parameters in memory and speed while still clipping the dense parameters.
bullets: Addresses GPU memory growth caused by retaining gradients for all MoE experts until the optimizer step.
Updates batched expert tensors in backward, limiting retained expert gradients to one layer at a time.
Reduces peak memory by 19–22% and step time by 17–23% in the reported bf16 fine-tuning experiments.
Preserves bitwise-identical updates without expert gradient clipping, while held-out loss remains within 0.003 of baselines.
Whole-batched-tensor updates avoid the slowdown associated with updating experts individually; dense parameters can still use gradient clipping.

papers.title: Sonar-MoE: In-Backward Expert Updates for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Training

papers.abstract: Exemplar-free continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers increasingly relies on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), yet prevailing methods govern the low-rank update space through strict subspace isolation. By projecting each incoming task into the approximate null space of historical token activations, isolation-based learners equate any cross-task feature overlap with catastrophic interference. We show that this orthogonality premise induces a structural bottleneck we term \emph{spectral starvation}: when down-projection bases are locked before task optimization, the gradient norm reaching the trainable up-projection is upper-bounded by the energy of current-task features captured by the chosen basis. Because natural visual tasks share low- and mid-level covariance structure, historical null tails contain barely $5.5\%$ of incoming task variance, starving new-class plasticity while blocking positive consolidation along shared directions. We propose BISECT (Bilevel Spectral Decomposition), a continual LoRA framework that partitions a fixed rank-$r$ budget into two orthogonal functional blocks: an invariant carrier spanned by the dominant modes of the joint historical-and-current Gram matrix, and a novelty complement extracted via generalized Rayleigh whitening followed by orthogonal complement projection. After single-task training, BISECT folds both blocks back into the frozen backbone using a closed-form precision gate that scales each rank-1 invariant atom by its current-to-joint Rayleigh ratio while preserving novelty atoms at unit gain. Across eight incremental settings on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and DomainNet, BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines with zero extra inference parameters or FLOPs, and remains complementary to sparse analytic expansion.
bullets: Isolation-based LoRA methods can suffer from “spectral starvation” when historical null spaces contain little incoming-task variance.
BISECT splits a fixed rank budget into an invariant block from joint historical/current spectral modes and a novelty block from whitened orthogonal complements.
A closed-form precision gate consolidates invariant atoms while retaining novelty atoms at full gain.
Across eight incremental settings spanning five benchmarks, BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines without extra inference parameters or FLOPs.
The method remains complementary to sparse analytic expansion.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of BISECT at session t. (I) Using the historical Gram state G<t and current-task Gram Gt, BISECT determines the layerwise rank split (kinv, knov) from the top-r spectral energy threshold η, extracts the invariant carrier Pinv from the joint Gram G1:t via randomized SVD, and synthesizes the orthogonal novelty complement Pnov via Cholesky-whitened generalized Rayleigh extraction. (II) Both basis blocks Pinv, Pnov remain locked while the up-maps Qinv, Qnov are optimized by SGD on Dt. (III) Each rank-1 invariant atom is folded into W (t−1) with its closed-form posterior precision weight ω⋆ j ∈ [0, 1], while novelty atoms fold at unit weight, yielding zero inference overhead.

(b) Distribution of task-t signal across quartiles of the historical eigenspectrum G<t on ViT-B/16: the bottom 30% null tail holds only 5.5% of raw task energy, starving gradient flow, whereas generalized Rayleigh whitening shifts selection to the mid-spectrum where unexplained variance peaks (51.6%). (c) Historical retention vs. emerging-class accuracy on 10S-ImageNet-R; varying the spectral threshold η traces a Pareto frontier above isolation and gradient-splitting baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces BISECT, a continual learning framework for Vision Transformers that partitions low-rank adaptation budgets to mitigate interference, directly addressing continual learning challenges.
papers.title: BISECT: Bilevel Spectral Decomposition for Low-Rank Continual Learning
papers.tldr: BISECT improves exemplar-free continual learning with LoRA by preserving shared knowledge while allocating capacity to genuinely novel task information.

papers.abstract: Timely and accurate crop health diagnosis is essential for sustainable agricultural production, yet accurate diagnosis often requires expert knowledge that is not readily available. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, and natural-language interaction, creating new opportunities for intelligent crop health assessment. However, deploying VLMs on resource-constrained devices remains challenging due to their substantial computational and memory requirements. This paper presents PlantVLM-Edge, a quantized vision-language framework for conversational crop health diagnosis that can run entirely on resource-constrained edge devices. PlantVLM-Edge combines agricultural domain adaptation, post-training quantization, and on-device serving with an offline chat interface, allowing growers to ask open-ended questions and receive diagnoses, symptom explanations, and management guidance without cloud connectivity. The framework is backbone-agnostic: we validate it with two different VLM types with varying scale and architecture (Qwen3-VL-2B and LLaVA-1.5-7B), four quantization schemes, and two diagnostic domains (plant diseases and insect pests), and we deploy all variants on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Eight-bit quantization affects answer quality minimally relative to the full-precision model, and 4-bit activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) retains 98.6% of full-precision answer quality on both domains while reducing the weight memory of the 2B backbone by 49%. In its most compact form, PlantVLM-Edge requires 2.01 GiB of weight memory, returns its first token in about 0.12 s, and completes a 64-token diagnostic response in 0.78 s. These results demonstrate that timely and accurate crop health diagnosis is practical on edge devices, providing a foundation for next-generation crop monitoring and decision support systems.

papers.abstract: This work investigates human-swarm interaction (HSI) for steering large collectives through an intermediary robot helper. While prior robot-swarm control and HSI techniques commonly assume swarm members are addressable, these assumptions often fail for ``ungovernable'' swarms such as wildlife flocks and schools of fish. Motivated by pastoral shepherding, we compare low-level teleoperation to a higher-autonomy motion-primitives interface in a virtual reality (VR) shepherding task under varied swarm cohesion dynamics. Results indicate that motion primitives that operate on collective shape (e.g., boundary-based control) improve task performance and reduce perceived workload.
bullets: Addresses human–swarm interaction when individual swarm members cannot be directly controlled.
Compares low-level teleoperation with higher-autonomy motion primitives in a VR shepherding task.
Evaluates performance across different swarm cohesion dynamics.
Shape-based primitives, including boundary control, improve task performance and reduce perceived workload.

papers.abstract: We introduce CoLa3D, a simple and effective model for composable 3D scene decomposition that, given a single whole-scene latent from either a single image or an existing scene mesh as input, directly outputs a set of object meshes with consistent spatial layout that can be assembled back into a coherent scene. CoLa3D introduces a novel paradigm for 3D scene decomposition within a shared whole-scene latent, unlike alternatives that perform per-object generation in canonical spaces and then glue the objects back together with fragile pose and scale estimation. The network is a lightweight, flexible, and scalable query-based transformer that accepts various types of queries, including 2D masks, 3D points, and learnable queries, and learns to decompose the scene into objects in a compact latent space. On both synthetic and real-world datasets, CoLa3D achieves state-of-the-art performance on composable 3D scene decomposition, substantially improving global scene-level consistency and object-level quality while running 2 times faster and using less than 1% of SAM 3D's training data. Visible depth on par with MoGe2 further confirms that latent decomposition preserves accurate visible scene geometry while producing physically complete, decomposable object meshes.
bullets: Takes a single-image or existing-mesh whole-scene latent as input and outputs object meshes that reassemble into a coherent scene.
Uses a lightweight, scalable query-based transformer with 2D-mask, 3D-point, or learnable queries.
Performs decomposition directly in a shared latent space, preserving global layout and object-level quality.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on synthetic and real-world datasets, runs 2× faster, and uses less than 1% of SAM 3D’s training data.
Produces physically complete meshes with visible depth comparable to MoGe2.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of CoLa3D. Starting from an RGB image or a holistic scene mesh, CoLa3D first obtains a structured scene latent zs geo with TRELLIS.2 [76] and augments it with 3D semantic features zs sem from Utonia [87]. A lightweight decomposition transformer then uses mask, learnable, or point queries to decompose zs = zs geo + zs sem through L blocks of self-attention, cross-attention to frozen DINOv3 [52] features f img, and alternating Latent-to-Query/Query-to-Latent cross-attention. Finally, a multi-hot assignment extracts per-instance latents {zo k}, which are decoded in parallel by the shared decoder D into aligned object meshes and can be recomposed in the global 3D space.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparisons on synthetic data. Compared with baselines, CoLa3D produces spatially coherent object meshes with correct relative positions and scales.

papers.abstract: Computer programmers chain together the same reusable computational primitives, for example, conditional statements or loops, but in different orders to implement different algorithms. In contrast, existing language model architectures always execute their layers in the same order. We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically orders its layers during inference to solve the problem at hand. LoL has a single hyperparameter, the size of its global library of transformer blocks, that allows it to transition seamlessly between parameter reuse and sparsity, generalizing the parameter-efficiency and FLOPs-efficiency tradeoffs of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts architectures in one unified family. We show that LoL achieves competitive performance with all three above baselines when pretrained on text data. On synthetic sudoku and maze data, we observe that the model employs distinct layer orderings to implement different solution strategies, and we can intervene on routing to force a model to apply a specific solution strategy to a problem instance. In a multilingual natural language setting, we find that LoL chooses different layer order patterns based on language and script. Similarly, we train LoL on safety data and fit probes to its router outputs, finding that these probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC. LoL provides a path toward a future in which models dynamically compose their own computational graph, enabling more efficient and controllable reasoning.
bullets: Addresses the fixed layer ordering used by standard language models.
Uses a global library of transformer blocks whose runtime routing determines layer order.
A single library-size hyperparameter spans parameter reuse and sparsity, unifying efficiency tradeoffs across dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture-of-experts models.
Matches the performance of these baselines on text pretraining and exhibits distinct routing patterns for sudoku, mazes, languages, and scripts.
Routing can be intervened on to force solution strategies, while router probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC.

figures.caption: Figure 1: We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), a novel architecture where the next executed transformer layer is chosen at runtime. We use strided window attention within the routed core to allow information to flow through the sequence dimension while using the same attention and MLP parameters for all tokens within each window.

Figure 6: Library of Layers is competitive with mixture of experts models. Left: Cross-entropy training loss over training FLOPs, averaged over 3 random seeds. We see growing gives LoL an early loss advantage and both models finish training with similar training losses. Right: Heatmap of expert utilization of one LoL model. We see some experts are heavily used by specific routed depths or neighboring groups of depths, while others are used diversely over depths, showing LoL learns to use the sparsity effectively.

Figure 3: Library of Layers learns distinct paths for different languages and distinct strategies when solving sudoku puzzles and mazes. Left: PCA projection of the routing paths of a 360M parameter LoL model trained on an equal mixture of 10 languages. We see the paths taken are distinct per language and Latin-script languages use similar paths. Middle and Right: We train 360M parameter LoL models to solve sudoku (middle) and mazes (right), using 5 different strategies. We then force each strategy’s mode path at inference time and see the models use the correct strategy (algorithm) with close to 100% accuracy.

Figure 5: Library of Layers is competitive with looped transformer models. Left: Cross-entropy evaluation loss, matching the number of unique layers in the core block of the LoL and looped transformer. We see LoL performs competitively with looped transformer models and offers more flexibility in layer ordering. Error bars are min/max loss over 3 random seeds. We note larger variance for the LoL models as changing the random seed changes the paths explored during training. Right: Cross-entropy training loss over training FLOPs, averaged over 3 random seeds per model.

Figure 4: Library of Layers is competitive with vanilla dense models. Left: Cross-entropy training loss over training FLOPs for 1B models. We see growing gives LoL an early loss advantage and all models finish with comparable training loss. Right: Heatmap of expert utilization of one LoL model. We see experts mainly tend to be used in groups of neighboring depths, but some are used throughout the model.

Figure 2: Library of Layers uses strided window attention and a top-1 router to allow for efficient training. LoL is made up of a prelude, a routed core, and a coda. The layers in the prelude and coda can attend over the whole sequence. In the core, the sequence is split into windows of W tokens, and at every routed depth a router selects one layer from the shared library per window (topleft). Attention is restricted to each window, but the window boundaries shift by S tokens between successive routed depths, allowing information to flow across windows (Strided Window Attention, top-right). Window 0 has no history, so its router uses the first token and a learned vector e(ℓ) for routed depth ℓ (bottom-left). For window i > 0, the router averages the mean hidden states of earlier windows 0, . . . , i − 1 and selects one layer (bottom-right). With W = 4 and S = 2, Layers 1 and 3 share the same boundaries while Layer 2 is offset, so information can pass between neighboring windows. Token 5 is highlighted in red to show this: in Layer 1 it is the first token in a new window, while in Layer 2 its window includes tokens 3 and 4.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation benefits from tactile feedback that captures both detailed contact geometry and interaction forces. When scooping grains, contact patterns help infer spoon orientation, while resistance transmitted through the grasp guides motion. To provide these complementary sensing capabilities, we present PanoTac, a low-cost, compliant tactile fingertip designed for dense three-axis tactile sensing. Each fingertip provides a $12 \times 32 \times 3$ tactile representation, with one normal ($z$) and two shear ($x$, $y$) response components at each taxel. The sensor operates at 60 Hz and costs less than $50 per fingertip. Sensor characterization quantifies response repeatability and consistency across sensor instances and contact locations. We integrate PanoTac into a robotic system with a visuo-tactile pipeline. Across test-tube preparation, grain scooping, and salt pouring, the resulting policies outperform vision-only baselines by an average of 46.7 percentage points. Ablations show that removing either spatial contact information or shear feedback reduces overall performance across the task suite. Our project page is available at https://panotac.github.io.
bullets: Captures a 12 × 32 × 3 tactile representation: normal force plus two shear components at each taxel.
Operates at 60 Hz and costs under $50 per fingertip.
Integrated into a visuo-tactile pipeline for test-tube preparation, grain scooping, and salt pouring.
Policies outperform vision-only baselines by an average of 46.7 percentage points.
Ablations indicate both spatial contact information and shear feedback are important for performance.

papers.abstract: LLM agents for GPU kernel optimization sit at two ends of a structure-freedom tradeoff. Scripted agents fix what the model does at each step, via a learned policy, an optimization menu, or fixed roles, and are sample-efficient where the recipe applies and stall where it does not. Open-ended agents let a self-directed model mutate a population of kernels and pay for the freedom in trials: thousands of evaluations, repeated edits, and wrong candidates. Both respond to hard targets by equipping the agent with more: parsed profiler output, disassembly analysis, retrieval over documentation and libraries, and stores of lessons. We argue that both lack direction, a hypothesis about where the remaining gap is, and that a short question asked at the right moment supplies it without narrowing what the agent may do next. We present KernelSeek, a question-driven agent that makes an existing CUDA kernel faster with no operator-specific knowledge and no faster implementation to imitate: a general-purpose coding agent, a minimal harness that enforces a verifiable goal, and questions at decision points, first from a human, then from a bank the agent applies to itself. On the same task, evaluator, hardware, and week, a tool-rich autonomous agent built in the prevailing style plateaued at 0.50x FlashAttention-3 after 133 model-driven steps; KernelSeek reached 1.13x. It then produced dependency-free FlashAttention forward kernels for Hopper and Blackwell, single CUDA files with no CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, or cuDNN, correct on all 182 scenarios per architecture and 1.16x FlashAttention-3 and 1.46x FlashAttention-4 (geometric mean). Across 162 human messages and 11.5K agent tool calls, every large gain followed a question that moved the agent to a different layer of the system or rejected a claimed limit, never one that supplied information. We release the kernels, harness, question bank, and all traces.
bullets: Open-ended kernel-optimization agents can waste many evaluations, while scripted agents may stall outside their prescribed recipes.
KernelSeek combines a general-purpose coding agent with a minimal verifiable harness and questions from humans or a self-applied question bank.
On the reported task, a prevailing tool-rich agent plateaued at 0.50× FlashAttention-3, whereas KernelSeek reached 1.13×.
It produced dependency-free CUDA FlashAttention forward kernels for Hopper and Blackwell, correct across all reported scenarios.
The study reports that every large gain followed a question prompting a new system layer or challenging an assumed limitation, rather than providing information.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers largely relies on a costly premise: preventing catastrophic forgetting requires either spawning a dedicated LoRA branch per session---causing adapter parameters to scale linearly with task horizon---or applying sparse Mixture-of-Experts gating symmetrically to both forward and backward passes, which sacrifices representational rank at test time. We argue that reading consolidated knowledge and writing new task credit are fundamentally asymmetric operations. Because visual features in a shared low-rank space distribute across rank-1 atoms rather than localizing in disjoint task silos, forward inference should read all atoms at full rank capacity, whereas backward optimization should restrict plasticity to a sparse subset of input-aligned channels. We introduce RASP (Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity LoRA), which adapts a single stationary-size adapter across sequential tasks. At each step, a scene-modulated cosine router selects the top-$q$ unlocked atoms to receive gradients, blocks updates on the remaining $r-q$ channels, and penalizes Frobenius Gram coherence between active and non-updated output directions. Across sessions, the router's empirical activation trace and each atom's exact spectral norm form a zero-overhead geometric consolidation index $ω_j = \sqrt{\tilde{c}_j \tildeσ_j}$ that drives Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking. Across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, RASP matches or surpasses branch-expanding LoRA learners under a strictly constant parameter footprint.
bullets: Targets catastrophic forgetting without adding a new LoRA branch for each task.
Uses asymmetric read/write behavior: full-rank forward inference and sparse, input-aligned backward updates.
A cosine router selects the top-q unlocked atoms for gradients, while coherence regularization protects inactive directions.
Tracks activation history and spectral norms to attenuate updates and lock consolidated adapter atoms.
Across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, matches or surpasses branch-expanding LoRA methods with constant parameter count.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the RASP pipeline. Stage 1 (Left): Every input batch traverses all r rank-1 atoms in the forward pass without truncation; a cosine probe modulated by an image-level scene gate ϕ(x̄) and a usage-equalizing prior scores the unlocked pool Pt−1. Stage 2 (Middle): Only the top-q unlocked channels At receive backward gradients, while a Frobenius Gram coherence penalty Rdec pushes active synthesis columns orthogonal to non-updated and locked columns. Stage 3 (Right): Cumulative routing trace c̃j and rank-1 spectral norm σ̃j form the consolidation index ωj = √ c̃j σ̃j , driving continuous Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking.

Figure 4. Trajectories, resilience, and system cost. (a) On CIFAR100, RASP matches the top expansion method across all 10 sessions at constant size. (b) On CUB-200, shared forward reading yields a +8.48 pp final lead over branch-isolated SplitLoRA. (c) Silencing the top-m task-associated atoms after training collapses isolated branches (−23.84% at m = 10) but costs < 1% on RASP, confirming distributed encoding. (d) Training time and peak VRAM on CIFAR-100.

Figure 3. Mechanistic analysis of RASP. (a, b) Effect of plasticity ratio q/r on ∆FAA (relative to q = r) and Average Forgetting across four benchmarks; stars mark the operating configurations in Table 2. The optimal q/r shifts rightward as domain divergence from ImageNet-21K increases. (c) Spearman rank correlation ρs of consolidation indices ω(t) against session t−1 and final session T , showing rapid stabilization after session 3. (d) In the 2D trace-spectral plane (c̃j , σ̃j), hyperbolic contours of ωj = √ c̃j σ̃j isolate true high-trace, high-energy anchors (crimson diamonds) while rejecting single-cue outliers (amber triangles).

papers.abstract: Matrix multiplication dominates both PHY signal processing and Deep Neural Network (DNN) inference, yet these domains place opposing demands on the matrix engine. Signal processing requires low-latency execution of relatively small matrix operations, whereas DNN inference, particularly at large batch sizes, prioritizes high throughput and energy efficiency for large matrix multiplications. While offering efficient memory access profile, a Systolic Array (SA) adds fill and drain delays per matrix. Those can be amortized for large matrices but not for small matrices. Conversely, a tensor unit completes the kernel in few cycles but would require repeated reads of same operand tiles over large matrices. This makes SA too slow for signal processing and tensor too inefficient for AI. We show that this need not be a choice between systolic and tensor structuring of Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) units. We propose a single engine that operates primarily as a SA and, through low-cost reconfiguration, transforms into a tensor-style engine on a per-operation basis. MUXes create both the spatial reduction adder tree and temporal reduction accumulators from the existing MACs and registers within the systolic array. The proposed reconfigurable SA simulated using modified SCALESim simulator, verified on an Zynq 702 FPGA and synthesized using ASAP 7nm FinFET library. SCALE-Sim simulations shows up to 7.5x lower latency for small complex value PHY kernels. Even on DNN workloads, it achieves up to 1.65x speedups over vanilla SA execution with trivial increase of memory accesses, retaining the systolic array's memory access advantage. Synthesis results estimate reconfigurable fabric costs only 8% power and 13.6% area overheads.
bullets: Signal processing favors low latency for small matrices, while DNN inference favors throughput and energy efficiency for large matrices.
The design reconfigures a systolic array into a tensor-style engine on a per-operation basis using MUXes, existing MACs, and registers.
Simulations report up to 7.5× lower latency for small complex-valued PHY kernels and up to 1.65× speedup on DNN workloads versus a vanilla systolic array.
The design preserves the systolic array’s memory-access advantages with only an estimated 8% power and 13.6% area overhead.
The engine was evaluated through simulation, FPGA verification on Zynq 702, and synthesis using a 7nm FinFET library.

papers.abstract: Conventional robot arms can be extremely heavy compared with the everyday objects they manipulate, creating a significant inertia mismatch at contact. Even a small accidental bump from a heavy arm can knock a light object out of place. Modern learning methods have nevertheless demonstrated a wide range of successful manipulation behaviors on these platforms, suggesting that even extreme inertia mismatch can be overcome with sufficient data. However, it remains unclear whether high inertia imposes a hidden cost on learning, potentially worsening scaling with data or lowering the performance ceiling of modern robot learning methods. We investigate this question through controlled simulation experiments that vary robot and object masses. We find that reinforcement learning succeeds across a broad range of mass combinations, while behavior cloning learns more reliable policies when a lighter robot manipulates a heavier object. Heavier robots require more demonstrations to attain the same performance as lighter robots. Finally, because new hardware is rarely an option, we explore ways to lower an existing arm's inertia at contact with existing hardware, either by choosing a lower-inertia workspace before collecting data or by steering the demonstrator toward lower-inertia configurations during the task. In both cases, the lower-inertia demonstrations are imitated more reliably. Project website: https://younghyopark.me/inertia-mismatch/
bullets: The study examines whether heavy robot arms create hidden costs for manipulation policy learning.
Controlled simulations vary robot and object masses to compare reinforcement learning and behavior cloning.
Reinforcement learning succeeds across a broad range of mass combinations.

Collecting demonstrations in lower-inertia configurations improves imitation reliability without replacing hardware.

papers.abstract: Navigating crowded urban environments requires robots to avoid pedestrians while adhering to social norms such as remaining on sidewalks. Existing approaches typically address either crowd avoidance or semantic path planning in isolation. We propose a reinforcement learning (RL) navigation policy that jointly reasons about semantic terrain and dynamic obstacles from a single semantically annotated bird's-eye-view (BEV) map, without relying on explicit human-state estimation. Our policy outperforms established crowd-navigation and semantic-aware baselines and transfers zero-shot to a legged robot, demonstrating socially compliant navigation in highly dynamic real-world scenarios.

Combines semantic terrain and dynamic-obstacle reasoning in one navigation policy.
Uses a single semantically annotated BEV map instead of explicit pedestrian-state estimation.
Outperforms established crowd-navigation and semantic-aware baselines.
Transfers zero-shot to a legged robot in dynamic real-world scenarios.

papers.abstract: Language models in customer-facing products must be continually updated, since the data they serve shifts over time. As retraining on the full accumulated data is impractical, each update should instead run on a small set of examples carrying the training signal of all data seen so far. The strongest current methods build this set by gradient matching, which synthesizes examples whose training gradients match those of the full data. However, they require ground-truth labels, run once on a fixed snapshot rather than on a growing stream, and are slow on large data. We introduce \textbf{OLGA}, which lifts these limitations. It distills unlabeled data by drawing the gradient matching targets from the model's own next-token predictions. Across five text classification benchmarks with phi-1.5, it improves accuracy by 10 percentage points over the strongest selection baseline using as few as five examples. OLGA also distills online data streams by keeping a running rehearsal memory of synthetic examples, which is re-distilled together with each new batch as it arrives. In the online setting, it outperforms the strongest selection-based continual baseline by 6.6 stream-AUC percentage points. Finally, our method scales to large data by pairing distillation with selection in a hybrid pipeline, letting selection handle the mild stage of compression and distillation the extreme one. It cuts runtime by 30\% versus distillation alone at similar accuracy, and beats the best selection-only pipeline by up to 12.6 percentage points.
bullets: Addresses continual training under shifting data without retraining on the full history.
Uses the model’s own next-token predictions to create gradient-matching targets from unlabeled data.
Maintains a rehearsal memory and re-distills it with each incoming batch for online updates.
Across five text classification benchmarks with phi-1.5, gains 10 accuracy points using as few as five examples.
A hybrid selection–distillation pipeline reduces runtime by 30% at similar accuracy and improves over selection-only methods by up to 12.6 points.

papers.abstract: Pre-touch sensing, or sensing information about an object before contact, is an attractive modality for robot hands as it can allow a robot to anticipate and respond to a contact before it happens. In this work, we introduce ToFTouch, a multimodal tactile sensor combining three multizone (4$\times$4 resolution) time-of-flight sensors with an optics-based pressure sensing array. We mount this sensor on a parallel jaw gripper and demonstrate its utility on three distinct tasks: (i) pre-grasp adjustment, (ii) item extraction from clutter, and (iii) item insertion into tight spaces. For pre-grasp adjustment, ToF feedback reduced cycle time by 7.4$\%$ by enabling anticipatory gripper closure during approach. For extraction, ToF sensing enabled successful retrieval across all tested depth offsets ($\pm$2 cm) deviating from the nominal pick point, including conditions where baseline approaches failed, with standard deviations below 0.4 cm. For insertion into dense clutter, we explore the proximity and tactile information provided from ToFTouch during an insertion trajectory. The results demonstrate the utility of multizone ToF sensing in a manipulation environment.
bullets: Enables pre-touch sensing so the gripper can respond before physical contact.

papers.abstract: High frame rate HDR video is important in applications such as autonomous driving and scientific imaging, where rapid motion and extreme illumination often occur simultaneously. Conventional frame cameras face a trade-off between temporal resolution and dynamic range, while event cameras provide complementary high-speed brightness-change measurements over a wide illumination range. These properties have motivated event-based HDR reconstruction, with existing methods broadly following event-only and hybrid event-frame paradigms. Event-only HDR reconstruction, however, suffers from brightness and color drift due to the lack of absolute intensity references. Hybrid event-frame methods alleviate this ambiguity using low-dynamic-range (LDR) frames as anchors, but most perform one-to-one HDR reconstruction at available LDR timestamps. In this work, we investigate single-reference HDR temporal expansion, reconstructing N HDR frames from one LDR reference and events instead of N aligned LDR observations. We develop HIVE-Diff, an event-conditioned video diffusion framework that decomposes the task into event-guided temporal generation and HDR content completion. Because paired real HDR-event data are scarce, we train on synthetic data and adapt the model to real event domains using LDR-event sequences as proxy supervision with teacher-student distillation. Experiments on synthetic and multiple real-world datasets demonstrate strong reconstruction quality and robust real-data adaptation.
bullets: Addresses the need for simultaneous high temporal resolution and wide dynamic range in fast, high-contrast scenes.
Generates N HDR frames from one LDR reference and events, avoiding the need for aligned LDR frames at every timestamp.
Uses event-guided temporal generation followed by HDR content completion in a video diffusion framework.
Trains on synthetic data and adapts to real event domains through teacher-student distillation with LDR-event proxy supervision.
Reports strong reconstruction quality and robust real-data adaptation across synthetic and multiple real-world datasets.

papers.abstract: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) is an effective treatment for acute ischemic stroke, yet access remains limited by the availability of neurointerventional expertise. Telerobotic and AI-assisted systems may help address this challenge, but it remains unclear how clinicians interact with different levels of autonomy and how autonomous navigation systems perform in realistic environments. This work introduces Copilot Assistance Modes (CAMs), a framework for clinician-AI collaboration in robotic endovascular navigation spanning the autonomy spectrum from manual operation to full autonomy. In the first in-vitro user study comparing clinician-AI collaboration strategies, 11 experts and two students evaluated six navigation modes in a patient-specific vascular phantom. Objective performance metrics were combined with subjective assessments, including workload and usability. Autonomous performance was additionally evaluated both in silico and in vitro to investigate sim-to-real transfer. Hands-on manual navigation achieved the strongest overall performance (100% success). While fully autonomous navigation achieved 81% success in simulation, performance dropped to 23% in vitro. In contrast, several clinician-AI shared-autonomy modes achieved success rates of 92-97%, approximately four times higher than full autonomy and comparable to direct robotic control (95%), demonstrating mitigation of sim-to-real domain shift through clinician-AI collaboration. Among the evaluated AI-driven approaches, user-directed task delegation and rotational shared control demonstrated the most favorable balance between performance and clinician acceptance. These findings suggest that effective clinician-AI collaboration and allocation of control authority may currently be more important for reliable robotic neurointerventional navigation than increasing autonomy alone.
bullets: Evaluated six Copilot Assistance Modes spanning manual control to full autonomy in a patient-specific vascular phantom with 11 experts and two students.
Combined navigation success metrics with clinician workload and usability assessments.
Manual navigation achieved 100% success; full autonomy fell from 81% in simulation to 23% in vitro.
Several shared-autonomy modes achieved 92–97% success, comparable to direct robotic control at 95%.
User-directed task delegation and rotational shared control offered the best balance of performance and clinician acceptance.

papers.abstract: Foundational vision models have become the de facto standard for many vision tasks due to their strong performance. However, they are notoriously opaque and remain hard to interpret. We present ALOE (ALign Once to Explain), a one-time, label-free feature alignment approach that efficiently converts foundational vision models into inherently interpretable B-cos variants. Once aligned, the B-cos backbone is used as a drop-in replacement across several downstream tasks-amortizing the cost of interpretability. ALOE is robust across pre-training paradigms (supervised, self-supervised, vision-language) and can preserve teacher-level generalization with orders of magnitude less data than training from scratch. On classification, it strongly outperforms vanilla B-cosification (e.g., +10.5 p.p. top-1 on ImageNet for DINOv3 ViT-B/16), retains strong linear probing, k-NN, and zero-shot transfer competitive with foundational backbones (DINOv3, SigLIP2) across diverse downstream datasets. It also preserves spatially structured features useful for dense prediction, while yielding well-localized and highly human-interpretable explanations by design.
bullets: Addresses the opacity of foundational vision models and the high cost of making them interpretable.
Uses a one-time, label-free feature-alignment procedure to convert pretrained models into B-cos variants.
Works across supervised, self-supervised, and vision-language pretraining paradigms, using far less data than training from scratch.
Preserves strong classification, linear-probe, k-NN, zero-shot, and dense-prediction capabilities while producing localized, human-interpretable explanations.
On ImageNet, improves over vanilla B-cosification by 10.5 percentage points in top-1 accuracy for DINOv3 ViT-B/16.

(3) Deploy—freeze the aligned B-cos backbone for linear probing and zero-shot transfer; faithful, welllocalized explanations follow directly from W (x) (i.e., model summary), amortizing interpretability across tasks (Sec. 5.1).

papers.abstract: Despite their widespread success across machine learning, the learning dynamics and generalization properties of neural networks remain poorly understood. The neural tangent kernel (NTK) provides an analytical characterization of the learning dynamics of infinitely wide neural networks and serves as a useful proxy for finite-width networks in supervised learning. In this work, we extend the NTK framework to reinforcement learning (RL) by introducing a temporal-difference (TD) flow formulation that accommodates time-varying mini-batches and TD targets, yielding a closed-form solution for value function evolution in an overparametrized setting. We also devise an optimization-based state-space exploration method that leverages the closed-form solution, coupled with constraints on the environment, to model the set of feasible states. On a deterministic grid environment, we validate that the proposed RL-based NTK formulation is indeed learning efficiently and adapting to the distribution shift in the training data distribution, and we demonstrate that the resulting exploration strategy improves sample efficiency. To our knowledge, this is the first work to extend NTK theory to characterize the learning dynamics of RL training with time-varying mini-batches and TD updates.
bullets: Formulates an NTK-based temporal-difference flow for RL with changing mini-batches and TD targets.
Derives a closed-form description of value-function evolution in the overparameterized setting.
Uses this solution with environment constraints to identify feasible states for optimization-based exploration.
On a deterministic grid environment, the method adapts to training-distribution shifts and improves sample efficiency.
Scope is validated on a deterministic grid environment; broader generalization is not established in the abstract.
