papers.tldr: Extends neural tangent kernel theory to reinforcement learning by modeling time-varying temporal-difference updates and using the resulting dynamics to improve state-space exploration.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobility is essential for sustained lunar surface operations, as communication delays and line-of-sight occlusions limit continuous teleoperation. Although recent traversability estimation methods increasingly rely on deep learning, the domain gap between terrestrial analogue environments and real lunar terrain can limit their generalisation, and real lunar traversability labels are scarce, making fully supervised training difficult. To address these challenges, we build a weakly supervised framework trained on sparse pairwise annotations and study whether augmenting visual features with depth-derived geometric information: depth, surface normals, and combined geometric descriptors. We evaluate the models in both in-domain and cross-domain settings using two terrestrial analogue datasets and the real lunar Chang'E PCAM dataset. Contrary to expectations, we find that naive geometric augmentation yields no consistent improvement over a strong visual-only baseline in either setting, with effects small relative to seed-to-seed variance. Instead, the choice of training source emerges as the dominant factor in transfer quality: models trained on domain-relevant sources transfer substantially better to real lunar imagery than the geometric fusion strategy improves any single model. Our evaluation runs onboard a resource-constrained edge device and provides a controlled baseline for designing more expressive multimodal fusion architectures in future lunar perception systems.
bullets: Addresses limited real lunar labels and the domain gap between terrestrial analogues and lunar terrain.
Uses a weakly supervised framework trained from sparse pairwise annotations.
Compares visual-only models with depth, surface-normal, and combined geometric feature augmentation.
Evaluates in-domain and cross-domain transfer across two terrestrial analogue datasets and the real lunar Chang’E PCAM dataset.
Runs on a resource-constrained edge device; results motivate more expressive multimodal fusion methods.

papers.abstract: A robot that acts around people needs a world model of the human: a belief over the person's body state and a dynamics model that predicts where that state goes next. This abstract argues that two published components form exactly these two halves, and specifies how to couple them. KNOWN [1] reconstructs the 3D human body while estimating both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in real time (11.6 ms per frame); its aleatoric term identifies unreliable observations, its epistemic term identifies inputs from low-density regions of the training data, and refinement driven by the epistemic term reduces the error on such inputs from 81.3 to 70.3 mm. PhysMoP [2] predicts future body configuration by solving the Euler-Lagrange equations of the body with learned dynamics terms, reducing the 80 ms prediction error from 9.6 to 2.1 mm on Human3.6M and from 12.1 to 0.7 mm on 3DPW. We define the interface between the two, propose three mechanisms by which KNOWN's uncertainty enters PhysMoP, and specify an evaluation protocol on in-the-wild video. No new experimental results are reported here.
bullets: KNOWN estimates 3D body state plus aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in real time.
PhysMoP predicts future body configurations using Euler–Lagrange physics with learned dynamics.
The work defines an interface and three mechanisms for incorporating KNOWN’s uncertainty into PhysMoP.
It proposes evaluating the coupled system on in-the-wild video; no new experiments are reported.
Prior results cited in the abstract show improved performance for both reconstruction and prediction, but are not results of this work.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The two halves of the human world model. (b) PhysMoP [2]: a physics branch predicts the Euler–Lagrange terms M , C, G and integrates them, a data branch predicts the whole future, and a fusion network combines the two. The arrow is the coupling proposed in Sec. 4: KNOWN’s per-frame belief becomes the history q1:T that PhysMoP integrates forward.

papers.abstract: Video dubbing aims to synthesize lip movements that match target speech while preserving the speaker identity, head pose, and background of a source video. Existing editors are predominantly trained via self-reconstruction under original paired audio, even though the source mouth becomes a conflicting target when driving speech is replaced. We introduce \emph{replacement-aware cross-audio supervision}: paired-audio samples use full-frame reconstruction, whereas unpaired replacement-audio samples mask out source-mouth reconstruction losses and supervise the mouth solely through audio--visual synchronization while preserving unmasked facial regions and background. Because offline dubbing provides the complete source video and target speech beforehand, we present \method, a full-context diffusion editor that uses matched trajectory regression to transfer CFG-guided teacher trajectories to a two-step student and distribution matching to recover visual quality after compression. We will release the curated training dataset, VidDub-Bench, fixed paired- and cross-audio evaluation manifests, preprocessing outputs, and unified evaluation code. Across three training seeds, masking out conflicting source-mouth reconstruction improves cross-audio Sync-C by 0.833. At two NFE, the final student provides the strongest cross-audio synchronization and visual-speech recognition among the evaluated methods, with competitive visual fidelity and source preservation.
bullets: Existing self-reconstruction training conflicts with replaced target speech because the source mouth is an incorrect target.
Replacement-aware cross-audio supervision masks source-mouth losses for unpaired replacement audio while preserving other facial regions and the background.
A full-context diffusion editor uses matched trajectory regression and distribution matching to produce a two-step student.

Masking improves cross-audio Sync-C by 0.833 across three training seeds; the two-step student achieves the strongest reported cross-audio synchronization and visual-speech recognition, with competitive fidelity and source preservation.
The authors will release VidDub-Bench, evaluation manifests, preprocessing outputs, and unified evaluation code.

papers.abstract: Streaming digital humans produce detailed video while continuing speech as new text arrives. High-resolution denoising is costly, and text updates can cause repeated or interrupted speech. We present TaoMate-HD, an autoregressive model for high-resolution audio-video streaming. For each short segment, or chunk, two denoising steps establish coarse video structure at low resolution. A final step refines the video to high resolution, with audio generated throughout the same trajectory. Each stage passes its audiovisual predictions to the same stage of the next chunk as history. Across text updates, the model retains this history to infer what has already been spoken. Continuation training utilizes asymmetric text conditioning, with separate text windows for generation and distillation. Experiments show a 1.6x speedup over direct high-resolution generation with the same model and hardware. Optimized stage-parallel deployment provides a further 1.9x overall speedup over serial progressive generation. Our continuation training reduces character error rate by 11.18 percentage points relative to the baseline. The model also supports hour-long audiovisual generation. Our project page is https://taoliveaigc.github.io/TaoMate-HD.
bullets: Addresses the high cost of high-resolution denoising and speech interruptions caused by incremental text updates.
Uses low-resolution coarse denoising followed by high-resolution refinement, while generating audio along the same trajectory.
Passes stage-wise audiovisual predictions between chunks and retains history to continue previously spoken content.
Achieves 1.6× speedup over direct high-resolution generation, with stage-parallel deployment adding a further 1.9× speedup.
Continuation training lowers character error rate by 11.18 percentage points and supports hour-long generation.

papers.abstract: Low-quality facial videos suffer from missing fine details, while AI-generated videos may additionally contain implausible teeth and lip movements that do not match the speech. Restoring the mouth region is particularly challenging: enhancing existing details can preserve structural errors, whereas regenerating them risks changing facial identity and articulation. We propose an audio-guided facial video restoration framework that reconstructs unreliable mouth details and aligns lip movements with the speech while preserving facial identity and temporal consistency. Built on a video diffusion transformer, our framework mixes input video latents with noise to retain useful source information while allowing corrupted details to be regenerated. Audio guides lip movements, reference images constrain facial appearance, and previously generated frames promote temporal consistency. We train the model in two stages, first learning visual restoration from degraded images and videos, then learning audio-guided lip correction from degraded dubbed videos. The resulting model supports both restoration with the original audio and visual dubbing with replacement audio. On talking-head restoration benchmarks, our method achieves the lowest LPIPS and DISTS and the best lip synchronization scores among the evaluated restoration baselines. Qualitative results on AI-generated videos further show improvements in facial detail and mouth-region appearance, including clearer tooth boundaries and lip contours.
bullets: Addresses low-quality or AI-generated talking-head videos with missing facial detail and speech-inconsistent teeth or lip movements.
Uses a video diffusion transformer that mixes video latents with noise, combining source information with controlled detail regeneration.
Audio guides lip motion; reference images preserve facial appearance; prior frames support temporal consistency.
Trains in two stages for visual restoration and audio-guided lip correction, supporting original-audio restoration and visual dubbing.
Achieves the best reported LPIPS, DISTS, and lip-synchronization scores among evaluated restoration baselines, with qualitative gains in tooth boundaries and lip contours.

papers.abstract: Earth observation (EO) workflows require selecting among known outcomes, estimating confidence, and processing large volumes of imagery. Generative vision-language models can address these tasks, but autoregressive decoding is computationally costly and their confidence estimates are unreliable. Decision models offer an alternative, returning probabilities over candidate answers in a single forward pass. However, their accuracy, calibration, and transfer across EO tasks remain insufficiently understood. We investigate these properties through a diagnostic study of d3-flash (8.4B parameters) across 30 settings from 23 public EO benchmarks. We find that compositional reasoning transfers well and calibration improves over its Qwen3.5-9B backbone on 24 settings, while counting, change quantification, damage grading, and absent-object recognition remain challenging. To address these limitations, we adapt d3-flash through low-rank fine-tuning on public EO training splits, producing EO-Jev. EO-Jev improves significantly over d3-flash on 26 of 30 settings and matches or exceeds specialist references on 20 of 28. It also achieves an average gain of 8.0 points across 12 held-out settings and lower expected calibration error than specialists on 21 of 28 settings. These improvements come at a modest cost of 1.8 points in general decision performance. Our results demonstrate the potential of adapting general decision models into competitive EO generalists while highlighting persistent challenges in quantitative perception, option-order consistency, and calibration under distribution shift.
bullets: Decision models provide single-pass probabilities over candidate answers, avoiding the costly decoding and unreliable confidence of generative vision-language models.
A diagnostic study evaluates d3-flash across 30 settings from 23 public EO benchmarks.
Compositional reasoning transfers well, but counting, change quantification, damage grading, and absent-object recognition remain difficult.
Low-rank fine-tuning yields EO-Jev, which improves over d3-flash on 26 of 30 settings and matches or exceeds specialist references on 20 of 28.
EO-Jev gains 8.0 average points on 12 held-out settings and improves calibration, with a modest 1.8-point decline in general decision performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2 EO-Jev Architecture and Training. EO images (single images, pre/post pairs or time series) are paired with typed questions with predefined answers. General decision data is replayed in 20% of each batch. The vision encoder and text tower Φθ process the images and questions, respectively. A frozen readout Wr converts the final hidden state h into option probabilities p. Training: LoRA adapters in the vision encoder and text tower are optimized using KL divergence against target distributions q, with an additional ranked probability score (RPS) on ordinal questions. Inference: merged adapters (W + BA) enable single-pass predictions at d3-flash cost. Answers are accepted when confidence exceeds a per-question threshold τq and otherwise deferred to an analyst. Examples and probabilities are illustrative.

Badges give the specialist’s best-accuracy mode (P: prompted, W: wrapped/generative). All models run on the same exclusive node (4×A100, BF16), on the same 160-question seeded sample per row, with image decoding inside the timed region. Medians: 3.2× in (a) and 6.4× in (b).

papers.abstract: Multimodal retrieval must integrate complementary evidence from views that may be missing, noisy, or unequally informative. When a sample provides limited reliable evidence, learning from its views alone can hinder the acquisition of useful retrieval representations. Semantically related training samples may provide complementary observations, yet existing volume-based objectives jointly align modalities within each sample without explicitly enabling information exchange across samples. We therefore propose a training-time hypergraph fusion framework that connects observed modalities both within samples and across semantically related samples, allowing representation learning to draw on evidence beyond an individual sample while leaving the retrieval pipeline unchanged at inference. The framework includes HyVol as a special case and introduces two configurations: wHyVol learns view contribution weights and symmetric semantic affinities, whereas wRHG additionally models typed interactions and participant roles through relational propagation. Missing modalities are omitted rather than imputed, and the hypergraph is discarded after training, incurring no additional inference cost. Experiments on eleven zero-shot video-text and audio-text retrieval benchmarks demonstrate broad improvements with both GRAM and HyperGRAM. Across 17 video benchmark-modality settings evaluated in both retrieval directions, wRHG outperforms GRAM in all 34 comparisons and HyperGRAM in 33 of 34. Mean text-to-video R@1 increases from 63.4 to 68.2 with GRAM and from 64.8 to 68.4 with HyperGRAM, while the largest video-to-text gain reaches 13.3 percentage points on ActivityNet. Under missing-modality evaluation, both weighted configurations retain positive text-to-video gains over GRAM across seven benchmarks at every evaluated missingness rate, even when 90% of clips lack one modality.
bullets: Addresses noisy, missing, or unevenly informative modalities and the limits of per-sample alignment.
Connects modalities within samples and across semantically related samples through hypergraph regularization.
wHyVol learns view weights and semantic affinities; wRHG further models typed interactions and participant roles.
Improves retrieval broadly across 11 zero-shot video-text and audio-text benchmarks, with no added inference cost.
Maintains positive gains under missing-modality conditions, including when 90% of clips lack one modality.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed framework. (a) Existing methods score each clip alone: a clip’s score depends only on the caption and the clip’s own views, and every other clip in the batch, even a related one, is pushed apart as a negative. (b) Our training-time hypergraph: observed views form vertices, document hyperedges group the views of each clip, and caption-guided semantic hyperedges connect related clips through same-modality and cross-modality links; missing views have no vertex and are not imputed, and each vertex receives a learned reliability weight. (c) At test time the hypergraph is removed: each clip is encoded and scored independently with the original backbone score, so the inference cost equals that of the backbone.

Figure 2: Overview of training-time hypergraph refinement. Each observed modality becomes a weighted vertex, and stop-gradient captions connect semantically related candidates through mutual top-k neighbors. Information is then exchanged either by weighted additive propagation (WHYVOL) or by typed relational messages (WRHG), and the refined embeddings are scored by the unchanged GRAM/HYPERGRAM objective. The hypergraph is used only during training and is removed at inference.

Figure 4: Zero-shot text-to-video retrieval under missing modalities with the GRAM backbone on seven video benchmarks. Each panel shows the R@1 gain of +HYVOL, +WHYVOL and +WRHG over GRAM (dashed line at zero) as a fraction r of the gallery clips that lose one randomly chosen modality; the per-clip masks are fixed and identical for all methods, and r=0 is the standard setting. MSR-VTT and VATEX use the T–VAS modality set, and the other benchmarks use T–VA.

papers.title: Fuse To Align: Multimodal Representation Learning for Retrieval via Hypergraph Regularization

papers.abstract: **Purpose:** Ultrasound biometry is widely used across various clinical applications, including prenatal and cardiac examinations, to obtain quantitative measurements by placing calipers at anatomical landmarks. However, these measurements remain subject to interoperator variability as they rely largely on manual caliper placement. Conventional methods often use specialized prediction heads for different ultrasound tasks, whereas vision-language models offer flexibility through text instructions. However, direct coordinate prediction does not explicitly model spatial likelihood distributions, limiting the representation of localization ambiguity. **Methods:** We propose Kev-Bio, a vision-language model that uses clinical measurement questions to guide ultrasound landmark detection. Inspired by System One decision models, Kev-Bio uses decision representations of the language model to generate queries for each caliper endpoint. These queries are matched against shared dense ultrasound features to produce spatial probability maps, from which landmark coordinates and clinical measurements are derived. The model is trained end-to-end using both landmark localization and clinical measurement losses. **Results:** On the nine-view FU/GU Biometry 2026 dataset, Kev-Bio achieves a mean radial error (MRE) of 22.50 pixels and a clinical measurement mean absolute error (MAE) of 15.38, outperforming the compared baselines in overall performance. **Conclusion:** These results demonstrate the effectiveness of Kev-Bio for ultrasound landmark detection and clinical measurement across different anatomical views. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/moeinheidari7829/Kev-Bio.
bullets: Addresses interoperator variability caused by manual caliper placement in ultrasound biometry.
Uses clinical measurement questions and language-model decision representations to query shared dense ultrasound features.
Generates endpoint probability maps rather than directly predicting coordinates, capturing localization uncertainty.
Trains jointly with landmark-localization and clinical-measurement losses.
On the FU/GU Biometry 2026 dataset, reports 22.50-pixel MRE and 15.38 measurement MAE, outperforming compared baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of Kev-Bio. Qwen3.5 and USFM provide visual tokens to the language model, while DINOv2 contributes additional localization features. Clinical questions are encoded into decision states at ⟨decide⟩ tokens, which generate queries for each landmark endpoint. A convolutional-based Pixel Neck combines features from the three visual encoders into a shared dense feature map. Endpoint queries are matched against this map to produce spatial probability maps, from which landmark coordinates and clinical measurements are derived.

papers.abstract: Actor--critic methods rely on critic gradients to improve continuous-action policies, yet finite-sample guarantees must control both value and gradient errors and their propagation through the actor. We develop a neural actor-critic procedure that combines a regularized minimax Bellman estimator over sigmoid networks with a finite reflected Langevin sampler driven by the fitted critic gradient. Under uniform Bellman regularity and covered reset sampling, a positive high-order action-derivative penalty yields value and action-gradient risk bounds with classical nonparametric minimax exponents up to logarithmic factors. We propagate estimation, mixing, discretization, temperature, and policy-iteration errors to obtain return guarantees, with refinements for bounded multimodal potentials and strongly concave regimes. Empirical studies across controlled simulations, logged continuous-control data, and a simulated decision task show favorable performance relative to the considered baselines.
bullets: Targets the challenge of propagating finite-sample critic value and gradient errors into actor updates.
Estimates the Bellman critic with a regularized minimax objective over sigmoid networks and a high-order action-derivative penalty.
Uses a finite reflected Langevin sampler driven by the fitted critic gradient to improve continuous-action policy updates.
Derives value, action-gradient, and return guarantees accounting for estimation, mixing, discretization, temperature, and policy-iteration errors.
Experiments on simulations, logged continuous-control data, and a simulated decision task report favorable performance against the considered baselines.

papers.abstract: Attention remains a substantial computational cost in Transformer training, particularly at long context lengths. NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs provide high-throughput low-precision matrix multiplication, but exploiting it in attention requires addressing quantization overhead, causal information leakage through shared scales, and numerical inconsistencies between the forward and backward passes. We present FLAMIA, a family of attention kernels for Blackwell with MXFP8 and mixed NVFP4/FP8 training paths. Our design combines token-block scaling that reuses quantized operands across matrix orientations, targeted safeguards against scale-induced leakage, and consistent forward and backward computations. Fused quantization and architecture-specific kernel optimizations reduce overhead, while document-local scaling and workload-aware scheduling support variable-length documents directly in packed layouts without repacking. Across various causal packed-document workloads, the MXFP8 path accelerates the combined forward and backward attention call, including quantization, by factors of $1.10$--$1.40\times$ on B200 and $1.06$--$1.42\times$ on B300 relative to the fastest evaluated baseline for each workload. We validate training stability and quality preservation on pretraining Llama-style models. These results show how jointly designing quantization, training numerics, and document scheduling translates low-bit hardware throughput into practical attention acceleration.
bullets: Targets attention’s high computational cost at long context lengths on Blackwell GPUs.
Introduces MXFP8 and mixed NVFP4/FP8 attention kernels with reusable token-block scaling and leakage safeguards.
Maintains consistent forward and backward computations while fusing quantization and applying architecture-specific optimizations.
Supports variable-length causal documents in packed layouts through document-local scaling and workload-aware scheduling.
Achieves 1.10–1.40× speedups on B200 and 1.06–1.42× on B300 for the MXFP8 path, while preserving training stability and quality in Llama-style pretraining.

papers.abstract: Geospatial text spotting involves locating and transcribing geographic labels, such as road names, district names, and landmarks, in raster maps. These labels are often small, densely arranged, and arbitrarily oriented. Although Arabic text recognition has been studied extensively in documents and natural scenes, Arabic geospatial text spotting remains underexplored. We introduce ARABGEOTEXT, an Arabic-centric benchmark covering 970 geographic locations in Riyadh and Jeddah, with 17,875 manually annotated text instances per view type. For each location, we pair an OpenStreetMap (OSM) rendering with a composite created by overlaying that rendering on the corresponding remote sensing (RS) imagery. The paired views preserve label content and pixel geometry, allowing evaluation across different backgrounds. Geographic partitions support in-city and city-disjoint evaluation of detection, recognition, and end-to-end spotting. Experiments with direct Qwen3.5-4B spotting show difficulties in recovering all labels within a tile. We therefore propose a tool-augmented vision-language framework that combines YOLO26 localization and crop rectification with Qwen3.5-4B recognition adapted through low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The framework outperforms direct LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-4B spotting across both image views and test cities. With localization held fixed, reader adaptation further improves recognition over the pretrained zero-shot reader. The dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yakoubbazi/ArabGeoText.
bullets: Addresses the underexplored task of locating and transcribing small, dense, arbitrarily oriented Arabic geographic labels.
Provides 970 locations in Riyadh and Jeddah with 17,875 manually annotated text instances per view type, pairing OpenStreetMap renderings with remote-sensing composites.
Supports in-city and city-disjoint evaluation of detection, recognition, and end-to-end spotting across different visual backgrounds.
Combines YOLO26 localization, crop rectification, and LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-4B recognition.
The framework outperforms direct LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-4B spotting, while reader adaptation improves recognition over the pretrained zero-shot reader.

papers.abstract: Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs without per-LLM fitting, and no law names the factors that set it. From closed-form expressions of LLM inference's computational and memory-access complexity, we derive the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache and next-token computation cost. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from several families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1-3.5x below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration. SIMPLE explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and higher GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy linearly relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; accuracy rises but energy rises faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x range. Moving to agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0x, as both prefill and KV-cache terms grow with input length; prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%), but not KV-cache cost, so even a cached agentic request costs 4.8x more.
bullets: Derives energy scaling from inference computation and memory-access complexity, separating prefill from decode costs.
Evaluated on 13 dense LLMs across NVIDIA H100 traces, achieving R² = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE without per-LLM fitting.
Shows prefill energy grows quadratically with hidden dimension, while higher GQA grouping linearly lowers per-token energy versus MHA.
Longer reasoning budgets can exceed the energy-minimizing output length: accuracy improves, but energy rises faster and Intelligence per Joule declines.
Agentic serving greatly increases request energy; prefix caching removes most prefill cost but leaves substantial KV-cache cost.

papers.abstract: Previous research shows that vision-language (VL) models struggle to understand fine-grained image details and tend to focus on the overall layout. Moreover, any weakness in English tends to be further amplified in the multilingual setting. To study that, we extend InpaintCOCO, an English dataset focused on fine-grained visual details, to 13 typologically diverse languages across five language families, creating MultiInpaintCOCO - a new multilingual benchmark of 953 minimal-pair examples. We further test several state-of-the-art models in multilingual multimodal retrieval, considering both light VL CLIP-like encoders and large language models. Our results show that performance degrades substantially for lower-resource languages, with the strongest predictor being the data resources available for the languages rather than typological similarity to English. In cross-lingual retrieval, most models exhibit a systematic bias toward English: when given a correct caption in a non-English language and an incorrect one in English, models preferentially select the English caption. This bias varies considerably across architectures. Among the tested models, Gemma 3 shows the strongest English preference while Qwen 3 is the least biased, despite both reaching similar monolingual accuracy across languages. The code is available at https://github.com/ufal/multi-inpaint-coco.
bullets: Extends InpaintCOCO to 13 typologically diverse languages across five language families.
Introduces 953 minimal-pair examples for multilingual fine-grained visual understanding.
Evaluates CLIP-like vision-language encoders and large language models on multilingual and cross-lingual retrieval.
Lower-resource language performance is driven more by available language data than by typological similarity to English.
Models often prefer incorrect English captions over correct non-English captions; English bias varies by architecture, with Gemma 3 strongest and Qwen 3 weakest among tested models.

papers.abstract: Ball-balancing robots (ballbots) must lean to accelerate, and the lean is limited by the wheel torques and by safety. Planners that use the full robot model are expensive, while planners that ignore the balance dynamics produce references that cannot be followed. This paper presents a two-layer navigation scheme for a three-omni-wheel ballbot. The upper layer is a model predictive controller on a \emph{jerk model} of the ball position, with discrete-time control barrier functions for static, moving, rotating and concave obstacles. The lower layer is a hierarchical sliding mode controller with an extended state observer and a robust exponential control barrier function on the tilt (HSMC-ESO-ECBF). The layers are linked by an acceleration bound derived in closed form from the largest steady tilt that the barrier function admits, so that the plan never asks for a lean the tracker refuses. For obstacles whose motion is only predicted, the obstacles are inflated by conformal prediction radii that bound the prediction error with a prescribed probability. In MuJoCo, with omni-wheel roller contacts and torque saturation, the scheme keeps at least $10$\,cm of clearance, tracks the plan within $2$\,cm RMS, keeps the tilt below the limit and plans in $9$--$12$\,ms, $10$--$15$ times faster than a full-model nonlinear MPC that enters the inflated obstacles; with predicted obstacles, the conformal inflation removes the collisions of a constant-velocity predictor in $30$ random crossing scenarios and reduces them in an endless run on a closed path.The source code and video illustrations are available at https://safe-ballbot.github.io
bullets: Uses an upper-layer MPC with discrete-time control barrier functions for static, moving, rotating, and concave obstacles.
Uses a lower-layer hierarchical sliding-mode controller with state estimation and a tilt barrier function to enforce balance limits.
Derives an acceleration bound from the allowable steady tilt, linking planning and tracking so references remain feasible.
Inflates predicted obstacles using conformal prediction radii to account for motion-prediction errors.
In MuJoCo, maintains at least 10 cm clearance, 2 cm RMS plan-tracking error, tilt limits, and 9–12 ms planning times; conformal inflation reduces collisions with predicted obstacles.

papers.abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) aims to recover expert rewards that transfer across environments with differing dynamics. Prior work has shown that such transfer is possible when gathering expert demonstrations across sufficiently different dynamics. In practice, however, expert demonstrations are costly, making it critical to select the right dynamics to reduce the quantity of expert data required for learning transferable rewards. We propose a two-phase approach: we first cycle through the available dynamics to obtain a reliable reward estimate, then actively select dynamics to reduce our uncertainty about the expert reward. Crucially, this yields novel sample complexity guarantees on transfer that hold for any dynamics, with a rate independent of the number of available dynamics. Empirically, our method significantly reduces the number of expert demonstrations needed to learn a transferable reward.
bullets: Targets the high cost of collecting expert demonstrations for transferable reward learning.
First cycles through available dynamics to obtain a reliable initial reward estimate.
Then actively selects dynamics that reduce uncertainty about the expert reward.
Provides transfer sample-complexity guarantees for arbitrary dynamics, independent of their number.
Experiments show substantially fewer expert demonstrations are needed to learn transferable rewards.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires fine-grained control and complex physical interactions with the environment, posing significant challenges for robot policy learning. Vision-only policies struggle with such tasks, as contact states and interaction forces are difficult to infer from visual observations alone. Existing methods mitigate this issue by incorporating force or tactile sensing. However, they often treat these signals as auxiliary observations without fully exploiting their role in modeling future interaction dynamics. To address this, we propose ForceLDM, a force-aware latent dynamics model that learns future contact and motion dynamics to guide action generation. Rather than directly predicting future observations, which can entangle task-relevant dynamics with irrelevant sensory details, ForceLDM learns a compact representation of future dynamics through knowledge distillation. Specifically, a teacher network with privileged future force/torque and optical flow signals extracts future dynamic features, which are then distilled into a student network trained only on current observations. This enables the student model to reason about upcoming contacts and physical dynamics without relying on future sensory inputs at deployment. To improve robustness and generalization, we further introduce a curriculum-based progressive noise injection strategy to mitigate over-reliance on future features. Experiments on five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks demonstrate that ForceLDM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, generalizes effectively to novel objects, and remains robust to environmental perturbations. Project page and code are available at https://tpy001.github.io/ForceLDM/.
bullets: Vision-only policies struggle to infer contact states and interaction forces during manipulation.
A teacher uses future force/torque and optical-flow signals to extract dynamic features, which are distilled into a student using only current observations at deployment.
The model predicts compact future contact and motion dynamics rather than full future observations.
Progressive curriculum-based noise injection reduces reliance on privileged future features and improves robustness.
Experiments across five real-world tasks show strong performance, generalization to novel objects, and robustness to environmental perturbations.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient large language model (LLM) fine-tuning, and recent methods incorporate curvature-aware strategies. However, in the high-dimensional parameter space of LLMs, these methods inherently suffer from exploding gradient variance and prohibitive costs. Conversely, confining updates to a low-dimensional subspace reduces variance but discards critical high-dimensional information, degrading performance. This creates a fundamental dilemma: full-space optimization is informative but has high variance, while subspace optimization has low variance but loses information. To break this trade-off, we propose ENGINE (Endogenous Variational MultiScale). Inspired by computational mechanics, we adapt static Variational MultiScale (VMS) theory to dynamic optimization, treating low- and high-dimensional spaces as resolved coarse and unresolved fine scales. Through a multigrid-style V-cycle, ENGINE alternates between spaces, dynamically probing fine-grained information in the high-dimensional space and injecting it to correct the efficient low-dimensional sampling process. Under appropriate assumptions, statistical analysis characterizes variance reduction and correction of curvature-induced bias, and convergence analysis establishes a stationarity bound for the corrected coarse updates. Evaluations on standard LLM benchmarks show that ENGINE achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence than existing ZO methods, achieving up to a $2.61\times$ speed-up in forward passes with zero additional peak memory overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/ENGINE.
bullets: ZO fine-tuning is memory-efficient but faces high gradient variance in full parameter spaces and information loss in low-dimensional subspaces.
ENGINE applies dynamic Variational MultiScale optimization, treating low- and high-dimensional updates as coarse and fine scales.
A multigrid-style V-cycle alternates between spaces to inject fine-scale information into efficient coarse-space sampling.
Theoretical analysis addresses variance reduction, curvature-induced bias correction, and convergence to stationarity.
On standard LLM benchmarks, ENGINE improves accuracy and convergence, with up to 2.61× fewer forward passes and no additional peak memory overhead.

papers.abstract: A memory-augmented agent must decide which memories to keep, merge and retrieve, and its only evidence of their value is its retrieval log: the memories it retrieved in each episode and whether it succeeded. Existing methods assign every memory a value from this log, even when the log cannot separate one memory's contribution from another's. We treat the log as an experiment that nobody designed and ask which memory values it determines. Two counts answer this before any outcome is observed: how often each memory was retrieved, and how often each pair was retrieved together. From these counts, we prove that top-$k$ retrieval leaves every memory value undetermined, however many episodes are logged, and that a question with its own memories, asked once, determines at most one of their values. On fourteen standard memory benchmarks, no memory value is determined in any of 55 configurations. Both causes are choices about retrieval. We introduce LEDGER, which estimates each determined Shapley value in closed form with a confidence interval and reports every other value as undetermined. It merges memories with identical histories without losing a determined value, and it retrieves so that the next log determines more. On pooled HotpotQA, LEDGER raises the fraction of memories determined from 0.001 to 0.797, at a cost of 2.6 accuracy points on HotpotQA and with a gain of 2.7 on LoCoMo.
bullets: Memory value is identifiable only when retrieval histories distinguish a memory’s contribution from others.
Two retrieval statistics—individual counts and pairwise co-retrieval counts—determine identifiability before observing outcomes.
The authors prove that standard top-$k$ retrieval leaves every memory value undetermined, regardless of log length; single-use question memories determine at most one value.
Across 55 configurations on 14 benchmarks, no memory value was determined.

LEDGER estimates determined Shapley values with confidence intervals, merges memories with identical histories, and improves the determined-memory fraction from 0.001 to 0.797 on pooled HotpotQA, with a 2.6-point HotpotQA accuracy cost and a 2.7-point LoCoMo gain.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation goals are easier to visualize than to specify numerically through explicit geometric constraints. We present VerifLM, a framework that converts image-edited goal configurations into physically verified 6-DoF object poses for planning. Using an edited image, VerifLM recovers an initial relative pose between an active object and a passive object, then prompts a vision-language model to generate axis-wise sampling constraints and a task-specific validation program. Candidate poses are evaluated in a physics simulator, and the VLM selects the most task-consistent retained candidate. To operate without predefined object meshes or physical parameters, VerifLM reconstructs metric object geometry from RGB-D observations and constructs multiple hypothetical simulations with varying physics and geometry. Parallel-world validation evaluates candidates across geometry--physics variations and ranks them by the number of worlds in which they satisfy the validation program. We evaluate VerifLM on nine manipulation tasks. VerifLM achieves the highest task success on eight of nine tasks, with the largest performance gain on goals requiring precise orientation and contact relationships.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of specifying manipulation goals with explicit geometric constraints.
Uses a vision-language model to generate axis-wise pose constraints and task-specific validation programs from edited images.
Reconstructs metric object geometry from RGB-D data and tests candidate poses across simulations with varied geometry and physics.
Ranks candidates by how consistently they satisfy the validation program across parallel simulated worlds.
Evaluated on nine tasks, achieving the highest task success on eight, with the largest gains for precise orientation and contact goals.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising approach for memory-efficient large language model (LLM) post-training, yet its reliability in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) under the mismatched-data regime produces a $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification that sets an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale $μ$ decreases, whereas Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT) under the matched-data regime eliminates this amplification via noise cancellation. We further derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants that cleanly separate the two regimes. These results motivate the ZO-BOLT algorithm, which builds on BOLT's matched-data advantage for reliable ZO optimization of an RLVR-aligned objective. Controlled perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched end-to-end comparisons validate the predicted effect of data matching. Experiments across three models and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks further show that ZO-BOLT consistently improves over the pretrained baseline while retaining a near-inference memory footprint. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianmin-chen/the_cost_of_mismatch.
bullets: Studies why zeroth-order gradient estimation is unreliable in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.
Shows that mismatched data causes $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification and an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale decreases.
Finds that matched-data evaluations, as in BOLT, cancel this amplification and yield cleaner convergence guarantees.
Introduces ZO-BOLT, which applies this matched-data principle to a ZO RLVR-aligned objective.
Experiments across three models and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks support the predicted effect and show gains over pretrained baselines with near-inference memory use.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) typically process large numbers of multimodal tokens from audio-visual inputs, incurring substantial computational costs and a large memory footprint for the key-value (KV) cache. Aggressive token pruning can alleviate this problem while maintaining competitive performance on multiple-choice tasks, which require only a single option as output. However, we observe substantial quality degradation when generating long-form, open-ended responses. We attribute this gap to query-guided selection, which can retain sufficient evidence for answer selection while discarding details needed for comprehensive generation. This motivates reducing overlapping information across tokens, termed structural redundancy, while preserving diverse content. However, the retained representations may still contain precision redundancy due to unnecessarily high numerical precision in their cached values. To address these two levels of redundancy in token representations, we introduce a training-free framework named R$^2$-Omni. First, Structure-Aware Token Consolidation (STC) consolidates redundant representations using spatiotemporal similarity in video and local continuity in audio. Then, Semantic-Sensitivity Guided Precision Allocation (SSPA) allocates value precision to the retained representations according to the estimated reduction in attention-output error under quantized keys, with query attention and audio-visual alignment providing a semantic prior. Extensive experiments on long-form generation benchmarks demonstrate an average 5.0$\times$ reduction in the memory footprint while preserving 97.98% of baseline generation quality and achieving a 1.48$\times$ end-to-end speedup, highlighting the benefits of jointly reducing structural and precision redundancy.
bullets: Targets quality degradation from aggressive token pruning in long-form, open-ended generation.
Uses Structure-Aware Token Consolidation to merge structurally redundant video and audio representations.
Uses Semantic-Sensitivity Guided Precision Allocation to assign lower or higher value precision based on estimated attention-output sensitivity.
Achieves a 5.0× average memory-footprint reduction, 97.98% of baseline generation quality, and a 1.48× end-to-end speedup.
The framework is training-free and evaluated on long-form generation benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Semantic change detection in remote sensing aims to identify and characterize land-cover transitions observed in pairs of satellite or aerial images. Existing methods assume a fixed set of change categories, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios where changes of interest may vary, for example across geographies or over time. In this work, we tackle the problem of class-incremental semantic change detection, where a model progressively learns to detect new types of semantic change. To do so, we exploit the hierarchical structure of land-cover semantics, where newly introduced categories correspond to fine-grained refinements of existing ones, and represent said semantic categories in hyperbolic space, which is particularly well suited to represent such hierarchical relationships. To capture semantic changes, we introduce HyperFlow, a method relying on Busemann prototypes, modeling change as an anomaly in a learned semantic flow within the hyperbolic embedding space induced by segmentation. HyperFlow couples change detection to class-incremental semantic segmentation, enabling class-incremental semantic change detection. We also present HiChange, a new large-scale, high resolution remote sensing dataset with detailed, fine-grained hierarchical labels. Experimental results demonstrate that HyperFlow achieves both strong change detection and semantic segmentation performance across incremental steps. In particular, we show that progressively refining semantic categories, rather than considering them all directly, yields improved change detection, highlighting the benefits of incremental learning for semantic change detection.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed change categories in remote sensing, where new categories may emerge across regions or over time.
Represents hierarchical land-cover categories in hyperbolic space and uses Busemann prototypes to model semantic flow anomalies.
Couples change detection with class-incremental semantic segmentation to progressively learn new change types.
Introduces HiChange, a large-scale, high-resolution dataset with fine-grained hierarchical labels.
Experiments show strong detection and segmentation across incremental steps, with category refinement improving change detection.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CI-SCD via Hyperbolic Flow. (1) Land-cover semantics are naturally organized in hierarchies. (3) Hyperbolic semantic flow: a vector field transforming the embeddings of the first image into the embeddings of the second image is learned. The hyperbolic distance between the positions of the predicted embeddings and the observed positions indicates change. papers.abstract: Computer-use agents for scientific software require application-specific expertise. Much of this expertise is documented in human-authored software manuals and web pages. However, turning these resources into executable, reusable skills remains challenging due to mismatches between documented and deployed software versions and differences in scope between documentation coverage and task requirements. We introduce ScienceCUA, a two-stage framework combining resource-to-skill construction with execution-guided skill evolution. First, ScienceCUA identifies tasks supported by the software from its documentation, infers operational trajectories, and generalizes them into reusable Skills. Command catalogs, syntax constraints, and shortcuts are organized separately as References for on-demand lookup. Then, ScienceCUA uses execution feedback to drive skill self-evolution by contrasting successful and failed trajectories for the same task, identifying deficiencies, revising existing skills or adding new ones, and updating the skill library only after repeated validation in real environments. To enable reliable evaluation without benchmark noise or task leakage, we introduce two improved benchmarks. ScienceBoard-Verified provides an audited and corrected basis for measuring task performance, while ScienceBoard-VE separates skill evolution from final testing through disjoint evolution and test tasks and further supports native-agent evaluation. Experiments show that the initial Skills and References improve average task success rate by up to 7.23 percentage points over the base model, while skill self-evolution increases the total gain over the baseline to as much as 17.12 percentage points. ScienceCUA turns software documentation into an evolving set of executable skills and queryable references, offering a practical way for general-purpose agents to use scientific software reliably and at scale.
bullets: Addresses the gap between human-authored documentation, deployed software versions, and real task requirements.
Constructs reusable Skills from documented tasks and trajectories, while organizing commands, syntax constraints, and shortcuts as queryable References.
Evolves skills by comparing successful and failed executions, revising or adding skills, and validating updates repeatedly in real environments.
Introduces ScienceBoard-Verified and ScienceBoard-VE to reduce benchmark noise, task leakage, and confounding between evolution and testing.
Initial resources improve average task success by up to 7.23 percentage points; self-evolution raises the total gain over baseline to up to 17.12 points.

papers.abstract: We introduce Axion 1.0, a fully open agent foundation model that combines strong and broad agentic capabilities with a remarkably simple training recipe. Axion 1.0 is trained in only three stages: two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization (DPO), or on-policy distillation (OPD). The first SFT stage develops strong self-contained reasoning through model-aware data construction, where we synthesize challenging problems and adversarially strengthen them based on the base model's own successful solution strategies. The second stage extends these capabilities to tool-dependent reasoning through a scalable pipeline for constructing diverse and automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real-world data sources and deterministic computation. Finally, reinforcement learning further strengthens long-horizon reasoning and interaction with external tools and environments. Despite this compact training recipe, Axion 1.0 achieves strong performance across a broad suite of agentic benchmarks and is competitive with leading commercial models on several of them. Equally importantly, Axion 1.0 is open beyond model weights: we release the complete recipe, including data construction, generation, filtering, verification, prompts, and training code, enabling the entire development process to be reproduced and extended. Axion 1.0 demonstrates that strong agent foundation models can be both open and simple, offering a practical and reproducible path toward advancing open agentic intelligence.
bullets: Uses two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, DPO, or on-policy distillation.
Builds self-contained reasoning through model-aware synthesis and adversarial problem strengthening.
Extends reasoning to tool use via diverse, automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real-world data and deterministic computation.
Reinforcement learning improves long-horizon reasoning and interaction with tools and environments.
Reports strong results across agentic benchmarks, including competitiveness with leading commercial models on several tasks; releases the full development recipe and code.

papers.abstract: Multimodal test-time adaptation (TTA) enables pretrained multimodal models to accommodate distribution shifts during inference using only unlabeled test data, without recourse to the original training data. Compared with unimodal adaptation, multimodal adaptation is further complicated by the coexistence and interaction of multiple representation perspectives. This complexity is particularly pronounced under modality reliability shifts, which preserve modality availability but degrade information quality, and modality availability shifts, which render the corresponding modality entirely inaccessible. Category-conditional Gaussian modeling offers a natural starting point for handling such distributional variations, having proven effective in unimodal test-time adaptation for characterizing representation distributions, yet its extension to multimodal settings requires a more elaborate formulation. To this end, we propose Adaptive Probabilistic Gaussian Calibration (AdaPGC), which extends category-conditional Gaussian modeling across modality-specific and multimodal fusion representations for probabilistic calibration under multimodal distribution shifts. AdaPGC continuously updates category-conditional Gaussian models over modality-specific and fusion representations, using the resulting probabilistic predictions to calibrate source model predictions and guide reliability based rectification, while exploiting their joint distributions to recover unavailable fusion representations. Extensive experiments under diverse modality corruption and missingness conditions demonstrate that AdaPGC effectively improves robustness under both modality reliability and availability shifts. Our source code will be released at https://github.com/XuJinglinn/AdaPGC-plus.
bullets: Addresses multimodal distribution shifts caused by reduced modality reliability or complete modality unavailability.
Extends category-conditional Gaussian modeling to modality-specific and multimodal fusion representations.
Continuously updates Gaussian models during inference using unlabeled test data.
Uses probabilistic calibration for prediction correction and joint distributions to recover unavailable fusion representations.
Experiments across diverse corruption and missingness conditions show improved robustness to both shift types.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed multimodal test-time adaptation framework. The input consists of paired video and audio streams affected by reliability shifts (modality corruption) or availability shifts (missing video/audio). For complete instances, the pretrained source model feeds the fused representation zF into the shared classifier to obtain source logits s; for incomplete instances, it instead uses the representation of the available modality, zV or zA. The category-conditional Gaussian means and priors are initialized from the pretrained classifier, while the covariance and cross-covariance matrices are initialized as identity matrices. During adaptation, these parameters are updated using target-stream statistics to define the discriminants gV , gA, and gF and conditional estimators EV →F and EA→F . For incomplete instances, the available modality representation is used to estimate category-conditional fused representations, whose Gaussian predictions are combined with the unimodal predictions to obtain calibration logits r. For complete instances, the fused Gaussian discriminant produces the calibration logits r = gF (zF ), while discrepancies between unimodal and fused Gaussian predictions guide reliability-aware one-sided alignment.

papers.abstract: Class-incremental learning (CIL) for outdoor 3D object detection remains largely underexplored. Existing outdoor studies are limited to single-benchmark evaluations, with SDCoT++ considering KITTI and CL2OD considering nuScenes under different incremental settings. This makes it difficult to assess whether observed continual-learning behavior generalizes across autonomous-driving benchmarks. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first unified cross-benchmark analysis of outdoor class-incremental 3D object detection across multiple autonomous-driving benchmarks, covering both two-task and multi-stage settings. We investigate: (1) how severely existing 3D detectors forget previously learned classes, (2) how incremental training exposes the stability-plasticity dilemma between knowledge retention and new-class acquisition, and (3) which forms of supervision are most effective for balancing these objectives. We introduce CL3DOD, a class-incremental 3D detection framework that restores missing supervision for previous classes using predictions from the previous-stage detector, preserves old-class responses through query-wise knowledge distillation, and employs EMA-based temporal consistency regularization. Experiments on KITTI and nuScenes reveal a consistent stability-plasticity dilemma across both benchmarks. CL3DOD generally achieves a more favorable stability-plasticity balance than controlled incremental baselines and improves upon published prior methods in the reported benchmark comparisons. This advantage persists across multiple incremental stages, demonstrating strong retention of previously learned knowledge while maintaining effective new-class acquisition. Our code, evaluation setup, and incremental task splits will be publicly released.
bullets: Provides the first unified cross-benchmark study covering two-task and multi-stage incremental settings.
Finds consistent forgetting and a stability–plasticity trade-off across both autonomous-driving benchmarks.
Restores previous-class supervision using prior-detector predictions, query-wise knowledge distillation, and EMA temporal consistency.
Reports a more favorable stability–plasticity balance than controlled baselines and improvements over published methods in the evaluated comparisons.
Scope is limited to the KITTI and nuScenes benchmarks and the incremental settings studied.

papers.abstract: Most image-based 3D reconstructors primarily recover visible surfaces, producing partial point clouds with large holes and leaving unobserved geometry unresolved. To address this limitation, we introduce AnchorComplete, a framework that reconstructs complete scene meshes from partial point clouds while preserving observed geometry and supporting scenes of varying scales. Building on TRELLIS.2, our method combines partial-point conditioning, which integrates global scene tokens with local spatial evidence to anchor generation to the input, and metric-scale coarse-to-fine generation, which progressively refines scene geometry within fixed-size windows while maintaining global structural consistency. Experiments on Replica and SCRREAM demonstrate that AnchorComplete consistently outperforms strong baselines in complete-scene reconstruction, particularly under sparse-view settings.
bullets: Addresses holes and unresolved geometry in image-based 3D reconstruction, which typically recovers only visible surfaces.
Combines partial-point conditioning with global scene tokens and local spatial evidence to preserve input geometry.
Uses metric-scale coarse-to-fine generation in fixed-size windows while maintaining global structural consistency.
Outperforms strong baselines on Replica and SCRREAM, especially in sparse-view settings.

Each window is conditioned on its parent occupancy and visible points through the local path (warm start) and on its points through anchor tokens read by cross-attention (global path).

papers.abstract: LLM agents compact long histories to fit their context windows, but the compacted context must still carry the operating rules that govern later actions. Prior work shows that violations rise after compaction, but measures compliance outside a complete agent harness and does not identify where each violation comes from. We introduce ARCBench(Agent Rule Compliance Benchmark), a configurable benchmark built on the open-source pi agent harness. Its tool-calling agent loop lets us measure rule compliance from actions taken during execution, bringing the evaluation closer to deployed agent workflows. Using ARCBench, we examine where violations after compaction come from, and how different compaction configurations and adversarial settings change their sources. We find that compaction rarely deletes the rule: most violations after compaction occur while the rule is still in the compacted history, with the agent treating a later request as permission, ignoring the rule, and proceeding anyway. Where violations come from depends on the configuration: how the rule is delivered decides whether the agent would break it even without compaction, while the compaction strategy and budget decide whether the rule survives. The strongest compactor-targeted attack more than doubles violations by corrupting the rule in the summary and changing how the agents behave, whereas the strongest defense restores the rule in most summary but still violates. Finally, retaining a rule does not guarantee compliance: compacted runs that retain the rule violate more than twice as often as runs with the full history.
bullets: Introduces ARCBench, a configurable benchmark that measures rule compliance through tool-calling actions in an open-source agent harness.
Most post-compaction violations occur even when the rule remains in the compacted history: agents treat later requests as permission or ignore the rule.
Violation sources depend on configuration: rule delivery affects baseline willingness to break rules, while compaction strategy and budget affect rule preservation.
A compactor-targeted attack more than doubles violations by corrupting summarized rules; the strongest defense restores rules in most summaries but does not eliminate violations.
Retaining a rule is insufficient: compacted runs with retained rules violate more than twice as often as full-history runs.

papers.selection_reason: Studies how context compaction affects LLM agent rule compliance, relevant to long-context processing and context management.
papers.title: Do Agents Still Follow the Rules? Benchmarking Rule Compliance under Agent Context Compaction
papers.tldr: ARCBench shows that context compaction usually preserves rules but can still sharply reduce agent compliance, especially when summaries corrupt rules or alter behavior.

papers.abstract: Recently, harness self-evolution has emerged as an important paradigm for improving agent performance. Prior studies show that evolving the agent harness can effectively enhance agent capabilities without modifying the foundation model's parameters. We find that existing approaches largely study agent evolution on a single task. In practice, coding agents may need to handle multiple task types over time. Whether an agent harness can continuously evolve across multiple tasks without suffering from catastrophic forgetting remains an important open question. In this paper, we investigate this open question through a comprehensive empirical study of continual harness self-evolution. We organize three software engineering task datasets into six different evolution directions and apply two representative harness evolution methods to perform continual evolution along these directions. Our experimental results show that evolution on a subsequent dataset can substantially undermine the performance on previously seen datasets. For example, with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, Meta-Harness improves its performance on SWE-Bench to 94.0% after evolution. However, after further evolution on FeatureBench, its performance on SWE-Bench drops to 32.0% by the fifth round, corresponding to a 66% relative decrease. Finally, based on our experimental findings, we identify several insights, providing directions for the continual self-evolution of agent harnesses. Code is available at https://github.com/THU-Agent/continual-harness-evolution.
bullets: Prior harness self-evolution studies largely focus on single-task improvement, leaving continual multi-task evolution underexplored.
The study evaluates continual harness self-evolution across three software-engineering datasets, six evolution directions, and two representative methods.
Subsequent evolution can substantially degrade earlier capabilities: SWE-Bench performance fell from 94.0% to 32.0% after further FeatureBench evolution in one example.
The findings reveal challenges in sustaining continual evolution and provide insights for developing less forgetful agent harnesses.
Scope: an empirical study of harness evolution; it does not modify foundation-model parameters.

papers.abstract: Soft robot co-design methods can jointly optimise morphology and control, but the resulting designs are often difficult to manufacture, while manufacturable approaches typically restrict actuator placement or require manual assembly. We present a simulation-based co-design framework that jointly optimises material distribution, pneumatic actuator placement and orientation, and control, while producing designs that can be fabricated monolithically using fused deposition modelling. The framework uses a differentiable 2D plane-stress Material Point Method simulator, incorporating an experimentally validated material model and an empirically derived surrogate model of a 3D-printed inflatable actuator. We demonstrate gradient-based optimisation soft robotic arms for prescribed tip trajectories. Optimised designs are transferred directly from simulation to one-shot monolithic FDM fabrication, with integrated actuators and no post-assembly. Physical experiments demonstrate that the resulting arms reproduce the behaviour predicted in simulation. This framework provides a path from task-level objectives to physically realisable soft robots while retaining substantial freedom over both morphology and actuation.
bullets: Addresses the gap between flexible co-design and manufacturable soft robots without manual assembly.
Optimises material distribution, actuator placement/orientation, and control for prescribed arm tip trajectories.
Uses a differentiable 2D plane-stress Material Point Method with validated material and actuator models.
Produces monolithic FDM-printed arms with integrated actuators, transferred directly from simulation.
Physical experiments confirm that fabricated arms behave as predicted by simulation.

papers.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is costly because attention repeatedly reads a growing key-value (KV) history. We introduce Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention (CISA), which retrofits pretrained dense attention models without gradient updates. CISA selects fixed-size KV chunks using compact summaries of existing keys, avoiding token-level indexing and a separate full-length index cache. It uses one indexing query per KV group and shares selected chunks across queries in that group. During prefill, QShare reuses selections across adjacent queries to reduce indexing cost and improve KV reuse and GPU utilization. We evaluate CISA on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano and Ultra, and Inkling-Small. In one-layer BF16 benchmarks at batch size 32 using Ultra's per-device attention dimensions, core attention is 11.7x faster for prefill queries near the end of a 1M-token prompt and 13.0x faster during decode. Including chunk scoring, selection, and all other measured GPU work, speedups are 8.6x and 3.0x. On Ultra NVFP4 with a 4,096-chunk budget, aggregate scores stay within 1.5 percentage points of dense attention on MRCR, LongBench v2, and GraphWalks. RULER sweeps on Nano and Ultra BF16 up to one million tokens show scores within 2.05 percentage points of dense attention with 8-16x fewer KV reads. Serving million-token prompts with 32 concurrent requests and 4K output tokens per request, CISA achieves 2.29x the end-to-end throughput of dense attention using Nemotron 3 Ultra NVFP4 on four NVIDIA B300 GPUs. Selecting fewer chunks increases throughput to 2.61x; in separate GraphWalks evaluations, the smaller budget widens the aggregate score gap from 1.49 to 3.59 percentage points. These results expose a practical quality-speed tradeoff without sparse training.
bullets: Targets the high cost of repeatedly reading growing KV histories during long-context inference.
Indexes fixed-size KV chunks using compact key summaries, with one query per KV group and shared selections across group queries.
QShare reuses chunk selections across adjacent prefill queries to reduce indexing overhead and improve KV reuse.
Reports up to 8–16× fewer KV reads, 2.29× end-to-end throughput, and quality within roughly 1.5–2.05 percentage points of dense attention in evaluated settings.
Using fewer chunks raises throughput to 2.61× but widens the GraphWalks quality gap to 3.59 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in cowork agents are shifting human-AI collaboration toward real-world automation, delivering software, designs, and other artifacts. However, such productivity work demands both high-quality delivery on complex productivity tasks and continued monitoring and decision-making over long horizons, a combination that remains an open challenge. We introduce CoworkOS, a general-purpose harness for long-horizon work that separates task strategy from execution management: the model decides actions, delegation, and acceptance, while the runtime maintains state and feedback. Its three-layer architecture enables direct execution or delegation to Subagents, synchronously or asynchronously, under stable responsibilities. Through a shared application layer, humans and agents inspect and revise the same evolving documents, presentations, CAD models, and Blender scenes, so human-in-the-loop participation can enter both through conversation and through direct modification of the work itself. To sustain continuity across agents and sessions, CoworkOS further introduces hierarchical workspaces and persistent semantic memory, so working files, key decisions, and long-running Job logs remain shareable, reusable, and resumable after interruption. Across 12 benchmarks and 6 categories of real-world applications, CoworkOS proves highly competitive with frontier agent applications such as Codex and DeepSeek Harness. As a sustained-work case study, CoworkOS uses GLM-5.3 as its backbone to conduct RSI-driven automated post-training on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Over five rounds, the model's average score across eight benchmarks rose from 33.19 to 42.95 (+9.76). Looking ahead, we believe CoworkOS opens a meaningful path toward general cowork-agent intelligence.
bullets: Targets the challenge of combining high-quality work on complex productivity tasks with sustained monitoring and decision-making.
Separates task strategy from execution management: models choose actions, delegation, and acceptance while the runtime maintains state and feedback.
Supports direct or delegated execution, synchronous or asynchronous subagents, and shared editing of documents, presentations, CAD models, and Blender scenes.
Uses hierarchical workspaces, persistent semantic memory, and job logs to make work resumable across agents and sessions.
Across 12 benchmarks and six application categories, it was highly competitive with Codex and DeepSeek Harness; a five-round post-training case study improved average scores from 33.19 to 42.95.

papers.abstract: On July 1, 2025, Vietnam reduced its 63 provinces to 34, abolished its 696 districts, and replaced its 10,035 commune-level units (wards) with 3,321. ViAdminShift, a Vietnamese language resource about this event, consists of 7,995 benchmark items, 2,281 retrieval passages from pre- and post-reform Wikipedia revisions and dated templates, and old-to-new tables that a released script rebuilds from the official conversion table (not redistributed). Changed items store the pre-reform answer (except 121 address items), a $2\times2$ design uses untouched units as controls, and 400 addresses appear without diacritics. The tables agree with an independent lineage on 10,564 of 10,565 official pairs, disagreements were settled against the resolutions, and the probing-track scorer agrees with both authors' blind labels (Cohen's $κ=0.91$ and $0.89$). Data, outputs, code, and a datasheet are released. In the probing track, at least 20 of 67 models know the reform. Fourteen of them give the new province alone for at most 11% of plain questions about old addresses (old province only: 14-100%); a bare date recovers up to 100%. Post hoc (80 province-free addresses, single runs), with reasoning off, today's date in the system prompt leaves 68-100% old-province-only answers for 10 of 12 models; with reasoning, an "as of" prefix in the question leaves none for seven of eight. On the 1,262-item benchmark subset, with same-source old and new passages, small models unaware of the reform give 14-30% outdated answers and the five benchmark-track knowers (also differing in size or provider) 0-5%.
bullets: It covers 7,995 benchmark items, 2,281 dated retrieval passages, old-to-new administrative tables, and 400 undiacritized addresses.
A 2×2 design uses changed units and untouched controls; tables are reconstructed from the official conversion table and validated against an independent lineage.
At least 20 of 67 tested models show awareness of the reform, but plain questions about old addresses often produce outdated or incomplete answers.
Adding a date or explicit “as of” context substantially improves temporal disambiguation in the reported probes.
The dataset, outputs, code, scorer, and datasheet are released.

papers.abstract: We release all 3,718 episodes from the ArmnetBench v0.1 evaluation (arXiv:2607.24481), which contains 600 teleoperated demonstrations and 3,118 rollouts of seven imitation-learning and vision-language-action policies on 12 tabletop tasks, recorded on low-cost SO-101 arms; 73% of the rollouts are failures. Every policy for a task was trained or fine-tuned on the same 50 demonstrations and rolled out on the same cell, so the corpus contains many policies' failures on shared tasks. An operator labelled every rollout successful, suboptimal or failure. Each episode has three camera views, joint states and actions and is available on the Hugging Face Hub in LeRobot v3.0 and a reward-model format. This note documents how the episodes were collected and the limitations that could affect their use.
bullets: Includes 600 teleoperated demonstrations and 3,118 policy rollouts on low-cost SO-101 arms.
All policies for each task used the same 50 demonstrations and robot cell, enabling shared-task comparison of failures.
An operator labelled every rollout as successful, suboptimal, or failure; 73% of rollouts were failures.
Episodes contain three camera views, joint states, and actions, with LeRobot v3.0 and reward-model formats available on Hugging Face.
The note documents collection procedures and limitations affecting corpus use.
