papers.abstract: Fine-grained manipulation couples instruction grounding, local visual precision, and sustained execution. We present FineCraft, a framework that adapts pretrained models for fine-grained manipulation in the MetaFine Challenge. A task-routed mixture of policies selects independently adapted DINOv2-DiT or pretrained $π_{0.5}$ policies through a common observation-action interface. Local visual features help identify the instructed object parts, demonstrations and expert continuations teach the required actions, and new observations guide replanning during execution. FineCraft ranks fourth with an overall score of $0.878$, exceeding the published reference on all five tasks. Official results and local diagnostics characterize performance across visual perturbations, instruction changes, and multi-stage manipulation. Code is available at https://github.com/eqcy/FineCraft
bullets: Addresses instruction grounding, precise local perception, and sustained multi-stage execution.
Uses a task-routed mixture of independently adapted DINOv2-DiT and pretrained π₀.₅ policies via a shared observation-action interface.
Combines local visual features, demonstrations, expert continuations, and observation-guided replanning.
Placed fourth in the MetaFine Challenge with an overall score of 0.878, outperforming the published reference on all five tasks.
Evaluates robustness across visual perturbations, instruction changes, and multi-stage manipulation.

papers.abstract: Knowledge is how understanding accumulates across people and generations: durable records that outlive their producers and that others can check, combine, teach, and correct. AI agents are now built and run by many independent users and organizations, and each agent is upgraded, replaced, or retired within months. Yet what an agent learns stays trapped in model parameters, a transient context window, or a system-specific memory store that is appended to and retrieved from rather than processed. We argue that the next generation of AI should be knowledge-centric, built around an explicit, continuously evolving knowledge layer independent of any single agent. In this loop, agents discover knowledge from their environments and trajectories; the layer internalizes it by turning fragmented, heterogeneous records and experience into composable, revisable understanding; and agents across systems and generations use the result and return new outcomes for revision. While discovery and use have advanced rapidly with large language model agents, internalization remains the bottleneck. We argue that internalization should become a persistent object of training and maintenance-centered on condition-preserving conceptualization of events and deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning across noisy, heterogeneous representations (text, tables, graphs, rules, and programs). To power this layer, we call for knowledge foundation models that provide shared neural capacity for knowledge computation, and outline a research agenda showing how an explicit knowledge layer delivers reuse, cost efficiency, auditability, and continuity across agent generations.
bullets: Current agents keep learning trapped in parameters, context windows, or system-specific memories, limiting reuse and continuity.
The proposed loop separates knowledge discovery, internalization, and use, with internalization identified as the main bottleneck.
Internalization requires condition-preserving conceptualization and deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning over heterogeneous, noisy representations.
The paper calls for knowledge foundation models to provide shared neural capacity for knowledge computation.
An explicit knowledge layer could improve reuse, cost efficiency, auditability, and continuity across agent generations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The knowledge-centric loop across agents and generations. Independent agent systems, built on different models and run by different organizations, discover knowledge and contribute it to an explicit knowledge layer. The layer is internalized by transformations and reasoning, and the results are used by other systems and by later generations, which inherit, revalidate, and revise them.

Figure 2: A knowledge foundation model inside the knowledge layer. It combines explicit knowledge, supporting observations and experience, and the implicit capacities of existing models, organizes shared computation across transformation and reasoning layers while delegating exact computation to symbolic components, and produces deductive, inductive, and abductive results whose status is recorded before they are written back. Implicit priors inform inference but do not become knowledge without evidence.
Table 1: Four types of knowledge [66] and their counterparts in AI systems.
Table 2: Qualitative comparison of explicit knowledge forms. Aggregation refers to counting, ranking, and comparing over many units. Ratings are our assessment.

Table 5: Routes to reasoning over knowledge and what each leaves open in the setting of §5.3, in our assessment. Each route is a candidate component of a knowledge foundation model rather than a competitor to it.
Table 3: Maturity of each stage of the knowledge-centric loop, in our assessment of the literature we examined.

papers.title: Toward Knowledge-Centric AI: Discovering, Internalizing, and Using Explicit Knowledge Across Agents and Generations
papers.tldr: The paper argues that future AI should use a shared, explicit knowledge layer that agents continuously discover, internalize, revise, and reuse across systems and generations.

papers.abstract: LLM post-training via reinforcement learning has shown consistent improvements in accuracy at the cost of reducing behavioral coverage - a phenomenon known as sharpening that can stall progress on difficult tasks. Repeated sampling objectives such as $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ are known to mitigate sharpening, but the mechanism behind it remains poorly understood. Moreover, existing approaches for $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization use dedicated algorithms, and no general framework exists for adapting established policy optimization methods from $\mathrm{@}1$ to $\mathrm{@k}$. We derive the optimal policies for KL-regularized $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ objectives in closed form. Our explicit solutions reveal that $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization naturally redistributes learning pressure based on prompt difficulty, directing it toward harder problems. Crucially, we show that standard $\mathrm{@}1$ objectives achieve these exact same optimal policies through prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation. Ultimately, this yields an optimizer-independent explanation for why $\mathrm{@k}$ objectives reduce sharpening on easy tasks while prioritizing success on harder ones. Building on these insights, we introduce $\mathrm{@k}$ Adaptive Pressure for Policy Optimization (KAPPO). Following a one-time reference calibration, KAPPO seamlessly adapts existing $\mathrm{@}1$ methods to $\mathrm{@k}$ via prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation, without otherwise altering their training procedures. Experiments with several RL methods on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that KAPPO provides direct control over sharpening. Crucially, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{@k}$ pressure can be fully realized with single completion training, matching the performance of multi-completion $\mathrm{@k}$ optimizers at a fraction of the cost.
bullets: Sharpening improves accuracy but reduces behavioral coverage, hindering difficult-task progress.
Closed-form analyses of KL-regularized pass@k and max@k explain their prompt-difficulty-adaptive learning pressure.
The same optimal policies can be achieved with standard @1 objectives using adaptive regularization or reward transformation.
KAPPO applies this adaptation to existing policy optimizers after a one-time reference calibration.
Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show single-completion KAPPO can match multi-completion @k optimization at lower cost.

figures.caption: Figure 3: MATH Level 5 validation performance of the starting checkpoints, @k-A⋆PO checkpoints, and PKPO checkpoints. @k-A⋆PO matches the performance of PKPO at a fraction of the on-policy training rollouts, requiring only a single-time reference calibration at ≤ 5% training time overhead.

Figure 2: pass@keval on AIME 2026 as the sampling budget at test time (keval) increases. Setting k > 1 during training consistently reduces sharpening. In Figure (a), we plot standard GRPO and @k-A⋆PO trained with k ∈ {1, 2, 4}. In Figure (b), we plot @k-DPO trained with k ∈ {1, 2}.

Figure 1: Adaptive pressure induced by @k objectives. (a) For binary rewards, increasing k strengthens regularization on easy tasks while retaining greater optimization pressure on difficult tasks. papers.selection_reason: Provides closed-form analysis and a general framework for pass@k objectives in LLM post-training, a meaningful contribution to LLM training methodology.
papers.title: Controlling Sharpening in LLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: KAPPO adapts standard single-completion RL objectives to control LLM sharpening, emphasizing harder prompts while reducing unnecessary pressure on easy ones.

papers.abstract: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity. Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3. These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/DepthGraft.
bullets: Addresses information dilution in deep Pre-LN language models without adding substantial cross-layer computation or memory access.
Uses stride-aligned shallow–middle source pairs to reconstruct deep-layer keys and values.
KV-sharing edges provide non-local gradient paths that sharpen key retrieval directions and enrich value representations.
Evaluated on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters under GQA and MLA, with consistent downstream gains.
On a 16B MoE model, reports improvements of 7.0% on MMLU-Pro, 6.6% on CMMLU, and 6.4% on C3.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a hierarchical KV-sharing LLM architecture that reduces KV cache by a third while improving downstream performance, fitting both efficiency and LLM architecture interests.
papers.title: DepthGraft: Structural Regularization through Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction
papers.tldr: DepthGraft hierarchically reuses KV projections across layers to regularize deep representations, reduce KV-cache memory by roughly one third, and improve language-model performance.

papers.abstract: Progress in robot learning, particularly physical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), is currently challenged by a limited availability of accessible, standardized benchmarks. While simulation-based MARL has produced remarkable emergent behaviors, from coordinated team play to complex tool use, translating these advances to physical systems remains difficult. A key barrier is infrastructural: physical platforms are often prohibitively expensive, require specialized facilities, or lack open mechanisms and designs for reproducibility. We introduce KlaskTron, an open-source, low-cost (<\$2500 USD), desktop-scale robotic testbed for adversarial MARL based on the dynamic tabletop game KLASK. The platform features dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors, enabling the high-speed, precise manipulation required for competitive play. Crucially, we provide a complete ecosystem: hardware designs (CAD, BOM), a GPU-native digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab for high-fidelity modeling and simulation, and a validated sim-to-real baseline using a learned neural actuator model. We demonstrate that this baseline enables zero-shot policy transfer, with trained agents exhibiting emergent adversarial behaviors. To ensure full reproducibility of our results, all project assets are released publicly: hardware CAD/BOM and assembly documentation at [https://idscethzurich.github.io/klask_hardware], inference software stack at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_software] and the simulation and MARL setup at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_rl].
bullets: Addresses the lack of accessible, standardized physical MARL benchmarks.
Uses dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors for fast, precise tabletop manipulation.
Provides open hardware designs, assembly documentation, inference software, and MARL simulation assets.
Includes an NVIDIA Isaac Lab digital twin and a learned neural actuator model for sim-to-real transfer.
Demonstrates zero-shot policy transfer with emergent adversarial behaviors.

papers.abstract: Fingerspelling - the sequential signing of letters that compose proper names, technical terms, and out-of-vocabulary words - is an integral component of any sign language. Despite Russian Sign Language (RSL) being used by more than 150,000 native signers, no public fingerspelling dataset for RSL exists, in contrast to American, British, German, and several other sign languages. We introduce Znaki the first open RSL fingerspelling dataset: 37,252 video recordings (35.4 hours) of 1,593 unique sequences - proper names sampled from 16 domain categories - recorded by 68 native RSL signers (37 Deaf, 29 hard-of-hearing, and 2 certified interpreters) through a crowdsourcing pipeline with a two-stage signer qualification procedure and expert validation. The dataset covers all 33 Cyrillic handshapes, and its letter-frequency distribution matches the Russian National Corpus. As reference points for future research, we establish two baselines adapted from American Sign Language fingerspelling recognition: a Squeezeformer-based encoder-decoder, reaching a character-level accuracy ($1-\mathrm{CER}$) of 0.932 and a sequence accuracy of 0.596, and Fingerspelling-PoseNet, reaching 0.886 and 0.545, respectively.
bullets: Addresses the lack of public RSL fingerspelling data despite widespread use of RSL.
Contains 37,252 recordings totaling 35.4 hours, covering 1,593 sequences across 16 proper-name domains.
Includes contributions from 68 native RSL signers and all 33 Cyrillic handshapes.
Uses crowdsourced collection with two-stage signer qualification and expert validation.
Provides two baselines: Squeezeformer achieves 0.932 character-level accuracy and 0.596 sequence accuracy; Fingerspelling-PoseNet achieves 0.886 and 0.545.

papers.title: Znaki: A Russian Fingerspelling Recognition Dataset
papers.tldr: Znaki is the first open Russian Sign Language fingerspelling dataset, with validated video recordings and baseline recognition results for future research.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) mitigates the student's exposure bias by optimizing on student-generated trajectories. However, student-generated prefixes may contain reasoning errors or follow patterns unfamiliar to the teacher, undermining the reliability of its token-level supervision. This degradation becomes more pronounced as prefixes grow longer. To address this teacher-side distribution mismatch, we propose Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation (SPTA), which adapts the teacher to the states on which it is queried during distillation. Specifically, before OPD starts, we collect student rollout prefixes with random lengths and continually train the teacher to continue from the prefixes using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). By treating each prefix as context and rewarding correct final answers, the teacher learns to recover from student-induced states rather than imitate the student's reasoning. Then, the adapted teacher is used for standard OPD, with no changes to the distillation objective. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that our SPTA improves average student performance over standard OPD and OPD with task-level RLVR-adapted teachers. These results highlight the importance of adapting teachers not only to solve problems independently, but also to provide reliable guidance on the states their students actually visit.
bullets: Problem: Longer or erroneous student prefixes create a teacher–student distribution mismatch that weakens token-level supervision.
Method: Train the teacher on randomly sized student rollout prefixes using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards before standard OPD.
The teacher learns to recover from student-induced states and produce correct continuations rather than imitate student reasoning.
SPTA leaves the standard OPD objective unchanged.
Experiments show higher average student performance than standard OPD and OPD using task-level RLVR-adapted teachers.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Standard OPD and Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation (SPTA). (a) In standard OPD, student rollouts may enter regions unfamiliar to the teacher, reducing supervision reliability. (b) SPTA first adapts the teacher through prefix-conditioned RLVR, using student prefixes as context and final-answer correctness as reward, then freezes it for standard OPD. Shaded regions indicate prefixes familiar to the teacher before and after adaptation.

Recovery improves at every evaluated nonzero ratio, even though Qwen34B’s clean-prompt accuracy decreases.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a teacher-adaptation method for on-policy distillation of LLM reasoning, a technically meaningful contribution to LLM training methodology.
papers.title: Meet Students Where They Are: Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation for On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: SPTA adapts the teacher to student-generated reasoning states before on-policy distillation, improving guidance and average student performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: An image that is hard to classify on its own may have a helpful neighbor in the same unlabeled batch. Zero-shot vision-language models (VLMs) score images independently and leave this evidence unused. We study small unlabeled query batches with no labeled examples. Visual similarity can reflect pose or background, so it may connect images from different classes. Each image's scores over the class vocabulary offer another way to choose neighbors. We introduce Behavioral Affinity Transduction (BAT), which builds a sparse graph from these class-response profiles. The graph supplies neighbor evidence during prediction. For EM-Dirichlet, it also screens candidate classes and initializes assignments. BAT plugs into direct and iterative readouts of a frozen VLM. Across diverse datasets, BAT improves the mean accuracy of every tested readout. In the main RN50 comparison, soft and hard EM-Dirichlet gain $4.22$ and $2.72$ percentage points.
bullets: Addresses the limitation that frozen VLMs classify images independently and ignore batch-level evidence.
Builds a sparse graph from each image’s class-response profile rather than relying only on visual similarity.
Uses graph-based neighbor information with direct and iterative readouts of a frozen VLM.
For EM-Dirichlet, BAT screens candidate classes and initializes assignments.
Improves mean accuracy across all tested readouts; in the main RN50 comparison, gains are 4.22 and 2.72 percentage points for soft and hard EM-Dirichlet.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential in robotic surgery for question answering, scene understanding, and grounded assistance, but their high computational cost limits real clinical deployment. Knowledge distillation provides a practical way to build compact surgical MLLMs, yet direct distillation is not well suited to surgical data because surgical samples vary greatly in difficulty, visual ambiguity, and required clinical context, making uniform teacher-student transfer unstable. In addition, the role of supervision changes during training: early stages require stronger teacher guidance for multimodal alignment, while later stages rely more on task supervision for effective optimization. To address these challenges, we propose SurgPace, a complexity-aware continuous curriculum framework for progressive distillation of surgical vision-language models. SurgPace estimates sample complexity using predictive confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency, and uses the fused score to guide a continuous easy-to-hard training process. We further introduce hierarchical representation alignment, which aligns the student with the teacher at the feature, logit, and probability levels, while gradually shifting the training focus from teacher imitation to task supervision. This design separates sample-level curriculum from objective-level scheduling, leading to more stable and effective distillation. We evaluate SurgPace on Surg-396K, a benchmark built from four public surgical datasets and covering five dialogue paradigms. SurgPace consistently outperforms strong MLLM distillation baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness for building compact, memory-efficient surgical MLLMs with faster decoding under controlled benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/hezhicheng2002/SurgPace.
bullets: Addresses unstable uniform distillation caused by varying surgical sample difficulty, ambiguity, and clinical context.
Uses predictive confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency to create a continuous easy-to-hard curriculum.
Aligns teacher and student at feature, logit, and probability levels while shifting from teacher imitation to task supervision.
Evaluated on Surg-396K across five dialogue paradigms, where it consistently outperforms strong distillation baselines.
Produces memory-efficient models with faster decoding under controlled benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed complexity-aware curriculum framework for progressive distillation. Teacher confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency are fused into a permissive complexity score, which guides continuous curriculum pacing from easy-first sampling to balanced training. This pacing is coupled with progressive objective interpolation and hierarchical representation alignment, jointly establishing a more structured optimization process that enables stable and efficient compression of surgical vision-language models.

Figure 1: Overview of the proposed SurgPace framework. Given surgical multimodal data, a teacher model first estimates sample complexity offline using complementary confidence and geometric consistency signals, which are permissively fused so that lower scores indicate easier samples. The resulting complexity estimates are then used to guide online curriculum training, where easier samples are emphasized earlier and harder samples are gradually incorporated as training progresses. During this process, the student model learns from the teacher through hierarchical representation alignment at the probability, logit, and feature levels, while a progressive objective schedule adjusts the balance of supervision over time. Together, these components enable stable and efficient compression of surgical MLLMs into a lightweight student model with reduced computational demands.

For the same surgical scene, the figure compares ground truth, teacher, and student outputs for single-phrase QA, visual QA, region-based QA, grounding QA, and detailed description. The example shows that the student preserves the main clinical semantics and spatial relationships while remaining compact.

papers.selection_reason: Progressive distillation for compact surgical multimodal LLMs, improving efficiency.
papers.title: SurgPace: Complexity-Aware Progressive Distillation for Surgical Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: SurgPace makes surgical multimodal language models more compact and efficient through complexity-aware, progressive knowledge distillation.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a vital tool in novel view synthesis. 3D Gaussian functions with attributes like color, opacity, and scale are stacked together to explicitly model a radiance field. However, discrete 3D Gaussians usually produce poor depth with few geometry details but lots of floaters, which hinders the effective modeling of smooth radiance fields. To address this issue, we propose to learn a radiance field within a continuous view-dependent color field parameterized by neural networks. With continuous constraints in color, the bias on low-frequency signals of neural networks can highly encourage the geometry modeling to contribute to high-frequency color variations on images, getting rid of solely relying on the color attribute itself. Moreover, we impose a constraint to improve the Lipschitz continuity of the neural color field, making large changes of each Gaussian's color also match with large changes of its position in terms of a ratio. To this end, we additionally introduce novel self-learning strategies to improve the learning of the neural view-dependent color field without any external knowledge or priors, aiming for better generalization on unseen scenes. Our numerical and visual comparisons on widely used benchmarks justify our idea and show better ability of high fidelity geometry recovery in 3DGS. Project page: https://github.com/yangyixi21/Neural-Color-Fields-3DGS.
bullets: Addresses poor depth, limited geometric detail, and floaters caused by discrete 3D Gaussians.
Represents view-dependent color with neural networks to encourage geometry to explain high-frequency image variations.
Adds a Lipschitz-continuity constraint linking large color changes to proportionally large positional changes.
Uses self-learning strategies to improve neural color-field learning and generalization to unseen scenes.
Experiments on widely used benchmarks show improved high-fidelity geometry recovery in 3DGS.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our framework. We first use Gaussian centers to query multi-resolution feature grids to obtain features. Then, together with view directions, we employ an MLP to predict view-dependent colors for each Gaussian. The predicted colors and Gaussian attributes are then rendered by the differentiable rasterizer. We impose self-learned supervision on the neural color field.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward general-purpose robot manipulation. While inference latency can affect task success in a constantly evolving physical world, the relationship between latency and task success rate remains poorly understood. In this paper, we introduce VLALagBench, a comprehensive benchmark for studying VLA inference latency sensitivity across task types, object speeds, execution modes (synchronous and asynchronous), and VLA policies. Using VLALagBench, we find that even a modest inference latency of 100 ms can nearly halve task success on moving targets, with sensitivity varying substantially across tasks and policies. These differences reflect task-specific requirements for precision and continuous motion. By overlapping inference with action execution, asynchronous execution can recover some of the lost success at the cost of more frequent inference requests. Building on these findings, we develop an empirical model that predicts task success from limited calibration data, achieving root-mean-square prediction errors of only 5.7-7.8% across various VLA policies. Given an inference system's latency and per-robot throughput, these predictions guide the selection of system-specific VLA algorithm configurations to maximize task success. We believe VLALagBench and these findings provide a solid foundation for future robotics algorithm-system co-design.
bullets: Benchmarks latency sensitivity across tasks, object speeds, execution modes, and VLA policies.
A 100 ms latency can nearly halve success on moving-target tasks, with effects varying by task and policy.
Latency sensitivity reflects task-specific needs for precision and continuous motion.
Asynchronous execution recovers some success by overlapping inference and action, but requires more frequent inference.
An empirical model predicts task success from limited calibration data with 5.7–7.8% RMSE and supports system-specific configuration selection.

papers.title: VLALagBench: Understanding When and Why VLA Inference Latency Matters
papers.tldr: VLALagBench shows that even small VLA inference delays can sharply reduce robotic manipulation success, while calibration-based modeling and asynchronous execution help mitigate the impact.

papers.abstract: We classify real and complex state-space models (SSMs) with linear transitions, distinguishing fixed-basis diagonal equivalence from input-output equivalence and tracking coefficient-conditioning windows under coordinate changes. We characterize diagonal equivalence through commuting transition families whose members are diagonalizable over the chosen field. With time-shared token-local matrix maps, we identify this class's state-mediated kernels with unnormalized scalar-mode linear attention with multiplicative masks. Mamba 3's multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) construction lifts one value per local interface; SSD-MIMO routes independent values for local retrieval rank above one. HybridMamba combines Mamba 1's per-coordinate decay, Mamba 2-style heads and Mamba 3's complex rotations and two-endpoint writes, mixing real and rotating state blocks with different decay laws. They recover Mamba 1-3 single-input, single-output (SISO) configurations as exact special cases. On five large H100 bfloat16 workloads, our fused GPU kernels improve geometric-mean training time over official Mamba 1/3 in matched SISO recoveries, with Mamba 2 near parity at SSM-core scope. Memory tradeoffs depend on the baseline and metric: saved-for-backward versus peak allocation. In small-model multi-token recall experiments, both designs outperform Mamba 1-3 on the hardest tier; higher routing ranks perform best in gated or phase-diverse configurations. In single-seed language models with about 500M parameters, both improve on Mamba 1/2 in test loss at 2B tokens, but the routing gains do not translate into lower language-model loss. Our best configurations approach Mamba 3 SISO through 10B tokens while remaining behind it and Mamba 3 MIMO in language-model loss.
bullets: Characterizes diagonal equivalence via commuting, jointly diagonalizable transition families, while distinguishing it from input-output equivalence and tracking conditioning under coordinate changes.
Shows that time-shared token-local matrix maps yield state-mediated kernels equivalent to unnormalized scalar-mode linear attention with multiplicative masks.
Introduces SSD-MIMO and HybridMamba to support retrieval rank above one and combine real decays, complex rotations, multiple heads, and two-endpoint writes.
Fused kernels improve training time over matched Mamba 1/3 SISO recoveries; Mamba 2 is near parity at SSM-core scope, with memory effects depending on the measurement.
Higher routing ranks improve small-model multi-token recall, but routing gains do not translate to lower language-model loss; the best models remain behind Mamba 3 variants.

papers.title: Diagonal Equivalence in State Space Models: Characterization, Retrieval Rank, and Selective Extensions

papers.abstract: Among visual localization strategies, scene coordinate regression (SCR) has emerged as an attractive approach for its compactness, accuracy, and speed. Despite these advantages, SCR models generalize poorly across substantially different camera models, such as omnidirectional or strongly rectified imagery. This limitation arises because, changes in field of view, lens distortion, or rectification-induced resampling can make the same scene content appear differently depending on its pixel position, degrading localization accuracy. To cope with this limitation, we introduce Ray-SCR, a lightweight extension to existing SCR architectures that conditions local visual features on their calibrated viewing rays and refines neighboring ray-conditioned features with a shallow local Transformer. We further formulate supervision directly in ray space and use sparse SfM points as metric anchors that link observations across views and camera models. Taken together, these components enable a single scene representation built from a panoramic mapping sequence to accurately localize query images captured with very different cameras, including pinhole, fisheye, and omnidirectional cameras. We evaluate Ray-SCR across multiple SCR architectures and on datasets with pinhole, fisheye, and omnidirectional cameras. The proposed ray conditioning substantially improves generalization across cameras and leads to state-of-the-art localization performance in these challenging cross-camera settings. The project page is available at https://jaeminch0.github.io/ray-scr-generalizing-scene-coordinate-regression-across-camera-models/.
bullets: Addresses poor SCR generalization caused by changes in field of view, lens distortion, and rectification.
Adds ray-conditioned local features and a shallow local Transformer to refine neighboring features.
Uses ray-space supervision and sparse SfM points as metric anchors across views and cameras.
A single panoramic scene representation supports localization from pinhole, fisheye, and omnidirectional queries.
Evaluations across multiple SCR architectures and camera datasets show improved cross-camera generalization and state-of-the-art localization performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Ray-SCR scene-training pipeline.We first extract encoder features from the training images, optionally augmented with sampled virtual views. SfM points are projected into each view, and features whose angular distance θi from the corresponding viewing ray ri is below a predefined threshold are retained in the training buffer. The Ray Adapter then injects camera-geometry information by encoding the associated viewing rays into the features and locally processing groups of neighboring features with a lightweight Transformer. The adapted features are subsequently passed through the standard SCR pipeline. Here, ACE-G is shown as an example, using a DINO encoder together with trainable scene-specific map codes.

Figure 3. Ray Adapter Architecture. Feature tiles sampled from the training buffer are paired viewing rays. Each ray is encoded and used to condition the visual feature through FiLM modulation and an additive ray embedding. The resulting features are then jointly refined within each local tile using a local Transformer before being passed to the SCR prediction head.

papers.abstract: Complex documents such as scientific papers contain rich information in tables, figures, and equations; however, existing deep research (DR) agents typically reduce papers to OCR-extracted text. We instead ask whether vision-language models (VLMs) can enable page-native deep research: directly retrieving and reasoning over rendered document page images. We introduce DR Pixel, the first open-source end-to-end multimodal DR agent that uses rendered page images as its sole retrieval and reasoning unit, operating over a corpus of 1.06M pages. To evaluate this setting, we construct DRPixelBench, a benchmark on scientific papers requiring reasoning over text, figures, tables, and equations. Surprisingly, page-native DR already works well without training, outperforming OCR-based baselines across state-of-the-art models like GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Qwen3.6-27B, while requiring fewer tool calls. We next turn to DR training. A key challenge is that teacher trajectories for agentic supervised finetuning are noisy, mixing critical reasoning and action steps with redundant or failed attempts. To address this, we introduce counterfactual credit reweighting, a fine-grained credit assignment method that weights individual reasoning and action steps by their counterfactual contribution to the final answer. Our training improves retrieval recall by about 15 points and final accuracy by over 10 points on DRPixelBench, and likewise outperforms the untrained baseline on four existing benchmarks. On out-of-distribution ViDoRe-V3, DR Pixel comes within 1.8 points of an oracle that is given the gold pages directly. Our results suggest that the conventional OCR-then-retrieve pipeline is not only unnecessary but suboptimal: directly retrieving and reasoning over visual document pages makes complex DR both more effective and more efficient.
bullets: Targets the loss of information from OCR-only processing of figures, tables, equations, and layout.
Introduces an open-source multimodal agent that uses rendered page images as its sole retrieval and reasoning unit over 1.06M pages.
Introduces DRPixelBench, a scientific-paper benchmark requiring multimodal document reasoning.
Counterfactual credit reweighting improves retrieval recall by about 15 points and final accuracy by over 10 points.
On out-of-distribution ViDoRe-V3, the system comes within 1.8 points of an oracle with gold pages; scope is centered on complex scientific documents.

papers.abstract: Theoretical limitations of transformers on state tracking---the ability to track information about entities or variables over long contexts---have motivated new recurrent language modeling (LM) architectures such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN). These architectures have, in particular, been benchmarked against the $S_5$ word problem, a theoretically hard state-tracking task that captures abilities such as code evaluation under arbitrary variable assignment. It, however, remains open whether other, simpler forms of state tracking might both be more relevant in practice and already explain observed differences between these architectures. We propose evaluating state tracking using a hierarchy of word problems with four increasing levels of difficulty: r-trivial, corresponding to immutable assignment to variables in programming; aperiodic, where assignments are mutable; soluble, where assignments are self-referential; and general finite state tracking. Theoretically, we show that the class of problems transformers are thought to length-generalize on does not even contain all aperiodic state tracking. On the other hand, we prove that GDN with positive eigenvalues expresses all aperiodic problems, and the regular languages recognized by certain transformers are precisely all soluble ones, thus providing a fine-grained picture of state tracking capabilities of various architectures. Taking these ideas to practice, we construct StateBench, a 4-tier long-horizon state-tracking benchmark. Our systematic direct training experiments across architectures largely align with theoretical expectation, albeit with interesting observations at very large scale length-generalization. Additionally, we also evaluate pretrained models---both open hybrid and closed frontier ones---on StateBench, finding that none of them robustly solves even soluble state tracking, suggesting a direction for future improvement.
bullets: State tracking is organized into r-trivial, aperiodic, soluble, and general finite-state problems of increasing difficulty.
Theoretical results show transformers may fail on some aperiodic tracking, while Gated DeltaNet can express all aperiodic problems; certain transformers correspond precisely to soluble problems.
StateBench provides a four-tier, long-horizon benchmark for systematic evaluation across architectures.
Direct training results broadly match theory, but pretrained open and closed models do not robustly solve even soluble state-tracking tasks.
Very large context lengths reveal additional, notable deviations from expected length-generalization behavior.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Placement of various language model architectures within the hierarchy of state-tracking (monoid word problem) complexity, along with examples of the kinds of tasks that fall into these categories. The two log-precision architectures extend into TC0. Dashed lines represent conjectured strict boundaries between classes.

papers.abstract: KlaskTron is an open-hardware physical platform for two-player adversarial reinforcement learning, with a learned actuator model that supports zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of trained policies. Building on this platform, we contribute KlaskTron-IL: a multi-tier imitation learning dataset (80k human demonstration timesteps collected directly on the physical robot, 320k symmetry-augmented timesteps, and synthetic expert trajectories up to 5M steps generated by the zero-shot-validated PPO policy), and diagnostic baselines that expose three characteristic failure modes of standard IL methods under contact-rich adversarial dynamics: BC's data scaling plateau, GAIL's interpretable but weak-gradient discriminator (Spearman $ρ= -1.0$ peg-ball proximity recovery, but a logit span under 0.1), and an asymmetric BC-prior x reward-density interaction. Because the policy interface used throughout this paper is the same one the actuator model bridges to hardware, a policy trained on this benchmark can run unchanged on the physical robot, as we demonstrate zero-shot for the strongest BC baseline, so long as its commands respect the actuator model's $\pm 0.2$ m/s identification range.
bullets: Uses 80k human demonstration timesteps from the physical robot, 320k symmetry-augmented timesteps, and up to 5M synthetic expert timesteps.
Benchmarks standard IL methods in two-player adversarial dynamics and identifies BC scaling plateaus, weak GAIL gradients, and asymmetric BC-prior/reward-density interactions.
GAIL’s discriminator provides interpretable peg-ball proximity recovery but produces weak logits.
The strongest BC baseline transfers zero-shot to the physical robot without policy changes.
Transfer is scoped to commands within the actuator model’s ±0.2 m/s identification range.

figures.caption: Figure 1: KlaskTron-IL system architecture. Dashed blocks are inherited from the platform [7]. Solid blocks are contributions of this paper. Demonstrations come from two sources: the inherited PPO expert acting in simulation (Tier 3, Section 4) and human play recorded on the physical robot (Tiers 1–2). BC learns offline from demonstrations alone, GAIL and BC+RL additionally optimize against the environment (Section 5).

Figure 4: Discriminator probing. Top: logit vs. peg–ball distance (Spearman ρ=−1.0). Bottom: data coverage. The perfect rank ordering confirms feature discovery; the narrow logit range is consistent with the weak reward signal under this configuration.
Figure 2: Peg occupancy: BC rollout (left) vs. human demonstrations (right). The BC policy occupies wall regions; expert demonstrations do not.

papers.abstract: While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has significantly advanced multimodal reasoning, existing frameworks suffer from a critical "perception-reasoning gap." Due to an over-reliance on seemingly relevant visual tokens, even minor perceptual perturbations can propagate through the reasoning process, leading to compounding hallucinations. To address this issue, we propose MIRA, a training framework that improves robustness to erroneous visual contexts while enhancing logical reasoning ability. By injecting filtered, deceptive visual contexts during training, we construct challenging "hard traps" that stress-test the model's robustness to misleading information. Furthermore, we introduce a group-wise reflection-triggering mechanism that enables the model to autonomously detect and rectify inconsistencies between visual cues and logical constraints, which is ultimately internalized as an intrinsic policy behavior. Importantly, MIRA does not rely on human annotations. Experimental results across multiple reasoning and perception benchmarks show that MIRA yields an average 7% improvement on in-domain benchmarks, with consistent improvements on vision-centric benchmarks. These findings highlight that active error recovery is essential for robust multimodal reasoning. Comprehensive ablation studies and analyses further provide insights into why MIRA is effective.
bullets: Addresses the perception–reasoning gap, where small visual errors can trigger compounding hallucinations.
Injects filtered deceptive visual contexts to create challenging “hard traps” during training.
Uses group-wise reflection triggers to help models identify and correct conflicts between visual evidence and logical constraints.
Reports an average 7% improvement across in-domain benchmarks, with consistent gains on vision-centric benchmarks.
Ablations and analyses support the importance of active error recovery for robust multimodal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Real-world driving requires context-aware decision-making. Existing end-to-end driving benchmarks primarily assess trajectory quality through safety, compliance, comfort, and driving progress, leaving context-dependent decision-making insufficiently characterized. To fill this gap, we present PlanContext, a benchmark for evaluating in-context driving decision-making. PlanContext constructs paired evaluations by varying high-level driving intentions while keeping the observed scene fixed, enabling a natural and controllable assessment of context-dependent decision-making. We further define six representative driving contexts and jointly evaluate contextual decision correctness, road compliance, and dynamic safety with class-balanced metrics. Experiments on 9,561 scene-condition instances from NAVSIM and 23 public end-to-end driving models show that high conventional driving-quality scores do not consistently correspond to strong route-level in-context driving decision-making. Further analysis shows that model behavior varies with decision timing, road structure, and traffic interaction depending on the decision required by the current context. Our results highlight in-context driving decision-making as an important complementary dimension for evaluating end-to-end driving systems.
bullets: Pairs evaluations with different high-level driving intentions while keeping the observed scene fixed.
Defines six representative driving contexts and measures decision correctness, road compliance, and dynamic safety.
Evaluates 9,561 scene-condition instances from NAVSIM across 23 public end-to-end driving models.
Finds behavior varies with decision timing, road structure, and traffic interaction.
Positions in-context driving decision-making as a complementary evaluation dimension for end-to-end driving systems.

papers.abstract: Complex video editing requires understanding complex instructions while jointly fulfilling multiple editing requests. Meeting these demands through dense model scaling substantially increases computational cost. We introduce VideoEditor-MoE, the first open-source mixture-of-experts framework for video editing. Beyond sparse MLP-MoE layers, MoE-Attention expands attention capacity through routed key--value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens. Initialized from a 5B video editing model, VideoEditor-MoE scales to 14B and 56B parameters, with approximately 8B parameters activated per token in both variants. Comparisons with existing methods and two complementary baselines, Explicit-MoE and MLP-MoE, assess its benefits over explicit expert guidance and MLP-only expert architectures. Further analyses demonstrate that all experts remain active and reveal that learned routing responds more strongly to sample content and diffusion noise levels than to human-defined editing categories. Spatial analysis further indicates sensitivity to object-level semantic features. We also identify decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling.
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of dense scaling for complex, multi-request video editing.
Introduces MoE-Attention, which routes key–value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens.
Scales from a 5B initialization to 14B and 56B parameters, activating approximately 8B parameters per token in both variants.
Analysis finds routing responds more to sample content and diffusion noise levels than to human-defined editing categories, with sensitivity to object-level semantics.
Identifies decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling; evaluations compare against existing methods and complementary MoE baselines.

papers.abstract: Multimodal fusion is studied under hybrid federation, where data are partitioned across samples and feature blocks. The proposed two-dimensional federated smooth multiple-kernel large-margin learning method (2D-FedSMKL) integrates availability-corrected modality scores, group-kernel regularization, and smooth worst-site risk aggregation. For fixed maps and propensities, the objective is convex and smooth. Curvature bounds and exact synchronous block-gradient equivalence are established for binary and multiclass scores, giving a conditional accelerated rate. An oracle-propensity binary risk bound and a propensity-perturbation result are also derived. Simulations and two public activity-recognition benchmarks assess site heterogeneity and modality absence. Worst-site aggregation improves worst-site performance under heterogeneity, including reversed and size-balanced designs. On the benchmarks, validation selects the correction; the selected model is not significantly worse than the strongest reference at the worst site, and group-regularization benefits vary by dataset.
bullets: Addresses hybrid federation where data are split across samples and feature modalities, with modality absence and site heterogeneity.
Combines availability-corrected modality scores, group-kernel regularization, and smooth worst-site risk aggregation.
Establishes convexity and smoothness under fixed maps and propensities, plus curvature, optimization-rate, and risk-bound results.
Worst-site aggregation improves performance under heterogeneous and reversed or size-balanced site designs.
On two activity-recognition benchmarks, the selected correction is not significantly worse than the strongest reference at the worst site; regularization effects vary by dataset.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustrative sample and modality partitions in hybrid federated fusion. Sites group distinct patient records vertically; independently held modality blocks form the horizontal partition. Original device icons depict baseline records, ECG monitoring and wrist/ankle inertial sensors (IMUs). Check marks indicate observed blocks and crosses indicate record-level absence; the baseline remains observed. IDs, devices and availability patterns are schematic, not clinical study data. Computational row groups need not coincide with statistical sites. Raw feature blocks remain with their custodians. 2D-Fed denotes 2D-FedSMKL.

Figure 2: Availability-corrected additive fusion for one sample. Observed modalities are inverse-probability weighted, whereas an absent block contributes zero rather than an imputed signal. Under the stated missing-at-random assumption and with the true observation propensities, the correction recovers each full-data linear score contribution in expectation. Estimated propensities are clipped to limit instability, which can introduce bias.

Figure 4: Compact simulation trends for the three incomplete-sample fusion methods. The legend label 2D-Fed denotes the proposed 2D-FedSMKL method. Left: the robust objective separates from mean-risk alternatives as site heterogeneity increases. Right: the methods remain close at moderate modality absence, with only modest separation at severe absence. Error bars show standard deviations across matched replicates.

Figure 3: Smooth worst-site aggregation. Log-sum-exp provides a differentiable approximation to the largest site risk, and its gradient gives the adaptive weight qs. Decreasing ρ approaches worst-site training; increasing ρ approaches π-weighted mean-risk training.

Figure 5: Paired component effects in the secondary factorial study under controlled MAR block absence. Panels correspond to MHEALTH and UCI HAR at 35% and 65% target absence. Points are paired mean differences in worst-site macro-F1 and horizontal bars are unadjusted 95% paired t intervals over 20 matched masks. Positive values favor the first-listed component: robust minus mean aggregation, conditional on IPW or zero filling; and IPW minus zero filling, conditional on mean or robust aggregation. papers.abstract: Cloth-changing person re-identification (CC-ReID) is still very challenging, and no method clearly dominates: methods that lead on one benchmark collapse on the others, because they rest on different identity cues. We show that a general-purpose vision-language model (VLM), used zero-shot as a judge for reranking a short candidate list, beats the expert retrieval models it reranks by a wide and consistent margin. On the four scenarios of CHIRLA, a long-term CC-ReID benchmark that no publicly released Re-ID model is trained on, reranking the candidates of two frozen experts raises rank-1 on every scenario, by 12.9 points on average over the best expert and 9.4 over the best naive ensemble of the two, with no component fine-tuned on the target data. Merging both experts' shortlists matches or beats reranking the stronger expert's shortlist alone, at lower cost. Introducing a VLM does, however, come at a cost: almost all of the pipeline's FLOPs are spent on it. We therefore borrow a criterion from ensembling and invoke the VLM judge only where the two experts disagree at rank 1. This threshold-free gate removes 40% of the calls, and a comparable share of total compute, with no significant drop in rank-1, trading 1.8 to 3.8 points of mAP. Judging remains the dominant cost, but on a benchmark where dedicated experts stall, we find a frozen general-purpose model to be the strongest judge of identity. The code is available at https://github.com/bdager/JudgeReID.
bullets: CC-ReID remains difficult because existing methods rely on different identity cues and do not generalize consistently across benchmarks.
The method uses a VLM as a zero-shot judge to rerank short candidate lists from two frozen expert retrieval models.
On all four CHIRLA scenarios, reranking improves rank-1 by an average of 12.9 points over the best expert and 9.4 over their naive ensemble, without target-data fine-tuning.
Merging both experts’ shortlists matches or exceeds reranking the stronger expert alone at lower cost.
Calling the VLM only when experts disagree at rank 1 removes 40% of calls with no significant rank-1 loss, though mAP drops by 1.8–3.8 points; VLM judging remains the main computational cost.

papers.abstract: Misleading charts can lead vision-language models to conclusions that conflict with underlying data. Existing work focuses on inference-time strategies, while training-time supervision remains less explored. We present VizDAGuide, a DAG-structured supervision method for misleading-chart question answering. The method represents intermediate reasoning states and their dependencies as a directed acyclic graph, assigns supervision weights according to their roles, and serializes the graph into a unified training target for open-ended and multiple-choice QA with single-pass inference. Experiments on two benchmarks across Qwen3-VL and InternVL3.5 models show improvements over a content- and weight-matched Linear CoT-SFT baseline on both answer formats. Process-level evaluation shows gains in grounding and operation execution, while ablations indicate that dependency structure and weighted supervision are most effective when combined. These results support DAG-structured weighted supervision for misleading-chart question answering.
bullets: Targets chart questions where visual presentation can conflict with the underlying data.
Represents intermediate reasoning states and dependencies as a directed acyclic graph.
Serializes weighted graph supervision into one training target for open-ended and multiple-choice QA with single-pass inference.
Improves answer performance over a matched Linear CoT-SFT baseline across two benchmarks and Qwen3-VL and InternVL3.5 models.
Process-level gains occur in grounding and operation execution; dependency structure and weighting work best together.

papers.abstract: Two machines can each recognize an object well and still fail together. We study classifiers that see different parts of one object and send short messages to a receiver that identifies its class. Coordination asks how to design messages together; cooperation asks whether the team outperforms one sender given the whole budget. On three digit datasets, messages designed together beat messages designed apart by 18.07 to 22.68 percentage points on average with two-bit messages, with gains in all 24 configurations. A fixed agreement, you report the row and I the column, recovers about half this gain, with only the receiver learned. Senders that draw the same distinctions waste a narrow vocabulary, and senders whose distinctions cross multiply it. A team has no more possible messages than one sender with the same budget, so a partner must bring evidence the first lacks. A solvable model shows individual statistics alone cannot determine whether a partnership helps. On MNIST digits, six shared bits remove 49.54 percent of the strongest tested solo's errors on average. Paired measurements correctly predicted most sensor teams would reduce average accuracy on new participants. Who should speak is a property of the pair, and must be measured in pairs.
bullets: The study examines classifiers that observe different parts of an object and send short messages to a receiver.
Jointly designed messages outperform separately designed ones by 18.07–22.68 percentage points across 24 two-bit configurations on three digit datasets.
A fixed row/column communication scheme recovers about half the coordination gain while learning only the receiver.
Senders should make complementary distinctions: overlapping distinctions waste limited message capacity, while cross-cutting distinctions expand useful information.
Pairwise measurements predicted that most tested sensor teams would improve average accuracy on new participants.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a decentralized guiding vector field framework for rigid formation path following in multi- UAV systems based on the superposition of simple rule-driven vector fields. Each control objective is encoded as a dedicated vector-field component: a normalized tangential term to ensure progression along a prescribed geometric path at a desired speed, a convergence term driving the formation toward the path, a local coordination term that preserves the desired formation shape through a pseudo-path parameter, and a local separation term for inter-agent collision avoidance. The coordination mechanism requires the exchange of only a single scalar per agent, resulting in low communication bandwidth. Partial theoretical results establish convergence of the swarm to the desired path and formation in the absence of the sepa- ration term, while collision avoidance is formally guaranteed. The approach is experimentally validated using a swarm of five quadrotors executing two 3D choreographies. The first experiment involves tracking a helical path while maintaining a rigid V-shaped formation. The second demonstrates a spiral- like motion obtained by a rotating circular formation tracking a vertical line. The experimental results support the effectiveness and practical applicability of the proposed framework.
bullets: Combines tangential, path-convergence, formation-coordination, and inter-agent-separation vector fields.
Each agent exchanges only one scalar, reducing communication requirements.
Provides partial convergence guarantees for path and formation tracking without the separation term, while collision avoidance is formally guaranteed.
Validated with five quadrotors on helical and spiral-like 3D choreographies.
Experiments support the framework’s practical effectiveness for rigid formation path following.

papers.abstract: With the popularization of livestreaming applications, automatic camera tuning has become indispensable for ordinary users to enjoy high Quality of Experience (QoE). However, the existing Image Quality Assessment (IQA) methods face two challenges in camera tuning. First, they struggle to identify subtle quality difference between images, which is common in camera tuning. Second, the ability to explain fine-grained differences and to provide suggestions for camera tuning are even more lacking. To address these challenges, we first construct FGLive-Comments, an instruction tuning dataset with rich annotations of both preferences for fine-grained image pairs and quality reasoning from global and local visual evidence, which supports selective adjustment recommendations of camera parameters. Based on FGLive-Comments, we develop Q-CamTuning, a multimodal large language model for livestreaming camera tuning. Its progressive perception-evidence-guidance framework learns quality-aware visual representations, enhances fine-grained reasoning with global-local evidence, and maps quality issues to camera-parameter adjustment directions. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that Q-CamTuning outperforms existing IQA models in both quality scoring and fine-grained image pair ranking. User study also validates its ability to recommend camera tuning suggestions.
bullets: Addresses IQA limitations in distinguishing fine-grained quality differences and generating actionable tuning guidance.
Introduces FGLive-Comments, an instruction-tuning dataset with pairwise preferences, global-local quality reasoning, and adjustment recommendations.
Uses a progressive perception-evidence-guidance framework to connect visual quality issues with camera-parameter directions.
Outperforms existing IQA models in quality scoring and fine-grained image-pair ranking.
A user study supports its ability to provide useful camera-tuning suggestions.

papers.abstract: Markerless hand-eye calibration under continuous motion requires jointly resolving camera geometry and the time offset between images and joint states. We present SyncHeC (Synchronized Hand-Eye Calibration), a dense differentiable-rendering framework that estimates both from a single robot trajectory. Continuous-time forward kinematics makes latency differentiable, metric depth complements mask contours, and an offline planner combines spatial sensitivity with temporal excitation. Alternating updates support Eye-to-Hand, Eye-in-Hand, and multi-camera calibration. On a 7-DoF arm, one $6.5$\,s motion yields $0.21$\,cm translation error against a marker-board reference, $0.34$\,cm touch-test error, and $2.7$\,ms latency error relative to an $87$\,ms reference with $95\%$ uncertainty of $\pm1.5$\,ms. Against CM-Calib on matched recordings, translation and nominal latency errors improve by $3.7\times$ and $2.3\times$. Experiments span seven arms and four depth sensors. Compensating the recovered offset during policy training and deployment increases success by $8.1$ percentage points across six families and six tasks ($1{,}800$ matched pairs; paired $95\%$ confidence interval $[6.3,9.9]$ points).
bullets: Addresses markerless hand-eye calibration when camera observations and joint states have an unknown time offset.
Uses dense differentiable rendering, continuous-time forward kinematics, metric depth, and an excitation-aware motion planner.
Supports Eye-to-Hand, Eye-in-Hand, and multi-camera calibration through alternating optimization.
On a 7-DoF arm, one 6.5-second motion achieved 0.21 cm translation error, 0.34 cm touch-test error, and 2.7 ms latency error.
Validated across seven arms and four depth sensors; offset compensation improved policy success by 8.1 percentage points across six tasks.

papers.abstract: Autonomous robots are gaining traction in off-road environments, driven by their rising demand in agriculture, defense, and search-and-rescue operations. However, these environments are inherently unpredictable and navigation remains a formidable challenge given the complex environmental conditions including challenging terrain and varying illumination. Off-road autonomy requires robust perception across multiple spatial scales and imaging modalities, yet most sensing setups struggle to capture both far-field environmental context and near-field terrain detail simultaneously across various illumination conditions. To facilitate development of robust off-road perception and traversability estimation systems, we propose MS-DOTT (Multi-Sensor Dataset for Off-road Terrain Traversability) a comprehensive multi-modal off-road dataset with long-range 3D sensing and short-range, fine-grained perception to facilitate high-fidelity terrain understanding by combining proprioceptive signals for tracking vehicle dynamics with exteroceptive imaging and pointcloud data. The dataset includes trajectories recorded across nominal lighting, low-light, and no-light conditions with diverse 2D and 3D sensing for both long-range large-scale and short-range high-resolution sensing, as well as 4D RADAR measurements that provide velocity estimates for detected pointclouds. We demonstrate the utility of the dataset by adapting a SOTA multi-sensor fusion method for the purpose of traversability estimation. This dataset will aid the robotics community in advancing research and development of methods for traversability estimation, off-road perception and multi-sensor fusion in unstructured environments.
bullets: Targets the challenges of off-road autonomy, including complex terrain, unpredictable environments, and changing illumination.
Combines long-range 3D sensing with short-range, fine-grained 2D/3D perception for multi-scale terrain understanding.
Includes proprioceptive vehicle-dynamics signals, exteroceptive images and point clouds, and 4D RADAR with pointwise velocity estimates.
Covers nominal-light, low-light, and no-light trajectories using diverse sensing modalities.
Demonstrates the dataset’s utility by adapting a state-of-the-art multi-sensor fusion method for traversability estimation.

papers.abstract: Contact transitions allow humanoid robots to redistribute object support across the whole body, enabling manipulation beyond hand-only grasps. Human videos provide a scalable source of such transitions for robots to learn from. However, body occlusion disrupts object pose tracking and corrupts retargeted motion. Moreover, accurately reproducing the object trajectory does not ensure that the robot applies stabilizing forces at the intended contacts, risking slips or drops in later phases. To address these challenges, we propose ReContact, which reconstructs and retargets human-object interactions through an object-centric contact plan. The plan specifies contact phases, contact pairs, anchors, pressing directions, and sticking or sliding modes. Contact priors stabilize object pose reconstruction through occlusion. A residual policy over a frozen whole-body tracker is rewarded for making contact at planned anchors with forces aligned to the specified directions. In simulation, on a thigh-supported regrasp task, ReContact achieves the planned two-palm bottom hold in 83.5 of episodes over three training seeds, versus 0.16% for the best adapted baseline. One policy trained on 247 references re-solved for new placements raises in-workspace tube-transfer success from 20.4% (source reference only) to 97.8%. On a real Unitree G1, policies execute seven contact-rich manipulation and two loco-manipulation tasks.
bullets: Addresses occlusion-corrupted object tracking and the gap between matching object motion and applying stabilizing contact forces.
Uses an object-centric contact plan with phases, contact pairs, anchors, pressing directions, and sticking/sliding modes.
Stabilizes pose reconstruction with contact priors and adds a residual policy over a frozen whole-body tracker to achieve planned contacts and force directions.
In simulation, the method achieves the planned two-palm bottom hold in 83.5% of episodes versus 0.16% for the best adapted baseline.
A policy trained on 247 references generalizes to new placements, increasing tube-transfer success from 20.4% to 97.8%; real-robot tests cover seven manipulation and two loco-manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Block-scaled lookup-table (LUT) formats, which represent weights as indices into a small value set (the grid), have become standard for low-bit LLM quantization, ranging from NF4 and BOF4 to the 3-bit LUT instruction in NVIDIA Rubin. While these formats leave the grid definition flexible, existing implementations rely on fixed grids derived either from numerical data types (INT, FP) or assumed weight distributions (NF, BOF). We demonstrate that no single fixed grid is universally optimal; the best fixed grid varies with bit-width: BOFS at 2 bits, NF at 4 and 5 bits, and INT at 6 bits. We introduce SHq, a closed-form family of grids parameterized by two critical degrees of freedom: a companding strength α that interpolates level spacing from uniform to floating-point-like, and an offset c that introduces asymmetry. This offset allows the sign bit of the FP8 block scale, otherwise unused, to select between the grid and its mirror image, up to doubling the number of distinct values available per block. SHq modifies only the lookup table contents and serves as a drop-in replacement for the grid in any such format. Across five models ranging from 3B to 35B parameters, including a mixture-of-experts architecture, evaluated at 2-6 bits using RTN and GPTQ, SHq achieves the lowest KL divergence in every setting at 3 and 4 bits and in most settings at 2, 5 and 6 bits. It outperforms the best fixed grid by up to 34% and remains superior under mixed-precision configurations. At 4.5 bits per weight, the SHq format reduces the KL divergence of NVFP4 by 41-67% while improving downstream accuracy. Grid families incorporating both spacing and offset parameters perform comparably, whereas those lacking an offset exhibit clearly higher error, confirming that these two degrees of freedom drive the observed gains. We therefore propose SHq as the standard grid for block-scaled lookup-table formats.
bullets: Fixed grids are not universally optimal: the best choice varies with bit-width.
SHq uses companding strength α and offset c to control spacing and asymmetry; the offset can exploit the FP8 scale sign to select mirrored grids.
It is a drop-in replacement for lookup-table grids in block-scaled formats and supports 2–6-bit quantization with RTN or GPTQ.
Across five 3B–35B models, SHq achieves the lowest KL divergence in all tested 3- and 4-bit settings and most other settings.
SHq improves KL divergence by up to 34% over the best fixed grid and reduces NVFP4 divergence by 41–67% at 4.5 bits while improving downstream accuracy.
