papers.abstract: Pose-driven human video diffusion animates a person from a single reference image and a target pose sequence, yet it struggles to preserve identity, rendering the face and garments unfaithfully as the pose departs from it. Personalization is the standard remedy, but its supervision is missing: one image fixes identity at a single pose, while a multi-pose subject video cannot be assumed in practice. Instead, we synthesize the missing supervision. A domain-tuned, pose-conditioned generator produces pseudo-ground-truth frames at selected key poses. An inference-time reference-only sampler steers these candidates toward the subject and keeps the most identity-consistent. A per-subject low-rank adapter then trains on static clips of them, configured from the reference alone, with no subject video, ground truth, or labels. Although lower in fidelity, these synthetic frames supervise more effectively than real ones. Real frames as captured carry motion that erodes the temporal prior, while a static clip conveys appearance alone. On TikTok and UBC Fashion, the adapted model improves the base on every metric, inverts the identity-versus-motion trade-off, and matches or surpasses adaptation on five real frames despite using none. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/SadmanPinon/one-image-is-enough.
bullets: Addresses identity drift in faces and garments when the target pose differs substantially from a single reference image.
Generates pseudo-ground-truth frames at key poses, filters them with a reference-only sampler, and trains a per-subject low-rank adapter on static clips.
Requires only one reference image—no subject video, ground-truth frames, or labels.
On TikTok and UBC Fashion, improves the base model on every reported metric and matches or surpasses adaptation using five real frames.
Synthetic static clips can supervise more effectively than real motion videos because they preserve appearance without disrupting temporal priors.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. From one reference image xref and a driving pose sequence P , a pose-conditioned generator G synthesizes pose-targeted pseudo-ground-truth frames Dpseudo of the subject. (a) Reward-guided generation: for each key pose, G draws several candidates as an interacting particle system and resamples them in-loop toward a DINO body-similarity reward to xref , then selects the final frame by ArcFace face identity. Every reward is read from the reference alone (our reference-only reward-guided sampler). (b) Test-time personalization: a per-subject LoRA ∆θ adapts the frozen base animator Fθ on static clips of the selected frames. The adapted model Fθ+∆θ renders the personalized video V̂ . No subject video, no ground truth, and no human feedback are used.

Figure 3. Temporal stability. Top: the driving frames. For Base (middle) and Ours (bottom), the leftmost column is that method’s output frame and the remaining columns are consecutive framedifference maps over the same frames. The non-personalized base produces widespread inter-frame residual across the face and torso (temporal flicker), whereas our adapted model confines residual to true motion boundaries and stays stable, reducing mean interframe residual by 60% over the frames shown. Brighter indicates larger frame-to-frame change.

Figure 7. Human preference study. Distribution of 1–5 ratings for ours, Animate-X, the unadapted base, and Moore-AnimateAnyone, on four axes. Thirty-four respondents, 180 ratings per bar group. Ours places 93% of appearance-alignment ratings at 4–5, against 38% for the base model; the ordering is the same on all four axes. Protocol in Appendix B.2.

Figure 8. In-Domain Comparisons: Diverse Motions and Backgrounds. Examples illustrating variations in background, motion complexity, and clothing style. Our approach consistently preserves holistic appearance and pose alignment while producing sharper, more realistic details than competing methods.

Figure 9. In-Domain Comparisons: Diverse Appearance and Illumination. Examples covering variations in skin tone, lighting conditions, and clothing texture. Our approach maintains consistent subject appearance and realistic fine-grained details across all scenarios, clearly outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

Figure 6. Pose-conditioned generator G. G is built on FLUX.1 Kontext [21] paired with a pose ControlNet [57]. The target pose is VAE-encoded and read by a frozen ControlNet (14 joint blocks, 38 unified blocks), whose pose-aware features condition the main DiT. The reference image and initial noise are encoded and denoised by the main DiT, into which we inject the trainable LoRA [13]; a text encoder supplies the prompt. The output latent is VAE-decoded to the subject rendered under the target pose. Backbone weights are frozen (snowflake); only the LoRA adapters are trained (flame).

Figure 5. Pseudo-frame count and supervision source. (a) FVD (orange) is lowest at K=5; FaceID (teal) dips at K=9 and peaks at K=21 at a similar FVD (values from Tab. 6). (b) Seven-metric comparison of supervision sources (outward = better, per-axis min–max over the rows of Tab. 5): Ours forms nearly the outer envelope, while self-distillation collapses on body similarity and temporal consistency.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on hard poses. For two subjects we show the reference and driving pose alongside the base, our adapted model, and ground truth. Insets crop the face. The base reconstructs identity and garment detail inconsistently as the pose departs from the reference, while our adaptation preserves both.

Figure 10. Cross-Domain Comparisons: Animated Characters. Examples from the Unseen100-Val evaluation set featuring 2D and 3D animated characters unseen during training. Our approach generalizes beyond photorealistic subjects, faithfully preserving stylized appearance details and character proportions while maintaining temporal coherence under complex motion.

Figure 11. Adaptation is bounded by pseudo-frame quality. Top (HQ): high-quality pseudo frames (Supervision) yield faithful adapted outputs (Output frames). Bottom (LQ): degraded pseudo frames for the same subject yield weaker outputs. This is why the reference-only sampler selects high-quality frames before adaptation.

Table 12. Sensitivity to the generator’s domain tuning. G’s LoRA receives from no tuning (off-the-shelf FLUX.1 Kontext with the pose ControlNet) to our default of 4,000 steps, with the rest of the pipeline fixed. Teacher is the fidelity of the selected pseudo-frame to the real frame at that pose, and downstream is the adapted model’s video quality (trim, 3 TikTok sequences).

Table 2. Quantitative comparison on cross-domain performance on the Unseen100-Val set after training on TikTok. Off the training distribution, our adaptation reaches the only FVD below 100 (92.5) and the lowest dtSSD, while every other method stays above 125.

Table 4. Component ablation. Each designed component is removed and compared against real-frame supervision (Real-5) and the unadapted base. FaceID and BodySIM are over the full video. Generator G is a per-frame reference with no temporal model, so it lacks FVD/dtSSD and is not ranked.

Table 17. Per-stage test-time cost, single H100 80 GB, 832×480, one TikTok subject, with 81-frame inference. Time is generation only for the inference rows and wall-clock elsewhere. Peak GPU is the maximum resident device memory during the stage, and Alloc. the torch allocator peak where the pipeline reports it (protocol in Appendix F.1).

Table 8. Test-time cost per reference image on a single H100 (TikTok, 81-frame inference, adaptation at 832×480, generation at 576×1024). The one-time peak is the maximum over the two stages, not their sum. Of it, 43.6 GiB is the frozen base and 9.2 GiB our update (Tab. 18). Inference costs what the base costs, as the merged adapter adds no parameters. Protocol in App. F.
Table 7. Reward-design ablation (on a tuning subset). The two reference-only rewards assigned to in-loop steering versus final selection. Steering with DINO and selecting with ArcFace is best.

Table 6. Number of pseudo frames K. We sweep the number of self-generated supervision frames used for per-subject adaptation. FaceID and BodySIM are over the full video; K=5 is the best balanced configuration.

Table 11. Per-subject LoRA rank r (on a tuning subset). Adaptation quality as the rank of the per-subject update varies. Quality improves with capacity up to r=128, our default; beyond it (r=256) the adapter over-fits the few pseudo-frames and quality regresses, marking a clear optimum. Absolute scores differ from the main tables because this sweep runs on a tuning subset.

Table 5. Supervision source. All rows share the adaptation recipe; only the supervision source changes. FaceID and BodySIM are over the full video, on the TikTok dataset. The standalone quality of G appears in Tab. 4.

Table 3. Cross-reenactment (Unseen100-Val). Each subject is driven by a different subject’s motion, so no aligned ground truth exists; we measure identity against the reference (FaceID, BodySIM) and pose obedience against the driving sequence (PoseAcc). Adaptation raises appearance fidelity while leaving pose obedience essentially unchanged, as the pose-conditioning pathway is frozen.

Table 18. Composition of the adaptation memory peak. Resident sizes follow from each checkpoint’s parameter count and load precision: bf16 for the frozen modules, and fp32 with gradients and two AdamW moments for the low-rank update. The final line is the measured peak minus the resident modules above it.

Table 10. Quality versus fine-tuning time. Per-subject adaptation quality at different numbers of fine-tuning steps and the time they take on a single H100 (K=5, TikTok). Quality saturates within the first five steps, our default. Longer budgets improve only identity, and not monotonically.

Table 14. Resampling schedule. Selected pseudo-ground-truth frame fidelity to the real frame as a function of the denoising window over which particles are resampled and the churn strength η that re-noises duplicated particles (N=8; mean over the K supervised poses × 3 sequences). Pseudo-ground-truth frame quality is largely insensitive to the schedule; the back-half-with-churn default is used for its downstream stability.

Table 13. Particle count N . Selected pseudo-ground-truth frame fidelity to the real frame (mean over the K supervised poses × 3 sequences) and per-pseudo-frame generation time, as the number of reward-guided particles varies. Frame quality is largely saturated already by our default N=8, while sampling time grows roughly linearly, so larger populations cost compute without further gain. Time is the per-pseudo-frame sampling cost on a single H100.

Table 16. Composition of the Unseen100-Val dataset. Each attribute group independently covers all 100 videos; rows within a group sum to 100 (or to 80 for appearance and setting, which apply only to the real-human videos).

Table 9. Identity measured by recognizers not used by the pipeline. Pseudo-frames are selected with ArcFace, so identity is re-scored with FaceNet512 and SFace, which are not used in selection. Faces are detected once and every recognizer embeds the identical crop. A frame is scored only when a face is found in the ground truth and in both arms (33 pairs for base vs ours, 30 for the three-arm comparison, trim regime, 3 TikTok sequences). Ours-FN selects with FaceNet512 instead of ArcFace.

Table 15. Key-pose selection. How the K supervised poses are chosen from the driving sequence, at fixed K: farthest-point sampling in keypoint space (ours) vs. random and uniform-in-time selection, each adapted with an identical step budget and evaluated on the generated video (mean over 3 sequences). On this subset the three strategies are within noise of one another, indicating the gain comes from supervising diverse poses at all rather than from the specific selection rule.

Table 19. Amortization of the one-time cost. Adaptation (9.3 min) is paid once per reference image, and each subsequent video of that reference costs only inference. Since adapted and base inference are the same computation (Tab. 17), we use a single render time for both, the measured 7.46 min for a full-length 305-frame video, so the ratio reflects the one-time cost alone. Average cost per video is (9.3 + 7.46n)/n, which decays as 1/n and is within 5% of the unadapted base by n=25.

papers.title: One Image Is Enough: Self-Generated Supervision for Personalizing Human Video Diffusion at Test Time
papers.tldr: A test-time personalization method uses self-generated multi-pose supervision from one reference image to improve identity preservation in pose-driven human video diffusion.

papers.abstract: Collision-free reaching is central to manipulation, yet real cells often leave the size and exact position of an obstacle unobserved, which excludes reinforcement learning controllers that take obstacle geometry as input. A reward limited to a collision penalty does not depend on the clearance outside the obstacle, so under a step cost its learned policy skims the obstacle surface and fails once the obstacle radius exceeds its training value. We investigate whether a single analytic reward term can induce a safety margin without exposing the obstacle to the policy. We augment the reward of a simulated Franka Emika Panda reaching task with a horizontal artificial potential field that penalizes proximity within a safety margin around each of two pillars (fixed nominal layout, random drift). Under hidden observation, policies trained with this term maintain a safe success rate above 88% across a radius sweep from 0.03 m to 0.055 m (30 seeds), while policies without it fall below 10% at the maximum tested radius; the term induces a minimum clearance of 47.9 mm against 9.6 mm without it and eliminates training collisions at least eight times earlier (median steps). The advantage is statistically significant at all out-of-distribution radii and holds across three reinforcement learning solvers and under full observation. Its safe success rate is comparable to that of a classical potential-field planner given the pillar positions. The margin is a fixed buffer rather than an adaptation to the radius, and it lengthens the path by about 19%.
bullets: Without clearance-aware rewards, policies skim obstacle surfaces and fail when obstacles are larger than during training.
The method adds a horizontal potential-field penalty around two pillars without revealing their size or exact position to the policy.
Across obstacle radii of 0.03–0.055 m, augmented policies maintain over 88% safe success, versus under 10% without augmentation at the largest radius.
The method increases minimum clearance to 47.9 mm from 9.6 mm and works across three reinforcement-learning solvers and full observation.
The induced margin is fixed rather than radius-adaptive and increases path length by about 19%.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Observation model. Top: workspace (top view); the dark polyline denotes the schematic manipulator from its base to the end-effector at p. Bottom: observation vector received by the policy, with segment widths equal to the corresponding dimensions. (a) Hidden observation (R9): the policy receives p, ṗ and g; the pillars are withheld. (b) Full observation (R9+4N ): the per-pillar features fi = [ci,x − x, ci,y − y, dc,i, h − z] are appended.

papers.abstract: Fusing independently normalized attention heads can increase the number of explicit key-value entries, or atoms, needed to preserve their output. We prove a sharp separation for $W_d(q)=\sum_{j=1}^dσ(q_j)$: its $d$ two-atom heads use $2d$ head-atom terms, whereas its minimum single-head representation has exactly $2^d$ atoms, even with arbitrary fixed replacement keys, scalar values, and positive masses. The same lower bound holds for every fixed uniform error below $1/2$ on $\mathbb R^d$, and the threshold is sharp. The proof uses exposed-key normal cones; exact equality on any nonempty open query domain inherits the bound. The resulting atom bound for a fixed head count is tight when that count divides $d$. A normalized family retains its exponential exact minimum while approaching a constant on fixed-radius query balls. For pretrained-model caches, a classical affine-rank bound and a certified instance exclude exact vector preservation at a specified atom count. Learned-cache comparisons on two disjoint banks of 64 contexts show budget-dependent reversals and calibration effects.
bullets: A function formed by d two-atom heads uses 2d head-atom terms but needs exactly 2^d atoms in any equivalent single-head representation.
The 2^d lower bound holds for every fixed uniform error below 1/2 on all of R^d and for exact equality on any nonempty open query domain.
The proof uses exposed-key normal cones; the bound is tight for fixed head counts when the count divides d.
A normalized construction preserves the exponential exact minimum while approaching a constant on fixed-radius query balls.

Cache experiments on two disjoint 64-context banks show budget-dependent reversals and calibration effects; a classical affine-rank bound and certified instance rule out exact preservation at a specified atom count.

papers.abstract: Representation alignment (REPA) is widely used to accelerate the training of latent-space diffusion transformers (DiTs). However, applying it to pixel-space models such as Just Image Transformers (JiT) is challenging. Our analysis reveals a pronounced representation conflict between discriminative alignment and pixel-space generation. Compared with its latent counterpart, JiT learns representations that are substantially less aligned with DINOv2. Applying REPA to JiT consistently reduces the reconstructability of its intermediate representations, whereas this effect is not observed in Latent JiT. We attribute this conflict to JiT directly reconstructing pixels, which requires its representations to hierarchically encode discriminative semantics and reconstruction-relevant visual information across network depths. To address these challenges, we propose Routed Representation Alignment (RouteREPA), which uses lightweight, representation-dependent routers to adaptively route task-oriented representations for alignment and generation. We further apply routing across multiple network depths to accommodate their depth-dependent representation requirements. Extensive experiments on ImageNet-1K at 256x256 resolution show that RouteREPA consistently improves JiT across model scales and training budgets, outperforming standard REPA. On JiT-H/16, RouteREPA further surpasses PixelREPA using only one-third of its training epochs without classifier-free guidance.
bullets: REPA is difficult to apply to pixel-space JiT because discriminative alignment can harm intermediate representation reconstructability.
JiT representations must encode both hierarchical semantics and pixel-reconstruction information, unlike latent JiT representations.
RouteREPA uses lightweight, representation-dependent routers to direct task-specific features for alignment or generation.
Multi-depth routing accounts for different representation requirements across network layers.
On ImageNet-1K at 256×256, RouteREPA consistently improves JiT over standard REPA and surpasses PixelREPA on JiT-H/16 with one-third the training epochs, without classifier-free guidance.

papers.abstract: Social navigation is essential for autonomous service robots operating in human environments, but progress remains constrained by the lack of extensive real-world benchmarks. This paper presents the Real Social Navigation Testbed (RESONATE), a reproducible benchmark for human-aware navigation based on a unified robotic platform, a shared ROS 2 software stack, precise trajectory ground truth, and structured social interaction scenarios. We evaluate eight controller configurations, combining classical and predictive local planners with different social modeling strategies, over eight representative scenarios with five repetitions each, yielding 320 physical experiments. The benchmark combines quantitative navigation and social metrics with participant-based qualitative assessments to jointly measure efficiency, safety, comfort, and perceived social behavior. Results reveal scenario-dependent trade-offs among the tested methods. The algorithms that stands out for their performance are the DWA with Gaussian social costmaps for its reliability, and the SFM-MPPI to provide the best balance between robustness, navigation efficiency, and social acceptance. Overall, RESONATE supports the robotics community with a real-world benchmark, reusable baselines, data, and testbed, and a consistent evaluation protocol for advancing socially aware navigation research.
bullets: Addresses the lack of extensive, standardized real-world benchmarks for social navigation.
Provides a unified robot platform, ROS 2 stack, trajectory ground truth, structured scenarios, reusable data, and baselines.
Evaluates eight controller configurations across eight scenarios and 320 physical experiments using quantitative and participant-based qualitative measures.
Measures navigation efficiency, safety, comfort, and perceived social behavior together.
Finds scenario-dependent trade-offs; DWA with Gaussian social costmaps is reliable, while SFM-MPPI offers a strong balance of robustness, efficiency, and social acceptance.

papers.abstract: Generalization remains a central challenge in robotics, calling for policies that address domain variations from multiple dimensions such as diverse embodiments, camera poses, and/or scene layouts. In order to approach this problem, we introduce PointPilot, a task-focused and 3D aligned manipulation framework built on a 3D space point-flow prediction. Rather than modeling the global scene, PointPilot only represents task-focused objects (robot grippers treated as objects), avoiding the prediction of potentially redundant scene parts unrelated to the manipulation tasks. Moreover, PointPilot aligns 3D spatial representation in one unified coordinate and supports closed-loop and fully automatic action execution across different manipulation modes from object point flow without a separately trained action expert, while existing works typically need an extra action head or are (semi-)automatic and single-arm mode specific. Given sensor observations and language instructions, our model jointly learns subtask planning, task-relevant object grounding, and 3D point flow prediction in an end-to-end way. By processing heterogeneous data in a shared 3D point flow space, PointPilot is able to absorb demonstrations from different embodiments. Extensive simulative and real world experiments validate our method. Notably, we demonstrate zero-shot embodiment generalization with PointPilot. A single trained policy can be deployed on previously unseen embodiments and successfully complete manipulation tasks without any additional fine-tuning.
bullets: Targets generalization across embodiments, camera poses, scene layouts, and manipulation modes.
Represents only task-relevant objects, including grippers, in a unified 3D coordinate space rather than modeling the full scene.
Jointly learns subtask planning, object grounding, and 3D point-flow prediction from sensor observations and language instructions.
Supports closed-loop, fully automatic action execution without a separately trained action expert.
Simulated and real-world experiments validate the approach, including zero-shot deployment on previously unseen embodiments without fine-tuning.

Right: PointPilot unifies in different manipulation modes and embodiments, thus supporting single-arm and bimanual gripper to execute any manipulation tasks by object-centric prediction. We further demonstrate real-world manipulation and promising zero-shot cross-embodiment skills transfer.

Predicted object motion is converted to end-effector trajectories through a learning-free geometry adapter for closed-loop execution.

papers.abstract: Long-lived agents rely on persistent memory of users, tasks and decisions, and this memory must stay consistent with a world that keeps changing. When an upstream fact changes, however, memory systems can revise the contradicted memory itself while the beliefs, plans and actions derived from it remain accepted, even though they have lost their support. We therefore formulate dependency-aware state revision, which asks not only what changed but also which dependent states should no longer be trusted. To address it, StateGraph maintains an evolving state dependency graph whose edges are recovered from interaction histories. Its core design is counterfactual verification: each candidate edge is tested by asking whether the dependent state would survive the loss of its premise, which separates support dependence from semantic relatedness, and revision then invalidates a dependent state only when a strict dependency fails and no independent support path survives. To test this design, we introduce StateChangeBench, a controlled benchmark of 50 author-constructed cases annotated with cascade depth, hard negatives and action consequences. On it, StateGraph's Impact-F1 margin over a CUPMem reimplementation is 6.9 percentage points at depth 1 and 26.0 at depth 3+. On public long-term memory benchmarks, its point estimates are comparable to or higher than those of the evaluated baselines on most datasets. These results provide initial evidence that explicit dependency tracking can improve selective memory revision under changing conditions.
bullets: Targets a key consistency problem: revising an upstream fact can leave its dependent memories incorrectly accepted.
Builds an evolving dependency graph from interaction histories.
Uses counterfactual verification to distinguish true support dependence from mere semantic relatedness.
Invalidates a dependent state only when a strict dependency fails and no independent support path remains.

On StateChangeBench, its Impact-F1 margin over a CUPMem reimplementation is 6.9 points at depth 1 and 26.0 points at depth 3+; results on public benchmarks are comparable to or higher than evaluated baselines on most datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The StateGraph pipeline. (A) Direct revision settles what the observation itself contradicts, yielding the seed set It. (B) Dependency reasoning—this paper’s contribution—proposes candidates from six bounded sources, then verifies each counterfactually, so the verified graph is a subgraph of the candidate graph. (C) Conservative revision maps each verified edge to a status instead of invalidating everything reachable. (D) Premise and action gating turns status into behavior. Panels correspond to §4.1–§4.5.

papers.abstract: Recent advancements in sign language processing can be attributed to developments in both large-scale dataset collection and algorithmic complexity in areas such as pose estimation techniques, signal processing through Transformer models, and model optimization. However, only a handful of sign languages, such as the American, British, and German, from over 200 globally recognized sign languages, reap the benefits of such advancements, while the rest lag behind. In this study, we aim to address this technological disparity by proposing a framework for the automatic collection and preparation of sign language datasets, with very minimal human-labour intervention, using the South African Sign Language (SASL) as a testbed. Specifically, we automatically collect SASL video content using public resources such as news broadcasts. Additionally, we convert their accompanying audio streams into text using available Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) tools. Furthermore, we crop the sign language area in the videos and use gradient descent to locate valleys of non-motion to determine end-of-sentence points within long videos to create our weakly sentence-aligned parallel corpora -- the Maswao (Signs) dataset. Finally, we benchmark the weakly aligned dataset on the task of Sign-to-text Translation using Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformer models to compare their individual intricacies. Our results show that Transformer models proposed in the literature outperform recurrent baselines, with the best-performing Transformer achieving BLEU-1 to BLEU-4 scores of 13.78, 5.21, 2.52, and 1.54, respectively, as well as ChrF = 18.09 and ROUGE-L = 10.51. These results indicate that the task remains promising and warrants further investigations.
bullets: Addresses the underrepresentation of South African Sign Language in sign-language processing resources.
Collects SASL videos from public sources such as news broadcasts with minimal human intervention.
Uses ASR transcripts, video cropping, and motion-based sentence-boundary detection to create weakly aligned sign–text pairs.
Benchmarks recurrent neural networks and Transformer models for sign-to-text translation.
Transformers outperform recurrent baselines, though the reported translation scores show the task remains challenging.

papers.abstract: In the prediction and control of physical systems, combining records from different experiments and operations is expected to supply information that no single experiment provides on its own. Time-series foundation models, which learn a shared predictor from diverse time series, offer a framework for treating such records as a common training resource. Moreover, query-based prediction models, which switch between known and target signals within the same time series, make it possible to handle response prediction and control-input generation in a unified manner. However, in control-experiment data, the connections between signals change with the experimental stage, such as system identification, filtering, and feedback control, which calls for a formulation that handles signal values and connection structures dynamically and in a unified way. We formulate a control foundation model that defines a data space of dynamic graphs containing connections, signal values, and missing values, together with an operation on this space that specifies the known signals and the prediction targets. This allows response prediction and control-input generation to be described as a common masked prediction problem, even for experimental data with different connections and recorded signals. The Block Diagram Transformer (BDT), which implements this formulation, combines attention along the time axis with a graph neural network that follows the block-diagram connections, and can be initialized with the pretrained parameters of existing time-series foundation models. Trained on control-experiment data that mix multiple experimental settings, the proposed model stabilized an unstable system through feedback control, which is difficult to achieve by fine-tuning existing time-series foundation models. Ongoing work applying this approach to a wide range of target systems is also yielding promising results.
bullets: Addresses control data whose signal connections change across stages such as identification, filtering, and feedback.
Formulates response prediction and control-input generation as one masked prediction problem over dynamic graphs with missing values.
Introduces the Block Diagram Transformer (BDT), combining temporal attention with a graph neural network guided by block-diagram connections.
BDT can be initialized from pretrained time-series foundation models and trained on mixed control-experiment settings.
The model stabilized an unstable system through feedback control, an outcome reported as difficult for fine-tuned existing time-series foundation models.

papers.title: Control Foundation Models across Changing Block Diagrams: Generalizing Time-Series Prediction to Dynamic Graphs
papers.tldr: A control foundation model represents changing block-diagram connections and signal values as dynamic graphs, enabling unified prediction and control across experiments.

papers.abstract: Accurate long-horizon probabilistic predictions of dynamical systems are a prerequisite for model-based decision-making. Variational Bayesian last layers (VBLLs) are an attractive model class for this setting, offering tractable uncertainty at near-deterministic cost, yet they are trained exclusively with single-step likelihood objectives that may be insufficient for reliable multi-step rollouts. We revisit VBLLs through the lens of Gibbs variational inference, which decouples posterior inference from the choice of training loss. Building on this perspective, we introduce a family of multi-step training losses that progressively incorporate long-horizon structure, robustness via continuous ranked probability scores (CRPS), and training on full autoregressive rollouts. Our approach retains the simplicity of VBLLs while directly optimizing for multi-step predictive quality. Across illustrative synthetic environments, a diverse suite of chaotic dynamical systems, and real-world data, we show that multi-step, CRPS-based objectives substantially improve long-horizon accuracy and distributional fit, consistently outperforming single-step likelihood training.
bullets: Targets unreliable multi-step rollouts from variational Bayesian last layers (VBLLs).
Uses Gibbs variational inference to decouple posterior inference from the training loss.
Introduces losses that progressively capture long-horizon structure, CRPS robustness, and full autoregressive rollouts.
Evaluations span synthetic environments, chaotic systems, and real-world data.
Multi-step CRPS objectives improve long-horizon accuracy and distributional fit over single-step likelihood training.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinating object acquisition, transport, and release from onboard sensing while responding to user commands and incomplete visual observations. We present ReGATE, a whole-body controller that combines egocentric depth, proprioception, and online locomotion and contact commands. Built on a teacher-student framework, ReGATE integrates interaction-state estimation through a recurrent adapter that predicts object geometry and physical contact without an external object-pose estimator. Head-wise and global gates regulate visual updates to a proprioceptive pathway. A visual-grounding and corruption curriculum trains the adapter, while phase-aware initialization increases coverage of brief contact transitions. In simulation, ReGATE achieves 85.2% success across 330 static-object acquisition trials, compared with 48.5% for VisualMimic under the same protocol, and 85.9% across 440 moving-object acquisition trials. Deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates commanded grasp-transport-release sequences and acquisition of laterally displaced boxes. A qualitative hardware experiment further demonstrates successful box acquisition when the camera is occluded after an initial observation and before the contact command. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to extend recurrent gated fusion of onboard depth and proprioception from perceptive locomotion to humanoid loco-manipulation under interrupted visual sensing.
bullets: Addresses whole-body loco-manipulation from onboard sensing and user commands, including brief or interrupted visual observations.
Uses a teacher–student controller with a recurrent adapter that estimates object geometry and contact state without an external pose estimator.
Head-wise and global gates regulate visual information, supported by visual-grounding, corruption, and phase-aware training curricula.
Achieves 85.2% success on 330 static-object trials and 85.9% on 440 moving-object trials in simulation, versus 48.5% for VisualMimic on the static protocol.
Hardware demonstrations on a Unitree G1 show grasp–transport–release behavior, laterally displaced box acquisition, and acquisition after camera occlusion.

papers.abstract: Classical structure-from-motion reconstruction proceeds iteratively, refining camera poses and scene geometry from a current estimate. This allows maps to easily expand without recomputing already computed views, or geometry estimates to improve as more observations are provided. Most geometric foundation models, however, predict entire geometry in a single forward pass or update a recurrent state as frames arrive sequentially, making this expansion and refinement non-trivial. We introduce Solv3R, a looped transformer that learns to continue solving multi-view geometry from its current state. Importantly, its update operator is independent of the iteration count, allowing previously refined and newly introduced views to be jointly updated regardless of how ``solved'' they are. We train the operator to preserve accurate reconstructions under continued iteration and correct inaccurate states, enabling refinement of fixed image collections and integration of new observations. Representations of solved views can also be cached once and reused as geometric context across iterations, enabling compact and efficient key-value caching. We analyze the solver dynamics and compare it with the state-of-the-art, demonstrating that a single learned solver supports offline reconstruction, incremental reconstruction, relocalization, and streaming without task-specific training or modules. The code and models will be made publicly available at https://ubc-vision.github.io/solv3r/.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of refining or adding views in geometric foundation models that rely on one-shot or sequential-state prediction.
Uses an iteration-independent update operator that jointly updates previously solved and newly added views.
Trains the solver to preserve accurate reconstructions while correcting inaccurate intermediate states.
Caches solved-view representations as reusable geometric context for more compact and efficient iterations.
Demonstrates broad reconstruction capabilities without task-specific training or separate modules.

papers.selection_reason: Looped transformer for iterative multi-view geometry is a generalist 3D foundation model with reusable geometric context caching.
papers.title: Solv3R: 3D Looped Transformer as a Multi-view Solver
papers.tldr: Solv3R is a looped transformer that iteratively refines and expands multi-view 3D reconstructions, supporting offline, incremental, relocalization, and streaming use cases with one learned solver.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving policies require effective visual representations that capture both spatial scene structure and temporal dynamics. Video latent prediction has emerged as an effective paradigm for learning spatiotemporal visual representations, yet it remains unclear whether scaling this objective with action-free driving videos can yield representations that benefit end-to-end planning. We study action-free video latent prediction as a scalable pretraining objective and introduce ScaleDrive, a driving-oriented framework pretrained exclusively on large-scale internet open-world driving videos, without action annotations or benchmark-specific data. We keep the pretrained video encoder frozen during downstream end-to-end planning training to isolate the transferability of representations learned from internet driving videos. Ego-motion and depth probes show that scaling action-free video pretraining progressively strengthens the temporal and geometric information encoded in the frozen representation. We systematically study the visual representation transfer across different end-to-end driving policies and closed-loop benchmarks, where ScaleDrive consistently improves downstream performance and demonstrates that scaling action-free video latent prediction yields representations that generalize across both planning policy architectures and evaluation scenarios and protocols.
bullets: Addresses whether action-free video pretraining can learn representations useful for downstream driving.
Pretrains a video encoder exclusively on large-scale internet open-world driving videos, without action labels or benchmark-specific data.
Freezes the encoder during downstream planning training to isolate representation transferability.
Probes indicate that scaling strengthens encoded temporal and geometric information, including ego-motion and depth cues.
Improves performance consistently across driving policy architectures, closed-loop benchmarks, and evaluation protocols.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by reducing the sequential cost of token-by-token generation. Advanced SD methods reduce proposal cost with parallel drafters that predict entire blocks in one forward pass, but overall speedup still depends on acceptance length. On-policy distillation (OPD) can push well-trained drafters beyond acceptance-length plateaus, yet conventional pipelines collect supervision through sequential draft-and-verify rollouts. Our key insight is that on-policy supervision need not inherit these dependencies: a draft block can be supervised using only its reference prefix and draft-sampled history. We propose SpecOPD, a branch-parallel OPD framework that parallelizes draft sampling and target supervision across independent branches drawn from the evolving drafter policy at reference anchors. We pack these branches into proposal trees to share target-prefix computation, using tree masks for full attention, branch-consistent indexer groups for sparse attention, and indexed state replay for linear attention to preserve each branch's history. We train the drafter with an E2E-TV surrogate that directly targets acceptance length. Our study spans 8B full-attention (GQA), 27B full-linear (GQA--GDN), and 125B sparse-linear (QSA--GDN) targets, three parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark, and DFlash V2), and four task domains (dialogue, coding, mathematics, and agentic). SpecOPD achieves up to 41.45% higher mean acceptance length, $16.09\times$ supervised-token throughput over sequential-rollout OPD under native configurations, and up to $3.56\times$ generation speedup over autoregressive decoding.
bullets: Addresses the sequential rollout bottleneck in conventional on-policy distillation for speculative decoding.
Samples independent draft branches from reference anchors and supervises them in parallel using draft-sampled histories.
Packs branches into proposal trees to share target-prefix computation while preserving branch-specific histories across attention types.
Uses an E2E-TV surrogate that directly optimizes acceptance length.

Across multiple target architectures, draft models, and domains, achieves up to 41.45% higher mean acceptance length, 16.09× higher supervised-token throughput, and 3.56× generation speedup over autoregressive decoding.

papers.abstract: Urban photogrammetric point clouds are commonly processed as local 3D patches, limiting the context available for distinguishing geometrically similar categories. Orthographic projection of the same data yields a co-registered digital orthophoto map (DOM)/RGB-D representation that supports efficient large-context modeling but compresses vertical geometry. Existing projection--point methods mainly fuse these two representations at the feature level while retaining a classifier shared across all samples. We present the Aerial Content-Aware Sample-Adaptive Classifier (ACASAC), which complements feature fusion with decision-level adaptation. A point-aligned aerial region bridges the full aerial crop and local 3D patch. ACASAC models scene-to-local variation within the projection and the representation discrepancy between aligned 2D and 3D supports, then transfers both relations to refine the local point class representation. The refined representation, scene-level aerial context, and fixed fused-head prior jointly form a classifier for the current sample. ACASAC improves the fixed dual-representation head by 2.1 and 2.7 mIoU points on SensatUrban and UrbanBIS, respectively, and by 2.1--2.3 points across four tested encoder combinations.
bullets: Local 3D patches lack sufficient context for distinguishing geometrically similar urban categories.
The method combines orthographic DOM/RGB-D large-context information with local 3D point features.
A point-aligned aerial region links the full aerial crop and local 3D patch.
It models scene-to-local variation and 2D–3D representation discrepancies to refine per-sample class representations.
It improves the fixed dual-representation head by 2.1 mIoU points on SensatUrban and 2.7 on UrbanBIS, with gains of 2.1–2.3 points across four encoder combinations.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in production agents involves transforming accumulated experience into reliable model updates while adapting to evolving business policies. We present CARE (Customer-service Agent Retrospective and Evolve), a grounded RSI framework that operationalizes this process in customer service. Its goal is to replace a frontier proprietary incumbent with an in-house mid-sized model that continues learning after deployment. After a one-time cold start on governed production traces, the current model serves production traffic alongside the incumbent, and its own failures drive the next update. A 24/7 inspection process establishes failures through evidence-blinded, independently reviewed judgments. Attribution separates model errors from defects in Skills, tools, or the harness, routing component failures to repair. Model-attributable trajectories are truncated at the first erroneous decision and paired with verified repairs. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) then updates the model using the same model as teacher, with the diagnosis and repair supplied as privileged information unavailable to the student. To support continued evolution as business requirements change, training mixes failures from different Skill/SOP versions, each judged against the policy in force when it occurred. Candidates run an executable simulation test compiled from the latest SOP and then frozen, followed by offline inspection of the resulting traces. Promotion requires a combined simulation-and-inspection score at least at parity with the deployed version, confirmation through an online comparison with the incumbent, and human approval.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reliable recursive self-improvement under changing business policies.
Uses evidence-blinded, independent review to identify failures and attribute them to the model, Skills, tools, or harness.
Truncates model-error trajectories at the first wrong decision and trains with verified repairs via on-policy self-distillation using privileged diagnoses.
Mixes failures across Skill/SOP versions and evaluates candidates in frozen, executable simulations plus offline trace inspection.
Requires parity with the deployed version, online comparison with the incumbent, and human approval before promotion.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CARE. Phase I bootstraps an in-house policy πθ0 from governed production traces of the incumbent system. Phase II is the recursive loop. The current model πθk serves part of the production traffic; 24/7 online inspection turns its own conversations into reviewed failures; attribution separates model-attributable failures from component failures, which are repaired outside the model; model-attributable failures are cut at the first erroneous decision and repaired, and the model distills from itself on that decision, with the hindsight visible only to the teacher. The candidate is measured by the evaluation system, where it runs a simulation test compiled from the latest Skill/SOP and then frozen, and its simulation traces are inspected offline; it is promoted only if the combined score of the two is at least at parity with the deployed version and an online comparison with the incumbent confirms it. After cold start, training data come from the model’s own failures and the teacher is the model itself. Stages tagged in red are driven by an external frontier model rather than by the in-house model. The operating context is revised independently of the loop: a revision reaches the deployed model through its input and the evaluation system through a recompiled test (Section 3.3).

Figure 3: Online inspection and attribution. Production conversations of the in-house model are frozen into a case set Qt and pass an evidence-blinded inspection (Eq. 18) that separates ranking, capacity-aware admission from three strata (Eq. 20), analysis, and independent review with reconciliation, and ends in one of four terminal states (Eq. 21). Terminal states feed back to the screener (Eq. 23). Only confirmed failures reach attribution, which routes model-attributable cases, together with their diagnosis d, to incremental task construction, routes component failures to repair, and holds cases whose cause cannot be isolated.

Figure 2: The cold-start data engine. (a) Admission keeps complete, context-keyed conversations that pass language, structural, and evidence-anchored semantic checks; only no_problem conversations enter Ds, and rejected or unresolved records are never backfilled. (b) Allocation splits a fixed budget N over region groups, the scenarios of each group, and the regions of GCC4, applying the capacity-constrained equal split of Eq. 8 at every level, and then freezes the selected members S. (c) Refinement borrows tone from linked human conversations for eligible turns while preserving every protected field; a rejected rewrite keeps the original conversation, and only a failed final check removes it.

Figure 4: Retrospective repair construction. (a) A confirmed failure is cut at the first decision the model got wrong. Everything the model could see at that moment becomes the student input; the erroneous output, the rest of the conversation, the outcome, and the diagnosis become hindsight. (b) The proposer uses hindsight to write a minimal repair that remains justified by the decision-time input alone, an independent verifier accepts or rejects it, and each accepted tuple can be projected into SFT, DPO, or OPSD data. Every case ends in exactly one terminal state.

Figure 6: The executable simulation environment. Before the run, the frozen case is split into one view per module (Eq. 38): the user simulator receives the user’s goal, initial knowledge, and signal-gated reactions; the system simulator the initial state and event schedule; the agent only its operating context; and the assessment the branch and the oracle, which no participant sees (Eq. 37). During the run, the orchestrator mediates every exchange, only the system simulator changes business state, and each participant receives its own projection of that state. After the run, the trace and the state log are judged against the oracle, and each case ends in pass or fail (Eq. 41). The traces are also inspected offline (Section 7.2).

Figure 5: Attribution-guided on-policy self-distillation at the failing decision. The student samples a fresh decision ŷ from the decision-time input x. A frozen copy of the same model, additionally given the privileged information I (diagnosis, incident-time SOP, and verified repair), reads the same prefixes, so at every token position both models give a distribution over the vocabulary. The loss compares the two on the teacher’s top-K tokens, in the forward direction with a floor at zero in the deployed configuration, and is backpropagated directly. Gradients flow only into the student, and I stays on the teacher side of the privileged boundary. The direction of the KL divergence, K, and the floor are ablated in Section 8.7.

papers.abstract: Real-time omnimodal assistants are expected to support people in everyday life, but audiovisual understanding alone does not establish whether they can provide timely and appropriate help. We introduce Omni-Life, a benchmark grounded in real-world user needs, deployment scenarios, and device-dependent observations. It combines controlled video synthesis for hazardous situations and edge cases with annotated real-world videos under a shared temporal protocol. The benchmark contains 400 videos: 290 requiring assistance, with 555 required intervention events, and 110 requiring silence throughout to test whether models can withhold unnecessary responses when no assistance is needed. We evaluate twelve configurations featuring mainstream real-time omnimodal models, jointly assessing event coverage, response content, timing, and unwanted output. At most 4.48% of videos requiring assistance are handled completely correctly. To examine practical deployment strategies, we study task reminders and response-latency tolerance. Reminders can improve recall by 17.12 percentage points but add approximately 4.6 unwanted responses per minute of reference silence. Increasing latency tolerance by 10s improves recall by at most 5.95 percentage points. These results show that existing models remain insufficient to deliver reliable assistance in real-life applications, calling for tailored model optimization in instruction following, timely proactive intervention, and withholding responses when assistance is not needed.
bullets: Evaluates assistance quality across event coverage, response content, timing, and unwanted output.
Combines controlled videos of hazards and edge cases with annotated real-world videos under a shared temporal protocol.

Across 12 model configurations, at most 4.48% of assistance-needed videos are handled completely correctly.

papers.abstract: AI scientists are expanding automated research across scientific domains, yet their ability to turn the scientific record into a foundation for autonomous discovery remains elusive. Here we uncover a fundamental barrier to this transition and demonstrate a route to overcome it in computational quantum science, where advances shape both what we can learn from complex quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. To identify this barrier, we introduce OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment that converts published studies into executable reproduction tasks. Across 59 papers spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization, we systematically evaluate five agentic systems powered by large language models and six third-party agent harnesses. Our findings reveal that current AI scientists often fail to reproduce published results, exposing a fundamental mismatch between what scientific papers communicate and what autonomous agents require. By contrast, human expert intervention can turn these failures into successful reproductions, showing that the missing information can be identified and converted into reusable research experience. Guided by this observation, we develop Residual Agents (RA), a quantum-tailored self-improving AI scientist that distils externally verified workflow repairs into such experience. RA substantially improves research performance under fixed base models and limited adaptation budgets. For example, RA raises DeepSeek V4.1 Flash performance from 68% to 85%, matching Claude Code with Opus 5 at a third of its cost despite using a weaker base model. We integrate all reproduced results into an extensible platform built on the model context protocol, making verified research workflows directly accessible to AI scientists and allowing new scientific papers to be continuously incorporated.
bullets: Evaluates five LLM-based agents and six agent harnesses on 59 papers spanning simulation, quantum algorithms, and quantum-property characterization.
Finds a fundamental mismatch between information communicated in scientific papers and what autonomous agents need for executable reproduction.
Shows that human intervention can identify missing information and repair failed reproduction workflows.
Introduces Residual Agents, a quantum-tailored self-improving system that reuses externally verified workflow repairs under fixed models and limited adaptation.
Builds an extensible model-context-protocol platform for incorporating verified research workflows and new papers.

figures.caption: FIG. 3. Performance of RA for computational quantum science. Reproduction success across 59 reproduction tasks is plotted against model-inference cost per task on a logarithmic scale. Marker shape denotes the agent system or harness type, marker color denotes the underlying model family or access mode, and marker size indicates wall-clock time per task; semitransparent markers denote earlier model generations. Labels identify the corresponding model or harness. RA, the proposed self-improving AI scientist, runs DSH as its executor and is drawn as the DSH marker inside a gear; the dashed line indicates the Pareto frontier between reproduction success and inference cost. A brown ring marks GPT models accessed through an application programming interface (API).

FIG. 2. AI-assisted reproduction reveals inconsistencies in the scientific record. a, Reproduction assessment across three directions of computational quantum science. Grey denotes studies with no identified problem, whereas increasingly dark red indicates Level I–III issues according to their severity and resolvability. b–d, Representative Level I–III cases. From top to bottom, each case shows the scientific problem, the identified reproduction issue—including the paper’s claim, the contradiction found by the AI scientist and expert feedback—and the reproduced results before and after expert correction, each compared with the original result. For the panel b, a machine-learning configuration discrepancy resolved using the released code. For the panel c, an ambiguous experimental procedure requiring expert resolution. For the panel d, a fundamental inconsistency between the reported quantity, released code and theoretical constraints that cannot be resolved from the available scientific record. Dashed black and solid red curves denote the reported and reproduced results, respectively.

FIG. 1. Paper-to-result reproduction in computational quantum science. a, Scientific papers from three research directions in computational quantum science are converted into reproduction tasks centred on a target figure within OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment. In OmniQ, a plan agent and an execute agent reproduce the source code and the target figure, and a judge agent compares the reproduced figure with the published one. b, The mechanism of the self-improving AI scientist RA for computational quantum science. The planner decomposes a research plan into sub-plans, each executed by an executor and evaluated by a critic. Failed steps are revised and re-executed, with the planner replanning when necessary. A judge evaluates the assembled result. Upon failure, expert feedback is processed by the residual agent to refine executor guidance, critic criteria and planner strategies.

papers.abstract: Language model agents often struggle with complex tasks even when equipped with expert-written skills. Such skills encode declarative knowledge, whereas successful execution requires procedural knowledge tailored to the task at hand. Natural language skills may leave conditions and dependencies implicit, and tasks involving multiple skills further require agents to coordinate intermediate results and execution order. We introduce Think with Skills, a method that trains reasoning models to turn relevant skill descriptions into task-specific pseudocode plans before execution. The pseudocode explicitly represents operations, conditions, intermediate results, and dependencies, providing a structured bridge from skill descriptions to agent actions. We construct training data that pairs tasks and skills with pseudocode plans and execution trajectories, use supervised fine tuning to initialize this behavior, and further optimize end-to-end task performance with Group Relative Policy Optimization. On SkillsBench, Think with Skills raises task success from 35.0% to 62.0%. These results show that proceduralizing expert knowledge before execution substantially improves skill use.
bullets: Addresses the gap between declarative skill knowledge and the procedural reasoning needed for complex tasks.
Plans encode operations, conditions, intermediate results, dependencies, and execution order.
Training uses task–skill–plan–trajectory examples, supervised fine-tuning, and Group Relative Policy Optimization.
On SkillsBench, task success increases from 35.0% to 62.0%.
The approach focuses on tasks requiring coordinated use of multiple skills.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of the Think with Skills training pipeline. A Draft Agent constructs and validates tasks from related skills. Strong and weak Solvers then attempt each task. Tasks solved by the strong Solver but not the weak Solver are retained, and the corresponding trajectories provide pseudocode and execution supervision for SFT. GRPO continues training from the SFT checkpoint with verifier rewards.

Figure 2. Illustrative comparison of direct skill use and Think with Skills on a routing-diagnosis task with the same input files and expert skill. Direct skill use consults relevant guidance during execution. Think with Skills first expresses the skill as task-specific pseudocode, then follows its branches and checks while executing. Failed checks trigger diagnosis and revision of the affected step. Passed checks allow execution to continue or finish.

Figure 3. Verifiable and difficulty-calibrated data construction. (A) A Draft Agent constructs a task, input files, and verifier from related skills and self-validates the candidate. (B) The strong and weak Solvers independently attempt the same candidate once, and the task-specific verifier scores both outputs. (C) Their joint outcome determines whether to retain the candidate, increase its difficulty, repair or simplify it, or discard it. Revised tasks return to self-validation before another independent evaluation by both Solvers.

papers.title: Think with Skills: Pseudocode Planning Before Execution for Advanced Reasoners
papers.tldr: Think with Skills improves language-model agents by converting expert skill descriptions into explicit pseudocode plans before execution.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models (AR-VDMs) enable real-time, long-horizon video generation but degrade rapidly once the inference horizon outruns the training horizon, due to compounding exposure bias. To stabilize long rollouts, recent methods heuristically adopt frame sink, keeping initial frames as a persistent model context, inspired by attention sinks in LLMs. We revisit this design and find that the mechanism by which initial frames stabilize long-range consistency in AR-VDMs is not an LLM-style attention sink; instead, long-range consistency is anchored through a sparse subset of attention heads, while the majority of heads predominantly capture local temporal dynamics. This observation reveals an over-conditioning pathology in existing frame-sink strategies: by universally exposing every head to the pinned initial-frame context, the model becomes prone to collapsing motion toward the low-dynamic modes of the teacher during model distillation. We propose Disen-Forcing, a distillation-time plug-in for AR-VDMs that disentangles and reinforces this head specialization through disentangled context routing and motion-disentangling regularization. On long-horizon video generation benchmarks, Disen-Forcing simultaneously improves long-range consistency and motion dynamics of base AR-VDMs, a trade-off that sink-based methods fail to balance.
bullets: AR-VDMs suffer compounding exposure bias when generating beyond their training horizon.
Long-range consistency relies on a sparse subset of attention heads, not a universal LLM-style attention sink.
Conventional frame-sink strategies over-condition all heads and can collapse motion toward low-dynamic modes.
Disen-Forcing uses disentangled context routing and motion-disentangling regularization during distillation.
Experiments show improved long-range consistency and motion dynamics without the trade-off of sink-based methods.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) elevates joint audio-video generation, but optimizing heterogeneous, modality-specific audio and video rewards often introduces cross-modal interference. On-policy distillation (OPD) alleviates this issue by transferring the capabilities of specialized audio and video RL teachers into a single student model. However, a significant imbalance in cross-modal token counts leaves audio with sparse supervision, causing unstable distillation. We observe that naively increasing the audio loss weight fails to solve this problem since audio learning relies heavily on visual context, indicating richer visual cues are crucial to offset sparse audio signals. To address this, we propose OmniOPD, a modality-wise on-policy distillation framework designed for balanced and stable audio-video generation. First, we construct privileged visual information using asymmetric noise scheduling, allowing the audio teacher to generate more informative targets from cleaner video context. Second, we introduce grouped multi-noise sampling to expand audio supervision coverage and stabilize training. Third, we introduce timestep-wise importance weighting based on teacher-student transition divergence, preserving reliable supervision while down-weighting unreliable learning signals, to stabilize fluctuations in audio learning. Evaluated on JavisBench and VBench demonstrate OmniOPD preserves audio quality while significantly enhancing video generation, achieving effective joint distillation.
bullets: Joint audio-video RL can suffer from cross-modal interference when audio and video rewards are optimized together.
Audio receives sparse supervision because audio has fewer tokens, and simply increasing its loss weight is ineffective.
The method uses asymmetric noise scheduling to provide the audio teacher with cleaner, more informative visual context.
Grouped multi-noise sampling broadens audio supervision, while timestep-wise importance weighting down-weights unreliable signals.
On JavisBench and VBench, OmniOPD preserves audio quality while significantly improving video generation.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of OmniOPD. (A) On-policy modality-wise distillation transfers knowledge from frozen video and audio teachers to a joint audio-video student using student-generated rollouts. (B) Privileged visual guidance provides the audio teacher with cleaner video context while sharing the same audio state with the student, yielding more informative audio supervision. (C) Multinoise sampling expands audio supervision across noise realizations and denoising steps, while statereliability weighting controls the contribution of unreliable learning signals.

Figure 4: Qualitative examples of joint audio-video generation by OmniOPD. These examples demonstrate improvements in audio diversity, voice–character alignment in multi-character scenes, visual aesthetics, and audio fidelity.

The middle row compares three joint-reward configurations, including increased audio reward weights. The bottom row compares audio-only optimization with two Cascade variants that optimize video first and then audio. (1) Audio-only reward optimization is unstable and can degrade video quality; increasing audio reward weights fails to resolve these conflicts and can further destabilize training.(2) Joint-reward optimization yields limited gains due to conflicts among reward objectives across modalities. (3) Sequential video-to-audio optimization stabilizes training, suggesting that cleaner and more stable video context is important for audio learning.

papers.abstract: Robust multimodal perception for soft robotic grasping is challenged by modality-dependent noise, semantic ambiguity, and limited coordinated multisensory data. We introduce Soma, a dataset containing 100 objects, 1,000 continuous grasping trajectories, and 74,914 multimodal samples grouped by software acquisition cycle, spanning remote RGB, hand RGB, depth, tactile, IMU, and structured text observations. We also collect Soma-Success, an independent grasp-outcome dataset with 1,000 trials (998 retained after quality control), to evaluate frozen-encoder transfer for post-hoc grasp outcome classification and early grasp success prediction. Built on Soma, SomaAlign learns multimodal representations in three stages: masked reconstruction estimates relative modality reliability; reliability-aware contrastive alignment uses pair-specific adaptive temperatures to adjust alignment sharpness; and conflict-aware semantic constraints improve intra-sample cross-modal consistency while preserving global feature geometry. SomaAlign achieves an average Recall@10 of 90.66% across 30 directed cross-modal retrieval tasks. The learned representations also support physical attribute recognition, multimodal question answering, cross-modal generation, and cross-dataset transfer to grasp outcome prediction. On Soma-Success, frozen SomaAlign encoders with lightweight probes achieve 94.59% post-hoc classification accuracy and 84.07% early prediction accuracy. Together, Soma, Soma-Success, and SomaAlign provide a data and representation-learning foundation for robust and transferable multimodal perception in soft robotic manipulation.
bullets: Addresses modality-dependent noise, semantic ambiguity, and limited coordinated multisensory data in soft robotic grasping.
Introduces Soma, with multimodal RGB, depth, tactile, IMU, and text observations from 1,000 continuous grasping trajectories, plus the independent Soma-Success evaluation set.
Uses masked reconstruction for modality reliability, adaptive-temperature contrastive alignment, and conflict-aware semantic constraints.
Reports 90.66% average Recall@10 across 30 directed cross-modal retrieval tasks.
Frozen encoders with lightweight probes reach 94.59% post-hoc and 84.07% early grasp-success prediction accuracy.

figures.caption: Fig. 5. Overview of the SomaAlign framework. SomaAlign follows three progressive optimization stages: (1) Reconstruction-Based Modality Reliability Estimation estimates modality reliability from normalized masked-reconstruction difficulty and constructs pairwise reliability scores; (2) Reliability-Conditioned Contrastive Alignment uses the pairwise reliability scores to adapt cross-modal contrastive temperatures and learn a shared representation; and (3) BatchAdaptive Conflict-Aware Geometry-Preserving Refinement calibrates pairwise similarities, estimates fuzzy sample-level conflict, and adaptively modulates intra-sample refinement while imposing conflict-consistency and reference-center anchoring constraints. The reference geometry constructed from Stage-II representations, including the sample-specific centers and global representation scale, is frozen and reused during Stage-III optimization. After training, only the modality-specific encoders are retained for inference.

Fig. 1. Overview of Soma, Soma-Success, and the SomaAlign framework. The soft robotic platform acquires six coordinated modalities: Remote RGB, Hand RGB, Depth, Tactile, IMU, and Text. Soma comprises 100 objects, 1,000 trajectories, and 74,914 aligned multimodal samples, while Soma-Success contains 1,000 collected grasp trials, of which 998 valid trials are retained for downstream evaluation. SomaAlign learns a unified semantic representation through Reliability Assessment, Adaptive Feature Alignment, and Conflict-aware Refinement. The learned representation supports cross-modal retrieval, physical attribute recognition, multimodal question answering, cross-modal generation, and frozen-encoder grasp success prediction.

Fig. 2. Overview of the Soma acquisition system. A unified software polling loop coordinates remote RGB-D sensing, hand-mounted RGB cameras, finger-mounted IMUs, and flexible tactile pressure arrays. Structured text descriptions are generated from experimental metadata using predefined templates. Representative sensor outputs and an example text annotation are shown on the right.

Fig. 4. Soma-Success collection protocol. The action-triggered snapshots Ta, Tb, and Tc correspond to the pre-grasp, closed-gripper, and terminal-lifting stages, respectively. The same snapshot-selection rule is applied to successful and failed trials. Representative examples are shown for the two-finger (2F) and three-finger (3F) configurations.

Fig. 9. Attribute classification accuracy retention under cross-modal generation, measured relative to the corresponding real-data baseline. (a) Single-modality probes. (b) Multi-modality probes with one generated modality replacing its real counterpart. (c) Average retention for the two strategies.
Fig. 3. Object collection in Soma. The 100 everyday objects cover diverse materials, shapes, sizes, hardness levels, colors, and functional purposes.

Fig. 6. Conceptual illustration of pair-specific distribution calibration and fuzzy membership assignment. Different modality pairs may exhibit different raw similarity distributions; therefore, the same similarity value can represent different degrees of relative inconsistency. Pair-specific ECDFs convert raw similarities into comparable conflict indicators ξi,π . The calibrated indicator is then softly assigned to overlapping ordered Gaussian fuzzy sets, allowing transitional cross-modal conflicts to partially activate multiple adjacent conflict levels.

Fig. 7. Motivation of the center-protection loss. Local cross-modal refinement may cause sample centers to deviate from the geometry established in Stage II. The center-protection constraint penalizes excessive center drift while allowing local multimodal representations to become more compact.

Fig. 8. Recall@1, Recall@5, and Recall@10 across 30 directed cross-modal retrieval tasks. Sensory-only retrieval uses paired temporal-window correspondence; text-related retrieval uses identical structured descriptions. Remote and Hand denote remote-view and hand-mounted RGB, respectively. Same-modality retrieval is excluded.

papers.abstract: Range-image-based point cloud super-resolution provides an effective way to reconstruct sparse outdoor point clouds by projecting low-resolution LiDAR scans into a regular 2D representation. However, current methods still face three challenges. First, range images exhibit pronounced vertical nonuniformity, with sparse observations in distant regions and denser observations in nearby regions. Some cross-scale fusion mechanisms do not account for the varying reliability of features at different vertical positions, allowing invalid values and noise from distant sparse regions to propagate into the decoder. Second, a single convolutional or sequence-modeling architecture often struggles to preserve both local high-frequency geometric details and global long-range dependencies, resulting in over-smoothed reconstructions. Third, smooth transition depths near foreground-background boundaries can produce spike artifacts when the 2D range image is back-projected into 3D. To address these issues, we propose a point cloud super-resolution method based on multi-scale spatial priors and joint local-global modeling. The design comprises a spatially gated fusion module, a multi-granularity local-global cooperative perception module, and 2D median-residual denoising. Experiments on KITTI-360 and nuScenes demonstrate effective reconstruction, with IoU scores of 0.4703 and 0.3593, respectively, supporting the feasibility of the proposed method for range-image super-resolution.
bullets: Addresses vertical nonuniformity in range images, loss of fine geometric detail, and spike artifacts at foreground-background boundaries.
Uses a spatially gated fusion module to limit the propagation of unreliable features from sparse distant regions.
Employs multi-granularity cooperative local-global perception to capture both high-frequency local structure and long-range dependencies.
Applies 2D median-residual denoising to reduce artifacts before back-projecting the range image into 3D.
Experiments on KITTI-360 and nuScenes report IoU scores of 0.4703 and 0.3593, respectively.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient generation, yet maintaining consistency over long rollouts remains challenging, especially when subjects or scenes reappear after going out of sight. Despite progress in fidelity and rollout robustness, existing distillation methods do not fully exploit richer historical information to constrain the student's current prediction. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{History Forcing}, a unified on-policy distillation framework that strengthens historical supervision for few-step autoregressive video generators. The framework uses the residual between teacher predictions with and without informative historical context to decouple this supervision. Such a historical context can be obtained using earlier generated chunks with less accumulated drift or a fixed-view teacher rollout that keeps the scene visible while the student looks away. The residual is then weighted and added to the score or velocity prediction used for distillation, forming a corrected target. By aligning the student with this corrected target through distillation, History Forcing incorporates long-range historical constraints into autoregressive generation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance among 1.3B models, with a VBench quality score of 85.07 for 15s video generation and a VBench-Long aggregate score of 79.82 for 60s generation. For out-of-sight world modeling, evaluations further demonstrate more plausible scene evolution and more consistent states when the camera returns, with Evolution Quality improving from 2.35 to 2.70 on PlayWorld and Object Consistency from 58.43 to 62.18 on MemoBench.
bullets: Addresses scene and subject inconsistency when content reappears after going out of view.
Uses teacher-prediction residuals between context-rich and context-poor rollouts as corrected distillation targets.
Historical context comes from earlier, less-drifted chunks or fixed-view teacher rollouts that preserve scene visibility.
Reports strong results for 15–60-second generation and improved out-of-sight scene evolution and object consistency. The abstract does not state limitations.
