papers.abstract: Interleaved multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning improves the visual reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models by dynamically incorporating visual evidence during reasoning. However, existing methods primarily select evidence from historical context. When the reasoning focus shifts, history-guided evidence may remain focused on prior regions and fail to cover the visual information required by the next step. We refer to this lag between visual evidence and subsequent reasoning demands as Temporal Evidence Myopia. To address this issue, we propose Lookahead Prediction-guided Adaptive Visual Refocusing (LPAVR), a training-free test-time framework. LPAVR transforms Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) from a decoding acceleration mechanism into a lookahead signal for anticipating upcoming reasoning intent. During MTP decoding, the draft head generates multiple future tokens, while the target model verifies them in parallel and retains the longest prefix consistent with its decoding trajectory. This target-verified prefix contains near-future semantics, which LPAVR uses to construct lookahead-guided visual evidence and assess whether history-guided evidence covers the indicated regions. If the coverage is sufficient, the history-guided evidence is retained; otherwise, LPAVR switches to the lookahead-guided evidence. This better aligns the visual context with upcoming reasoning and improves consistency between draft predictions and target-model decoding. Experiments on multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that LPAVR improves both reasoning accuracy and the acceptance rates of MTP speculative tokens, jointly enhancing visual reasoning and speculative decoding efficiency.
bullets: Addresses Temporal Evidence Myopia, where history-based visual evidence lags behind shifts in reasoning focus.
Uses Multi-Token Prediction as a lookahead signal rather than only for decoding acceleration.
Retains historical visual evidence when coverage is sufficient and switches to lookahead-guided evidence otherwise.
A training-free, test-time framework evaluated across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
Reports improved reasoning accuracy and higher acceptance rates of speculative tokens.‌
papers.selection_reason: Improves interleaved multimodal reasoning in MLLMs via lookahead-guided visual refocusing, fitting multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Lookahead Prediction-Guided Adaptive Visual Refocusing for Interleaved Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: LPAVR uses verified future-token predictions to refocus visual evidence toward upcoming reasoning needs, improving multimodal reasoning and speculative decoding efficiency.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can handle noncritical stages of long-horizon manipulation yet fail during short precision-critical phases. Lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) specialists can address these failures without directly applying RL to the full VLA, but retain auxiliary controllers and switching mechanisms at deployment. We study how to transfer their capabilities into a single flow-matching VLA. Direct imitation of specialist rollouts can reproduce action jitter and leave the VLA unprepared for states encountered during its own execution. We introduce REPAIR, a value-guided distillation framework that combines offline initialization with on-policy refinement. At each critical-phase observation, REPAIR queries the corresponding specialist for multiple action candidates and weights them using its critic to construct a supervision distribution. A shared weighted flow-matching objective trains the VLA first on observations from specialist-assisted rollouts, then on observations collected through its own execution. Specialists provide supervision without taking control during on-policy collection and are removed at deployment. Across six real-robot tasks with 30 evaluation trials per task, REPAIR achieves 100% success on all six tasks, with lower mean end-effector jerk than specialist-assisted execution on every task.
bullets: Targets short, precision-critical phases where VLAs often fail during long-horizon manipulation.
Uses specialist critics to weight multiple candidate actions within a shared flow-matching objective.
Combines offline training on specialist-assisted rollouts with on-policy refinement on the VLA’s own observations.
Avoids reproducing action jitter and reduces distribution mismatch from direct imitation.
Achieves 100% success across six real-robot tasks and lower mean end-effector jerk than specialist-assisted execution on every task.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Training framework of REPAIR. (a) Human demonstrations initialize the base VLA π0.5. (b) With this VLA frozen, critical-phase RL trains multiple specialist actors and their critics. (c) Offline observations from DE and on-policy observations from Dπ feed a shared value-refined supervision mechanism. For each critical observation, the selected phase specialist generates the action candidates and its critic determines their relative weights. The VLA learns from these targets in critical phases and replayed VLA actions in noncritical phases. Only the VLA is deployed.

Figure 1: Overview of REPAIR. Local RL expertise provides value-guided supervision for offline initialization and on-policy repair. The VLA acts without specialist takeover during online distillation and is deployed as a single policy.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic novel- view synthesis with real-time rendering, yet fine-grained di- agnosis of its rendering artifacts remains challenging. These artifacts are typically spatially localized and exhibit diverse degradation patterns, making them difficult to character- ize using global quality metrics and image-level assessment benchmarks, which provide no explicit indication of where they occur or what types of artifacts they represent. To ad- dress this limitation, we introduce GaussFlaw-80K, the first large-scale dataset for fine-grained perceptual diagnosis in 3DGS. Constructed through a model-assisted human-in-the- loop pipeline, GaussFlaw-80K contains 80,049 artifact re- gions across 14,289 rendered images, each annotated with a pixel-level mask and one of eight flaw labels spanning ge- ometric, blending, and photometric degradations. These an- notations turn 3DGS artifact diagnosis into an explicit and measurable task. Building on this dataset, we propose Ge- oCritic, a geometry-guided multi-task model that integrates RGB appearance with depth-derived cues to jointly localize artifacts and classify their flaw types. Beyond evaluation, we further demonstrate the downstream benefits of fine-grained diagnosis through three complementary targeted operations: Gaussian densification, attribute correction, and outlier prun- ing. Experiments show that GeoCritic achieves an AUC-J of 0.9507 and an Acc@1 of 80.08%, while diagnosis-guided re- finement improves all reported global and crop-level metrics across diverse datasets and 3DGS backbones.
bullets: 3DGS artifacts are spatially localized and varied, which global quality metrics and image-level benchmarks cannot adequately diagnose.
GaussFlaw-80K contains 80,049 artifact regions from 14,289 rendered images, with pixel-level masks and one of eight flaw labels.
GeoCritic combines RGB appearance and depth-derived cues to jointly localize artifacts and classify their types.
The model achieves an AUC-J of 0.9507 and Acc@1 of 80.08%.
Diagnosis-guided densification, attribute correction, and outlier pruning improve reported global and crop-level metrics across datasets and 3DGS backbones.

papers.abstract: Prompt compression is aimed at reducing input prompt lengths to enable cheaper, faster, and potentially higher-quality LLM predictions. However, existing prompt compression methods are often limited by modest compression gains, a risk of hallucination, and/or high compression latency. We propose EffComp, an Efficient prompt Compression framework for RAG-based question answering (QA). EffComp employs BERT-style document reranker and sentence selector models to allow fast extractive prompt compression at the sentence level. Its extractive nature prevents hallucinations in the compressed prompts. Additionally, the training process using a hybrid reinforcement and supervised learning approach is designed to optimize the compression ratio while preserving LLM accuracy. Experiments on various QA datasets demonstrate that EffComp outperforms state-of-the-art prompt compression methods achieving the best trade-off between compression ratio and accuracy with minimal latency. This makes it practical for real-world applications.
bullets: Targets costly, slow, and potentially unreliable prompt compression for RAG-based QA.
Uses BERT-style document reranking and sentence selection for efficient extractive compression.
Combines reinforcement and supervised learning to optimize compression while maintaining LLM accuracy.
Experiments across QA datasets show the best reported trade-off between compression ratio and accuracy with minimal latency.
Extractive compression limits hallucination risk and supports practical deployment.

papers.abstract: Understanding how objects and their spatial relationships evolve in 3D space over time remains challenging for vision-language models (VLMs), particularly under changing viewpoints. Recent approaches incorporate geometric information into reasoning, but explicit supervision for temporally ordered 4D state evolution and its use as intermediate evidence remains limited. We introduce \textbf{Trace4D}, which trains VLMs to predict 4D state sequences and reason over their inter-timestep changes alongside temporal visual observations. Its 4D-grounded chain-of-thought (CoT) explicitly represents 4D states, analyzes temporal visual context, and connects both as evidence for the answer. We construct Trace4D-Train from in-the-wild videos with 600K 4D perception examples and approximately 70K grounded QA examples, and train with joint supervised fine-tuning followed by geometry-aware GRPO. At inference, Trace4D predicts 4D states and reasoning directly from video without reference annotations or an external geometric model. Experiments on Trace4D-Bench and VLM4D show improved QA accuracy over the base VLMs and benefits from reasoning over 4D state changes and temporal visual observations.
bullets: Targets VLM difficulty in tracking object states and spatial relationships over time under changing viewpoints.
Predicts temporally ordered 4D states, analyzes their changes, and combines them with temporal visual observations in grounded chain-of-thought reasoning.
Trains on in-the-wild videos with 4D perception and grounded QA supervision, followed by geometry-aware GRPO.
Performs inference directly from video without reference annotations or an external geometric model.
Shows improved QA accuracy on Trace4D-Bench and VLM4D over the base VLMs.

papers.abstract: We reimplement the dynamics model of the Robotic World Model (RWM) and test the uncertainty estimate that its follow-up, RWM-U, uses to penalize reward in offline policy optimization. Our implementation matches the released model's gradients. On held-out data, training on the model's own rollouts beats one-step training at the preregistered long horizon for all ten episodes, but loses on short one-step windows. RWM-U's ensemble disagreement ranks rollout errors better than forecast step (Spearman rho = 0.90 at 100 steps), yet its spread substantially understates error: one-sigma coverage on the released checkpoint is 4.6% at 100 steps, versus 68% for a calibrated Gaussian. Rolling ensemble members on their own predictions raises coverage to 33%. The implemented squared-error loss on sampled predictions drives each member's variance toward zero. A horizon-specific rescaling restores one-sigma coverage under leave-one-episode-out evaluation, but not two-sigma coverage. We also identify two defects in the released evaluation pipeline. The study covers one robot, one gait and one dataset; it trains no policy.
bullets: The reimplementation matches the released model’s gradients.
Training on model-generated rollouts outperforms one-step training at the preregistered long horizon, but not on short windows, across all ten episodes.
RWM-U ensemble disagreement strongly ranks rollout errors (Spearman ρ = 0.90 at 100 steps) while substantially understating their magnitude.

Released-checkpoint one-sigma coverage is 4.6% at 100 steps; rolling members on their own predictions raises it to 33%, and rescaling restores one-sigma coverage under leave-one-episode-out evaluation.
The study finds a variance-collapse issue in the squared-error loss and two defects in the released evaluation pipeline; it trains no policy and covers one robot, gait, and dataset.

The runs are drawn individually but are visually coincident within each objective, so the 28 read as two lines, one falling and one rising – which is the point: the trajectory does not vary visibly from run to run. papers.selection_reason: Reproduces and evaluates the uncertainty estimation of a robotic world model's dynamics, directly relevant to world-model reliability.
papers.title: Right Ranking, Wrong Scale: Reproducing the Robotic World Model's Dynamics Model and Testing the Uncertainty of Its Follow-up

papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents that act in the open world need two abilities: world knowledge to interpret what they see, and exploration to find what they cannot yet see. We study how agents combine the two through interactive visual geolocation. GeoGuesser Bench contains 282 tasks in an offline Street View environment where agents rotate, zoom, and move between real panoramas. Its three task types shift the balance from knowledge to exploration: agents (1) report the coordinates of their starting location, (2) name the enclosing street, city, state, or country, or (3) find, read, and count nearby objects. The coordinate tasks in (1) also include 42 real GeoGuessr World Championship rounds, whose expert guesses provide a human reference. We evaluate 23 VLMs: the best accuracy is 62.5% on place naming and 35.0% on object finding, and the best agent averages 4352.4 GeoGuessr points on the championship rounds, against 4770.3 for the better expert in each round. Beyond these headline numbers, world knowledge and exploration are only weakly correlated across models: agents that localize well do not necessarily explore well. To understand where agents fail, we categorize their errors into vision, navigation, and tool-use failures. Further ablations show that the strongest agents, such as Claude Opus 4.8, still perform well with limited views, while weaker agents degrade; customizing the environment thus adjusts task difficulty. The environment's verifiable rewards and restorable state also support training, and our Planner-Worker-Compressor harness cuts planner tokens by 57-61% by compacting the interaction history. We hope GeoGuesser Bench and its environment serve as a high-quality foundation for simulating real-world exploration at scale.
bullets: Introduces 282 offline Street View tasks involving panorama rotation, zooming, and movement, plus 42 expert-referenced GeoGuessr championship rounds.
Tests three task types: coordinate localization, place naming, and finding, reading, or counting nearby objects.
Evaluates 23 VLMs; best reported accuracy is 62.5% for place naming and 35.0% for object finding, while the strongest agent approaches expert GeoGuessr performance.
Finds only weak correlation between localization and exploration ability, with errors categorized as vision, navigation, or tool-use failures.
Shows that environment difficulty can be adjusted through view limits and that a Planner-Worker-Compressor harness reduces planner tokens by 57–61%.

papers.title: GeoGuesser Bench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Agents on Interactive Geolocation
papers.tldr: GeoGuesser Bench evaluates how vision-language agents combine world knowledge and interactive exploration in realistic geolocation tasks.

papers.abstract: Agentic Real2Sim2Real systems can reconstruct a scene in simulation from camera observations, but contact-rich dynamics such as friction and restitution cannot be observed without interaction. We call this the dynamics gap and present CUE, an agentic system that closes it by interacting with the environment itself. Given only a high-level instruction and no resets, the agent builds its own perception, identifies physical parameters, and targets interactions where its simulation is least accurate. On billiards, CUE reduces held-out ball-position error by 72% relative to the strongest baseline across 25 hidden-physics conditions in simulation, and we further deploy it on a real pool table. More details can be found on the project website: https://cue-dynamics.github.io/
bullets: Addresses unobservable contact-rich properties such as friction and restitution.
Uses agent-directed interaction to identify physical parameters and target regions where simulation is least accurate.
Operates from a high-level instruction without environment resets, while building its own perception.
On billiards, reduces held-out ball-position error by 72% versus the strongest baseline across 25 hidden-physics simulation conditions.
Also demonstrates deployment on a real pool table.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Held-out ball-position error after k real interactions, mean over 25 hidden-physics conditions (shaded: 25th–75th percentile).

papers.selection_reason: Agentic robot system that self-directs physical interaction to learn environment dynamics and close the simulation gap; fits robot learning and physical interaction.
papers.title: Closing the Dynamics Gap through Self-Directed Robotic Interaction
papers.tldr: CUE closes the Real2Sim2Real dynamics gap by autonomously probing an environment to identify hidden contact physics and improve simulation accuracy.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic assembly requires reliable perception and action across grasping, alignment, and insertion. Vision captures global object pose and scene context, where as fingertip touch provides local contact cues that are especially useful as contact states change. We present a visuotactile diffusion policy that combines four-step histories from two camera views and two fingertip tactile images to condition action-sequence generation. A recurrent temporal representation integrates recent observations from both modalities. To encourage it to capture how contact evolves under action, an auxiliary objective predicts fingertip-image changes two steps ahead from the temporal representation and demonstrated actions. This objective is used only during training and adds no inference-time computation. Across three independent training seeds in MuJoCo assembly experiments, the full model achieves an average success rate of $59.0\% \pm 2.6\%$, improving on the visual-only baseline ($42.7\% \pm 1.5\%$) by 16.3 percentage points.
bullets: Targets reliable perception and action across grasping, alignment, and insertion, where touch provides local contact information beyond vision.
Conditions action-sequence generation on four-step histories from two camera views and two fingertip tactile images.
Uses a recurrent temporal representation to integrate multimodal observations.
Adds a training-only objective that predicts fingertip-image changes two steps ahead from the representation and demonstrated actions, with no inference-time cost.
In MuJoCo assembly experiments, it achieves 59.0% ± 2.6% success across three seeds versus 42.7% ± 1.5% for a visual-only baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Visuotactile diffusion policy for robotic manipulation.
papers.title: Visuo-tactile Diffusion Policy for Robotic Manipulation with Auxiliary Tactile Dynamics Prediction
papers.tldr: A visuo-tactile diffusion policy improves long-horizon robotic assembly by using visual and fingertip-tactile histories with an auxiliary contact-dynamics prediction objective.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations can sound plausible while having little influence on a model's final answer. We study four rewards that use the policy's own signals to encourage reliance on generated reasoning: gradient sensitivity, confidence gaps, progressive confidence gains, and reasoning--prompt swaps. We add each reward to group relative policy optimization (GRPO) and evaluate two small instruction-tuned models on GSM8K and StrategyQA using reasoning edits, paraphrases, and prompt hints. Several configurations increase answer reliance to reasoning edits, while effects on accuracy and paraphrase robustness vary. We also observe answer copying at a high reward weight and high reliance in decomposition settings with poor task accuracy. The study compares practical objectives for reasoning reliance, confirms the trade-off between reliance and performance, and proposes four lightweight rewards that can improve reasoning reliance.
bullets: Targets the gap between plausible reasoning traces and reasoning that actually influences final answers.
Uses gradient sensitivity, confidence gaps, progressive confidence gains, and reasoning–prompt swaps as rewards within GRPO.
Evaluates two small instruction-tuned models on GSM8K and StrategyQA with reasoning edits, paraphrases, and prompt hints.
Several reward configurations increase reliance on reasoning edits, while accuracy and paraphrase robustness vary.
High reward weights can cause answer copying, and decomposition settings may show high reliance despite poor task accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Training objectives to improve reasoning reliance in LLMs.
papers.title: Chain of Faith: Policy-Internal Rewards for Reasoning Reliance
papers.tldr: The study introduces four lightweight policy-internal rewards that can make models rely more on their chain-of-thought, but greater reliance does not consistently improve accuracy or robustness.

papers.abstract: Personalizing large language model assistants requires adapting their responses to individual users, including the selection of content, reasoning approach, level of detail, and form of presentation. Such preferences are often latent, becoming visible only when users respond to an initial answer and request revisions. We investigate whether these feedback trajectories can be converted into a reusable personalization signal without explicit preference profiles or labels, prompt-time access to interaction histories, or model parameter updates. We introduce UPSHIFT (User Preference Steering from Human-AI Interaction Feedback Traces), a training-free method that compares the hidden representations of initial and feedback-conditioned responses within each session, averages the resulting trajectory displacements across a user's sessions, and injects the aggregated preference direction when answering a new query. The method is motivated by the implicit-preference hypothesis: although an individual conversational transition may reflect topic progression or task-specific correction, changes that recur across sessions retain a component that captures how the user wants responses to be adjusted. We validate the preference-representation capability of UPSHIFT on PrefEval. In evaluations with 40 simulated users, every tested configuration improves preference alignment over the unsteered baseline on held-out topics for both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B; the best configuration increases macro-averaged Elo from 1364.0 to 1605.2 and from 1341.9 to 1591.8, respectively. Matched-user and positive-versus-negative controls further demonstrate that these gains arise from the user-specific preference direction and its learned orientation. These results show that interaction histories can provide compact, reusable supervision for lightweight personalization.
bullets: Addresses latent user preferences revealed through requests to revise initial answers.
Compares hidden representations of initial and feedback-conditioned responses, then averages session-level changes across a user’s interactions.
Injects the aggregated, user-specific preference direction into responses to new queries using a training-free procedure.
On PrefEval with 40 simulated users, all tested configurations improved held-out preference alignment for both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B.
Controls indicate gains come from the user-specific preference direction and its learned orientation.

figures.caption: Table 1: PrefEval accuracy (%) by preference domain. The best result in each column within each evaluation mode is bold.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free method to steer LLM responses using feedback traces, a form of test-time adaptation.
papers.title: UPSHIFT: User Preference Steering from Human-AI Interaction Feedback Traces
papers.tldr: UPSHIFT extracts recurring user-preference directions from feedback-driven interaction traces to personalize LLM responses without profiles, prompts containing histories, or parameter updates.

papers.abstract: When a masked diffusion language model is sampled in a few parallel steps in a random order, the model actually run is a mixture over reveal plans, while cross-entropy training fits token conditionals rather than this mixture. We introduce mixture-likelihood fine-tuning (Mix-FT), which fine-tunes a pretrained model on an importance-weighted bound of its own sampler's likelihood, with no teacher and no change to the architecture or the sampler. On LLaDA-8B, a LoRA fine-tune for 0.002% of the pretraining compute writes better OpenWebText continuations than continued cross-entropy and Alpha diffusion given the same compute, at every tested step count. With half the model evaluations, 16 rather than 32 steps per block, its continuations score better than the original model's in every seed under three judges, with confidence-based decoding as well as random order, and under confidence-based decoding two blinded LLM raters from different model families prefer them in 69 and 71% of pairs. On a public 110M-parameter block diffusion model, Mix-FT takes under four T4-hours and beats continued cross-entropy, Alpha diffusion and SDTT distillation at 4, 8 and 16 steps per block, under two judges in every seed. Exact likelihoods on text8, with a control that weights every plan equally, attribute about three quarters of the likelihood gain over continued cross-entropy to weighting each plan by how well it explains the sequence.
bullets: Few-step random-order sampling mixes over token-reveal plans, but standard cross-entropy does not optimize this mixture likelihood.
Mix-FT uses an importance-weighted likelihood bound for the model’s own sampler, requiring no teacher, architectural changes, or sampler changes.
On LLaDA-8B and a public 110M-parameter block diffusion model, it outperformed continued cross-entropy and competing diffusion fine-tuning methods across tested step counts and judges.
It maintained gains with half as many model evaluations and under both random-order and confidence-based decoding.
Text8 likelihood controls attribute roughly three quarters of the gain over continued cross-entropy to weighting reveal plans by how well they explain the sequence.

papers.selection_reason: Fine-tuning method for diffusion language models to improve few-step sampling.
papers.title: Train the Sampler You Run: Few-Step Masked Diffusion Language Models via Mixture-Likelihood Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: Mix-FT trains masked diffusion language models against the likelihood of the few-step sampler they actually use, improving generation quality without changing the model or sampler.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled fine manipulation capabilities, yet performing tasks that require working memory remains a key challenge. Most existing VLA architectures operate under a Markovian assumption, mapping only the current observation to an action, which leads to failure in non-Markovian environments. Inspired by the human 'inner monologue', we propose Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory (HeLM), a hierarchical VLA framework that maintains task-relevant history in explicit language through factorized event detection and event-triggered memory updates. We evaluate HeLM across 10 non-Markovian real-world tasks with 56 variants, including five newly formulated inter-episode tasks that require persistent context across task boundaries. HeLM improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and achieves 78% subtask success on compositional generalization tasks, while using up to 4.5x less memory and running 2.5x faster than the keyframe baseline at long horizons.
bullets: Addresses failures of Markovian VLA models on tasks requiring working memory and persistent context.
Uses factorized event detection with event-triggered updates to maintain task-relevant language history.
Evaluated on 10 real-world non-Markovian tasks with 56 variants, including five inter-episode tasks.
Improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and reaches 78% subtask success on compositional generalization.
Uses up to 4.5× less memory and runs 2.5× faster than a keyframe baseline at long horizons.

papers.tldr: HeLM enables VLA agents to handle non-Markovian manipulation by storing task-relevant history as hierarchical, explicit language memory.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has shown considerable potential for novel view synthesis (NVS) and 3D reconstruction. Feed-forward methods avoid costly per-scene optimization, but fixed image or spatial resolutions limit their ability to allocate primitives according to local complexity. We present OctreeSplat, a hierarchical octree-guided feed-forward Gaussian splatting. OctreeSplat extracts multi-view features and geometric priors from a frozen visual foundation model (VFM), constructs a hierarchical octree, and predicts densification scores. The resulting representation allocates Gaussian primitives at spatially varying densities according to local complexity. Stochastic solids volume rendering improves depth rendering, strengthens geometric supervision, and supports surface reconstruction. When camera parameters are available, an optional test-time optimization (TTO) module improves agreement between predicted and ground-truth parameters. Training updates only 76 million additional parameters and requires 35 GPU-hours. Experiments on Replica, TUM, Tanks and Temples, and DTU demonstrate competitive RGB view synthesis, depth synthesis, and surface reconstruction. OctreeSplat reduces the number of Gaussian primitives while maintaining high reconstruction quality.
bullets: Addresses fixed-resolution limitations in feed-forward Gaussian splatting by adapting representation density to local scene complexity.
Extracts multi-view features and geometric priors from a frozen visual foundation model to build an octree and predict densification scores.
Uses stochastic solids volume rendering to improve depth rendering, geometric supervision, and surface reconstruction.
An optional test-time optimization module improves camera-parameter agreement when camera information is available.
Experiments across Replica, TUM, Tanks and Temples, and DTU show competitive RGB/depth synthesis and surface reconstruction with fewer Gaussian primitives.

Stochastic-solid volume rendering provides RGB and geometric supervision.

papers.title: OctreeSplat: Hierarchical Octree-Guided Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: OctreeSplat uses a VFM-guided hierarchical octree to adaptively allocate Gaussian primitives for efficient feed-forward 3D reconstruction and view synthesis.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing detailed geometry and realistic appearance from a single RGB image is essential yet fundamentally challenging due to inherent ambiguities such as occlusion, lighting variations, and texture-geometry entanglement. While recent diffusion-based generative models have significantly improved novel view synthesis, existing approaches suffer from two critical limitations: lack of cross-view geometric consistency and insufficient cross-domain semantic alignment. To address these issues, we introduce UniCross3D, a unified cross-view and cross-domain diffusion framework designed explicitly for consistent and physically coherent 3D generation. UniCross3D features two novel contributions: (1) a cross-view latent regularization that enforces cross-view geometric consistency across synthesized viewpoints by penalizing latent variance, and (2) a cross-domain mutual information objective grounded in the physics of image formation, explicitly aligning synthesized color and normal maps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniCross3D achieves significantly improved view consistency and semantic alignment over state-of-the-art methods and yields higher-fidelity reconstructions, particularly under challenging textures and ambiguous viewpoints.
bullets: Addresses ambiguities from occlusion, lighting, and texture–geometry entanglement in single-RGB-image 3D generation.
Uses cross-view latent regularization to reduce geometric inconsistencies across synthesized viewpoints.
Introduces a physics-grounded mutual information objective to align synthesized color and normal maps.
Experiments report better view consistency, semantic alignment, and reconstruction fidelity, especially for challenging textures and ambiguous viewpoints.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of UNICROSS3D framework.

Figure 4: For text-to-3D evaluation, we compare two categories of methods based on their input modality. Image-to-3D approaches such as UNICROSS3D and CRM [WWC*24] take as input the image generated by a text-to-image model (SDXL [PEL*23]) from the given text prompt (see first column). In contrast, text-to-3D methods such as IT3D [CZY*24] and JointDreamer [JZH*24] directly consume the raw text prompt as input to synthesize the 3D shape.

Figure 1: Comparisons with the state-of-the-art 2D-to-3D method [LLL*24]. The proposed method, UNICROSS3D, addresses two fundamental limitations of the previous 2D-to-3D generation methods: (a) cross-view inconsistency and (b) cross-domain inconsistency. (a) Previous approaches suffer from geometric distortions and inconsistent appearances across synthesized views due to stochastic sampling and insufficient latent regularization. These issues become especially severe when generating views from novel, unseen viewpoints. (b) Existing methods lack strong consistency between color and normal maps, often misinterpreting texture patterns as geometry or producing shading that does not align with the actual surface normals. This results in semantic misalignments that degrade the physical plausibility of the reconstructed 3D shapes.

papers.tldr: UniCross3D improves single-image 3D reconstruction by jointly enforcing cross-view geometric consistency and cross-domain alignment during diffusion generation.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon dexterous manipulation remains a fundamental challenge for robot learning, requiring the composition of multiple skills, precise bimanual coordination, generalizable visual understanding, and robust skill transitions. Yet existing manipulation benchmarks largely emphasize isolated skills or support only a limited range of end-effectors, making these capabilities difficult to evaluate systematically. We introduce DexArena, a benchmark designed to evaluate learning and generalization in long-horizon bimanual dexterous manipulation. DexArena features 10 long-horizon tasks and 30 stage-level tasks spanning diverse household and industrial scenarios. Each long-horizon task is composed of explicitly defined stages with physically grounded success conditions, enabling reliable evaluation of both intermediate progress and end-to-end task completion. A unified benchmark interface and verified human-teleoperated demonstrations enable testing different policy learning algorithms, with standardized simulation configurations, scene randomization, trajectory replay, and task-level evaluation. Through extensive baseline experiments, we identify substantial challenges in precise manipulation, generalization to scene variation, and skill composition. DexArena establishes a challenging and reproducible benchmark for developing robot learning methods that move toward generalizable long-horizon dexterous behavior.
bullets: Covers 10 long-horizon and 30 stage-level tasks across household and industrial scenarios.
Tasks use explicitly defined stages and physically grounded success conditions to measure both intermediate progress and end-to-end completion.
Provides a standardized interface with human-teleoperated demonstrations, simulation configurations, scene randomization, trajectory replay, and task-level evaluation.
Baseline experiments reveal persistent challenges in precise manipulation, scene-variation generalization, and composing skills.

papers.abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) are a standard way to keep a planner inside a safe set, but they assume control affine dynamics, a barrier function given in closed form, and a known nominal controller. Integral control barrier functions (ICBFs) remove the first assumption and absorb input constraints, yet they still assume a given nominal controller and a barrier function. In this work, we present an approach to learn all three from data, using neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs) for the dynamics, imitation for the nominal controller, and supervised regression for the barrier function. The learned dynamics, nominal controller, and the barrier function are used to build the ICBF filter constraint analytically. Furthermore, the barrier is trained on viability rather than geometry, meaning that a state counts as safe only if some emergency maneuver can still avoid the constraint under the actuator limits, a correction that geometric labels miss entirely and that grows with speed. Actuator limits then enter the online program as hard bounds while the learned barrier rows may be relaxed, which keeps the program solvable at every state and the actuator limits exact, and we bound how far the input it returns can drift from the one the true models would give. On agile racing with a 6-D dynamic bicycle, the filter removes all 12 unsafe episodes from 200 held out layouts at an unchanged success rate and above 100 Hz on one CPU core, holds the input constraint on every episode of a benchmark where a jointly trained baseline holds it on 53.38%, and keeps that advantage under large errors in the plant friction.
bullets: Addresses CBF limitations requiring control-affine dynamics, known barriers, and a nominal controller.
Learns dynamics with neural ODEs, the nominal controller by imitation, and the barrier through supervised viability regression.
Uses emergency-maneuver viability labels, capturing speed-dependent safety that geometric labels miss.
Keeps actuator limits hard, allows learned barrier constraints to relax for solvability, and bounds deviation from the true-model input.
On agile racing tasks, removed all 12 unsafe held-out episodes, ran above 100 Hz on one CPU core, and maintained actuator constraints under friction-model errors.

(c) Fraction of geometrically safe states that viability relabels unsafe, by speed: the signature of a viability set rather than a smoothed obstacle indicator.

papers.abstract: With the growing deployment of large language models (LLMs) across diverse domains, concerns regarding their safety have grown substantially. LLM unlearning has emerged as a pivotal approach to removing harmful or unlawful content while maintaining utility. Despite increasing interest, the challenges of continual unlearning, which is common in real-world scenarios, remain underexplored. Successive unlearning tasks often lead to intensified utility degradation. To effectively unlearn targeted knowledge while preserving LLM utility, it is essential to minimize changes in model parameters by selectively updating those linked to the target knowledge, thereby ensuring other knowledge remains unaffected. Building on the task vector framework, we propose a new method named ALKN (Adaptive Localization of Knowledge Negation), which uses dynamic masking to sparsify training gradients and adaptively adjusts unlearning intensity based on inter-task relationships. Comprehensive experiments across three well-established LLM unlearning datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms baseline methods in both unlearning effectiveness and utility retention under continual unlearning settings.
bullets: Addresses utility degradation caused by successive unlearning tasks.
Uses a task-vector framework with dynamic masking to sparsify training gradients.
Adaptively adjusts unlearning intensity according to relationships between tasks.
Evaluated on three established LLM unlearning datasets under continual unlearning settings.
Reports better unlearning effectiveness and utility retention than baseline methods.

papers.abstract: Universal humanoid motion tracking is essential for enabling humanoid robots to perform diverse tasks in human environments. To capture the wide diversity of human motions, mixture-of-experts (MoE) policies have been widely adopted, leveraging dynamic routing to enhance policy expressiveness. However, we identify that divergence between old and updated policies can be misestimated during policy-gradient updates of MoE policies, due to their dynamic routing. Because most policy-gradient algorithms regulate policy updates based on the divergence, this misestimation can lead to either overly conservative or excessively large updates, which can yield a suboptimal policy. In this paper, we propose Mixture of Experts with Alternating Policy Optimization (MAPO), which alternately optimizes the router and the experts to avoid the divergence misestimation. MAPO consistently tracks 182 motions that PPO with MoE fails to track, whereas PPO with MoE tracks only one motion that MAPO fails to track. MAPO also attains the highest tracking success rate among the compared methods and the lowest tracking error across most error metrics, demonstrating its superior performance. Videos can be found on the project website: https://mapo-corl2026.github.io/MAPO/
bullets: MoE policies can misestimate old–updated policy divergence because their routing changes dynamically.
This misestimation may cause overly conservative or excessively large policy updates, producing suboptimal policies.
MAPO alternates optimization of the router and expert policies to address this issue.
MAPO consistently tracks 182 motions that PPO with MoE fails to track, while PPO with MoE tracks only one motion MAPO fails to track.
Among the compared methods, MAPO achieves the highest tracking success rate and lowest error across most metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Comparison of update mechanisms between MAPO and PPO. Pink, blue, and blue-green indicate the router, experts, and mixed policy, respectively. The bars in the center show the magnitudes of each component and the mixed policy. The shaded regions show the implicit trust regions induced by clipping. (a, c) MAPO measures the KL divergence of each component separately, allowing proper regulation of the updates. (b, d) In contrast, because PPO measures the KL divergence of the mixed policy, the clipping mechanism may fail to regulate the updates properly.

Figure 1: MAPO resolves the divergence misestimation problem that hinders policy-gradient training of MoE policies, enabling effective humanoid motion tracking. Consequently, MAPO successfully tracks a wide variety of human motions, including complex whole-body motions, such as (a) sitting in mid-air, (b) abrupt full-body turns, (c) deep crouching, and (d) one-footed spinning. Red spheres denote the reference motion targets.

papers.abstract: Enterprise conversational systems require memory to personalize interactions, retain information across sessions, and maintain conversational coherence. At enterprise scale, however, memory must not only retrieve relevant information accurately but also provide it efficiently to the answer-generation model. Existing memory systems face a trade-off between retrieval accuracy and context efficiency. Retrieving more context can improve recall but increases inference cost and latency. We present Scalaris, a scalable enterprise memory architecture that addresses this trade-off through a unified long-term and short-term memory design. We propose that user interactions and assistant responses possess distinct characteristics and roles in a conversation: user interactions capture evolving knowledge about the user and provide value across sessions, whereas assistant responses must be stored efficiently so that only information relevant to the current query is retrieved. We therefore treat them separately and support each with specialized representations and ingestion/retrieval pipelines. Scalaris reaches 92.2 % accuracy on LongMemEval-S and 90.77 % on LoCoMo using Qwen3-32B, state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks, while supplying the answer-generation model with approximately 10 times fewer retrieved context tokens than Hindsight, a leading memory system for conversational AI. When integrated with our proprietary closed-source AI assistants, Scalaris improved overall response quality by 36 %. Together, these results establish Scalaris as a cost-effective framework for building scalable, personalized conversational AI systems.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between memory retrieval accuracy and inference cost/latency at enterprise scale.
Uses unified long- and short-term memory with specialized representations and ingestion/retrieval pipelines for user interactions versus assistant responses.
Achieves 92.2% on LongMemEval-S and 90.77% on LoCoMo using Qwen3-32B, reported as state-of-the-art on both benchmarks.
Supplies roughly 10× fewer retrieved context tokens than Hindsight and improved response quality by 36% in proprietary assistants.
Scope: evaluated on two memory benchmarks and proprietary closed-source assistants; broader applicability is not established by the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Flow diagram of the ingestion and retrieval pipeline of Scalaris. The ingestion phase organizes user interactions as facts, entities, and summaries in the graph store, assistant responses as atomic units in the vector store, and stores each incoming user query and AI response verbatim in the history store. The retrieval pipeline begins by reformulating the incoming query, which is then used to retrieve information from the graph and vector stores. Summaries are fetched directly from the graph store, and the N most recent exchanges from the history store. All retrieved components are combined during context assembly and passed to the answering system.

Figure 1: Overview of Scalaris’s source-aware memory organization. User interactions are processed to maintain relevant facts, relevant entities, and user and session summaries in a temporal knowledge graph. Assistant responses are decomposed into independently retrievable atomic units and stored in a vector store. In parallel, both user interactions and assistant responses are preserved verbatim in a shared history store.

Figure 2: An illustrative instance of context retrieval in Scalaris. Long-term memory supplies the user’s preference for fuel economy together with prior Honda Civic interactions, while short-term memory supplies the Relevant Assistant Messages, session summary, and recent turns (only the latest exchange is shown, for visual clarity). Together these resolve the referent, let the agent determine that only Corolla information must be retrieved, and enable personalization by focusing on fuel economy and including trade-offs.

Figure 4: Evaluation prompt used by the GPT-4o judge to compare two AI assistant responses. papers.abstract: On-device multimodal agents are limited by two deployment mismatches: pretrained attention structures may not divide evenly across the compute cores of an edge accelerator, causing irregular partitions; and standard prefix caching keeps historical visual tokens in the persistent KV cache, whose capacity grows with the number of rounds. We present PARC, which combines parallelism-aligned structured pruning with lifetime-aware KV-cache reorganization. At the model level, it uses first-order Taylor importance and grouped-query-attention-aware selection to make attention dimensions divisible by the target core count while preserving the query-to-key/value ratio and head dimension. At runtime, it separates the system prompt, persistent text history, and transient visual observations by lifetime, updating text history during tool execution so that historical images leave the persistent cache and more interaction rounds fit a fixed budget. On 2,062 GUI actions, the incremental interface shows no accuracy regression, and task-aware recovery training restores 98.7% of the action-type accuracy gap and the coordinate hit rate to the original level. Under seven-core deployment, hardware-aligned pruning reduces vision-encoder latency by 11.4%, improves decoding throughput by 23.8%, and lowers per-heap high-water memory by 12.7%; a parameter-matched control confirms that the speedup stems mainly from core alignment rather than parameter reduction.
bullets: Addresses uneven attention partitioning across edge-accelerator cores and cache growth from multi-round visual interactions.
Uses Taylor-based, grouped-query-attention-aware structured pruning while preserving key attention dimensions and target-core divisibility.
Reorganizes KV-cache contents by lifetime, updating text history during tool execution so past images do not remain persistent.
On 2,062 GUI actions, the incremental interface shows no accuracy regression; recovery training restores 98.7% of the action-type accuracy gap and coordinate hit rate to the original level.
With seven cores, pruning reduces vision-encoder latency by 11.4%, raises decoding throughput by 23.8%, and lowers per-heap memory high-water usage by 12.7%.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have recently shown great promise in robotic control, benefiting from the future imagination capability of large-scale pretrained video models. However, most existing WAMs require explicitly imagining future states at test time, incurring substantial computational overhead and latency that make them unsuitable for real-time robotic control. In this paper, we propose W2A, a two-stage distillation framework for real-time robotic manipulation that distills intermediate denoising representations from a video diffusion model into an action model during training, while entirely discarding the video model at test time. We hypothesize that although video latent representations are high-dimensional, a compressed low-dimensional subspace is sufficient to provide effective supervision for action generation. This makes it possible to transfer such information effectively into an action model. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world settings demonstrate competitive success rates while significantly improving inference efficiency. On LIBERO, W2A achieves a 95.9% average success rate. More importantly, W2A achieves about 21x faster inference than the representative WAM baseline.
bullets: Existing world action models often imagine future states at test time, creating prohibitive computational overhead for real-time control.
W2A uses two-stage training to transfer intermediate denoising representations from a pretrained video diffusion model into an action model.
The approach assumes effective supervision can be compressed into a low-dimensional subspace of the video latent space.
The video model is discarded at deployment, reducing inference cost while retaining useful world priors.
W2A reports a 95.9% average success rate on LIBERO and approximately 21× faster inference than a representative WAM baseline.

papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is increasingly constrained by the cost of maintaining an ever-growing KV-cache. Low-rank K/V projections provide a promising way to compress the KV-cache with minimal quality loss, but prior work has largely optimized KV-cache compression in isolation, leaving distributed inference, especially with tensor parallelism where attention computation is partitioned across multiple GPUs, largely underexplored. We make two observations: (i) tensor-parallel communication is an important cost when deploying low-rank KV-cache compression in distributed inference; and (ii) Value compression can be associated with the output projection, allowing the same low-rank Value representation to reduce both Value-cache width and tensor-parallel communication. Based on these observations, we propose BasisKV, a low-rank KV-cache compression method for communication-intensive, long-context LLM inference. BasisKV jointly optimizes the low-rank factors across per-GPU attention partitions against the complete attention output, rather than fitting each partition in isolation. The compressed Value cache is further reused to help identify which Key pages should be accessed: it predicts part of the Key information needed for routing, while a Key-specific residual stores what cannot be recovered from Value. The original Keys are then retrieved only for the selected pages to compute exact QK scores. Across multiple LLM families and system settings, BasisKV achieves a better quality--efficiency tradeoff than existing low-rank baselines, reaching up to 1.42x end-to-end speedup under 8-GPU tensor-parallel inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/alexz949/BasisKV
bullets: Targets KV-cache growth and communication overhead in distributed, tensor-parallel inference.
Jointly optimizes low-rank factors across GPU attention partitions against the complete attention output.
Uses compressed Values to predict routing-relevant Key information, with a Key residual for unrecoverable details.
Retrieves original Keys only for selected pages to compute exact query–key scores.
Reports a better quality–efficiency tradeoff than low-rank baselines, with up to 1.42× end-to-end speedup in 8-GPU tensor-parallel inference.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents are vulnerable to perturbations of their observed state inputs. Prior works often constrain state adversaries with $L_p$-norm uncertainty sets and evaluate policy performance under the resulting perturbations. However, in continuous control tasks like robotics control, different state dimensions have distinct physical meanings and influence policy behavior to different degrees, which $L_p$-norm sets fail to capture or explain. Moreover, it is important to identify when and along which state dimensions a policy is vulnerable, independently of the algorithm used to train it. In this paper, we focus on evaluation-time attacks applied to pretrained policies. We propose \textbf{P}erformance-\textbf{D}egradation \textbf{N}on-\textbf{U}niform \textbf{U}ncertainty \textbf{S}et (\method{}), an interpretable formulation of uncertainty sets for state perturbations. \method{} is state-dependent, dimension-wise non-uniform, and can be synthesized online during policy evaluation. We first formulate an ideal constrained optimization problem for \method{} computation, then introduce a surrogate constraint to make the problem tractable. Experiments across multiple continuous-control environments, policy algorithms, and state attacks show that \method{} reveals variation in policy sensitivity across states and dimensions, while its performance degradation is moderately controlled.
bullets: Targets a limitation of uniform $L_p$-norm sets, which overlook the differing meanings and policy influence of state dimensions.
Focuses on attacks against pretrained policies during evaluation, independently of the training algorithm.
Formulates an ideal constrained optimization problem and uses a tractable surrogate to synthesize the uncertainty sets online.
Experiments across continuous-control environments, policy algorithms, and state attacks show varying sensitivity across states and dimensions with moderately controlled performance degradation.

papers.abstract: 3D generation, editing, and completion are typically treated as regenerating the complete 3D asset under task-specific constraints, even when only a local region needs modification. This leads to task isolation, inconsistency in content that should remain unchanged, and dependence on task-specific paired data. We address these issues with a key observation: the three tasks all synthesize a designated region while keeping the rest intact---the full region for generation, the target region for editing, and the missing region for completion. We term this paradigm Selective Modeling and build SeMo3D upon it; it naturally unifies the three tasks, preserves unchanged content by construction, and enables training without paired editing or completion data, since any 3D asset can be partitioned into a selected region and its context. For training, we propose region-selective denoising, which randomly selects regions of varying sizes on standard 3D assets and applies noise and loss only to them, jointly learning all three tasks. For architecture, we propose Omni3DiT, a multi-condition 3D diffusion transformer that distinguishes regions to create from those to retain and fuses image, text, and point guidance for fine-grained control. Experiments across three benchmarks show SeMo3D surpasses state-of-the-art methods on all tasks, delivering multimodal controllability in generation and strong consistency and accuracy in editing and completion. SeMo3D further serves as a unified modeling tool for agents, enabling efficient 3D creation through natural-language interaction. Project page: https://xiaokunsun.github.io/SeMo3D.github.io/.
bullets: Reframes all three tasks as synthesizing a selected region while retaining contextual content.
Uses region-selective denoising to train jointly on standard 3D assets without paired editing or completion data.
Introduces Omni3DiT, a multi-condition 3D diffusion transformer supporting image, text, and point guidance.
Experiments across three benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance across generation, editing, and completion, with controllability and consistency.
Supports natural-language-driven 3D creation for agents.

papers.abstract: A competent learned controller already recovers from many disturbances. Improving it means learning a correction, and learning when not to apply it. Freezing a skill's parameters does not settle the second half. In a controller that routes among frozen skills, a new entry rule can redirect the states an old skill succeeded on. We therefore constrain entry instead of parameters. Each update searches for a feedback skill at a measured failure. It fits an entry rule that reads observations and rejects every state on an accumulated successful trajectory. The skill is admitted only if the composed controller reproduces the new recovery on its own and replays every protected trajectory exactly. A finite-trajectory condition states when this preserves the previous controller. One mechanism runs on four streams: two motions on each of two humanoid systems. Two updates per stream add 62 recoveries over 192 withheld perturbations, and lose none of the base controller's successes. We then price that guarantee. Removing the constraint recovers 33 more conditions but stops eight protected ones from completing at all, and excluding only what admission proves necessary recovers none of that cost.
bullets: Targets the problem of new skill-entry rules redirecting states where existing skills already succeed.
Learns a feedback recovery skill at a measured failure and an observation-based entry rule.
Admission requires reproducing the new recovery and replaying every accumulated protected trajectory exactly.
Across four humanoid motion streams, two updates per stream added 62 recoveries over 192 withheld perturbations without losing base successes.
Removing the preservation constraint recovered 33 additional conditions but caused eight protected trajectories to fail; the approach is scoped to finite recorded trajectories.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical control scales robot behavior by separating task-level planning from low-level control. In dynamic, high-dimensional tasks, however, a fixed planner-to-policy interface can fail when contacts, balance, or disturbances evolve faster than high-level policy updates. Execution therefore requires choosing not only which low-level policy to run, but also which policy-specific goal should be given to it. We formulate this problem as policy orchestration: runtime selection of a policy-goal pair that is likely to remain feasible while tracking the planner target. We develop EPO, an energy-based policy orchestrator for modular goal-conditioned policy families. For each policy, EPO learns a composite energy over low-level goals, where lower energy corresponds to higher feasibility and more accurate target realization. At runtime, EPO refines each policy's goal and executes the lowest-energy policy-goal pair. Because energies are policy-specific, new policies can be incorporated by learning their own energy models, without retraining the existing policies or a centralized scheduler. In simulation, EPO improves the empirical precision-robustness trade-off by refining policy-specific goals before selectively switching among policies based on energy scores. We further demonstrate sim-to-real deployment of the same frozen policies and energy models on real humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://yewr.github.io/epo
bullets: Addresses failures of fixed planner-to-policy interfaces when contacts, balance, or disturbances change faster than high-level updates.
Learns a composite energy for each modular goal-conditioned policy, where lower energy indicates greater feasibility and more accurate target realization.
Refines candidate goals and executes the lowest-energy policy–goal pair during runtime orchestration.
New policies can be added by learning separate energy models without retraining existing policies or a centralized scheduler.
Simulation shows improved precision–robustness trade-offs, with sim-to-real deployment on humanoid loco-manipulation tasks using frozen policies and energy models.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate visual assets through text-based formats such as SVG and CAD, but these symbolic representations describe images using high-level primitives rather than explicit raster values. We ask whether LLMs can instead generate pixel images directly through their existing vocabulary, without a learned image tokenizer or decoder. We introduce PixelBench, a benchmark for text-to-pixel (T2P) and image-to-pixel (I2P) generation across multiple resolutions, together with a complementary pixel-understanding evaluation. Models generate an RGB color palette followed by a grid of indices specifying the palette color of each output pixel. In T2P, the strongest models produce recognizable images directly from text. In I2P, the strongest models outperform palette-matched downsampling and specialized pixelization algorithms at low resolutions. Pixel-understanding performance correlates strongly with generation performance. A resolution-scaling study shows that pixel-generation performance often improves initially before declining at high resolutions. Finally, we introduce Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which augments visual instruction tuning with caption-palette-grid trajectories. We post-train Molmo2-4B from its pretraining checkpoint by mixing general instruction data with our curated PRT data, improving performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks, indicating that explicit pixel reconstruction can provide useful auxiliary supervision.
bullets: Benchmarks text-to-pixel, image-to-pixel, and pixel-understanding across multiple resolutions without image tokenizers or decoders.
Models generate an RGB palette followed by grid indices assigning a palette color to each pixel.
Leading models produce recognizable text-generated images and outperform palette-matched downsampling and specialized pixelization methods for low-resolution image-to-pixel tasks.
Pixel understanding correlates strongly with generation quality, while performance typically improves at first and then declines as resolution increases.
Pixel Reconstruction Tuning improves Molmo2-4B across 16 visual-centric benchmarks by adding caption–palette–grid trajectories to instruction tuning.

papers.abstract: Safe autonomous driving requires more than recognizing the current scene: the ego vehicle must anticipate how surrounding traffic participants will evolve under its own motion. However, existing end-to-end driving models typically encode scenes into dense visual or BEV features, leaving object-level interactions implicit. We propose (INTERACT INTERaction-aware Action-Conditioned Trajectory learning), a three-stage framework that learns a slot-based object-centric world model from unlabeled driving videos and transfers it to trajectory planning. INTERACT first learns recurrent slots that group dense visual features into temporally structured scene-entity representations without object annotations. It then infers latent ego actions from slot context and video transitions, and uses them to condition future slot prediction, capturing how ego motion and surrounding entities co-evolve. Finally, the learned slots, latent actions, and future slot predictions are distilled into a trajectory planner to guide trajectory generation and selection. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM and nuScenes validate the effectiveness of INTERACT. In particular, it achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM, with improvements in safety-critical collision metrics.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of predicting how surrounding traffic evolves in response to the ego vehicle’s motion.
Uses recurrent slots to discover temporally structured scene entities without object annotations.
Infers latent ego actions and conditions future slot prediction on those actions to model interaction dynamics.
Distills learned slots, actions, and future predictions into a trajectory planner.
Validated on NAVSIM and nuScenes, achieving state-of-the-art NAVSIM performance with improved collision-related metrics.

papers.abstract: Clinical evidence is inherently relational: medical images are interpreted with prior studies, cross-modal examinations, reports, and localized findings, and retrieving relevant evidence is therefore central to clinical interpretation. Recent foundation models increasingly encode these heterogeneous sources into shared embedding spaces, yet existing embedding evaluation often focuses on isolated matches, leaving unclear whether current models retrieve relevant evidence across changes in modality, appearance, and granularity. We introduce MedHEB, a unified benchmark with 107 retrieval tasks from 54 datasets, including both in-distribution and held-out-source evaluation, across three axes: evidence form (2D images, 3D volumes, text), pairing type (image--image, image--text, text--text, and modality-bridging visual matching), and relevance granularity (global, question-conditioned, region-level). Under a single ranking protocol, MedHEB varies clinically relevant evidence definitions to test whether embedding proximity remains meaningful across heterogeneous evidence, including modality-bridging visual retrieval and region-level text-to-region retrieval. Across representative models, performance is uneven across retrieval families: models strong on conventional image--text or text--text retrieval are less reliable on modality-bridging and region-level tasks. Current embedding spaces capture some clinical relationships well but do not yet provide balanced retrieval across heterogeneous evidence. We further provide MedEmb, an MLLM-based reference embedding model trained on the MedHEB ID split, as a reproducible baseline for unified 2D--3D--text medical retrieval. We release MedHEB with preprocessing scripts, evaluation code, access manifests, and MedEmb to support research on clinically meaningful medical embeddings.

Covers 2D images, 3D volumes, and text; image–image, image–text, text–text, and modality-bridging retrieval.
Tests global, question-conditioned, and region-level relevance under a unified ranking protocol.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in open-world environments where safety risks cannot be fully predefined. However, most existing guardrail mechanisms remain static, relying on fixed rules, prompts, or classifiers that generalize poorly to emerging risks. Here we present EVOLVE, a tool-level self-evolving defense framework that formulates agent security as a process of cumulative security evolution. Inspired by how human societies transform experiences into transferable protective knowledge, EVOLVE externalizes security knowledge into executable guardrail tools that are continuously inherited, independently audited, and iteratively refined through lifelong interaction. Across multiple benchmarks, backbone models, and embodied environments, EVOLVE consistently outperforms existing defenses across diverse risk scenarios with +22\% average F1 score. We further validate the framework in real-world robotic and autonomous agent systems. Our results suggest that scalable agent safety may require continuously evolving defense systems rather than static guardrails.
bullets: Targets the limitations of static rules, prompts, and classifiers in open-world environments with unforeseen safety risks.
Models security as cumulative evolution, externalizing protective knowledge into reusable executable guardrail tools.
Tools are continuously inherited, independently audited, and iteratively refined through lifelong interaction.
Across benchmarks, backbone models, and embodied environments, EVOLVE reports a 22% average F1 improvement over existing defenses.
The framework is additionally validated in real-world robotic and autonomous-agent systems, though its scope centers on continuously evolving defenses.

papers.abstract: Hyperspectral videos provide rich spectral signatures for robust tracking under challenging conditions such as camouflage and low illumination. However, limited hyperspectral annotations and the large RGB-hyperspectral domain gap hinder the direct use of modern temporally pretrained RGB trackers. We propose SProTrack, a multimodal framework that transfers temporal knowledge from pretrained RGB trackers to the hyperspectral domain through latent spectral prompting. The key idea is to decouple temporal modeling from spectral adaptation, allowing temporal dynamics to be inherited from RGB foundation models while hyperspectral information is learned from unlabeled data in a self-supervised manner. Unlike band-selection methods that discard most spectral information or prompt-based approaches that rely on local-search crops, SProTrack learns a global, scene-level spectral representation from the full hyperspectral frame using an autoencoder. This latent representation is used to guide spectral prompt extraction while a pretrained RGB tracker preserves strong temporal modeling on RGB-compatible inputs. By encoding spectral-spatial structure into compact latent prompts, SProTrack bridges the RGB-hyperspectral modality gap without extensive retraining or dense supervision. Experiments on HOT2020 and HOT2023 demonstrate that SProTrack achieves the best overall performance, with strong results across all spectral domains.
bullets: Addresses limited hyperspectral annotations and the RGB–hyperspectral domain gap in object tracking.
Uses an autoencoder to learn global spectral-spatial representations from full hyperspectral frames.
Decouples temporal modeling from spectral adaptation, retaining RGB tracker dynamics while adapting spectral information.
Avoids discarding bands and reliance on local-search crops by generating compact latent prompts.
Reports the best overall performance on HOT2020 and HOT2023, with strong results across spectral domains.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SProTrack. (a) Stage 1: a Spectral-Spatial AutoEncoder (SSAE) is trained self-supervisedly to encode hyperspectral frames into compact latent representations. (b) Stage 2: the frozen SSAE encoder generates latent spectral prompts, injected into a transformer-based RGB backbone for layer-wise modulation. (c) Spectral-Spatial block: a spectral branch models inter-band dependencies via Mamba and a spatial branch captures local patterns via convolution; their fused outputs, stacked across blocks, form the encoder, with a symmetric decoder for reconstruction. Detailed implementations are provided in the supplementary material.
