papers.abstract: Robot policies still fail at everyday manipulation: an unfamiliar task, an object never held before, a scene that changes mid-motion, a skill that should improve with use. They fail despite pretraining on over a million trajectories, pooled from dozens of robots at great expense, while a child acquires all of these abilities within a few years of learning from a single body. This survey argues that the gap is one of design, and proposes designs for the next generation of robot models, drawn from how the nervous system solves the same problems. From the body we take compliance: the policy commands stiffness alongside position, so the controller yields where the task allows and presses where it must, which greatly lowers the demand for precise position output. From the visual system, where a fast pathway for action runs in parallel with the slow pathway for recognition, we take a dedicated fast vision system for motor behavior: it precomputes the quantities the policy needs and drives a reactive policy at camera rate. From the cerebellum we take a predictor beside the policy that forecasts the consequence of each command and recalibrates from its own error. From motor cortex we take a single model that composes action units from primitives, verifies each at a sensory boundary, practices the weakest unit with a hypothesis in mind, and reasons each attempt closer to the goal. Proven primitives are then consolidated from code into weights, so they run fluently and respond quickly the next time. Together these describe a robot that acts on its own initiative, the basis of deployment and recursive self-improvement, and we offer each proposal as a hypothesis to be tested.
bullets: Robot policies struggle with novel tasks, objects, changing scenes, and continual skill improvement despite extensive trajectory data.
It draws design principles from the body, visual system, cerebellum, and motor cortex.
Key proposals include stiffness-aware control, a fast action-oriented vision pathway, predictive models for self-calibration, and compositional primitive-based planning.
The framework emphasizes sensory verification, targeted practice, reasoning toward goals, and consolidating successful primitives into model weights.
The proposals are presented as hypotheses for future testing, with autonomous initiative and recursive self-improvement as the broader goal.

figures.caption: Figure 26: Consolidation advances a primitive from a script over many functions to an end-to-end policy. (a) At first the model writes a perception pipeline that computes the slot’s pose and the key’s geometry in the hand before calling the orient template, which runs by Cartesian control. (b) Next the model outputs both values directly from the images and supplies them to the same template, so the explicit measuring code is no longer needed. (c) In the end the template lives in the orient experts of the model’s mixture-of-experts trunk: the action head of the same model reads their latent, no number is passed, and the action stream reacts at the control rate.
Figure 3: Opposing muscles set torque and stiffness separately. The difference of flexor and extensor pull sets the net torque, and their sum sets the stiffness at the same pose.

Figure 1: A child has three abilities that current robot policies lack. Top: a boy opens an unfamiliar drawer on the first try, while a policy finds no training handle to copy. Middle: a girl catches a flying toy, while a robot is still reasoning about shape and coordinates when the toy lands. Bottom: the boy’s piano playing improves with days of practice, while a robot never trained on the piano cannot learn it or improve over time, because its learning stopped the day it was deployed.

Figure 7: Vision and touch build a single object model, and each sense fills in what the other cannot. Vision covers the visible surfaces, while touch supplies weight, texture, slipperiness, and compliance, and explores the occluded back.
Figure 4: Contact supplies the surface detail. A yielding wrist and a soft towel follow the bumps, so the controller computes fewer corrections.

Figure 6: Slowly adapting (SA) afferents report steady pressure and rapidly adapting (RA) ones report change, so the four classes split what touch carries. The traces are schematic responses to a ramp-and-hold skin indentation: SA afferents sustain firing during the hold, RA afferents respond transiently during pressing and release, and SA2 afferents also fire at a low rate before contact, driven by resting skin stretch. RA afferents can also fire during ongoing motion or vibration. Spike counts and timing are illustrative rather than measured; responses depend on the stimulus and afferent [194, 2].

Figure 13: In the prevailing model, the dorsal stream is a bank of parallel channels. The figure expands the dorsal branch of Figure 12 and draws the motion areas MT and MST, which that figure folds into the parietal box, as a separate stage. Each visual area estimates one quantity the body needs (where to look, what is moving, what is within reach, where to reach, how to turn and shape the hand, and what a tool in hand reaches) and sends it to a partner in premotor, motor, or oculomotor areas; the italic line in each visual box names the reference frame the channel works in (Section 4.2.4). Each label names an area’s dominant contribution rather than its only one [331].
Figure 9: Descending signals from cortex turn down predicted or irrelevant tactile channels and turn up the task-relevant one, so the fingertip signal arrives at high contrast.

Figure 17: Joint World Action Models let the prediction loss train the action head, while cascaded ones only pass predicted frames forward. In the cascaded design a video generator synthesizes predicted frames and a separate inverse-dynamics module reads actions off them. In the joint design a shared backbone trained under one generative objective feeds a state head that generates future frames, which some variants skip at test time, and an action head that emits the executed chunk.

Figure 27: The practice agent finds the error-prone part across attempts, corrects it during inference, and hands the corrected record to consolidation. (a) Over seven episodes of opening a lock, insert passes rarely, and the blame falls on orient’s angle, which is solved with an arbitrary offset after several model calls and fails most first attempts; it is unfamiliar and error prone and is practiced first. (b) During practice the direction to move after each attempt comes from the graded goal test, the forecast against the outcome, or the model’s reasoning; the interval halves until the goal test fires, and the angle that passed is stored. (c) Consolidation then improves the coding strategy that finds the keypoints, trains the model to output the values directly, and trains the orient experts of the trunk, so the orient primitive becomes familiar.

Figure 21: Actions attach to a vision-language backbone in one of three ways. (a) The first generation bins each action dimension and decodes actions as text tokens, one at a time. (b) The current generation keeps the backbone and attaches a small action expert that attends to its features and denoises a noisy chunk into continuous actions by diffusion or flow matching; proprioception enters the expert, as drawn, in 𝜋0 and GR00T N1, and the backbone in SmolVLA [42, 40, 354]. (c) An omni model has no head. Images, text, and actions are tokens in one sequence, so the same network predicts the next action and the next image. Purple: transformer with pretrained weights. Teal: images, text, proprioception, and the action expert. Gray: discrete action tokens and the noise the expert denoises.

Figure 20: One model composes familiar primitives into a new solution. Reach, grasp, orient, and tool use, none of them learned for this task, combine to retrieve an out-of-reach key, and the same model turns the plan into movement.
Figure 10: When an object’s properties cannot be seen, the robot should probe before it commits. Lifting, tilting, and pressing within safe bounds each test a hypothesis the camera cannot settle.
Figure 2: The slot walls supply the rod’s trajectory. The hand pushes along the slot and yields across it, so the walls shape the path and the controller has far less of the curve to compute.
Figure 11: The same ball is read twice, by the two visual streams in the brain. The ventral stream resolves its pattern and identity; the dorsal stream resolves its trajectory and guides the catch.
Figure 5: Touch alone finds the handle and opens the door. With eyes closed the hand feels its way to the handle, turns it and pushes the door open; in the dark a camera has nothing to offer.

Figure 24: Motor cortex is M1, premotor cortex, and SMA, reciprocally connected, with three cortical inputs: prefrontal goals enter through SMA and premotor cortex, the parietal state enters through premotor cortex and, from S1 and area 5, M1 directly, and ACC reaches SMA and M1 through the cingulate motor areas [364]. M1 carries most of the corticospinal tract, and SMA, premotor, and cingulate areas each add a direct projection that bypasses it [100]. Motor cortex also drives the brainstem pathways and runs loops through the basal ganglia and cerebellum [230]; reflex afferents return to the cord and touch and proprioception return to parietal cortex. Only the principal pathways are drawn.

Figure 14: A visually guided action must re-express the retinal report in the frame its effector needs. The same dumpling has different coordinates in each frame along the chain: eye, head, body, hand, tool, and object.

Figure 8: Three neurons carry a fingertip signal to primary somatosensory cortex (S1), a chain short enough to leave time for a tactile correction within about 75 ms. The first-order neuron ascends on the same side through the spinal dorsal column to the cuneate nucleus of the medulla; the second-order neuron crosses there and ascends to the ventral posterolateral (VPL) thalamus; the third-order neuron projects to S1 on the side opposite the stimulated hand. Each line ends in a dot at its synapse, and the legend colors mark the three cell bodies. Other branches and circuits are omitted [197].

Figure 15: A second viewpoint reveals what the head camera cannot see. The mug body partly hides its far-side handle from the head camera. Moving the wrist camera of the free hand to a side viewpoint reveals more of the handle before grasping. Teal arrows mark viewing directions; the curved gray arrow marks the wrist motion.

Figure 19: The same nuclear prediction leaves by two routes. Ascending (left), it reaches cortex through the ventrolateral thalamus. Descending (right), it joins the command in flight at the brainstem and spinal cord. Both arrive within tens of milliseconds of the command, before sensory feedback could alter it through cortex.

Figure 18: The cerebellar circuit is three synapses deep, wide in the middle, and local along its length. The highlighted paths trace one local circuit: parallel fibers run only a few millimeters [315], and about forty Purkinje cells converge on one nuclear neuron [309], so coupling between body parts is local by construction. The inferior olive (amber) returns the prediction error over one climbing fiber per Purkinje cell, which adjusts the parallel-fiber synapses that were active when the faulty prediction was made. Counts are rough human figures [12, 285, 202].

Figure 16: Having tossed the ball herself, she knows from the throw where and when it will land. A copy of the tossing command is enough to forecast the ball’s arrival, so the right hand is already in place while the ball is still in the air. The faint circles show predicted positions of the same ball.

Figure 22: A robot learns mostly before it leaves the factory and afterwards executes the learned policy; a human begins with a genome rather than pretrained weights and does most of its learning after birth, through play, practice, and observation.

Figure 25: One action unit runs as a loop; the arrows show the flow of control rather than anatomical pathways. Purple marks the four stages, run clockwise, and teal what each stage reads. Solid teal arrows have direct support: the cerebellar forecast amends the unit in flight [31, 252] and sustains and times the cortical preparation of the next [122, 60]. Dashed arrows are hypotheses: whether the forecast also times the basal ganglia release is untested, and pre-SMA, which launches units and switches between them [205, 178], is proposed here to do so on the ACC verdict. Assigning one area to each stage is a simplification; each area takes part in more than one.

Figure 12: Vision for action and vision for recognition separate after V1, and a collicular route bypasses cortex entirely. The geniculate route through V1 divides into a dorsal stream through posterior parietal cortex to premotor and motor areas (vision for action) and a ventral stream through V2 and V4 into inferotemporal cortex (vision for recognition); a separate collicular route drives fast orienting of eyes and head without cortex.

Figure 23: Unlocking a door is four action units in a fixed order, reach, orient, insert, and rotate, and each ends at a sensory event: the tip reaches the slot, the key aligns, it stops at the end, the lock turns.

Table 1: No single sensor family combines fine resolution, kilohertz speed, and shear. Resolution and speed are order-of-magnitude values typical of each family, and the cited works are representative examples. A taxel (“tactile pixel”) is one sensing point on the skin.
Table 3: Discrepancies between the current robot stack and the nervous system, stage by stage, and the proposal each chapter derives from the gap.

Table 2: Four afferent classes split touch by receptive-field size and adaptation [186, 389, 194]. The pairing of SA2 afferents with Ruffini endings is disputed, since the human fingertip holds few such endings [303]. Figure 6 uses the same codes.

papers.tldr: This survey proposes brain-inspired designs to make robot learning more adaptive, efficient, and capable of everyday manipulation beyond large-scale pretraining.

papers.abstract: Learned sparse attention, used in production models such as DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5, lets each query attend to only k keys chosen by a lightweight indexer, but the indexer still scores every key in the prefix. At one million tokens, this selection takes more than half of prefill time. Two-stage selection over contiguous blocks, as in HiSA, reduces this cost, but its recall declines as context grows at a fixed candidate budget. We present AttentionIndex, which routes each query over an inverted-file index that groups indexer keys by similarity and refines the candidates with the native indexer score. AttentionIndex builds the index during prefill, making new keys searchable immediately, reusing previous clustering to keep maintenance cheap, and exposing each query only to clusters built from its own prefix. On GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at one million tokens, AttentionIndex delivers 1.3-1.8 times the prefill throughput of exhaustive selection, and at throughput within 5% of HiSA, it recovers 17.0 and 10.0 percentage points more of the exhaustive top-k, respectively. AttentionIndex also improves accuracy on long-context benchmarks by up to 18.4 percentage points over HiSA at the same candidate budget.
bullets: Exhaustively scoring every prefix key makes sparse-attention selection a major prefill bottleneck at long contexts.
It routes queries through a causal inverted-file index, then reranks retrieved candidates with the native indexer score.
The index is built online during prefill, immediately includes new keys, reuses prior clustering, and restricts queries to prefix-derived clusters.
On GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at one million tokens, it achieves 1.3–1.8× exhaustive-selection prefill throughput.
At similar throughput to HiSA, it recovers 17.0 and 10.0 more percentage points of exhaustive top-k recall and improves long-context accuracy by up to 18.4 points.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of AttentionIndex for one indexed layer. Update path: new keys enter an open window and are searchable at once; every W keys the window is sealed into local clusters, and every R tokens a refit regroups the prefix. A new index version is visible only to queries whose prefix contains all of its keys.

papers.abstract: General-purpose robot policies must work across robots, tasks, and environments, yet the variation that makes physical trials informative also makes them difficult to reproduce. We introduce RoboColosseum, a distributed evaluation framework that combines unified policy serving and standardized protocols across a network of locally operated robots in diverse environments. Our initial study evaluates five vision-language-action (VLA) policies and three frontier AI agents across four embodiments (SO-101, Franka, Bimanual-YAM, and G1 Humanoid). The Open Track compares models without task-specific adaptation in blinded, pairwise trials under matched local conditions. The Fine-tune Track measures how well VLA policies adapt to 20 tasks across all four embodiments when each policy receives the same 100 demonstrations per task. Across 5,699 pairwise Open Track comparisons at 124 sites, frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies, while all systems struggle to complete open-world tasks reliably. After fine-tuning, GR00T N1.7 leads on SO-101 and pi0.5 leads on Franka and Bimanual-YAM. Policy rankings show weak agreement across embodiment-specific task suites (Kendall W = 0.24). Open Track rankings poorly predict relative performance after fine-tuning, with substantial rank reversals on all three embodiments shared between tracks. Measuring partial progress reveals differences that task success alone misses. On the G1 Humanoid, no policy completes any of the five tasks, yet average progress ranges from 13.3% to 23.2% across policies. Open Track rankings stabilize as trials accumulate, and active matchmaking achieves comparable ranking agreement with substantially fewer physical trials than uniform sampling. These results show how distributed physical evaluation can reveal where robot policies generalize, how well they adapt to new tasks, and how far they progress on tasks they fail to complete.
bullets: Standardizes policy serving and evaluation protocols across locally operated robots at 124 sites.
Evaluates five VLA policies and three frontier agents across four embodiments using open and fine-tuning tracks.
Frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies in open-world trials, but all systems struggle with reliable completion.
Fine-tuning changes model rankings substantially across embodiments; Open Track rankings poorly predict adapted performance.
Partial-progress metrics and active matchmaking provide more informative and trial-efficient evaluation than success rates and uniform sampling.

figures.caption: Figure 1 RoboColosseum overview. RoboColosseum connects distributed evaluation sites through shared robot interfaces, policy-serving infrastructure, and two complementary evaluation tracks. In the Fine-tune Track, policies receive the same 100 demonstrations per task and are evaluated on predefined tasks using common success and progress criteria. In the OpenTrack, policies are evaluated without additional task-specific adaptation through blinded, pairwise comparisons under matched local conditions, while tasks and environments vary across comparisons. The results shown for both tracks are based on evaluations we conducted from 17 September to 28 October 2026. The project spans SO-101, Franka in the DROID configuration, Bimanual-YAM, and Unitree G1, with participation determined by track and model compatibility. The lower panels illustrate track-specific evaluation outputs and examples of physical evaluation settings. The global network depicts the broader project vision; the scope of completed experiments is reported separately.

papers.abstract: Online Active Learning (OAL) aims to extend deep learning from static inference after offline training to continuous adaptation during real-time interaction with a changing physical environment. This transition is essential for safety-critical applications, but it raises a central theoretical question: whether the online parameter update process remains stable when scaled to multilayer neural architectures. This paper develops a stability-focused OAL framework. The framework uses prediction error as a feedback signal to update a structured deep model, thereby linking online learning with Lyapunov-based energy minimization. We show that prediction error convergence alone is insufficient for global parameter convergence because multilayer networks may admit high-dimensional manifolds of equivalent output solutions. The analysis therefore separates output error regulation, internal zero dynamics, interlayer coupling, and parameter convergence. Persistency of excitation and active damping are then used to remove the residual null-space modes that remain after output error convergence. A cascaded Lyapunov analysis establishes asymptotic stability of the overall OAL learning process, while monotonic activation functions and diffeomorphic layer mappings provide the uniqueness condition for the target parameter trajectory. The resulting proof provides a theoretical basis for applying online adaptive learning to large-scale neural systems in nonstationary and safety-critical settings.
bullets: Addresses whether online parameter updates remain stable as neural systems adapt continuously in changing, safety-critical environments.
Uses prediction error as feedback and decomposes stability into output regulation, internal zero dynamics, interlayer coupling, and parameter convergence.
Shows that prediction-error convergence alone cannot ensure unique parameter convergence because multilayer networks may have equivalent-output solution manifolds.
Uses persistency of excitation and active damping to eliminate residual null-space modes.
A cascaded Lyapunov analysis proves asymptotic stability under monotonic activations and diffeomorphic layer mappings.

papers.abstract: Long-term conversational memory faces a timing mismatch: write-time summaries and graphs organize history before a future query is known, while independent retrieval can allocate a limited evidence budget to redundant or fragmented turns. We introduce Chain on Demand (CoD), a query-time evidence organization framework over an unchanged turn-level memory. Given a broad candidate pool, CoD constructs a temporary evidence chain by allocating a fixed anchor budget according to query relevance, lexical diversity relative to selected anchors, and newly covered query terms, followed by deterministic restoration of each selected anchor's same-session neighborhood. The resulting chain is used only for the current query, while the underlying conversational memory remains unchanged. In a paired comparison over all 1,986 LoCoMo questions, CoD achieves 82.2% accuracy on 1,540 non-adversarial questions and 76.3% on all 1,986 questions. On LongMemEval-S, one fixed configuration that indexes both user and assistant turns obtains 86.6% across all 500 questions. These results show that long-term memory can preserve the original conversation while deferring evidence organization until the information need is known.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between write-time memory organization and unknown future queries.
Builds a temporary evidence chain from relevant, lexically diverse anchors that add new query terms.
Restores each selected anchor’s same-session neighborhood to preserve conversational context.
Achieves 82.2% accuracy on 1,540 non-adversarial LoCoMo questions and 76.3% across all 1,986; reaches 86.6% on LongMemEval-S.
Scope: results use fixed configurations and depend on the evaluated conversational-memory benchmarks.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict scene changes to guide robot actions, yet their RGB futures entangle state changes with appearance and lack 3D geometry. Recent WAMs add geometry as a training signal or a control interface, or build native 3D models, but decide what geometry to model rather than how the action should read it. Intuitively, control-relevant cues lie at embodiment--object interactions and their transitions, yet probing existing WAMs reveals that their action attention underweights these interactions in favor of the rest of the embodiment. To focus the action on these interactions, we present Gnomon4D, a WAM that jointly generates future video, robot actions, and GeoDelta, a video-aligned 4D geometric motion field recording the image-plane displacement and depth change of embodiment and object points. With the embodiment and objects in one field, their relative motion, which marks an interaction, can be read off. Guided by this motion and the task, Interaction-Salient Attention (InSAttn) selects where the action reads, and Transition-Anchored Aggregation (TransAgg) selects when, around grasp and release. As GeoDelta encodes surface motion rather than embodiment-specific controls, it serves as a human--robot quasi-action that links action-free pretraining on EgoManip-5000H, which we curate, to robot mid-training on Robot-30H. Gnomon4D leads on RoboTwin~2.0, VLABench, and RoboDojo, and outperforms real-robot baselines, especially under visual shifts. Project page: https://droliven.github.io/Gnomon4D.
bullets: Addresses the problem that RGB-based world-action models entangle appearance and state changes, while action attention often overlooks control-relevant interactions.
Jointly predicts future video, robot actions, and GeoDelta, a video-aligned 4D field of image-plane displacement and depth changes for embodiment and object points.
Uses Interaction-Salient Attention to select where to attend and Transition-Anchored Aggregation to focus around grasp and release transitions.
GeoDelta enables action-free pretraining on EgoManip-5000H and robot mid-training on Robot-30H by acting as a human–robot quasi-action.
Leads on RoboTwin 2.0, VLABench, and RoboDojo, and outperforms real-robot baselines, particularly under visual shifts.

papers.abstract: A GUI command can be correct at the interface level yet still produce an incorrect assembly. An agent must identify the relevant components, respect their structural relationships, and determine which parts should move during recovery. We introduce MAGAR-Bench, a benchmark of 4,000 multimodal samples from 26 assembly families that separates Assembly Decision, Atomic Action, and Minimal Rework. For rework, the objective counts distinct moved parts within the validated recovery candidate set for each state, rather than the number of actions. We also introduce MAGAR, a selective correction framework built on a frozen policy obtained by supervised fine-tuning. Its key design matches correction granularity to output dependencies. Structured candidates revise assembly fields and rework scope, while complete action candidates keep native GUI primitives coupled with their parameters. A learned selector retains the original prediction unless a candidate passes a task-specific intervention threshold. On recorded states from held-out assembly families, MAGAR improves Overall, the task-balanced aggregate, from 37.50 to 41.39, with gains on all three tasks. Across 209 interventions, 70 correct an error and 22 introduce one. These results support task-specific correction while highlighting the remaining tradeoff between fixing errors and preserving reliable predictions.
bullets: MAGAR-Bench contains 4,000 multimodal samples across 26 assembly families and evaluates Assembly Decision, Atomic Action, and Minimal Rework separately.
Minimal Rework measures the distinct parts moved within a validated recovery candidate set, rather than counting actions.
MAGAR uses a frozen supervised-fine-tuned policy, task-specific candidate structures, and a learned selector with intervention thresholds.
On held-out assembly families, Overall task-balanced performance rises from 37.50 to 41.39, with gains on all three tasks.
Among 209 interventions, 70 fix errors and 22 introduce errors, showing a remaining tradeoff between correction and prediction preservation.

papers.abstract: Does effective swimming with multiple underactuated soft arms require explicit coordination between arms? We hypothesize that an eight-arm swimmer can control its swimming speed and direction by independently learning each arm's actuation amplitude under a shared rhythmic drive, without prescribed inter-arm phase coupling. To test this hypothesis, we compare three reinforcement learning-based control strategies using proximal policy optimization (PPO): (1) learning arm-specific actuation amplitudes without inter-arm phase coupling, (2) learning actuation amplitudes with prescribed inter-arm phase coupling, and (3) directly learning actuator commands through end-to-end PPO without an explicit rhythmic structure. Across 200 episodes with randomized three-dimensional velocity commands, the controller without phase coupling satisfies the tracking criterion in 169 episodes, compared with 117 for the phase-coupled controller and 28 for end-to-end PPO. Straight-line swimming and commanded direction-change trials further demonstrate more accurate velocity tracking without phase coupling. These findings suggest that effective eight-arm swimming does not require prescribed inter-arm phase coupling, but can instead be achieved through learned arm-specific amplitude modulation within a rhythmic control structure.
bullets: The study tests whether explicit inter-arm coordination is necessary for swimming with underactuated soft arms.
It compares three PPO controllers: amplitude learning without phase coupling, amplitude learning with prescribed coupling, and end-to-end actuator-command learning.
Without phase coupling, the controller met the tracking criterion in 169 of 200 randomized 3D-velocity episodes, versus 117 with coupling and 28 for end-to-end PPO.
Straight-line and direction-change trials also showed more accurate velocity tracking without prescribed phase coupling.
The result is scoped to the tested eight-arm swimmer and control setup; it supports learned amplitude modulation within a rhythmic structure.

Observations from MuJoCo drive the policy, while rewards guide updates to the policy and value networks. The policy modulates a shared Hopf oscillator and the actuator mapping. papers.abstract: Semantic-ID-based (SID) generative recommendation (GR) represents each item as a sequence of discrete tokens and predicts the next item through autoregressive SID generation. However, existing methods face two challenges. First, insufficient shared context modeling for user sequences: full-history and recent behaviors provide overlapping yet complementary evidence, but modeling them within a single sequence may dilute current cues, whereas processing them through separate streams may fail to coordinate them. Second, insufficient personalized adaptation in progressive SID decisions: although decoder states evolve with generated prefixes, existing models typically use a shared output-side transformation across recommendation instances, without explicitly selecting a transformation suited to the current user need. To address these challenges, we propose Multi-View Thinking with Adaptive Generation (MV-Thinker), a framework that Thinks Globally and Generates Personally. First, Multi-View Temporal Thinking uses view-specific thinking queries and readers over overlapping full-history and recent-history views, coordinating both sources into complementary user-conditioned contexts before SID generation. Second, Hierarchical Residual Adaptation organizes lightweight adapters into nested residual paths before a shared vocabulary projection, adaptively transforming context-bearing decoder states for SID decisions. Extensive experiments on four public datasets demonstrate that MV-Thinker consistently outperforms strong discriminative and generative recommendation baselines across multiple ranking metrics. The implementation code and datasets are available on: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MV-Thinker
bullets: Addresses weak coordination between full-history and recent-history user views, and limited personalization during progressive SID generation.
Uses Multi-View Temporal Thinking with view-specific queries and readers to combine complementary history contexts.
Applies Hierarchical Residual Adaptation to transform decoder states through lightweight, nested residual paths before SID prediction.
Experiments on four public datasets show consistent gains over discriminative and generative baselines across multiple ranking metrics.
Scope: focuses on semantic-ID autoregressive recommendation and relies on overlapping full- and recent-history views.

papers.abstract: Treating morphology and control as separate design problems has constrained the efficiency and adaptability of quadrupedal robots, while current co-design approaches are often constrained by restricted design spaces. We overcome this limit by introducing Dogger, a bio-inspired quadruped with modular three-segment legs, four-bar linkages and adjustable passive knee compliance. A two-stage framework combining reinforcement learning and Bayesian optimization is developed: the morphology-conditioned control policy is trained across designs and then held fixed during task-specific design selection. The resulting designs and policies deployed zero-shot reduce the cost of transport by 18.6% and 35.7% for inspection and payload-carrying tasks. Comparisons demonstrate that full geometry-compliance co-design outperforms fixed and restricted design scopes. Cross-task tests further reveal distinct task-specific morphologies with shared mechanical trade-offs. These results provide hardware-level evidence that expanding the physical design space alongside learned control is essential to realize the full potential of task-driven morphology-control co-design in legged robotics.
bullets: Introduces Dogger, a bio-inspired quadruped with modular three-segment legs, four-bar linkages, and adjustable passive knee compliance.
Trains a morphology-conditioned control policy across designs, then selects task-specific designs while keeping the policy fixed.
Zero-shot deployments reduce cost of transport by 18.6% for inspection and 35.7% for payload-carrying tasks.
Full geometry–compliance co-design outperforms fixed or restricted design spaces.
Cross-task results show distinct task-specific morphologies sharing mechanical trade-offs.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Two-stage optimization for morphology-control co-design. In Step 1, a universal control policy πu is trained in simulation across a broad design space D using RL. papers.abstract: Numerical labels often specify a set of possible values: a measurement is rounded, a laboratory test reports only a bound, or a program is stopped at a timeout. We introduce boundary marginalization, the first method that trains an autoregressive language model on the exact likelihood of such observations through its existing digit tokens. A fixed-width, order-preserving numeral representation groups consecutive grid values under shared digit prefixes. An interval is a union of such groups, so its exact probability and gradient follow from at most two boundary paths, the successive digit prefixes of its endpoints, each of length logarithmic in the number of grid values. The resulting objective unifies precise, rounded, bounded, and censored supervision and trains digit decisions at the resolution supplied by each observation. The same computation supports exact distributional queries and unbiased gradients for the continuous ranked probability score on exact labels. Experiments show recovery of a conditional distribution from rounded and censored reports alone, improved likelihood on naturally censored molecular measurements, and more accurate code latency distributions on two backbones. Exact interval updates remain tractable as the numerical support grows to one million values.
bullets: Represents numerical values with fixed-width, order-preserving digit strings so observed intervals share digit prefixes.
Computes exact interval likelihoods and gradients using at most two endpoint paths, with logarithmic complexity in support size.
Unifies precise, rounded, bounded, and censored supervision while matching training resolution to observation precision.
Also enables exact distributional queries and unbiased continuous ranked probability score gradients for exact labels.

Experiments recover distributions from incomplete reports and improve likelihood or latency-distribution accuracy across molecular measurements and two code models; tractability extends to one million values.

papers.abstract: Reasoning-augmented recommender systems (RecSys) enhance user preference modeling by generating reasoning trajectories over historical interactions before making recommendations. Knowledge distillation provides a practical paradigm for transferring such reasoning capabilities from powerful large language models to lightweight RecSys. However, existing methods typically rely on a single fixed teacher, remain constrained by the teacher knowledge ceiling, and indiscriminately distill teacher-generated trajectories without assessing their actual utility for downstream recommendation. To address these limitations, we propose MUSE (Multi-Teacher Utility-guided Selection with Self-Exploration), an adaptive reasoning distillation framework that jointly improves reasoning generation and reasoning utilization. MUSE first constructs a diverse reasoning pool using multiple teacher LLMs and progressively augments it via student self-exploration, enabling the student to leverage the strengths of different teachers and gradually explore reasoning strategies beyond teacher imitation. We then develop Rank-Gain Utility Assessment (RGUA), which evaluates each candidate according to the normalized full-catalog rank improvement of the ground-truth item and identifies the most and least recommendation-beneficial trajectories. Based on these utility-aware trajectory pairs, we introduce dual-level contrastive learning objectives that guide the student generator to prefer beneficial reasoning while training the recommendation encoder to more effectively exploit recommendation-relevant preference evidence. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of single-teacher distillation and indiscriminate use of generated reasoning.
Builds a diverse reasoning pool from multiple teacher LLMs and expands it through student self-exploration.
Uses Rank-Gain Utility Assessment to identify reasoning trajectories that improve the ground-truth item’s catalog ranking.
Applies dual-level contrastive learning to favor beneficial reasoning and strengthen recommendation-relevant preference encoding.
Experiments on three real-world datasets show effectiveness and robustness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of MUSE. Figure 1: Illustration of the limitations of existing reasoning distillation methods and the proposed MUSE. MUSE instead adaptively selects recommendation-beneficial reasoning from multiple teachers and progressively incorporates superior student-generated reasoning through self-exploration, enabling more effective reasoning distillation for recommendation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has improved the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) across a wide range of tasks. However, token-level RL assigns an action's advantage to the entire generated response, including tokens specifying the parsed action, reasoning chains, and malformed content. Although the environment executes only the parsed action, variation in how the action is expressed in natural language can introduce additional variance into policy-gradient estimates. We propose RLiD (Reinforcement Learning in the Decision plane), a framework that directly optimizes the probabilities of executable action options. RLiD compiles observations, an optional compact memory, and a labeled action menu into the model input, and uses a large decision model (LDM) to select an action in a single forward pass. By eliminating autoregressive token generation and bypassing action parsing, RLiD avoids invalid action outputs and improves RL rollout efficiency. Our analysis shows that, within a fixed text policy, marginalizing over alternative realizations of the same action removes a zero-mean gradient component without changing the expected update. We further distill trained LDM policies into generative LLMs through supervision on their action trajectories. Experiments on ARC, Countdown, and Sokoban demonstrate improved performance or lower computational cost across several settings. On ALFWorld, the complete training and distillation pipeline reaches 99.3% success in 12.7 H100 GPU-hours, compared with 86.6% in 17.3 GPU-hours for token-level RL of the same LLM. With compiled memory, our strongest Qwen2.5-1.5B LDM and distilled generative LLM achieve 100% success on all 134 unseen and 140 seen ALFWorld evaluation games.
bullets: Token-level RL adds gradient variance because rewards are assigned to reasoning, action-expression, and malformed-output tokens that the environment does not execute.
RLiD compiles observations, optional compact memory, and a labeled action menu, then selects an action in one forward pass with a large decision model.
The framework avoids autoregressive generation and action parsing, reducing invalid actions and computational overhead.
Its analysis shows that marginalizing over equivalent textual realizations removes a zero-mean gradient component without changing the expected update.

Across ARC, Countdown, Sokoban, and ALFWorld, RLiD improves performance or reduces cost; on ALFWorld, the full pipeline achieves 99.3% success in 12.7 H100 GPU-hours versus 86.6% in 17.3 GPU-hours for token-level RL.

papers.abstract: Cohort memory can support LLM-based recommendation planning through group-level user profiles and advice. As outcome feedback becomes available, this guidance may need to be updated while preserving the underlying observations. We present RecGroupMemory, a workflow that provides this memory to an orchestration LLM and separates memory construction from feedback-based revision. It uses feedback from the previous day to revise decision guidance, while validation checks keep selected source values unchanged. Online comparisons were conducted among Taobao users with low purchasing power selected by the business team. Relative to a no-memory baseline, memory without feedback and memory with feedback showed increases of 1.58% and 1.78%, respectively, in the number of guided transaction users.
bullets: Addresses the need to revise recommendation guidance as outcome feedback arrives without changing underlying cohort data.
Separates memory construction from feedback-based revision for an orchestration LLM.
Uses previous-day feedback to update decision guidance, with validation checks protecting selected source values.
In an online Taobao comparison, guided transaction users increased 1.58% without feedback and 1.78% with feedback versus no memory.
Evaluation focused on Taobao users with low purchasing power selected by the business team.

papers.abstract: LLM planning often relies on reactive executors (e.g., ReAct) that generate a single action at each step to remain grounded in the latest observations, incurring substantial inference cost. Batched executors reduce this cost by predicting multiple actions in a single model invocation, yet they are prone to compounding errors, as intermediate observations are ignored. We propose an expectation-observation consistency verification (EOCV) mechanism for batched executors, preserving grounding while improving efficiency. The mechanism generates expectations of action outcomes and compares them with the resulting observations. Consistency permits continued execution, whereas mismatches trigger early termination and replanning from the current observation. Experiments on text-based and multimodal benchmarks across multiple backbones show broadly comparable average task performance between EOCV and reactive executors, with a 29-35% reduction in average weighted token usage. Moreover, the mechanism is model-agnostic and remains effective when integrated into state-of-the-art planners.
bullets: Reactive executors stay grounded but require costly per-step inference; batched executors are cheaper but can compound errors.
EOCV generates expectations for batched actions and compares them with observed outcomes during execution.
Consistent observations allow execution to continue, while mismatches trigger early termination and replanning.
Across text-based and multimodal benchmarks, EOCV maintained broadly comparable average task performance to reactive executors while reducing average weighted token usage by 29–35%.
The mechanism is model-agnostic and integrates with state-of-the-art planners.

figures.caption: Figure 2: An overview of EOCV. papers.abstract: Residual connections give each Transformer block access to all earlier layers only through one fixed sum, broadcast to all of the block's inputs. This broadcast bottleneck imposes three constraints: the query, key, value and residual inputs of a block, which we call its roles, read the same vector; all hidden dimensions within a role share one set of weights over earlier layers; and every earlier layer has the same fixed weight for every token. We propose the Multi-Role Multi-Group Mixing Residual (M3), which removes all three: every role, and every group of hidden dimensions within a role, reads its own token-dependent mixture of all earlier layers. M3 starts as an exact residual connection and adds as little as 1.4% parameters and 1.8% FLOPs. From 100M to 1.4B parameters, M3Former outperforms the Transformer and coarse-grained cross-layer connections at every size, matching a Transformer 1.19-1.34x the size of the one it modifies, trained with 1.4-1.8x the compute. Relaxing only some of the constraints recovers only part of this gain. M3Former also improves sparse mixture-of-experts models of up to 4.6B parameters and trains more stably in deeper networks. Code: https://github.com/Kingchet10/m3former
bullets: Fixed residual connections force query, key, value, and residual inputs to share the same earlier-layer mixture.
M3 gives each role and hidden-dimension group its own token-dependent mixture of all preceding layers.
It begins as an exact residual connection and adds only 1.4% parameters and 1.8% FLOPs.
Across 100M–1.4B parameters, it outperforms standard Transformers and coarser cross-layer methods, with gains comparable to scaling the Transformer 1.19–1.34×.
It also improves sparse mixture-of-experts models up to 4.6B parameters and stabilizes deeper networks.

papers.abstract: Engineering drawings specify mechanical parts through orthographic projections. Recognizing which part a drawing depicts underlies part search, design reuse, and digitization, yet no public benchmark measures whether vision models can do it. We introduce Blueprint2CAD, a benchmark for drawing-to-render correspondence: given an orthographic line drawing and a shaded render, usually from another viewpoint, decide whether they show the same part. Its data layer, BlueCAD-30K, applies an open drafting pipeline to 29,925 Zero-to-CAD models, adding view-aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings from six viewpoints, and surface-type metadata. Frozen encoders retrieve the matching part from a 10,000-model gallery with up to 65% Recall@1 when viewpoints are known but 43% when they are not, and the four encoders we test lie within six points of each other: viewpoint, not backbone, is the bottleneck. Six zero-shot vision-language models reach only 0.52-0.67 verification accuracy, with model-specific Yes/No biases that chain-of-thought shifts but does not remove; a quick LoRA fine-tuning on in-domain pairs improves verification accuracy by a few points but sharpens these biases and leaves the viewpoint failure intact.
bullets: Introduces drawing-to-render correspondence: deciding whether an orthographic drawing and shaded render depict the same part.
Builds BlueCAD-30K from 29,925 CAD models with aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings across six viewpoints, and surface metadata.
Frozen encoders achieve up to 65% Recall@1 with known viewpoints, falling to 43% when viewpoints are unknown.
Zero-shot vision-language models reach 0.52–0.67 verification accuracy and exhibit model-specific Yes/No biases.
LoRA fine-tuning slightly improves accuracy but does not solve viewpoint failures and intensifies bias.

papers.abstract: Geometry-aware neural operators face substantial computational and memory demands when learning across complex physical domains. We introduce Architecture-Aware Mixed Precision (AA-MP), a replica-exchange training strategy that allocates numerical precision according to replica roles and architecture-specific operations. By retaining FP32 for refinement while selectively employing BF16 for exploration, AA-MP preserves predictive accuracy while improving training efficiency. Across fluid dynamics and three-dimensional structural mechanics benchmarks, AA-MP achieves comparable accuracy to full-precision training over an ensemble of runs, while reducing hot-replica peak GPU memory by 46.9% and training time by up to 25.8%. It also outperforms naive Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) in memory efficiency and computational cost, with increasing memory advantages at larger model and geometry scales. Ablation studies show that retaining FP32 in the cold-replica is important for predictive accuracy, while additional FP32 operations in the exploratory replica provide limited benefits relative to their computational cost. Finally, conformal prediction for uncertainty calibration shows that AA-MP achieves near-nominal coverage with narrower prediction intervals than the alternatives. These results advance the scalability of geometry-aware scientific machine learning by reducing computational costs without compromising predictive accuracy or uncertainty quantification.
bullets: Targets the computational and memory demands of neural operators on complex physical domains.
Assigns precision by replica role and architecture operation, using FP32 for refinement and selective BF16 for exploration.
Maintains accuracy comparable to full-precision training across fluid dynamics and 3D structural mechanics benchmarks.
Reduces hot-replica peak GPU memory by 46.9% and training time by up to 25.8%, outperforming naive AMP in efficiency.
Conformal prediction achieves near-nominal coverage with narrower prediction intervals; scope is evaluated on the reported benchmark domains.

The exploratory hot replica uses a manually controlled BF16 live model, while the latent reduction, prediction-error and energy reductions, master parameters, and optimizer states are maintained in FP32. papers.abstract: Cooperative perception (CP) requires substantial communication bandwidth to exchange sensing information among connected agents. A variety of compression techniques have been proposed to reduce transmission costs while retaining task-relevant information. However, most existing methods follow a frame-wise compression paradigm, overlooking temporal predictability and repeatedly transmitting information that could be inferred from historical context. To address these limitations, we propose MirrorComm, the first world model-based communication-efficient CP framework. Specifically, mirrored world models at the transmitter and receiver predict the transmitter's current observation from a shared history of its reconstructed observations. The transmitter compares this prediction with its current observation and selectively transmits observation updates to correct prediction errors, reducing repeated transmission of predictable information. Experiments on the OPV2V dataset across two downstream tasks including object detection and semantic segmentation show that MirrorComm reduces communication bandwidth requirements by up to approximately 66-fold while maintaining comparable performance to a state-of-the-art (SOTA) method. Ablation studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of the individual components.
bullets: Targets the bandwidth burden of exchanging sensing information among connected agents.
Predicts current observations from shared histories at both transmitter and receiver, exploiting temporal predictability.
Sends only updates that correct prediction errors instead of repeatedly transmitting predictable content.
On OPV2V object detection and semantic segmentation, reduces bandwidth by up to approximately 66-fold with comparable performance to a SOTA method.
Ablation studies support the effectiveness of its individual components.

papers.abstract: No algorithm is best on all problems, but a real warehouse is a narrow problem: its layout and processes rarely change. Operators still run one general multi-robot planner at many sites, because experts cannot tune it for each one. In this work, which we call Late Autumn, we explore whether LLM coding agents running autonomous research can specialize a general planner for one site, trading generality for throughput, much as post-training adapts a pretrained LLM to one task. We study six campaigns on a lifelong planner that combines task assignment with multi-agent path finding, on a floor modeled on an existing automated warehouse. We find that (1) the agents raise throughput by 22--60%, and the gains hold on unseen seeds; (2) they rediscover known MAPF mechanisms, such as corridor-exit priorities, local guidance, and rollouts, and independent campaigns find the same bottleneck; (3) the gains largely carry over to another layout, a larger fleet, and other service times, shrink with a smaller fleet, and mostly vanish under an outbound-heavy demand mix; and (4) each final patch (0.7k--2.4k lines) is a chain of scored commits with a median step of 27 lines, so experts can review it, and review finds problems that the score misses; some patches multiply planner compute by over 100x. LLM agents can therefore turn each site's bias into extra throughput at little engineering cost, with reviewable patches; we expect experts to shift toward designing insightful metrics and fast simulators that mirror the real problem.
bullets: Specialization targets fixed warehouse layouts and processes, where site-specific tuning can trade generality for throughput.
Across six autonomous campaigns, agents improved throughput by 22–60% and retained gains on unseen seeds.
Agents rediscovered MAPF techniques including corridor-exit priorities, local guidance, and rollouts, with campaigns identifying similar bottlenecks.
Benefits mostly transferred across layouts, fleet sizes, and service times, but weakened with smaller fleets and largely disappeared for outbound-heavy demand.
Final patches were reviewable chains of small scored commits, but review exposed issues missed by scoring and some patches increased planner compute by over 100×.

papers.title: Late Autumn: LLM Agents Specialize a General Multi-Robot Planner for One Warehouse
papers.tldr: LLM coding agents can specialize a general multi-robot warehouse planner for one site, substantially improving throughput through small, reviewable code changes, though gains depend on workload and may require much more computation.

papers.abstract: Hyperspectral image (HSI) classification requires the representation of contiguous spectral signatures and spatial context under limited labeled supervision. Vision test-time training (TTT) offers an alternative to fixed-weight token mixing by performing self-supervised inner-model updates on the input sequence, but its application to center-pixel HSI classification remains insufficiently characterized. We present ViTTT-HSI, a spectral-spatial adaptation of the vision test-time training (ViT3) architecture. A spectral-aware embedding stem extracts ordered-band information using spectral convolution and forms spatial tokens without reducing their spatial resolution. Two ViT3-based TTT encoder blocks perform patch-conditioned token mixing, followed by the fusion of center-pixel and neighborhood-average features for classification. We evaluate the framework on Indian Pines, Pavia University, Salinas, and Houston 2013 using ten random seeds and dataset-specific training fractions of 1% or 5%. The mean overall accuracies are 97.6390%, 98.8753%, 99.3292%, and 98.4283%, respectively. Ablations reveal a substantial contribution from the TTT inner update on Indian Pines and a smaller positive contribution on Pavia University, while the relative benefits of the spectral stem and feature fusion depend on the dataset. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using patch-conditioned vision TTT for spectral--spatial HSI classification and highlight the role of the inner adaptation mechanism.
bullets: Targets HSI classification with limited labeled supervision while preserving spectral signatures and spatial context.
Uses a spectral convolution stem, resolution-preserving spatial tokens, and two patch-conditioned ViT3-based TTT encoder blocks.
Fuses center-pixel and neighborhood-average features for final classification.
Evaluated on Indian Pines, Pavia University, Salinas, and Houston 2013, achieving mean overall accuracies of 97.6390%, 98.8753%, 99.3292%, and 98.4283%, respectively.
Ablations indicate that TTT inner updates are especially beneficial on Indian Pines, while other component benefits vary by dataset.

papers.abstract: Can a language model that reads the full history of an access log say whether a service may act now? On an executable benchmark of grants, withdrawals, reinstatements, expiries, groups and change windows under a known policy, scored on pairs of histories that differ only in the order or one field of the deciding events, open models of 7 to 32 billion parameters fall from 72 to 86 percent after eight or sixteen events to 48 to 55 percent after 256, while reasoning-trained 32B models reading the current state reach 96 and 98 percent. A reasoning model of 120 billion parameters trails the state by four and seven points at 256 and 512 events and by about ten at 1,024, so the length beyond which explicit state outlasts long context grows with the reader. We treat agent memory as recursive filtering. The decision depends on the history only through a state whose size is set by the number of tracked keys. A store holding fewer component records than the state forgets on a time scale set by its capacity, and a reader model predicts its accuracy within 0.02 on average in a registered test. Retaining log lines without regard to time order errs with probability approaching one half, a bound that is attained. A filter in which a model parses each line and an explicit rule applies the updates answers 80 to 89 percent at 256 events and beats relevance retrieval, model-kept ledgers, a reimplementation of StateMem and the Mem0 library. A retriever that selects at query time the lines the queried state depends on matches it at 256 events on the first domain, so what decides is selection by the state's dependencies, which the filter performs when writing, without the query. Applying parsed updates themselves, the models fall to 58 and 59 percent. A frozen replication on a second domain with fresh wording reproduces the horizon.
bullets: Long-context models degrade sharply on access histories: accuracy falls from 72–86% after 8–16 events to 48–55% after 256, while models given current state reach 96–98%.
The effective horizon of long-context reading grows with model size, but even a 120B reasoning model trails explicit state by 4–10 points at 256–1,024 events.
Agent memory is modeled as recursive filtering: only the state relevant to tracked keys needs to be retained, and undersized stores forget on a capacity-dependent timescale.
A parser-plus-rule-update filter achieves 80–89% at 256 events, outperforming relevance retrieval, model-kept ledgers, StateMem, and Mem0.
Selecting history lines by the queried state’s dependencies matches the filter on one domain; a frozen replication on a second domain reproduces the horizon effect.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates agent memory vs long context and proposes filtering, fits LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: Agent Memory as Rate-Limited Filtering: Explicit State Outlasts Long Context Beyond a Reader-Dependent Horizon
papers.tldr: Explicit, dependency-aware state filtering preserves policy decisions far better than relying on long, unordered histories, with its advantage increasing as histories grow and reader capacity limits are reached.

papers.abstract: Recent interactive video world models generate visually compelling videos from a single image, following user-provided camera motion and text prompts. However, such low-level control demands substantial user effort to realize a high-level intent, and the generated world struggles to remain persistent as the exploration proceeds. In this work, we present AgiWorld, an agentic video world model that explores and builds a persistent world from a single image and a free-form instruction. For high-level planning, our agent AgiWorld-Agent designs the world and the journey through it in a world state and directs the exploration. For low-level realization, our video world model AgiWorld-WM generates the video chunk by chunk and stores it with its geometry in a spatial memory, from which the agent updates its world state. This closed loop keeps the world faithful to the user's intent and keeps the agent's world state consistent with the generated content throughout the exploration. We co-design the two levels around the shared spatial memory and an interface of metric camera trajectories and structured prompts. In AgiWorld-WM, to handle occlusion and accumulated geometric errors in the spatial memory over long rollouts, we propose occlusion-aware history selection, which retrieves past views by surface visibility, and reliability-based memory maintenance, which prefers reliable geometry and earlier observations. AgiWorld-WM achieves state-of-the-art overall performance on world revisiting and exploration benchmarks, and qualitative results and ablations show that AgiWorld builds persistent worlds from free-form instructions over minute-long journeys. Persistence thus arises not from the video model alone but from its closed loop with the agent.
bullets: Addresses the user effort required by low-level camera control and the loss of world consistency during extended exploration.
AgiWorld-Agent plans the world and journey from a free-form instruction, while AgiWorld-WM realizes exploration as video chunks.
A shared spatial memory stores generated views and geometry, enabling the agent to update its world state and maintain consistency.
Occlusion-aware history selection and reliability-based memory maintenance mitigate visibility and accumulated geometric errors.
Reports state-of-the-art overall performance on revisiting and exploration benchmarks, with qualitative results and ablations supporting persistence over minute-long journeys.

papers.abstract: AI assistants store values that a language model derived from a person's records under the person's own definitions, such as their important contacts. Keeping such a value correct takes two steps: detection, noticing that an input changed, and repair, producing the correct new value. Benchmarks that score only the final answer cannot tell which step failed, and they state every change as new text. Seeing this limitation, we present MemShift, a benchmark of five shifts: source revision, deletion, redefinition, writer switch, and export. The first three fork a synthetic world into branches that differ only in the shift. Gold values and dependencies are fixed before any text, and a deterministic scorer replaces an LLM judge. For a memory that reports its invalidations, MemShift shows for each changed item whether the memory noticed the change and whether its repair was right. Moreover, we build a reference memory with known detection and repair to validate the measure. By evaluating four open-weight LLMs, we find that detection helps only as much as repair allows: the LLMs re-derive few values computed by the person's definitions correctly, and programs that the LLM writes over typed records close most of the gap to exact recomputation. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zichuanxu/memshift.
bullets: Separates memory-update performance into change detection and value repair, revealing which step fails.
Covers five shifts: source revision, deletion, redefinition, writer switch, and export.
Uses controlled branch construction, fixed gold dependencies, and deterministic scoring instead of LLM judging.
Evaluations of four open-weight LLMs show limited accuracy when re-deriving values from personal definitions.
LLM-generated programs over typed records approach exact recomputation, closing much of the repair gap.

papers.abstract: Looped language models can stop iterating early, and recent work shows that post-hoc readouts of the loop trajectory often rival the learned exit gate of the looped model Ouro. Such comparisons reduce each method to one operating point chosen by a selection rule. We ask whether that rule decides the outcome. On a frozen Ouro-1.4B with four loops, we compared a trained stability probe ($π_1$-x) with Ouro's native gate, adapted to a per-question stopping decision, in pre-registered studies; the confirmatory study was designed after an exploratory finding on development data and evaluated once on a sealed test set of 8,517 questions. In the pre-registered confirmatory comparison, which selected operating points with a bootstrap-screened 1 pp accuracy-loss rule, the probe saved more of the four-loop budget than the native gate (+0.053 gross macro saving over three benchmarks, 95% CI [+0.049, +0.057]), mostly from CommonsenseQA, where the probe's test upper bound on accuracy loss exceeded 1 pp. Under a point-only rule, a pre-specified secondary analysis on the same test set reversed the preference (-0.022 [-0.026, -0.018]), with operating points that exceeded the budget. In pre-specified secondary comparisons, the probe showed no demonstrated advantage over an untrained KL divergence between successive loops (+0.00125 [-0.0041, +0.0065]); we emphasise this result post hoc and claim no equivalence. The probe also broke its budget on one of two out-of-distribution benchmarks (3.26 pp loss on Social IQa). Savings are estimated from stored full-depth traces, not measured inference time, and our screen carries no formal risk-control guarantee. We conclude that halting methods should be compared as signals together with selection procedures, with strong untrained baselines and out-of-distribution checks.
bullets: On frozen Ouro-1.4B with four loops, a trained stability probe was compared with Ouro’s native gate for per-question stopping.
Under a bootstrap-screened 1 percentage-point accuracy-loss rule, the probe saved more loop budget than the native gate across three benchmarks.
Under a point-only rule, the preference reversed, with operating points exceeding the budget.
The probe showed no demonstrated advantage over an untrained KL-divergence baseline and exceeded its budget on one out-of-distribution benchmark.
Savings came from stored full-depth traces rather than measured inference time, and the selection screen has no formal risk-control guarantee.

papers.abstract: Spatial audio conveys not only what sounds are present, but where they originate and how they interact with the environment. Recent audio-language models increasingly understand and reason about such scenes, yet spatial audio understanding, generation, and editing remain largely separate. We present Spatial Transfusion, a unified first-order ambisonics (FOA) framework that extends a pretrained spatial audio understanding model to generation and editing through flow matching over VAE latents. We formulate editing as a structured scene transformation over a taxonomy of atomic edits. Keeping the pretrained backbone frozen, we introduce modality-based LoRA routing and a curriculum that progressively adds generation, editing, and natural-language interaction. Experiments show that Spatial Transfusion largely preserves spatial understanding while outperforming full fine-tuning in generation and editing. The resulting model supports controllable FOA generation and editing through both structured and natural-language interfaces. Audio samples are available at https://microsoft.github.io/spatial-transfusion/
bullets: Addresses the separation between spatial audio scene understanding, generation, and editing.
Extends a pretrained spatial audio understanding model using flow matching over VAE latents.
Models editing as structured scene transformations with atomic edits and supports natural-language control.
Uses frozen-backbone modality-based LoRA routing and a curriculum spanning generation, editing, and interaction.
Experiments indicate preserved spatial understanding and stronger generation/editing than full fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Computed tomography (CT) provides diverse patient information and various clinical tasks, for which numerous deep learning models have been investigated. Recent years have seen the development of vision-language foundation models that can comprehensively extract clinical features, driven by representation learning that combines CT volumes with radiology reports. Existing approaches typically adopt Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)-based representation learning, where pairs from different cases are, in principle, treated as negative pairs such that the volume and report embeddings are pushed apart. In the biomedical imaging, however, treating different cases as negative pairs is not always appropriate, particularly when clinical similarity exists. In this study, we propose a supervised representation learning framework grounded in clinical knowledge from language foundation models, rather than the weak supervision used in CLIP. Specifically, we utilized a large language model to extract abnormal finding phrases from reports. We then explicitly constructed the target features that the image encoder should output, as the semantic representation of the extracted findings using a biomedical text embedding model. Our Findings-aware Language-Image Pre-training (FiLIP) outperformed weakly supervised approaches in multi-label zero-shot finding classification in both in-domain and external-domain evaluations, and also proved effective when fine-tuned for the downstream task of radiology report generation.
bullets: CLIP-style training can incorrectly separate clinically similar CT volumes and reports.
An LLM extracts abnormal finding phrases from radiology reports.
A biomedical text encoder converts findings into target semantic representations for supervised image training.
FiLIP outperformed weakly supervised methods in multi-label zero-shot finding classification across in-domain and external-domain evaluations.
It also supported downstream radiology report generation after fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Sycophancy in language models is well documented as a behaviour but poorly localised as a mechanism. We ask whether capitulation under user pushback, the abandonment of a correct answer when a user objects, corresponds to a linear direction in the residual stream, and whether such a direction emerges with scale. Across eight instruction-tuned models spanning 0.5B to 14B parameters in two families, under a pre-registered protocol with leave-one-question-out cross-validation, within-question permutation nulls, and a positive control, we find no usable direction below 7B and a direction that clears our validation gate at 7B, 8B and 14B. Ablating that direction in Qwen2.5-7B reduces the rate at which the model reverses a correct answer by 4.8 percentage points, roughly a quarter in relative terms, while the identical intervention on a gate-failing direction and on a marginally passing one produces no effect. Probe quality, not statistical significance, predicts causal relevance. Behaviourally, pushback destroys three to five times more correct answers than it repairs at 1B and reaches parity by 7B, falsifying our own pre-registered prediction, and a sign-reversing crossover between pushback types survives an order of magnitude of scale in Qwen and holds at 8B in Llama, with marginalisation over five paraphrases per type. We additionally quantify five measurement hazards, including a numerical-precision effect that changes roughly one episode label in ten.
bullets: Across eight instruction-tuned models from 0.5B to 14B parameters in two families, no usable direction appeared below 7B.
Directions passed the validation gate at 7B, 8B, and 14B, but not smaller scales.
Ablating the validated direction in Qwen2.5-7B reduced reversals of correct answers by 4.8 percentage points; control directions had no effect.
Pushback harmed correct answers more often than it repaired them at 1B, reached parity by 7B, and showed a persistent sign-reversing pattern across pushback types.
Five measurement hazards were identified, including numerical precision changing roughly one in ten episode labels.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress in 3D scene understanding from multi-view RGB observations. Yet a fixed object and query can elicit inconsistent target-related responses across camera viewpoints, a phenomenon we characterize as viewpoint-induced semantic drift. We introduce LieVLM, a Lie routing framework for view-robust 3D understanding. Motivated by the rotational component of viewpoint change, Lie routing adapts visual representations by applying local $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ transformations to projected features within learned three-dimensional subspaces. Geometry tokens extracted by VGGT predict local rotation parameters and channel-wise routing coefficients. A closed-form Padé--Cayley map transforms projected visual features, whose identity-relative corrections are projected back and gated into the original visual and geometry features. This design retains the pretrained semantic and direct spatial context while learning view-dependent feature adjustments. Experiments on 3D captioning, grounding, detection, and spatial reasoning show consistent improvements over additive fusion across training scales and backbones. Controlled ablations examine the roles of geometric conditioning and transformation structure. Viewpoint analyses further reveal systematic variation in the predicted routing states alongside more localized target responses and stronger task performance across viewpoint changes.
bullets: Addresses inconsistent target-related responses from different camera viewpoints in MLLMs.
Uses geometry tokens to predict local SO(3) rotations and channel-wise routing coefficients in learned feature subspaces.
Applies a closed-form Padé–Cayley transformation and gates identity-relative corrections into visual and geometry features.
Improves 3D captioning, grounding, detection, and spatial reasoning across training scales and backbones compared with additive fusion.
View analyses show changing routing states, more localized target responses, and stronger performance across viewpoints.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM serving by drafting tokens that the target model verifies in one pass, and its gain grows with the drafts the target accepts. Structured outputs should be an ideal case, because much of a record follows from relations among its fields: an itinerary's days follow from its cities' stays and flights. Serving engines, however, draft such text by proposing it from the prompt or a learned head, and their grammar masks enforce only syntax, so the model must satisfy the relations, which it violates: on NATURAL PLAN's trip problems, Qwen3-8B writes a valid itinerary for 10%, and retries that name the violated relation raise this to 14%. We present FactorSpec, which serves exact relational constraints as speculative drafts. FactorSpec compiles a JSON Schema and its relations into a factor graph with an exact feasibility check, drafts every token the constraint determines as certain, verifies each request at a width chosen for it, and computes the masks in worker processes outside the scheduler while the GPU runs. In SGLang, its drafts yield up to 10.5 tokens per verify step, up to 1.9x those of the fastest n-gram drafter, and it decodes up to 1.43x faster than speculators tuned per load, at a grammar mask's cost; it also leads in vLLM. Because every record is also valid, it serves up to 13.9x the valid records per GPU-second of syntax-only baselines.
bullets: Targets relational violations in structured generation, which grammar masks alone cannot prevent.
Compiles JSON Schema and field relations into a factor graph with exact feasibility checking.
Drafts constraint-determined tokens, adapts verification width per request, and computes masks off the scheduler path.
In SGLang, reaches up to 10.5 tokens per verify step and 1.43× faster decoding than load-tuned speculators; it also leads in vLLM.
Produces only valid records, reaching up to 13.9× more valid records per GPU-second than syntax-only baselines.
