papers.selection_reason: Speculative decoding for LLM serving reduces latency, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: FactorSpec: Serving Exact Relational Constraints as Speculative Drafts
papers.tldr: FactorSpec accelerates structured-output serving by drafting tokens that are guaranteed by exact relational constraints, achieving faster decoding and far more valid records than syntax-only approaches.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models process hundreds of visual tokens, making visual representations a major computational bottleneck. We argue that visual token pruning should be formulated not as identifying individually important tokens, but as preserving the dominant low-rank spectral structure of the visual representation. Based on this formulation, we introduce SVD-Prune, a training-free framework that leverages Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and statistical leverage scores for globally informed token selection. SVD-Prune is architecture-agnostic and can be applied at different stages of the multimodal pipeline, including encoder-side, decoder-side, and hybrid configurations Extensive experiments across VLM and VLA benchmarks demonstrate strong robustness under extreme compression. SVD-Prune reduces the visual token. SVD-Prune cuts the visual token budget by up to 99.3%, while, at a 16-token budget, encoder-side pruning lowers inference FLOPs by 82.4% and achieves a 4.18x end-to-end speedup, including pruning overhead.
bullets: Targets the computational bottleneck caused by hundreds of visual tokens in VLMs and VLAs.
Formulates pruning as preserving dominant low-rank spectral structure rather than ranking tokens independently.
Uses training-free SVD and statistical leverage scores for globally informed, architecture-agnostic selection.
Supports encoder-side, decoder-side, and hybrid multimodal pipeline configurations.
At 16 tokens, encoder-side pruning reduces inference FLOPs by 82.4% and achieves a 4.18× end-to-end speedup, including pruning overhead.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models answer better when they think longer, but a thinking trace keeps going well after its answer has formed. We measure this slack in Qwen3.5-9B and remove most of it with concise self-training: two rounds of on-policy rejection-sampling fine-tuning that keep the shortest correct samples, plus a small share of answer-synthesis targets, giving Concise-9B. On 8,983 held-out problems (competition and hard mathematics, SuperGPQA, a five-area confirmation set and MMLU-Pro), Concise-9B generates 0.66x the tokens of Qwen3.5-9B at a 32K thinking budget, with accuracy equivalent within +/-1 point (-0.20 [-0.77, +0.36] points). Forcing each trace on the hard and confirmation sets to answer every 2,048 thinking tokens, we find that 54-64% of Qwen3.5-9B's thinking tokens come after the point from which every forced answer equals the final one (41-48% for Concise-9B). Stopping there would keep every answer at 0.35-0.44x the base model's tokens, but finding that point takes hindsight: stopping when three consecutive forced answers agree costs the base model 2.4-9.2 points. Concise self-training removes slack without that cost: 86% [83, 90] of the thinking tokens it saves come after the answer has formed. It has a limit: with traces continued to 80K tokens, Concise-9B solves 25 fewer of 1,276 hard problems (-25 [-49, -1]), mostly in competition mathematics. The measurement also yields a cheap commit signal for adaptive sampling that matched two-sample escalation within +/-1 point at 0.67x its tokens in a pre-registered test. Results on Qwen3.5-4B, on which the recipe was developed, and a replication on Olmo-3-7B-Think suggest that the saving depends on how verbose the base model is.
bullets: Qwen3.5-9B’s reasoning traces contain substantial slack: 54–64% of tokens occur after the answer has effectively formed.
Two rounds of on-policy rejection-sampling fine-tuning retain the shortest correct traces and some answer-synthesis targets.
Concise-9B uses 0.66× as many tokens as the base model with accuracy within ±1 percentage point on 8,983 held-out problems.
The method removes slack without the accuracy cost of naïvely stopping based on agreement among intermediate answers.
At 80K-token traces, Concise-9B solves fewer hard problems, mainly in competition mathematics; savings also depend on base-model verbosity.

papers.selection_reason: Directly about a reasoning LLM and its training to reduce thinking tokens; relevant to LLM research.
papers.title: Concise-9B: Removing the Slack from a Reasoning Model's Thinking
papers.tldr: Concise self-training removes much of a reasoning model’s redundant thinking while preserving accuracy, though very long reasoning can reveal a small loss on the hardest problems.

papers.abstract: Scaling laws predict the outcome of large, expensive training runs by extrapolating trends from smaller, cheaper runs. On downstream accuracy evaluations, these predictions fail when the weaker models produced by the cheaper runs score near zero accuracy, because these scores give no trend to extrapolate to larger scales. We introduce hinted scaling laws, which use privileged information to turn a benchmark into a continuum of easier versions so that even the small models score above zero. We find that accuracy rises smoothly and predictably with the hint level, enabling new types of scaling laws that operate below the noise threshold. On the Delphi pretraining ladder, a hinted scaling law fit on models trained with at most $10^{20}$ FLOPs forecasts the GSM8K accuracy of a $10^{23}$ FLOP model (25.9%) to within 3 percentage points; a standard scaling law under-forecasts it by 13 percentage points when fit on the same models and by 12 even with models up to $10^{22}$ FLOPs in the fit. Across both this pretraining ladder and a collection of post-trained model families, hinted scaling laws reduce the median forecasting error on GSM8K, AIME and HLE from 21 percentage points to 4.3. Hinting also reduces the number of test examples needed to tell whether one model is better than another by widening the accuracy gaps between models while approximately preserving their order: a single hinted rollout per problem ranks nearly indistinguishable models as accurately as five unhinted rollouts. Our results suggest that hinting is a general primitive for improving the accuracy and cost of downstream scaling laws and other prediction tasks in model development.
bullets: Standard scaling laws fail when small models score near zero, leaving too little signal to extrapolate.
The method introduces benchmark hints that create a continuum of easier tasks where weaker models achieve nonzero accuracy.
Hinted accuracy varies smoothly with hint level, enabling scaling-law fits below the usual noise threshold.
On GSM8K, hinted fits reduced median forecasting error across GSM8K, AIME, and HLE from 21 to 4.3 percentage points.
Hinting also improves model comparisons: one hinted rollout ranked nearly indistinguishable models as accurately as five unhinted rollouts.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces hinted scaling laws to improve downstream accuracy prediction for LLM training runs, a core LLM development methodology.
papers.title: Hinted Scaling Laws
papers.tldr: Hinted scaling laws make near-zero downstream accuracies informative by converting benchmarks into easier, hint-assisted versions, substantially improving forecasts of larger-model performance.

papers.abstract: When a deployed model degrades under concept drift, an operator can retrain it, raise an alert and monitor, or roll back. Yet most drift-adaptation methods consider only retraining. We present RAR (Retrain-Alert-Rollback), a state machine that gives each response an explicit trigger and cost. Retraining is gated on drift detection, label availability, and measured degradation. Every retrained model must pass a two-stage canary before promotion, and corruption-triggered and quality-triggered rollbacks enter different hold states. Under a prospectively specified protocol we compare RAR with six baselines, including a cost-aware retraining policy, on 13 streams: eight real public streams and five semi-synthetic streams derived from them. RAR does not dominate. At low retraining cost, retrain-heavy baselines lead, and no policy's rank differs significantly from RAR's. At higher cost, RAR beats detector-triggered retraining, periodic retraining, and no response simultaneously on four streams, each within a bounded cost window. Its advantage over detector-triggered retraining is consistent with a latency-feasibility condition stated in advance. Against the cost-aware policy, results are heterogeneous. RAR retrains before true drift onsets one eighth to one third as often as detector-triggered retraining, but at lower net utility on most semi-synthetic streams. On H2's designated corruption stream (a registered follow-up), rollbacks fire yet RAR loses to retraining baselines. At $ρ= 1$, removing the canary, and thus rollback, raises utility on 11 of 13 streams. On a post-hoc follow-up stream, cause-specific hold release resumes adaptation where a single cooldown does not. We provide the harness, configurations, and per-cell results for reproduction.
bullets: Frames drift response as a state machine with explicit triggers and costs for retraining, alerts, and rollbacks.
Gates retraining on detected drift, label availability, and measured degradation; promoted models must pass a two-stage canary.
Evaluated prospectively against six baselines across 13 real and semi-synthetic streams.
At higher retraining costs, RAR outperformed three alternatives on four streams within bounded cost windows, but results versus the cost-aware policy were heterogeneous.

papers.selection_reason: Decision framework for retraining/rollback under concept drift, relevant to continual adaptation of deployed models.
papers.title: Retrain, Alert, or Rollback? A Three-Response Decision Framework for Production ML Under Concept Drift
papers.tldr: RAR chooses among retraining, alerting, and rollback under concept drift, improving cost-aware performance in some high-cost settings but not consistently outperforming simpler policies.

papers.abstract: Safe navigation in interactive traffic requires autonomous vehicles to reason about unobservable human characteristics and the reciprocal nature of multi-agent interactions. Traditional architectures often decouple prediction from planning, leading to the "Frozen Robot Problem" or unsafe maneuvers under high ambiguity because they treat risk assessment and information acquisition as independent objectives. We argue that the notion of safety should not remain static but must instead dynamically co-evolve with the system's internal confidence: the robot should actively clarify ambiguity when necessary while also recognizing the diminishing returns of information, and naturally transition toward task execution. We introduce a unified belief-space Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework that couples multistep information planning with a clarity-adaptive Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) barrier mechanism. By treating clarity, a scalar informational state, as an explicit planning variable, the controller co-designs its probing strategy with its safety specification, tightening conservatism under high ambiguity and relaxing constraints as confidence improves. We further provide a performance analysis showing that the cost of information seeking and the expected planning-cost gap to a controller that knows the true human characteristic are bounded by residual ambiguity and solver error. We evaluate the framework in lane-merging and unsignalized-intersection scenarios against representative interactive-planning baselines. Across 5,000 simulations, the proposed method achieves the highest success rates (94.6% and 93.2%) and the lowest collision rates (1.2% and 1.4%) among the compared methods, providing a principled foundation for robust decision-making in human-centric environments.
bullets: Addresses unsafe or overly hesitant driving caused by separating prediction, planning, risk assessment, and information gathering.
Models clarity—an informational confidence state—as an explicit planning variable.
Combines multistep information planning with a clarity-adaptive CVaR safety barrier that is more conservative under ambiguity and relaxes as confidence improves.
Provides bounds linking information-seeking cost and planning-cost gap to residual ambiguity and solver error.
In 5,000 simulations across lane merging and unsignalized intersections, it reports 94.6%/93.2% success and 1.2%/1.4% collision rates, respectively, outperforming compared baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Timestep-by-timestep overview of the proposed framework executing an unsignalized intersection crossing. Yellow and black denote the ego and human-driven vehicles, respectively; translucent silhouettes show past positions. Each row presents vehicle trajectories, the belief over the human characteristic θ summarized over cooperative, neutral, and aggressive regions, the safety-margin distribution with lower-tail CVaR0.05, clarity βk , and control effort. At t1 = 0.0 s, the ego approaches the intersection with a nearly uniform belief over θ and a broad safety-margin distribution. Low clarity yields a large safety demand hsafe + κ(1/βk − 1) in Eq. (7). At t2 = 1.3 s, a cautious forward probe is followed by a shift toward an aggressive characteristic. The safety-margin distribution narrows and shifts left as the vehicles approach the conflict region, while clarity and control effort increase. At t3 = 2.6 s, the belief further favors an aggressive characteristic. Increasing clarity reduces both the additional safety buffer and the information penalty Φ(βk) = 1 − βk , supporting a shift toward task execution. At t4 = 3.9 s, the belief over θ is more concentrated and the safety-margin distribution becomes sharper as the crossing progresses. At t5 = 5.5 s, the ego has cleared the intersection, with a narrow predicted safety-margin distribution and reduced control effort. The sequence illustrates how evolving belief confidence jointly shapes information-seeking and safety conservatism, supporting a transition from cautious probing to task execution without explicit mode switching.

Fig. 3: Behavioral comparison across lane-merge runs (mean ± std). (a) Task progress: all methods achieve comparable route progress. (b) Clarity: the proposed method reaches higher reference-observer clarity than the baselines. (c) True safety margin: mean margins are initially similar but diverge near the merge region; the proposed method maintains a positive mean margin, while several baselines exhibit greater variability or reduced clearance. (d) Information gain: the proposed method exhibits a pronounced early peak followed by diminishing information gain as clarity increases, consistent with an early emphasis on information acquisition followed by task execution.

Fig. 4: CVaR barrier value versus clarity βk for each ablation variant, across all simulation runs. The proposed method concentrates in the high-clarity region while maintaining positive barrier values, illustrating the combination of belief refinement and safety preservation.

Fig. 2: Qualitative lane-merging comparison in a selected episode. Faded vehicles indicate historical poses, while solid vehicles show the states at lane-change completion. The proposed method is the only method that merges ahead of the cooperative human driver in this episode, achieving the shortest task completion time of 5.4 s. RA-MPPI, AIG-MPC, D-MPPI, and ID-SMPC merge behind the human, completing the task in 6.1 s, 5.8 s, 6.4 s, and 5.9 s, respectively.

TABLE I: Quantitative comparison across lane-merge and unsignalized-intersection scenarios (500 runs per method per scenario). The proposed method achieves the highest success rates (94.6% and 93.2%) and lowest collision rates (1.2% and 1.4%), respectively, together with the highest mean clarity and information gain in both scenarios. D-MPPI has the shortest completion times, while AIG-MPC uses the least control effort. RA-MPPI achieves the largest CVaR margin in lane merging, whereas the proposed method achieves the largest margin at intersections.

TABLE II: Ablation study across all scenarios (2,880 runs). The proposed method achieves the highest success rate (92.9%) and mean final clarity (0.85 ± 0.06). Fixed CVaR attains the lowest collision rate (0.5%) but the longest average time (7.92 ± 2.31 s). Certainty-Eq is fastest (5.01± 1.88 s) but has the highest collision rate (5.6%) and negative mean CVaR safety slack, indicating repeated safety margin violations.

papers.selection_reason: Belief-space MPC for interactive driving navigation, relevant to embodied navigation safety.
papers.title: When to Probe and When to Act: Clarity-Aware Risk-Adaptive Control for Interactive Driving
papers.tldr: A risk-adaptive MPC controller jointly decides when to probe uncertain human behavior and when to act, improving interactive-driving safety in simulated traffic.

papers.abstract: Search-based planning remains a powerful policy improvement paradigm in reinforcement learning, driving milestone successes in discrete domains. However, extending this paradigm to continuous control exposes a structural mismatch: search evaluates a finite set of action candidates, whereas continuous RL typically relies on Gaussian policies. We show that winner-action distillation into a continuous Gaussian induces a \textit{projection error} and a stepwise variance-expanding gradient tendency when the selected action is sufficiently far from the current mean. Empirically, this tendency is associated with elevated terminal variance and a return gap on the evaluated tasks. To address this, we propose \textbf{Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP)}. By adopting a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, IGP naturally aligns the policy support with the search candidates, eliminating the projection error and reducing the residual approximation to a bounded discretization error. To bypass the combinatorial explosion of high-dimensional discrete action spaces, IGP pairs Gumbel Top-$K$ candidate sampling with an MPPI-style multi-round iterative search to refine the policy at each state. Empirically, IGP achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency on DMControl and HumanoidBench. Furthermore, it produces more stable action sequences with lower temporal variance, demonstrating its practical potential for real-world robotic deployment.
bullets: Gaussian winner-action distillation can introduce projection error and increase action variance when selected actions lie far from the policy mean.
IGP uses a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, replacing projection error with bounded discretization error.
Gumbel Top-K sampling and MPPI-style iterative refinement avoid the combinatorial cost of high-dimensional discrete search.
On DMControl and HumanoidBench, IGP reports state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency.
IGP also generates more temporally stable action sequences, supporting potential robotic deployment.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Comparison of MPPI and Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP). While standard MPPI refines trajectories over an unbounded continuous action space, IGP natively operates in a factorized discrete policy space. papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention scores, and each layer scores its own cache. To our knowledge, no eviction method asks which layer should score. We find, across twenty-one models, that the depth of the scoring layer governs eviction quality. On the eighteen models with per-layer caches, spanning 0.5B to 109B, long-context retrieval accuracy collapses at shallow layers, peaks between 0.4 and 0.75 of depth, and degrades at the last layer. The curve arises because a layer judges tokens well only once it has used the question to find the answer, which takes several layers. Modeling eviction as a top-$k$ cut, we compute answer survival probability from prefill attention and reproduce the measured curves. This approach selects the scoring layer using calibration prompts with known answers, and the selected layer is the best layer measured on most models and never significantly below it. It improves on the own-layer default on sixteen of the eighteen models, with significant gains on seven, all at 14B or below, while on larger models the default is already close to the best mid-depth layer. Scoring every cache from the selected layer while keeping one set of tokens for all heads also beats per-head SnapKV by 18 to 43 points on five models up to 14B under tight budgets. This gain carries over to financial filings at 32K context, all at the same memory budget, with no extra forward pass. The same curve explains a penalty in shared-cache models, where several layers read one cache and the layer that writes it scores by default. On Gemma-4-E2B the writer is shallow and loses 28 points to a mid-depth reader at a 10% budget. We also find that in open-book question answering (LongBench) no mid-depth layer beats the own-layer default.
bullets: Eviction quality depends strongly on scoring-layer depth: it is poor near the input, peaks around 40–75% depth, and declines at the final layer.
The pattern reflects when layers have incorporated the question enough to identify answer-relevant tokens; a top-k survival model reproduces the observed curve.
Calibration prompts with known answers select an effective scoring layer, improving on the default in 16 of 18 per-layer-cache models and significantly in 7.
Using the selected layer to score all heads beats per-head SnapKV by 18–43 points on five models up to 14B, including financial filings at 32K context, without extra forward passes.

The benefit is model- and task-dependent: larger models often have near-optimal defaults, shared-cache writers can be substantially worse, and no mid-depth advantage appears on LongBench open-book QA.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates which layer should score KV-cache eviction, directly improving cache efficiency.
papers.title: Who Should Score the Cache? Mid-Depth Layers Are the Best Judges of KV-Cache Eviction
papers.tldr: Mid-depth transformer layers are generally the best judges for KV-cache token eviction, improving long-context retrieval when a single selected layer scores caches.

papers.abstract: RL locomotion policies trained under nominal simulation conditions may encounter distribution shifts that compromise safety. Predictive monitors could anticipate violations, but their world-model forecasts may become unreliable under shift, and ensemble disagreement is not calibrated. We evaluate predictive Signal Temporal Logic (STL) monitoring for frozen Ant-v5 and HalfCheetah-v5 policies using closed-loop world-model rollouts and a three-model ensemble. Across external-force, observation-noise, and mass shifts, predicted robustness ranks HalfCheetah's future STL violations strongly, whereas disagreement does not reliably track observation prediction error or violations. Under severe noise, violations remain common ($64.2\pm24.4\%$ at $K{=}20$ across three PPO seeds), yet current-state robustness without prediction comes within $0.03$ AUROC of predictive robustness. Penalizing predicted robustness by disagreement does not consistently improve ranking. Ant provides complementary per-specification evidence, but its composite target has no positive violations and its any-violation target is single-class in most evaluated seed-condition slices. Overall, predictive robustness provides useful STL-specific ranking but little demonstrated additional ranking value over the current state; these findings caution against treating ensemble disagreement as a reliable indicator of safety uncertainty.
bullets: Studies frozen Ant-v5 and HalfCheetah-v5 policies under external-force, observation-noise, and mass distribution shifts.
Uses closed-loop world-model rollouts with a three-model ensemble to predict STL robustness and future violations.
Predictive robustness ranks HalfCheetah violations strongly, while ensemble disagreement does not reliably indicate prediction error or safety violations.
Under severe noise, violations remain frequent, but current-state robustness performs nearly as well as predictive robustness.
Results are limited for Ant because several violation targets are non-positive or single-class across evaluated slices.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Predictive STL monitoring pipeline. The current observation ot feeds the frozen PPO policy and the world-model ensemble, whose members each generate a K-step closed-loop rollout by repeatedly querying the policy on predicted observations. Predicted trajectories are evaluated with STL and aggregated into predictive robustness P and STL disagreement Uρ; independently, O is evaluated on the observed trajectory τt:t+K , and SUP penalizes P by Uρ.

These condition-level results provide no consistent evidence that ensemble STL robustness disagreement reliably identifies future STL violations.

papers.abstract: Repeated satellite imagery permits understanding of how our planet changes over time, letting us predict its future and plan mitigating actions. Most existing studies that rely on a time series of satellite observations forecast the spectral values at each pixel for a future target date. However, clouds, shadows, and sensor noise often corrupt these observations, so that spectral forecasters waste much of their capacity on low-level features or noise rather than real change. With the advent of Earth foundation models, we argue that forecasting in embedding space is a feasible and more effective alternative. To this end, we design a token space that handles irregular histories from different sensors and foundation models and supports forecasts at any query date. Tokens from this space are inputs to our proposed forecaster, E$^2$Forecast, which is a transformer with two branches: a Gaussian branch that directly predicts a mean point forecast and per-dimension standard deviations, and a rectified-flow branch that generates forecast ensembles. On Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 benchmarks, forecasting embeddings instead of spectral values halves the cosine distance (from 0.20 to 0.10) and greatly reduces overconfidence, lowering the z-score standard deviation from 2.63 to 1.22. By comparing new observations with its forecasts, E$^2$Forecast can also detect anomalous changes without labels or retraining, raising F$_1$ from 41.58 to 48.70 on a global benchmark. This consistent superiority is validated on nine remote sensing foundation models. Beyond change detection, we believe our approach advances the field by permitting effective reuse of diverse pretrained task heads. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ucam-eo/e2forecast.
bullets: Pixel-level spectral forecasting is easily disrupted by clouds, shadows, sensor noise, and irregular observations from different sensors.
The method uses a token space for irregular histories and arbitrary query dates, with a two-branch transformer: Gaussian forecasts and rectified-flow ensembles.
On Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 benchmarks, embedding forecasts reduce cosine distance from 0.20 to 0.10 and improve uncertainty calibration.
Forecast-versus-observation comparisons enable anomaly detection without labels or retraining, increasing F₁ from 41.58 to 48.70 on a global benchmark.
The approach supports reuse of diverse pretrained remote-sensing task heads; scope is demonstrated across nine foundation models.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of E2Forecast. (a) Each image in an irregular time series is converted into an Earth embedding ei by an Earth foundation model si, which may differ across observations. (b) The historical embeddings with their dates, the location and the query date τ∗ form a token sequence for a masked transformer fθ . In one pass, the probability-estimation branch predicts the per-dimension Gaussian (µ,σ) of the future embedding, and the embedding-generation branch denoises a noisy target zt = t z1 + (1 − t) ϵ by flow matching. papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation aims to predict depth maps from single RGB images (forgoing the need for stereo camera pairs) and has seen impressive leaps in performance in recent work due to the introduction of affine-invariant losses and the use of foundation model features. These monocular depth models predict affine-invariant depth, which describes the relative positions of objects in the scene instead of absolute depth. While these models demonstrate strong performance on single image benchmarks and qualitatively consistent predictions in video, their effectiveness at preserving consistent spatial structure has been less thoroughly explored. Many potential real-world applications, such as handling video streams as input, rely on coherent three dimensional consistency in scenes. Further, anchoring relative depth predictions to a metric reference for a given scene is a key challenge for applying monocular depth models to real-world situations. We develop a novel evaluation protocol for monocular depth models using video sequences with moving camera positions to test the consistency of prediction across variation in viewpoint. We demonstrate this methodology over diverse, real-world video sequences where we are able to anchor depth model output to metric depth values using structure from motion. Our work demonstrates open challenges in the development of broadly applicable monocular depth foundation models, particularly with their ability to provide temporal consistency over long time frames. We also identify challenges in the straightforward adoption of structure-from-motion as a metric grounding tool for monocular depth estimation models.
bullets: Motivation: Strong single-image benchmark performance does not guarantee coherent 3D structure over video or viewpoint changes.
Method: Evaluate predictions on real-world video sequences with moving cameras and use structure from motion to anchor affine-invariant depth to metric values.
Findings: The evaluation exposes challenges in achieving temporal consistency over long time periods.
Scope: It also reveals limitations in directly using structure from motion for metric grounding of monocular depth.
Contribution: A viewpoint-sequence benchmark methodology for assessing consistency and metric applicability of monocular depth models.

papers.abstract: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) follows the pretrain-finetune paradigm: an agent is first pretrained on historical data and then adapted through online interaction. We study offline-to-online adaptation without offline replay, where the agent must improve using only the pretrained model and newly collected experience. A key challenge is to avoid catastrophic failure, a sharp early performance collapse during online fine-tuning, while still achieving strong asymptotic performance. Through controlled experiments, we show that removing offline replay can induce catastrophic failure, while retaining strong conservative regularization from offline RL can suppress final online performance. We also find that common stabilization strategies do not reliably prevent early collapse, and that the critic-side mechanisms we test are insufficient on their own. Motivated by these findings, we propose ANCHOR, a simple adaptation method that anchors the actor to the offline-pretrained policy early in online fine-tuning, anneals this constraint over time, and retains only a small residual conservative critic regularizer. We provide a theoretical interpretation showing that KL anchoring helps preserve critic reliability across nearby occupancy distributions, with a two-phase regret bound explaining when anchoring should be maintained or relaxed. Across FrankaKitchen, AntMaze, and Adroit tasks, ANCHOR substantially reduces catastrophic failure while maintaining strong asymptotic performance. Ablations show that KL annealing and the residual conservative weight are important for balancing early stability and online adaptation, while additional analysis shows that ANCHOR is most beneficial when the pretrained policy contains useful behavior to preserve. Code is available at https://github.com/Cho-Geonwoo/ANCHOR.
bullets: Offline-to-online adaptation without offline replay can cause catastrophic early performance collapse.
Strong conservative regularization may prevent collapse but limit eventual online improvement; critic-only stabilization is insufficient.
ANCHOR anchors the actor to the pretrained policy early, anneals the KL constraint, and keeps a small residual conservative critic regularizer.
Theory links KL anchoring to critic reliability under nearby occupancy distributions and gives conditions for maintaining or relaxing the anchor.
Experiments on FrankaKitchen, AntMaze, and Adroit show reduced catastrophic failure with strong asymptotic performance; benefits are greatest when pretrained behavior is useful.

figures.caption: Figure 2: ANCHOR improves both early stability and final performance. Existing methods do not consistently achieve both low catastrophic failure and strong asymptotic performance across tasks. In contrast, ANCHOR reduces early performance collapse while attaining strong final performance across tasks. The aggregate curve reports the mean success rate averaged over the six tasks.

Figure 1: Controlled analysis of offline data and conservative regularization. Success rates of CQL during online fine-tuning across four tasks. (a) Keeping the conservative regularizer α during online fine-tuning can reduce asymptotic performance. (b) Removing offline replay can induce early performance degradation.

Figure 6: SQOR and SQOG do not reliably predict catastrophic failure. We compare success rate, the spurious Q-optimism ratio (SQOR), and the spurious Q-optimism gap (SQOG) across four tasks. Both metrics show task-dependent and inconsistent alignment with early performance collapse. The vertical dashed line marks the timestep at which the largest performance drop occurs.

Figure 7: Q-update volatility does not reliably predict catastrophic failure. We compare success rate and critic-update volatility across four tasks. Volatility shows weak and inconsistent correspondence with early performance collapse.

Figure 4: Benefit of ANCHOR depends on pretrained policy quality. ANCHOR reduces catastrophic failure more clearly when the offline-pretrained policy starts from a higher initial success rate. Curves with the same color correspond to the same pretrained policy. Results are averaged over three seeds.

Figure 5: Hyperparameter and architectural tweaks do not consistently mitigate catastrophic failure. From top to bottom, the plots correspond to: batch size, actor learning rate, critic learning rate, critic hidden dimension, actor hidden dimension, LayerNorm in the critic, LayerNorm in the actor, and the duration of the offline pretraining phase. Across all settings and tasks, none of these factors consistently mitigates catastrophic failure.
Figure 10: Applying KL anchoring to IQL. Adding KL anchoring with annealing to IQL reduces the initial performance drop, but does not improve asymptotic performance over the IQL baseline.

Figure 11: Additional environments reveal limitations of KL-anchored adaptation. In kitchencomplete, ANCHOR remains competitive despite near-zero initial success. In relocate-binary, all methods fail to make meaningful progress. In antmaze-ultra-diverse, most methods do not improve over the offline-pretrained policy, suggesting that harder sparse-reward exploration requires mechanisms beyond KL anchoring alone.

Figure 17: Hyperparameter sensitivity of ANCHOR. We vary the initial KL weight β0 (top), the KL annealing interval TKL (middle), and the residual online conservative weight αon (bottom). Here, α∗ denotes an intermediate value between 0 and αoff , where αoff is the conservative regularization weight used during offline pretraining. ANCHOR remains stable under moderate changes to KL-related hyperparameters, while αon controls the balance between early stability and final improvement.

Top: UTD ratio; Middle: warmup length; Bottom: Cal-QL conservative-regularizer weight, αCal-QL. Increasing UTD, extending warmup, or tuning αCal-QL does not reliably prevent early performance collapse.

Figure 16: Critic-shift regularization does not prevent catastrophic failure. Effects of varying the critic-shift penalty strength αKL across four tasks. Top: critic distribution shift during online fine-tuning, measured by DKL ( softmax(Qoff) ∥ softmax(Qθ) ) . Bottom: corresponding success rates. Increasing αKL slows the critic shift, but does not reliably prevent early performance collapse.

Figure 3: KL annealing improves early stability while preserving final performance. ANCHOR is compared with the fixed-KL and no-KL variants. The fixed-KL variant improves early stability but can limit final improvement, while the no-KL variant adapts aggressively but causes early collapse.

Figure 8: Sensitivity to batch size and UTD ratio. We vary the batch size (top) and UTD ratio (bottom) across three tasks. ANCHOR is generally robust to these choices, although larger batch size and larger UTD can increase learning instability.

Figure 12: Stronger preservation is insufficient in antmaze-ultra-diverse. Keeping both the conservative coefficient and KL coefficient fixed yields a higher mean success rate than ANCHOR during online fine-tuning, but does not significantly improve asymptotic performance.

As the KL coefficient is annealed, the gap between β0 = 0.5 and β0 = 2.0 gradually narrows.

papers.abstract: Dexterous in-hand manipulation is commonly formulated around explicit object pose estimation, yet reliable pose tracking is challenging under severe hand-object occlusions and often requires object-specific supervision. This dependence creates a bottleneck between perception and control that can limit robustness and scalability. We present an end-to-end visuomotor framework for dexterous in-hand reorientation that operates on RGB observations and proprioception without intermediate pose estimation. Our approach jointly learns visual representations and control policies through behavior distillation from privileged state teachers and auxiliary reconstruction objectives. Furthermore, we introduce image-goal-conditioned reorientation, allowing desired object configurations to be specified directly through images rather than canonical pose representations. We evaluate our approach across a diverse set of object geometries and instances in simulation, where it consistently outperforms pose-based methods and policies built on pretrained visual encoders. Finally, we demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer of a single image-goal-conditioned policy across five real-world objects, showing that accurate dexterous reorientation can be achieved without explicit pose estimation. For videos and code release, please refer to the project website: https://rffr.leggedrobotics.com/works/goaldex/
bullets: Addresses the brittleness and scalability limits of pose tracking under severe hand–object occlusion.
Jointly learns visual representations and control policies using privileged-state behavior distillation and auxiliary reconstruction.
Specifies target object configurations through goal images rather than canonical poses.
Outperforms pose-based methods and pretrained-encoder policies across diverse simulated object geometries and instances.
Transfers a single image-goal-conditioned policy directly to real-world reorientation across five objects.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed image-goal-conditioned framework for dexterous in-hand reorientation. The policy maps RGB observations, proprioception, and visual goal images directly to joint actions, eliminating the need for explicit pose estimators or canonical object-frame representations. We demonstrate languageguided reorientation using a VLM to select visual goals from natural language instructions.

Figure 2: Training architecture for image-goal-conditioned visuomotor distillation. Current RGB observations and goal images are encoded into visual representations and fused with proprioceptive inputs. A recurrent policy integrates the multimodal features over time to predict joint position targets, while auxiliary reconstruction and continuous contrastive objectives shape the latent representation using privileged simulation supervision.

papers.abstract: Learning accurate value functions is central to reinforcement learning (RL), yet remains challenging because supervision is limited and indirect: ground-truth values are unavailable, and each transition in the data only provides an immediate reward that can be used to construct bootstrapped targets as supervision. This challenge is particularly pronounced when data is limited or reward signals are sparse, as is common in real-world applications such as robotics. We argue that the key to accurate value learning in this limited data regime is extracting richer learning signals from the available data. In this paper, we introduce Value Forcing, a new approach that uses flow matching to estimate return distributions and enables accurate value learning from limited data. Our key insight is that we can extract richer learning signals by enforcing Bellman consistency at every noise level. Empirically, Value Forcing improves the accuracy of estimating the return distribution, and prevents the distribution from collapsing to a single value, as occurs with prior methods. We instantiate Value Forcing with two practical value-learning algorithms: VF, an actor-critic method, and IVF, an implicit value-learning method. We evaluate both algorithms across $26$ long-horizon tasks in the offline RL setting and find that they outperform prior value-learning methods, with particularly large gains when data is limited. Our project website is available at https://chongyi-zheng.github.io/value-forcing.
bullets: Addresses inaccurate value estimation under sparse rewards and limited data, where only bootstrapped supervision is available.
Uses flow matching to estimate return distributions and applies Bellman consistency at every noise level.
Introduces two practical algorithms: VF for actor-critic learning and IVF for implicit value learning.
Across 26 long-horizon offline RL tasks, both methods outperform prior value-learning approaches, especially with limited data.
Better preserves return distributions instead of collapsing them to a single value.

figures.caption: Figure 1: We introduce Value Forcing, a new approach to learning distributional value functions with flow matching that supervises the learned return distribution at every flow noise level through Bellman consistency. Unlike prior methods that provide supervision only at selected noise levels or use inaccurate targets at others, Value Forcing provides substantially richer learning signals and enables much more accurate estimation of the return distribution, preventing it from collapsing around a single value. This in turn leads to better policy performance, especially in the limited-data regime.

Figure 2: Value Forcing learns more accurate return distributions than prior flow-based return estimators. (Left) We collect datasets to conduct policy evaluation experiments at a single state from each of the four OGBench domains. papers.abstract: Standard attention forms query (Q), key (K), and value (V) matrices through learned linear projections of input hidden states. Architectures such as GAU and Mega incorporate nonlinear transformations into attention. In this paper, we propose GatedV, a simple attention variant that applies SiLU only to V before aggregation without introducing additional trainable parameters. We evaluate GatedV against a standard decoder-only Transformer using matched parameter counts, paired initializations, and equal training-token budgets. At 2.33M parameters, GatedV reduces mean held-out perplexity from 59.1 to 57.9 (2.0%), with improvements across all five paired seeds. At 26.16M parameters, following an equal-budget learning-rate search, mean held-out perplexity falls from 20.2 to 19.7 (2.4%), with improvements across all three paired seeds. Small-model ablations show that the tested affine rescaling of values does not fully reproduce GatedV's gains. A short interleaved benchmark on NVIDIA DGX Spark measures approximately 0.7% higher full-context forward latency for the larger model, based on synchronized wall-clock timings. These findings suggest that value-only self-gating can improve language modeling performance without increasing parameter count or redesigning the attention-weighting mechanism.
bullets: Modifies standard attention by applying SiLU only to the value (V) representations before aggregation.
Adds no trainable parameters and leaves the attention-weighting mechanism unchanged.
Improves mean held-out perplexity by 2.0% at 2.33M parameters and 2.4% at 26.16M parameters across all paired seeds tested.
Ablations suggest tested affine value rescaling does not fully explain the gains.
incurs approximately 0.7% higher full-context forward latency for the larger model in a short DGX Spark benchmark.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own generations by matching the teacher's token probabilities. These probabilities entangle two kinds of information: which tokens the teacher prefers, and how confident it is. The latter reflects the teacher's own capacity and calibration, which a smaller student may be unable to reproduce. Because the teacher temperature changes these values without changing the ordering, OPD is also sensitive to the temperature choice. We ask whether the teacher's ordering of candidate tokens is enough, and propose Order-Only On-Policy Distillation (O$^{3}$PD). At each student-generated prefix, O$^{3}$PD trains the student to reproduce the order of the teacher's top-$K$ tokens, without fitting their probability values. The objective is therefore invariant to the teacher temperature and needs no temperature tuning. Across six teacher--student pairs, O$^{3}$PD outperforms OPD on the average over HMMT25, AIME24, and AIME25 in every pair, by up to 2.9 points, with gains of up to 5.6 points on AIME25. Other ranking losses yield similar gains, so the benefit comes from ordinal supervision itself. Analysis shows that O$^{3}$PD departs further from the teacher's probabilities than OPD, yet reproduces its ranking more faithfully and yields a stronger student. The ranking, not the probability values, thus carries the knowledge that on-policy distillation needs to transfer.
bullets: OPD’s probability targets mix token preference with teacher confidence, which smaller students may not reproduce and which vary with temperature.
O³PD trains on the teacher’s ordering of top-K tokens at prefixes generated by the student.
The ranking-based objective is invariant to teacher temperature and requires no temperature tuning.
Across six teacher–student pairs, O³PD outperformed OPD on the average of HMMT25, AIME24, and AIME25 in every pair, with gains up to 2.9 points overall and 5.6 points on AIME25.
Similar gains from other ranking losses indicate that ordinal supervision, rather than a specific loss, drives the benefit.

papers.abstract: Effective multi-agent collaboration requires finalizing solutions from reasoning that is distributed across the individual attempts of many agents. However, useful intermediate reasoning can remain unexploited when collaboration is limited to voting on conclusions reached among individual agents, or aggregating long, noisy collections of reasoning trajectories in context. In this work, we propose TTT-Consolidate, a framework that uses multi-agent reasoning trajectories as adaptation data to improve a model's subsequent reasoning. TTT-Consolidate jointly consolidates trajectories into parametric representations through test-time training, then generates a new solution by conditioning on the consolidated information. We meta-learn how to consolidate using bi-level optimization at training time, where an inner loop encodes reasoning trajectories into a lightweight LoRA adapter, and an outer loop learns meta-parameters for the inner loop such that the consolidation is helpful for the model to synthesize a final solution. As no large-scale corpus of diverse reasoning trajectories exists for training aggregation methods, we construct the OpenParallelThinking corpus composed of 12,810 math problems paired with a mixture of trajectories from six LLMs. Evaluated on challenging math and STEM benchmarks, TTT-Consolidate outperforms the best aggregation baselines by up to 20 percentage points, even under matched compute and runtime settings, with the gap widening at larger model scales. TTT-Consolidate also recovers from unsuccessful individual trajectories more robustly, an ability that improves as the number of available (even incorrect) trajectories increases. Finally, we demonstrate that TTT-Consolidate benefits from both SFT and RL-based outer loop objectives. We will release TTT-Consolidate and OpenParallelThinking for use in future work on reasoning aggregation.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of voting and aggregating noisy reasoning traces in context.
Encodes multiple trajectories into a lightweight LoRA adapter during an inner-loop test-time training phase.
Uses bi-level meta-learning to optimize how trajectory information is consolidated for final-solution synthesis.
Introduces OpenParallelThinking, a corpus of 12,810 math problems with trajectories from six LLMs.
Outperforms aggregation baselines by up to 20 percentage points on challenging math and STEM benchmarks, including under matched compute and runtime.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models now act in a closed loop, yet their safety is evaluated one variation at a time: robustness benchmarks perturb the scene while assuming instantaneous inference, and real-time execution methods study inference delay in nominal scenes. We argue that physical safety is not a property of the model alone, but emerges from how variations in the physical environment, the model, the computing platform, and execution interact in closed loop. We formalize this as cross-layer variation propagation across these system layers and use an interaction contrast to measure when joint variation creates more risk than the sum of its parts. In 4,000 paired closed-loop episodes of the pi0.5 vision-language-action model on LIBERO, a 400 ms inference delay raises the safety-violation rate by 3.5 percentage points under the training viewpoint but by 37 percentage points under a 60-degree camera shift: 33.5 percentage points (95% CI: 25-43) more than the two effects combined. We close with a research agenda toward predictable physical intelligence: predicting when variation becomes risk, and adapting compute, power, and control accordingly.
bullets: Existing evaluations often test scene variation and inference delay separately, missing their closed-loop interaction.
The paper formalizes cross-layer variation propagation and measures excess joint risk with an interaction contrast.
Across 4,000 paired LIBERO episodes using pi0.5, a 400 ms delay was far more harmful under a 60° camera shift than under the training viewpoint.
The results motivate predicting when variation becomes dangerous and adapting compute, power, and control accordingly.

papers.abstract: Financial time-series forecasting is still difficult owing to the non-stationary nature of the market, regime changes, and catastrophic forgetting, which makes conventional deep learning models hard to adapt in the long term. To achieve uncertainty-aware robust financial forecasting in the face of changing market conditions, this study proposes a Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Network with Continual Learning (HQNN-CL). The proposed framework combines Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (HMM) based regime detection, BiLSTM temporal encoding, adaptive-depth parameterized quantum circuits, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), experience replay, and probabilistic forecasting in a single architecture. The framework was tested on four real-time stock datasets: Microsoft, Systems Limited, Teradata and Tata Consultancy Services, and compared with seven state-of-the-art forecasting models, including recurrent and Transformer-based models. The experimental results show that HQNN-CL has outperformed other methods on the Systems Limited (RMSE = 3.0149) and Teradata (RMSE = 0.8909) datasets and is within 0.32% and 0.40% of the best baseline method for Microsoft and Tata Consultancy Services, respectively. The proposed framework also generates well-calibrated probabilistic forecasts within the range of 89.5% to 96.5% empirical coverage rate, has zero catastrophic forgetting (BWT = 0.0000) for all sequential learning tasks, and consistently shows positive forward transfer. Ablation and statistical significance analyses also validate the performance of adaptive quantum feature learning and continual adaptation under heterogeneous market conditions, regime-wise.
bullets: Targets non-stationary markets, regime shifts, and catastrophic forgetting in long-term financial forecasting.
Combines Gaussian HMM regime detection, BiLSTM temporal encoding, adaptive-depth quantum circuits, EWC, experience replay, and probabilistic forecasting.
Evaluated on Microsoft, Systems Limited, Teradata, and Tata Consultancy Services stock datasets against seven forecasting models.
Outperformed comparison methods on Systems Limited and Teradata, while remaining close to the best baseline on Microsoft and Tata Consultancy Services.
Produced calibrated forecasts with 89.5%–96.5% empirical coverage, zero catastrophic forgetting, and positive forward transfer across sequential tasks.

papers.abstract: Diffusion driving vision-language-action models repeatedly execute the backbone at every denoising stage, incurring substantial inference cost, while it remains unclear whether all scenes require the same decoding computation. To distinguish when a trajectory becomes readable from how much further refinement it requires, we analyze trajectory readout across network depth and decoding progress. We identify a depth-decoding dissociation in which late-layer representations already support useful trajectory readout after the first forward sweep, whereas early-layer representations benefit more from continued decoding. We further find that both the preferred readout layer and decoding depth vary across scenes. Based on these observations, we propose a scene-adaptive readout and decoding framework. A scene-conditioned readout MoE adaptively weights and combines trajectory predictions from layer-specific late-layer representations after a single backbone sweep, while an adaptive decoding policy applies additional native refinement only when required by the scene. We evaluate our framework on two diffusion driving VLAs across the Waymo E2E and nuScenes benchmarks. Our method improves validation RFS by up to 0.56 while also improving test performance, and achieves an end-to-end speedup of up to $6.0\times$ on Waymo E2E, while consistently reducing trajectory error on nuScenes. These results demonstrate that scene-level readout and decoding allocation improves planning quality while avoiding unnecessary decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjyu001/SARD
bullets: Diffusion driving VLAs repeatedly run the backbone during denoising, but scenes differ in the decoding needed for reliable trajectories.
Late-layer features can support useful readout after one backbone sweep, while early-layer features benefit more from continued refinement.
A scene-conditioned readout MoE combines layer-specific predictions, and an adaptive policy adds native decoding only when needed.
Across two VLAs on Waymo E2E and nuScenes, the method improves planning quality, reduces trajectory error, and achieves up to 6.0× end-to-end speedup on Waymo E2E.
papers.selection_reason: Scene-adaptive readout and decoding for diffusion driving VLAs, improving planning quality while cutting inference cost; fits VLA and efficiency.
papers.title: Scene-Adaptive Readout and Decoding in Diffusion Driving VLAs
papers.tldr: A scene-adaptive framework reduces diffusion driving VLA inference cost by selecting where to read trajectories and how much to decode per scene.

papers.abstract: Retrieving objects from densely packed storage requires anticipating how contact disturbs surrounding objects when limited clearance prevents lifting the target over clutter. However, contact can propagate beyond the target's immediate neighbors, while accumulated prediction errors make learned dynamics unreliable over long planning horizons. We introduce DARE (Disturbance-Aware REtrieval), a geometry-aware relational dynamics framework that uses retrospective correction to improve long-horizon prediction for disturbance-aware retrieval. DARE encodes compact object descriptors and predicts action-conditioned disturbance propagation through object-level message passing. When a sparse observation becomes available, a learned corrector uses the prediction discrepancy to amend an earlier predicted state and reruns the intervening dynamics, propagating the correction through the predicted contact chain. These predictions guide a receding-horizon planner that balances retrieval progress against displacement and rotation of surrounding objects, permitting necessary contact while discouraging harmful disturbance. Experiments in planar and RoboCasa environments evaluate long-horizon prediction, generalization, and robustness for disturbance-aware retrieval in dense clutter. See our project website: https://the-back-to-the-future.github.io
bullets: Targets retrieval when limited clearance requires contacting surrounding objects.
Uses geometry-aware object descriptors and relational message passing to predict action-conditioned disturbance propagation.
Applies a learned corrector to sparse observations, amending earlier states and rerunning dynamics through predicted contact chains.
Guides receding-horizon planning that balances retrieval progress with surrounding-object displacement and rotation.
Evaluated in planar and RoboCasa environments for prediction, generalization, and robustness in dense clutter.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Pipeline Overview: Given object geometry and the current scene state, DARE propagates action-conditioned interactions over an object graph to predict scene evolution under candidate target motions. The resulting rollouts capture direct and indirect disturbances to surrounding objects, enabling the planner to select a retrieval trajectory that balances goal progress against collateral disturbance.

Fig. 1: Disturbance-aware retrieval. (a) Collision avoidance leaves the target blocked. (b) Direct retrieval topples a neighboring object. (c) Our method predicts contact-induced disturbance to plan retrieval through controlled contact, preserving stability of surrounding objects.

papers.abstract: Language and vision models became data-efficient by pretraining on plentiful unlabelled data; physical field models have such data, over ten million 3D shapes, but geometry pretraining designs its targets rather than deriving them from the physics. Euler-Lagrange geometry pretraining derives them: for attached flow, a shape enters the flow's Euler-Lagrange equation only through coefficients that distance and normal line (the normal up to sign) fix to first order. Their reconstruction error therefore bounds what a representation loses about any field, and fine-tuning on costly simulations need only assemble the global field. We realise it in AREALS, a masked surface autoencoder whose areal tokens carry position, normal and area, pretrained self-supervised and sign-free on 61,822 raw meshes. Because the operating condition enters only through the far field, sensors can supply it: AREALS completes a hidden field in one forward pass without condition labels. It matches the accuracy of the same architecture trained from scratch with half the simulations on DrivAerML and DrivAerNet++ and about a quarter on WindsorML. On DoubleDelta wings, 20 sensors give $3.9\times$ and $4.0\times$ lower field and force error than GABI, a Bayesian inversion method with a learned prior, and beyond the training angles pretraining halves the error.
bullets: Motivated by the abundance of unlabeled 3D shapes and the cost of physics simulations, the work derives geometry-pretraining targets from the Euler-Lagrange equation for attached flow.
AREALS is a sign-free masked surface autoencoder using tokens that encode position, normal, and area, pretrained self-supervised on 61,822 raw meshes.
Sensors provide operating conditions, allowing one-pass completion of hidden fields without condition labels.
AREALS matches a scratch-trained model using half the simulations on DrivAerML and DrivAerNet++, and about one quarter on WindsorML.
With 20 sensors on DoubleDelta wings, it achieves 3.9× lower field error and 4.0× lower force error than GABI; pretraining also halves error beyond training angles.

figures.caption: Figure B.1. The Euler–Lagrange construction and its guarantees. Assuming only locality, the shift symmetry, rotations and Galilean boosts fixes the flow’s Lagrangian density as the pressure, with the gas’s equation of state the only free function; making its integral stationary gives the Euler–Lagrange equation, the law the flow obeys. Each guarantee on the right follows from this construction, and its last line says what AREALS builds in or learns from it.

Figure B.2. Near the wall the Euler–Lagrange equation needs only local geometry, the distance encodes it, and pretraining reads it (schematic; computed counterparts in Figure 2). (A) Bodies with the same wall around p, the wall point nearest x, have the same Euler–Lagrange equation at x, though not the same flow: in wall coordinates the Lagrangian density, the pressure times √ g, sees the shape only through the surface metric gS and the shape operator W at p. (B) The level sets and steepest lines of the distance are those coordinates; the value, Hessian and third derivative of ηS = 1 2 d2S give the wall, its normal lines and their spreading W (Lemma 1). (C) The pretrained decoder reads the distance and normal line at each query’s nearest wall point from nearby tokens; W is not supervised. Widths and the dashed radius in C are schematic; the 52% is measured on 16 DoubleDelta test wings (Section K).

Figure B.3. Wall coordinates and the half squared distance on the car of Figure 2. (a) Round the windscreen, cells between levels of t stretch by 1 + tκ: to 0.81 over the concave and 1.26 over the convex part, at t = 0.21. (b) On the centre plane, the bands of ηS vanish on S; its Hessian gives the normal lines (purple) and its third derivative the shape operator W , drawn as osculating arcs at two points. Right: through p, ηS is 1 2 t2 along the normal and flat along the surface.

Figure 2. What the flow equation needs from geometry, computed on one car mesh in potential flow (Section B). Tags say how each panel is established: derived for attached flow, or proved. (a) Surface pressure; a point x near the wall is its foot p plus a distance t along the normal. (b) The Hessian of the half squared distance ηS gives the normal lines (purple), and its third derivative the shape operator W , whose norm sets the colour. (c) Field error against shape distance for 30 perturbed shapes, with the flow re-solved on each: per unit distance it grows from 1.8 to 24 as the perturbing waves shorten when the distance counts position alone (open), but stays at 0.45–0.57 when it also counts normal lines (filled), so ω(r) ≤ 0.57 r. Figure B.3 draws the wall coordinates and ηS on the centre plane.

papers.abstract: Large language models show large and seemingly arbitrary performance drops when a task is rewritten in ways that leave its requirements untouched. We recast task difficulty as a causal quantity: the treatment effect of meaning-preserving perturbations on a model. A meaning-preserving rewrite can only be observed to hurt a task the model can already solve, so we place the estimand on the principal stratum where the degradation occurs: the conditional causal difficulty (CCD), the probability that a randomly drawn twin breaks a solvable task. Because harder tasks tend to be more phrasing-sensitive, complexity enters as an effect modifier rather than a confounder, and we residualize it out to obtain complexity-residualized difficulty (CRD); zero for a task exactly as fragile as its complexity predicts, positive for anomalously fragile ones. Current benchmarks do not supply the data CCD requires, so we introduce GlassGSM and GlassMATH, augmenting GSM8K and MATH with twins built from perturbation families, raising fragility on GlassGSM by $\approx 12\times$ over GSM-IC-style distractors on the same problems ($3.7\%\to44.9\%$) while keeping the answer key unchanged. Our predictor Frail learns the per-perturbation break probability and reaches $0.613{\pm}0.023$ of the suite reliability ceiling on GlassGSM and $0.557{\pm}0.023$ on GlassMATH, against $0.171$/$0.401$ for a surface-feature baseline and $0.444$/$0.463$ for supervised baselines such as VAP3, and, at a $5\%$ curation budget on GlassGSM, doubles random recall of fragile items, matching an oracle ranking. Additionally, cross-fitted residualization leaves CRD uncorrelated with the declared proxy in practice. Code is available at https://github.com/upwork/Conditional_Causal_Difficulty_for_LLMs
bullets: It proposes conditional causal difficulty (CCD): the probability that a meaning-preserving “twin” breaks a task the model can already solve.
Complexity-residualized difficulty (CRD) removes fragility explained by task complexity, highlighting anomalously fragile tasks.
GlassGSM and GlassMATH augment existing benchmarks with perturbation-generated twins while preserving answer keys.
On GlassGSM, the proposed perturbations increase observed fragility from 3.7% to 44.9% compared with GSM-IC-style distractors.
The Frail predictor estimates per-perturbation break probability and improves fragile-item selection over stated baselines; results are reported relative to each suite’s reliability ceiling.

papers.title: Fragility Is Not Reducible to Hardness: Conditional Causal Difficulty for LLMs

papers.abstract: Embodied agents that answer questions about their route need a memory of what they saw, and scene graphs are a natural form for it. A vision-language model (VLM) can receive such a graph as text or through a graph encoder, but accuracy alone cannot show whether the graph holds the episode's facts, reaches the model, or is actually relied on. In this diagnostic study, we introduce a graph-swap test for the last of these: each episode is given another episode's graph, and we count how many answers change. On an embodied question-answering benchmark with routes through two to seven rooms, we use it to compare ways of delivering scene-graph memory to a fine-tuned VLM. As text, the memory is used strongly, adding 30 points on route questions. As a graph, it is not, and we trace why: the encoder preserves the information, but standard pooled and late fusion discard it. Giving each node its own input token recovers part of it, a gain of 8.3 points on route questions that the swap test confirms comes from the graph. The test also exposes a shortcut that accuracy hides: when the same facts appear in the text, the model ignores its graph. The test thus offers a cheap check of whether a VLM uses its scene-graph memory, and our analysis points to how that memory should be delivered.
bullets: The study tests whether scene-graph memory is represented, reaches the VLM, and actually influences answers.
It swaps each episode’s graph with another episode’s graph and counts answer changes to measure graph reliance.
Text-based graph memory is strongly used, improving route-question performance by 30 points.
Graph encoders preserve information, but standard pooled and late fusion discard its usefulness.

Giving each graph node its own input token recovers part of the benefit, with an 8.3-point route-question gain confirmed by the swap test; duplicated text facts can cause the model to ignore the graph.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a novel 'graph-swap test' to diagnose whether embodied VLMs actually utilize their scene-graph memory, finding that standard graph encoders often discard information via pooling and identifying a shortcut where models ignore graph memory when text is present.
papers.title: Do Embodied VLMs Actually Use Their Scene-Graph Memory?
papers.tldr: A graph-swap diagnostic shows that embodied VLMs often fail to use scene-graph memory unless graph information is delivered through node-level input tokens.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) suffer from visual hallucination, such as saying an object that is not present in an image. We ask a more fundamental question: whether a VLM is even aware of where it is looking before understanding the semantic meaning in the image. We formulate this question as a LOOK task: identifying which parts of its visual input were available to the model. We construct the task in a self-supervised way without manually labeling the available region to the model. Our experiments show that existing VLMs fail to localize the visible region. We further show that fine-tuning VLMs on the proposed LOOK task improves a model's awareness of visual input.
bullets: Targets visual hallucination and the more basic issue of visual-input awareness.
Defines LOOK as identifying the portions of an image available to the model before semantic interpretation.
Constructs the task without manually labeling visible regions.
Finds that existing VLMs struggle to localize their visible input.
Shows that fine-tuning on LOOK improves visual-input awareness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Where does a hallucination originate? In this example, we ask what animal is grazing in a photograph of a dog on grassland, a model answers “a sheep”. The same wrong answer can arise at two levels of the hierarchy. At the Perceive level, the model uses the image but misrecognizes the dog. At the Look level, the model does not rely on the image at all, and “sheep” follows from the textual context.

Figure 1: Hierarchy of visual understanding: LOOK → Perceive → Understand. We introduce a hierarchical visual grounding structure and argue that visual hallucination can arise from any level. This work focuses on the fundamental Look level.

Figure 4: Illustration of VisABench construction. All conditions use the same prompt, “Does this image contain: dog? Answer with Yes or No.”, with the only difference being the visual input. The grounded answer is Yes in (i) and No in (ii) and (iii).

Figure 7: Permutation test. The grey bars mean IoU after re-pairing each prediction with the window of another image while the color lines show the IoU on the given image. The pretrained and SFT models show no positive dependence on the view.

Figure 5: Four ways to probe visual awareness. The green box shows the available visual region while the red dashed box shows the prediction. (i) We input the full image, but the model boxes the dominant person rather than the whole canvas. (ii, iii) When the context pixels are greyed out or its embeddings are zeroed, the model still locates the dominant person, likely using semantic shortcuts. (iv) In LOOK, the model answers with the whole canvas.
Figure 6: Learning to look dynamics.

Figure 3: Constructing a LOOK example. We select a merge-block-aligned viewport and encode only its pixels for the VLM. Importantly, we restore positional metadata from the full canvas without encoding the excluded image content. The crop’s coordinates provide the target automatically.

Table 3: Performance on VisABench. All models are evaluated on the same 10,752 items. For each condition, we report the Yes rate (%) and mean p(Yes). Gap denotes the real-image Yes rate minus the no-image Yes rate. The bottom rows report results for additional pretrained VLMs (Bai et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024b; Gemma Team, 2026). † The image-placeholder embedding of this model is untrained, causing it to produce neither Yes nor No without an image. IoU counts answers without a valid box as zero.
