papers.selection_reason: Introduces a self-supervised LOOK task probing whether VLMs localize their visible input region, a spatial-awareness diagnostic with transferable value for spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Learning to Look: A Foundation for Visual Understanding
papers.tldr: The paper introduces LOOK, a self-supervised task for testing and improving whether vision-language models know which image regions they can actually see.

papers.abstract: Gradients are no longer used only to train models: Gradient magnitudes are now measurement instruments, used to rank attention heads for pruning, to decide per-example clipping in private training, to allocate adapter rank budgets, and to debug models. Across these workflows, larger gradient magnitudes are taken to mean greater importance. Even for a fixed input--output function, these gradients are computed in one of many possible parameter coordinate systems. For example, attention scores depend on the query and key projections only through the paired product $W_QW_K^\top$. Scaling a head's query projection by $c$ and the corresponding key projection by $1/c$ therefore leaves every output logit unchanged. This change in parameter coordinates rescales the corresponding query and key gradient norms by $1/c$ and $c$, respectively. To test whether gradient-based decisions remain unchanged under these coordinate changes, we introduce Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization (GRR). GRR rewrites a trained model in new parameter coordinates that compute exactly the same function, verifies that predictions are unchanged, and then tests whether the decisions derived from the gradients are unchanged too. Our audits span GLUE classifiers, a ViT on CIFAR-10, GPT-2-medium and GPT-2-large, a 1.1B-parameter Llama-style model on WikiText-2, and six trained LoRA adapters. Empirically, predictions are preserved throughout, but both the gradients and the gradient-based decisions change. Across 66 GLUE attention audits, the median top-3 overlap of raw head-gradient rankings is only $1/3$, and rankings and pruning masks change even under the mildest rescalings we test. In the largest of 14 global-pruning audits, the shifted ranking selects head masks that differ in four of 22 pruned heads and reach $50.92\%$ and $94.84\%$ validation accuracy on one ELECTRA SST-2 model.
bullets: Gradient magnitudes depend on the chosen parameter coordinates, so larger values may not consistently indicate greater importance.
The study introduces Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization (GRR), which rewrites models into functionally equivalent coordinates and compares gradient-derived decisions.
Audits cover GLUE classifiers, a CIFAR-10 ViT, GPT-2 models, a 1.1B-parameter Llama-style model, and six LoRA adapters.
Predictions remain unchanged, but gradients, rankings, and pruning masks change; across 66 GLUE attention audits, the median top-3 overlap is only 1/3.
In the largest global-pruning audit, four of 22 pruned heads differ, with the resulting masks reaching 50.92% and 94.84% validation accuracy on one ELECTRA SST-2 model.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the GRR audit. Scaling a head’s query projection by c and the corresponding key projection by 1/c preserves the model’s function and predictions. This coordinate change rescales the query and key gradients by 1/c and c, respectively. Applying different scales across heads changes the raw-gradient head ranking. Gradient-guided pruning therefore keeps different heads, and the two pruned ELECTRA models differ substantially in SST-2 validation accuracy, as detailed in Sec. 4.3.

Figure 4: Token-level anatomy of the largest layer-local decoder-only pruning gap: GPT-2-medium on WikiText-2, layer-2 V–O gauge, with raw-gradient bottom-3 pruning. Test perplexity is 46.75 for the dense model, 46.92 after pruning with the original-coordinate mask, and 50.09 after pruning with the reparameterized-coordinate mask, giving a 3.17-point gap. (a) With zero next-token argmax flips and maximum logit difference 3.36 × 10−3, the coordinates select disjoint head sets with Jaccard 0. (b) The reparameterized-coordinate mask is worse on 120 of 128 blocks. (c) The most affected block localizes the additional next-token negative log-likelihood. Canonical balancing makes the two raw-gradient masks identical, while function-space scores also agree across coordinates.

Figure 2: Executing Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 on a trained checkpoint. (a) Each head’s raw score follows the corresponding exact scalar-gauge orbit; circles mark the checkpoint and diamonds the constructed representative. (b) Applying the constructive proof exactly reverses the 12-head ranking. (c) Raw top-3 overlap becomes 0, whereas path-normalized, canonically balanced, and functionspace decisions are unchanged. Engineered scales lie in [0.159, 4.53]; the maximum logit difference is 7.63 × 10−6; prediction flips are 0.0%; and realized scores deviate from the prescribed score targets by at most 1.2× 10−6 in relative terms.

Figure 7: Cross-task global V–O pruning calibration. Each point is a raw same-function comparison for a 15% global-pruning decision with RoBERTa on SST-2, QNLI, or MRPC, with bottom pruning and top ablation split across the two plots. Mild gauges are enough to move masks substantially; whether that mask disagreement becomes a large validation gap is task- and decision-dependent.

Figure 6: Anatomy of the largest GLUE global-pruning gap: ELECTRA on SST-2 under an aggressive global Q–K gauge, with bottom-15% pruning. (a) The two 22-head masks share 18 removed heads, with four removals unique to each coordinate. This difference amounts to four head substitutions and gives Jaccard 18/26 = 0.692. (b) The original-coordinate mask removes every final-layer head, whereas the reparameterized-coordinate mask retains H1 and H8. Before any pruning, the two coordinates have zero prediction flips on the 128-example audit subset and a maximum logit difference of 1.25 × 10−5. (c) The two masks yield 50.92% and 94.84% accuracy on the full 872- example validation set. Canonical balancing makes the masks identical, eliminating the coordinate discrepancy but not guaranteeing a useful pruning heuristic.

Figure 5: Iterative pruning schedules for RoBERTa on MRPC. The right plot shows that raw samefunction reparameterization changes the accumulated masks, and the center plot shows that the same reparameterization also changes the accuracy trajectory under top-head ablation. Canonical balancing maps both coordinates to the same schedule for the V–O scalar gauge, so the balanced curve tracks the original coordinate and the final mask Jaccard is 1.000.

Figure 3: Summary GRR diagnostics. (a) Raw GLUE attention gradients and paired-product tangents have low same-function top-3 agreement, whereas path-normalized, function-space, and canonically balanced scores are stable under the scalar gauges tested; bars show medians and pale bands show observed ranges. (b) Decoder-only raw rankings and pruning masks also have low agreement. The scale sweeps in (c) and (d) show that DistilBERT stability decreases smoothly as the gauge range grows, with zero prediction flips; shading gives bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for the mean.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the reliability of gradient-based decisions (like pruning) under reparameterization in LLMs, providing insights into LLM architecture and optimization, fitting 'Language Foundation Models'.
papers.title: Same Function, Different Gradients: Evaluating Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization
papers.tldr: Gradient-based importance decisions can change substantially under parameter reparameterizations that leave a model’s predictions exactly unchanged.

papers.abstract: Monocular semantic SLAM aims to reconstruct scene geometry and build semantic maps from RGB observations. Existing Gaussian-based methods often attach semantic labels or features to evolving Gaussian primitives, making semantic fusion difficult to maintain and increasing reconstruction overhead. Hybrid Gaussian--voxel representations provide more stable semantic support, but often rely on RGB-D input or known poses and do not revise historical semantic evidence after geometry updates. We present UniGS-SLAM, an RGB-only framework that decouples open-vocabulary semantics from Gaussian reconstruction while preserving bidirectional interaction. Foundation priors enhance monocular depth and pose estimation, while semantic observations are fused into an independent sparse voxel map with observation provenance, enabling historical contributions to be revised as reconstruction evolves. The fused semantics further guide Gaussian filtering and local surface refinement. Experiments on Replica, ScanNet, and KITTI-360 show leading tracking, rendering, and geometric reconstruction performance among representative RGB-only methods, together with strong open-set semantic mapping on Replica and ScanNet. We also achieve a 2.37-fold reconstruction speedup over the fastest compared semantic SLAM baseline. Project page: https://3dagentworld.github.io/UniGS-SLAM/.
bullets: Addresses unstable semantic fusion and costly reconstruction in Gaussian-based monocular semantic SLAM.
Uses foundation priors to improve monocular depth and pose estimation while decoupling semantics from Gaussian reconstruction.
Stores semantics in a provenance-aware sparse voxel map, allowing historical evidence to be revised after geometry updates.
Uses fused semantics to guide Gaussian filtering and local surface refinement.
Reports leading performance among representative RGB-only methods on Replica, ScanNet, and KITTI-360, with a 2.37× reconstruction speedup over the fastest compared semantic SLAM baseline.

papers.title: UniGS-SLAM: Monocular Gaussian SLAM with Enhanced Geometry and Open-Vocabulary Semantics

papers.abstract: Complex systems, from ecosystems to brains, are usually modeled as modular components coupled through feedback rather than as indivisible wholes. Can a transformer trained on the joint behavior of a group of interacting agents be understood in the same way? In this work, we develop a computational-mechanics framework to study agents interacting in feedback loops. We formally prove that any joint stochastic process can be presented as resulting from the behavior of agents interacting in feedback, and the resulting process is generated by a hidden Markov model whose Bayesian beliefs factorize into separate components per agent. Furthermore, our experiments show that transformers trained on such feedback sequences make use of this separability, disentangling the beliefs about the underlying factors into separate subspaces of their residual stream. This representation is found to scale linearly (instead of exponentially) with the number of agents. Moreover, interventions show that these representations are causally efficacious, allowing for targeted steering of individual agents' beliefs by selectively inserting counterfactuals. However, coarse-graining the behavior is found to disrupt the factorization, and can force a higher-dimensional representation. Together, the results establish both the dimensional advantage of a factorized representation and the ability of transformers to exploit it, laying the groundwork for investigating traces of compositional predictive architecture in pretrained models.
bullets: A computational-mechanics framework shows any joint stochastic process can be represented as interacting agents in feedback, with beliefs factorized by agent.
Experiments find transformer residual streams disentangle these agent-specific beliefs into separate subspaces.
The factorized representation scales linearly rather than exponentially with the number of agents.
Causal interventions enable targeted steering of one agent’s beliefs through counterfactual insertion.
Coarse-graining behavior can break factorization and require higher-dimensional representations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Beliefs can be patched factor by factor. Belief patching for the system with beliefs as in Fig. 2: a counterfactual belief is spliced into one factor’s residual-stream subspace, and the joint next-token distribution is compared in KL with the Bayes prediction for the patched beliefs (edit), the unedited model (floor), a write with no effect (null), and an unrelated sequence (unrel.). Annotated: fraction of the null-to-target gap closed (mean ± sd, five seeds). Protocol is described in Appendix L.

Figure 4: The dimensionality advantage of factored representations grows with the number of agents. (a) A social network in which a central hub exchanges perceptions and actions with N agents; the agents (green band) can be read as a single macro-agent, the tensor product of the individual agents, so the network is a binary feedback loop between the hub and this macro-agent. (b) Cumulative explained variance (CEV) of the final-layer residual stream follows the factored prediction for the telephone process with three mess3 sub-agents. Solid curves: mean over five seeds (see Table 2); shaded bands: min–max across seeds. Dashed: CEV of the factored concatenation of the Bayes-optimal per-agent belief states on the same sequences; dotted: CEV of their tensor product (Kronecker). (c) Effective rank nc—the smallest number of principal components whose CEV reaches 80% (red) resp. 95% (blue)—for telephone processes with N mess3 sub-agents (BOS position excluded, 4096 sequences). Solid lines: the final-layer residual stream (mean over five seeds per N ; the shaded min–max band never exceeds one component). Bayes-optimal belief states themselves are the factored concatenation of the per-agent belief states (dashed; simplex dimension ∑ i(di − 1) = 8N ) and their Kronecker product (dotted; simplex dimension ∏ i di − 1 = 9N − 1). For N ≥ 3 the residual stream matches the factored belief states to within one component at both thresholds, while the Kronecker belief states require 2.5–11× more. (d) Coarse-graining forces a higher-dimensional representation: CEV by PCA rank, one color per observed interface, dashed lines the Bayes-optimal belief state and solid lines the trained transformer (mean over five independent draws of the process, one model per draw and interface; shaded bands: min–max across draws). Under full observation, the belief state factorizes, and the theory curve saturates at the 8-dimensional factored concatenation, whereas the coarse observers must track the entangled joint belief state (∼ 22 dimensions). Process and model parameters in Appendix K.

Figure 2: Separable linear representations of beliefs emerge in transformers trained on joint feedback processes. A coupled process with mess3 as agent T (top row) and fractal2 as agent U (bottom row). (Leftmost column) States of the MSP of each factor (top two PCA directions; colored by the belief resp. the emission probability). (Remaining columns) linear reconstruction from the final-layer residual stream at different points through training (held-out linear probe refit per checkpoint, same PCA basis; held-out R2 annotated). The experimental protocol is described in Appendix K.

Figure 17: Belief edits track the Bayes prediction continuously along the interpolation path. KL divergence (median over interventions; bands: interquartile range) between the edited next-token distribution and three references, as a function of the edit dose λ: the Bayes prediction at the interpolated tuple (bf (λ), b−f ) (on-path, solid), and the Bayes predictions at the two endpoints (λ = 0: original; λ = 1: full counterfactual; dashed). Rows: the two feedback setups; columns: the patched factor; n: evaluable interventions pooled over five seeds per setup. The dashed horizontal rule is the unedited model’s own fidelity floor; the dotted curve is the untouched factor’s component against its original prediction (leakage). At λ = 0.5 the nearest endpoint reference is 16–56× farther from the edited output than the interpolated target. Panel counts differ only through the identifiability gate (0.05 total variation between the endpoint references): the candidate pool is identical across panels, but the fractal2 belief distribution concentrates on a near-degenerate one-dimensional set, so swapping a fractal2 belief more often produces indistinguishable references.

Figure 8: There are four different readily accessible presentations for a feedback process between agents T and U . Which one you arrive at depends on 1) whether you choose to model the simultaneous process X0:tY0:t or the shifted process X1:t+1Y0:t, and 2) whether you box circuit elements so that Agent U or Agent T operates first. All presentations modify the linear operator of one of the transducers, either delaying the action or the perception.

Figure 11: Probe selectivity controls and layer-wise emergence. All panels show the held-out linear-probe error 1 − R2 on the residual stream over training (mess3–fractal2 feedback loops). Solid curves: mean over five seeds per setup—the canonical run plus four reruns (Table 2); shaded bands: min–max across seeds. (a,b) Final-layer probes fitted to the true per-factor beliefs and to two controls: the same sequence’s belief two positions earlier (time-shifted) and beliefs of shuffled sequences (a derangement of the batch). The shuffled floor stays at 1−R2 ≈ 1 throughout; the true factors improve by 40–280× over training. (c–f) The true-belief probe refit at each residual-stream depth (embedding, blocks 1–4, final LayerNorm). Blocks 1–2 acquire essentially all of the structure; the action-delayed factor U is complete by block 2, while factor T sharpens to the last layer. The embedding row is training-invariant by construction (a linear probe on it can realize any function of token and position).

Figure 14: The base HMMs (edge labels read “emission : probability”). (a) mess3(x, a): three states, three symbols; with b = (1 − a)/2 and y = 1 − 2x. A transition into state s′ emits symbol s′ with probability ax ≡ ax and each other symbol with probability bx (independent of the source state, so both incoming arrows share the label shown by each vertex); a self-loop at s emits s with probability ay and each other symbol with probability by. Its mixed-state presentation is the fractal simplex of Fig. 2 (top row). (b) fractal2(b, p, q): two states, two symbols; state s re-emits its own symbol with probability b and stays, otherwise emits the other symbol and moves with probability p (resp. q). Its two-state belief simplex is the barcode of Fig. 10c. (c) sns(p, q): the simple nonunifilar source; symbol 1 is emitted only on the resetting B → A transition, giving a Cantor-like 1-D belief geometry, drawn as a barcode like the fractal2 factor of Fig. 10c.

Figure 16: Belief patching under the unprojected and the encoder-orthogonalized write. (a) Fraction of the null-to-target distance closed by the edit, per setup and patched factor (large markers: ratio of means over seeds; small dots: individual seeds; filled: unprojected write ∆, open: ∆⊥ of Eq. (67)). Every setup without an sns factor closes 89.5–99.6% of the gap under either construction. The two sns loops fail under both, and are the only setups the construction changes qualitatively: under the unprojected write, editing the mess3 partner in the sns→mess3 loop leaves the output farther from the target than no edit at all (−41%), which the projection turns into +14%—the raw write was corrupting the sns encoding directly. (b) The between-factor encoder subspace overlap (share of the edited factor’s encoder span lying in its partners’) against the gap difference between the constructions. The overlap is substantial everywhere (0.13–0.58) and does not separate fragile from robust writes—the sns loops are the outliers in both directions—so the deviations are not explained by overlapping belief encodings.

Figure 9: Belief-state geometry of the role-swapped setup likewise refines over training. Rows: both factors of setup B (agent T fractal2, agent U mess3); setup A is shown in Fig. 2. Leftmost column: ground-truth MSP. Remaining columns: linear reconstruction from the final-layer residual stream at checkpoints 0, 500, 5k, and 50k (probe refit per checkpoint; same PCA basis and color conventions as Fig. 2; held-out R2 per panel). Both factors are already reconstructed to R2 ≥ 0.83 at initialization and are refined by training to R2 ≥ 0.998 by step 50k.

Figure 10: Both mess3–fractal2 setups are represented by factorized, causally load-bearing beliefs in the residual stream. The final-checkpoint reconstruction of Fig. 2 with the role-swapped arrangement alongside it: mess3 as agent T and fractal2 as agent U (setup A, panels a,b,e,f— the setup reproduced in the main text) or vice-versa (setup B, panels c,d,g,h). Top row: Bayes-optimal belief states; bottom row: reconstruction from the final-layer residual stream at step 50k. Panel and color conventions and the probe protocol are as in Fig. 2; the belief patching in (i,j) is as in Fig. 3.

Figure 15: All runs converge to their Bayes-optimal floors. Evaluation loss over training (log scale); solid curves are means over five seeds per setup, shaded bands the min–max across seeds (mostly narrower than the line). Dashed lines: each setup’s Bayes-optimal floor, position-averaged and estimated with 32768 MC samples (per-seed floor estimates differ by ∼10−3 nats; the line shows the family mean). (a) The four main-text setups: the mess3–fractal2 feedback loops A and B of Figs. 2 and 10 and the two telephone processes. (b) The telephone-mess3 N -sweep of Fig. 4c. Every setup reaches its floor within ∼103 steps; final losses lie within 1–5× 10−3 nats of the floor, i.e. at the precision of the MC estimate for all runs except two of the five N=4 seeds, which plateau 3–5 × 10−3 nats above it. papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of how transformers represent interacting agents in feedback loops, providing a mechanistic understanding of multi-agent reasoning in LLMs, fitting 'Language Foundation Models'.
papers.title: Beliefs in feedback: Factored representations of interacting agents in transformers
papers.tldr: Transformers trained on feedback-driven multi-agent sequences can factorize and causally manipulate beliefs about individual agents, using representations that scale linearly with agent count.

papers.abstract: The efficiency and fidelity of 3D Gaussian Splatting critically depend on adaptive density control, which grows and suppresses Gaussian primitives throughout optimization. However, the standard pipeline still relies on heuristic view-space gradients, scale thresholds, and global opacity resets, rather than explicitly assessing the loss-reducing effect of each split, clone, or opacity update. This mismatch can allocate primitives to already-sufficient regions, miss under-reconstructed structures, and destabilize training through blanket opacity changes. In this work, we recast adaptive density control as a collection of local loss-reduction decisions. We derive efficient Taylor-based per-Gaussian surrogates that predict the objective change caused by three primitive-level operations: splitting, cloning, and opacity decay. This yields a unified loss-aware framework with three components. First, we extend second-order splitting to a normalized joint position-scale space, enabling children to adapt not only their locations but also their anisotropic extents. Second, we formulate duplicate cloning as a surrogate minimization problem, selecting only Gaussians whose duplicated contribution is predicted to improve reconstruction and assigning each child a principled opacity. Third, we replace global opacity reset with selective soft opacity decay that weakens harmful primitives while preserving useful ones. Across standard 3DGS benchmarks, our method produces more targeted primitive allocation and achieves improved rendering quality with comparable or smaller Gaussian budgets compared to baselines.
bullets: Replaces heuristic gradients, scale thresholds, and global opacity resets with per-Gaussian loss-reduction decisions.
Uses efficient Taylor-based surrogates to estimate the objective change from primitive-level operations.
Extends second-order splitting to joint position-scale space for adaptive child locations and anisotropic extents.
Selects beneficial clones with principled opacity and applies selective soft decay to harmful primitives.
Improves rendering quality with comparable or smaller Gaussian budgets across standard 3DGS benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our framework. (a) During training, we accumulate per-Gaussian surrogate statistics, including the joint splitting matrix and surrogate terms for cloning and opacity decay. At each densification interval, these surrogates determine whether each Gaussian is split, cloned, or assigned opacity decay. (b) For each Gaussian, we sequentially evaluate splitting, cloning, and opacity decay using accumulated loss-aware surrogate statistics. Joint splitting computes a loss-reducing direction in the joint position-scale space and initializes two children with corresponding position and log-scale perturbations. Cloning minimizes a local Taylor-based surrogate with respect to the duplicate opacity and appends a duplicate child when it is predicted to decrease the loss. Opacity decay similarly estimates a loss-reducing opacity decay strength and selectively decreases the opacity of Gaussians whose current contributions are predicted to be harmful.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on standard 3DGS benchmarks. Red boxes highlight zoom-in regions where our method better preserves fine details and object boundaries.

Figure 1: Intuition of our loss-aware adaptive density control (ADC). We visualize the effect of each density-control operation from the same intermediate state at the 3,000th training iteration. (a) Splitting: we compare the position-only split of [32] with our position-scale split, visualizing splitting Gaussians as ellipsoids. While the position-only split produces misplaced offspring around the thin bicycle handle, our position-scale split places offspring more appropriately and forms the handle structure more faithfully. (b) Cloning: we compare standard 3DGS and ours by individually cloning candidate Gaussians and measuring the resulting loss change; green/red indicate candidates whose duplication decreases/increases the loss. Our cloning selects mostly loss-reducing candidates and recovers missed structures, whereas heuristic cloning introduces loss-increasing candidates. (c) Opacity decay: we compare the opacity reset of standard 3DGS with our selective opacity decay. Opacity reset makes all Gaussian primitives nearly transparent, leading to unstable training. In contrast, our method weakens only Gaussians predicted to hinder optimization. (d) Component comparison: standard 3DGS relies on heuristics. SteepGS improves splitting with a position-only loss-aware rule but keeps cloning and opacity update heuristic. Our method applies loss-aware decisions to position-scale splitting, cloning, and opacity decay.

papers.abstract: Studies of neural network generalization and robustness often summarize smoothness with a single number, such as a Lipschitz constant or a Hessian curvature statistic. However, Lipschitz constants summarize global worst-case sensitivity and Hessian statistics summarize local curvature; neither captures how model responses vary with the size, direction, and location of perturbations encountered in real-world deployment. To measure smoothness under these perturbations, we introduce a finite-difference roughness spectrum that profiles model responses across these conditions. Our roughness spectrum generalizes scalar smoothness measures, bringing Lipschitz sensitivity and directional Hessian curvature into a common framework across perturbation scales. We connect this spectrum to classical Besov theory, which describes how a function's variation changes with scale. Our theoretical analysis also proves that a larger output shift can cause less task damage than a smaller one, and that local curvature alone can miss the blocks most vulnerable to finite perturbations. In image classification, Roughness Source Control (RSC) suppresses margin roughness along noise directions and improves noise robustness in a comparison of 80 checkpoints across four model--dataset combinations. In post-training quantization, we identify blocks that need higher precision by measuring task-loss increases from perturbations matched to the size and direction of each block's quantization error. Our mixed-precision allocation achieves lower perplexity than the Hessian-based HAWQ-V2 baseline under the same GPTQ weights and bit budgets in all 14 settings across seven held-out large language models.
bullets: Scalar Lipschitz and Hessian measures miss how responses vary with perturbation size, direction, and location.
A finite-difference roughness spectrum unifies global sensitivity and directional curvature across scales, grounded in Besov theory.
The analysis shows that larger output shifts can sometimes cause less task damage than smaller shifts, and local curvature can overlook vulnerable blocks.
Roughness Source Control improves noise robustness across 80 image-classification checkpoints spanning four model–dataset combinations.
For post-training quantization, spectrum-guided mixed precision achieves lower perplexity than HAWQ-V2 in all 14 tested settings across seven held-out language models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the roughness spectrum. A single scalar does not describe which scales, directions, or blocks carry sensitivity. A roughness spectrum measures smoothness at the perturbation scale a model will encounter. The block ranking at that scale can reverse the ordering suggested by a scalar summary. papers.selection_reason: Introduces a theoretical framework for measuring neural network smoothness (roughness spectrum) and applies it to improve mixed-precision allocation in GPTQ, contributing to the 'Efficient AI' subtopic of memory/compute efficiency.
papers.title: Scalar Smoothness Is One Point on a Besov Spectrum
papers.tldr: The paper replaces single-number smoothness metrics with a perturbation-scale roughness spectrum that better identifies task-relevant vulnerabilities and improves robustness and quantization decisions.

papers.abstract: Robust 4D reconstruction of deformable endoscopic scenes from monocular videos remains challenging due to non-rigid tissue deformation, illumination changes, occlusions, and unknown camera trajectories. Reliable dynamic reconstruction of endoscopies could significantly enhance visualization, diagnostic accuracy and intraoperative guidance of minimally invasive procedures. We propose SurgicalTS, a self-supervised triangle-splatting framework for dynamic endoscopic scene reconstruction from static monocular cameras. The scene is represented by a canonical set of triangles jointly optimized with a deformation network. We introduce a quaternion-based deformation model, an improved color parametrization, spatio-temporal priors, and a redefined initialization strategy that improves completeness under occlusions. Extensive evaluation on challenging in-vivo endoscopy videos from diverse procedures shows that SurgicalTS successfully models soft-tissue deformations and tool-tissue interactions over time, while consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Our method also reduces training times while maintaining competitive geometric and photometric accuracy results, highlighting the effectiveness of quaternion-based deformation modelling with physical consistency for robust and efficient 4D reconstruction of endoscopic scenes.
bullets: Targets non-rigid tissue motion, illumination changes, occlusions, and unknown camera trajectories in endoscopic videos.
Represents scenes with canonical triangles jointly optimized with a deformation network.
Introduces quaternion-based deformation, improved color modeling, spatio-temporal priors, and occlusion-aware initialization.
Evaluated on diverse in-vivo procedures, where it models tissue deformation and tool-tissue interactions over time.
Reports consistent outperformance of prior methods, reduced training time, and competitive geometric and photometric accuracy.

papers.title: 4D Triangle Splatting Reconstruction of Dynamic Endoscopic Scenes from Monocular Videos

papers.abstract: The spatial intelligence of large vision-language models (LVLMs) requires the ability to combine local visual observations into a geometrically consistent representation of the physical world. Many static benchmarks assess isolated spatial judgments, such as relative direction or distance, while interactive embodied evaluations combine perception with exploration, planning, control, and simulator-specific execution. To bridge this gap, we introduce RECONSPATIAL, a benchmark centered on multi-view 3D scene reconstruction across indoor, tabletop, and outdoor environments. Given real multi-view images and target-object queries, LVLMs are required to jointly predict oriented 3D bounding boxes in a shared, camera-anchored metric coordinate frame. Reconstructions are evaluated along two complementary axes: Structure for relative layout and Metric for physical scale and camera-anchored placement. Nine atomic spatial QA tasks, grouped into Geometric Perception and Spatial Relations, probe spatial capabilities involved in joint reconstruction. Offline navigation extends evaluation to path planning. Evaluation of 18 frontier LVLMs reveals a consistent gap between relative scene structure and metric reconstruction; even GPT-6-Astra scores 81.4% on Structure but only 58.7% on Metric. Tracing this gap, diagnostic analyses link atomic spatial capabilities to reconstruction quality and show that relational consistency alone does not ensure metric accuracy. Experiments with 3D map injection further separate scene construction from path planning, revealing how these geometric errors limit navigation success. Finally, spatial fine-tuning yields broad transfer across both spatial and general vision-language benchmarks.
bullets: Benchmarks joint prediction of oriented 3D bounding boxes in a shared, camera-anchored metric coordinate frame across indoor, tabletop, and outdoor scenes.
Separates evaluation into Structure, measuring relative layout, and Metric, measuring physical scale and camera-anchored placement.
Includes nine atomic spatial QA tasks and offline navigation to connect reconstruction quality with spatial reasoning and path planning.
Evaluation of 18 frontier LVLMs finds a consistent Structure–Metric gap; even GPT-6-Astra scores 81.4% on Structure versus 58.7% on Metric.
Diagnostic studies show relational consistency does not guarantee metric accuracy, while spatial fine-tuning transfers across spatial and general vision-language benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Software development sessions often involve several unfinished tasks rather than one issue carried through to completion. As coding agents take on repository-level development, they need to recover an earlier task's requirements and partial progress after intervening work. Existing repository-level benchmarks typically score one issue-to-patch episode and do not directly measure whether an agent can resume a task after advancing other unfinished work in the same repository. We introduce \textbf{\ourmethod}, a benchmark for focus-task resumption in sessions that interleave unfinished tasks drawn from the same source repository, with a persistent checkout for each task. Each focus task is evaluated in matched uninterrupted and switched sessions with identical focus requirements and executable verifiers. The switched session interleaves ordered stages from other unfinished tasks in the same repository, while only the final focus patch is scored. \ourmethod~contains 200 focus tasks from 19 Python repositories, reconstructed from issue, pull-request, and review histories and rendered as 400 matched session specifications. Across 7 coding agents, interleaved unfinished work produces an average focus-task resolution gap of 11.5 percentage points, ranging from 6.0 to 15.0 percentage points. Trajectory analysis identifies cross-task requirement confusion and loss of task state as recurrent resumption behaviors. We introduce a plug-in context-management module that selects task-relevant history and maintains concise task-state summaries. On OpenCode, the module improves focus-task completion under same-repository task switching by 5.5 to 15.5 percentage points across the evaluated models. Code is available at github.com/Miraclecsc/Switch-SWE.
bullets: Introduces a benchmark for evaluating focus-task resumption in interleaved coding sessions, unlike standard single-issue evaluations.
Matches uninterrupted and switched sessions using persistent task checkouts and executable verifiers; only the final focus-task patch is scored.
Across 7 agents, switching causes an average 11.5-percentage-point drop in focus-task resolution, with gaps from 6.0 to 15.0 points.
Common failures include confusing requirements across tasks and losing track of partial task state.
A context-management module that selects relevant history and summarizes task state improves completion by 5.5–15.5 points on OpenCode.

papers.abstract: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. Reasoning models that fit edge memory budgets can produce long reasoning traces, increasing sequential decoding, end-to-end latency, energy consumption, and KV-cache memory pressure. We present MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models designed for edge deployment, targeting this accuracy-generation-efficiency trade-off. Our recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine, and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused LLM teacher; a four-stage post-training curriculum comprising two SFT stages followed by two RL stages with hard-sample mining; and an edge deployment evaluation spanning multiple GGUF quantization variants and real-device inference on laptop and smartphone hardware. On seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B while being 6.75x smaller; MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points despite being less than half its size. On HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses it by 11.66 points despite being ~16x smaller. Beyond accuracy, MedPsy reduces average response length by 1.7x (1.7B) and 3.2x (4B) versus its Qwen3 backbones, while Q4_K_M quantization preserves the aggregate score within 1 point of BF16 with ~69% lower disk footprint. In real-device inference, MedPsy-4B's shorter generations translate into 75% lower median end-to-end latency and estimated energy per answer than its Qwen3 backbone at matched quantization, while peak RAM remains below 5 GB across our tested laptop and smartphone configurations.
bullets: Targets the gap between capable but oversized medical LLMs and compact models that struggle on knowledge-intensive healthcare tasks.
Uses synthetic medical data, teacher-generated chain-of-thought targets, two SFT stages, and two RL stages with hard-sample mining.
Across seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B and matches MedGemma-27B; MedPsy-1.7B also exceeds MedGemma-1.5-4B.
MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B on HealthBench-Hard while using far fewer parameters.
Shorter outputs, quantization, and edge testing yield lower latency, energy use, and storage needs, with peak RAM below 5 GB in tested configurations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective post-training paradigm for vision-language models (VLMs). Standard RLVR, however, assigns identical outcome-derived credit to all generated tokens regardless of their perceptual relevance. Recent perception-aware methods estimate visual reliance through image perturbation or masking. These indirect proxies require perturbation branches, while corruption sensitivity does not necessarily identify the visual evidence used for reasoning. We instead shape model perception through native attention, an intrinsic model signal. Rather than treating attention as a post-hoc explanation, we formulate it as a reward-anchored, token-aligned routing signal that encourages attention patterns supporting visually grounded reasoning. To this end, we propose NAS-PO, a Native Attention-Strategy Policy Optimization framework. NAS-PO analyzes native attention with a visual mass policy that quantifies visual allocation and a conditional visual policy that captures spatial routing over visual tokens, making the optimization well-posed. Based on this, Native Attention-Strategy Advantage Shaping (NAS-AS) draws on the visual-mass policy to redistribute signed policy-gradient credit for visually engaged rollouts. The Adaptive Attention-Coupled (AAC) loss then aligns the visual-mass policy on all response tokens and the conditional visual policy on visually active ones, consolidating the visual-routing patterns that drive successful trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that NAS-PO substantially surpasses leading RL-tuned VLMs across 7 out-of-domain reasoning and perception benchmarks, with its effectiveness consistently validated across 8B and 32B. Visual-Routing Sensitivity (VRS) analysis further indicates that the optimized attention prioritizes visually load-bearing regions.
bullets: Standard RLVR gives identical outcome-based credit to all generated tokens, ignoring their visual relevance.
NAS-PO models visual allocation with a visual-mass policy and spatial routing with a conditional visual policy.
NAS-AS redistributes signed policy-gradient credit for visually engaged rollouts, while AAC aligns attention patterns with successful trajectories.
It substantially outperforms leading RL-tuned VLMs across 7 out-of-domain benchmarks at both 8B and 32B scales.
VRS analysis suggests optimized attention focuses on visually load-bearing regions.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of NAS-PO. Given an image–query pair (I,Q), the standard GRPO pipeline produces G clean rollouts and verifier-derived group-relative advantages Ai. Using the same clean rollouts, NAS-PO reads native attention ai,t(j) and losslessly decomposes its visual component into a visual-mass policy qi,t, which captures whether and how much a response token relies on the image, and a conditional visual policy ρi,t, which captures where attention is routed over visual tokens. The visual-mass policy also provides visually active indicators ci,t shared by NAS-AS and the conditional branch of AAC. At the trajectory level, NAS-AS summarizes visual reliance into a bounded factor αi and forms Ãi = αiAi. At the token level, AAC aligns q on all valid response tokens and ρ on visually active ones under the unshaped positive-advantage gate [Ai]+. The shaped policy-gradient objective and the adaptively weighted AAC loss jointly update the policy.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a deployed model using only unlabeled target data, but standard entropy-based methods often rely on deterministic confidence and can reinforce overconfident errors under distribution shift. We propose MIRA, Mutual Information guided calibration for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation, a source-free online adaptation method that uses lightweight last-layer Gaussian perturbations to probe prediction reliability. For each target batch, MIRA reuses a single feature extraction pass and samples perturbed classifiers around the source classifier, forming an efficient local predictive distribution. Rather than fitting a Bayesian posterior, MIRA treats the perturbation scale as a local probing radius and selects a batch-specific scale using mutual information (MI) and prediction agreement. The resulting perturbation-sensitivity signal identifies predictions that are confident and locally stable under classifier perturbations, while suppressing brittle predictions with high stochastic disagreement. MIRA then performs adaptation with an MI-confidence weighted entropy loss, which down-weights perturbation-sensitive or low-confidence samples before they drive entropy minimization. This weighted loss reduces the influence of brittle predictions that can otherwise cause harmful adaptation under distribution shift. The method requires no source data, retraining, model ensembles, or offline posterior fitting, and can be applied as a plug-and-play modification to entropy-minimization TTA. Experiments on distribution-shift benchmarks show improvements in accuracy, calibration, and negative log-likelihood, suggesting that mutual-information-guided perturbation probing and weighted adaptation yield more robust online TTA than deterministic confidence.
bullets: Addresses the tendency of entropy-based TTA to reinforce overconfident mistakes under distribution shift.
Uses lightweight last-layer Gaussian perturbations and one feature-extraction pass to estimate local prediction reliability.
Selects a batch-specific perturbation scale using mutual information and prediction agreement rather than fitting a Bayesian posterior.
Applies an MI-confidence weighted entropy loss that down-weights uncertain or perturbation-sensitive samples.
Experiments on distribution-shift benchmarks report improved accuracy, calibration, and negative log-likelihood.

papers.abstract: Memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated mostly on social dialogue, where facts accumulate and rarely change, so remembering reduces largely to finding the turn in which something was said. Financial dialogue breaks this assumption: figures are revised, stances shift without being restated, rules stated once govern later questions, and a single company is discussed under several analytical lenses. Memory systems that retrieve the passages most similar to a question, or the most recent ones, therefore return superseded values, miss rules that share no wording with the question, and cannot recover a stance spread across sessions. We present TrackMem, a per-speaker graph memory that tracks the history of figures, separates perspectives by entity and lens, and preserves each speaker's actions in chronological order. To evaluate it, we introduce FinLoCoMo, a benchmark of 15 long-horizon investment conversations with 765 questions in two splits: one following the LoCoMo categories and one targeting four failure modes. With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits. On the failure-mode split it reaches 73.9% macro accuracy against 69.4% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on questions about revised figures (86.5% against 73.4%).
bullets: Financial conversations challenge standard retrieval because values change, stances evolve implicitly, rules may be stated only once, and entities are discussed through multiple lenses.
TrackMem uses a per-speaker graph memory to preserve figure histories, distinguish entity–perspective combinations, and order actions chronologically.

papers.abstract: Surgical video understanding is essential for intraoperative assistance such as workflow monitoring, instrument preparation and procedural documentation. Delivering such assistance in real time requires a model to jointly perceive the ongoing scene, remember past surgical events, and respond before clinically relevant moments pass. Existing approaches provide limited support for jointly retaining procedural evidence and deciding when to respond in streaming surgical video. In this work, we propose SurgStream, a workflow-anchored proactive streaming framework for real-time surgical video understanding. We first introduce Workflow-Anchored Memory (WAM) to record structured instrument-action-target observations and fold them into phase-level summaries, providing compact and queryable surgical memory. Deadline-aware Transition Learning (DTL) is then devised to supervise response states within clinical windows, enabling timely responses before procedural deadlines. We further introduce SurgStream-Bench, comprising 11.7K streaming interactions across various tasks covering real-time perception, backward memory queries, forward proactive QA, proactive alerts and caption memory. Experiments on SurgStream-Bench show gains over state-of-the-art methods, especially in memory and forward proactive QA. The source code will be available.
bullets: Targets streaming assistance that must perceive scenes, remember prior events, and respond before clinically relevant moments pass.
Workflow-Anchored Memory records instrument–action–target observations and compresses them into phase-level summaries.
Deadline-aware Transition Learning supervises response timing within clinical windows.
Introduces SurgStream-Bench with 11.7K streaming interactions spanning perception, memory queries, proactive QA, alerts, and caption memory.
Experiments report gains over existing methods, particularly for memory and forward proactive QA.

papers.abstract: Stress is a leading contributor to long-term physical and mental health decline. The automatic assessment of stress is a promising approach for continuous monitoring and mitigating human biases. However, the development of automated systems remains challenging due to the heterogeneity of physiological and behavioral signals. This paper presents MUPA${}^2$S, a multimodal framework for automatic stress assessment that combines facial video and ECG signals within a unified perception architecture. Both modalities are mapped into a shared token representation without modality-specific components, and processed through asymmetric attention comprising segment-local cross-attention and global self-attention across segment states. Experiments on a newly collected 58-subject stress dataset, evaluated under a stratified subject-level protocol, show that facial video achieves 69.44% test accuracy, while ECG-only performance remains close to chance under the proposed representation. Unified Video-ECG fusion achieves a test accuracy of 69.58% at approximately half the number of parameters of feature-level fusion, with negligible additional computational cost. Feature-level fusion does not exceed the video-only baseline, while unified input-level integration provides a parameter-efficient mechanism for jointly processing the two modalities.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of heterogeneous physiological and behavioral signals in automated stress assessment.
Maps facial video and ECG into a shared token representation without modality-specific components.
Uses segment-local cross-attention and global self-attention across segment states.
On a 58-subject dataset, video-only accuracy is 69.44%, while ECG-only performance is near chance.
Unified video–ECG fusion reaches 69.58% accuracy with roughly half the parameters of feature-level fusion and negligible extra computation.

papers.abstract: Frequent urban floodwater poses a serious threat to the safety and efficiency of intelligent transportation systems. Existing vision-based methods for floodwater level detection face two main limitations. First, the lack of explicit reasoning leads to poor detection performance and little interpretability. Second, these methods struggle to generalize to the complex and varied real-world road scenes seen from different viewpoints. To address this, we reformulate the task as an explicit visual reasoning problem and propose HydroReasoner, a floodwater level reasoning framework designed for cloud-edge collaboration. HydroReasoner builds on Qwen2.5-VL and is trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization. To address the scarcity of reasoning process annotations, we build a floodwater domain knowledge graph HydroKG and design a novel KG path reward. Through deterministic graph traversal over HydroKG, this reward supervises the model's reasoning process at a fine granularity, which improves both reasoning and generalization. For edge deployment, we apply 4-bit quantization to the model, cutting GPU memory usage by 57% and inference latency by 43% while out-of-domain accuracy drops by only 0.2 percentage points. We also propose a confidence-based cloud-edge routing mechanism, which improves system safety and eases the computational load on the cloud. In addition, we build HydroLevel, a floodwater benchmark dataset of 3,000 images, for training and evaluating the model. Experimental results show that HydroReasoner achieves detection accuracy 4.0 and 13.6 percentage points higher than conventional vision baselines in the in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations respectively, with performance dropping by only 4.4 percentage points out of domain.
bullets: Reframes floodwater-level detection as an explicit visual reasoning task to address weak interpretability and poor cross-scene generalization.
Uses Qwen2.5-VL with Group Relative Policy Optimization and a HydroKG-based path reward to supervise reasoning without requiring extensive reasoning annotations.
Introduces HydroLevel, a 3,000-image floodwater benchmark for training and evaluation.
Outperforms conventional vision baselines by 4.0 percentage points in-domain and 13.6 percentage points out-of-domain; out-of-domain performance drops 4.4 points.
4-bit quantization reduces GPU memory usage by 57% and latency by 43%, while confidence-based routing improves safety and reduces cloud computation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed collaborative edge-cloud traffic monitoring network. The system leverages 5G technology to aggregate multi-source floodwater imagery from Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), vehicles (dashcams), and Roadside Units (RSUs). These diverse data streams, captured from heterogeneous viewpoints, are transmitted to the cloud server or processed locally, where the proposed HydroReasoner framework performs efficient and interpretable floodwater level reasoning.

Fig. 2. The overall framework of HydroReasoner. The pipeline comprises three stages: (I) Reasoning Path Generation: the policy model performs explicit reasoning on the input floodwater image and outputs a structured reasoning path. (II) HydroKG Path Verification: the reasoning path is parsed into candidate triples and verified against HydroKG for structural completeness and consistency with domain grading rules. (III) Reward Shaping and GRPO Update: the verification result, together with format and accuracy signals, forms a composite reward that drives the policy update.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) can improve answer accuracy while weakening responsiveness to supporting evidence. We investigate this separation in scientific-document question answering through matched document interventions that change the supported answer while preserving the question and unrelated context. We identify evidence bypass: a student retains an originally correct answer after the document changes to support a different one. On QASPER with a Qwen3-4B student, standard OPD raises original-document accuracy by 3.4 percentage points, lowers counterfactual accuracy by 5.3 points, and increases bypass by 15.7 points; the same directional pattern appears on PeerQA. Controlled perturbations localize the shift to answer-critical evidence, and bypass grows with the student's pre-distillation closed-book preference for the original answer. A factorized study of teacher targets, privileged information, divergence, and supervision density finds that explicitly supplying the teacher with annotated answer-critical spans yields the largest joint improvement in evidence response and claim support. These findings motivate Evidence-Paired OPD (EP-OPD), which combines on-policy supervision on matched documents supporting different answers to the same question with an answer-level margin that favors each document's supported answer over its paired alternative. Across both datasets and two student sizes, EP-OPD recovers 54-66% of standard OPD's counterfactual-accuracy loss while preserving 80-85% of its original-document accuracy gain. Our results establish evidence responsiveness as a distinct training and evaluation target alongside answer accuracy. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/RuoranXu/EP-OPD.
bullets: Identifies “evidence bypass”: students retain an original answer even when matched document edits support a different answer.
On QASPER, standard OPD increases original-document accuracy by 3.4 points but decreases counterfactual accuracy by 5.3 points and increases bypass by 15.7 points; PeerQA shows the same pattern.
Bypass is localized to answer-critical evidence and is stronger when the student initially prefers the original answer in closed-book settings.
Teacher access to annotated answer-critical spans provides the largest joint improvement in evidence response and claim support among tested factors.
EP-OPD recovers 54–66% of OPD’s counterfactual-accuracy loss while retaining 80–85% of its original-document accuracy gain across two datasets and student sizes.

papers.abstract: Reverse and forward Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergences provide complementary supervision in on-policy distillation: reverse KL refines the student's active token rankings, and forward KL allocates mass to teacher-supported candidates. At student-generated prefixes, we form a four-observation matrix by treating the student and teacher as both candidate sources and evaluators. The diagonal self-observations measure uncertainty, while source-centered cross-observations recover the two KL objectives. We establish an exact identity equating the Fisher inverse-metric coupling of their logit gradients with the sum of these contrasts, yielding a common local descent direction for distinct positive distributions. Observation-coordinated on-policy distillation (OC-OPD) uses observations to set preferences, closed-form bargaining to coordinate gradients, and distributional discrepancy to scale the update. Across three heterogeneous student settings (non-thinking generation, thinking generation, and base-model initialization), OC-OPD achieves strong gains in mathematical reasoning and transfers effectively to out-of-distribution scientific question answering and code generation. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/RuoranXu/OC-OPD.
bullets: Addresses the complementary roles of reverse KL for refining active token rankings and forward KL for covering teacher-supported candidates.
Builds a four-observation matrix from student/teacher candidate sources and evaluators at student-generated prefixes.
Uses an exact Fisher inverse-metric identity to align the two KL objectives toward a common local descent direction.
Coordinates gradients via closed-form bargaining and scales updates using distributional discrepancy.
Reports gains in mathematical reasoning with transfer to out-of-distribution scientific QA and code generation across three student settings.

papers.abstract: Event-based optical flow estimation using spatiotemporal planar approximation inherently assumes constant velocity and tends to average out temporal velocity variations. In this paper, we propose a flow estimation method that extends this planar approximation along the temporal axis. The resulting event-based optical flow constraint allows existing variational optical flow formulations to model temporal motion variation. Specifically, we partition the space-time volume into sub-intervals and apply a two-step planar approximation to track object edges consistently. Moreover, a spatial compensation mechanism and a temporal regularization term are incorporated to compensate for edge displacements and temporally stabilize the flow estimation, respectively. The experimental results show that modeling temporal motion variation improves flow estimation accuracy over conventional methods.
bullets: Addresses the constant-velocity assumption in conventional spatiotemporal planar approximation.
Partitions the space-time volume into sub-intervals and applies two-step planar fitting to track object edges.
Adds spatial compensation for edge displacement and temporal regularization for stable flow estimates.
Integrates with existing variational optical-flow formulations.
Experiments show improved accuracy when temporal motion variation is modeled.

papers.abstract: Embodied question answering asks an agent to navigate, observe, and then answer questions about what it saw, yet answer accuracy alone cannot tell whether any of this happened. A plausible answer can come from the question, the room label, or the answer choices, and a correct answer does not show that the supporting observation was ever made. We present a multi-room benchmark whose 200 test episodes and 800 questions are stratified by route extent, with an evaluation ladder that holds the questions fixed while varying only the evidence supplied to the answerer, from text-only probes through closed-loop agents to replay of the reference trajectory. Questions are generated from symbolic records of rooms, visible objects, and frames, so every answer can be traced to the observations that support it. A closed-loop vision-language agent reaches no target in 200 episodes yet answers 45.5% of questions, within 0.1 points of the same model given no images; replaying the reference trajectory raises the same model to 57.4%, so the evidence exists along the route but is not gathered. A family-level audit then shows that access to evidence is not the same as use of it. Four of eight families are largely answerable from text, one cites frames that cannot establish its own answer, and the oracle conditions reach 59.5% on Rooms-visited by counting the supplied images. Evidence acquisition, answer coverage, and shortcut sensitivity must therefore be established before an accuracy gain can be credited to memory.
bullets: Evaluates 200 multi-room episodes and 800 questions across route extents.
Uses fixed questions with progressively richer evidence: text-only, closed-loop agents, and reference-trajectory replay.
The tested agent reaches no targets but answers 45.5% of questions, nearly matching its no-image performance.
Replay of the reference trajectory raises accuracy to 57.4%, indicating evidence is available but often not acquired or used.
The audit finds substantial text shortcuts and shows that answer accuracy alone cannot establish grounded observation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Benchmark and evaluation pipeline. (A) Episode generation produces a reference route and a privileged symbolic record; the example strip shows a bed visible at t=0 and t=1 and gone by t=2. The question shown is answerable from the full trajectory, but its cited frames {0, 1} omit the later absence, the evidence-selection defect of Section 4. papers.abstract: Networks that keep learning overwrite what they know. Prevailing remedies replay stored data, distil from old models or freeze the backbone. The brain suggests a different division of labour: the hippocampus indexes where experience lies in cortex while the cortex keeps learning. We show that this division lets a fully trainable network keep learning without cross-task replay, a teacher or inference-time memory. After each task, a training-only hippocampal memory indexes the input geometry of every group of synapses sharing an input, residual energy included, and limits each synapse's movement per direction before and after the optimizer. This class-free geometry carries most of the protection; with conflict detection on top, the method cuts absorption of established classes by near-duplicates several-fold against every compared method. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of one principle keeping whole networks learning across four architecture families and models up to 8 billion parameters. Methods that freeze the backbone hold up only as far as its representation already separates the classes; here the whole network keeps learning to tell near-duplicates apart, leading the frozen-backbone baseline by 17.5 points on TACRED. Without the memory, much old knowledge stays decodable but beyond the network's reach.
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting caused by continual learning overwriting established knowledge.
Indexes input geometry and residual energy for synapse groups, constraining synaptic movement before and after optimization; conflict detection adds further protection.
Works across four architecture families and models up to 8 billion parameters.
Reduces absorption of established classes by near-duplicates several-fold versus compared methods.
On TACRED, outperforms a frozen-backbone baseline by 17.5 points; without memory, old knowledge may remain decodable but inaccessible.￼

papers.selection_reason: Proposes continual learning without replay using hippocampal-style memory indexing, directly fitting continual and online learning.
papers.title: Hippocampal consolidation without replay in fully fine-tuned networks

papers.abstract: Factual recall in language models is typically framed as retrieving a factual association: a subject--relation pair maps to a single object. However, many facts are context-dependent: the same pair maps to different objects depending on a condition such as time. We introduce anchored factual recall, in which the model receives an explicit conditioning expression, an anchor, and must select the object valid under it. This raises questions that single-object recall does not: where the anchor enters the computation, what it changes, and how that change selects the answer. Focusing on temporal anchors, we answer them with causal interventions on four open-weight models on English prompts and identify two routes. In a subject-mediated route, the anchor resolves the final subject-token representation to the queried year, and the relation redistributes the readout of this state across attention heads. In a direct route] the final position attends to the anchor, and upper-layer MLPs turn this signal into a preference for the time-appropriate object. The two routes are parallel channels: their contributions add up, most queries use both, and their balance depends on the query, e.g., on the relation, consistently across models. This reframes mechanistic accounts of factual recall from retrieving a single stored object to selecting among context-dependent alternatives.
bullets: Introduces anchored factual recall, where a subject–relation pair maps to different objects depending on an explicit condition such as time.
Uses causal interventions on four open-weight models with English prompts to trace how temporal anchors affect recall.
Identifies a subject-mediated route: the anchor makes the subject representation year-specific, while the relation redistributes its readout across attention heads.
Identifies a direct route: the final position attends to the anchor, and upper-layer MLPs favor the time-appropriate object.
Both routes usually contribute additively, with their balance varying by query and relation across models.

papers.abstract: Data-driven sequential decision making in marketing and healthcare can benefit from observations collected in related environments, particularly when data in the environment of interest are limited. Transferring such information requires accounting for differences in rewards and transition dynamics across environments. We study knowledge transfer for offline reinforcement learning through a joint estimation framework that directly integrates source information into target value-function learning. We propose Direct Transfer Fitted Q-Iteration (DFQI), which updates the target Q-function while simultaneously borrowing the source information through an L1 penalty that links the target coefficients to a weighted aggregate of source coefficients, with both determined jointly within each Bellman update. Using sieve approximation, we establish statistical guarantees for target estimation and policy learning in stationary discounted environments with common or heterogeneous transition kernels. Empirical studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed DFQI framework in transferring source information to improve policy learning with limited target data.
bullets: Addresses offline reinforcement learning when target-environment data are scarce but related source-environment data are available.
Introduces Direct Transfer Fitted Q-Iteration, which jointly estimates the target Q-function and a weighted source-coefficient aggregate during each Bellman update.
Uses an L1 penalty to connect target and transferred source coefficients, allowing information sharing despite differing rewards or transition dynamics.
Provides statistical guarantees for target estimation and policy learning under common or heterogeneous transition kernels.
Empirical studies show improved policy learning with limited target data; results are scoped to stationary discounted environments.

papers.abstract: Delta-rule linear attention underlies language models such as Kimi Linear and Qwen3-Next. Chunkwise implementations expose matrix parallelism, but their backward passes compute unnecessary auxiliary adjoints. We present ReWY, an algebraic reformulation that reduces this work before optimizing accelerator execution. Differentiating the chunk correction as one triangular residual system eliminates the inverse adjoint and reduces seven local WY matrix products to three. Two complementary transformations expose further reuse: centered matrix contractions replace pairwise vector-gate processing, and scalar-gate reductions reuse key-gradient products instead of forming a key Gram matrix. These identities simplify backward computation for DeltaNet, GDN, KDA, and GDN2 while preserving the recurrence and gradients in exact arithmetic, without changing the architecture or training objective. We implement the reduced graph on GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Under matched recomputation and full-saving policies, precision-qualified six-shape comparisons with frozen FLA references yield 1.15-1.81$\times$ geometric-mean complete low-level backward speedups on NVIDIA GPUs. All four operators achieve 1.18-1.70$\times$ on H100 and H200 while retaining original FP32 working matrices. A separate public-autograd evaluation on Ascend 950DT, including gradient conversions, yields 1.09-2.89$\times$ under available matched policies. Paired ablations establish further ReWY gains after optimizing the complementary contractions. Complete-gradient checks validate the recorded operator cases; supplementary full-model backward measurements assess integration into community FLA models and a GDN2 layer port. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/flashserve/ReWY.
bullets: Targets redundant auxiliary adjoints in chunkwise Delta-rule linear-attention backward passes.
Uses a triangular residual-system formulation plus centered contractions and scalar-gate reductions to expose reuse.
Applies across DeltaNet, GDN, KDA, and GDN2 without changing the architecture or training objective.
Reports 1.15–1.81× geometric-mean low-level backward speedups on NVIDIA GPUs and 1.09–2.89× on Ascend 950DT under matched policies.
Validation includes precision-qualified operator checks, ablations, complete-gradient checks, and selected full-model integration measurements.

papers.selection_reason: Presents an algebraic reformulation that reduces backward-pass matrix multiplications for delta-rule linear attention, directly improving attention efficiency.
papers.title: ReWY: Faster Backpropagation for Delta-Rule Attention - From 7 to 3 Matrix Multiplications
papers.tldr: ReWY reformulates Delta-rule attention backpropagation to reduce seven local WY matrix multiplications to three, delivering faster GPU and NPU backward execution while preserving exact gradients.

papers.abstract: Learning semantic representations for 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently emerged as a promising direction for 3D scene understanding. However, existing 2D-to-3D semantic lifting approaches rely primarily on 2D segmentation supervision and lack object-level priors, causing the learned representation to be driven by local mask evidence rather than holistic object structure. In this paper, we present VLSplat, a vision-language guided approach for object-centric semantic lifting in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our method augments mask-based lifting with object-level semantic priors derived from vision-language models and refines Gaussian representations using an object-group scene graph. The refinement is performed through two language-guided modules: intra-group refinement suppresses semantic noise within object groups, while inter-group acquisition expands object support regions by incorporating structurally relevant candidates from neighboring groups. Extensive experiments on indoor scene datasets demonstrate that VLSplat improves the semantic consistency and structural completeness of object-level categories. Our code and models are available at https://vlsplat.github.io/.
bullets: Targets semantic lifting methods that rely on local 2D mask evidence and lack holistic object-level structure.
Uses vision-language models to provide object-level semantic priors alongside mask-based lifting.
Builds an object-group scene graph with intra-group refinement to reduce semantic noise.
Uses inter-group acquisition to expand object support with structurally relevant neighboring candidates.
Experiments on indoor scene datasets show improved semantic consistency and structural completeness of object categories.

The scene graph further guides language-based intra-group refinement and inter-group acquisition, improving semantic consistency and structural completeness.

papers.abstract: We introduce Spade-SLAM, a self-supervised dense visual SLAM framework that substantially narrows the long-standing performance gap to supervised methods in a zero-shot setting. By demonstrating that high-fidelity tracking can be achieved without explicit ground-truth pose and depth labels, our approach offers a highly effective and label-efficient alternative to fully supervised pretraining. Our core contribution is a complementary sparse-to-dense training regime: While a warping-based photometric loss provides a dense training signal, we stabilize the optimization and suppress drift in ambiguous regions using a sparse correspondence loss derived from image feature matches. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Spade-SLAM significantly improves robustness and accuracy compared to existing self-supervised baselines, closely rivaling SLAM systems trained with explicit pose and depth supervision. The code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/JulianPSchmitt/Spade-SLAM.
bullets: Addresses the performance gap between self-supervised and supervised dense visual SLAM.
Combines dense warping-based photometric loss with sparse correspondence loss from image feature matches.
Uses sparse matches to stabilize training and reduce drift in ambiguous regions.
Experiments show improved robustness and accuracy over self-supervised baselines, approaching supervised systems.
Code is planned for public release.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Spade-SLAM pipeline. Trained end-to-end via self-supervision, Spade-SLAM leverages photometric warping and sparse correspondence-based reprojection, eliminating the need for ground-truth pose or depth annotations.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents need physical intelligence to understand their surroundings through physical perception, physical knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning. These capabilities must work together to interpret events and make quantitative judgments. Existing benchmarks advance physical understanding and general-purpose tool use, yet the coordination of these capabilities in physical scenarios remains insufficiently characterized. Inspired by Popper's Three Worlds, we introduce TriPhysBench, a benchmark of 410 questions from 200 videos that brings physical perception, physical knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning into a shared evaluation setting. Its measurement-grounded and knowledge-grounded subtasks impose complementary demands on obtaining observations and acquiring external specifications, then applying them to quantitative problems. Among six representative vision-language models, the best achieves an answer accuracy of only 50.38%, revealing limited performance on tasks that require these capabilities to work together. We further introduce TriPhys, a framework that learns a unified policy for physical perception, knowledge retrieval, and quantitative reasoning from complete tool-integrated trajectories. The policy uses intermediate reasoning to guide retrieval and computation, then incorporates tool feedback into subsequent physical inference. On 110 questions from videos excluded from training, TriPhys improves answer and solution scores across three Qwen configurations, with a 17.7% relative gain in answer accuracy for TriPhys-27B over its Qwen3.6-27B backbone. This work provides a benchmark and a learning pathway toward embodied agents that move beyond recognizing events to understanding and reasoning about the physical processes behind them.
bullets: Introduces 410 questions from 200 videos covering physical perception, knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning.
Measurement- and knowledge-grounded subtasks test whether agents can obtain observations or specifications and apply them quantitatively.
The best of six evaluated vision-language models reaches only 50.38% answer accuracy, indicating substantial difficulty with coordinated physical reasoning.
TriPhys learns a unified policy that uses intermediate reasoning to guide retrieval and computation, then incorporates tool feedback into later inference.
On 110 held-out questions, TriPhys improves answer and solution scores across three Qwen configurations; TriPhys-27B achieves a reported 17.7% relative answer-accuracy gain over its backbone.
