papers.abstract: Geometry is the very form that connects space, time, and matter, serving as the fundamental fabric of the physical world, from continuous fields to discrete structures. Despite its importance, deep learning is inherently blind to geometry. Riemannian geometry stands as a well-established mathematical foundation for studying geometry, yet it remains largely incompatible with deep learning architectures. To bridge this gap, we establish a new learning framework--Geometric Morphology Learning--that learns geometric or topological structures, shapes or conformations for representation learning, reasoning and action modeling. Moving beyond early attempts limited to specific geometric priors, this theory centers on modeling the intrinsic geometry of objects and learning from such geometric or topological knowledge. Specifically, we construct a neural bundle, a unified scaffolding linking local and global structures, and formulate differentiable operators, including connection and curvature, thereby enabling the study of geometry with advanced geometric concepts such as holonomy and cohomology. Consequently, Geometric Morphology Learning opens new horizons in foundation models, reasoning and planning, graph modeling, physical simulation, PDE systems, and dynamics, marking a fundamental shift toward instilling systematic geometry in artificial intelligence.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between geometry’s role in physical systems and deep learning’s limited geometric awareness.
Introduces a neural bundle to connect local and global structures in a unified scaffold.
Defines differentiable geometric operators, including connections and curvature, and supports concepts such as holonomy and cohomology.
Targets applications in foundation models, reasoning and planning, graph modeling, physical simulation, PDEs, and dynamical systems.
The abstract presents a broad theoretical framework but reports no specific experiments or quantitative results.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes geometry-aware learning framework for foundation models, targeting spatial reasoning and dynamics.
papers.title: Geometric Morphology Learning: Empowering Foundation Models from Structure to Spacetime Intelligence
papers.tldr: Geometric Morphology Learning proposes a framework for integrating intrinsic geometric and topological structure into deep learning, enabling more geometry-aware representation, reasoning, and action modeling.

papers.abstract: LLM agents operate Web infrastructure from the command line and rely on a return assumption, namely that each tool call returns within a bounded time and with its requested action finished. Many commands, however, ask a question before they act, and the agent's harness either closes the program's input or keeps it open as a terminal at which nobody types. With closed input, the program can return status 0 without the requested action. With open input, it waits until a time limit, and the agent pays in time and tokens. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first to measure and repair the return assumption. We collect 91,469 production tool calls and 89,047 public agent trajectories, test how 8 widely used harnesses launch commands, and build Litmus, a catalog of 158 checked command-line invocations, and Tripwire, a benchmark of 25 task pairs that differ only in whether a question guards the requested action. We then propose RECEIPT, which keeps the input open, reads what each process waits for from system calls, and returns this state to an unmodified agent through a model-checked protocol. On Litmus, closed input causes 11.5% of tested invocations to return status 0 without performing the requested action, and 7 of 8 harnesses close input when no terminal is attached. An unanswered question at a plain terminal multiplies a task's token use by 2.9, and the input connection moves an LLM from 7th to 3rd place among 8. Across 5 LLMs, RECEIPT reduces false claims of success by 73.5% and completes all 25 guarded tasks on a second harness. An agent's reliability therefore depends on what its harness lets it observe as well as on its LLM. Agent builders should report what each tool call did, not only how it ended, and benchmark maintainers should fix and report the input connection before they rank LLMs.
bullets: The study examines the return assumption that every tool call finishes its requested action within a bounded time.

Across 91,469 production calls, 89,047 public trajectories, and 8 harnesses, closed input sometimes produces status 0 without performing the requested action, while open input can cause waiting and token waste.
The authors introduce Litmus, a catalog of 158 checked invocations, and Tripwire, a benchmark of 25 task pairs involving question-guarded commands.
RECEIPT keeps input open, observes what processes await through system calls, and reports that state to an unmodified agent using a model-checked protocol.
Across 5 LLMs, RECEIPT reduces false success claims by 73.5% and completes all 25 guarded tasks on a second harness.

papers.selection_reason: Measures and repairs tool-call return assumption for LLM agents, improving reliability in web operations.
papers.title: RECEIPT: Measuring and Repairing the Return Assumption of LLM Agents in Web Service Operations
papers.tldr: RECEIPT shows that terminal input handling can cause LLM agents to falsely report success or waste tokens, and repairs this by exposing interactive command state to the agent.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon terminal tasks are used to evaluate and train agents. Human-curated datasets are scarce, so many synthesis methods have emerged. They usually measure the length of a task by the turns a model needs to pass it, and its difficulty by labels the LLM sets during generation. We find, however, that the turn count largely reflects the habits of the model, not only the demands of the task, and that the labels barely track how often models pass. We describe a terminal task by its work, the number of operations it requires, and its depth, the number of turns that must happen in sequence because the commands of each turn can only be chosen after reading the output of the previous one. Estimating depth as the smallest turn cap, stated to the agent, under which the task passes, we audit 734 tasks from six existing datasets. Synthesis has mostly added work, not depth: 94% of the solved synthetic tasks pass within three turns, yet depth, unlike the turn count, predicts difficulty beyond work. We propose DEPTH, in which a generation agent writes each task one segment at a time in a real software environment, carrying out each segment before writing it and starting the next from the state it leaves. Our 105 tasks exceed every audited dataset in depth and work, and none of six current models passes half of them. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on runs from these tasks improves it on two terminal benchmarks.
bullets: Task turn counts often reflect model behavior, while generated difficulty labels poorly predict success.
The paper defines depth as the minimum number of sequential turns required when later commands depend on earlier outputs, separate from total work.
Auditing 734 tasks across six datasets found that 94% of solved synthetic tasks finish within three turns, and depth predicts difficulty beyond work.
DEPTH generates tasks segment by segment in a real software environment, executing each segment before continuing from the resulting state.
Its 105 tasks exceed audited datasets in depth and work; six current models each fail to pass half, and fine-tuning Qwen3-8B improves performance on two terminal benchmarks.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agentic systems are increasingly combined with CoT reasoning to solve tasks that require accurate reasoning, external knowledge, and multi-step deliberation. Yet, explicit CoT incurs substantial generation overhead, while implicit CoT, which replaces textual rationales with compact continuous tokens, does not naturally support the explicit communication interface required for agentic tool-use. We propose TAC-CoT, a tool-empowered adaptive implicit CoT framework that replaces explicit reasoning traces with compact latent reasoning segments while retaining textual tokens only for tool calls, observations, and final answers. This interleaved design enables agentic tool-use without verbalizing every intermediate reasoning step. Experiments on agentic math and QA benchmarks show that TAC-CoT improves accuracy by up to 8.8 points while reducing model forward passes by up to 6.8x. Furthermore, analyses show that TAC-CoT improves tool-use quality in both single- and multi-tool settings.
bullets: Addresses the generation overhead of explicit chain-of-thought and the limited tool-use interface of implicit reasoning.
Uses compact latent reasoning segments, while retaining textual tokens for tool calls, observations, and final answers.
Evaluated on agentic math and question-answering benchmarks.
Reports accuracy gains of up to 8.8 points and up to 6.8× fewer model forward passes.
Analysis indicates improved tool-use quality in both single- and multi-tool settings.

papers.abstract: Understanding mobility dynamics and the effects of urban transportation management policies requires examining how individual travel decisions, traffic conditions, and policy interventions influence one another over time. We present AgenticMobility, an open-source experimental platform for studying how mobility AI agents and other AI agents interact, adapt through repeated experience, and collectively shape mobility outcomes. Persistent agents retain identities and relevant states across rounds, with explicit interfaces defining information access, admissible actions, and decision schedules; linked records trace decisions, execution, and feedback. In the current implementation, large language model (LLM) agents act as travelers choosing routes and departure times and as a manager periodically adjusting link charges within MATSim. A preliminary demonstration spans 100 simulated days in each of five configurations, with one run per configuration and a shared simulation seed. In the joint traveler--manager run, all 1,179,300 finalized target decisions satisfied action constraints; execution checks verified implementation of accepted choices and preservation of personal memories across days. Trajectories show stable route choices alongside departure-time adjustments and differences between controlled-trip and population-wide outcomes. The platform supports experiments on individual adaptation, collective outcomes, and management interventions by varying information access, retained experience, and management feedback. Source code is available at https://github.com/Agentic-City-Research/Agentic-Mobility
bullets: Models repeated interactions among travelers, traffic conditions, and transportation policies.
Uses persistent agents with defined information access, actions, decision schedules, and traceable feedback records.
Implements LLM travelers selecting routes and departure times, plus a manager adjusting link charges in MATSim.
A preliminary 100-day, five-configuration demonstration verified action constraints, choice execution, and memory preservation.
Enables experiments varying agent information, retained experience, and management feedback; scope is currently experimental with one run per configuration.

papers.abstract: Reasoning about surgical video -- which phase is underway, which instruments act, and when events occur -- underpins operative documentation, workflow analysis, and skill assessment. Yet surgical visual question answering is still largely built on single frames and closed labels that cannot express a duration, an ordering, or a count, and the video models that lift the frame limit typically compress every clip the same way regardless of the question, discarding the temporal evidence the answer needs. Worse, the answers are structurally heterogeneous, spanning five incompatible structures -- binary, classification, multi-label, counting, and sentence-temporal -- that no single training signal scores uniformly well. We propose SurgQ-VLM, a two-stage model for surgical video question answering. Stage 1 trains a question-conditioned dual-stream (slow/fast) compressor for a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-VL-7B: cross-attention conditions both streams on the question, and each clip's visual tokens shrink 49x from the raw ViT patches (11x vs. post-merge backbone tokens). Stage 2 post-trains with GRPO under an answer-type-aware reward that scores each question on the metric matching its answer structure (micro-F1 for label sets, normalised error for counts, a content-timing blend for temporal windows). On a sealed 21,840-question test split over Cholec80 and CholecT50, SurgQ-VLM reaches 0.779 keyword accuracy and a 10x BLEU-4 gain over zero-shot; GRPO adds 2.5 pp K-Acc (2.0 pp attributable to the answer-type-aware reward), concentrated in the structurally hard types, with answer format unchanged (ROUGE-L). Code is available at https://github.com/DhruvMakwana/SurgQ-VLM.
bullets: Targets limitations of frame-based and uniformly compressed video QA, especially for duration, ordering, and counting questions.
Uses a two-stage architecture: question-conditioned slow/fast visual compression followed by GRPO post-training.
Applies answer-type-specific rewards for binary, classification, multi-label, counting, and sentence-temporal answers.
On a sealed 21,840-question test split from Cholec80 and CholecT50, achieves 0.779 keyword accuracy and a 10× BLEU-4 gain over zero-shot.
GRPO improves keyword accuracy by 2.5 percentage points, with gains concentrated in structurally difficult answer types.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models interleave linear-attention layers with a small number of softmax-attention layers. Prior work largely attributes in-context retrieval to softmax attention, treating linear attention primarily as a mechanism for compressing past context. We revisit this division of labor and show that linear attention plays a direct role in retrieval by constructing the query used by softmax attention. Studying Qwen3.5 (Gated DeltaNet) and Granite4.0 (Mamba-2), we identify an Encode--Address circuit. An early Encode block preserves token identity, while an Address block constructs the final-position representation from which a softmax \emph{reader} forms its attention query. Transplanting this representation between prompts with different queried keys redirects retrieval in 0.97--0.99 of cases. The Address block's recurrent state carries the retrieval target, and its computation transfers across architectures: replacing Granite's Address block with Qwen's restores retrieval accuracy to 0.92--0.94 without updating either model's weights. Across six Qwen3.5 models, Address computation becomes distributed at larger scales over a chain of blocks, each guiding a successive reader, as the query no longer passes from one reader to the next through attention. These findings reveal a division of labor in hybrid retrieval: linear attention constructs the query, while softmax attention performs the lookup. Code is available at https://github.com/yuang-chen/LinearQuery
bullets: Identifies an Encode–Address circuit: early linear-attention blocks preserve token identity, while later blocks build the final-position representation used by a softmax reader.
Transplanting the Address representation between prompts redirects retrieval in 0.97–0.99 of cases.
The retrieval target is carried in recurrent state, and Address computation transfers across Qwen3.5 and Granite4.0 architectures.
Replacing Granite’s Address block with Qwen’s restores retrieval accuracy to 0.92–0.94 without changing model weights.
At larger Qwen3.5 scales, Address computation becomes distributed across a chain of blocks and readers.

papers.abstract: The transition of information-centric artificial intelligence to safety-critical applications is impeded by the limitations of conventional offline-training paradigms in open-world environments. This paper presents Control AI, an architecture for Online Active Learning (OAL) inspired by the continuous Prediction-Evaluation-Correction process of biological intelligence. The framework combines the hierarchical representation capacity of deep neural networks with the real-time error-feedback adaptation of adaptive control. A prediction model maps sensory input into a latent manifold, an optional latent model represents transitions in that space, and a reconstruction model maps the latent state back to observable signals. Residuals between predictions and measurements provide the internal learning signal. Spatial and temporal cross-reconstruction architectures prevent OAL from collapsing to a trivial identity mapping, while coupled, dual, and localized variants shorten error-transmission paths. Localized predictive coding style OAL is implemented through guidance-backpropagation and target-backpropagation architectures, and hybrid and scaled variants support high-dimensional deployment. The paper focuses on the architectural rationale and the progression from a conceptual feedback loop to practical large-scale configurations.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of offline training when safety-critical systems encounter changing, unanticipated conditions.
Combines deep hierarchical representations with real-time adaptive-control feedback.
Uses prediction, optional latent transition modeling, reconstruction, and residual errors as the learning signal.
Introduces spatial and temporal cross-reconstruction plus localized, dual, coupled, hybrid, and scaled variants to avoid trivial identity mappings and support larger deployments.
The abstract emphasizes architectural rationale and configuration progression rather than reporting quantitative experimental results.

papers.abstract: When user queries are incomplete, large language models should ask targeted questions before committing to an answer, a capability we call proactive elicitation, yet evaluation on real user-assistant queries across seven LLMs (8B to frontier) shows that fewer than 11% of underspecified queries trigger a follow-up question. To benchmark and train this capability, we introduce VagueBench, where each seed query is annotated with structured intent and detail units then degraded into intent-vague and fully-vague variants via controlled removal of linguistic cues, yielding known hidden information sets for evaluating both when and what to ask. We propose DialogGRPO, an offline reinforcement learning method that organizes multi-turn elicitation as a dialogue-state directed acyclic graph, where candidate questions at each node receive dense turn-level rewards combining immediate information gain with lookahead value through group-relative comparison, enabling fine-grained credit assignment without runtime simulation. DialogGRPO elicits missing information on over 88% of vague queries with substantial gains in both recovery efficiency and answer coverage, without over-asking on complete queries, outperforms prompting and test-time-scaling baselines, and generalizes zero-shot to MultiWOZ 2.4 and AmbigQA.
bullets: Fewer than 11% of underspecified queries prompt follow-up questions across seven evaluated LLMs.
VagueBench creates controlled intent-vague and fully-vague queries with known missing information for evaluating when and what models should ask.
DialogGRPO uses a dialogue-state DAG and dense rewards based on information gain and lookahead value to train multi-turn elicitation.
The method elicits missing information on over 88% of vague queries, improving recovery efficiency and answer coverage without over-asking on complete queries.
It outperforms prompting and test-time-scaling baselines and generalizes zero-shot to MultiWOZ 2.4 and AmbigQA.

papers.abstract: Zhuangzi dreamt he was a butterfly and, on waking, could not tell which was the dream. We ask a version of his question of a model of the fly brain: placed inside a world generated by a world model, can a fixed brain tell that the world is a dream? We treat it as a question about what a connectome-constrained model trained on one task makes available beyond that task: do its responses make the defects of a dream linearly decodable? The observer is a published model of the fly visual system trained only for optic-flow estimation; reality is the MPI-Sintel movie on the model's 721-column retina; dreams are continuations of five real frames by three small world models (a persistence random walk, an MDN-RNN and an RSSM) at three temperatures. The judge is a classifier two-sample test on temporal statistics of cell-type responses, with sequence-level cross-validation. In the trained observer's responses all nine dreams are separable from reality (AUC 0.85-0.99, mean over 50 trained models), in those of the same network before training much less so (0.58-0.75 for the learned world models; paired difference 0.20-0.37), equally on sequences the observer never saw, and in an order unrelated to pixel error. Because these AUCs are near ceiling, we add graded probes made of each window's own real frames with only their order broken. Swapping one adjacent pair of the 14 generated frames gives 0.73 on the trained responses against 0.54 before training and 0.56 for pixel statistics; the trained curve reaches 0.75 at 1.1 swapped pairs of seven, the pixel statistics at 4.7, and the untrained network not at all. A detection horizon, the test on the first k generated frames, orders the world models where the full-length AUC saturates.
bullets: The study asks whether a fixed, biologically constrained visual model exposes detectable defects in generated worlds beyond its optic-flow task.
It compares responses to MPI-Sintel reality with continuations produced by three small world models under three temperatures.
A classifier two-sample test on temporal statistics of cell-type responses evaluates dream–reality separability with sequence-level cross-validation.
All nine dreams were separable in trained-model responses (AUC 0.85–0.99), substantially more than in the untrained network; separability was unrelated to pixel error.
Breaking temporal order in generated frames was detectable earlier from trained neural responses than from pixel statistics, and detection horizons differentiated the world models.

papers.abstract: Linear recurrences are becoming an increasingly common building block in large language models, replacing the growing KV cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state that enables efficient decoding. However, the quantization stack has largely been developed around softmax Transformers, whose numerical properties and inference state differ from those of recurrent models. Our goal is to understand these differences and study the design space of quantization methods for recurrent models. In our analysis, we differentiate between two targets. First, extra-state quantization concerns weights and activations outside the recurrent state, whose distributions are shaped indirectly by the sequence mixer during training. In controlled 1.3B parameter models, we find that decayed recurrences develop weaker residual outlier channels than softmax attention and are therefore easier to quantize without incoherence processing. Second, intra-state quantization concerns the recurrent state itself during decode, where repeated updates create a different numerical problem from KV cache quantization. We instantiate our findings as LoReS, a state quantization pipeline combining value-axis scale grouping to match output channel magnitude, decay-based mixed-precision to protect slowly decaying heads or channels, and stochastic rounding to limit error accumulation under repeated requantization. Across Qwen-3.5 9B, Nemotron-H 8B, and Kimi-Linear 48B-A3B, LoReS supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower effective precision on shorter decode horizons. We implement LoReS in vLLM and demonstrate end-to-end decode speedups.
bullets: Recurrent models require separate treatment of extra-state weights/activations and the recurrent state itself.
Decayed recurrences develop fewer residual outlier channels than softmax attention, reducing the need for incoherence processing.
LoReS combines value-axis scale grouping, decay-aware mixed precision, and stochastic rounding to control recurrent-state quantization error.
It supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower precision for shorter decode horizons across several large models.
A vLLM implementation demonstrates end-to-end decoding speedups.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generation has achieved impressive results on short clips, yet generating long videos remains challenging due to error accumulation over extended horizons, where each predicted frame depends on potentially imperfect previous frames. Existing approaches typically rely on static context management strategies, such as sliding-window caches that discard early frames or fixed sink frames that permanently preserve initial content. These designs either lose critical long-range context or anchor generation to outdated information, which can lead to degraded fidelity, motion stagnation, and reduced diversity. In this paper, we propose Learning to Memorize (L2M), a learned context memory management framework that dynamically retains, evicts, and evolves historical frames according to predicted importance. The framework consists of an importance prediction router that estimates the relevance of each historical frame, degradation-aware training that improves robustness to noisy or corrupted context, and a dynamic memory initialization and evolution mechanism that updates long-term memory using exponential moving average (EMA) importance scores. This allows high-quality frames to replace stale anchors and enables memory to adapt naturally to scene evolution. Trained with a teacher-student distillation objective and sparsity regularization, L2M makes efficient use of a fixed KV-cache budget while preserving the most informative contextual information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that L2M improves long-horizon video generation quality and temporal consistency over existing baselines, providing a learned strategy for context memory management in long autoregressive video generation.
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and degraded quality in long video generation caused by static context strategies.
Uses an importance-prediction router to retain, evict, and update historical frames based on relevance.
Combines degradation-aware training, EMA-based memory evolution, teacher–student distillation, and sparsity regularization.
Experiments report improved long-horizon video quality and temporal consistency over existing baselines.
Scope: focuses on learned context management within a fixed KV-cache budget.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of L2M. (a) Training phase: Given the current chunk feature f̄b and historical latent frame features {f̄i}i<(b−1)Bf+1, the importance-aware frame router predicts importance scores for each historical latent frame. Binary frame selection masks mi ∈ {0, 1} are obtained via GumbelSoftmax discretization. The pruned context is fed to the student network, which is supervised by the teacher operating on the full context. Degradation-aware training augments a subset of historical frames with degradations, encouraging the router to assign them lower retention probabilities. (b) Inference phase: The router predicts frame importance scores, and low-scoring latent frames are evicted to meet the cache budget. High-scoring frames are dynamically selected as long-term memory and periodically updated using maintained EMA scores, continuously promoting informative historical frames.

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers have become the most powerful models for visual generation, but still suffer from massive computation costs. To solve this problem, feature caching has been proposed to cache the features of diffusion models in the previous computation steps and then reuse them in the following caching steps, which brings significant acceleration but also degradation in generation quality. To address this problem, this paper proposes Z-cache as a feature caching method that can maintain high-quality generation through self-reflection. Concretely, we observe that the error from feature caching tends to be sharply reduced after each full computation. Based on this observation, Z-Cache is designed to first predict the features in the future caching steps and then perform a full computation. After that, Z-Cache returns to the caching steps and re-predicts them based on the previous and the current computation steps, which brings correction in features. Experiments demonstrate that with Z-Cache, diffusion transformers achieve comparable generation quality to the original model but with faster inference speed, for instance, 6.22X acceleration on FLUX-dev for text-to-image generation. Our code is released on GitHub.
bullets: Feature caching reduces diffusion-transformer computation but can degrade image quality.
Z-Cache predicts features for future caching steps, periodically performs full computation, and uses it to correct subsequent predictions.
Experiments report comparable generation quality with faster inference, including 6.22× acceleration on FLUX-dev for text-to-image generation.
The method targets inference acceleration for diffusion-transformer-based visual generation.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Visualization of videos generated by Hunyuan Video with different feature caching methods. The annotated speedups denote FLOPs reductions relative to 50-step sampling.

Figure 3: Pipeline of Z-Cache. The figure uses the reverse-diffusion notation t, t − 1, . . . for visualization, while the text uses a sampling-order index that increases along denoising. Traditional feature caching forecasts an active window from a past full-computation anchor and directly moves to the next window. In contrast, Z-Cache treats the window as provisional: after obtaining the next scheduled full-computation anchor, it revisits the same window, constructs dual-anchor hidden estimates, re-samples the window trajectory, and commits the reflected window-end latent. Z-Cache therefore performs in-loop trajectory correction without adding extra full-computation steps.

papers.abstract: Navigation world models predict future observations conditioned on navigation actions to support planning, but their generalization across real-world environments remains constrained by the limited coverage of action-labeled data. Action-free navigation videos provide diverse visual experience, yet lack the recorded actions required for action-conditioned training. We introduce OpenNWM, a generalist navigation world model with latent action pretraining. It learns universal latent actions from large-scale action-free videos through visual prediction pretraining, and further aligns them with physical motions via action-conditioned post-training. To support video pretraining, we curate NavAnywhere, a large-scale action-free navigation video dataset comprising 17.5 million visual observations from 15 heterogeneous sources. It captures navigation by ground robots, humans, and drones, with diverse viewpoints and motion patterns across five broad scene types: residential areas, public and commercial spaces, urban settings, parks, and natural landscapes. Experiments demonstrate improved visual prediction on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, together with improved navigation performance. These results show that latent-action pretraining enables diverse, action-free videos to improve dynamics learning and generalization for open-world navigation.
bullets: Addresses limited action-labeled data and poor cross-environment generalization in navigation world models.
Pretrains universal latent actions through visual prediction on action-free navigation videos.
Post-trains the latent actions with action-conditioned data to align them with physical motion.
Introduces NavAnywhere, a dataset of 17.5 million observations from 15 sources spanning varied agents, viewpoints, motions, and environments.
Reports improved visual prediction on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, as well as better navigation performance.

papers.abstract: Agentic workflows organize complex tasks into reusable procedures. However, invoking an LLM at every step incurs repeated inference costs and delays. We propose a framework for self-evolving agentic workflows through semantic task decomposition. Each subtask has explicit applicability conditions and a procedure that executes code or invokes a model as needed. An agent uses execution feedback to refine the decomposition and update these procedures. Experiments in the GLEE competition show the framework on bargaining, negotiation and persuasion. Most observed final-decision procedures are implemented in code. Code is available at https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/NeurIPS2026_SeaFlow.
bullets: Addresses the repeated inference cost and latency of invoking LLMs at every workflow step.
Represents each subtask with explicit applicability conditions and an executable procedure.
Uses execution feedback to refine task decompositions and update procedures over time.
Evaluated in the GLEE competition on bargaining, negotiation, and persuasion tasks.
Observed final-decision procedures were mostly implemented in code.

papers.abstract: Residents who contact a community service desk about a repair or a service charge need answers they can act on, with facts that hold for their case and commitments the desk can keep. In tool-augmented LLM agents, such facts come from documents and records, and the conduct of a service answer is usually specified in a system prompt. We present NEIGHBOR, an LLM agent for community resident services that trains this conduct into the model that drives its tools. NEIGHBOR is deployed on a live resident-service platform for a district of an East Asian city of more than ten million people. It adapts Qwen3-235B-A22B with LoRA on 7,824 supervised fine-tuning examples built from public community-service materials around six service-behaviour targets, among them commitment control and human referral, and the adapted model plans document retrieval and read-only text-to-SQL over the resident's own records. In an offline evaluation with seven configurations, an independent domain expert rated all 350 answers to 50 stratified held-out queries. NEIGHBOR scores 7.74/10 against 5.86 for the same agent running the un-tuned model (+1.88; paired Wilcoxon $p<10^{-8}$; higher on 46 of 50 queries) and improves all six rated dimensions. No tool-augmented answer received a red-line flag (standalone models: 8-14% of answers). An LLM judge ranks the seven configurations much as the expert does (Spearman $ρ=0.93$). Its rubric counts specifics absent from the reference answer as fabricated, so it scores tool-grounded answers 1-2 points lower, enough to change which configuration ranks first. For resident-facing agents, service behaviour is a practical fine-tuning target that raises expert-rated answer quality with the tools held fixed.
bullets: Targets six service behaviors, including controlling commitments and referring cases to humans.
Uses LoRA fine-tuning on 7,824 supervised examples while retaining document retrieval and read-only text-to-SQL tools.
In an expert evaluation, the tuned agent scored 7.74/10 versus 5.86/10 for the untuned agent across 50 queries.
The tuned agent improved all six rated dimensions, and no tool-augmented answer received a red-line safety flag.
LLM-judge rankings broadly matched expert rankings, but the judge penalized grounded specifics absent from reference answers.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex speech models execute dense model inference for every audio frame throughout a live interaction. This uniform framewise schedule creates sustained GPU load across dialogue states whose computation has strong, reusable temporal structure. ReFrame formulates full-duplex inference as a silence-aware computation problem. Mutual Silence Speculation (MSS) operates when both participants are silent: it evaluates multi-frame Temporal continuations, verifies text and hidden-state stability, and applies batched Mimi audio-token correction. Listening Frame Folding (LFF) operates while the user speaks and the agent listens: it processes already-arrived user frames through parallel Temporal execution and frame-batched audio-token generation while accepting only the verified prefix. Frame-Budget Reinvestment (FBR) assigns the released frame intervals to resumable external retrieval and language-model workers, then injects timely references through Moshi's conditioning interface. We instantiate ReFrame on five full-duplex models spanning Moshi-family, phase-structured, and flattened autoregressive generation. Across the complete 1,225-conversation FDBench, ReFrame reduces measured GPU execution time by 18.80-31.01% and retains 96.92-100% non-PAD text agreement on five different models. On HaluEval tests, FBR increases the number of correct generated spoken answers from 86 to 205 under the same auxiliary-service budget. ReFrame turns recurring dialogue structure into lower inference cost and higher end-to-end service capability.
bullets: Targets the sustained GPU cost of dense frame-by-frame inference during silence and listening phases.
Uses Mutual Silence Speculation, Listening Frame Folding, and verified-prefix processing to reuse and batch temporal computation.
Reinvests freed compute intervals in resumable retrieval and language-model workers via the model’s conditioning interface.
Evaluated on five full-duplex models across 1,225 FDBench conversations, reducing measured GPU execution time by 18.80–31.01%.
Maintains 96.92–100% non-PAD text agreement; retrieval reinvestment increased correct spoken answers from 86 to 205 under the same auxiliary-service budget.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have enabled generative video compression to reconstruct details lost during coding using pretrained spatiotemporal priors. However, a substantial gap remains between codec-induced degradation and the perturbation trajectories learned by flow-matching models. In this paper, we identify a compression-dependent directional mismatch that degradation-strength-based timestep calibration alone cannot resolve. Compressed latents remain strongly aligned across codec operating points, while their reconstruction residuals vary substantially in magnitude and direction. To bridge this gap, we propose RIFT, a Residual-Informed Flow Transfer framework for one-step generative video compression. At its core, RIFT introduces a Residual Geometry Inducer (RGI) that converts the pretrained flow prediction into a content-adaptive restoration update using decoder-visible codec cues. RGI integrates flow-timestep conditioning with a learned full-band residual-strength estimate and content-conditioned direction and gain modulation, aligning the orientation and magnitude of the update with the compression-dependent residual geometry. Extensive experiments on three public video compression benchmarks show that RIFT outperforms competing generative video compression methods. The code is publicly available on RIFT.
bullets: Compression artifacts differ in residual magnitude and direction, which timestep calibration alone cannot address.
RIFT uses decoder-visible codec cues to make restoration updates content-adaptive.
Its Residual Geometry Inducer combines flow-timestep conditioning with learned residual strength, direction, and gain modulation.
Experiments on three public video-compression benchmarks show RIFT outperforms competing generative compression methods.
The method targets one-step reconstruction using pretrained spatiotemporal priors.

papers.abstract: LLM-based role-playing agents are fluent at imitating a character's style, yet struggle to make role-consistent decisions over long narrative horizons. Such decisions are shaped by experiences spanning many prior scenes, which are often partial and may point in different directions. Existing methods inject cross-scene memories as context, but do not reason about how past events shape a character's current motivations and behavior. We propose MemRole, a framework that makes this memory-to-decision process explicit. It introduces Long-Horizon Memory Thinking (LHMT), a reasoning schema that decomposes hidden reasoning into context understanding, memory activation, and response strategy planning, trained on a novel-derived dataset whose character-grounded, timeline-constrained memory pools limit each character to what it could plausibly know at the current narrative point. Beyond supervised fine-tuning, we propose Self-Refining On-Policy Self-Distillation (SR-OPSD): the model critiques its own rollouts against the reference under a data-driven rubric, and a critique-conditioned teacher view of the same model distills token-level guidance back into the policy. MemRole-32B improves over its backbone by 15.2 points on memory-grounded role-playing, performs on par with frontier LLMs such as GPT-5.4, and achieves the best character-motivation recognition accuracy on CroSS-MR.
bullets: Addresses role inconsistency when prior experiences are partial, conflicting, and spread across many narrative scenes.
Uses Long-Horizon Memory Thinking to understand context, activate relevant memories, and plan response strategies.
Trains on character-grounded, timeline-constrained memory pools that restrict knowledge to what a character could plausibly know.
Adds Self-Refining On-Policy Self-Distillation, where self-critiques guide token-level policy refinement.
MemRole-32B improves its backbone by 15.2 points, matches reported frontier-LLM performance, and leads on CroSS-MR character-motivation recognition.

papers.abstract: A poor start lowers the ceiling, but does not negate the value of finishing well. In autoregressive video temporal grounding, models systematically exhibit an endpoint performance asymmetry, predicting ends significantly worse than starts. A committed flawed start acts as an immutable physical constraint, irreversibly capping the attainable overlap as a sunk loss. While models should minimize the remaining conditional regret, standard post-training paradigms fail to teach this adaptation. Specifically, teacher-forced SFT suffers from strict prefix exposure bias, and holistic trajectory evaluation in standard GRPO inadvertently penalizes conditionally optimal ends if they follow a poor start. To address this, we introduce FinishStrong, a novel two-stage post-training framework explicitly designed to teach optimal continuations. First, Online-start SFT exposes the end prediction to the model's own generated contexts. Second, Conditional-tree GRPO restructures the sampling topology, centering end rewards exclusively within the same-start branch to mathematically isolate the conditional end quality from the inherited start penalty. FinishStrong-9B achieves a state-of-the-art 61.7\% overall IoU on TimeLens-Bench, remarkably outperforming flagship closed-source models like Gemini-3.8-Flash and Qwen3.8-Max. Crucially, when forced to continue from imperfect starts, it reduces the subsequent end prediction error by 36.5\%, proving its exceptional ability to end well after flawed starts. Code will be open.
bullets: Autoregressive models predict temporal segment ends worse than starts, and flawed starts can cap the achievable overlap.
Standard teacher-forced SFT and holistic GRPO do not adequately reward conditionally good continuations after poor starts.
The two-stage framework uses Online-start SFT to expose models to their own generated starts.
Conditional-tree GRPO evaluates end quality within the same-start branch, separating continuation quality from inherited start errors.
FinishStrong-9B reports 61.7% overall IoU on TimeLens-Bench and reduces end prediction error by 36.5% after imperfect starts.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a teleoperation system for service robots that integrates human pose estimation with virtual reality (VR) to enable intuitive remote control. By using the Mediapipe framework for 2D pose detection and extending it with RGB-D data from the Intel RealSense D455 camera, a comprehensive 3D human pose estimation is achieved. This data is then mapped to the robot's kinematics, allowing the operator to control the robot's movements naturally. A VR interface was developed to provide an immersive perspective, enhancing the operator's situational awareness. Real-world experiments were conducted using the CHARMIE service robot to validate the system's effectiveness in tasks involving object manipulation. While the current system successfully demonstrates the potential of VR-based teleoperation, challenges remain in accurately capturing certain joint angles (e.g., wrist yaw) and ensuring precise mapping between human and robot movements. Future work includes the integration of inertial measurement units (IMUs) for improved rotational tracking and the implementation of more advanced control algorithms. Overall, this research contributes to the development of more intuitive and effective teleoperation systems for service robots, facilitating their deployment in complex and dynamic environments. This work further introduces a novel approach to teleoperation by combining RGB-D sensing with an innovative algorithm for real-time joint angle computation using Mediapipe, enhancing the precision of human-robot motion mapping and enabling immersive control through a VR interface. These contributions represent significant advancements in the field of human-robot interaction, particularly for service robot applications.
bullets: Combines Mediapipe 2D pose detection with Intel RealSense D455 RGB-D data to estimate 3D human pose.
Maps estimated human joint movements to the robot’s kinematics for natural control.
Provides an immersive VR interface intended to improve operator situational awareness.
Validated through real-world object-manipulation experiments with the CHARMIE service robot.

papers.abstract: Humanoid controllers need the ability to yield to external forces while retaining the capacity to resume their original tasks. However, tracking objectives penalize the deviations needed for yielding, while relaxing tracking goals persistently can make task recovery harder. Existing approaches often rely on task-specific interaction command interfaces or constructed compliant motion data and reference trajectories, limiting the direct reuse of their compliance-training mechanisms across different task interfaces. We introduce CompliantBot, a compliance-training framework for motion tracking and velocity-command locomotion. It preserves the original task inputs and requires no preconstructed compliant data or target trajectories. A state-dependent interaction force field couples applied loads to the robot's motion, enabling local articulation and whole-body movement to change the forces experienced. A complementary force-magnitude reward encourages lower interaction loads, while task rewards are downweighted during loading and restored after release to coordinate yielding and task resumption. The trained policies use task inputs and proprioceptive history without explicit external-force measurements. Across both task interfaces, CompliantBot yields farther under constant pulls and experiences lower spring interaction loads than matched baselines, while resuming task tracking after force removal. CompliantBot achieves the highest task completion among the compared methods under stronger pulls. Power evaluations further show that CompliantBot has the lowest mean joint mechanical power among the compared methods. Real-robot demonstrations further illustrate compliant responses through arm motion, stepping, and body reorientation.
bullets: Addresses the conflict between force yielding and maintaining or recovering task objectives.
Uses a state-dependent interaction force field, force-magnitude reward, and adaptive task-reward weighting during loading and release.
Supports both motion-tracking and velocity-command locomotion while preserving their original task inputs.
Outperforms matched baselines in yielding distance, spring-load reduction, strong-pull task completion, and mean joint mechanical power.
Real-robot demonstrations show compliant arm motion, stepping, and body reorientation.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents accumulate experience from task streams, but existing frameworks typically rely on fixed pipelines to retrieve and utilize this experience, neglecting when and how to deploy it. We introduce Online Meta-Control of Experience (OMCE), a framework that updates experience memory and learns a meta-control policy from task feedback during test-time adaptation. OMCE employs a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller that uses compact retrieval signals to select among four cognitive actions: DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL. This routing mechanism operationalizes three coupled decisions: whether to invoke experience, which memory format to utilize, and when to consolidate new guidance. OMCE evolves online, leveraging task feedback to update the memory bank and refine the routing policy via contextual bandit updates. Experiments on four online adaptation benchmarks across four backbones show that OMCE improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points over the strongest compared baseline, while reducing per-task token use by a factor of 5.7 to 62.5 relative to ACE with GPT-5.2. Controlled ablations further support the benefits of learned routing and continued routing policy adaptation.
bullets: Addresses fixed experience-retrieval pipelines that do not adapt experience use to task context.
Uses a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller to choose among DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL actions.
Jointly decides whether to invoke experience, which memory format to use, and when to consolidate guidance.
Updates both the experience memory and routing policy online from task feedback.
Across four benchmarks and four backbones, improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points and reduces token use by 5.7–62.5× versus ACE with GPT-5.2.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of OMCE. The lightweight Meta-Controller selects a cognitive action specifying whether and which experience to inject into the task prompt. The agent solves the task with the augmented context containing the query and any injected experience. Figure 1: From Fixed Pipelines to Learned Meta-Control. Up: Existing methods typically follow a fixed routine for using and consolidating experience, even when the retrieved experience does not help the current task. Down: OMCE learns from task feedback when to use experience, whether to draw on past cases or general guidance, and when to distill new guidance.

papers.abstract: Position-independent caching reuses chunk KV caches across positions and requests. Independent encoding, however, omits cross-chunk interactions and can degrade accuracy. In our study, neither PIC training nor rule-based recomputation, alone or combined, consistently recovers full-prefill accuracy. Oracle-guided recomputation on PIC-trained models improves accuracy at the same budget, motivating better selection. We present CacheWeave, which adapts the full backbone to PIC, then freezes it and trains a model-native block selector on the adapted model's oracles. The selector uses compact cached chunk features and question hidden states without extracting backbone attention scores. It selects contiguous token blocks aligned with KV blocks to support efficient recomputation and limit copy-on-write amplification. Its runtime, CacheWeave-Serve, supports private and shared KV caches, keeps selection and recomputation on the GPU, and stages sliding-window KV for hybrid attention models. Across three models and four tasks, CacheWeave outperforms CacheBlend and ProphetKV by 7.2 and 3.5 percentage points on average at a 5% recomputation budget, with a mean relative accuracy loss of 1.6% to full prefill. With 32-token blocks, CacheWeave-Serve cuts single-request TTFT by up to 16.1x over full prefill and 1.7x over ProphetKV, and raises SLO goodput under load by up to 7.8x.
bullets: Position-independent KV caching is efficient but loses cross-chunk interactions, hurting accuracy.
CacheWeave adapts the backbone to position-independent caching, then trains a model-native selector using oracle-guided recomputation.
The selector uses compact cached features and question hidden states, avoids backbone attention extraction, and chooses contiguous KV-aligned blocks.
Across three models and four tasks, it improves over CacheBlend and ProphetKV by 7.2 and 3.5 percentage points at a 5% recomputation budget, with 1.6% mean relative accuracy loss versus full prefill.
CacheWeave-Serve supports private/shared caches and hybrid attention; with 32-token blocks, it cuts single-request TTFT by up to 16.1× and improves loaded-system SLO goodput by up to 7.8×.

Figure 2. Each PIC method alone. Lines: non-native recomputation on the untrained base model at 5–20% recomputation budget. Dashed: lossless (base model, full prefill), base PIC, and trained PIC without recomputation (green). Figure 1. Attention patterns for system prefix S, chunks D1, D2, and question Q; rows attend to coloured columns. (a) Full prefill. (b) PIC removes cross-chunk interactions. papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) read knowledge-graph facts ranked by relevance, leaving open whether they suffice or conflict. Our checks use relation knowledge, written by hand or learned from training questions labelled with their relation paths. It selects a compact context of facts yielding an answer, and derives it; a derivability check tests whether an answer follows, a consistency check whether facts conflict, and a validation-chosen routing gate decides where the derived answer replaces the LLM's. Seven open LLMs read the compact context better in exact match than relevance-ranked facts; on ComplexWebQuestions (CWQ) they match SubgraphRAG's facts at a quarter of the prompt tokens, and stronger LLMs read SubgraphRAG's better. Where the routing gate passes, ours leads SubgraphRAG's in exact match in all 53 LLM, benchmark and prompt settings. A precision gate, returning the derived answer only when the check passes with exactly one derived entity, answered 18 and 5 percent of held-out WebQSP and CWQ questions in a pre-specified test, right for 90 and 96 percent. The consistency check judges facts by path evidence only where another path joins their entities, true of 2.5 percent of named-entity facts in our compact WebQSP and CWQ contexts.
bullets: The work addresses whether relevance-ranked graph facts are sufficient or may conflict when LLMs answer questions.
Hand-written or learned relation knowledge selects facts along answer-supporting relation paths and derives an answer.
Derivability and consistency checks, combined with a validation-selected routing gate, determine when to replace the LLM’s answer.
Across seven open LLMs, compact contexts outperform relevance-ranked facts in exact match; on CWQ, they match SubgraphRAG’s facts using one-quarter as many prompt tokens.
A precision-only gate answered 18% of WebQSP and 5% of CWQ held-out questions, with 90% and 96% accuracy respectively; consistency checks applied to only 2.5% of named-entity facts.

papers.title: Less but Sufficient: Relation Knowledge Selects Compact Knowledge-Graph Contexts, and What External Checks Can and Cannot Catch

papers.abstract: Most robot policies, whether trained by imitation learning (IL) or reinforcement learning (RL), map observations to action values at discrete control steps and leave the continuity of physical motion to be learned implicitly. We propose ODE policy, which learns the dynamics of the action rather than the action itself. A neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) learns the vector field of the action by matching the integrated actions to the targets over short action chunks in IL and single control steps in RL. A lightweight diversity head captures multi-modal behavior by randomizing the direction of the field. At deployment, each action is integrated from the previous one, so the executed trajectory is continuous by construction. We evaluate it as a visuomotor policy, as the action head of vision-language-action (VLA) and world action models (WAMs), and as the actor of model-based RL against 14 baselines on unimanual, bimanual, dexterous, locomotion, and loco-manipulation tasks. In IL, against flow matching, it reaches 5.9$\times$ the success, 5.4$\times$ the generalization, and 3.9$\times$ the mode balance after one epoch, and generates actions 10.8$\times$ faster. It mostly moves more smoothly than human demonstrations. On 14 real-world tasks across single-arm, dual-arm, dexterous, and humanoid robots, it achieves the highest success rate. In RL, it further speeds up SuperMimic for humanoid motion tracking and smooths its actions. Efficient in learning, data, parameters, and execution, ODE policy offers a promising path to scaling robot learning.
bullets: Addresses the discontinuity of policies that predict discrete actions directly.
Uses a neural ODE to learn an action vector field and integrates actions from the previous action at deployment.
A diversity head supports multimodal behavior by randomizing the field direction.
Evaluated across visuomotor policies, VLA/WAM action heads, and model-based RL on diverse real-world robotic tasks.
Reports strong gains over flow matching in early IL training, faster action generation, smoother motion, and the highest success rate across 14 real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: Task success, retrieval quality, and cost do not show whether an LLM agent used a delivered memory or what followed from that use. We introduce MemUse, which evaluates memory at its point of use in recorded trajectories: each memory delivery is compared with what the agent could already see and followed through the agent's later actions and their consequences. An agentic judge rates each delivered entry's relevance, accuracy, novelty, influence, and observed effect; programmatic checks enforce complete reading of cited evidence, and fixed rules aggregate the ratings into verdicts linked to memory histories and delivery cost. On 8,000 SWE-bench Verified episodes from three memory systems, resolve rates stay within 0.4 percentage points of a no-memory baseline, yet MemUse shows that most delivered entries were irrelevant, most relevant entries went unused, and in two systems most deliveries restated content the agent could still see. It also surfaces effects that outcomes hide: 23.2\% of episodes with beneficial memory use still failed, and 5 of 16 with harmful use still succeeded.
bullets: Evaluates memory at its point of use by comparing each delivery with the agent’s visible context and tracing subsequent actions and consequences.
An agentic judge scores relevance, accuracy, novelty, influence, and observed effect, with programmatic evidence checks and fixed aggregation rules.
Across 8,000 SWE-bench Verified episodes and three memory systems, resolve rates stayed within 0.4 percentage points of the no-memory baseline.
Most delivered entries were irrelevant, most relevant entries went unused, and two systems often repeated information already visible to the agent.
Memory effects were not captured by outcomes alone: 23.2% of episodes with beneficial memory use still failed, while 5 of 16 with harmful use still succeeded.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of MemUse. The memory bridge connects agents to memory systems and annotates memory operations. The trajectory recorder captures model calls, with token usage and cost when available. Within each episode, data processing groups identical repeated deliveries into injection spans while earlier copies remain visible and assigns each entry a credit window for attributing actions. The memory graph links deliveries to recorded entry histories across trajectories. For each eligible span, an agentic judge assesses each entry’s information quality, use, and observed effects from its exposed text, prior context, and subsequent trajectory. Programmatic checks enforce evidence coverage and credit windows, and fixed rules derive the span verdict.

Figure 2: Credit windows and judge routing. (a) A’s deliveries at steps 2 and 4 share S1; re-entry after removal starts S4 with a fresh prior context. (b) The shorter copy A′ adds no text or identifier beyond the visible A, so A′ in S3 receives an empty window and A in S1 retains credit through step 9. Effects of credited actions are followed through the episode end. (c) S1, S2, and S4 are judged; S3 receives a rule-derived neutral triage label without a judge call. Empty deliveries receive a neutral placeholder and are excluded from triage rates.

Figure 3: Six-axis memory profiles, pooled over four runs per configuration, with each profiled span weighted equally. (a) The radar plot uses a common logarithmic radial scale from 0.001% at the center to 100% at the outer ring, with tenfold increases between adjacent rings. (b) Heatmap cells report the same means as percentages, with shading on the same logarithmic scale. Lower harm shares are better. Table 7 reports these shares alongside uncertainty and token efficiency.

Figure 4: Memory effects concealed by task outcomes. (a) A TencentDB skill for a different Napoleon bug directs the agent into the wrong component (steps 2–5). A reproduction rules out Napoleon at step 7, and the agent fixes sphinx/util/docfields.py at step 9; the task passes despite the detour. (b) A MemGovern card guides the agent to add a subset handler at step 8, changing the reported subset check from None to True. The equality error persists, and at step 14 the agent decides to leave it unfixed despite the card’s advice to repair it; the task fails. Timelines show complete episodes with steps numbered locally. Arrows mark first consumption, shading marks credit windows, and blue steps mark actions based on memory. Red and green annotations highlight problems and repairs. Memory effects are judge assessments; task outcomes come from the SWEbench harness.

Figure 5: Delivered-token and beneficial-entry shares by delivery form. Circles show each form’s share of estimated delivered tokens, including restatements, and diamonds show its share of beneficial entries. Values pool four runs per configuration, with both Mem0 configurations combined. Forms with no beneficial entries and less than 0.1% of tokens are omitted from the plot but retained in the token denominators. Full cards, task recall, and full skills supply most beneficial entries at small token shares. Table 11 gives the detailed breakdown.

Figure 6: Run variation and effects conditional on use. (a) Markers show each of four runs per configuration on logarithmic scales; within a row, runs 1–4 are offset from top to bottom, and shading spans the four runs. Relevance is the mean entry share across profiled spans; token efficiency divides beneficial-entry counts by all estimated delivered tokens, including restatements and spans without profiles. (b) Effect counts are pooled across four runs and divided by the number of acted-on entries, n. Labels give improved and undetermined shares; every segment retains its proportional width.

Omitted empty and automatic-copy forms each contribute less than 0.1% of tokens and remain in the denominators.

Input tokens are split into uncached and cached tokens as reported by the provider.

Yields count beneficial or harmful entries per 100 profiled spans. Coverage uses all 2,000 episodes per configuration; recurring items occur in at least 50 episodes of a run. Delivered tokens include restatements and spans without profiles. Unknown novelty share is zero in every configuration.

Delays compare the first anchored action with the first consuming step. Episode counts exclude the three episodes without a harness result; one MemGovern episode belongs to both effect groups.

Table 8: Results of each run. Resolved, relevance, acted on, benefit, and harm are percentages, with entry shares averaged over the profiled spans of the run. Efficiency counts beneficial entries per million delivered tokens, and spans counts profiled spans. The no-memory baseline resolved 75.0%, 72.0%, 73.0%, and 71.8% of the tasks in its four runs.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a point-of-use evaluation framework for LLM agent memory, fitting the LLM memory topic.
papers.title: Delivered, Not Used: Evaluating Agent Memory at Its Point of Use
papers.tldr: MemUse evaluates whether an agent actually uses delivered memory and what effects that use has, revealing that outcome metrics alone can hide substantial memory waste and harm.

papers.abstract: Query-conditioned sparse KV selection reduces long-context inference cost by attending to a subset of historical KV entries at each decoding step. Existing selectors must wait for the target-layer query before scoring candidates and generating indices, placing routing on the immediate pre-attention path. We introduce EarlySelectKV, a training-free transformation that uses proxy queries from earlier hidden states to precompute selected KV indices while retaining the real target-layer query for final attention. Tests with RocketKV, Quest, and Loki show no consistent pattern of quality degradation across the evaluated settings. In the primary RocketKV evaluation, ES-RocketKV differs by +0.018 points on LongBench, approximately -0.01 points on RULER, and +0.25 percentage points on representative NIAH/Passkey settings. In a TensorRT-LLM deployment with CPU-offloaded routing, ES-RocketKV improves end-to-end output throughput by up to 12.4% and reduces GPU-resident memory by 11.1% of the combined KV/K-summary pool. This makes routing timing an explicit optimization target alongside KV subset selection in sparse long-context decoding. Code is available at https://github.com/sea-with-sakura/EarlySelectKV.
bullets: Addresses routing latency caused by waiting for each target-layer query before selecting historical KV entries.
Uses a training-free transformation to anticipate selected KV indices from proxy queries in earlier hidden states.
Evaluated with RocketKV, Quest, and Loki, with no consistent quality degradation reported across tested settings.
In TensorRT-LLM with CPU-offloaded routing, improves output throughput by up to 12.4% and reduces combined KV/K-summary GPU memory by 11.1%.
Frames routing timing—not only KV subset selection—as an optimization target for sparse long-context inference.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of EarlySelectKV. The main flow gathers selected KV using precomputed page indices and performs sparse attention with the real query. The side flow constructs a proxy query from an earlier hidden state and precomputes next-layer page indices. Early and Mid taps represent two timing–fidelity trade-offs: the former offers a longer preparation window, while the latter provides higher selection fidelity.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models can generate task-oriented robot actions, but they do not guarantee safe execution in obstacle-rich manipulation scenes. Although CBF-QP safety filters can locally project unsafe actions into a safe set, such correction may push the robot away from the learned task trajectory and leave the VLA policy without a reliable recovery direction. We propose Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair, a post-hoc repair module that uses the short-horizon action chunk predicted by the VLA to detect blocked nominal trajectories and generate entry-exit-rejoin guidance around obstacles. The selected route is added to the CBF-QP objective as a soft guidance term, while the CBF safety constraint remains hard. On SafeLIBERO, our method improves collision avoidance, task success, and SafeSuccess compared with AEGIS. Our project page is available at GitHub.
bullets: VLA-generated actions lack guaranteed safety in obstacle-rich manipulation scenes.
Standard CBF-QP filters enforce local safety but can divert the robot from its task trajectory without providing recovery guidance.
The method detects blocked short-horizon action chunks and generates entry-exit-rejoin routes around obstacles.
These routes softly guide the CBF-QP objective, while safety constraints remain hard.
On SafeLIBERO, it improves collision avoidance, task success, and SafeSuccess over AEGIS.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair. The method uses the VLA action chunk to estimate a nominal future trajectory and detect obstacle-induced blockage. When the nominal trajectory is blocked, it generates an entry-exit-rejoin route around the obstacle and adds the selected route to the CBF-QP objective as soft guidance. The CBF constraint remains hard, so the repaired action preserves safety while following a recoverable route toward task completion.
Fig. 2: Qualitative comparison on SafeLIBERO. Task: pick up the chocolate pudding and place it in the basket. Top row: AEGIS (Success, Collision). Bottom row: Ours (Success, Collision-free).
TABLE I: Quantitative results on the SafeLIBERO benchmark.
TABLE II: Ablation study of route-guided CBF-QP components.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses safe VLA robot manipulation with a post-hoc safety repair module.
papers.title: Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair for Safe Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair improves VLA robot safety by steering corrected actions around obstacles while preserving the model’s intended task route.

papers.abstract: Analog In-Memory Computing (IMC) is a promising paradigm for accelerating GEMM-based AI workloads by executing computations directly within the memory array in the analog domain. While IMC delivers substantial energy and throughput improvements, it can suffer from significant task accuracy degradation due to analog-to-digital converter (ADC) quantization noise, which occurs at the GEMM output and is thus different from weight/activation quantization, which occurs at the GEMM input. Mixed ADC resolution allows IMC modules to choose between high- and low-resolution ADC modes with different energy costs, offering a compelling accuracy-energy trade-off. However, selecting ADC resolutions across IMC units while respecting hardware granularity constraints remains challenging. In this paper, we propose SMART-AIMC, a Sensitivity-aware Mixed ADC Resolution framework with fine-grained Tunability for Analog In-Memory Computing. SMART-AIMC correlates the algorithmic task loss to hardware ADC quantization noise in the form of an ADC Channel Sensitivity (ACS) metric. Using this metric, SMART-AIMC systematically, and in a disciplined manner, allocates ADC resources to critical computations. Furthermore, we introduce a sensitivity-based channel reordering scheme that overcomes the hardware granularity constraints with no runtime overhead and approaches the optimal ADC quantization possible for the model. Evaluated across diverse workloads, SMART-AIMC unlocks a superior accuracy-energy Pareto frontier, providing (1) higher task accuracy at matched energy budgets and (2) fine-grained tuning across efficiency targets, from aggressive energy savings to near-digital inference accuracy. At the latter operating point, SMART-AIMC achieves $6.99\times$ higher modeled system-level energy efficiency for linear projections than the INT8 digital baseline with negligible accuracy degradation.
bullets: ADC quantization noise at GEMM outputs can significantly degrade IMC task accuracy, creating a distinct challenge from input quantization.
The framework uses an ADC Channel Sensitivity metric to relate algorithmic loss to ADC noise and prioritize critical computations.
Sensitivity-based channel reordering bypasses hardware granularity constraints without runtime overhead.
Across diverse workloads, SMART-AIMC offers higher accuracy at matched energy and fine-grained tuning from aggressive savings to near-digital accuracy.
Near the digital-accuracy operating point, it reports 6.99× higher modeled system-level energy efficiency than an INT8 digital baseline for linear projections, with negligible accuracy degradation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: IMC architecture, signal swing reduction, and ADC resolution-energy trade-off.

Figure 2: Variations in ADC sensitivity. Sensitivity to ADC quantization varies significantly not only across decoder blocks, but also among individual channels, necessitating a systematic approach for optimal compute-to-ADC resolution mapping. The experiment setting is detailed in Appendix H.
Figure 5: IMC accelerator architecture. Static-weight linear projections are mapped to analog IMC, while attention matrix multiplications and vector operations are executed on digital engines.

Figure 7: SMART-AIMC fidelity–energy efficiency Pareto analysis. KL divergence and perplexity versus system-level energy-efficiency gain for linear projections over digital INT8 for LLaMA-2-7B on WikiText-2. Dashed lines show digital INT8 fidelity; lower fidelity metrics and higher gain are better. SMART-AIMC establishes a superior frontier over the heuristic and random baselines.
Figure 12: Channel reordering is compatible with rotation methods, allowing optimizations on both input quantization and ADC quantization.

Figure 3: Channel reordering for ADC allocation. Without reordering, high-sensitivity channels can be inadvertently mapped to low-resolution IMC units. Channel reordering strictly ensures that the high-sensitivity channels are mapped to high-resolution ADCs. The setting is detailed in Appendix H.
Figure 4: Sensitivity-aware channel reordering across a decoder layer. Output channels with similar sensitivity are grouped to reduce IMC unit-level mixed-resolution loss during ADC quantization.

Figure 6: SMART-AIMC ADC-resolution allocation. SMART-AIMC identifies distinct sensitivities across projections and blocks to optimize fine-grained ADC assignments under a budget of 20% 12-bit and 80% 9-bit ADCs.

Figure 8: ADC quantization noise distributions. Both 9-bit and 12-bit ADC configurations exhibit near-uniform quantization noise, aligning with the statistical theory of quantization (Widrow et al., 1996).

Figure 11: Hierarchical energy breakdown across ADC resolutions (9–12 bits). (a) Energy consumption of the IMC and non-IMC execution paths, with their respective operation counts. (b) Component-level breakdown of Eproj. (c) IMC macro energy breakdown, showing that ADC-related energy is the primary resolution-dependent component. All energies are reported per decoder block.

papers.abstract: Recently, speech-driven facial and oral animation technologies have been used in various fields such as education, speech therapy, and healthcare. But methods to objectively evaluate the quality of generated results are still limited. Accordingly, we propose the Fréchet Oral Distance (FOD), which uses embeddings from an Oral Motion Encoder (OME) and a TIMIT-Vis reference distribution. In experiments, FOD reproduced model rankings similar to the coordinate-based metric, Lip Vertex Error (LVE), and showed trends consistent with user preference. Our framework provides objective and reproducible benchmarking without relying on expensive equipment or subjective evaluation, and it can be extended to compare a variety of 2D/3D models.
bullets: Addresses the limited availability of objective evaluation methods for generated facial and oral animation.
Computes distance between Oral Motion Encoder embeddings and a TIMIT-Vis reference distribution.
Reproduced model rankings similar to the coordinate-based Lip Vertex Error metric.
Showed trends consistent with user preference in experiments.
Enables reproducible evaluation without expensive equipment or subjective assessment, with potential use across 2D and 3D models.

papers.tldr: Fréchet Oral Distance (FOD) is a coordinate-free metric for objectively benchmarking speech-driven oral animation in alignment with established metrics and user preferences.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture has been widely adopted in large language models (LLMs) since it reduces the computational cost through sparse expert activation. However, the massive parameter scale of MoE models hinders their deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. Although existing mixed-precision quantization reduces the model size, they are inherently static, fixing the bit-width of each expert across decoding steps. Such static schemes yield suboptimal performance as they overlook the dynamic variation in expert importance during decoding. Furthermore, they fail to adapt to the dynamic latency constraint driven by the fluctuating system utilization. To address these challenges, we propose MatMoE, a dynamic mixed-precision quantization framework for efficient MoE inference. MatMoE features: (1) a Matryoshka MoE PTQ algorithm that enables experts to operate flexibly at multiple precisions within a stringent memory budget; (2) a floor-and-compensation quantization method that eliminates redundant memory accesses in the Matryoshka representation; and (3) a dynamic bit-width allocation strategy that determines the precision for each expert based on their routing scores to satisfy the dynamic latency requirement. We implement our MatMoE system atop llama.cpp for both CPU and GPU platforms. Extensive evaluations across three modern MoE models and challenging benchmarks demonstrate that MatMoE achieves $4.0\% \sim 18.3\%$ higher accuracy than state-of-the-art static mixed-precision method. Compared to llama.cpp, MatMoE delivers $1.3\times \sim 3.7\times$ speedup on Raspberry Pi 5, and $1.2\times \sim 1.3\times$ speedup on NVIDIA RTX 4090 and Jetson AGX Orin.
bullets: Targets the large memory footprint and inflexibility of static mixed-precision quantization for MoE deployment on edge devices.
Uses Matryoshka MoE post-training quantization so experts can operate at multiple precisions within a fixed memory budget.
Introduces floor-and-compensation quantization to reduce redundant memory accesses.
Dynamically allocates expert bit-widths from routing scores to meet changing latency requirements.
Across three MoE models, reports 4.0%–18.3% higher accuracy than a static mixed-precision method and 1.2×–3.7× speedups over llama.cpp across tested CPU/GPU platforms.
