papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based video object removal/inpainting with a training-free evidence-guided sampling method; fits video diffusion and editing.
papers.title: Recoverability-Aware Evaluation of Diffusion Video Inpainting and Object Removal
papers.tldr: Recoverability-aware evaluation separates copying from generation in video object removal and shows that diffusion removers underuse content visible in other frames, while training-free evidence reuse offers only partial or unreliable gains.

papers.abstract: In modern robot learning, generative robot policies are first pretrained through supervised learning from demonstrations, then refined through reinforcement learning, supervised finetuning, or other forms of posttraining. Yet conventional pretraining metrics, such as validation loss and average task success, provide an incomplete account of which policies support both effective direct deployment and subsequent posttraining. In this work, we study closed-loop pass@k, which evaluates the probability that k rollouts from the same initial condition attain at least one success. Thus, pass@1 measures mean task success; large-k pass@k measures whether success remains reachable under repeated sampling. Across a wide range of posttraining recipes, we show that large-k pass@k reveals posttraining differences not captured by pass@1. In particular, checkpoints with similar pass@1 but different large-k pass@k have different posttraining performance. Moreover, we show pass@k peaks at different checkpoints during supervised pretraining, revealing a coverage-reliability tradeoff over the course of training. Based on these observations, we propose two practical interventions: (1) a purely offline checkpoint-selection criterion that balances coverage and reliability without closed-loop evaluation, and (2) a generative data augmentation procedure that expands supervision beyond the finite demonstration set, preserving large-k pass@k while maintaining or improving pass@1 and raising the observed coverage-reliability Pareto frontier. Together, our results motivate evaluation, checkpoint selection, and training procedures that explicitly account for posttraining. Blog post, visualizations, and code are available at https://zhanyisun.github.io/robot-policy-learning-dynamics/.
bullets: Pass@1 measures average success, while large-k pass@k measures whether success remains reachable through repeated sampling from the same initial state.
Policies with similar pass@1 can differ substantially in posttraining performance when their large-k pass@k differs.
During supervised pretraining, coverage and reliability peak at different checkpoints, revealing a coverage–reliability tradeoff.
The work proposes offline checkpoint selection and generative data augmentation to preserve or improve coverage and reliability.
The findings motivate evaluation and training procedures that explicitly account for downstream posttraining potential.

figures.caption: Figure 5: During pretraining, generative augmentation preserves coverage while maintaining, and in some tasks improving, reliability (pass@1). Across most MimicGen tasks and RoboCasa, Baseline DP loses pass@10 at later checkpoints. JointAug prevents this loss of coverage while maintaining or improving pass@1. PostBC also preserves pass@10 better than Baseline DP, but can do so at the cost of pass@1.

Figure 1: Later checkpoints trade large-k pass@k for mean task success; checkpoints with similar pass@1 can lead to different posttraining performance. Left: single-task BC followed by residual RL on two representative MimicGen tasks, with (a) showing pass@k during BC and (b) residual RL from different BC checkpoints. Right: multitask pretraining on RoboCasa tasks followed by SFT on target tasks, with (c) showing pass@k during pretraining and (d) downstream SFT. Across (a,c), larger-k pass@k peaks and declines earlier than pass@1, so later checkpoints increasingly favor mean task success at the expense of large-k pass@k performance. Orange marks the earlier checkpoint selected by our offline coverage–reliability criterion (Sec. 4), while blue marks the final supervised-training checkpoint; matching dashed lines in (a,c) indicate the initializations used in (b,d). Despite similar pass@1, finetuning from the orange checkpoint achieves stronger performance than finetuning from the blue checkpoint across both settings.

Figure 7: Real-robot Push-T. (a) Task setup. (b) Best-of-k validation action MSE across training epochs. (c) Quantiles of validation action error across training epochs. (d) Normalized coverage and reliability scores with the selected checkpoint at epoch 46. (e) Pass@1 and pass@5 success rates of the selected (epoch 46) and final (epoch 200) checkpoints over 20 fixed initial states.

Figure 4: Held-out action-MSE quantiles expose the coverage–reliability balance. (a) Held-out action-MSE quantiles across training, colored by percentile u from 0.05 (red) to 0.95 (blue). (b) For a held-out observation, 64 matched-noise samples from ep50 and ep800, plus the expert action, are projected with PCA; rings mark the minimum-MSE sample. ep50 is more dispersed yet has lower best-of-64 MSE, whereas ep800 contracts but its best sample lies farther from the expert. Consistent with (a), lower quantiles favor earlier checkpoints, while higher quantiles improve later. (c) We summarize the lower and upper halves as rcov|H(τ) and rrel|H(τ) and select the checkpoint minimizing max{rcov|H(τ), rrel|H(τ)}; the selected ep350 matches the closed-loop oracle.

Figure 3: Best-of-k action MSE selects earlier checkpoints than closed-loop pass@k. (a) Held-out best-of-k action MSE across training checkpoints for different k. (b) Closed-loop pass@k success rate across the same checkpoints. Matching colors and marker shapes denote the same value of k across panels; hollow markers indicate the minimum MSE in (a) and maximum pass@k in (b). As k increases, both optima shift earlier, but the best-of-k MSE minimum precedes the corresponding pass@k peak, with a larger separation at higher k.

Figure 9: Residual RL finetuning across the coverage–reliability tradeoff. We additionally finetune an earlier baseline checkpoint (ep.200/100/100 for Threading/Hammer Cleanup/Mug Cleanup) with lower pass@1 and higher coverage than the checkpoint selected by our criterion. Its performance relative to later checkpoints depends on the available online budget.

Figure 12: Observation conditioning exacerbates the deterioration in held-out denoising during late training. Relative change in held-out ϵ-prediction MSE from epoch 200 to 800 for the image-conditioned and action-only models, evaluated on the same noisy action chunks. Negative values indicate lower held-out loss at epoch 800; positive values indicate higher loss. The conditional model exhibits held-out loss deterioration at higher diffusion noise levels.

Figure 10: Flow-matching policy pretraining and OGPO finetuning. Each row shows a MimicGen task with 200 demonstrations. (a) Best-of-k validation action MSE. (b) pass@k during BC pretraining. (c) Validation error quantiles. (d) Coverage–reliability scores and selected checkpoint. (e) OGPO finetuning from the selected versus final BC checkpoint. The selected initialization generally achieves better downstream RL performance.

Figure 20: JointAug retains favorable-tail coverage while improving typical action accuracy. For four held-out Mug Cleanup states, we jointly project 64 action samples from baseline ep50, baseline ep800, and JointAug ep800 with PCA. Stars mark expert actions and rings mark the minimum-MSE sample. The baseline ep50 is dispersed with low best-of-64 but high mean MSE; baseline baseline ep800 contracts and lowers mean MSE but worsens best-of-64 MSE; JointAug ep800 achieves best of both worlds.

Figure 21: Context-Smoothed Pre-training from TMRL does not preserve coverage under prolonged training. Across five MimicGen tasks, TMRL generally underperforms JointAug in pass@10 and often loses both pass@10 and pass@1 at later checkpoints.

Figure 28: Late-training coverage loss also occurs with low-dimensional state observations. Across five tasks, baseline diffusion policies lose pass@10 at later checkpoints despite using no visual encoder. Joint (o, a) augmentation preserves substantially more pass@10.

Figure 19: JointAug is relatively robust to generator checkpoint selection. We compare the five-checkpoint mixture used in our main experiments against individual generator checkpoints from the same run . Across four tasks, single-checkpoint variants have similar pass@10 gains over the baseline, while the mixture performs similarly overall and slightly improves pass@1 on Mug Cleanup and Threading.
Figure 16: Extended training on Threading D2. The coverage–reliability dynamics persist to 1600 epochs, and the offline criterion continues to select an intermediate checkpoint.

Figure 18: JointAug enables residual RL finetuning on 3-Piece Assembly (D2). Left: JointAug substantially improves pass@1 and pass@10 during BC pretraining. Right: residual RL from the final JointAug checkpoint reaches over 0.8 success, while finetuning from the baseline checkpoint remains near zero.

Figure 6: Generative augmentation produces stronger checkpoints for posttraining. Columns correspond to Fig. 5. We compare posttraining from the baseline checkpoint selected by our coverage–reliability criterion (Sec. 4), the final Baseline DP checkpoint, and the final checkpoint from our generative augmentation run. Across MimicGen tasks, the final generative-augmentation checkpoint substantially outperforms the final baseline and often matches or exceeds the selected checkpoint. On RoboCasa, it matches the selected checkpoint on both pass@1 and pass@32.

Figure 24: The late-training coverage loss persists across denoiser widths. We vary the U-Net from 24M to 1.0B parameters while keeping the encoder, data, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and sampler fixed. All four models show a similar peak and subsequent decline in pass@10.

Figure 8: Distribution of condition-level success counts over supervised pretraining. For each checkpoint, we run pass@32 on each of 500 evaluation conditions and bin each condition by its number of successful rollouts within 32 trials. The stacked bands show the fraction of conditions in each success-count bin; each vertical slice sums to one. During late training, the fraction of conditions with zero successes increases, while the fraction with high success counts also increases.

Figure 14: Full MimicGen results across tasks and dataset sizes. Results for all five tasks with 200 and 500 demonstrations. Each row reports best-of-k validation loss, closed-loop pass@k, the full error-quantile profile, coverage–reliability checkpoint selection, and downstream residual RL finetuning.

Figure 13: Late-training held-out denoising loss increases more at lower diffusion noise levels and with sparser local conditioning support. Relative change in mean held-out ϵ-prediction MSE from epoch 200 to epoch 800, ∆rel,g(t) (Eq. D.6), for queries divided into equal thirds by local conditioning support. Negative values indicate lower mean loss at epoch 800; positive values indicate higher mean loss. At a fixed noise level, the relative loss change is generally larger for queries with sparser local conditioning support.

Figure 30: Qualitative world-model predictions on real-robot Push-T. The top row shows ground truth; the middle and bottom rows show predictions from world models trained on rollouts from the selected early and final policy checkpoints, respectively. Each model predicts four frames from two history frames (Chunk 1), then autoregressively predicts four more frames (Chunk 2). The earlyrollout model achieves higher PSNR in both chunks.

Figure 25: Longer EMA memory delays and smooths the pass@10 decline but does not fundamentally remove it. Holding βmax = 0.9999 fixed, increasing p from 0.75 to 0.9 gives the EMA a longer memory earlier in training, causing pass@10 to peak and decline later. Holding p = 0.9 fixed, increasing βmax from 0.9999 to 0.99995 allows the EMA memory to continue growing later in training and further smooths the decline. Pass@10 still decreases under all schedules.

Figure 22: Pass@k training dynamics are stable across sampling configurations. Pass@1 and pass@10 are evaluated using DDIM with different numbers of denoising steps and η, and using DDPM. All settings show the same late-training decline in pass@10.

Figure 27: Fresh denoisers reproduce the pass@10 decline with fixed encoder representations. New denoisers are trained from scratch with either the epoch-150 or epoch-800 encoder frozen throughout training. Both show a later decline in large k pass@k.

Figure 26: Freezing the encoder does not prevent the late-training large k pass@k decline. From epoch 150 onward, the encoder is fixed and only the denoiser is trained. Pass@10 still decreases at later epochs. The overall training dynamics is largely the same as baseline run.

Figure 29: Best-of-k off-manifold error reveals the same coverage–reliability tradeoff. At k = 1, ep800 has slightly lower off-manifold error; from k = 2 onward, ep400 is better and the gap grows with k.
Figure 17: Robustness to training horizon. Offline selection tracks the closed-loop oracle as H increases.

Figure 11: Later checkpoints exhibit higher held-out denoising loss near the low-noise end, and changes to the final denoising calls substantially affect pass@k profle. (a) On training demonstrations, ϵ-prediction MSE decreases with further training across all noise levels. (b) On unseen demonstrations, later checkpoints have higher denoising loss near the low-noise end than earlier checkpoints despite lower training loss. (c) In a 10-step DDIM sampler, replacing any one of the first four two-step bands (Q1–Q4) of the epoch-800 checkpoint with the corresponding epoch200 weights has little effect on pass@1 or pass@10. Replacing Q5, the final two calls, restores most of the epoch-200 checkpoint’s pass@10 advantage while reducing pass@1.

Figure 23: Learning-rate schedule ablation on Threading D2 Each panel overlays one ablated schedule (colored) with the default single-cosine schedule (gray). Solid and dashed curves denote pass@10 and pass@1, respectively. Across schedules, large-k pass@k peaks earlier and declines as pass@1 improves later in training; changing the learning-rate schedule primarily shifts the timing of these changes.
Figure 15: Full RoboCasa multitask pretraining results. Best-of-k validation loss, pass@k, error quantiles, coverage–reliability checkpoint selection, and downstream SFT.

papers.selection_reason: Robot policy pretraining, coverage-reliability dynamics, and checkpoint selection; directly relevant to robot learning.
papers.title: Beyond Validation Loss: Coverage and Reliability Dynamics in Robot Policy Pretraining
papers.tldr: Large-k closed-loop pass@k exposes robot-policy coverage and posttraining potential that validation loss and pass@1 can miss.

papers.abstract: Robot-use Agents (RUAs) have shown promising zero-shot manipulation capabilities, but reliance on frontier, proprietary models limits research into further training. To democratize RUA research, we introduce uni-robot-agent, a unified harness for competitive open-weight robot use that supports further training. Without privileged inputs, an out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, surpassing the published GPT-6 Astra-RoboProbe result of 28.97 and many VLA/WAM baselines, and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks. Our analysis across model generations, families, and sizes links effective robot use to four general capabilities, suggesting that future RUA training should develop them jointly.
bullets: Addresses the dependence on proprietary frontier models that limits further RUA training research.
Introduces a unified harness for training and evaluating open-weight robot-use agents.
An out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39 and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks.
Analysis across model generations, families, and sizes identifies four general capabilities linked to effective robot use.
The work suggests future RUA training should develop these capabilities jointly.

papers.abstract: Advances in monocular depth estimation (MDE) now let an attacker generate depth from publicly available RGB images and submit forged RGB-D queries. Such attacks break a core assumption of RGB-D place authentication: that depth comes from a sensor. We study a presentation attack detection (PAD) classifier that uses geometric consistency between the enrollment and query views, as a software-layer defense. A three-stage evaluation shows how far this classifier detects software-injected depth, depending on how accurately the attacker knows the camera intrinsics. In the first stage, the attacker has only an estimate of the intrinsics, and the PAD classifier separates forgeries generated by all three MDE models with a validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.997-0.999. In the second stage, the attacker obtains the exact intrinsics, and the original PAD classifier falls to near chance (AUC 0.54-0.61); a retrained PAD classifier, however, still has the registration residual between enrollment and query as a cue. In the third stage, an oracle evaluation, in which the evaluator fits warps using the ground-truth 3D geometry, shows that detection falls to near chance only in its strongest case, where every valid query keypoint is given its ground-truth 3D coordinate. Of the detection cues, the reprojection error captures the attacker's misestimate of the intrinsics, whereas the registration residual remains even when the attacker knows the exact intrinsics.
bullets: Generated depth from public RGB images violates the assumption that RGB-D authentication depth comes from a sensor.
With only estimated camera intrinsics, the classifier detects forgeries from all three evaluated MDE models with validation AUC of 0.997–0.999.
Knowing the exact intrinsics reduces the original detector to near-chance performance (AUC 0.54–0.61), while retraining preserves detection using registration residuals.
Reprojection error reflects intrinsic-parameter mismatch; registration residual remains informative even when intrinsics are known.
Under an oracle using ground-truth 3D geometry, detection becomes near chance only in the strongest attack case, where all valid query keypoints receive ground-truth 3D coordinates.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates attacks on depth estimation for place authentication, relevant to 3D geometry and security in embodied systems.
papers.title: Detecting Generated-Depth Injection Attacks on RGB-D Place Authentication
papers.tldr: Geometric-consistency PAD can detect generated-depth injection attacks, but its effectiveness depends strongly on the attacker’s knowledge of camera intrinsics and 3D geometry.

papers.abstract: Concerns about LLM homogeneity are typically quantified with embedding similarity, which reduces two texts to a single score. We revisit homogeneity with 25 interpretable metrics spanning five dimensions: semantic, lexical, syntactic, structural, and stylistic & presentational. A human study shows that perceived similarity depends on both content (what responses say) and form (how they say it), yet embedding similarity correlates less with human meaning judgments than sentence-level matching ($ρ=0.417$ vs. $0.606$) and not significantly with form judgments ($ρ=0.140$). Across 18 contemporary LLMs, models say similar things in different words: they share global semantics and broad linguistic profiles but remain distinct in lexical characteristics, structural patterns, and interactional conventions. Across releases from 2024 to 2026, models become more like themselves but not more like one another: among significantly changing metrics, intra-model distances decrease for 17 of 22, and inter-model distances increase for 14 of 21. Across two post-training pipelines, model-specific conventions emerge during SFT and are selectively reshaped by preference optimization. These results suggest that homogeneity is multidimensional and evolving, and that embedding similarity alone can overstate cross-model homogeneity while concealing diverging intra- and inter-model trends.
bullets: A 25-metric framework covers semantic, lexical, syntactic, structural, and stylistic/presentational similarity.

Human-perceived similarity reflects both response content and form; sentence-level matching aligns better with meaning judgments than embeddings, while embeddings do not significantly track form judgments.
Across 18 contemporary LLMs, responses share global semantics and broad linguistic profiles but differ in lexical, structural, and interactional characteristics.
From 2024–2026, models become more consistent with themselves without becoming more alike: intra-model distances generally shrink while inter-model distances often grow.
SFT introduces model-specific conventions, and preference optimization selectively reshapes them.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes LLM homogeneity using multidimensional metrics, contributing to the understanding of LLM behavior and architecture.
papers.title: Revisiting LLM Homogeneity Through a Multidimensional Lens
papers.tldr: LLM homogeneity is multidimensional: models share broad meaning but differ in wording, structure, style, and interaction conventions, which embedding similarity alone fails to capture.

papers.abstract: Interactive world generation requires both accurate local control and stable scene consistency over long rollouts. Existing methods improve local generation through camera or geometry conditioning and extend historical context with memory mechanisms. However, long-horizon exploration remains challenging due to incomplete target-view guidance and inconsistencies accumulated during scene updates. We present \textbf{GSExplorer}, a generation--reconstruction framework built around a persistent 3D Gaussian world state. At each step, the current 3DGS scene provides multimodal rendering conditions for a video generator, while camera geometry is injected through a separate Relative Ray Encoding branch. Generated videos are then fed back to a SLAM-based reconstruction backend, where appearance and geometric consistency checks produce a shared support mask for selective scene updates and cross-chunk pose refinement. We further design a data-construction pipeline that reproduces realistic 3DGS degradation during scene extrapolation, yielding 293K training pairs of degraded multimodal renderings and real target videos. GSExplorer achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods on both single-step and three-step WorldScore evaluation, including a Camera Control score of 99.07 in single-step extrapolation. On 481-frame leave-and-return rollouts, it also shows strong revisit consistency.
bullets: Addresses incomplete target-view guidance and accumulated inconsistencies during long-range scene exploration.
Conditions a video generator on multimodal renderings from the current 3DGS state plus camera geometry via Relative Ray Encoding.
Uses SLAM reconstruction with appearance and geometry checks for masked scene updates and cross-chunk pose refinement.
Trains on 293K pairs designed to mimic 3DGS degradation during scene extrapolation.
Reports best overall performance among compared methods on single- and three-step WorldScore evaluations, with strong 481-frame revisit consistency.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of GSExplorer. Starting from a 3DGS scene initialized from a single image, we render multimodal scene conditions along the planned camera trajectory at each step. These conditions, together with camera geometry and text prompts, guide the conditiondriven generator to produce a completed video. The generated video is then fed back to the SLAM-based world update, where content and geometric masks are combined into a support mask for selective scene updates. The support mask also filters correspondences for cross-chunk alignment, as indicated by the dashed arrow. The updated 3DGS world state then provides reliable conditions for the next step, forming a generation–reconstruction loop.

Figure 2. Architecture of the condition-driven video generator. Multimodal 3DGS renderings are encoded as scene conditions and injected into the diffusion backbone through one input projection and five residual projections. Camera intrinsics and poses define tokenwise ray geometry, which is incorporated through a separate RRE attention branch in every DiT block using geometry-aware Q/K/V and output transforms. Text prompts follow the original Wan cross-attention pathway.

Figure 3. Training-pair construction pipeline. First, long sequences are filtered and sampled into 57-frame clips containing 8 context frames and 49 target frames. Next, we reconstruct the full sequence with 3DGS-SLAM while forcing Gaussian insertion at the first target frame. Together, these steps improve target-view alignment while preserving the desired context-limited degradation. We then retain only Gaussians born within the context frames, recovering the desired context-limited degradation. Finally, the retained 3DGS is rendered at the target poses to produce multimodal degraded conditions paired with the real target frames.

Figure 4. Qualitative WorldScore results across one-, two-, and three-step extrapolation. P and C denote the text prompt and camera instruction. GSExplorer accurately follows both controls while maintaining high visual quality and coherent spatial structure.

Figure 8. Additional qualitative comparison of long-horizon revisit results. After extended leave-and-return exploration, GSExplorer better preserves the scene content and spatial layout of the initial view.
Figure 7. Additional qualitative results on WorldScore. GSExplorer follows the specified text and camera controls while maintaining coherent scene appearance and geometry during extrapolation.
Figure 5. Qualitative comparison of long-horizon revisit results. GSExplorer better preserves the content and details of the starting view after long-range exploration.

Figure 6. Cost across generation steps on WorldScore. Step time, peak GPU memory, and scene storage over three extrapolation steps for outdoor (top) and indoor (bottom) scenes. Each additional step increases runtime by only a few seconds and scene storage by a few hundred MiB, keeping incremental costs modest.

papers.title: GSExplorer: Interactive World Generation with a Persistent 3DGS World State
papers.tldr: GSExplorer enables consistent long-horizon interactive world generation by maintaining and selectively updating a persistent 3D Gaussian scene state.

papers.abstract: Motion language models (MoLMs) encode 3D human motion as discrete tokens for language-based understanding. Deploying them on monocular video raises two problems. Pose detection yields 2D joint sequences, leaving a dimensional gap from the 3D motion used in training. Moreover, the 2D observation changes with the camera viewpoint, while the depth lost in projection makes the 2D pose ambiguous across viewpoints. We propose MoPort, a view-aware 2D interface that enables MoLMs to take 2D observations as input. We introduce Paired View Alignment (PVA), which gives two views of the same motion a shared 3D teacher target and directly constrains the consistency of their latents, so that 2D observations from different viewpoints are mapped to a consistent semantic representation. Camera-Modulated Encoding (CME) estimates the camera extrinsics from the 2D sequence and uses them to modulate encoding, providing the 2D latents with geometric information about the viewpoint. MoPort achieves R@1 of 0.5674 on HumanML3D and 0.3286 on KIT-ML, outperforming all evaluated baselines. On HumanML3D, its R@1 decreases only from 0.5763 on in-distribution viewpoints to 0.5585 on out-of-distribution viewpoints. We validate portability on three downstream MoLMs. Furthermore, on the real-world RGB video dataset Fit3D, MoPort achieves 80.36\% accuracy. Code will be released upon acceptance.
bullets: Addresses the 2D–3D representation gap and viewpoint ambiguity when applying MoLMs to monocular video.
Uses Paired View Alignment to map different-view 2D observations of the same motion to consistent semantic latents.
Uses Camera-Modulated Encoding to estimate camera extrinsics and incorporate viewpoint geometry during encoding.
Reports R@1 of 0.5674 on HumanML3D and 0.3286 on KIT-ML, outperforming evaluated baselines.
Shows robustness across viewpoints, portability to three downstream MoLMs, and 80.36% accuracy on Fit3D.

figures.caption: Figure 2. MoPort framework. (a) A shared MoPort encodes different 2D projections of one 3D motion and aligns them with latent and token targets from a pretrained 3D encoder. The view loss pulls the two latents together, and sampled cameras supervise the camera head. (b) The camera head estimates the extrinsics as a, and Gram-Schmidt gives R̂, which rotates the rays into the 3D reference frame. An MLP maps the standardized R6D representation c of R̂ to multi-scale FiLM parameters. (c) At inference, YOLOv8x [11] and ViTPose-H [37] extract 2D tracks, which MoPort maps to the native tokens of a pretrained MoLM. Dashed arrows indicate training supervision.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes MoPort, a view-aware interface for Motion Language Models to handle 2D observations of 3D motion, addressing spatial understanding and geometric consistency.
papers.title: MoPort: A View-Aware 2D Interface for Motion Language Models
papers.tldr: MoPort lets motion language models interpret monocular 2D pose sequences by aligning views and encoding camera geometry, achieving strong cross-view motion-text retrieval and real-video recognition.

papers.abstract: Registering intraoperative Ultrasound (US) bone-surface point clouds to preoperative Computed Tomography (CT) models can support radiation-free orthopedic navigation. Differences in imaging physics produce distinct surface sampling patterns, complicating cross-modal feature matching. Bone strongly reflects ultrasound and casts an acoustic shadow, so US captures only the probe-facing bone surface and leaves most CT points unmatched. This partial coverage makes correspondences ambiguous on near-symmetric bones. We propose CUFormer, a modality-aware registration framework. We introduce a Modality-Aware Transformer (MAT) that encodes input modality through identity embeddings and updates features through modality-specific adapters within a shared geometric matcher. We model imaging visibility and use predicted reference-side visibility to weight coarse and fine correspondences. CUFormer achieves the lowest mean registration errors among evaluated methods on two CT-US datasets, UltraBones100k and UltraBonesHip, and the CT-RGB-D dataset SpineDepth. On UltraBones100k, it reaches mean rotation error 4.53$^\circ$, translation error 3.19\,mm, and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) 2.54\,mm, reducing RMSE by 65.8\% relative to the best-performing baseline by this metric. These results demonstrate CUFormer's effectiveness in aligning partial bone surfaces with preoperative CT across anatomical sites.
bullets: Addresses mismatched CT and ultrasound surface sampling, including partial US coverage and ambiguous correspondences on near-symmetric bones.
Uses a Modality-Aware Transformer with identity embeddings and modality-specific adapters in a shared geometric matcher.
Predicts reference-side visibility to weight both coarse and fine point correspondences.
Achieves the lowest mean registration errors among evaluated methods across UltraBones100k, UltraBonesHip, and SpineDepth.
On UltraBones100k, reports 4.53° rotation error, 3.19 mm translation error, and 2.54 mm RMSE; RMSE is 65.8% lower than the strongest baseline by that metric.

papers.title: CUFormer: Modality-Aware CT-Ultrasound Point Cloud Registration for Orthopedic Navigation
papers.tldr: CUFormer improves CT–ultrasound bone point-cloud registration for radiation-free orthopedic navigation by modeling modality differences and visibility.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting sorts every splat by depth in every frame. Viewers that draw splats with the hardware rasterizer and sort them on the CPU, as most web and mobile viewers do, spend most of the frame time in this sort. We present AbacusGS, which stores the blending order of a 3DGS scene in the scene layout. AbacusGS groups the splats into octree boxes of at most 128 splats and stores each box in order along an axis chosen at write time. In each frame, AbacusGS sorts only the visible boxes, and one dot product per box decides whether the box is read forward or backward. A short order-aware fine-tuning converts an existing 3DGS model, and the over operator of 3DGS stays unchanged. On 13 standard scenes, AbacusGS loses 0.13 dB PSNR on average against an equally fine-tuned 3DGS model. In an OpenGL viewer that orders splats on the CPU, AbacusGS renders frames 4.5 times faster than per-splat sorting. We also present a compact format of 17 bytes per splat and a CUDA tile renderer that use the same order. The code will be released.
bullets: Targets CPU-based per-splat sorting, a major bottleneck in web and mobile viewers.
Groups splats into octree boxes of up to 128 and sorts only visible boxes; one dot product selects each box’s traversal direction.
Uses short order-aware fine-tuning while keeping 3DGS’s blending operator unchanged.
Across 13 standard scenes, loses 0.13 dB PSNR on average versus equally fine-tuned 3DGS and renders 4.5× faster in an OpenGL CPU-sorting viewer.
Also provides a 17-byte-per-splat format and a CUDA tile renderer using the same ordering scheme.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces AbacusGS, an efficient rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that avoids per-splat sorting, improving the efficiency of 3D foundation models.
papers.title: AbacusGS: Gaussian Splatting without Per-Splat Sorting
papers.tldr: AbacusGS accelerates Gaussian Splatting by storing approximate blending order in the scene, avoiding expensive per-splat depth sorting with only a small image-quality loss.

papers.abstract: Homogeneous gradient functions have widespread significance, including applications in maximum energy subspace selection and retrieval problems. Euler's homogeneous function theorem specifies how the potential associated with a positively k-homogeneous gradient field can be recovered directly from the field itself. We use Euler's theorem to build on GradNets and propose a homogeneous gradient network architecture that is guaranteed to correspond to the gradient of a homogeneous function. Then, we describe how monotone homogeneous GradNets universally approximate the gradients of k-homogeneous convex functions. The inductive bias of homogeneous GradNets enables them to outperform baseline ICNNs by up to 7dB in our max energy subspace projection experiment and by up to 13% higher accuracy, 98% fewer parameters, and 70% fewer FLOPS in our amortized inner product search experiment.
bullets: Addresses learning gradient fields with positive homogeneity, relevant to energy-based subspace selection and retrieval.
Uses Euler’s homogeneous function theorem to construct GradNets guaranteed to be gradients of homogeneous functions.
Shows monotone homogeneous GradNets universally approximate gradients of k-homogeneous convex functions.
Outperforms baseline ICNNs in max-energy subspace projection and amortized inner-product search experiments, with reported gains in quality and efficiency.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a homogeneous gradient network architecture (GradNets) with theoretical guarantees, contributing to the understanding of network architectures and optimization efficiency relevant to LLMs.
papers.title: Learning Gradients of Homogeneous Functions
papers.tldr: A homogeneous gradient network architecture learns gradients of homogeneous functions while guaranteeing valid gradient structure and enabling efficient applications.

papers.abstract: Representation steering methods like difference-in-means (DIM) offer a lightweight approach to controlling LLM behavior, but their effectiveness varies widely across concepts, datasets, and layers, making principled deployment costly without exhaustive hyperparameter sweeps. We build on the discriminability index $d'$, a compute-cheap geometric measure of how well contrastive training activations separate along the steering direction. Across five behaviors on 3 models, we demonstrate uses beyond its established role as a dataset-level steerability predictor. First, in the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) setting, we show that $d'$ reliably identifies performant layers at which to steer, eliminating the need for a layer-wise sweep. Second, we extend this analysis to open-ended multi-token generation, and find that $d'$ remains successful for layer selection across different settings. Lastly, we test whether the position of a generated token's representation on the DIM line predicts steering success on that individual example. In the MCQA setting, this works for high-$d'$ datasets but is inconsistent across behaviors, models, and training-token choices in open-ended generation. This highlights that methods developed and conclusions drawn in single-token MCQA settings do not necessarily transfer to open-ended generation.
bullets: The study uses the discriminability index, d′, to measure how well contrastive activations separate along a steering direction.
Across five behaviors and three models, d′ identifies effective steering layers in MCQA without exhaustive layer-wise sweeps.
d′ also supports layer selection for open-ended multi-token generation across multiple settings.
A token’s position on the DIM line predicts individual-example steering success for high-d′ MCQA datasets, but is inconsistent in open-ended generation.
Results caution against assuming that single-token MCQA findings generalize directly to open-ended generation.

papers.selection_reason: Uses activation-steering geometry to reduce hyperparameter search and select layers in LLMs, directly relevant to language foundation model control.
papers.title: Sweep Less, Steer More: Using Activation Steering Geometry for Reduced Hyperparameter Search
papers.tldr: Activation-separation geometry can reduce layer-search costs for activation steering, but example-level predictions transfer inconsistently from MCQA to open-ended generation.

papers.abstract: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time by adding a vector to their internal representations. Most work asks how to build that vector, and far less attention has gone to where to add it, even though steering at a poorly chosen layer can be worse than not steering at all. Prior selectors choose a layer without ever steering the model to test it: they score how separable the target behavior is at that layer, and how consistently the individual examples point along the steering direction. We argue that what matters is not the separability of the two activation clouds, nor the alignment of individual displacements with their mean, but the extent of the cloud of per-example displacements that mean-difference steering averages. We propose a topology-based layer selection method, called TopoSteer, which scores a layer by the total H_0 persistence of its displacement cloud, computed as the length of the cloud's Euclidean minimum spanning tree. We show that the score focuses on the displacement cloud's relative geometry, while class separation affects it only through standardization. We also provide a theoretical explanation for our method by proving that, as example-level variation increases, TopoSteer and discriminability move in opposite directions, so the two criteria can rank layers in opposite ways. Across multiple language models and steering tasks, TopoSteer provides a principled alternative to discriminability- and separability-based layer selection and yields more effective steering without requiring held-out validation.
bullets: Layer choice is crucial: steering at a poor layer can underperform doing nothing.
It replaces separability and displacement-alignment criteria with total H₀ persistence—the Euclidean minimum spanning tree length of the displacement cloud.
The method captures relative displacement geometry, with class separation affecting the score only through standardization.
Theory shows that increasing example-level variation can make TopoSteer and discriminability rank layers oppositely.
Across multiple language models and steering tasks, TopoSteer yields more effective steering without held-out validation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Layer choice decides the outcome, and LayerNavigator and TOPOSTEER choose differently. With large variation, the two classes overlap, so discriminability D drops, while the displacements keep a common direction but vary widely in length. papers.selection_reason: Topological layer selection for activation steering in LLMs is directly relevant to controlling and understanding large language foundation models.
papers.title: TopoSteer: Topological Layer Selection for Activation Steering in LLMs
papers.tldr: TopoSteer selects activation-steering layers by measuring the topological spread of per-example displacement vectors, improving steering without held-out validation.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing plays a crucial role in everyday human interaction. Consider inserting a plug into a tight socket, vision alone provides limited guidance during the final insertion stage, and we instead rely on both anticipated contact and realized tactile feedback to ajust the insertion motion. The same capability is equally important for robots, particularly in dexterous manipulation tasks. Yet many contemporary robot policies remain vision-dominant. This visual bias, compounded by limited tactile data and sparse contact events, can cause directly incorporated tactile signals to be ignored or even compromise the policy's pretrained capabilities, yielding degrading performance as observed in our experiments. We present $TF^2$-Steering, which refines actions via learned residual steering of the flow-matching action expert's velocity field, using a tactile mixture-of-experts architecture to integrate both tactile forecasts and real-time tactile feedback. Together with specific designed three stages training recipe, $TF^2$-Steering enables tactile signals to correct and, when necessary, redirect the flow-matching action-generation process, while building on the strong action-generation capacity of the vision-based foundation policy. Extensive experiments across six simulated and six real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of $TF^2$-Steering. It outperforms the strongest evaluated baselines by 10.7 percentage points in average simulation success rate and 9.1 percentage points in average real-world progress success rate. Project page: https://yiming-cc.github.io/tf2-steering/.
bullets: Addresses the tendency of vision-dominant policies to ignore or weaken performance when directly given sparse tactile signals.
Learns residual corrections to a flow-matching action expert’s velocity field.
Uses a tactile mixture-of-experts architecture to combine tactile forecasts with realized feedback.
A three-stage training recipe lets tactile input correct or redirect the pretrained vision policy’s actions.
Evaluated on six simulated and six real-world tasks, improving average success by 10.7 and 9.1 percentage points, respectively, over the strongest baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Tactile-forecast and feedback action refinement for dexterous robot manipulation directly fits embodied robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: $TF^2$-Steering: Action Refinement with Tactile Forecasts and Feedback via Velocity-Field Steering

papers.abstract: Causal masking obstructs the column balancing used by optimal-transport (OT) attention. We study an unbalanced OT operator that uses only current and earlier rows and characterize its induced positional prior. For bounded scores and any fixed balancing strength below one, its fixed point assigns vanishing mass to every fixed window as context grows. With constant scores, the prior has an exact scale-invariant form. We classify positional encodings by whether they prevent this dilution. We also derive finite-length window-mass bounds for log-distance priors with exponents near one. Preregistered experiments use 25M- and 100M-parameter language models. The OT operator improves loss extrapolation over softmax, while exploratory comparisons favor an explicit distance bias at a fraction of the cost. Changing only the bias beyond the training length moves long-context loss in the predicted direction on all 30 tested checkpoints. During training, learned exponents approach one even when constrained above it. A margin chosen from prior calculations controls distant-mass growth in the tested setting.
bullets: Causal masking prevents standard OT column balancing, motivating an unbalanced OT operator over current and earlier rows.
For bounded scores and fixed balancing strength below one, mass in any fixed-size window vanishes as context length grows; constant scores yield an exact scale-invariant prior.
The work classifies positional encodings by whether they prevent this dilution and derives finite-length bounds for log-distance priors with exponents near one.
Experiments with 25M- and 100M-parameter language models show improved loss extrapolation over softmax, while explicit distance bias performs favorably at a fraction of the cost.
Modifying only the bias beyond the training length shifts long-context loss as predicted across 30 checkpoints; learned exponents approach one in training.

papers.selection_reason: Studies causal optimal-transport attention, positional priors, and length extrapolation for language models, directly relevant to long-context LLM research.
papers.title: Causal Optimal-Transport Attention: Positional Priors and Length Extrapolation
papers.tldr: Causal OT attention develops a scale-invariant positional prior that can dilute local attention over long contexts, but suitable distance-based biases can improve length extrapolation at lower cost.

papers.abstract: We present See, Think, Use, a protocol that traces each answer of a vision-language model to perception, reasoning or the use of perception. The diagnosis shows a developer which stage to improve and directs test-time compute to the stage that fails. Benchmarks score the final answer, and an answer that rests on the image earns the same credit as a guess or a memorized prior. The protocol asks the model two extra questions per item and needs no access to its weights. A localization probe asks for a box around every instance and measures seeing, and a text-replacement probe answers from a description and measures thinking. Use is the rate at which the answer follows the model's own perception across counterfactual image pairs. The rate needs no answer labels, because the question and its prior are the same on both images. On two model families and six datasets the protocol shows that the knob that helps follows the task family. Answers follow the model's perception except on images that contradict a common prior, and asking the model to localize first repairs this failure when its boxes are right. Allocating compute by the measured stages comes close to the best uniform policy at lower cost and beats a random allocation of the same compute wherever a knob raises the short stage. We will release the code, the prompts and the per-question outputs.
bullets: The protocol separates failures into seeing, thinking, and using visual evidence.
It uses localization and text-replacement probes, plus counterfactual image pairs, without model-weight access or answer labels for the use measure.
Across two model families and six datasets, the most effective intervention depends on the task family.
Models often follow their perception except when images conflict with common priors; localization-first prompting can repair this when localization is correct.
Stage-based compute allocation approaches the best uniform policy at lower cost and outperforms random allocation when a targeted intervention helps.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses perception and reasoning failures in vision-language models and allocates test-time compute, directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: See, Think, Use: Diagnosing Perception and Reasoning Failures in VLMs
papers.tldr: See, Think, Use diagnoses whether VLM errors arise from perception, reasoning, or failure to use perception, enabling targeted test-time computation.

papers.abstract: Resource managers typically encode what to do in a task-specific policy---a heuristic, an optimization procedure, or a model trained for the task---that must be developed before use and may need revision as the workload or system changes. We propose bypassing policy development and instead asking pretrained models to make resource-management decisions directly, given the current system state, desired outcome, and available choices. We evaluate this approach on microservice autoscaling, DRAM sizing, and video encoding, using a frontier LLM and two small decision models. On two microservice applications, a small decision model meets latency targets while using within 10% of the replicas allocated by policy-based autoscalers and within 13% of the frontier LLM. In DRAM sizing, a small decision model reduces DRAM usage by up to 27.5% relative to static provisioning while maintaining at least 95% of baseline performance. In video encoding, it completes encodes up to 4.3$\times$ faster than the frontier LLM, with an imperceptible 1.1-point decrease in Video Multi-Method Assessment Fusion (VMAF), a metric of perceptual video quality. Making individual resource-management decisions may be considerably simpler than developing a general strategy for making them.
bullets: Targets changing workloads and systems where hand-designed or trained policies require development and revision.
Provides models with the current system state, desired outcome, and available choices to select resource-management actions.
Evaluates the approach on microservice autoscaling, DRAM sizing, and video encoding using a frontier LLM and two small decision models.

Small decision models meet stated performance goals with competitive resource use, reduce DRAM usage by up to 27.5% while retaining at least 95% of baseline performance, and encode video up to 4.3× faster than the frontier LLM.
Scope is demonstrated across three resource-management tasks; the abstract does not establish that direct model invocation universally replaces specialized policies.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Architecture common to the DIMWIT autoscalers. At each tick, the autoscaler reads per-service utilization via the Kubernetes Metrics API and patches the service’s HPA object with the desired replica count R, causing HPA to adjust the service’s Deployment.

Figure 3. Per-endpoint median p95 latency when horizontally scaling replicas using HPA, Erlang, Agar, Claude Opus 5.5 (low and high reasoning effort), Laya, and Jev on CloudLab. Jev-Single sends a separate request per service every 15 s, while Jev-Batched sends one batched request for all services every 15 s. The horizontal dashed line marks the 300 ms SLO. For each application, the boundary boxes show average running replicas, except for Jev-Single on Social Network and TeaStore and Laya on TeaStore, where they show requested replicas; excess pods remain Pending due to cluster capacity limits.

Figure 4. DRAM usage and performance achieved with TierSizer, Laya, Opus 5.5 (low and high reasoning effort), and Jev, normalized to static 2:1 DRAM provisioning. Bars show average DRAM usage and performance, while black markers indicate minimum DRAM usage (peak savings). The dashed red line marks the 95% performance target.

Figure 5. Video quality (mean VMAF) versus encoding time across video clips, with encoding parameters updated every 5 seconds. Laya achieves the lowest encoding time on all videos while maintaining quality close to FFmpeg medium. A difference of 6 VMAF points is commonly considered barely perceptible to human viewers (Ozer, 2017). Smaller differences are generally imperceptible.

Figure 2. Example frame from Elephants Dream (Blender Foundation, 2006), shown uncompressed (left) and encoded at the same bitrate using two different x264 encoder configurations (center and right). The encoded versions achieve VMAF scores of 94.59 and 38.51, respectively, illustrating how encoder settings affect video quality.

Figure 6. Impact of decision interval, the time between encoding parameter updates, on encoding time and video quality for the three videos described in Table 4. Lower encoding time and higher VMAF are better.
Table 3. DRAM sizing workload characteristics. Resident set size (RSS) is in GiB.
Table 2. Past observations in each model’s state. Opus 5.5 also sees its own past reasoning for those decisions.
Table 1. x264 encoding parameters available to the LLMs, their allowed values, and the defaults under the medium preset.
Table 4. Videos used in our encoding experiments and their motion characteristics. All source videos are 720p at 24 fps, obtained from Xiph.org (Xiph.Org Foundation).

papers.selection_reason: Proposes DIMWIT, a method for using LLMs directly for resource management tasks (autoscaling, encoding) without task-specific tuning. Relevant to Large Language Models.
papers.title: DIMWIT: Directly Invoking Models Without Intensive Tuning
papers.tldr: DIMWIT uses pretrained models to make resource-management decisions directly, avoiding task-specific policy development and tuning.

papers.abstract: Assigning GWAS variants to causal genes requires evidence from multiple resources. We present V2G, an agentic pipeline that records evidence retrieval and returns ranked genes alongside the retrieved evidence. We evaluate whether language-model reranking improves gene prioritisation and whether its gains depend on the retrieved evidence or recall of known associations. On 135 held-out loci where candidate retrieval succeeded and Open Targets L2G predicts, reranking by a language model improves Precision@1 over the evidence ordering it receives, 0.793 against 0.711 (+0.081, 95% CI +0.038 to +0.129), and over nearest-gene assignment (+0.178); no difference from Open Targets L2G or from training-membership baselines was detected. Given only the trait and the candidate gene symbols, in shuffled order, the same model scores 0.864 on these loci (three seeds, 0.859 - 0.867) and names the reference gene at 0.594 of the loci where the pipeline never retrieved it; with each gene's symbol moved to another gene's evidence row it follows the top-scored row and scores 0.284. The gain over the evidence ordering is recall of known genes, and the evidence as presented anchors the model to the ordering rather than informing it. Across the 296 held-out loci (five seeds each) the model keeps the given top candidate at 86% of decisions; at naturally retrieved loci its departures select a reference gene in 85% of departure decisions (31 of 37 loci), and none displaced one. Its calls carry trait-matched mouse mutant or Mendelian phenotype annotations more often than other candidates at the same locus. Train-test overlap is reported throughout. The study includes a frozen benchmark, cached predictions and reproduction code.
bullets: Evaluated on held-out GWAS loci with retrieved candidate genes and Open Targets L2G predictions.
Language-model reranking improved Precision@1 over the supplied evidence ordering (0.793 vs 0.711), but not over Open Targets L2G or training-membership baselines.
With only trait and gene symbols, the model often identified reference genes, indicating gains depended on known-gene recall.
Swapping gene symbols across evidence rows caused the model to follow the top-scored row, showing sensitivity to presentation order.
At naturally retrieved loci, departures from the top candidate selected a reference gene in 31 of 37 cases; train-test overlap was reported.

figures.caption: Figure 1: An agentic variant-to-gene pipeline and a locus where the evidence ordering is incorrect. a, Pipeline stages. Each is a separate, recorded tool call: the genome build is inferred from the coordinates and GRCh37 input lifted to GRCh38; linkage disequilibrium is computed from local 1000 Genomes panels across five ancestry groups; loci are fine-mapped to credible sets by approximate Bayes factor or SuSiE; per-candidate evidence is retrieved gene by gene; and a language model reasons over the assembled evidence and returns a ranked list citing what it used, so any call can be traced to the measurements behind it. b, The evidence retrieved at 2:21155063 A>G, associated with LDL cholesterol (study GCST90002412, a held-out test locus). Score is the composite evidence score that determines the order in which candidates are presented; Dist is the distance from the lead variant to the gene’s transcription start site; eQTL is the number of GTEx v8 tissues with a significant eQTL; PP.H4 is the posterior probability of colocalization; OT L2G is the Open Targets locus-to-gene score. The curated gold gene, APOB, is shaded. All four candidates colocalize at PP.H4 ≥ 0.99; therefore, colocalization cannot discriminate between them, and Open Targets returns no L2G prediction at this locus. c, Ranking before and after the reasoning step. The composite score ranks TDRD15 first on proximity (31 kb, against 111 kb for APOB); the model promotes APOB in all five seeds, with rationales that cite its role in LDL particles (prior knowledge rather than a retrieved measurement). With the open-weights backbone (Qwen3-32B) the ordering is left unchanged in all five seeds. The values shown are the stored benchmark evidence, reproduced in Supplementary Table 7. Of these, the evaluated prompt showed the score and the eQTL and colocalisation flags; the distance, tissue count, PP.H4 and L2G columns were not shown (Methods).

Figure 4: The deployed implementation and what a user receives. The figure describes the application; the benchmark runs evaluated in this study used a narrower prompt (Methods, Reasoning, and output); therefore, panel a is not a description of the evaluated configuration. a, Deployment boundary. The application is distributed as a container image and runs inside the user’s own institution. The summary statistics are read inside the container and never leave it. Build inference, linkage disequilibrium, fine-mapping, expression-QTL retrieval, colocalization, Mendelian randomization, and reporting execute against local reference data. Annotation, the Open Targets, gnomAD, and GTEx lookups, and drug-target scoring send variant coordinates and alleles or gene symbols to public services, and the GWAS Catalog browser sends trait and study identifiers; the optional reasoning step sends the candidate genes, locus record, and assembled per-gene evidence to a language-model endpoint with a key the user supplies, and each such request is logged before it is sent as host, model, message count, and payload size, with no key and no prompt text. b, The audit trail behind a single call, shown for the locus of Fig. 1. The called gene is the consensus prediction of five GPT-5.2 runs; each row is that gene’s value in the released benchmark record, and the rationale is the text stored for it in the first run, quoted verbatim. The evaluated prompt held only the composite score and the eQTL and colocalisation flags for this gene (Supplementary Note 7); the panel marks which rows were shown. The rationale’s ‘lipid eQTL’ is an inference from the trait name, not a retrieved tissue: no tissue was supplied. A field the record does not hold is printed as not recorded rather than inferred: the fine-mapping method is not stored per locus, no coding consequence was flagged for this gene (which does not by itself show the variant is non-coding), and Open Targets returned no prediction. The colocalization value is computed from incomplete regional inputs (Methods). This schematic of the interface is generated from the recorded benchmark data.

Figure 2: The pipeline’s contribution is a rare, high-precision intervention rather than a uniformly better ranking. a, Frequency of each backbone departing from the order in which candidates were presented over 1,480 locus–seed decisions per backbone (296 held-out loci × 5 seeds). GPT-5.2 departed at 212 decisions (14.3%); Qwen3-32B departed once (0.1%), and its Precision@1 was consequently identical to the composite evidence ordering in every seed (0.395 in both cases, all five seeds; at that one locus, neither the initial nor the promoted gene was the reference gene). Bars represent counts over decisions, not loci; the 212 GPT-5.2 departures occur at 60 loci. b, Outcome of the 142 departures (37 loci) made by GPT-5.2 on loci whose reference gene was retrieved naturally, that is, excluding loci where the reference gene had to be added to the candidate set. A total of 120 promoted a reference gene (85%; 31 loci), and 22 did not (7 loci; one locus appeared in both counts because its seeds were split between the two outcomes). *Harmful count departures that displaced a candidate that was already a reference gene; its denominator was all 212 departures, including those on force-added loci, and none occurred. c, Paired outcomes against each comparator on the primary split (135 natural loci at which Open Targets also returned a prediction). The bars show discordant loci only (those where exactly one of the two methods is correct), because concordant loci carry no information in a paired test. The nearest gene was determined by the GENCODE TSS distance. P values are two-sided exact McNemar tests on discordant counts, unadjusted. The full results across all splits are presented in Supplementary Table 1.

Figure 3: The pipeline’s calls and curated reference genes carry trait-matched phenotype annotation more often than other candidates at the locus. Support is assessed against mouse mutant phenotypes (MGI, all allele classes) and human Mendelian disease phenotypes (HPO), with trait and phenotype terms mapped to 18 organ-system categories by versioned rules. These annotations are not GWAS associations but are not independent of the literature either (Results). Predictions are the consensus GPT-5.2 gene per locus. A gene is supported at a locus when any of its phenotype categories meets any of the trait’s. a, Support by arm, shown as supported/annotated loci out of 295 eligible loci, with 95% bootstrap intervals over loci; the random-candidate arm is the expected support of one uniformly drawn other candidate, so its count is fractional. Because mouse mutants are pleiotropic (an annotated gene carries a mean of 6.8 of the 18 categories), absolute rates are not interpretable on their own, and only within-locus differences are. b, Within-locus paired contrasts. Bars are the difference in support between the two arms at the same locus, with 95% intervals from a bootstrap over clusters of loci sharing a reference gene; n is the number of loci where both arms have an annotated gene. q values are Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted across the 11 contrasts for this source (exact McNemar or sign-flip permutation tests); solid fill marks q < 0.05 and hatched fill q ≥ 0.05. All contrasts, by source, are in Supplementary Table 5. Seed 20261017.

Table 1: Precision@1 by method and split. Force-added loci (reference gene added to the candidate set by the benchmark and so buried by construction) are reported separately from natural loci, with the pooled result alongside. The primary analysis is the natural loci where Open Targets also returns a prediction; it is conditional on candidate retrieval and Open Targets coverage. The lower two rows are diagnostics, not comparators: both reach 1.000 on force-added loci, which is the artifact those loci create rather than a result. Open Targets is scored with uncovered loci as failures; the other estimands are in Table 2. Every rate is rounded once from its count; the full grid with counts and Wilson intervals is Supplementary Table 1.

Table 2: Open Targets coverage under each estimand. Accuracy where Open Targets predicts (split by whether the credible set comes from the locus’s own study), accuracy with abstentions scored as failures, and, as a combined method rather than Open Targets alone, accuracy when the first stored candidate is credited where it abstains. Quoting the first alone flatters a method permitted to decline, while quoting the second alone penalizes abstention.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLM reranking for gene prioritization in a bioinformatics pipeline. A standard application of LLMs, relevant to Large Language Models.
papers.title: An auditable agentic pipeline for variant-to-gene prioritisation, validated against orthogonal functional evidence
papers.tldr: V2G is an auditable variant-to-gene pipeline, but its language-model reranking gains mainly reflect recall of known associations and evidence-row ordering rather than independent use of biological evidence.

papers.abstract: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of exploiting instructional videos when model parameters are frozen and large-scale updates are costly.
Builds a tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that generates hard, video-grounded questions to refine stored knowledge.
Uses a Table-of-Contents tree for reasoning-guided retrieval instead of embedding similarity alone.
Evaluated on VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark from 72 chess tutorials across 12 openings, with performance improving as more videos are consumed.
Also improves opening-phase gameplay and shows generality in a second domain.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL). In Stage I, TAL performs video-grounded agent– model adversarial consolidation, where a video agent harvests hard question–answer pairs from instructional videos that are supported by tutorial evidence yet unsolved by the frozen model, forming a question bank. In Stage II, TAL performs question–memory adversarial consolidation, using this question bank to iteratively refine tutorial memory through a read–write loop. At inference time, TAL retrieves relevant tutorial units via a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, enabling the frozen model to access structured tutorial knowledge for downstream reasoning without parameter updates.
Figure 1: Overview of learning paradigms for LLM agents, comparing parametric and non-parametric approaches along the dimensions of stored knowledge, inference-time usage, and update mechanism.
Figure 5: Comparison of learning curves on the held-out test set.
Figure 3: Scaling behavior of TAL vs. vanilla (GPT-5.2) on training (left) and test (right) splits.
Figure 4: Interactive user interface used for human evaluation.

Table 1: Comparison of baseline methods and TAL on the training and test sets under varying numbers of demonstration videos. Best results are in bold. TAL consistently outperforms all baselines across all settings, showing a clear scaling trend as more tutorial demonstrations become available.
Table 2: Comparison with stronger retrieval and memory baselines. Best results are in bold.
Table 3: Second-domain evaluation on Adobe Photoshop 2026 software tutorials. Best results are in bold.
Table 8: Impact of retrieval depth.
Table 4: Head-to-head TAL vs. vanilla results under fixed openings.
Table 5: Two-stage consolidation ablation.

Table 7: Vision-in-construction ablation on 110 held-out questions. Full TAL uses event-aligned frames and transcripts, while transcript-only TAL removes all visual inputs. Results are mean±standard deviation over three seeds; best results are in bold.
Table 9: The 12 classical openings covered in VidLearn.

Table 10: Nearest-neighbor overlap between each of the 110 test questions and the 174 training questions (left) / 2,564 training subtitle chunks (right). Lower values indicate weaker train–test similarity. No test question has a near-duplicate match (≥ 0.8) under any metric or pool, ruling out trivial lexical leakage.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric method for LLM agents to learn from instructional videos. This is a form of video imitation learning for agents, fitting Learning from Human Videos.
papers.title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?
papers.tldr: TAL enables LLM agents to continually learn from tutorial videos without parameter updates by building and reasoning over a structured, persistent tutorial memory.

papers.abstract: Localized false-merge correction in connectomics requires converting an identified error into an executable native 3D partition. Still, neither intermediate correction predictions nor seeded graph solvers alone determine which native source-sink constraints should define that partition. We formulate this problem as a 3D-native partition-aware contact selection problem: selecting candidate contacts based on the complete partitions they induce. Our solution comprises two components: ContactCut (CC)-Auto, which uses learned single-contact selection, and ContactCut (CC)-Search, which enables bounded paired-contact search, generates compact alternatives, and applies learned panel ranking. On historical two-way false-merge corrections from MICrONS and FlyWire, CC-Auto improves failure-aware 3D partition (FA-3D Part.) mIoU by 5.9 and 3.4 points over the strongest graph-based controls and by 12.5 and 10.0 points over the best learned baselines. A MICrONS-trained ranker transfers to FlyWire with negligible degradation. CC-Search expands oracle reachability and prioritizes near-oracle alternatives. The code is available at https://github.com/bentake/ContactCut.
bullets: Targets the gap between detecting a false merge and defining executable source–sink constraints for a native 3D partition.
CC-Auto learns to select individual contacts; CC-Search performs bounded paired-contact search and ranks compact alternatives.
On MICrONS and FlyWire corrections, CC-Auto improves FA-3D Part. mIoU over graph-based controls and learned baselines.
A ranker trained on MICrONS transfers to FlyWire with negligible degradation.
CC-Search increases oracle reachability and prioritizes alternatives close to oracle solutions.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Supervoxel contacts and candidate selection. (a) Supervoxels correspond to graph nodes. The voxel faces shared by two supervoxels form a contact, represented by a graph edge. (b) Candidate contacts have centroids within 500 nm of the localized error cue x0 (red). Shown candidate centroids are green. The crossed marker denotes an excluded contact.
Fig. 2. Qualitative 3D-native correction results. Predictions are shown against the historical reference.

Fig. 3. Effect of contact selection. The red marker in (a) is the localized cue x0. This example shows how nearby contacts induce different partitions under the same graph-cut setup. e2 is selected by CC-Auto.

Table 1. 3D-native automatic false-merge correction. Coverage and FA-3D Part. mIoU use the eligible TEST cohort. Eligibility requires a valid native two-way historical reference. The remaining metrics use the intersection of scorer-valid outputs across all applicable displayed methods. M→FW denotes zero-shot transfer. Best/second-best are bold/underlined.
Table 2. Contact-selection ablation and bounded search. 3D Part. mIoU on contact-valid TEST operations; † denotes reference-best reachable or best-in-panel quality.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces ContactCut, a learned framework for 3D false-merge correction in connectomics. It uses learned selection and ranking for 3D partitioning, fitting 3D Foundation Models.
papers.title: ContactCut: A Partition-Aware Contact Selection Framework for False-Merge Correction in Connectomics
papers.tldr: ContactCut selects native 3D contacts for correcting false merges in connectomics, improving partition quality and supporting transferable, near-oracle alternatives.

papers.abstract: Cryptographically secure inference faces two practical challenges: making secure programming accessible to AI developers and data scientists, and achieving efficient execution across deployment environments. Developers must compose cryptographic primitives correctly, while performance depends on hardware, networks, and evolving ciphertext states. We present CipherFlow, a compiler framework that takes a high-level AI computation graph, available cryptographic primitives, and a target hardware and network configuration to generate an executable, latency-optimized secure inference program. CipherFlow automates cryptographic execution decisions through three techniques: MicroBench profiles deployment-specific primitive costs; state-expanded planning jointly optimizes homomorphic encryption (HE) and secure multi-party computation (MPC) placement, conversions, and ciphertext maintenance under cryptographic-state constraints; and BlockFold summarizes branched regions to scale planning to Transformer graphs. Evaluation using measured HE/MPC backend costs across CPU/GPU and network settings shows up to 16.5$\times$ speedup on BERT-base and over 22$\times$ on ViT compared with static hybrid placement baselines. CipherFlow separates model programming from cryptographic execution decisions, enabling developers to express AI computations while the compiler constructs efficient secure programs.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of programming secure inference and optimizing it across hardware, networks, and evolving ciphertext states.
MicroBench profiles deployment-specific costs for available homomorphic encryption and secure multi-party computation primitives.
State-expanded planning jointly optimizes HE/MPC placement, conversions, and ciphertext maintenance under cryptographic-state constraints.
BlockFold summarizes branched regions to make planning scalable for Transformer graphs.
Measured evaluations report up to 16.5× speedup on BERT-base and over 22× on ViT versus static hybrid-placement baselines.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can autonomously run neuroimaging analyses from research questions to reported findings. Existing agentic systems use tools to check that code runs and reported values match its output, but rely on LLM judgment to decide which results warrant scientific reporting. We show that LLM judges endorse site-confounded findings even when the confound is presented as evidence. We present \textbf{CONFIRM}, a framework that separates running an analysis from deciding which findings to report. CONFIRM encodes each hypothesis as a machine-readable, pre-specified analysis plan that fixes the claim and its pass criteria before computing results. It then filters results through five deterministic gates (search history and multiplicity, confounds, power, analytic stability, and replication) under three configurable reporting standards, from least to most demanding: \textit{Screen}, \textit{Replicate}, and \textit{Full}. Failed claims receive diagnoses that guide follow-up analyses. To evaluate reporting decisions at the claim level, we introduce \textbf{NeuroClaimBench}, comprising 489 executable neuroimaging claims with frozen data, including literature-supported findings and 150 controls designed to violate individual methodological requirements. On NeuroClaimBench, CONFIRM falsely supports at most 3\% of controls, compared with 23--38\% for the baselines, while recovering up to 61\% of literature-supported claims. When auditing an existing agent, CONFIRM reduces false support on controls from 23\% to 0\% while retaining the agent's literature-supported claims. Its diagnostic feedback also produces more supported revisions than Self-Refine with fewer LLM calls. Together, CONFIRM and NeuroClaimBench show that basing reporting decisions on pre-specified analysis plans and deterministic gates is essential for trustworthy autonomous scientific discovery.
bullets: LLM judges can endorse site-confounded findings even when the confound is explicitly shown.
CONFIRM separates analysis execution from reporting and encodes each hypothesis with fixed claims and pass criteria before analysis.
Five deterministic gates assess multiplicity, confounds, power, analytic stability, and replication under Screen, Replicate, or Full standards.
NeuroClaimBench evaluates 489 executable claims, including 150 controls designed to violate specific methodological requirements.
CONFIRM falsely supported at most 3% of controls versus 23–38% for baselines, while recovering up to 61% of literature-supported claims; audited agents reduced false support from 23% to 0%.

If a required gate fails, the claim is withheld, and the LLM may propose revised analyses that keep the original question.
