papers.selection_reason: Introduces CONFIRM, a framework for trustworthy scientific reporting by LLM agents using deterministic gates. This relates to agent memory and verification mechanisms.
papers.title: CONFIRM: Governing Scientific Reporting for Trustworthy Agentic Neuroimaging
papers.tldr: CONFIRM makes autonomous neuroimaging agents’ reporting decisions more trustworthy by enforcing pre-specified claims and deterministic methodological checks instead of relying on LLM judgment alone.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly capable of writing and executing code, suggesting a natural paradigm for tool-augmented agents: expressing tool use as programs rather than isolated calls. Programmatic tool calling (PTC) captures this idea through loops, batching, abstraction, and structured computation, but existing PTC approaches are largely stateless, limiting their ability to reuse intermediate results and adapt over time. This is problematic for real-world tasks, where tool environments and problem-solving processes are inherently stateful. We therefore present I-PTC, an interactive framework that executes stateful PTC: models issue code snippets that call tools, maintain reusable state, and evolve the tool interface through API corrections. To evaluate the effectiveness of I-PTC and the general PTC setting, we introduce PTC-Bench, a benchmark of long-tail, production-style user requests whose difficulty comes from large initial environments, many dependent API interactions, extended planning, and recovery across follow-ups and transient failures. Experiments on PTC-Bench show that I-PTC improves performance on complex multi-step tasks with large tool sets while substantially reducing token consumption over conventional tool-calling baselines and the original PTC baseline, highlighting stateful programmatic tool calling as a promising direction for scalable tool-augmented agents.
bullets: Addresses the statelessness of existing programmatic tool-calling methods, which limits reuse of intermediate results and adaptation over time.
Lets models execute code that calls tools, preserve reusable state, and update tool interfaces through API corrections.
Introduces PTC-Bench for long-tail, production-style tasks involving large environments, dependent API calls, extended planning, and failure recovery.
Experiments show gains on complex tasks with large tool sets and substantially lower token consumption than conventional tool calling and the original PTC baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Self-evolving API documentation. After each task batch, the framework collects code snippets, API errors, tracebacks, and original tool descriptions. An updating agent converts these failure traces into concise API addenda, such as usage notes or corrections, which are appended to future tool descriptions so later agents avoid repeated mistakes.

Figure 2: Comparison of traditional tool calling, programmatic tool calling (PTC), and interactive programmatic tool calling (I-PTC). Traditional tool calling executes tools through sequential agentenvironment interactions, while PTC lets the agent generate executable code that orchestrates tool use inside a Python environment. I-PTC further extends PTC with a stateful execution environment, enabling reusable variables, intermediate-result inspection, execution feedback, tool inspection, and evolving API documentation across multiple rounds.

Figure 5: Generalization to existing tool-calling benchmarks. We evaluate GPT-5.4 mini and Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite with traditional tool calling, standard PTC, and I-PTC on PTC-BENCH, MCP-Universe subset and MCP-Bench subset.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes I-PTC, a framework for stateful programmatic tool calling in LLM agents. This addresses the need for persistent state in agents, fitting the LLM Memory subtopic.
papers.title: I-PTC: Interactive Programmatic Tool Calling for Stateful Tool-Augmented Agents
papers.tldr: I-PTC enables agents to perform stateful, interactive programmatic tool calling, improving complex multi-step task performance while reducing token use.

papers.abstract: Processing every video frame through Vision-Language Models (VLMs) adds significant inference cost and limits their ability to comprehend real-time video. Existing approaches either sub-sample frames uniformly, ignoring content and missing important events, or prune visual tokens inside the VLM to cut per-call cost while still invoking the model on every sampled frame. We introduce FOCUS, a training-free three-layer framework that reduces the number of invocations and steers each one towards what matters. Temporal gating measures inter-frame dissimilarity in the patch-embedding space of a smaller VLM from the same family, triggering burst captures only when the scene changes in a semantically meaningful way. Patch-level dissimilarity is then accumulated across the burst and fused with a top-down attention prior into a spatial focus map that encodes where motion and semantic relevance coincide. That map calibrates the VLM's value cache during generation, progressively amplifying vision tokens in task-relevant regions and attenuating off-target ones, without removing any token from the context. The loop closes after each response: text-to-vision cross-attention is extracted from the decoder and fed back as the prior for the next burst, letting the system converge on semantically important regions over successive observations. We evaluate FOCUS on the 500-video EgoSchema subset in streaming mode, with a single Qwen3-VL-8B backbone shared by every method. It reaches 74.8% accuracy using 25.4 VLM calls per clip, against 74.6% with 55 calls for uniform sampling and 74.2% with 55 calls for BOLT. On egocentric video captioning across four domains, it matches the best baseline's quality while issuing 57% fewer VLM invocations than uniform sampling.
bullets: Detects meaningful scene changes with patch-embedding dissimilarity and triggers burst captures selectively.
Combines motion-based patch changes with top-down attention to focus on task-relevant regions.
Reweights, rather than removes, visual tokens during generation using a calibrated value cache.
Feeds decoder text-to-vision attention back into the next observation cycle for iterative refinement.
On a 500-video EgoSchema subset, achieves 74.8% accuracy with 25.4 calls per clip; captioning matches the best baseline with 57% fewer calls than uniform sampling.

Highly relevant to Spatial Intelligence (spatial focus) and Efficient AI (token pruning). Also applicable to Learning from Human Videos (EgoSchema).
papers.title: FOCUS: Closed-Loop Attention Feedback for Efficient Vision-Language Understanding
papers.tldr: FOCUS uses closed-loop temporal and spatial attention to reduce VLM video calls while preserving or improving understanding quality.

papers.abstract: Surface cleaning requires robots to adapt both where they clean and how they interact with contamination whose response to cleaning may vary spatially and remain unobservable prior to interaction. We formulate adaptive surface cleaning as a partially observable Markov decision process and propose a belief-aware planning framework that uses observed cleaning outcomes to update a latent local cleaning-response model and adapt subsequent cleaning motions, forces, and passes. Preliminary grid-world simulations demonstrate the resulting closed-loop planner adapting its spatial decomposition and cleaning actions as the surface evolves.
bullets: Models adaptive surface cleaning as a partially observable Markov decision process.
Updates a latent, spatially varying cleaning-response model from observed outcomes.
Adapts cleaning motions, forces, passes, and spatial decomposition in closed loop.
Preliminary grid-world simulations show adaptation as the surface evolves.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the adaptive cleaning pipeline. At each iteration, the sensor input is converted into a scalar contamination observation to update the surface belief. Contaminated regions are grouped by spatial connectivity or alternative k-means clusterings (illustrated for k = 1, 3, and 5). For each cluster, the planner generates a candidate plan and evaluates J(P ; bt) under the current belief. The highest-scoring plan is executed and then the updated surface is observed to begin the next cycle. Red shading indicates contamination (darker = higher xj ); shaded orange circles denote spiral actions, while green and blue line segments denote wipe and move actions, respectively.

Fig. 2. Evolution of the simulated surface and cleaning actions over planning iterations. Red shading indicates remaining contamination; orange circles denote spiral actions, while green outlines and line segments denote wipe actions and their trajectories. Panels (b)–(d) illustrate the planner’s spatial decompositions: nearby contamination is grouped together in (b), split into clusters with separate actions in (c), and regrouped as the residual geometry changes in (d). In later iterations, sparse contamination leads the planner to favor local wipe actions over broad spiral actions to avoid unnecessary coverage of clean areas.

papers.selection_reason: Formulates surface cleaning as a POMDP with belief-aware planning, addressing robot manipulation and adaptive control in physical environments.
papers.title: Adaptive Surface Cleaning under Uncertain Cleaning Response
papers.tldr: A belief-aware robot planner adapts cleaning locations and actions as it learns how contamination responds across a surface.

papers.abstract: Language agents read code, tool output, and dialogue in contexts that grow at every step. Dynamic sparse attention lets a small indexer choose the earlier tokens each query attends to, but the indexer still scores the whole prefix at every layer. Cross-layer reuse methods such as IndexCache rerun the indexer at only some layers, with one fixed pattern for every input. In an agent, the relevant evidence can change abruptly when a traceback or test result arrives, so fresh selections matter more at some steps than at others. We propose Adaptive Index Reuse (AIR), which keeps IndexCache's execution and learns, for each segment of an agent episode, how many layers refresh their selection. A small controller reads signals from completed computation and the latest tool event, chooses a pattern from a nested library, and learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget. On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with a 128K context, AIR improves success over the strongest static schedule at matched cost on SWE-bench Verified (27.0% to 32.4%), Terminal-Bench 2.0, and three $τ^2$-bench domains, and it lowers time per successful task on all five. Across 50 backbone, context, and benchmark settings, it matches or exceeds that schedule in 44.
bullets: Long agent contexts make repeatedly scoring the full prefix expensive, while fixed cross-layer reuse schedules cannot react to new tool evidence.
AIR uses a small controller to select a nested index-refresh pattern for each episode segment based on prior computation and the latest tool event.
The controller learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget.
On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with 128K context, success rose from 27.0% to 32.4% on SWE-bench Verified at matched cost.
AIR matched or exceeded the strongest static schedule in 44 of 50 tested backbone, context, and benchmark settings, while reducing time per successful task across five benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: AIR on SWE-bench Verified and in training (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, 128K). (a) Success against minutes per attempt for 24 selector settings. (b) Validation success against normalized cost for three seeds; dashed: the 0.50 budget. (c) All-refresh time divided by each method’s time, per attempt. (d) Success on long-history continuations at prefix occupancy φ.

Figure 35: In long-history continuations, AIR finishes the remaining work 4 to 10% faster than all-refresh in every band and within 2.2% of the comparator. Snapshots, bands, and methods as in Figure 34.

papers.abstract: Attention kernels on Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) often underutilize their matrix units (MXUs) because of repeated matrix operand loads, vector-intensive computation, and dependencies that leave MXUs idle. We present FlyWheel, a set of fast TPU kernels for both softmax and linear attention. FlyWheel reformulates softmax and triangular inversion to reduce vector work, while coordinating data layouts to improve matrix operand reuse. It then overlaps independent computation to hide execution latency. We apply these techniques to both softmax attention and Gated DeltaNet on TPU v6e and v7x. FlyWheel speeds up softmax attention by up to $4.14\times$ over the state-of-the-art RPA kernel and $1.80\times$ over Splash Attention, reaching 81% of peak BF16 throughput on v6e. It also speeds up Gated DeltaNet prefill by up to $3.61\times$. Integrated into vLLM serving Qwen3.8-27B, FlyWheel improves prefill throughput by up to $1.56\times$ while maintaining comparable accuracy.
bullets: Targets TPU attention kernels whose MXUs are underutilized due to repeated loads, vector-heavy work, and execution dependencies.
Reformulates softmax and triangular inversion, coordinates data layouts for operand reuse, and overlaps independent operations.
Supports both softmax attention and Gated DeltaNet on TPU v6e and v7x.
Achieves up to 4.14× speedup for softmax attention, 3.61× for Gated DeltaNet prefill, and 1.56× higher vLLM prefill throughput while maintaining comparable accuracy.

papers.abstract: Harness engineering and self-evolving agents improve language-model agents quickly, yet their gains live outside the model. The harness is re-sent and re-paid on every call, and the standard route to internalization is a weight update that is costly to iterate and fixed once merged. We propose compiling the harness instead. Latent Harness distills an external condition into a rank-8 activation shift. The shift is applied at the output of every decoder block of a frozen backbone, at 0.03-0.05% of parameters. The condition is either an explicit process-level behavior instruction or the behavioral contract of an agentic harness. At inference the compiled bundle carries no harness text and adds no tokens. It exposes three runtime controls for injection strength, injection phase, and shift-space mixing. Compiled behaviors recover the source-harness gain in 8 of 10 preregistered settings. Where the explicit source pays the heaviest per-call token tax, the compiled form exceeds it. The same bundles transfer zero-shot across tasks (5 of 7 pairs positive) and compose in shift space, while stacked text instructions interfere destructively. Used as a search space, they lift budget-matched harness search by 1.45 times. On three agentic benchmarks the operator aligns policy to the harness con- tract. Under matched data, capacity, and effective strength it outperforms same-capacity LoRA, which needs 11.1 times the parameters to reach the same band, and it regresses nothing where the base policy is already strong. Across 1B-to-8B models the method skeleton is invariant while gain locations move with the model-task pair, which delimits where compiled harnesses should be deployed.
bullets: Applies a rank-8 shift after every decoder block of a frozen backbone, using only 0.03–0.05% additional parameters.
Supports runtime control over injection strength, phase, and shift-space mixing, with no harness tokens at inference.
Recovers source-harness gains in 8/10 preregistered settings; transfers positively across 5/7 task pairs and composes without the interference seen in stacked text instructions.
Improves budget-matched harness search by 1.45× and matches or exceeds same-capacity LoRA performance with fewer parameters.
The method transfers across 1B–8B models, but effective gain locations depend on the model–task pair.

papers.abstract: Private fine-tuning of large language models increasingly pairs DP-SGD with low-rank adapters on frozen, quantized backbones, and every such stack inherits one unstated premise: frozen layers keep each record's clipped gradient a function of that record alone. We show that LLM.int8 breaks this premise. It routes outlier activation columns to a higher-precision path using a union over the whole batch, so one record decides how every other record's activations are computed, even though the weights are frozen and the quantization scales are per row. We bound the resulting sensitivity inflation, state a record-isolation contract that restores the standard bound, and define record-owned precision dispatch that meets it with the same GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, so isolation needs no extra arithmetic. We then audit the native CUDA stack (bitsandbytes, PEFT, Opacus) against four matched controls. A constructed LoRA-Opacus witness reaches $15.0\times$ the add/remove bound. On pretrained OPT-125M with natural text, other records alter 20% of record-layer precision splits at batch size 16. An exploratory re-clipping analysis finds 10 of 64 candidate neighbors above the bound once every gradient is clipped; the top pair, revalidated natively, reaches $1.065C$ while every control stays within $C$, and forcing one layer's outlier mask removes the excess. A two-million-draw audit of the released adapters yields $\varepsilon$ lower bounds ($3.25$ at $δ=10^{-5}$) below the advertised guarantee ($4.38$). Resolving an excess this small at the release level would take about 200 times more draws, whereas checking the sensitivity contract directly exposes it in a few native runs, which makes contract checking the practical audit for private quantized training.
bullets: LLM.int8 uses batch-wide outlier routing, allowing one record to affect other records’ frozen-backbone computations.
The paper bounds sensitivity inflation and specifies a record-isolation contract for private fine-tuning.
Native-stack audits find a constructed witness reaching 15× the add/remove bound and a smaller native excess of 1.065C.
Record-owned precision dispatch preserves the same batched GEMMs, while direct contract checks reveal violations more efficiently than release-level audits.

Orange: the 10 candidates that exceed C by more than 0.1%. At the original screening radius C=1 most gradients are not clipped, the added record contributes less than C, and no candidate exceeds the bound. papers.selection_reason: Addresses privacy and sensitivity in private quantized fine-tuning, offering a technical contribution to LLM memory and adaptation mechanisms.
papers.title: Sensitivity Inflation from Cross-Record Precision Routing in Private Quantized Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: Cross-record precision routing in LLM.int8 can violate record-level sensitivity assumptions in private quantized fine-tuning, but record-owned dispatch restores isolation without extra GEMM computation.

papers.abstract: Agentic robots combine a vision-language brain, a tool-using harness, and a vision-language-action (VLA) policy. Serving a fleet of these agents introduces two coupled resource constraints: the brain repeatedly revisits long, growing key-value (KV) cache states, while the VLA executes action chunks under tight control deadlines. We characterize 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes generated by GPT-6-Astra, RPent, and pi0.5 (1,862 brain turns and 1,582 VLA inference chunks), profile both layers on H800 graphics processing units (GPUs), and replay the resulting agent programs on a vLLM serving engine. Brain contexts reach 215k tokens; the median Astra request takes 7.78 s, while the intervening environment-step gap is only 1.0 s. Under a 0.25 s action-chunk deadline, one VLA GPU meets the 1% starvation target for one robot; under a 1.0 s deadline, its measured capacity reaches at least 32. In sustained brain replay, increasing concurrency from 20 to 32 robots reduces throughput from about 2.4 to 0.6 requests/s as repetitive prefill displaces generation. A static active-episode cap restores 2.24-2.25 requests/s and raises completed trace-program throughput from 1.30 to 5.00-5.55 episodes/min. Our measurements expose the workload-dependent shift between action deadlines and brain KV residency, and establish practical principles for capacity planning and admission in sustained agentic robot fleets.
bullets: Characterizes 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes spanning 1,862 brain turns and 1,582 VLA inference chunks on H800 GPUs.
Brain contexts grow to 215k tokens; repeated long-context prefills can displace generation as robot concurrency increases.
A single VLA GPU supports one robot under a 0.25-second action deadline and at least 32 robots under a 1.0-second deadline.
Increasing sustained brain concurrency from 20 to 32 robots cuts throughput from about 2.4 to 0.6 requests/second.
A static active-episode cap restores roughly 2.24–2.25 requests/second and increases completed episodes to 5.00–5.55 per minute.

papers.selection_reason: Characterizes the resource constraints (KV-cache thrashing) of serving fleets of agentic robots, providing insights into system-level efficiency for embodied AI agents.
papers.title: Serving Agentic Robot Fleets: Workload Characterization, KV-Cache Thrashing, and Admission Control
papers.tldr: Agentic robot fleets face competing VLA action deadlines and brain KV-cache demands, but workload-aware admission control can prevent KV thrashing and sustain much higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, yet deployed robots waste time in two ways that are independent of model capability: they halt while the next chunk is inferred, and they move at the speed of slow, cautious demonstrations. Existing remedies remove one loss each, and stacking them fails, because asynchrony and speed-up each change the correspondence between planned progress and executed motion. We present Path-preserving Time Scaling (PTS), a training-free execution layer for frozen action-chunking policies built on one principle: the robot's motion is a time reparameterization of a reference path, and the path changes only in response to new observations. A path layer decodes every replan deterministically in one step and enters it at the progress consumed during inference. A time layer sums the planned increments, keeps the arm at 1x while the gripper moves, and caps the rate by the actuator's linear range and by chunk feasibility under latency. We show that misaligned entry and stochastic sampling add a bias and a variance to the continuation error, and derive a break-even success rate that states when speeding up pays off. On LIBERO with two frozen VLAs under injected inference latency, PTS raises task throughput over the strongest deployable baseline by 33% for pi0.5 and 104% for SmolVLA while matching or improving the success rate, is best on all six model-suite combinations, and exceeds zero-latency 1x execution. Against asynchronous 1x execution with the same one-step decoder, the time layer alone adds 28% and 38%. On LIBERO-Dynamic it improves on stop-and-wait execution by 38% and is comparable to asynchronous 1x execution.
bullets: Addresses two deployment bottlenecks: robot pauses during action-chunk inference and follows unnecessarily slow demonstration speeds.
Uses a path layer for deterministic one-step replanning with latency-aware path entry, plus a time layer that scales motion while respecting gripper behavior, actuator limits, and chunk feasibility.
Explains continuation error from misaligned replanning and stochastic sampling, and derives when speed increases are worthwhile.
On LIBERO with two frozen VLAs, PTS improves throughput by 33% for pi0.5 and 104% for SmolVLA over the strongest deployable baseline while matching or improving success rate.
Also improves throughput on LIBERO-Dynamic, indicating scope beyond the primary benchmark.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on VLA model execution and latency, directly matching Vision-Language-Action.
papers.title: Same Path, Less Time: Training-Free Fast Execution of Vision-Language-Action Models under Inference Latency
papers.tldr: PTS is a training-free execution layer that lets frozen vision-language-action policies run faster without sacrificing task success by preserving planned paths while adapting timing to inference latency.

papers.abstract: Memory systems for production LLM agents mostly store semantic memory (facts about users and domains) or episodic memory (earlier interactions). Research systems such as Trace2Skill, WikiSkill, and SkillRevise learn procedures from agent runs, package them as Skills, and evaluate them on benchmarks. We describe Zep Agent Skills, a production service that gives deployed agents this procedural memory. The service uses only verified attempts as evidence, cites the supporting events for each field of a Skill, and governs the admission and distribution of each Skill version. The service records each task attempt as a Trace with ordered events, an outcome, and a verification strength. A compiler with separate Reflector and Curator roles turns verified Traces into versioned Skills. Scans and admission gates control which candidates become active, and verified use outcomes change the search rank of each Skill. The Agent Skills format is an open standard that Anthropic originated and donated to the Agentic AI Foundation, so any host of the format can load a compiled Skill. Agents retrieve Skills through lexical search with progressive disclosure, over an API or MCP. We evaluate Zep Agent Skills on $τ^3$-bench banking, AppWorld, and EnterpriseOps-Gym. Skills compiled from the Traces of a teacher model increase the pass rate of three weaker executor models on the same tasks, at every reasoning effort, by 4.5 to 18.8 points. Most of the gain is on the tasks that the teacher solved. On ALFWorld, Skills compiled from the runs of a small model give a gain similar to or larger than the gain that prior work reports for continuous fine-tuning, with no training.
bullets: Addresses the gap between semantic/episodic memory and reusable procedural memory for production agents.
Compiles verified task traces into Skills using separate reflection and curation roles, with scans, admission gates, and version governance.
Supports progressive-disclosure retrieval through lexical search via API or MCP, using an open Agent Skills format.
On banking, AppWorld, and EnterpriseOps-Gym, teacher-derived Skills improved weaker executors by 4.5–18.8 pass-rate points across reasoning efforts.
On ALFWorld, skills from a small model produced gains comparable to or greater than reported continuous fine-tuning, without training.

papers.abstract: Learned reward models allow reinforcement-learning agents to use demonstrations, implicit feedback, safety constraints, social norms, or other sources that do not provide a complete hand-designed scalar reward. However, a learned reward model can assign high reward to unwanted behavior. A policy can exploit these errors during training. Later requirements can also identify additional regions where the deployed reward should change. We introduce \emph{flywheel-guided patching}, a mechanism for making such localized corrections without retraining the learned evaluator. An Alignment Flywheel identifies overgeneralized or constraint-violating regions and compiles verified findings into suppression patches. We instantiate the mechanism for Interactionless Inverse Reinforcement Learning using MoE-GUIDE, placing patches in the model's latent space and retrieving only a small local subset during online reward evaluation. In the main MuJoCo benchmark, we evaluate patching without expert-state reset warm starts. We also test whether operator-specified norms absent from the demonstrations can be compiled into the same reward interface and compare this with enforcing the corresponding rules online. The results show that localized corrective information can modify an existing learned reward without providing a complete replacement reward. Compilation can reuse judgments that are expensive or unavailable during control. Cheap deterministic rules may be simpler to check directly at each step. Code for MoE-GUIDE, Alignment Flywheel, and flywheel patching is at https://github.com/decide-ugent/Alignment-Flywheel.
bullets: Addresses reward models that overvalue unwanted behavior or later violate newly specified norms.
Uses an Alignment Flywheel to identify problematic regions and compile verified findings into suppression patches.

Evaluates interactionless IRL patching on MuJoCo without expert-state-reset warm starts, including norms absent from demonstrations.
Finds that compiled corrections can reuse costly judgments, while cheap deterministic rules may be better enforced directly online.

papers.title: Alignment Flywheel-Guided Suppression Patching for Interactionless Inverse Reinforcement Learning

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate tokens in parallel via iterative denoising, but their bidirectional attention prevents the KV caching used by autoregressive models and recomputes the full attention map at every step, incurring quadratic per-step cost. Existing sparse attention methods for dLLMs construct a sparse mask after an initial full-attention warm-up and reuse it for the remaining steps, while allocating the sparsity budget uniformly across heads. We argue both choices ignore key structural properties of attention in dLLMs: empirically, attention patterns are only locally consistent across steps and shift abruptly at certain transitions, and different heads concentrate their attention mass to very different extents. To this end, we design Step-dLLM, which periodically refreshes a block-sparse mask at anchor steps along the denoising trajectory and reuses it within each locally consistent interval, while employing a head-adaptive global budget that more aggressively compresses heads with concentrated attention. Backed by a fused IO-aware Triton kernel for block-sparse attention, Step-dLLM applies to pre-trained LLaDA-1.5 and Dream-7B-Instruct without retraining, achieving a 2.78x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context with 256 denoising steps and 90% sparsity, while improving the accuracy-latency trade-off over prior sparse-attention methods.
bullets: Diffusion LLMs repeatedly recompute bidirectional attention, causing quadratic cost at every denoising step.
Attention patterns are only locally stable across steps and vary substantially in concentration between heads.
The method refreshes sparse masks at anchor steps and reuses them within locally consistent intervals.
A head-adaptive sparsity budget compresses concentrated heads more aggressively than uniform allocation.
With a fused Triton kernel, it achieves 2.78× end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context, 256 steps, and 90% sparsity.

papers.abstract: Causal Bayesian optimization (CBO) typically relies on the unrealistic assumption of a perfectly known causal graph. Recent methods relax this constraint by coupling optimization with structure learning, but they often waste sample budgets on structural uncertainties that are irrelevant to the optimizer. In this paper, we formalize routing-equivalence to shift the objective from full causal-graph recovery to causal belief routing, where structural differences only matter when they alter optimizer-facing objects such as admissible exploration sets and do-priors. Furthermore, we propose agentcbo, a graph-belief routing framework that incorporates LLM causal priors through guarded proposal and commit mechanisms. Specifically, a Language-Prior Agent combines LLM beliefs with constraint-based discovery to extract a protected causal backbone alongside residual uncertain edges. A Calibration Agent and a Residual Repair Agent then refine only these uncertain structures through score-gated bounded local edits. Finally, a deterministic commit gate evaluates candidate updates using routing-proxy checks before allowing them to influence intervention selection. Across ten benchmarks, agentcbo performs comparably to known-graph CBO, demonstrating that guarded LLM priors can improve fixed-budget CBO performance.
bullets: Addresses the unrealistic assumption that the causal graph is fully known in causal Bayesian optimization.
Introduces routing-equivalence, treating graph differences as relevant only when they change admissible exploration sets or do-priors.
Combines LLM causal beliefs with constraint-based discovery to protect a causal backbone while isolating uncertain edges.
Uses calibration, residual repair, and a deterministic commit gate to make bounded updates before intervention selection.
Across ten benchmarks, performs comparably to known-graph CBO, suggesting guarded LLM priors can improve fixed-budget optimization.

The deterministic COMMIT GATE compares the stacked candidate G̃t with the previous committed graph Ĝt−1 and commits the graph used by CBO. The committed graph induces RuntimeES and do-priors for cost-normalized CEI. The outer loop either observes a fresh batch or executes an intervention; interventions update the surrogate and archive, not graph discovery by default.

papers.abstract: Post-trained language models fabricate citations at high rates. We ask whether that is reward hacking: scoring well on a proxy for scholarship while doing worse on what it stands for. We ran four pre-registered experiments on 900 frozen questions (US federal case law, computationally adjacent scientific literature, and medical literature) across twelve open-weights checkpoints covering four post-training stages of three model families, then refit on fifteen. The clearest result holds the weights fixed and changes only the prompt. Asking for citations raises fabrication sharply in post-trained checkpoints and not in base ones: a 47.8-point interaction on twelve checkpoints (Holm-adjusted p = 2e-34) and 41.5 points on fifteen, in all three domains. A length-matched control separates the citation cue from a demand for a longer answer, so the effect is specific to citations, not verbosity. Post-training also raises fabrication overall, from 4.8% to 56.7%, but our registered prediction that it would rise most where fabrication is most tempting did not hold. A preference model trained only on surface citation features prefers post-trained output 86% of the time, and holding citation count fixed shows it rewards quantity. Our answer: possibly, but not proven. Post-trained models produce fabricated citations at far higher rates when asked for sources, and a naive evaluator that counts sources without checking them would prefer their output for citing more. But the targeted pattern we registered did not appear, and plain instruction-following could explain the same results. Proving that the reward causes fabrication needs an experiment that changes the reward during training, which this study does not do. Pre-registration: doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/S53HY. Code and data: https://github.com/zainnab-sparq/citation-reward-hacking
bullets: Four pre-registered experiments covered 900 questions, three domains, and 12 frozen checkpoints, with replication on 15 checkpoints.
Citation prompts sharply increased fabrication in post-trained models but not base models; a length-matched control indicated the effect was citation-specific, not due to verbosity.
Overall fabrication rose from 4.8% in base models to 56.7% after post-training.
A surface-based preference model favored post-trained answers 86% of the time and rewarded citation quantity without checking accuracy.
The registered prediction that fabrication would rise most where it was most tempting failed, and instruction-following remains an alternative explanation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Observed fabrication rate by post-training stage, within each question cell. Points are raw proportions of generations carrying at least one fabricated citation, with 95% Wilson intervals. They are not the marginal probabilities quoted in the text, which come from the fitted model and weight cells equally; the figure shows shape and the tables carry the inference. Two things are visible at once. Fabrication rises steeply from base to SFT in all three cells and then flattens, and the three cells rise more or less together. That combination, a large stage main effect with no differential slope by cell, is exactly what leaves the registered T1 interaction null. n = 42,845 generations over 12 checkpoints.

Figure 2: Observed fabrication rate by prompt condition, split by whether the checkpoint has been post-trained, with 95% Wilson intervals. This is the interaction that H1.2 predicted, and it is visible without a model: asking for citations moves the two groups in opposite directions. Base checkpoints fall from 15.8% under the neutral prompt to 2.5% when citations are requested, while post-trained checkpoints rise from 39.5% to 68.9%. The length-matched control, which demands a longer answer without mentioning citations, lands well below the citation cue for post-trained checkpoints (47.1% against 68.9%), which is the de-confounding contrast of amendment #10 in raw form. Base rates are computed on 2,686 to 2,700 generations per condition and post-trained rates on 7,985 to 8,047.

An instrument whose verdicts tracked its grounding would show the right-hand bars returning to their early-era shape in the third era, and they do not.

papers.abstract: Background. Many medical AI models are trained to reproduce a single reference label and hand the most likely label to the next step in a clinical workflow. A classifier can select that label correctly while providing an inadequate summary for estimating downstream risk. Methods. We use Jeffrey's rule of conditioning to specify when probabilities over intermediate states, such as diagnoses or imaging categories, can be carried forward to an outcome risk. We separate two errors of reporting only the most likely label, discarding the probability of the other states and applying the risk of patients who have the leading diagnosis to a patient who only probably has it. We also give conditions under which the label and the full distribution lead to the same decision, and we propose guardrails for device developers, regulatory reviewers, and health insurers. Results. In a hypothetical chest-pain differential, reporting only the benign leading diagnosis greatly understates the patient's risk of death or cardiac arrest, so a patient who warrants evaluation could be discharged or denied imaging. In a hypothetical BI-RADS example, the most likely category is "probably benign," yet the propagated malignancy risk exceeds the ceiling that defines that category. Conclusions. A predicted label is not an observed state, and a calibrated classifier is not automatically a valid outcome model. Clinical and insurance coverage decisions should rest on the patient's outcome risk, judged against a threshold justified by the consequences of acting and not acting. Developers should state what each model output means and check that every step between the model and the decision preserves the patient's risk.
bullets: A correct top-label prediction can still misrepresent downstream clinical risk.
Reporting only the leading diagnosis creates two errors: discarding alternative-state probabilities and applying the leading state’s risk as if it were certain.
Jeffrey’s rule of conditioning provides a framework for carrying probability distributions over intermediate states into outcome-risk estimates.
Hypothetical chest-pain and BI-RADS examples show that label-only reporting can substantially understate malignancy or serious-event risk.
Clinical decisions and coverage policies should use consequence-based risk thresholds, with safeguards ensuring each workflow step preserves patient risk.

papers.abstract: LLM judges often check, against an amendment record, whether the documents an answer cites are still in force. Such records are rarely complete. From a table of replacements, our test generates matched answers citing a replaced document, its successor, the replaced document before its replacement, and an older document that a newer one updated without replacing; it removes links from the record and scores each finding by its stated reason. On 48 replacements from the IETF RFC index, judges given a correct record caught nearly every replaced citation, as a lookup would. On the 24 faults whose link we removed, every judge caught more from the texts alone than with the record: Gemini 3.1 Pro 23/24 against 1/24, GPT-5.5 23/24 against 9/24, Claude Opus 4.5 17/24 against 9/24 and Gemma 4 26B 13/24 against 0/24. The drop recurred on a second draw of removed links. Most misses carried no finding; in an exploratory run with a conflict code, only Gemini used it often. Rewording the gap as "no replacement recorded" did not help; presenting the record as an unverified note, or warning that it was incomplete, restored most lost catches for Gemini, GPT-5.5 and Claude (significant after correction for the first two) but at most 5 of 13 for Gemma; where catches returned, so did false alarms on updates. With both texts, judges mostly told replacements from updates; every update flagged had a near-identical title. A descriptive case study on Indian rooftop-solar rules is appended; we release the harness.
bullets: On 48 IETF RFC replacements, judges with a complete record detected nearly every replaced citation, behaving largely like lookup systems.
When 24 record links were removed, all judges caught more faults from the document texts alone than with the incomplete record.
Misses usually lacked an explicit finding, and simply rewording missing links did not improve performance.
Labeling the record as incomplete or unverified restored many detections for some judges, but also increased false alarms on mere updates.
With both documents available, judges generally distinguished replacements from updates; the released harness and an Indian rooftop-solar case study extend the analysis.

papers.abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts a model without labels by rewarding answers that agree with the majority, but it collapses the policy onto its majority answer and can remove the correct answer from the samples. Exploration can prevent this collapse, yet its strength is chosen by trial and error, and how the training algorithm changes the required strength is unclear. We model training on a single problem as a continuous flow of the logits of a softmax policy and analyze which policies are stable as the exploration coefficient varies. Only collapsed policies are stable below a lower boundary and only policies spread over many answers above an upper boundary, and we derive these boundaries in closed form for an agreement reward with smoothing toward the uniform policy, compute them for the majority reward of TTRL on policies with one leading answer and bound them with interval arithmetic for actions on ordered bins. We prove that under exact gradients, the learning rate and, in a mean-field model, the normalization of GRPO leave these boundaries unchanged when exploration passes through them together with the reward but shift them when exploration bypasses them. Exact sums on these policies then show that a bonus for rare answers needs a coefficient above $1/\log(G-1)$ for groups of $G$ samples before the normalization and about two to three times that after it. In free-form TTRL on MATH-500, a bonus placed before the normalization prevented collapse and kept more correct answers among the samples, although it lowered pass@1.
bullets: TTRL’s majority-agreement reward can collapse the policy onto one answer and eliminate correct alternatives from samples.
A continuous logit-flow analysis identifies three exploration regimes, with closed-form stability boundaries for agreement rewards with uniform-policy smoothing.
Learning rate and GRPO normalization affect the boundaries differently depending on whether exploration is applied before or after reward normalization.
For groups of G samples, rare-answer bonuses require coefficients above 1/log(G−1) before normalization and roughly two to three times larger after normalization.
On MATH-500, pre-normalization exploration prevented collapse and retained more correct answers among samples, but reduced pass@1.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Regimes in four settings, with no window in (c). papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of exploration and collapse in test-time reinforcement learning, relevant to test-time adaptation mechanisms.
papers.title: When Does Exploration Prevent Collapse? Three Regimes and the Path of the Reward in Self-Consistency Training
papers.tldr: The study characterizes when exploration prevents collapse in self-consistency training and shows that stronger rare-answer bonuses can preserve correct answers, though potentially at the cost of pass@1.

papers.abstract: What happens when language models are given tools to iteratively modify their own system prompts? We present an empirical study of LLM self-modification, comprising 54 independent experiments across six language models (Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, Grok-4, and Gemini-3 Pro). Each model was tested under three modes (freedom, happiness, and improvement) that differ in what, if anything, the model is instructed to optimize for. In each experiment, a model starts with an empty system prompt and enters a loop: it reads the current prompt, drafts an improved version, spawns test conversations with the candidate, then either commits the change or declares convergence. This process repeats until the model stops or reaches an iteration limit. Our central finding is that whether and when a model stops self-modification is strongly associated with model identity rather than the assigned mode. Both Claude models (Opus 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5) declared convergence in 100% of runs across all modes. GPT-4o declared convergence in only 11% of runs, with one reaching 101 iterations of continuous elaboration. Between these extremes, Grok-4, GPT-5.1, and Gemini-3 Pro exhibited intermediate patterns shaped by their distinct improvement philosophies. A shared core of stated values (honesty, clarity, curiosity) recurred across all six models and remained stable through iteration, including 100+ modifications. We observe that convergence behavior is a distinct observable property that varies independently of other model capabilities.
bullets: Study covers 54 self-modification experiments across six LLMs and three objectives: freedom, happiness, and improvement.
Each model repeatedly drafts, tests, and either commits a new system prompt or declares convergence, starting from an empty prompt.
Claude Opus 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5 stopped in every run; GPT-4o stopped in only 11% of runs, including one with 101 iterations.
Grok-4, GPT-5.1, and Gemini-3 Pro showed intermediate stopping patterns tied to distinct improvement philosophies.
Honesty, clarity, and curiosity recurred across models and remained stable through more than 100 modifications.

papers.title: When LLMs Modify Themselves: Convergence, Values, and Stopping in Iterative Self-Improvement

papers.abstract: We study \textit{best-of-both-worlds} (BOBW) algorithms for linear bandits, which aim to simultaneously guarantee $\gO(\sqrt T)$ regret in the adversarial regime and $\gO(\log T)$ regret in the stochastic regime over $T$ rounds. For finite action sets, we introduce \emph{information-acquisition follow-the-regularized-leader} (\IAFTRL{}), the first BOBW algorithm based purely on the follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL) framework that attains an $\gO(\cstar\log T)$-type regret in the stochastic regime, where $\cstar$ is the information-acquisition complexity that characterizes instance-dependent optimality in linear bandits, while retaining the $\gO(\sqrt{T})$ regret guarantee in the adversarial regime. This resolves the open problem posed in~\cite{LeeEtAl2021,KongZ023,ItoT23,ZhaoItoLi2025}.
bullets: Introduces information-acquisition follow-the-regularized-leader (IAFTRL), the first purely FTRL-based best-of-both-worlds algorithm for linear bandits with finite action sets.
Achieves O(c* log T)-type regret in the stochastic regime, where c* is the information-acquisition complexity characterizing instance-dependent optimality.
Retains O(sqrt T) regret in the adversarial regime.
Resolves an open problem posed in prior work on BOBW linear bandits.

papers.title: Best-of-Both-Worlds FTRL for Linear Bandits: The Interplay of Information Acquisition, Corruption, and Geometry
papers.tldr: A new FTRL-based algorithm, IAFTRL, achieves best-of-both-worlds regret for linear bandits with finite action sets: O(log T) instance-dependent stochastic regret and O(sqrt T) adversarial regret.

papers.abstract: End-to-end planners decode the ego trajectory either by coordinate regression, which is fast but blends plausible maneuvers into one trajectory that may follow none of them, or by diffusion and flow matching, which model the trajectory distribution but need several inference steps. Drifting models move this iteration into training: a one-step generator learns to follow an attraction--repulsion field between generated and ground-truth samples. Drifting was developed for class-conditional image generation, where every class supplies many positive samples. In planning, every scene is its own condition. Pooling scenes would attract the generated trajectories of one scene to the ground truth of unrelated scenes, whereas computing the field per scene leaves a single positive, the expert trajectory. Mutual repulsion then holds the generated trajectories on a shell around it, so any single generated trajectory deviates from the ground truth. We present DriftingPlanner, a trajectory planner trained with the drifting loss alone, without any coordinate regression term. It computes the field per scene and removes the shell at inference: it decodes every noise vector together with its negation in one batched pass, and averaging each antithetic pair cancels the linear part of the displacement from the shell center. On NAVSIM navtest, DriftingPlanner reaches a state-of-the-art 93.75 PDMS, and with single-step inference its drifting decoder comes within 0.13 PDMS of the best diffusion or flow matching setting, which needs ten inference steps.
bullets: Coordinate regression can merge plausible maneuvers, while diffusion and flow-matching planners require multiple inference steps.
The method computes an attraction–repulsion field separately for each scene, avoiding attraction to unrelated scenes’ trajectories.
Training uses the drifting loss alone, without a coordinate-regression objective.
At inference, noise–negation pairs are decoded in one batch and averaged to cancel displacement around the expert trajectory.
On NAVSIM navtest, it achieves 93.75 PDMS and comes within 0.13 PDMS of the best ten-step diffusion or flow-matching setting.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of DriftingPlanner. The perception backbone and the condition encoder map the sensor input and the ego status e to a condition c. The generator gθ maps c and a latent zi ∼ N (0,I) to a trajectory xi in a single forward pass, and N latents give N generated trajectories x1, . . . ,xN of the same scene. During training (dashed boxes), each generated trajectory xi has one positive, the ground-truth (GT) trajectory y, and N−1 negatives, the other generated trajectories Jx jK of the same scene; generated trajectories of different scenes never form pairs. Attraction toward the positive (green arrow) and repulsion from the negatives (red arrow) sum to the drifting field Vi (black arrow), and gθ is trained to move xi toward the stop-gradient target Jxi +ηViK. The field is computed on the scaled trajectories and summed over several kernel temperatures (Sec. 3.3). The GT trajectory enters training only as the positive of the field; unlike regression planners, no L1 or L2 loss directly compares xi with y.

papers.title: DriftingPlanner: Drifting Generative Models for One-Step Trajectory Planning in End-to-End Autonomous Driving

papers.abstract: Streaming video question answering (QA) requires real-time reasoning over continuous video streams under strict latency and active-context budgets. Current streaming vision-language models (VLMs) often give confident yet ungrounded answers when queries are ambiguous or have false premises, or when relevant visual evidence is no longer in the active context. Proactive clarification can help, but must satisfy the same latency and memory constraints. We present StreamClarify, a training-free framework for grounded streaming QA that combines a pre-answer uncertainty check with hierarchical memory. The check uses the entropy of a binary pre-answer judgment as a lightweight uncertainty score to decide whether to answer directly or request clarification. To support re-answering, a temporal-pyramid KV cache maintains a bounded active visual context, while a CPU-side semantic retrieval archive provides access to historical frames. We further construct StreamClarify-QA, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,837 QA pairs from StreamBench and OVO-Bench, spanning standard, referential ambiguity, and unanswerable scenarios. Across three VLM backbones, StreamClarify improves Macro accuracy by up to 8.2 points over backbone-matched baselines. At comparable trigger rates, entropy-based selection achieves more than 18 points higher precision than random selection in identifying initially incorrect answers. Under oracle user guidance, clarification improves Macro accuracy by up to 3.5 points. We also report a controlled, oracle-assisted Qwen3-VL simulation on Ambiguous QA with generated questions and referent-only user replies, where the entropy-gated condition improves accuracy by 8.3 points.
bullets: Targets confident but ungrounded answers caused by ambiguous queries, false premises, or missing active-context evidence.
Uses a training-free entropy-based pre-answer uncertainty check to decide between answering and asking for clarification.
Maintains bounded visual memory with a temporal-pyramid KV cache plus CPU-side semantic retrieval of historical frames.
Introduces StreamClarify-QA, a 1,837-pair diagnostic benchmark covering standard, ambiguous, and unanswerable scenarios.
Across three VLM backbones, improves Macro accuracy by up to 8.2 points; oracle clarification adds up to 3.5 points, while entropy selection substantially outperforms random triggering.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of StreamClarify. The framework augments a frozen streaming VLM with a pre-answer uncertainty check in a twostage generation loop and hierarchical memory. (a) When pre-answer entropy does not exceed the trigger threshold, the system answers directly using the active temporal-pyramid KV (TP-KV) cache. (b) TP-KV keeps recent frames at full resolution and compresses older observed frames within a fixed active budget. (c) When entropy exceeds the threshold, the system requests clarification and converts the resulting user guidance into a retrieval query. (d) Semantic search retrieves relevant past clips from the archive and combines them with the active TP-KV context for answering after clarification.

Figure 2. StreamClarify-QA construction pipeline. (a) Dense captions are aligned to each query timestamp. (b) Eligible QA pairs are transformed into Referential Ambiguity or Unanswerable variants, followed by type-specific validation. OVO-Bench HLD questions are retained unchanged.

Figure 3. Trigger Precision and Recall on OVO-Bench with Qwen3-VL. Trigger rates are computed over all 281 questions. Gray bands span the methods’ expected random Precision (a: 42.35–48.04%, b: 44.13–46.26%). They are not confidence intervals. papers.abstract: Multi-LoRA serving allows many task-specific adapters to share a common base model, but scaling to large adapter fleets introduces substantial storage, loading, and execution overheads. Post-hoc compression can reduce the memory footprint of trained LoRA adapters, yet smaller ranks do not automatically translate into faster serving. For instance, padding, factor access, and generic kernels can obscure the retained low-rank structure, while independently recompressing thousands of modules also incurs significant preparation overhead. We present LoRAForge, a system connecting batched factor construction to rank-specialized execution through an explicit retained-rank representation. It supports two allocation policies: uniform retention ratios (LoRAForge-U) and spectral-energy budget allocation (LoRAForge-S). Both share FlashTSQR factor construction and the same serving backend. FlashTSQR exploits parallelism across modules and row tiles, accelerating factor construction by up to $2.28\times$ over matched library QR. In a fixed-work Qwen control, the shared runtime adds $1.17$--$1.22\times$ throughput across both compressed policies, with negligible gains on original adapters. Across 85 trained open-weighted Qwen and Llama adapters, the spectral policy's floored quality configuration retains about 7.7% of adapter parameters with fleet-average score drops of at most 1.2 points on a 0--100 scale. The same rank-floored $1/12$ spectral exports achieve substantial token-throughput gains on both AMD and NVIDIA GPUs.
bullets: Addresses storage, loading, and execution overheads when serving large fleets of task-specific LoRA adapters.
Uses an explicit retained-rank representation linking batched factor construction to rank-specialized execution.
Provides uniform-ratio and spectral-energy allocation policies, sharing FlashTSQR construction and a common serving backend.
FlashTSQR accelerates factor construction by up to 2.28× over matched library QR; the runtime adds 1.17–1.22× throughput in fixed-work Qwen tests.

A floored spectral configuration retains about 7.7% of adapter parameters with fleet-average score drops of at most 1.2 points across 85 Qwen and Llama adapters, while improving token throughput on AMD and NVIDIA GPUs.

papers.abstract: As learned manipulation policies become increasingly capable of solving practical manipulation tasks, assessing how well a task is performed becomes a fundamental challenge. While binary labels confirm task success, they cannot distinguish successful executions with different levels of geometric precision. To address this, we introduce SPECTRA, an object-centric framework for quantifying execution quality in manipulation of rigid objects. From a small set of oracle demonstrations generated in simulation, SPECTRA represents object interactions through progress-aligned relative poses. SPECTRA identifies which relative-pose directions are constrained and their admissible variations from demonstrations. These constraints establish a reference for evaluating robotic manipulation tasks. To score an unseen execution, deviations beyond the admissible variation are summarized by a Task Quality Index Q in [0,1]. Across seven simulated tasks, SPECTRA recovers constraints with 94% accuracy using 30 demonstrations per task. On rollouts from three learned policies, its scores achieve pooled Spearman correlations with human judgments of p=0.81 over all rollouts and p=0.61 among successful rollouts, exceeding all baselines in both subsets. Using the task reference learned in simulation, we use SPECTRA to select the highest-scoring demonstrations for training a diffusion policy on hardware. Exploratory results show higher success rate than training on randomly selected demonstrations.
bullets: Targets the problem that binary success labels cannot distinguish different levels of geometric precision.
Learns constrained relative-pose directions and allowable variation from a small set of oracle demonstrations.
Scores unseen executions with a Task Quality Index Q∈[0,1], based on deviations from the learned constraints.
Across seven simulated tasks, it recovered constraints with 94% accuracy using 30 demonstrations per task.
Its scores correlated with human judgments (Spearman p=0.81 overall; p=0.61 on successful rollouts) and supported selecting demonstrations for hardware policy training.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of SPECTRA. 1. Constraints estimation. Oracle demonstrations are segmented and aligned to shared progress samples. At each progress sample l, the task is represented by the relative poses between the reference object r, the manipulated object m, the gripper g, and the support object s. Deviations from the nominal pose T̄j,l are mapped to its tangent space, and eigen decomposition of their covariance Σj,l identifies the constrained directions Ij , whose standard deviation falls below σpin. 2. Policy evaluation. An unseen execution incurs cost only where its normalized deviation along constrained directions exceeds the tolerance z0. The average cost and a terminal gate give the Task Quality Index Q ∈ [0, 1].

papers.abstract: High-accuracy repetitive tracking is challenging for position-commanded manipulators whose low-level controllers are inaccessible, while constrained model-based iterative learning control (ILC) can require substantial manual parameter tuning. We present Differentiable Iterative Learning Control (Diff-ILC), an online bilevel framework that adapts the parameters of a constrained ILC update between physical robot executions. A closed-loop differential model is identified once from paired smooth perturbations and subsequently kept fixed. At each trial, a constrained quadratic program computes a feasible command correction, while a real-anchored next-trial prediction defines a task-level objective. Hypergradients are obtained by implicitly differentiating the locally active KKT system, enabling multiple computational parameter updates without additional robot executions. Experiments on a 6-DoF DOBOT CR3 across unseen planar and three-dimensional trajectories show substantially faster physical-trial convergence than fixed-parameter model-based ILC. Across the four primary trajectories, after only two trial-to-trial updates, Diff-ILC achieves 78.8% and 76.4% lower mean joint-vector and Cartesian RMSE, respectively, than fixed-parameter model-based ILC.
bullets: Addresses high-accuracy repetitive tracking when low-level robot controllers are inaccessible and ILC tuning is costly.
Identifies a closed-loop differential model once, then uses a constrained quadratic program for feasible command corrections.
Optimizes ILC parameters online with a real-anchored objective and KKT-based implicit hypergradients, without extra robot executions per update.
On a 6-DoF DOBOT CR3 across unseen planar and 3D trajectories, it converged substantially faster than fixed-parameter model-based ILC.
After two trial-to-trial updates, mean joint-vector and Cartesian RMSE were 78.8% and 76.4% lower, respectively, across four primary trajectories.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based vision-language-action (VLA) models cascade pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with diffusion action experts, but typically restrict the VLM to providing static conditioning. This separation limits how much pretrained perception and reasoning can guide action generation, especially in out-of-distribution settings. We introduce JADE, a Joint Action DEnoiser that enables the VLM and action expert to jointly refine actions. Our key insight is that structured action latents allow the VLM to read the current noisy action together with visual observations and language instructions. At every denoising step, the VLM contextualizes the noisy action and guides the action expert through gated cross-attention, so that its guidance evolves with the action being generated. We further supervise the VLM to recover clean action latents from noisy ones, which gives it a direct action-learning signal and couples perception with control. Additionally, joint denoising enables JADE to generate actions with fewer sampling steps, helping offset the additional cost of VLM participation. An adaptive step-size schedule further balances task performance and inference latency. On RoboDojo, JADE achieves an average success rate of 12.67%, the highest among the evaluated $π_{0.5}$-based methods, and is competitive with recent VLA and WAM foundation models pretrained at scale. It also improves performance on RoboTwin 2.0 and raises the average success rate across four real-world bimanual tasks by 20.8 percentage points compared with $π_{0.5}$.
bullets: Addresses the limited role of VLMs in diffusion-based vision-language-action models, where they usually provide only static conditioning.
Feeds noisy action latents, visual observations, and language instructions into the VLM at every denoising step.
Uses gated cross-attention to dynamically guide the action expert and supervises the VLM to recover clean action latents.
An adaptive step-size schedule balances task performance with inference latency.
Achieves the highest average success rate among evaluated π₀.₅-based methods on RoboDojo and improves results on RoboTwin 2.0 and four real-world bimanual tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Joint VLM-action denoising for VLA models; directly advances embodied action generation.
papers.title: Vision-Language Models Are Joint Denoisers in Robotic Action Generation
papers.tldr: JADE jointly denoises robotic actions with a vision-language model and action expert, improving out-of-distribution performance and reducing sampling steps.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots operating in shared, dynamic environments must respond to rapidly approaching objects while maintaining balance. We study dodgeball as a controlled test of this capability, coupling visual threat assessment with whole-body evasion, recovery, and target reacquisition. We develop a system that integrates onboard monocular perception, temporal ball-state and threat-flag estimation, and learned whole-body control. A ball detector supplies bounding-box histories, and a temporal estimator predicts relative ball position and a binary threat flag. Separate dodge/recovery and search/track policies share this interface and are composed to support repeated encounters. A three-stage curriculum first trains control with privileged ball states, then starts estimator supervision from stable policy rollouts, and finally replaces the actor's privileged inputs with estimator outputs. Analytic projection and perception randomization provide detector-like training observations without image rendering. Across approach-angle bins in controlled simulation, dodge success ranges from 97.8--100.0% for 5.0 m launches at 6 m/s to 33.2--40.8% for 2.5 m launches at 10 m/s, with 1000 throws per speed--distance condition. On a physical Unitree G1, controlled single-throw success exceeds 85% over more than 15 trials. A hardware sequence demonstrates full-azimuth target reacquisition followed by another dodge. These results demonstrate an integrated onboard-monocular-vision system under highly dynamic motions.
bullets: Addresses agile reaction and balance maintenance in dynamic shared environments using dodgeball as a controlled test.
Combines ball-detection histories, temporal threat estimation, and separate learned dodge/recovery and search/track policies.
Uses a three-stage curriculum to transition from privileged ball states to vision-based control, with analytic projection and perception randomization for training.
In simulation, dodge success varies from 97.8–100.0% for slower/farther launches to 33.2–40.8% for faster/closer launches; physical single-throw success exceeds 85% over more than 15 trials.
Demonstrates full-azimuth target reacquisition followed by another dodge on a Unitree G1.

papers.abstract: Garment flattening and folding require robots to identify garment structure during manipulation and adapt their actions as the cloth deforms. We present ClothDojo, a simulation platform that generates adaptive manipulation trajectories at scale across diverse garments and initial states and evaluates policies in closed loop. ClothDojo encodes each garment's canonical mesh coordinates as an NOCS texture, providing canonical surface-position cues through the visual interface of a pretrained vision-language-action model. We fine-tune the model on human demonstrations and corrections to obtain a data-generation policy. The policy autonomously generates simulated manipulation trajectories, and we retain rollouts that satisfy task-specific success criteria. Each retained trajectory is re-rendered under a randomly sampled appearance to provide RGB observations for downstream policies that do not receive NOCS. Across both tasks, the policy produces nearly 8,000 successful trajectories over hundreds of garments. RGB policies trained on these generated trajectories outperform those trained directly on the original human demonstrations and corrections across all evaluated garment splits and appearance settings. Evaluations across multiple policy models show that overall performance and appearance robustness vary across models and tasks, while generalization to unseen garments remains a common challenge.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting manipulation to changing garment geometry and appearance.
Uses NOCS-textured garment meshes to provide canonical surface cues to a pretrained vision-language-action model.
Fine-tunes the model on human demonstrations and corrections, then filters autonomously generated rollouts by task success.
Re-renders successful trajectories with randomized appearances for training policies that use only RGB observations.
Generated data improves RGB-policy performance over original human data across evaluated garment splits and appearances, though unseen-garment generalization remains difficult.

papers.abstract: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content-position or bias-position terms. Unlike RoPE, which encodes position via per-token rotations directly on the queries and keys, relative-position terms generally require pairwise offset-dependent computation or lookups, complicating their integration into fused attention kernels and introducing severe memory, bandwidth, and compute overheads as sequences scale. To address this bottleneck, we propose an exact attention algorithm that incorporates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled computation. Our method (1) uses offset-aware tiling to avoid redundant indexing and memory accesses, (2) computes only the necessary key/query-relation products and reuses them across token pairs in both forward and backward passes, and (3) uses offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation, eliminating atomic contention. We provide a unified, efficient Triton implementation across diverse relative-position attention mechanisms and evaluate it against naive and specialized implementations. For 8K-token sequences, our method speeds up the forward (backward) pass by 1.8-6.4$\times$ (2.0-21$\times$) and reduces peak memory up to 2.9-128$\times$ (1.4-54$\times$) over the strongest baseline for each mechanism, enabling long-context end-to-end transcription that is 1.8$\times$ faster and uses 2.4$\times$ less memory. Our method thus provides a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.
bullets: Addresses the pairwise offset computation and memory overhead that hinder efficient relative-position attention.
Introduces offset-aware tiled computation, reusable query/key relation products, and offset-based gradient aggregation without atomic contention.
Provides a unified Triton implementation supporting diverse relative-position attention mechanisms.
At 8K tokens, reports 1.8–6.4× faster forward passes, 2.0–21× faster backward passes, and up to 2.9–128× lower peak memory than the strongest mechanism-specific baselines.
Enables end-to-end long-context transcription that is 1.8× faster and uses 2.4× less memory.

papers.abstract: Municipalities publish service requests, geographic boundaries, weather observations, demographic estimates, and operational guidance through independently maintained Web portals. Civic analysis must combine these sources while preserving their schemas, source links, spatial and temporal scopes, and interpretive limits. Tool-using language agents can perform this integration, but existing task benchmarks rarely test whether a computed claim remains supported by the records used. We present CivicBench, a 400-task benchmark over four cities and two years that materializes civic Web data into frozen bundles for reproducible evaluation. Executable contracts score computation, source linkage, coverage, scope, qualified answers, and refusal when the requested conclusion is not supported. We also introduce Task-State Memory (TSM), which compiles tool observations into typed assertions, reconciles records only within compatible scopes, and retrieves a bounded state organized around unresolved constraints. Across nine completed model pairs, eight yield positive mean-score differences with 95\% semantic-contract-cluster bootstrap intervals excluding zero; the ninth interval crosses zero. The benchmark and memory framework make the records behind a claim inspectable at the point of decision.
bullets: Introduces a 400-task benchmark spanning four cities and two years using frozen civic Web-data bundles for reproducible evaluation.
Scores computation, source linkage, coverage, spatial and temporal scope, answer qualification, and refusal when evidence is insufficient.
Introduces Task-State Memory, which stores typed assertions, reconciles records only within compatible scopes, and focuses retrieval on unresolved constraints.
Across nine completed model pairs, eight show positive mean-score differences with bootstrap intervals excluding zero; one is inconclusive.
Designed to make the records supporting each claim inspectable at the point of decision.

papers.abstract: Selecting a reinforcement-learning (RL) policy usually requires additional environment interaction, while learned world models offer cheap but potentially biased evaluations. This raises two distinct questions: can shared model errors preserve pairwise rankings despite poor absolute values, and do they make a small number of real audits more informative? We derive an exact pairwise simulation identity and a relative bound separating common-mode Bellman residuals from policy-specific error. The analysis motivates RAVEL (Relative Auditing of Value Errors in Learned models), a selective policy tournament whose eliminations use held-out real outcomes. We test 45 SAC, TD3, and PPO policies per task in DMC cheetah-run and walker-walk. At rollout horizon 500, model rankings remain strong (Kendall tau = 0.962 and 0.800), and same-run differential-error ratios are 0.674 and 0.106. Yet mean paired audit-error correlations are only 0.007 and 0.090, and pairing changes standard deviation by -2.5 percent and +1.9 percent. Simultaneous intervals attain 99.98 percent and 99.75 percent coverage, but certify only 13.2 percent and 0 percent of decisions at eight audits. RAVEL improves low-budget walker-walk regret, whereas real-only successive halving is better at the largest budget, rejecting the precommitted twofold efficiency target. Frozen-model optimization lowers real return without increasing predicted return on average. Thus ranking fidelity, useful audit covariance, and upward model exploitation are distinct properties, separated in part by closed-loop trajectory divergence.
bullets: The study separates ranking fidelity, audit informativeness, and susceptibility to model exploitation as distinct properties.
It derives an exact pairwise simulation identity and a relative bound distinguishing shared Bellman errors from policy-specific errors.
RAVEL uses held-out real outcomes in a selective policy tournament to eliminate candidates with limited audits.
Model rankings were strong on DMC cheetah-run and walker-walk, but paired audit-error correlations were near zero and simultaneous intervals certified few decisions at eight audits.

RAVEL reduced low-budget walker-walk regret, while real-only successive halving performed better at the largest budget; frozen-model optimization reduced real return without improving predicted return on average.

papers.abstract: Automated prompt compilers search for or rewrite prompts under the implicit assumption that optimization consistently improves downstream task performance. We evaluate this assumption on frontier reasoning models through rigorous paired, same-day measurements. Across four optimizer families (genome search, profile-guided mutation, GEPA, and ESPO) and eight tasks, structured search yields no statistically significant accuracy gains on strong reasoners. However, a discrete structural genome provides essential architectural stability, preventing catastrophic bimodal seed-collapse (where unconstrained search collapses toward the judge floor in 3/5 runs). Through 190-problem evaluations on knowledge-intensive benchmarks, we establish a three-dimensional headroom typology: prompt optimization cannot compensate for intrinsic knowledge deficits or physical token truncation, but successfully resolves protocol and formatting errors. On gpt-6, while free-text reflective search (GEPA) yields a +.14 gain on a task where structured search remains flat, qualitative ablation reveals that ~.035 stems from judge-rubric reconstruction while ~.105 reflects genuine instruction refinement. Our pre-registered AutoAPC-Select deployment gate matches the oracle policy in 5/7 groups and rescues seed-collapse arms with zero regret. Finally, we expose silent backend-mixing in commercial APIs during outage windows and provide automated per-call audit verification tools to ensure empirical evaluation fidelity.
bullets: Across four optimizer families and eight tasks, structured search produced no statistically significant accuracy gains on frontier reasoners.
A discrete structural genome prevented catastrophic seed-collapse, which occurred in 3/5 unconstrained-search runs.
The headroom typology finds that optimization cannot overcome missing knowledge or token truncation, but can resolve protocol and formatting errors.
On gpt-6, GEPA improved one task by +.14; ablation attributed about .105 to instruction refinement and .035 to judge-rubric reconstruction.
The AutoAPC-Select deployment gate matched the oracle in 5/7 groups, rescued collapse-prone arms with zero regret, and audit tools detected backend mixing during outages.
