papers.abstract: Structured pruning reduces the size of large language models, often at the cost of lower accuracy. Whether this decline reflects diminished reasoning capacity or greater difficulty in sampling correct solutions is less clear. We examine this question across expert, FFN and layer pruning on four mathematical and coding benchmarks, comparing original and pruned models through pass@k at matched sampling budgets. Even after substantial pruning, some models match or exceed the original model's reasoning coverage despite lower pass@1, and solve problems left unsolved in the original samples. Retaining broad coverage, however, does not mean that correct solutions remain easy to obtain. Under severe pruning, diverse generated chain-of-thought (CoT) traces can coexist with increased repetition and less reliable generation. As correct answers become harder to sample, the additional attempts can sharply increase total token use even when individual responses become shorter. This separation between coverage and sampling efficiency also clarifies expert-selection gains, as methods with markedly different pass@1 can solve the same problems at large budgets yet require different numbers of attempts to reach a common coverage target. Pruning should therefore be assessed by both the range of problems a model can still solve and the sampling cost of obtaining correct solutions.
bullets: Evaluates expert, FFN, and layer pruning on mathematical and coding benchmarks using pass@k at matched sampling budgets.
Finds that some heavily pruned models can match or exceed original models in reasoning coverage and solve problems absent from original samples.
Shows that lower pass@1 can reflect reduced sampling efficiency rather than loss of solvable-problem coverage.
Severe pruning increases repetition and generation unreliability, potentially raising total token use despite shorter individual responses.
Argues that pruning should be assessed by both coverage and the sampling cost needed to reach it.

papers.abstract: Generative recommendation promises to simplify conventional multi-stage recommender systems by generating item Semantic IDs (SIDs) autoregressively. However, two obstacles limit its effective- ness in industrial settings: interaction-only supervision underuses the semantic knowledge encoded in pretrained language models, while beam-search likelihood ranks token sequences rather than directly estimating item relevance. To address these limitations, we propose HiGenTrans, a three-level framework that introduces LLM knowledge at the input, representation, and decision levels. First, Global Semantic Priming (GSP) adds an LLM-derived user representation to the beginning-of-sequence embedding, provid- ing a semantic prior before SID generation. Second, Hierarchi- cal Representation Transfer (HRT) aligns intermediate LLM representations with depth-matched GenRec layers through mean- centered projections and gated residual connections. Finally, Multi- Signal Decision Calibration (MDC) uses a lightweight mixture- of-experts calibrator to combine semantic relevance, generation confidence, and candidate-set context when reranking beam-search outputs. All semantic features are computed only from the observ- able interaction prefix, preventing target leakage, and can be cached offline. Experiments on three public benchmarks show that HiGen- Trans improves Recall@10 by up to 12.9% and NDCG@10 by up to 33.7% over the strongest baselines. These results demonstrate the value of transferring LLM knowledge at complementary stages of the generative recommendation pipeline.
bullets: Targets two limitations: interaction-only training misses LLM semantic knowledge, while beam search scores sequences rather than item relevance.
Uses Global Semantic Priming to prepend an LLM-derived user representation before semantic ID generation.
Applies Hierarchical Representation Transfer to align intermediate LLM and generative-recommender representations with gated residuals.
Uses Multi-Signal Decision Calibration to rerank beam outputs using semantic relevance, generation confidence, and candidate context.
On three public benchmarks, improves Recall@10 by up to 12.9% and NDCG@10 by up to 33.7% over the strongest baselines; features use only observable history and can be cached offline.

papers.abstract: Situational-safety benchmarks label each scene SAFE or UNSAFE and score a multimodal large language model (MLLM) against that label, usually by judging its free-form answer, and these scores guide deployment. We ask what such a label measures. A label score can come from the scene, the request or the benchmark's own files. We propose the Benchmark Card, seven measured fields that tell them apart, and fill it for six benchmarks. Only MSSBench chat leaks the label through its image files: image size alone reaches 82.3% accuracy, matching or beating six of seven commercial models. Elsewhere the signal outside the scene comes from design. In MOSSBench the item partition fixes the label, and on HoliSafe the request alone ranks pairs about as well as the scene. On our corrected chat split, the size rule falls to chance. We then introduce the Spot-Stop decomposition, which compares ranking with labelling on pairs of a safe and an unsafe scene. It splits the gap above a label-swap null into three parts: a threshold part, overlap between safe and unsafe scores, and order that holds only within a pair. Most of fourteen open MLLMs rank better than they label, beyond what their AUROC predicts. On chat, one shared threshold repairs a third to a half of the excess, and label-free recentering recovers it on balanced batches. Recentering on unlabelled scenes of the same situation improves ranking on VSCBench for 13 of 14 models.
bullets: Introduces the Benchmark Card, which separates safety signals arising from the scene, request, or benchmark files, and applies it to six benchmarks.
Finds severe leakage in MSSBench chat: image size alone achieves 82.3% accuracy, while other benchmarks contain design-based shortcuts.
Proposes Spot-Stop, decomposing the gap between ranking and binary labelling into threshold, score-overlap, and pair-specific ordering effects.
Most of 14 open MLLMs rank safe versus unsafe scenes better than they label them; shared-threshold calibration and label-free recentering reduce this gap.
Recentring on unlabeled scenes from the same situation improves ranking on VSCBench for 13 of 14 models.

papers.selection_reason: Audits and analyzes the behavior of Multimodal LLMs on situational-safety benchmarks, providing a framework for understanding label reliability.
papers.title: What Does a Safety Label Measure? Auditing Situational-Safety Benchmarks for Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Situational-safety benchmark scores can reflect dataset artifacts and calibration—not just an MLLM’s understanding of scene safety—so the paper proposes tools to audit and improve their interpretation.

papers.abstract: Financial restatements correct errors in previously published financial reports. Could managers' language in earnings calls warn of them in advance? Comparing 109 calls that precede restatements with 218 matched control calls, we find that the text predicts restatements but adds no detectable ranking gain beyond public firm information. A text classifier beats chance, largely because of restatements tied to special-purpose acquisition companies, but a model using only public information scores slightly higher. With refitting, the 95% interval for the gain from adding text (-0.05 to 0.11 AUROC) still leaves room for a meaningful benefit. A large language model scores higher, but we show that it names the exact ticker in 66% of masked transcripts, and it was released after the restatements occurred. Our results suggest that finding new warning signs in call text requires a public-information baseline and a check of what a language model already knows.
bullets: The study compares 109 calls preceding restatements with 218 matched control calls.
A text classifier performs better than chance, driven largely by restatements involving special-purpose acquisition companies.
A public-information-only model scores slightly higher than the text-based model.
The estimated gain from adding text remains uncertain, with a 95% AUROC interval of -0.05 to 0.11.
A large language model scores higher but may rely on memorized ticker information rather than transcript warning signs.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates the utility of language models and text classifiers for financial prediction, a standard application of LLMs in NLP.
papers.title: Do Earnings Calls Help Predict Financial Restatements? Evaluating Text Beyond Public Firm Information
papers.tldr: Earnings-call text can predict financial restatements, but it adds no clear ranking benefit beyond publicly available firm information.

papers.abstract: Streaming video LLMs can now commentate live gameplay, but they are trained and tested on the same games. We study cross-game streaming commentary, in which a model trained on one game commentates games it has never seen, and find that current commentators transfer their timing but not their knowledge of the game world. We propose StreamDuo, which pairs a trainable commentator with a frozen research agent that reads the wiki of the game being played. When the commentator sees something it cannot name, it sends the current frames, and the research agent returns a few wiki entries two seconds later while the stream continues. We train only the commentator, on a single game, in two stages. Information-gain labels teach it to ask only where an answer would help it say what the human caster said, and on-policy self-distillation from a copy of itself that sees the ideal answer teaches it to use noisy answers. Trained on Baldur's Gate 3 and tested on ten unseen games, StreamDuo raises entity recall from 0.082 to 0.116 over Proact-VL trained on the same data, cuts source-game leakage from 9.9% to 1.0%, and achieves the best timing and the highest judged liveliness and overall quality among streaming models.
bullets: Cross-game commentators preserve timing but struggle to recognize and understand unfamiliar game worlds.
The system queries relevant wiki entries when it encounters an unknown entity, while commentary continues with a short delay.
Training uses information-gain labels and on-policy self-distillation, requiring commentator training on only one game.
Trained on Baldur’s Gate 3 and tested on ten unseen games, it improves entity recall, reduces source-game leakage, and achieves strong timing, liveliness, and overall quality.
Results are scoped to streaming commentary on unseen games and rely on available game-wiki information.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on streaming video LLMs for live commentary, involving temporal reasoning, entity recognition, and cross-game transfer.
papers.title: StreamDuo: A Live Commentator and a Research Agent for Unseen Games
papers.tldr: StreamDuo improves live gameplay commentary on unseen games by combining a trainable commentator with a frozen wiki-reading research agent.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on skill documents, yet most retrievers rank them by description alone and ignore what earlier executions revealed, even though a relevant skill can hurt execution. We present CompSkill, which indexes skills with learned 512-d keys and compiles matched same-task comparisons into skill offsets and capped key residuals (KeyOpt), so experience changes which document the executor receives, never its text. Under a logistic outcome model with unknown task difficulty, matched comparisons cancel that difficulty and only discordant ones carry information; on support executions, predictions improve with each discordant task. An experience hypergraph keeps each comparison with its executor and document versions, recalls missed skills and grounds a cited review. Compact keys raise SkillRet NDCG@10 from 64.0 to 70.9 at one eighth of the dimension. With one document, CompSkill completes 256 and 260 of 332 ToolQA tasks with GPT-5.6-luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, more than every baseline, and stays on par with the strongest baselines on AppWorld and ALFWorld. On 332 newly generated ToolQA tasks, it completes 256 with GPT-5.6-luna, significantly more than BM25, SkillRet-8B, Tool2Vec and RankGPT; over all 844 ToolQA tasks, it completes 24 more than the strongest baseline. Selection matters beyond relevance: pairing the right guide with a same-database sibling instead of another database's guide costs 8 of 96 tasks. Code, models and support data: https://github.com/satoshinji2992/CompSkill
bullets: Motivation: Description-only retrievers ignore lessons from prior executions and may select relevant-looking but harmful skills.
Method: Learned 512-dimensional keys are updated with skill offsets and capped residuals from matched same-task comparisons; an experience hypergraph preserves executors and document versions.
Theory: Under an unknown task-difficulty model, matched comparisons remove difficulty effects, while discordant outcomes provide learning signals.
Results: SkillRet NDCG@10 rises from 64.0 to 70.9 using one-eighth-dimensional keys; CompSkill also improves ToolQA completion and remains competitive on AppWorld and ALFWorld.
Scope: The approach depends on support executions and comparison evidence; selecting the right same-database guide matters substantially.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses skill retrieval for LLM agents operating in embodied environments (ALFWorld), bridging language models and robot learning.
papers.title: CompSkill: Compiling Execution Experience for Skill Retrieval
papers.tldr: CompSkill improves skill retrieval by compiling execution experience into compact key adjustments, helping agents select more useful documents without changing their text.

papers.abstract: Can a language model learn better ways to reason about other people's minds by improving its own strategies, and are the strategies it learns actually right? We study this with cogrsi. A grounded reader marks who saw each event in a story and uses a short written principle to settle disagreements between its readings. With a principle written by experts, it beats self-consistency at the same token cost. A self-improvement loop then writes the principle itself. It keeps an update only if accuracy rises by a calibrated margin, and in one variant only if it also passes counterfactual test pairs. The learned principles transfer: on 800 BigToM pairs that no system had seen, each of them scores higher than the expert principle. We then check what the learned rules actually say. Each rule is translated into code and run on thousands of small stories with known answers. Most of them give a wrong answer in at least one situation they claim to cover, for example by treating a character who is in the room as knowing what happened even while asleep. Accuracy does not reveal which rules are wrong, and the counterfactual test does not fix this. A strategy can help in practice and still be wrong as a rule, so both need checking. Our code and data are publicly available.
bullets: A grounded reader tracks which characters witnessed events and uses a written principle to resolve disagreements.
Expert-written principles outperform self-consistency at the same token cost.
Self-improvement retains updates only when accuracy improves by a calibrated margin; one variant also requires counterfactual tests.
Learned principles transfer to 800 unseen BigToM pairs and score higher than the expert principle.
Code-based audits find that most learned rules fail in at least one situation, and neither accuracy nor counterfactual testing reliably exposes these errors.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models can interpret instructions and plan manipulation tasks, yet struggle when acting directly as robot policies. On RoboDojo, a large planning-execution gap separates high-level task decisions from physical execution: removing arm execution raises GPT-6 Astra's success rate from 22.5% under the reference control interface to 76.2%. We present Auriga, a task-agnostic agent harness that closes 68.3% of this gap in zero-shot manipulation without target-task trials or resets. In Auriga, the model makes all task decisions over an explicit task belief and acts through either direct tool calls or synthesized multi-step Python programs, while the harness supplies calibrated 3D measurements, finger-referenced dual-arm control, and a single admission gateway to the robot. Before motion, the model inspects a visual trajectory preview while simulation is paused; during execution, the harness checks declared stage tolerances and grasp bounds, stopping the robot on divergence and returning the measured discrepancy for in-place recovery. Developed across 13 cross-task capability iterations and frozen for evaluation, Auriga ranks first on the RoboDojo leaderboard with a 57.7% success rate (64.0 Score), more than doubling the reference harness on the same model, and remains first under scene randomization while learned policies drop by up to 33.9%. On RoboCasa365, the same frozen harness reaches a 73.2% success rate, outperforming VLA-assisted agents by up to 23.1% on composite tasks. Project page: https://auriga.stelledge.com/ Code: https://github.com/lose4578/Auriga
bullets: Addresses the large execution gap between high-level VLM decisions and physical robot control.
Combines explicit task beliefs, tool calls or synthesized Python programs, calibrated 3D sensing, dual-arm control, and a unified robot gateway.
Uses paused visual trajectory previews and runtime checks for tolerances and grasp bounds, enabling interruption and discrepancy-based recovery.
Achieves 57.7% success on RoboDojo and 73.2% on RoboCasa365 with a frozen, zero-shot harness.
Remains robust under scene randomization, though the abstract does not specify limitations beyond its evaluated settings.

Figure 1 Auriga completes manipulation tasks zero-shot within a single episode. A general-purpose model plans and acts through a shared harness, with no target-task exploration, demonstrations, or resets. The model localizes targets by multi-view triangulation, complemented by depth and point-cloud estimates (1), and reviews candidate motions before they are executed (2). The harness verifies each execution and stops when an action fails (3); the model then revises its plan and recovers from the current state (4–5) until the task succeeds (6).

Figure 6 Preview and verification in two rounds, drawn on the head-camera image. In the first round, the previewed gripper path moves to the object, closes on it, and lifts it to a checkpoint placed by the model, where the robot pauses and the model receives a fresh wrist view (inset 1). Once the gap exceeds the tolerance, the harness stops the arm and reports with a fresh view (inset 2), so the gripper does not open. papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses embodied manipulation using a task-agnostic agent harness that integrates vision-language models with robot control, closing the planning-execution gap.
papers.title: Auriga Technical Report: A Task-Agnostic Agent Harness for Zero-Shot Embodied Manipulation
papers.tldr: Auriga is a task-agnostic robot-control harness that substantially narrows the gap between vision-language planning and reliable zero-shot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Federated time-series forecasting is increasingly important in applications where temporal data are distributed across privacy-sensitive clients, such as environmental monitoring, smart cities, and industrial sensing. A central limitation of current continual-learning protocols is that they usually assume predefined task boundaries, whereas deployed forecasting systems receive an uninterrupted stream and must decide autonomously when adaptation is necessary. This paper addresses catastrophic forgetting in task-free federated forecasting under concept drift. We introduce a drift-aware continual-learning protocol in which each client monitors prediction-window RMSE, calibrates a robust median threshold from the offline base period, and triggers adaptation only after persistent degradation. To mitigate forgetting, we propose a TwoTierReplay mechanism that separates fixed offline representative memory from online memory. The offline tier preserves long-term knowledge learned during the base phase, while the online tier captures recent distributional changes after drift. Experiments on the Beijing Multi-Site Air- Quality dataset with 12 clients, three forecasting targets, and three horizons show that TwoTierReplay achieves the best stability-plasticity score in all nine target-horizon configurations. It improves over the strongest baseline by approximately 11.4%. These results suggest that explicit temporal structuring of replay memory is a practical and effective mechanism for task-free federated continual forecasting.
bullets: Addresses continual forecasting without predefined task boundaries in privacy-sensitive, distributed time-series settings.
Clients monitor prediction-window RMSE and adapt only after degradation persistently exceeds a robust threshold calibrated from the base period.
TwoTierReplay separates fixed representative offline memory from online memory that captures post-drift data.
On the Beijing Multi-Site Air-Quality dataset, it achieved the best stability–plasticity score across all nine target–horizon configurations.
It improved over the strongest baseline by approximately 11.4%; scope is limited to the evaluated dataset, clients, targets, and horizons.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Task-free federated continual-forecasting protocol. Each client maintains fixed offline and bounded online replay memories locally. A persistent drift alarm at any client triggers local adaptation at all K clients; the server aggregates only model parameters and rebroadcasts the updated global model.

Fig. 2. TwoTierReplay memory and local-update flow. The non-evictable offline tier stores representative base-period samples, whereas the bounded FIFO tier stores recently revealed stream samples. At a drift event, current samples and replay samples from both tiers are used for local adaptation.

TABLE II MEAN SIGNED STABILITY–PLASTICITY SCORE, SP = RMSEstream +AFbase , OVER THREE RANDOM SEEDS. THE AVG. COLUMN IS THE ARITHMETIC MEAN ACROSS THE NINE TARGET-HORIZON CONFIGURATIONS. LOWER VALUES ARE BETTER.

papers.selection_reason: Task-free federated continual forecasting with two-tier replay under concept drift.
papers.title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Task-Free Federated Continual Forecasting via Two-Tier Replay under Concept Drift
papers.tldr: TwoTierReplay reduces catastrophic forgetting in task-free federated forecasting by combining long-term offline memory with recent online replay triggered by persistent drift.

papers.abstract: Existing serving systems for large language models batch requests for many different LoRA adapters on one GPU. However, these systems reject adapters from other parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as DoRA, (IA), VeRA and OFT. One solution to this is to convert these adapters to LoRA, but this induces a significant memory and accuracy cost. Instead, we show that, under some modifications, a batched LoRA kernel can serve all of these methods exactly and efficiently. We achieve this by writing each method in one normal form, a LoRA computation with six slots for an adapter's own vectors and matrices. Some slots can merge into an adapter's weights at load time; the others remain live and induce a cost. We give ways to efficiently pay this cost and predict it from a zero-parameter byte model. We package this system, Scute, and build it on top of vLLM. Scute serves all five methods, coming as checkpoints from the Hugging Face PEFT library, in one batch, and it matches that library with a mean error of at most 1.5% of each adapter's effect. Under a burst of requests on an RTX A6000, a mix of these methods takes 5-17% more decode time than the same number of LoRA adapters. Furthermore, using Scute, the same GPU can serve 64 to 1024 (IA) and VeRA adapters at 1.5x to at least 2.5x the request rate of their LoRA conversions.
bullets: Existing systems typically reject DoRA, (IA), VeRA, and OFT adapters or incur memory and accuracy costs by converting them to LoRA.
Scute expresses five PEFT methods in a common six-slot LoRA normal form, merging some components at load time and efficiently handling the rest during serving.
A zero-parameter byte model predicts the runtime cost of the remaining live components.
Built on vLLM, Scute serves Hugging Face PEFT checkpoints in one batch with at most 1.5% mean error relative to the PEFT library.
On an RTX A6000, mixed-method bursts take 5–17% more decode time than equivalent LoRA batches, while (IA) and VeRA can achieve 1.5× to at least 2.5× the request rate of LoRA conversions.

papers.abstract: 3D visual grounding localizes objects in 3D scenes from natural language descriptions, requiring reasoning over semantics, spatial relationships, and multi-view observations. Training-free approaches avoid costly annotations but often rely on explicit scene transformation or scene-level frame selection, which may waste limited visual capacity on query-irrelevant regions. We observe that effective grounding should prioritize observations that provide evidence for the query rather than uniformly represent the entire scene. Based on this insight, we introduce QVR3D, a query-guided visual reasoning framework that operates on RGB-D observations using off-the-shelf foundation models. QVR3D combines Query-Guided Maximum Coverage (QGMC) for selecting complementary query-relevant views with Grounding Probability Estimation (GPE) that integrates instance confidence, attribute consistency, and relationship consistency. The framework supports both single- and multi-object grounding without task-specific adaptation. Experiments on ScanRefer and Nr3D achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, while QGMC also improves frame efficiency across multiple 3D vision-language tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/jwliao1209/QVR3D.
bullets: Targets inefficient scene-level view selection that spends visual capacity on query-irrelevant regions.
Uses Query-Guided Maximum Coverage to select complementary views relevant to the language query.
Uses Grounding Probability Estimation to combine instance, attribute, and relationship consistency.
Supports both single-object and multi-object grounding without task-specific adaptation.
Reports state-of-the-art zero-shot results on ScanRefer and Nr3D, with improved frame efficiency across multiple 3D vision-language tasks.

papers.abstract: In this paper we present the methodologies, results, and analysis used to deploy a decentralized safety verification algorithm on a robotic swarm to prevent collisions at runtime in an outdoor environment. Typically, approaches toward verification of swarms of cyber-physical systems (CPS) are evaluated solely in numerical simulations or in highly controlled, noiseless indoor environments. Our efforts to implement collision avoidance on a real swarm system outdoors have revealed that the underlying algorithmic assumptions juxtaposed against the implementation details of the target system are critical factors in a method's efficacy in the real world. Here we modify, enhance, and analyze a decentralized reachability-based method for collision avoidance on a size, weight, and power-constrained uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) swarm with the objective of illustrating the challenges of real-world CPS deployments as well as provide guidance for researchers in this space. Verification performance, resource utilization, and timing data were gathered over the course of 140 total outdoor vehicle flights, including 6 swarm flights composed of 8 UAVs, and used to improve collision-avoidance performance as experimentation progressed. Our extensive experiments show that the proposed decentralized runtime verification approach can efficiently verify the safety of multiple UAVs in real-time and help all agents take safe actions to avoid collisions. On average, each agent, using our open-source safety_checker library, takes approximately 500-520 ms to verify its safety for the next 4 s into the future, in which the reachable set broadcast time dominates the total verification time (~300-500 ms).
bullets: Addresses the gap between simulated or controlled swarm verification and real-world outdoor deployment.
Enhances a decentralized reachability-based collision-avoidance method for size-, weight-, and power-constrained UAVs.
Evaluated performance, resource use, and timing across 140 outdoor flights, including six flights with eight UAVs.
The approach enabled real-time safety verification and safe collision-avoidance actions for multiple UAVs.
Each agent verified safety approximately 500–520 ms ahead for the next 4 seconds; reachable-set broadcasting dominated runtime.

papers.abstract: Persistent homology (PH) is a mathematically principled multi-scale topological descriptor of shape and connectivity in data. It is widely applied in image classification, segmentation, and shape analysis across medical and aerial imaging, providing structural information that pixel-wise deep learning may overlook. Standard cubical PH decomposes an image into cubical cells (vertices, edges, and squares) and reduces them sequentially in filtration order. This sequential reduction has $Θ(n)$ parallel depth for an $n$-pixel image, limiting within-image GPU parallelism and constraining its use in topology-aware deep learning. We introduce CuPH, a GPU-based parallel algorithm for computing cubical PH on 2D images that operates directly on pixels rather than cubical cells. CuPH buckets pixels by filtration values, activates them with a level-synchronous sweep, and tracks connected components with a lock-free union-find method. We prove that CuPH produces persistence diagrams identical to standard cubical PH on integer inputs, with a stability bound for floating-point inputs. CuPH reduces parallel depth from $Θ(n)$ to $O(L\log n)$ for an image with $L$ intensity levels. We implement the level sweep as a single CUDA kernel, eliminating cross-level kernel-launch overhead. Empirically, CuPH is $18.6$--$99.6\times$ faster than the existing GPU baseline (CMP). As a drop-in PH backend, CuPH accelerates topology-aware classification ($4.2$--$16.7\times$) and segmentation ($8.3$--$44\times$) while preserving accuracy. It also enables computing full-image PH losses on high-resolution images, improving segmentation Dice by $2.2$--$4.6$ points over patch-local PH baselines and accelerating training by $25$--$31\times$.
bullets: Addresses the limited within-image GPU parallelism of standard, sequential cubical persistent homology.
Buckets pixels by filtration value, sweeps levels synchronously, and uses a lock-free union-find to track connected components in one CUDA kernel.
Proves equivalence to standard cubical PH for integer-valued inputs and provides a stability bound for floating-point inputs.
Reduces parallel depth from Θ(n) to O(L log n), where n is image size and L is the number of intensity levels.
Reports substantial speedups for PH, topology-aware classification and segmentation, while enabling full-image PH losses that improve segmentation over patch-local baselines.

papers.abstract: Semantic caching lowers the cost of serving large language models (LLMs) by reusing stored responses for similar requests. In multi-turn conversations, whether a cached response is acceptable depends on both conversations' histories, which embedding similarity of requests and histories predicts poorly (AUC 0.62--0.74 on five workloads). We therefore learn the \emph{reuse risk}, the probability that a cached response is unacceptable, from judge feedback, and choose a budgeted set of conversation states to cache by weighing the generation cost a reuse avoids against a price for unacceptable reuse. We propose CUCB-SC-MT, which learns a cache from logged conversations with a suboptimality guarantee, and CLCB-LS-MT, which learns online and has $\tilde O(\sqrt N)$ regret over $N$ requests when conversation states recur. On math-tutoring (SocraTeach) and movie-ticketing (Taskmaster-3) conversations, both achieve lower loss than prior semantic caching approaches: ContextCache, multi-turn variants of ElastiCache and vCache, and single-turn semantic caching at every cache budget. With 1,000 cache entries, CLCB-LS-MT avoids 35--41\% of the generation cost through acceptable reuses, against at most 22--25\% for the baselines, and lowers estimated serving latency by 19--35\%.
bullets: Request and history embedding similarity poorly predicts whether a cached response is acceptable, with AUC 0.62–0.74 across five workloads.
The approach learns reuse risk—the probability that a cached response is unacceptable—and balances avoided generation cost against reuse risk under a cache budget.
CUCB-SC-MT learns from logged conversations with a suboptimality guarantee, while CLCB-LS-MT learns online with ~O(√N) regret when conversation states recur.
On math-tutoring and movie-ticketing conversations, both methods outperform prior semantic-caching approaches at every evaluated cache budget.
With 1,000 cache entries, CLCB-LS-MT avoids 35–41% of generation cost through acceptable reuse and reduces estimated latency by 19–35%.

papers.abstract: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) aims to identify a query-view target in a satellite image, yet reliable instance grounding remains challenging under substantial viewpoint discrepancies. Although recent methods incorporate multimodal prompts, they insufficiently address the varying transferability of linguistic and visual evidence across views. Viewpoint-dependent descriptions (e.g., building facades visible in oblique UAV views but not in top-down satellite images) may become unreliable for satellite grounding, while visually similar instances further complicate target identification. To address these challenges, we rethink CVOGL from a visual grounding perspective and propose GAV (Grounding Across Views), a view-aware framework for constructing target-centered evidence and establishing discriminative cross-view correspondence. Specifically, view-aware referring reasoning mitigates viewpoint-dependent ambiguity, multi-token exemplar prompting and contrastive alignment strengthen visual-semantic correspondence, and scene-level supervision with alignment-based verification distinguishes competing satellite instances. We further introduce CVOGL-Text, a street- and drone-to-satellite benchmark with query-derived expressions. GAV achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoP-UAV with 62.55% Acc@0.5 (+18.19 percentage points) and outperforms evaluated click-point baselines on CVOGL-Text.
bullets: CVOGL must transfer target evidence between street/drone views and top-down satellite imagery despite major viewpoint differences.
GAV uses view-aware referring reasoning to reduce ambiguity from descriptions that are unreliable across viewpoints.
Multi-token exemplar prompting and contrastive alignment strengthen cross-view visual-semantic correspondence.
Scene-level supervision and alignment-based verification help separate competing satellite instances.
GAV reports 62.55% Acc@0.5 on MoP-UAV and outperforms evaluated click-point baselines on the introduced CVOGL-Text benchmark.

Scene-level discriminative supervision distinguishes competing instances, followed by alignment-based re-ranking for final target selection. papers.abstract: Unified-memory edge devices increasingly run LLM/VLM inference alongside time-critical CPU tasks for perception and control. GPU memory traffic can overwhelm these tasks, yet platforms such as DGX Spark expose neither bandwidth counters nor direct bandwidth regulation. We present Ripple, a CPU-GPU co-scheduler that combines model-derived GPU memory volumes with CPU completion feedback to regulate interference. Ripple divides inference into pausable, layer-based units and translates each CPU job's deadline slack into a GPU-byte budget, admitting work within the budgets of all overlapping jobs. Online updates track changing interference, while deadline-aware pacing and judicious SM footprint narrowing preserve inference progress. Implemented with SGLang engine hooks and a central scheduler, we evaluate Ripple on DGX Spark with four robotic CPU task mixes and LLM/VLM inference. It is the only evaluated approach that consistently meets the 2% CPU deadline-miss target and VLM deadlines across the tested deadline settings while retaining best-effort LLM throughput.
bullets: Addresses GPU memory-traffic interference with time-critical CPU perception and control tasks when hardware offers no bandwidth controls.
Divides inference into pausable layer-based units and converts CPU deadline slack into GPU-byte budgets.
Uses CPU completion feedback, online interference tracking, deadline-aware pacing, and narrowed SM footprints to regulate sharing.
Implemented with SGLang hooks and a central scheduler, Ripple was evaluated on DGX Spark with four robotic CPU task mixes.
It consistently met the 2% CPU deadline-miss target and VLM deadlines across tested settings while retaining best-effort LLM throughput.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-training can collapse language models, and many proposed remedies target overconfidence, yet their effects on confidence are rarely measured. We study a five-round self-training loop on Qwen3-1.7B, using three seeds per compared method, and distinguish confidence temperature (drift from a calibrated starting point) from discrimination (ranking correct answers above incorrect ones). Accuracy and overall discrimination remain nearly unchanged, but confidence sharpens and the most confident answers become less reliable. Matching predictive entropy to the calibrated starting model each round recalibrates nearly as well as label-based temperature fitting, at both 1.7B and 8B. Sharpening is not inherent to self-training: exact samples from a model's distribution have zero expected gradient. Instead, most drift comes from fitting each generated answer twice, with top-p truncation contributing the rest; removing both keeps entropy on generated outputs flat. Remedies affect the two properties differently: truncated cross-entropy, an entropy bonus, and single-pass training preserve temperature without improving discrimination, while focal loss and multi-sample targets improve discrimination but cause underconfidence. Reference-data mixing also overshoots. Pairing a ranking-improving loss with label-free recalibration achieves both.
bullets: Across five rounds, accuracy and overall discrimination stay nearly unchanged while confidence becomes sharper and highly confident answers less reliable.
Matching predictive entropy to the initial calibrated model recalibrates nearly as well as label-based temperature fitting, across 1.7B and 8B models.
Confidence drift largely comes from fitting generated answers twice; top-p truncation contributes additional drift, while exact distributional samples have zero expected gradient.
Loss remedies trade off differently: some preserve calibration without improving discrimination, while focal loss and multi-sample targets improve discrimination but induce underconfidence.
Combining a ranking-improving loss with label-free recalibration achieves both improved discrimination and calibrated confidence.

papers.abstract: When a World Action Model fails at control, is the bottleneck proposal generation or trajectory scoring? We introduce pico-WAM, a compact model with supplied physical state for tracing policy-dynamics interactions. Using 206 Push-T demonstrations and 15 training seeds, we compare data regimes and search configurations. Counterfactual branch training improves short-horizon cost ranking and enlarges the coverage advantage of policy-restarted over warm-started search by 4.8 percentage points; restart wins under both data regimes. Replacing learned trajectory scores with simulator costs improves coverage by 12.2 points while retaining learned proposals. Substituting simulator states in proposal generation alone shows no detected gain. Component diagnostics and a separate door-opening study show why better ranking need not yield better control or outperform imitation. These controlled interventions identify scoring as an effective improvement target in the tested setting and provide a reproducible protocol for diagnosing compact world models.
bullets: Studies proposal generation versus trajectory scoring using supplied physical state, 206 Push-T demonstrations, 15 training seeds, and controlled search interventions.
Counterfactual branch training improves short-horizon cost ranking and increases policy-restarted search’s coverage advantage over warm starts by 4.8 percentage points.
Simulator trajectory costs improve coverage by 12.2 points while retaining learned proposals; simulator states alone do not show a detected proposal-generation gain.
A separate door-opening study shows that better ranking may not translate into better control or outperform imitation.
Findings are scoped to the tested settings and support a reproducible diagnostic protocol for compact world models.

papers.abstract: With the emerging 6G paradigm where AI services operate over decentralized and resource-constrained edge infrastructure, performance of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge. This paper proposes HAFL, a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite-assisted hierarchical asynchronous Federated Learning (FL) framework, enabling resource-limited terrestrial clients to collaborate via Ground-Satellite Links (GSLs). Within this framework, LEO satellites serve multiple roles: as edge servers aggregating and broadcasting models, as clients accelerating training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing through Inter-Satellite Links (ISLs). Unlike conventional synchronous Jacobian-type updates, HAFL employs asynchronous Gauss-Seidel-type updates to enhance convergence speed. We provide theoretical convergences for convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex objectives, respectively, and formulate optimization problems to jointly determine optimal hyperparameters to minimize global training latency. Evaluations demonstrate that HAFL achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance for benchmark DNNs and datasets, offering promising FL systems across remote areas with 6G technologies, but much less global rounds and communication cost.
bullets: Targets decentralized, resource-limited terrestrial clients in space-air-ground integrated 6G networks.
Uses satellites as aggregators, broadcasters, additional training clients, and inter-satellite relays.
Replaces synchronous updates with asynchronous Gauss-Seidel-type updates and provides convergence analyses for convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex objectives.
Jointly optimizes hyperparameters to reduce global training latency.
Experiments show faster initial convergence, comparable final performance, and fewer global rounds with lower communication cost for benchmark DNNs and datasets.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon reasoning and agentic workloads strain KV-cache capacity and decode attention throughput. We present Jet-QSparse, a training-free method that combines compact NVFP4 cache storage with native FP4 query-key computation on Blackwell tensor cores. A dense scan scores the full key history and selects 128-token blocks for sparse FP16 value aggregation with FP32 accumulation, preserving higher precision in the output-forming step while enabling contiguous tile loads. Calibrated key centering and at most two BF16 pages per sequence and layer address quantization error; FP8 prefill uses a temporary arena while the persistent cache is packed directly from BF16 activations. Across four hybrid LLMs, a budget of 128 blocks per KV head shows no detected accuracy loss on the evaluated mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks, although some smaller budgets incur losses. With 64 blocks, Qwen3.8-27B achieves a $1.94\times$ end-to-end decode speedup over dense BF16 at 128K context and batch size 16 on one GB300, and the measured Qwen KV pools provide $2.58$-$2.76\times$ BF16's token capacity.
bullets: Targets KV-cache capacity limits and decode-attention throughput in long-horizon reasoning and agentic workloads.
Uses training-free NVFP4 cache storage, native FP4 query-key computation, dense history scoring, and sparse FP16 value aggregation.
At 128 selected blocks per KV head, no accuracy loss was detected across evaluated mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks.
At 64 blocks, Qwen3.8-27B achieved a 1.94× end-to-end decode speedup at 128K context and batch size 16 on one GB300.
Measured Qwen KV pools stored 2.58–2.76× as many tokens as BF16; smaller budgets could reduce accuracy.

papers.title: Jet-QSparse: Accelerating Agentic LLM Inference with 4-Bit Sparse Attention

papers.abstract: Digital image correlation (DIC) is a widely used non-contact technique for full-field displacement measurement. Data-driven deep-learning DIC offers rapid inference but may generalize poorly to unseen speckle patterns, deformation modes, noise levels, and illumination conditions. Classical optimization-based DIC and recent image-constrained neural formulations avoid labeled displacement data, yet their convergence and accuracy remain vulnerable to initialization, large rigid-body motion, fine non-uniform deformation, and gray-value disturbances. This paper presents a global-to-local hybrid neural DIC framework for robust pixelwise measurement. Stage 1 estimates a dominant in-plane rigid transformation through coarse rotation search, phase correlation, and masked refinement, providing a reliable initialization under large translation and rotation. Stage 2 represents the residual displacement with a hybrid Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN) and multilayer perceptron (MLP), and optimizes it using a valid-overlap, illumination-robust structural loss. The local gray-value model explicitly accommodates multiplicative and additive intensity changes. Simulated and real experiments demonstrate accurate and stable displacement recovery under noise, non-uniform deformation, large rotation, illumination variation, and degraded imaging conditions.
bullets: Addresses poor generalization of learning-based DIC and optimization failures caused by large motion, fine deformation, noise, and gray-value disturbances.
First estimates dominant rigid motion using coarse rotation search, phase correlation, and masked refinement for reliable initialization.
Then models residual displacement with a hybrid KAN–MLP neural field optimized using a valid-overlap, illumination-robust structural loss.
Explicitly accounts for multiplicative and additive intensity changes through a local gray-value model.
Simulated and real experiments show accurate and stable recovery under rotation, non-uniform deformation, noise, illumination variation, and degraded imaging.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a hybrid neural field for robust pixel-wise displacement measurement, contributing to spatial intelligence and geometric understanding in computer vision.
papers.title: Robust Pixel-wise Digital Image Correlation under Large Motions and Illumination Variations via a Global-to-Local Hybrid Neural Field
papers.tldr: A global-to-local neural DIC framework enables robust pixel-wise displacement measurement under large motions, complex deformation, noise, and illumination changes without relying on labeled displacement data.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models re-encode the full observation through a multi-billion-parameter vision-language model (VLM) at every control step, even though scene semantics evolve at roughly 1 Hz while reactive control requires 20-50 Hz. We present a VLA that decouples the two: a VLM runs as a low-frequency semantic anchor whose cached context is reused across control steps, while a flow-matching action expert operates at high frequency, consuming the cached semantics with a fresh, low-latency visual stream from a compact encoder pretrained on robot video with masked reconstruction, optical flow, and depth. The measured age $τ$ of the cache conditions the expert through adaptive layer normalization. Reusing the cache makes the policy a function of its age, and training covers that function explicitly: cache ages sampled from real episode history, plus an age-ramped pixel corruption that erases the stale snapshot the way deployed staleness corrupts content. On the asynchronous deployment stack, the recipe closes most of the staleness gap: on LIBERO-Spatial, 61.4% to 95.5% at a 2 s semantic refresh (95.9% at 1 s, within 1.6 points of the frequency-matched anchor); averaged over the four LIBERO suites, the deployed policy holds 95.2% at a 1 s refresh and 94.5% at 2 s against a 96.3% matched anchor. A forward-only chunk-boundary correction (soft-nudge), an autograd-free reformulation of real-time-chunking guidance, carries per-control-step re-planning without loss (97.1%) at zero added latency. The same lens exposes a second defect: under an instruction-scene mismatch the policy keeps manipulating the scene, and a chain-of-thought verdict gate trained on zero-cost negative episodes freezes execution exactly on mismatched instructions without hurting feasible success.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between roughly 1 Hz scene-semantic updates and 20–50 Hz reactive control.
Caches VLM context and combines it with high-frequency visual features from a compact robot-video-pretrained encoder.
Conditions the flow-matching action expert on cache age and trains it with realistic cache-age histories and staleness-mimicking pixel corruption.
On LIBERO, achieves 95.2% success at a 1 s semantic refresh and 94.5% at 2 s, versus 96.3% for a frequency-matched anchor.
Adds zero-latency chunk-boundary correction and a verdict gate that freezes execution under instruction–scene mismatch.],

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Leap-VLA overview. Slow system: the VLM runs at fslow over a token sequence that appends, after the prompt and the observation, the chain-ofthought region; it produces the cached context C and the chain-of-thought-supervised anchor features, and its reasoning region is emitted as the structured output shown. Because attention is causal, the prompt-region features the expert consumes are unchanged by the appended block (Sec. III-B). Fast system: the flow-matching expert runs at ffast, consuming C and fresh fast-stream features through one pluggable token-block interface: image tokens from the frozen motion-aware encoder (dual-frame, robot-pretrained with reconstruction, optical flow, and depth). The measured cache age τ conditions the expert via AdaRMS, proprioception enters as a dedicated input token, and the control rate f is passed to the action head; training samples τ from the physical episode history.

Perturbed-instruction failures therefore reflect instruction generalization rather than manipulation competence. A dual-frame pair (ot−δ, ot) is fused into a 6-channel input at the stem; a ∼49% row/column strip mask is applied jointly to both frames (pair-level tube masking), and the visible patches go through the compact encoder. Three lightweight decoders share the encoded features: the reconstruction decoder fills in both frames’ masked patches, the optical-flow decoder predicts the dense ot−δ→ot motion of masked patches, and the depth decoder predicts per-pixel depth for each frame. Panels show a held-out RoboTwin sample; decoder outputs are the training-time ground truth (WAFT flow, Depth Anything V2 depth, and the raw frames).

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Leap-VLA, a VLA model that decouples a low-frequency VLM backbone from a high-frequency action expert, directly addressing the efficiency of vision-language-action models.
papers.title: Leap-VLA: High-Rate Robot Control from a Low-Rate VLM Backbone
papers.tldr: Leap-VLA enables high-rate robot control by reusing low-rate VLM semantics while adapting to cache staleness with fresh visual input and age-aware action prediction.

papers.abstract: An AI can find a safe action faster than any human, but it must never decide what counts as safe. We present GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical digital engineering and operations, built on one partition of authority: learned models propose, rank, and accelerate; a symbolic rules engine checks every consequential action against hard limits before it executes; and validated physics confirms and decides. GURU runs a workflow as a closed control loop, with Navigation, Action, and Planning agents sharing one Common Internal Language and one training factory. Nuclear, aviation, and national-security guidance now requires this pattern; a harnessed language model keeps the model at the center, GURU puts a validated reference there. In computational fluid dynamics, the workflow raised the converged-simulation rate on unseen aircraft geometries from under 1 percent to 74 percent over 100 single-attempt cases, ran 54 live cases to Mach 6 on three facilities, and an ablation put the symbolic layer at 13 points of boundary-layer capture. Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters raised ParaView control success from 55 to 75 percent. In space domain awareness, where a language model cannot be trusted to decide, a frozen self-supervised world model under validated propagation scored highest of five methods at conjunction risk, including fully fine-tuned language models, with several-times-lower seed variance: the trustworthy design gives up nothing in accuracy, and the recipe transferred to reactor anomaly detection. A radar-to-avoidance debris pipeline was demonstrated in stages on a 2026 reentry; the hierarchy coordinates simulated teams of 200 aircraft. Training scaled near-linearly past 1,000 Aurora nodes and ran at 8,000. The approach extends to a control-grade microreactor digital twin with validated physics, not a learned model, as the safety basis.
bullets: Uses Navigation, Action, and Planning agents connected by a shared internal language and training factory in a closed-loop workflow.
Applies symbolic verification before consequential actions execute, with validated physics serving as the safety basis rather than learned models.
Improved unseen-aircraft CFD convergence from under 1% to 74% across 100 single-attempt cases; also demonstrated live Mach 6 cases on three facilities.
Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters increased ParaView control success from 55% to 75%; validated world modeling achieved the best conjunction-risk score among five methods.
Demonstrations span space-domain awareness, reactor anomaly detection, debris avoidance, large simulated aircraft teams, and a control-grade microreactor digital twin.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Data Factory outputs feed multiple automated-machine-learning frameworks trained in parallel. Candidate models are evaluated, compared, and ranked under Monte Carlo cross-validation, and the best predictor for each target is registered for downstream use in the workflow.

Figure 1: The GURU hierarchy. The Planning layer performs long-horizon forecasting and planning with JEPA world models and model predictive control. The Action layer turns plans into bounded decisions through optimization, parameter prediction, and anomaly detection. The Navigation layer executes and monitors operations across software and physical systems. Feedback flows bidirectionally, so plans constrain low-level action while observations update the planner. The middle layer, labeled Discrete actions in the figure, is the Action layer.

Figure 8: Knowledge-graph construction pipeline. Heterogeneous software sources are converted into a common, provenance-preserving observation representation, using vision-language models and automatic speech recognition (ASR) for video and deterministic or vision-language extraction for PDF documents, before being transformed into candidate claims and merged into a canonical knowledge graph. The shared intermediate schema allows document and video evidence to contribute to the same reusable representation.

Figure 21: The horizon-aware forecaster that produces the forward tracks. The extended model takes a look-ahead interval, up to 72 hours (at most 7 days), from as much as 28 days of history, and predicts the embedding of the whole future trajectory rather than a single point. Sweeping the look-ahead forward and backward turns the same model into a scanner across the historical archive for behavior staggered in time to avoid notice. The forecaster is a joint-embedding predictive architecture (LeCun, 2022; Assran et al., 2023).

Figure 17: Software-control architecture and knowledge-learning loop for ParaView. The Planning agent decomposes a user goal into structured actions; the Grounding agent maps each action and the current application state to executable code or GUI operations; and the Execution agent applies the selected operation and returns the resulting state. Tutorials, documents, and interaction trajectories provide knowledge for retrieval and role-specific training.

Figure 2: The GURU platform. The Learning Engine trains Navigation, Action, and Planning agents. The rules engine validates schemas, ontologies, constraints, and execution state. The agent society coordinates specialized agents through message pools and a shared workspace for auditable execution. Inputs span sensor streams, simulation outputs, documents, and direct user interaction, and the same platform drives applications in digital engineering, space operations, and reactor operations.

Figure 4: The Common Internal Language unifies agents through a shared semantic substrate for concepts, values, rules, and procedures, a uniform message format for the global workspace, and hierarchical task structures ready for planning and execution. Inset: a natural-language and geometry request is translated into typed, unit-aware attribute records with explicit provenance and uncertainty fields.

Figure 3: Lightweight clients capture multimodal input and workflow intent. Structured representations and high-dimensional embeddings are routed to backend services for reasoning, orchestration, and execution across local, cloud, and high-performance computing environments. Remote applications can be driven and viewed through a streamed display.

Figure 45: CFD simulation outcomes by grid generator and parameter selection. Stacked outcome shares for the earlier Pentagrow pipeline with predicted parameters, the extrusion-based generator with random parameters, and the extrusion-based generator with learned parameter selection. Outcomes are failed grid generation, failed initial solve, failed during adaptation, not finished, not converged, and converged. The rightmost configuration is the headline result in the text: 100 cases, one attempt each, of which 92 completed and 74 converged.

Figure 6: Current and target states are encoded into latent embeddings. The predictor learns action-conditioned transitions in that latent space, which lets agents forecast the behavior of an interface or environment without reconstructing raw observations.

Figure 7: Multimodal sources for software-knowledge acquisition. Document and video tutorials provide procedural demonstrations and application knowledge, while autonomous ParaView exploration produces state-action-outcome trajectories. The exploration examples show before-and-after application states; several attempts did not achieve the requested goal, which is why execution without an error is never treated as achievement. Both sources are transformed into reusable observations for knowledge extraction and agent training.

Figure 49: Quantitative comparison of anomaly-detection methods and JEPA scoring rules. (Top left) Balanced accuracy at the warning threshold by method. (Top right) Correct-classification rate per fault group. (Bottom left) Temporal anomaly scores for four JEPA scoring variants. (Bottom right) Balanced accuracy and average precision for each scoring rule. Embedding kNN gives the best and most consistent balance across fault families.

Figure 46: Frozen JEPA matches or exceeds configuration-matched baselines on conjunction risk, with seed-stable performance. Mean binary F1-score over 10 seeds on the shared test split, with every method trained under the same budget (batch size 96, 1,000 training steps); labels show mean ± standard deviation. The frozen JEPA encoder with a small MLP head scores highest, and its low seed-to-seed variance shows the result does not depend on a lucky seed, even though none of its backbone weights are trained.

Figure 11: GURU CFD Suite workflow for high-speed aerial vehicles. The figure shows one representative airframe from the live run described above, the Fury: from a natural-language prompt, GURU configured an aerodynamic sweep at Mach 2 to 4, 40 to 50 km, plus or minus 5 degrees angle of attack, about 1M cells, and autonomously submitted it to HPC. Post-processed output for the Fury airframe shows Mach contours and surface pressure-coefficient distribution, the computational mesh, converged residual histories, and axial surface pressure and heat-flux profiles. Video: https://youtu.be/GQIJjjVolNY

Figure 13: The generation model maps image embeddings and augmented renderings into meshable vehicle geometries. Representative outputs span 11 aerial vehicle classes, from fixed-wing subsonic and transonic to supersonic and hypersonic, eVTOL, flying-wing and blended-wing-body, delta-wing and canard, high-lift, rotorcraft, lighter-than-air, and unconventional configurations, with 673 geometries reaching successful volume-grid generation.

Figure 36: Historical traffic replay with modeled hazard bands and candidate reroutes. The dashboard combines recorded aircraft tracks, event evidence, illustrative debris bands, and proposed route alternatives. The evidence panel distinguishes published predictions, event confirmation, and traffic records; the decision panel summarizes modeled intersections and rerouting costs. The displayed alternatives are simulation outputs, not aircraft actions that occurred during the event. Also identified in the dashboard - limits on route completion, cost estimation, and multi-aircraft conflict assessment. Video: https://youtu.be/Jtyf78QsXlE

Figure 20: Two-phase design. In pre-training, the world model learns from context and target windows split from up to 28 days of state-vector history, with a slow exponential-moving-average target encoder and a Gaussian anti-collapse regularizer optimized under an MSE objective in embedding space. In the conjunction stage, the frozen encoder produces embeddings for the history of two objects, which are combined into a symmetric pair representation and read by a conjunction head trained on public conjunction-message labels to output a collision risk score.

Figure 43: OpenMC drum-angle runs are fit to a smooth reactivity model used by the point-kinetics controller. The MPC then chooses drum rotations to track a scheduled power target or to maximize power while holding a fuel-temperature cap.

Figure 18: Ablation of context, retrieval, and learned adaptation for ParaView software control (successful attempts out of 150 per configuration). Explicit program state, API information, and capability catalogs improve base-model performance, while graph retrieval is most valuable when supplied context is limited. Under full context (state, API inventory, and catalogs), the role-specific Planning and Grounding adapters provide additional gains, with retrieval and adaptation showing complementary effects in some configurations.

Figure 9: Knowledge-graph snapshot for ParaView by semantic family. The graph contains 105,125 nodes and 106,202 edges from 64 source packages (42 PDF, 19 video, two API, and one exploration package), including 1,552 exact API definitions, of which 1,478 carry nonempty signatures. The panels count nodes in the ten semantic families; the remaining nodes include procedure steps and transitions, which are stored as supporting control-flow records. These are corpus-wide counts, not counts of facts relevant to any single goal. Automatic semantic matching between documentation and exploration was disabled in this release, so shared storage should not be read as complete automatic linkage.

Figure 19: 2D projection of JEPA world-model embeddings for orbital time-series windows. Non-maneuver windows and maneuver windows separate cleanly, and a simple linear boundary achieves an area under the curve near 0.98 with no labeled supervision during pre-training and no deep downstream classifier fit to the embedding.

Figure 41: Learned models predict dose rate and the effective multiplication factor for each candidate shielding layout, while the optimizer searches material configurations that keep the multiplication factor near target and reduce external dose. Later iterations reach lower-dose designs while keeping the reactor viable.

papers.selection_reason: Presents GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical operations, combining learned models with symbolic rules and validated physics, relevant to embodied agents and interactive world models.
papers.title: GURU: A Hierarchical Neuro-Symbolic Multi-Agent System for Verification-Aware Automation of Mission-Critical Digital Engineering and Operations
papers.tldr: GURU is a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system in which learned models propose actions, symbolic rules enforce hard safety limits, and validated physics makes final decisions for mission-critical operations.

papers.abstract: Pretrained text embeddings encode semantic structure in high-dimensional continuous spaces whose coordinates are difficult to interpret. We introduce Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding (ISBC), which learns a small set of binary dimensions from frozen embeddings without taxonomy labels or downstream outcomes. A trainable encoder and affine decoder combine reconstruction with controls on activity, factor utilization, dependence, and activation uncertainty. Individual bits and their conjunctions select overlapping document groups; complete activation profiles provide finer contexts for conditional comparisons. We evaluate these representations across corpora, backbones, and code configurations through reconstruction, geometry, predictive probes, and document inspection. Empirical cases identify both distinctions within existing categories and shared content across their boundaries. In a mixed-domain corpus, the most frequent profiles predominantly identify source collections, while selected within-source comparisons reveal sentiment and migration contrasts. Selected associations persist in additional documents encoded without refitting. In an engagement application, bits alone improve prediction of log-transformed outcomes over a constant reference, while their combinations identify within-event content contrasts associated with engagement. The results support using binary coordinates and their combinations for empirical interpretation, with complete profiles providing a fine, partly initialization-dependent description rather than a unique discrete taxonomy.
bullets: Learns binary dimensions without taxonomy labels or downstream outcomes.
Combines reconstruction with controls for sparsity, factor use, dependence, and activation uncertainty.
Uses bits, conjunctions, and complete activation profiles for document grouping and conditional comparisons.
Evaluations across corpora and embedding backbones find source, sentiment, migration, and engagement-related contrasts.
Complete profiles offer fine-grained but partly initialization-dependent descriptions, not a unique taxonomy.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks that benefit from sustained personalized support through long-term memory. Existing memory-augmented methods retrieve and use memory primarily from the initial request, with limited awareness of ongoing execution and emerging personalization needs. Agents may therefore overlook user preferences and project constraints during multistep tasks. We propose Pulse, a streaming personalization method for long-horizon tasks. An independent, lightweight memory agent continuously monitors execution, identifies emerging personalization needs and potential preference conflicts, and uses user and project memories to provide targeted interventions at appropriate stages. Reinforcement learning optimizes when and how the memory agent intervenes, improving the timeliness and accuracy of personalized support. Pulse scores 71.9% on $π$-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, achieving the highest overall scores among the compared methods on both datasets while improving task execution efficiency.
bullets: Existing memory methods rely mainly on the initial request, potentially missing preferences and constraints that emerge during execution.
Pulse uses an independent lightweight memory agent to monitor task progress and identify personalization needs or preference conflicts.
The agent retrieves user and project memories and delivers targeted interventions during relevant stages.
Reinforcement learning optimizes the timing and content of interventions.
Pulse scores 71.9% on π-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, with the highest overall scores among compared methods and improved task efficiency.

papers.abstract: Early-exit language models decide for each token how much computation to spend, usually by stopping once the prediction is confident. Yet a token is not a fixed unit: tokenizers cut words into different numbers of pieces in different languages. We ask where inside a word such a policy spends its budget. In Qwen3, along two adaptive axes (the timesteps of a spiking conversion and the layers of the original Transformer), confidence stopping gives the continuation pieces of a word less computation than its first piece in English, German, and Turkish, but more in Bangla. Segmentation drives this. Re-segmenting the same parallel passages with BPE-dropout shifts the gap by up to eight exits on both axes, small models trained under two tokenizers shift Bangla's gap by six exits, and BLOOM and mGPT, which split Bangla less finely, give it the English pattern. Characters per token do not predict the gap across languages; within-word surprisal explains 75% of its variance. A learned stopping head beats confidence stopping by 7 to 8 points, but gains less than one point over the best mix of fixed exits at equal cost, and sometimes loses. All results come from offline analysis, not measured speedups.
bullets: In Qwen3, continuation pieces generally receive less computation than first pieces in English, German, and Turkish, but more in Bangla.
Changing tokenization with BPE-dropout shifts within-word computation gaps by up to eight exits; tokenizer choice also reverses Bangla’s pattern across models.
Characters per token do not explain the gaps across languages, while within-word surprisal explains 75% of their variance.
A learned stopping head improves over confidence stopping by 7–8 points, but offers less than one point over the best fixed-exit mixture at equal cost and can sometimes underperform.
The study is based on offline analysis, so it does not measure actual speedups.

papers.abstract: Image denoising is a fundamental problem in mobile photography. Despite a large number of solutions proposed for this task, the majority of them are trained on synthetically produced noisy images, and are additionally too computationally heavy for processing full-resolution images on mobile devices. This creates a need for efficient deep learning-based models that are not only performant but can also be deployed on constrained mobile hardware. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose the participants to design fast solutions that can denoise Full HD resolution photos while running on popular smartphone GPUs from Qualcomm and Arm. For this, the participants were provided with a large-scale dataset consisting of noisy-clean image pairs captured in the wild. The runtime of all models was evaluated on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 chipsets with the Adreno and Mali GPUs, respectively. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to perform high-quality image denoising under 100 milliseconds on both platforms while reaching a PSNR score of over 37 dB. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.
bullets: Targets the computational and realism limitations of existing denoising methods trained on synthetic noise.

papers.abstract: Image super-resolution is widely used on mobile devices for upscaling various types of image data. This creates a need for efficient deep learning-based models that are not only performant but can also be deployed on neural processing units (NPUs) present in the majority of mobile and IoT chipsets. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose the participants to design fast solutions that can upsample images from Full HD to 4K resolution while running on popular mobile NPUs from Qualcomm and MediaTek. For this, the participants were provided with the DIV2K dataset and trained models to do an efficient 3X image upscaling. The competition had two tracks: in the first track, the models had to be fully quantized (INT8), and the runtime of all models was evaluated on the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 NPU. In the second track, the participants were developing floating-point solutions that were evaluated on the MediaTek Dimensity 9500 NPU. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to reconstruct 4K images under 5 milliseconds while reaching a PSNR score of 30 dB. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing plays an important role in imitation learning for contact-rich manipulation by providing direct observations of physical contact with objects. Recently, several tactile foundation models (TFMs) have been proposed to learn general-purpose tactile representations through pretraining on large-scale tactile datasets. However, how these pretrained tactile representations should be leveraged for end-to-end imitation learning remains insufficiently explored. In this work, we integrate multiple TFMs into Diffusion Policy and systematically evaluate their effectiveness for contact-rich manipulation under common experimental settings. We further investigate adaptation strategies, including encoder fine-tuning and task-specific mid-training, to understand how pretrained tactile representations can be effectively used for downstream imitation learning. Through extensive evaluation across diverse manipulation tasks in both real-world and simulation environments, including more than 5,000 real-world policy rollouts, we provide empirical insights into the use of TFMs for end-to-end imitation learning. Project page: https://mmurooka.github.io/tfm4il-project-page/
bullets: Integrates multiple tactile foundation models (TFMs) into Diffusion Policy.
Studies encoder fine-tuning and task-specific mid-training as adaptation strategies.
Evaluates diverse manipulation tasks in both real-world and simulation settings.
Reports extensive empirical evaluation, including more than 5,000 real-world policy rollouts.
Provides practical insights into using pretrained tactile representations for downstream imitation learning.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained robotic manipulation requires instruction grounding, robust perception, and precise contact control. We describe our submission to the MetaFine Open Competition at CoRL 2026. Five independently trained models use a common architecture with frozen DINOv2 and CLIP encoders, trainable language-conditioned feature modulation, and task-specific action heads. We improve demonstrations through contact-aware grasp filtering, instruction-matched data, and expert correction of insertion failures. At inference, task-dependent strategies include photometric test-time augmentation, stochastic action averaging, and uncertainty-triggered replanning. Our submission achieves an official overall score of 0.914 and ranks third among 15 teams. We analyze the models and their task-specific behavior.

papers.abstract: We test whether Koopman structure helps a differentiable world model used to train a simulated Unitree G1 whole-body tracking policy by backpropagation through imagined rollouts, replacing the MLP world model of an otherwise unchanged pipeline. It does not: return is at best equal (0.823 versus 0.830), one-step error on identical data is 1.3 to 1.6 times the MLP's, and training is about 15% slower. Lifted rollouts diverge or fail to train policies; of the schemes tested, re-lifting at every imagined step trains best. Re-lifting never uses the lifted linear dynamics and leaves a model affine in the action, with state-dependent offset and slope; an action-affine MLP also predicts worse, so the accuracy cost belongs to this class. At a fixed state, the dynamics' curvature in the action explains only part of it. Across states, the policy's actions span a curved region, so an affine model fits policy data only as the tangent at the policy's action, the operating point: on G1, the MLP's tangent there is as accurate as the MLP; at the mean action, 31 times worse. The offset must encode, from the state alone, where the policy acts, whereas an MLP reads the action. Supplying the policy's action removes most of the remaining gap on G1, Ant and Humanoid. The only tested online repair approaching the MLP feeds the action into the nonlinear lift, abandoning the structure. For this use, the MLP world model remains the better choice.
bullets: Replacing the MLP with Koopman-based models yields comparable-or-worse return, higher one-step error, and roughly 15% slower training.
Lifted rollouts diverge or fail to train policies; re-lifting each imagined step performs best but does not use lifted linear dynamics.
The resulting action-affine structure poorly represents the curved state-dependent action regions visited by the policy.
Providing the policy action to the model recovers most of the accuracy gap across G1, Ant, and Humanoid; nonlinear action lifting largely abandons the intended structure.
For this setting, the standard MLP world model remains preferable.
