papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generators produce videos block by block from historical context. They are trained within a bounded horizon, whereas inference can extend far beyond it, causing temporal consistency to gradually decrease. Existing methods focus on eliminating this mismatch, but we instead ask whether the historical context used in training remains suitable for inference. Each block reads historical context in two stages, when denoising generates it and when committing writes it into the KV cache for later blocks. We find that older historical context such as the sink helps denoising but can hurt later blocks when read during committing, even in generators trained to read it there. We also show that as committing reads more preceding blocks, clip-to-clip Subject Consistency rises, plateaus, and then declines. We therefore propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain. Each committing pass reads only the preceding block's stored KV, while denoising keeps the base historical context. Commit Forcing improves 60-second VBench Quality and Total on all 6 generators, by up to 1.27 and 1.10 points. Its consistency gains extend to 240-second videos, and it achieves an 82.9% win rate in overall human preference on 120-second LongLive videos.
bullets: Long-video autoregressive generators lose temporal consistency when inference extends beyond their training horizon.
Older context can help denoising but harm later blocks during KV-cache committing, revealing a mismatch in how history is used.
Subject consistency rises, plateaus, and declines as committing reads more preceding blocks.
The training-free Commit Forcing rule makes committing read only the preceding block’s stored KV while preserving the base context for denoising.
It improves VBench Quality and Total across all six generators, with consistency gains extending to 240-second videos and an 82.9% human-preference win rate on 120-second videos.

papers.abstract: Mobile UI understanding and generation require both fine-grained component perception and reliable structured synthesis. Inspired by the unified direction introduced by UI-UG, we present UI-UG 2, a compact 4B-parameter multimodal large language model (MLLM) that advances mobile UI Understanding and Generation with broader task coverage, a front-end-aligned taxonomy, and online render-aware reinforcement learning. UI-UG 2 constructs a multi-source understanding corpus from RICO, VINS, Android in the Wild, and Android Control, annotated with an 80-category two-level UI taxonomy aligned with front-end component semantics, and pairs it with over 5,000 requirement-screenshot-JSON tuples for progressive structured UI generation through a domain-specific language (DSL). For understanding, UI-UG 2 introduces decomposed rewards for category prediction, OCR fidelity, color recognition, dense grounding, and GUI grounding. Unlike the offline Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)-style generation optimization in UI-UG, UI-UG 2 optimizes generation through end-to-end online Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO): sampled DSL outputs are rendered with a Playwright-based server-side pipeline and evaluated using LLM-as-a-Judge and contrastive preference ranking. Experiments show that UI-UG 2 achieves the strongest referring and dense-grounding results among the evaluated models on our 80-category benchmark, and achieves the best composite generation score among compared models at a compact scale (4B). More importantly, we observe a consistent understanding-to-generation transfer: adding fine-grained UI perception supervision improves generation quality under a fixed training budget, suggesting that component-level semantics provide a shared representational foundation for both tasks.
bullets: Targets reliable perception of UI components and synthesis of structured, executable interfaces.
Uses an 80-category, two-level taxonomy with supervision for category prediction, OCR, color recognition, and grounding.
Generates UIs progressively as DSL outputs from requirement–screenshot–JSON training tuples.
Applies online GRPO with server-side rendering and LLM-based and contrastive preference evaluation.
Reports strongest referring/dense-grounding results on its benchmark and the best composite generation score among compared compact models; finer perception also improves generation.

papers.title: UI-UG 2: Advancing Mobile UI Understanding and Generation with Fine-Grained Supervision and Reinforcement Learning

papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of mobile devices has democratized video recording, but a stark aesthetic divide persists between casual, low-cost captures and high-cost cinematic productions. Bridging this gap requires upgrading heterogeneous production elements, such as lighting, specialized costumes, and materials, without altering the core layout, identity, and temporal motion of the original footage. However, this task is heavily bottlenecked by two important challenges: 1) Lacking a high-quality paired training data specifically designed to handle complex low-to-high appearance shifts. 2) Ignoring the capacity of current video editing models to perceive and enhance the multiple low-cost compositions. To address these issues, we present CineCraft-120K, a large-scale dataset of aligned low- and high-cost video pairs annotated with pair-aware editing prompts. CineCraft-120K features a diverse, high-resolution and high-cost Cinematic Crafting bank spanning decades of media production, meticulously taxonomized into 5 broad domains and 23 fine-grained sub-categories. It also provides element-level mapping between low- and high-cost counterparts, offering pair-aware rich textual prompts that precisely detail the required aesthetic transformations while anchoring structural layout. Architecturally, we propose a simple yet effective dual-memory feature adapter, where a text-memory expands semantic capacity for low2high appearance changes, and a hint memory supplies layer-wise visual feature corrections of high-cost element before context injection. Extensive experiments and ablation studies demonstrate the superiority of CineCraft-120K for low-to-high-cost video editing, alongside the effectiveness of our dual-memory adapter.
bullets: Addresses the gap between casual mobile videos and high-cost cinematic productions without changing core layout, identity, or temporal motion.
Introduces CineCraft-120K, a high-resolution dataset of aligned low-/high-cost video pairs with pair-aware editing prompts.
The dataset covers five broad domains and 23 fine-grained categories, with element-level mappings and structural editing guidance.
Proposes a dual-memory feature adapter: text memory expands appearance semantics, while hint memory provides layer-wise visual corrections.
Experiments and ablations report effective low-to-high-cost video editing and validate the adapter design.

papers.abstract: Simulation-based VLA evaluation often treats matching task, seed, and episode identifiers as sufficient evidence that two policies faced identical test conditions. Under specific vectorized reset and autoreset conditions, different termination timing can change subsequent initial-state assignment, so the same episode index need not mean the same test state. We present an evaluation-integrity framework for paired comparison - invariants I1-I5, provenance logging, optional scene fingerprints, and an automated checker - and a controlled LeRobot 0.6.1 LIBERO harness study with emulated controllers. Four evidence levels are kept separate: (A) mixed-horizon Sync wave-1 IDs [20, 5, 22, 7] vs [4, 5, 6, 7]; (B) homogeneous separate-job Sync control (16 cells, 0 ID/fingerprint mismatches); (C) Async+Freeze batch-size map differences (12 I3 mismatches; bs=8 incomplete; mechanism unisolated); (D) a synthetic McNemar illustration only. Controllers were emulated and no real-VLA shared-vector experiment was completed. We recommend checking declared/resolved init-state identity and provenance before paired statistics. We do not claim that published VLA leaderboards are generally invalid.
bullets: Vectorized reset and autoreset behavior can make identical task, seed, and episode identifiers refer to different states when termination timing differs.
The framework defines invariants I1–I5, provenance logging, optional scene fingerprints, and an automated checker.
A controlled LeRobot 0.6.1 LIBERO harness study found no mismatches in a homogeneous separate-job control, but identified 12 map mismatches in an Async+Freeze batch-size comparison.
The study used emulated controllers and did not complete a real-VLA shared-vector experiment.
The authors do not claim that published VLA leaderboards are generally invalid.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become an important paradigm for improving multimodal large language models (MLLMs), especially with automatically verifiable rewards. Self-supervised visual pretext tasks provide such rewards without human annotations. However, existing methods mainly exploit within-instance structure, offering limited supervision for cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison. We introduce Group-and-Order Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning (GO-SSL), a cross-instance jigsaw framework for vision-centric MLLM post-training. Given two visual instances, GO-SSL mixes their local elements and trains the model to group them by instance of origin while recovering the order within each group, coupling instance-level comparison with spatial, temporal, or geometric structure recovery. This paired formulation turns the same unlabeled data into richer verifiable supervision through diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum. We instantiate GO-SSL mainly on cross-image jigsaw tasks and further extend it to 3D depth and video temporal ordering. Across diverse benchmarks, GO-SSL consistently improves over the base MLLM and prior self-supervised post-training baselines, with clear gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding. Further evaluations across model scales and families support its generality. These results suggest that cross-instance comparison provides a useful self-supervised RL signal for improving transferable visual understanding in MLLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/SEU-VIPGroup/GO-SSL.
bullets: Addresses the limited cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison learned by prior within-instance self-supervised methods.
Pairs two visual instances, mixes their local elements, and trains the model to separate them by origin while restoring spatial, temporal, or geometric order.
Uses diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum to create richer automatically verifiable rewards from unlabeled data.
Applied to cross-image jigsaws, 3D depth, and video temporal ordering, with reported gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding across benchmarks.
Evaluations across model scales and families indicate broad generality, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results or limitations.

papers.selection_reason: Self-supervised RL post-training for vision-centric MLLMs that improves spatial understanding and extends to video temporal ordering.
papers.title: Learning to Group and Order: Cross-Instance Self-Supervised RL for Vision-Centric MLLMs
papers.tldr: GO-SSL improves vision-centric MLLMs by using self-supervised RL to group mixed visual elements by source and recover their original order across paired instances.

papers.abstract: Real-time long-video generation requires continuous output with consistent appearance and natural motion. Existing chunk-wise autoregressive methods face challenges in both generation efficiency and long-video quality: serialized denoising and history-cache refresh require two forward passes even with one-step denoising, and longer rollouts can degrade quality and cause camera drift. We propose Wave Forcing (WF), which co-designs generation, training, and execution for continuous video output with multi-step denoising. WF uses chunk-wise causal attention to access earlier, cleaner chunks before their denoising is complete, and distributes staggered denoising and cache-refresh stages across full-model replicas to achieve 1F1C: one output chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill. To adapt the model to this continuous generation process, we develop a three-stage training procedure that successively introduces mixed-noise denoising, motion supervision, and causal adaptation using self-generated history. To execute this process efficiently, Wave Runtime (WaveRT) uses Wave Parallelism (WP) for early K/V delivery and communication-computation overlap, together with optimized kernels and pipelined VAE decoding. Experiments on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B show that 5-step WF maintains overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing while achieving higher Dynamic Degree on both short and long videos. Our system efficiency experiments show that 4-step WF achieves 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, yielding 7.07x the single-GPU end-to-end throughput. In DiT-only tests with matched SageAttention+W8A8 backends, denoising steps, and GPU counts, WP delivers up to 2.53x the throughput of the faster of the Ulysses and Ring context-parallel baselines across six model scales (1.3B-14B).
bullets: Targets inefficiency and quality degradation in chunk-wise autoregressive video generation, including camera drift during long rollouts.
Uses chunk-wise causal attention, staggered multi-step denoising, and replicated model pipelines to produce one chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill.
Introduces three-stage training with mixed-noise denoising, motion supervision, and causal adaptation using self-generated history.
Wave Runtime combines early K/V delivery, communication-computation overlap, optimized kernels, and pipelined VAE decoding.
On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, 5-step WF has quality comparable to Rolling Forcing with higher Dynamic Degree; 4-step WF reaches 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs.

papers.abstract: We report the end-to-end deployment and measurement of MiniMax H3, a 20.38-billion-parameter video diffusion transformer (DiT) - the count measured from the safetensors headers of the Q8 checkpoint as deployed locally (Section 3.2) - running entirely on consumer Apple Silicon hardware: an Apple Mac mini with M5 Pro chip and 64 GiB of unified memory. Using the official bf16-to-Q8 (8-bit, group size 64) quantization path executed locally on the machine, we produced a working text-to-video pipeline with no cloud dependency. We document the full deployment procedure, including two non-trivial blockers and their fixes, and report measured figures for build time, peak memory, and per-clip render latency across four resolution tiers (Draft 384x640 through Native 768x1344). A 15.08-second 576x1024 clip rendered in 4838.49 seconds with a measured MLX peak of 27.467 GiB. We further operated the system as an unattended production pipeline, completing 17 clips in 26.49 hours with zero render failures. A blind human review of the 17 production clips (generation prompts withheld) averaged 3.12, 3.18, and 2.94 out of 5 for structural integrity, temporal consistency, and visible artifacts. All figures in this report are our own measurements except where explicitly labeled as third-party data. This is a systems/empirical report; we make no claim of model innovation.

papers.abstract: Reasoning-enabled model derivatives must turn intermediate deliberation into a usable answer within a deployment budget. We study that transition in an Ornith checkpoint adapted to multi-camera driving question answering with verifiable rewards. Paired archived outputs show that, on a selected 400-question development screen with a 256-token cap, GRPO increases answer extraction from 78.25% to 90.25% and accuracy from 55.50% to 63.75%. Of 39 wrong-to-correct transitions, 33 begin with an unextractable base response. The base's 87 unextractable responses all reach the token cap. Checkpoint-verified reconstruction on those same questions gives a much smaller first-pass accuracy gain at 512 tokens: +0.75 percentage points, versus +8.25 at 256. A later answer-cued continuation is analyzed separately; it helps the base more and narrows the adapter difference. On the full 2,511-question development set, this recovery-enabled pipeline reduces mean generated tokens from 108.6 to 47.1, while the paired accuracy interval includes zero gain. We frame these findings as adaptation of answer delivery under finite budgets, with explicit selection and provenance limits. Ornith's self-scaffolding lineage and newer reasoning-enabled derivatives such as Bonsai motivate the problem, but our measured results concern Ornith alone and do not establish a shared architectural mechanism or cross-model transfer.
bullets: On a selected 400-question screen capped at 256 tokens, GRPO raises answer extraction from 78.25% to 90.25% and accuracy from 55.50% to 63.75%.
Most wrong-to-correct changes involve previously unextractable responses: 33 of 39 transitions; all 87 base unextractable responses hit the token cap.
Checkpoint-verified reconstruction yields only a +0.75-point accuracy gain at 512 tokens, compared with +8.25 points at 256 tokens.
On the full 2,511-question development set, recovery-enabled tuning cuts mean generated tokens from 108.6 to 47.1, while the paired accuracy interval includes zero gain.
Results are limited by selected-screen and provenance constraints and apply to Ornith alone; they do not establish cross-model transfer.

papers.abstract: Multi-camera driving question answering provides a discrete test of vision-language models, but post-training gains can reflect changed selected answers or improved answer extraction. We investigate this distinction within the Gemma model family using archived, task-linked WaymoQA evaluations. A zero-shot diagnostic on 5,519 test questions spans effective-small, mixture-of-experts, unified, and dense checkpoints, with serving differences disclosed rather than interpreted as architecture effects. The strongest controlled evidence is a matched-harness Gemma-4-12B base/GRPO pair: accuracy rises from 73.78% to 75.43%, a gain of 1.65 percentage points with a scene-cluster bootstrap interval of [+0.84, +2.41]. There are 215 improvements and 124 regressions; 213 improvements start from an extractable but incorrect base answer, and only two recover previously unextractable responses. Crossing correctness with extraction state shows why correct noncompliant outputs cannot be counted as prediction errors. Category counts reveal a critical safety asymmetry: routine perception gains (+5.93 pp) mask a regression in safety-critical hazard prediction (-1.82 pp), demonstrating that unweighted outcome rewards can trade off rare edge cases for aggregate accuracy. Reward saturation describes sampled training dynamics rather than an architectural ceiling. A separate archived Gemma-31B thinking comparison yields no detected average improvement, with uncertainty that does not establish equivalence. These results support a modest answer-selection gain for the recorded tuning configuration and a reproducible diagnostic accounting, without attributing corrected labels to specific grounding mechanisms or claiming superiority over matched supervised tuning.

Findings are limited to the recorded tuning configuration and do not claim superiority over matched supervised tuning or identify specific grounding mechanisms.

papers.abstract: We present \textbf{UniCaMo}, an unified framework for joint control of camera and object motion in image-and-text-to-video diffusion models. Given a reference image, text prompt, sparse 3D object trajectories, and a 3D camera trajectory, UniCaMo constructs motion-consistent input noise that directly encodes the desired motion. Our 3D-grounded noise construction combines reference-derived noise propagation with a spherical Gaussian noise representation for newly revealed regions, providing a simple and effective motion prior without requiring reconstruction of unseen scene geometry. UniCaMo requires no architectural modifications or dedicated control modules and can be adapted using lightweight LoRA fine-tuning with low training data volume. Experiments on standard controllable video generation benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art motion controllability and high visual quality with minimal inference overhead.
bullets: Uses a reference image, text prompt, sparse 3D object trajectories, and a 3D camera trajectory as control inputs.
Constructs motion-consistent noise through reference-based propagation and spherical Gaussian noise for newly revealed regions.
Avoids reconstructing unseen scene geometry and requires no architectural changes or dedicated control modules.
Supports lightweight LoRA adaptation with low training data volume and minimal inference overhead.
Reports state-of-the-art motion controllability and high visual quality on standard controllable video-generation benchmarks.

The 3D-grounded noise is consumed by a LoRA finetuned video diffusion model to generate a video exhibiting corresponding object and camera motion.

papers.abstract: Virtual metrology (VM) aims to estimate costly or delayed metrology variables from heterogeneous sensor signals and in-line measurements, and it acts as a critical component of semiconductor manufacturing. While recent data-driven models have improved VM accuracy, most are trained in batch settings and assume stationary data distributions. In practice, however, production environments evolve continuously due to equipment degradation, process adjustments, and maintenance events, making conventional batch-trained VM models difficult to maintain under temporal distribution shifts. In this work, we propose GRAPE (Global Regression with Adaptive Prediction Enhancement), a practical online learning framework for VM in evolving wafer-processing environments. GRAPE integrates a stable global predictor based on interpretable representations with two lightweight streaming adapters that correct feature-level and environment-level shifts through online updates. Experiments on two real-world semiconductor manufacturing datasets, including chronologically held-out blind-test streams, show that GRAPE improves robustness and generalization under real temporal drift compared with both conventional batch-learning methods and existing online learning baselines.
bullets: Addresses the failure of batch-trained VM models under temporal shifts caused by equipment degradation, process changes, and maintenance.
Combines a stable global predictor with lightweight online adapters for feature-level and environment-level drift correction.
Evaluated on two real-world semiconductor manufacturing datasets with chronologically held-out blind-test streams.
Shows improved robustness and generalization under real temporal drift versus batch-learning and existing online-learning baselines.

Adapter I performs feature-level adaptation by adjusting the contributions of shift-sensitive features, while Adapter II corrects prediction offsets at the environment level. The final prediction is obtained by combining the outputs of these components, and the adapters are updated online to continuously adapt the model to temporal distribution shifts.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models and more recently Flow models have widespread application. In this work we consider degenerate Diffusion models in which the per-step generator is deterministic. We construct a modified variational framework and show a formal equivalence between Flow models and Degenerate Diffusion models. For our discrete-time variational objective we show that the optimal degenerate generator recovers the data distribution in the limit of an infinite number of generator steps. Our work therefore provides a unified perspective, showing that discrete-time implementations of flow matching and the discrete-time Degenerate Diffusion model can be considered within the same simple variational framework, removing the need for the continuous-time machinery normally used to justify flow matching models.
bullets: Studies degenerate diffusion models whose per-step generators are deterministic.
Constructs a modified variational objective for these discrete-time models.
Formally establishes equivalence between flow models and degenerate diffusion models.
Shows convergence to the data distribution with infinitely many generator steps.
Avoids relying on continuous-time machinery to justify flow matching.
papers.selection_reason: General flow-matching/diffusion theory with a unified variational objective; transferable to video diffusion and video world models.
papers.title: A Discrete-Time Variational Objective for Degenerate Diffusion and Equivalence to Flow Matching
papers.tldr: A discrete-time variational framework unifies degenerate diffusion and flow matching, showing that optimal deterministic generators recover the data distribution as the number of steps grows.

papers.abstract: Post training for large reasoning models remains insufficient on challenging problems, whose correct trajectories are hard to sample. Though prior works address this difficulty by integrating supervised fine tuning on expert trajectories with reinforcement learning, such external experts are not always available. Existing self improvement methods instead use reference solutions to create a privileged self-teacher. Yet privileged teacher correctness does not imply student reachability. Solution conditioning shifts the teacher distribution toward actions unlikely under the unprivileged student, producing seemingly "correct" trajectories that are unreachable or even mal-formed learning targets. Accordingly, we identify reachability alignment as the key to self constructed supervision and propose Self-Steered Reasoner (SSR). SSR realizes this principle through student support projection, which transforms the privileged teacher distribution into a directional signal only over reasoning actions locally reachable under the unguided student. Verification then retains correct trajectories sampled from this reachable space. To further boost the sampling efficiency, an iterative refinement framework is adopted, using diagnostic guidance based on current trajectories. On problems with pass@64 = 0 even after extensive RL, SSR recovers correct and learnable trajectories for 74.6% without parameter updates. Fine tuning on these trajectories followed by resumed reinforcement learning improves aggregate accuracy by 4.9 percentage points on AIME25/26 and HMMT26. These results show that privileged guidance becomes effective self-improvement data when aligned with the reasoning actions the student can reach.
bullets: Problem: Privileged teacher solutions may be correct but unreachable or malformed for the unguided student, limiting self-improvement.
Method: Project the teacher distribution onto the student’s local support, verify correct reachable trajectories, and iteratively refine sampling with diagnostic guidance.
Result: SSR recovers correct, learnable trajectories for 74.6% of problems with pass@64 = 0 after extensive RL, without parameter updates.
Further training on recovered trajectories followed by resumed RL raises aggregate accuracy by 4.9 percentage points on AIME25/26 and HMMT26.
Scope: The approach depends on verification and is evaluated on challenging mathematical reasoning problems.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the SSR framework. 1. Given a very hard question Q, we sample failed rollouts from the student model. The failed rollout is then summarized and diagnosed against the reference solution to produce a self-steer. The self-steer describes the error and provide fixing directions while avoiding directly offering the answer. 2. The self-steer is then used to construct the privileged self-teacher. The KL-divergence between teacher and student is calculated on the failed rollout to determine the proper intervention point. Everything after that point is discarded. 3. After the intervention point, for every decoding prefix, the student first calculate its support-set by retaining every token with a student possibility above a certain threshold δ. The teacher then rewights these tokens and choose the next token. For each new trajectory generated, it will be stored for further training if correct, and send back to a new round of refinement if incorrect. After the iterative refinement succeeds, the saved positive trajectory can be used to improve the student model.

Figure 1: RLVR can extend the model’s ability in its comfort zone, but it meets obstacles when coming to anxiety zone where correct trajectories are hard to sample. Privileged-teacher can provide aid signals on anxiety zone, but it can also select actions outside the student’s reachable region, producing unlearnable traces. Directly imitating these actions can corrupt the student’s reasoning ability(e.g., learning to hallucinate a non-existent hint). By projecting privileged preferences into the consensus region, SSR retains the learnable steering signals within the privileged preferences, effectively expands the student’s learning boundary.
Figure 3: Equal-budget search allocation. Iterative refinement recovers 147/197 problems, compared with 102/197 when all 64 initial failures receive one correction.
Figure 4: One SSR correction round. A failed trajectory is summarized and diagnosed, continued under student-support projection, and retained after verification.

papers.title: Steer, Don't Tell: Breaking Reasoning Plateaus with Reachability-Aligned Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: SSR makes self-distillation effective by steering privileged teacher guidance toward reasoning actions the student can actually reach, unlocking correct trajectories on hard problems.

papers.abstract: Remote smartphone recommerce is scaling quickly, and locking a repurchase offer from seller photos and diagnostic screens before the handset arrives has become a central operational task. Existing multimodal resources mainly target defect localization, catalog attributes, or screen reading. They overlook payout-facing scorecards with dual cosmetic and operational ground truth under a declared input contract. This gap stems from two challenges: (1) the lack of a large weakly labeled trade-in corpus kept separate from a compact audited ranking cut, and (2) architectures that either flatten unordered photo bags into one prompt or collapse evaluation into a single price scalar. To address these challenges, we propose PhoneValue-Bench, a dual-ground-truth recommerce framework with PhoneValue-Corpus for weak training on 21,550 orders and 278,748 images, and PV-Rank as the only leaderboard on 335 quality-gated orders. Systems are ranked by CardScore under LeadGate, with Cosmetic Fill and Operational Fill as diagnostics, while grade and price stay off the board. Notably, ValueAgent is a six-stage perception-fusion reference that canonicalizes views, detects regional defects, reads screenshots, and fuses evidence under warehouse-style rules, so bag-of-images prompting is not the only evaluation unit. On the same PV-Rank cut and frozen scorer, this full-system and input-contract comparison finds ValueAgent at 84.1 CardScore against the strongest Flat Vision-Language Model at 69.9, with the largest reported gap in CosFill, while OpsFill remains limited under the two declared contracts. CardScore measures field-fill completeness, not quote accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the lack of payout-facing benchmarks combining cosmetic and operational ground truth under a declared input contract.
Includes PhoneValue-Corpus with 21,550 orders and 278,748 images for weak training, plus 335 quality-gated orders in the PV-Rank leaderboard.
Ranks systems with CardScore and reports Cosmetic Fill and Operational Fill diagnostics; grade and price are excluded from ranking.
ValueAgent uses six-stage view canonicalization, defect detection, screenshot reading, and warehouse-rule evidence fusion.
On the PV-Rank cut, ValueAgent scores 84.1 CardScore versus 69.9 for the strongest flat vision-language model; CardScore measures field completeness, not quote accuracy.

papers.abstract: Replacing the matrix in an iteration with random low-rank matrices can reduce the cost of matrix-vector multiplication. However, even if the sampled matrices equal the original matrix in expectation, the expected squared norm of the random iterates may grow while the original iteration converges. Under a fixed rank bound, we study how to choose the distribution of these random matrices to minimize this growth when sampling independently at each step. We derive an exact formula for the optimal asymptotic growth factor and use it to determine when the expected squared norm can converge to zero. We then characterize precisely when a fixed sampling distribution achieves this optimal factor and construct finite-support optimal distributions in every attainable case. These results determine the minimum rank required for stability and provide optimal sampling designs under the prescribed rank constraint.
bullets: Unbiased random matrix approximations can still make expected squared iterates grow, even when the original iteration converges.
For independently sampled approximations with a fixed rank limit, the study derives the exact optimal asymptotic growth factor.
It establishes when the expected squared norm converges to zero and determines the minimum rank needed for stability.
The work characterizes all sampling distributions attaining the optimum and constructs finite-support optimal designs whenever attainable.

papers.selection_reason: Optimal low-rank sampling for repeated matrix-vector multiplication, a transferable efficiency technique for AI computation such as attention.
papers.title: Unbiased Low-Rank Approximation for Repeated Matrix-Vector Multiplication: Stability and Optimal Sampling
papers.tldr: The paper identifies optimal unbiased low-rank sampling strategies that minimize long-term growth in repeated randomized matrix-vector multiplication and characterizes when stable convergence is possible.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown promise for chest radiograph report generation, but adoption remains limited because of hallucinated findings that are not grounded in the image. Correcting these hallucinations and improving overall report quality remains a significant challenge. Prior work has addressed this problem by refining models with reinforcement learning, preference optimization, or chain-of-thought supervision, often at substantial compute cost. To address this gap, we introduce CheXPoT, a program-of-thought (PoT) framework that verifies each generated finding against image features and removes those it cannot ground. CheXPoT decomposes generated reports into predicates with RadGraph and an LLM, grounds these predicates against a DenseNet-121 and Grad-CAM visual evidence table, executes PoT verification code, and rewrites reports after removing unsupported predicates. On a 4,145-image held-out split, CheXPoT yields statistically significant precision gains on 8 of 14 CheXpert classes and F1 gains on 5, with no significant decreases in either metric. CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 19.2% (MedGemma-4B) to 46.8% (MedGemma-4B + CheXPoT) and micro-average F1 from 23.0% to 49.4%, absolute gains of 27.6% and 26.4% respectively. We also tested CheXPoT on other VLM report generators. On LLaVA-Med, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 4.5% to 17.7% and micro-average F1 from 6.3% to 19.4%. On MAIRA-2, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 15.6% to 42.1% and micro-average F1 from 21.0% to 45.3%. Our results suggest that inexpensive post-hoc visual verification may improve VLM trustworthiness by correcting unsupported findings from generated reports. CheXPoT lays a foundation for tools that help validate VLM-generated radiology reports and reduce unsupported findings. These innovations may subsequently help increase trust and adoption of VLM tools in Medicine.
bullets: Targets hallucinated or image-ungrounded findings that limit clinical trust in VLM-generated radiology reports.
Decomposes reports into predicates, grounds them using DenseNet-121 and Grad-CAM evidence, verifies them with program-of-thought code, and rewrites reports.
On a 4,145-image held-out split, it significantly improved precision for 8/14 CheXpert classes and F1 for 5, without significant metric decreases.

papers.abstract: Local image--text matching can find strong evidence for individual concepts yet favor captions with incorrect attribute--entity bindings. We introduce ConstraintMatch, a training-free inference method that turns entity-level regional consistency into an explicit matching cost. On the same frozen condition--region similarity matrix, it compares independent crop selection for each category and attribute with a shared crop choice within each entity. Their gap quantifies the score advantage obtained by relaxing the shared-region constraint. Spatial references from the same image calibrate this gap by keeping category evidence fixed while jointly shifting an entity's attribute maps. Per-entity clipping prevents cancellation across residuals, and the scaled mean cost is subtracted from global similarity. ConstraintMatch uses pooled embeddings, and spatial calibration requires no additional encoder calls. With parameters fixed per backbone across tasks, ConstraintMatch improves over global matching by 7.70 percentage points on full ARO Attribute and 5.63 points on held-out SugarCrepe++ attribute swaps, averaged across Qwen~2B and CORE~2B. Against SGI adapted to the same 13-crop budget, the respective gains are 4.85 and 3.51 points. Controlled analyses distinguish the effects of shared-region matching and candidate score calibration. The results establish entity-level evidence selection as a practical scoring principle for compositional multimodal retrieval.
bullets: Addresses incorrect attribute–entity bindings that can survive conventional local image–text matching.
Uses a training-free inference cost comparing independent versus shared regional evidence for each entity.
Calibrates the cost with spatial references, clips per-entity residuals, and subtracts the scaled mean from global similarity.
Uses pooled embeddings without extra encoder calls for spatial calibration.
Improves attribute-swap retrieval over global matching and a same-budget SGI baseline across ARO and SugarCrepe++ evaluations.

papers.abstract: Calling a tool through generated text adds decoding steps, even when the computation itself is short. We study an alternative: a small neural module that runs inside a language model's forward pass. A learned writer turns hidden states into a symbolic tape, a short sequence of discrete symbols that encodes the computation. The module, trained separately and then frozen, reduces the tape to a result, and a learned reader returns that result to the model. We evaluate arithmetic and object tracking in gemma-3-1b-it. With a writer trained on labelled tapes, the layer answers all 750 items of BIG-Bench Hard's tracking shuffled objects correctly. At seven people it needs about 1/10 of the GPU kernel time of a text-tool baseline that uses the same host model and exact code, with accuracy 1.00 against 0.99. The writer can also be learned from answers alone, guided by a hand-written copying prior, but less reliably: 5 of 6 runs succeed in the 1B host and 2 of 4 in the 4B host. Two independently trained layers keep their task accuracy when attached to one model, and a learned gate keeps them silent on the tested general-text and look-alike prompts. The results support a narrow use case: a bounded computation that returns one symbol can avoid the decoding cost of a textual tool call. Extracting the right input reliably, and deciding when to act, remain the main open problems.
bullets: Targets arithmetic and object-tracking tasks in Gemma-3-1B-IT.
A learned writer encodes hidden states into a short discrete symbolic tape; a frozen module computes on it, and a reader returns the result.
With labelled tapes, the layer correctly answers all 750 BIG-Bench Hard shuffled-object tracking items.
At seven people, it uses about one-tenth the GPU kernel time of a text-tool baseline, with accuracy 1.00 versus 0.99.
Answer-only tape learning is less reliable; extracting inputs and deciding when to invoke the module remain open problems.

papers.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) estimates advantages against the within-prompt mean reward, a baseline shared across the group. In practice, rollouts within a prompt are not always homogeneous, differing in their solution strategies and reasoning trajectories, along which they may group into subgroups. We further find that these heterogeneous subgroups may exhibit distinct reward distributions. The global baseline, however, collapses them onto a single credit axis, where the credit reflects neither a rollout's standing within its subgroup nor the subgroup's standing relative to the rest. We therefore study how to adjust the baseline when the rollouts of a prompt fall into heterogeneous subgroups. We define the \emph{subgroup offset} as the deviation of a subgroup mean from the global mean, and shift the baseline along it by a single signed coefficient $λ$. The sign of $λ$ yields two opposing directions: \emph{Alignment} ($λ{>}0$) adds the offset to the baseline, drawing credit toward a rollout's relative position within its subgroup; \emph{Contrast} ($λ{<}0$) subtracts it, drawing a rollout's credit toward the relative quality of the subgroup it belongs to. The adjustment acts on the baseline alone, leaving the reward signal and the optimization objective unchanged. In this work, we induce subgroups from strategies, grouping rollouts that share a strategy into the same subgroup. We evaluate both directions on Qwen3-8B-Base and Olmo3-7B-Base across four competition-level math benchmarks, against a $λ{=}0$ anchor that shares the same strategy-conditioned sampling and differs only in the baseline. Against this anchor each direction yields modest but consistent gains in multi-sample coverage, with Contrast the stronger of the two.
bullets: GRPO’s global within-prompt baseline can obscure both a rollout’s subgroup-relative quality and the subgroup’s overall quality.
The method computes each subgroup’s mean-reward deviation from the global mean and shifts the baseline by a signed coefficient λ.
λ>0 (Alignment) emphasizes position within a subgroup; λ<0 (Contrast) emphasizes the subgroup’s quality relative to others.
Subgroups are induced by grouping rollouts that share a solution strategy.
Across two base models and four competition-level math benchmarks, both directions consistently improve multi-sample coverage over the matched λ=0 anchor; Contrast is stronger.

papers.tldr: Subgroup Offset adjusts GRPO’s baseline using strategy-based subgroup reward differences, with both alignment and contrast improving multi-sample math coverage modestly, and contrast performing better.

papers.abstract: As large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks, memory has become an important component for supporting sustained decision-making and action. Existing methods primarily focus on memory storage, updating, and retrieval, but often overlook how memory scheduling affects task execution: the main agent must identify memory needs, initiate retrieval, and wait for results while advancing the task, increasing both scheduling burden and execution time. To address this problem, we propose MemSidecar, which decouples memory scheduling from task execution through two independently selectable modes. Hooks directly delivers bound memory to the main agent when execution events match predefined conditions. Foresight uses an independent agent to predict potential queries, retrieve results in parallel, and store them in a cache, delivering matching and valid results when actual requests arrive. Hooks and Foresight achieve scores of 41.23% and 44.34% on MCP-Persona, respectively, while effectively reducing execution costs and latency and improving the efficiency of long-horizon agent execution.
bullets: Targets the overlooked cost of having the main agent schedule memory retrieval while executing tasks.
Provides two selectable modes: Hooks for event-triggered delivery of bound memory, and Foresight for parallel query prediction, retrieval, and caching.
On MCP-Persona, Hooks and Foresight score 41.23% and 44.34%, respectively.
The approach reduces execution costs and latency while improving long-horizon execution efficiency.

papers.abstract: Despite recent progress in long-form video understanding, current benchmarks mostly focus on short clips or hour-scale videos. This leaves a major gap in evaluating ultra-long video understanding, where videos often last tens of hours. To bridge this gap, we introduce DramaVQA, a large-scale benchmark built upon long-form TV dramas. Containing approximately 20K question-answering (QA) pairs, the scale of DramaVQA exceeds previous long-video datasets, such as Video-MME and LVBench, by an order of magnitude. Our benchmark has two main features that make it stand out from existing datasets. First, we establish a scalable, LLM-assisted annotation pipeline that uses multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to generate complex questions, followed by strict human checking to ensure high data quality. Second, DramaVQA introduces a multi-level time structure; queries are designed across different video lengths, with the hardest questions requiring overall understanding across the entire drama. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art MLLMs face major challenges when tested on these very long videos, highlighting the need for agentic AI algorithms capable of managing long-term memory. The project is available at https://github.com/xinyuehuo/DramaVQA
bullets: Targets a gap in video benchmarks: understanding dramas lasting tens of hours rather than short clips or hour-scale videos.
Provides approximately 20K question–answer pairs, exceeding prior long-video datasets by an order of magnitude.
Uses an LLM-assisted pipeline to generate complex questions, followed by strict human verification.
Organizes questions across multiple temporal levels, including whole-drama reasoning.
Evaluations show state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle with ultra-long videos, motivating agentic methods with long-term memory.

papers.abstract: Lifelong Person Re-identification (LReID) aims to match the same person using sequentially collected data. In practical long-term deployments, however, the model must handle both domain shifts across cameras and scenes, and irregular clothing changes of the same identity. This gives rise to the Cloth-Hybrid Lifelong Person Re-identification (CH-LReID) task, which demands balancing cloth-relevant and cloth-irrelevant knowledge in streaming data. While existing LReID methods have explored replay-based or distillation-based anti-forgetting strategies, they typically fail to sufficiently model stage-aware domain distributions and cross-stage feature continuity under exemplar-free training. To address this problem, we propose a Distribution-Aware Adaptive Differentiated Knowledge Consolidation (DADKC) framework. The core idea is to enhance the existing Differentiated Knowledge Consolidation (DKC) paradigm with adaptive distribution modeling. To this end, three lightweight modules are designed: (1) an Anchor Pool Adapter (APA) to retrieve learnable anchor cues for refining identity features; (2) a Phase Path Mixer (PPM) to perform stage-aware expert routing for integrating domain-specific distribution paths; and (3) a Stage Bridge Alignment (SBA) module to regularize the continuity of base, anchor, and path representations between adjacent stages. Extensive experiments on the CH-LReID and LReID benchmarks show that DADKC gains 4.1%/4.5% mAP/R1 on Order-1 and 3.6%/3.4% mAP/R1 on Order-2 over the DKC baseline, and lowers weighted forgetting from 2.4%/1.7% to 1.8%/1.4%, while storing neither historical images nor per-image features. The code is available at https://github.com/fire667/DADKC.
bullets: Targets Cloth-Hybrid Lifelong Person Re-identification, where identities may change clothing across sequential domains.
Extends Differentiated Knowledge Consolidation with adaptive distribution modeling through three lightweight modules: APA, PPM, and SBA.
APA refines identity features using learnable anchor cues; PPM routes samples through stage-aware domain paths; SBA aligns representations across adjacent stages.
Compared with DKC, DADKC improves mAP/R1 by 4.1%/4.5% on Order-1 and 3.6%/3.4% on Order-2, while reducing weighted forgetting.
Operates without storing historical images or per-image features.

A DKC-style backbone extracts base and uncertainty representations; APA retrieves anchor cues, PPM routes through stageaware experts, and SBA aligns current and previous-stage base, anchor, and path features. The final model uses accumulated experts and an unknown-domain embedding at test time.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models draw each frame from a memory bank of earlier frames stamped with their capture times. With frames, weights and noise fixed, reversing the timestamps of two views flips the state that generators of two families draw: they take the newest timestamp as the truth. That reading is right as long as states never return. After an agent undoes an action, the newest view of a region is outdated and the only view of the present is older; memories for changing worlds delete that older view, and memories that keep it hand the generator the past. Temporal databases separate when a record is stored from when its content holds, its valid time. ReDate keeps every frame and dates each retrieved token by its valid time, read from the agent's action log. The frozen generator then reads a reverted region as one that has just reached a new state, so ReDate needs no training. We prove that trusting the newest timestamp is right exactly when every current view is dated after every outdated one, that without a view taken after the return only the action log tells a reverted region from an up-to-date one, and that a generator able to draw from its own prediction gains more from re-dating than from deletion when the moved tokens keep little weight. After an undo, ReDate raises the share of FAR's steps showing the current state from 0.36 to 0.62 and HY-WorldPlay's from 0.003 to 0.19. We also propose a calibrated state metric to test any memory after undos.
bullets: Problem: Using the newest capture timestamp as truth fails when an agent reverses an action and the current state is represented by an older frame.
Method: Retain all frames and re-date retrieved tokens using valid times inferred from the agent’s action log.
Theory: Newest-timestamp selection is correct only when all current views are newer than all outdated views; after a return, the action log may be essential.
Results: After undo, current-state coverage rises from 0.36 to 0.62 for FAR and from 0.003 to 0.19 for HY-WorldPlay.
Scope: Re-dating is especially beneficial when moved tokens receive little weight, and the paper introduces a calibrated metric for evaluating memory after undos.

papers.selection_reason: Valid-time memory mechanism for interactive video world models after action undos; directly targets action-conditioned world generation and embodied memory.
papers.title: Old Is Not False: Valid-Time Memory for Interactive Video World Models
papers.tldr: ReDate improves interactive video world models after undo actions by assigning memory tokens their valid state time rather than their capture time, requiring no retraining.

papers.abstract: Streaming 3D reconstruction models keep past video frames in a recurrent state, fast weights from test-time training, or a key-value (KV) cache. Each written frame shifts the coordinate frame of later cameras or occupies GPU memory. Training-free rules decide what to write from a signal of the current frame. How much they write accounts for their mean accuracy: spending the update budget of a gate at uniformly spaced frames, with no signal, matches nine published gates, and the budget bounds the drift of the state wherever the writes fall. We propose SceneBound, a training-free rule that writes a frame only when its predicted camera pose lies at least a fixed radius from every stored keyframe. Its keyframe count stays within a constant factor of the covering number of the visited poses, the fewest views that keep a keyframe near every camera, so the count grows with the places visited and stays flat when the camera returns. In large scenes, SceneBound closes a submap once decoding its first frame again reveals drift. SceneBound uses one radius across four released models and three memory types. In the recurrent state of CUT3R and the KV cache of StreamVGGT, it achieves the lowest mean trajectory error among the published training-free rules we evaluate, in one pass and over nine passes of a scene, where its keyframes grow by 3% to 6%.
bullets: Uniformly spacing updates can match published signal-based gates, suggesting update budget largely determines mean accuracy and bounds state drift.
SceneBound stores a frame only when its predicted camera pose is outside a fixed-radius neighborhood of existing keyframes.
Its keyframe count tracks the covering number of visited poses: it grows with exploration but remains stable when the camera revisits locations.
For large scenes, it closes submaps when decoding the first frame reveals renewed drift.
Across four models and three memory types, it achieved the lowest mean trajectory error among evaluated training-free rules for CUT3R and StreamVGGT, with only 3%–6% keyframe growth over nine passes.

papers.abstract: Persistent Web information assistants must combine evolving document facts with user requirements established and revised across sessions. Yet systematic evaluation of how changes in both sources affect response requirements and evidence attribution remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce Dual-Source Evolution Benchmark (DuSE-Bench), a benchmark comprising 1,000 tasks across five scenarios, including 700 whose required premises originate in both dialogue and documents. An evolving Support Graph guides task construction and preserves links from updated facts and reused conclusions to original turns and passages. Task annotations distinguish grounding source from state dependence and enable separate evaluation of response content, response type, and source attribution. Experiments across 11 baseline configurations reveal persistent challenges in joint reasoning over evolving dialogue and documents, with content accuracy on jointly grounded tasks reaching at most 56.7%. Moreover, improvements in content accuracy can coincide with poorer response choice, while content-correct responses frequently lack complete attribution to original evidence. Matched evidence substitutions further show that the effect of replacing one source's evidence depends on support from the other. These findings motivate coordinating dialogue memory and document retrieval to apply current user requirements and document facts together while preserving their original support. The data are available at https://github.com/JianfengGao7/DuSE-Bench.
bullets: Introduces 1,000 tasks across five scenarios, including 700 requiring premises from both dialogue and documents.
Uses a Support Graph to track updated facts and reused conclusions back to original conversation turns and document passages.
Separately evaluates response content, response type, and source attribution, distinguishing grounding source from state dependence.
Across 11 baseline configurations, jointly grounded content accuracy reaches at most 56.7%, and correct content often lacks complete evidence attribution.
Findings show that response quality depends on coordinating dialogue memory with document retrieval, especially when evidence from one source changes.

papers.abstract: Many questions about a book can only be answered by connecting passages chapters apart, such as a cough heard three times across a horse's life. We introduce CrossChapterQA, 1,853 such questions over 14 public-domain books. Each question lists the two to six chapters it needs (spanning half the book at the median) and the relation linking them, cites evidence from each, and has two independent reference answers graded blind. We use it to build LadderRAG, which indexes a book as passages, summaries and book-level cards for about $0.41 and answers a question for under a cent. Its first version failed mostly at retrieval. We redesigned it four times, steered by an LLM judge's verdicts and our analyses of failed answers: a design-level counterpart of RLAIF and RLHF in which feedback changes the architecture, not model weights. We also report the two redesigns that made answers worse. On the 191 questions its first version got wrong, the final version retrieves over twice as many required chapters on held-out books (recall 0.36 to 0.79), and ten annotators rate its answers 6.5/10 on average (764 ratings).
bullets: Introduces CrossChapterQA: 1,853 questions across 14 public-domain books requiring evidence from 2–6 chapters.
LadderRAG indexes passages, summaries, and book-level cards, costing about $0.41 per book and under a cent per answer.
Four redesigns were guided by LLM judge feedback and failure analysis, changing the architecture rather than model weights.
On 191 initially failed questions, required-chapter recall improved from 0.36 to 0.79 on held-out books.
Annotators rated final answers 6.5/10 on average across 764 ratings; two redesigns reduced performance.

figures.caption: Figure 3: LadderRAG at a glance. (A) Each book is indexed once, in four steps, into a ladder with three levels: passages (L1), section summaries (L2) and five book-level cards (L3). (B) The final version answers in four steps: it plans the question, finds evidence for each part among the passages, adds the book-level context, and answers in a single call (retrying with more passages if a part is missing). The coloured tags show which level of the ladder each step reads. (C) How v4b came about: each version answered the development questions, an AI judge flagged wrong answers, we analysed the failures, and the design changed (§5).

papers.abstract: Many systems are observed only through unpaired snapshots, with population samples available at each time point but no correspondence between samples at different times. These snapshots determine the one-time distributions but leave the temporal coupling unspecified, requiring a modeling prior to connect successive times. We propose the lift-project stochastic differential equation (SDE), an autonomous SDE on the observed coordinate and a few hidden coordinates, trained only to match the snapshots. Most existing methods, including time-dependent SDEs, Schrödinger bridges and optimal transport, evolve the observed coordinate alone. For a scalar observation, the classical comparison theorem implies that all such models have non-negative lagged covariance, so on data whose lagged covariance turns negative, their error has a computable floor. The lift-project SDE is not bound by this floor. On two representative partially observed systems, the Duffing and pendulum oscillators, at comparable fit to the snapshots, the proposed method reduces the lagged-covariance error by factors of 2.4 and 6.6 relative to the strongest baseline and is the only model below the error floor; one hidden coordinate is already enough for such improvement. Furthermore, if a second experiment changes only the initial state of the hidden coordinate, no single model that evolves the observed coordinate alone can fit both experiments, whereas a single lift-project SDE can.
bullets: Unpaired snapshots identify one-time distributions but not how observations are coupled across time.
The method trains an autonomous SDE jointly over observed and hidden coordinates using only snapshot matching.
For scalar observations, observed-only models have a non-negative lagged-covariance constraint and an associated error floor.
On Duffing and pendulum oscillators, the method reduces lagged-covariance error by factors of 2.4 and 6.6 versus the strongest baseline.
One hidden coordinate suffices for improvement, and a single lift-project SDE can fit experiments differing only in hidden initial state.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied manipulation requires policies to act on information that is no longer visible. Modified objects may leave the field of view, while completed subtasks continue to constrain future actions. Existing approaches extend temporal context through recurrent state updates, test-time training, or storage and retrieval of past observations. As horizons grow, these mechanisms can still leave the policy to infer task state from long, redundant, and viewpoint-dependent visual experience. We argue that long-horizon agents benefit not merely from remembering more, but from remembering task-relevant state changes and progress. We propose Memory of Object States and Task Progress (MOST), a policy-internal memory framework that compresses multi-view observations into temporal tokens. Historical and predictive future tokens are explicitly supervised with object states and subtask progress, structuring memory around what has changed in the world and what has already been accomplished. The resulting memory directly conditions action generation within a single end-to-end policy, without an external planner or retrieval stage. We further introduce RoboCasa-Long, a benchmark of multi-minute, multi-stage mobile manipulation tasks. Across RoboCasa365, RoboCasa-Long, and real-world robot experiments, MOST consistently outperforms Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (XR-1), the previous state-of-the-art model. It raises average success from 65.9% to 72.1% on RoboCasa365, average maximum task progress from 20.83% to 42.22% on RoboCasa-Long, and real-world success from 6.66% to 43.33%. MOST also outperforms a matched visual-history memory variant, showing that effective long-horizon memory depends not only on how much experience is retained, but on whether it preserves decision-relevant progress and world-state changes.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of acting on modified objects and completed subtasks that are no longer visible.
Compresses multi-view observations into temporal tokens representing historical object states and predicted future task progress.
Uses these tokens to condition action generation within a single end-to-end policy, without an external planner or retrieval stage.
Introduces RoboCasa-Long, a benchmark for multi-minute, multi-stage mobile manipulation.
Reports gains over XR-1 and a matched visual-history memory variant across simulation and real-world experiments.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Memory Expert architecture. Historical multi-view observations are encoded into history tokens, and future queries are appended to form the memory sequence. The sequence is processed with block-causal self-attention and conditioned on the instruction through cross-attention. During training, each token predicts its subtask and the state of every relevant object. The output of each Memory Expert layer conditions the corresponding Action Expert layer.

Figure 2: MOST overview. MOST integrates a Vision Language Model, a Memory Expert, and an Action Expert within one end-to-end policy. The Vision Language Model encodes the current observation and instruction. The Memory Expert represents sampled history as object states and task progress, and the Action Expert uses both contexts to generate continuous actions. Task-state supervision is training-only.

papers.abstract: Vision-language action (VLA) models excel for end-to-end autonomous driving, yet their tendency to over-invoke chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning mirrors a human cognitive pitfall: overthinking. Just as deliberate reasoning can slow or mislead human judgment in routine tasks, excessive CoT in VLA incurs unnecessary compute overhead and can paradoxically degrade planning performance. Recent research tackles this via adaptive reasoning, which dynamically modulates inference complexity by selectively triggering CoT for complex scenes while responding directly to routine ones. While prior adaptive methods rely on implicit adaptation, recent work shows that explicitly optimizing the route between CoT and direct responses yields superior performance, assuming scene-difficulty annotations which are labor-intensive, poorly scalable, and prone to error due to the subjectivity of judging driving complexity. We explore, for the first time, whether adaptive reasoning with explicit route optimization can be achieved without any scene-difficulty labeling. We introduce STEER, a generic over-reasoning mitigation strategy featuring two key components: (i) routing uncertainty-aware rollout, which calibrates sampling to align routing diversity with model uncertainty; and (ii) cross-route advantage credit assignment, which introduces a differential metric to reinforce optimal routing decisions based on environmental rewards rather than subjective labels. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 demonstrate that STEER is competitive with state-of-the-art methods in both planning quality and the Pareto front of inference efficiency.
bullets: Targets over-reasoning, which can increase inference cost and hurt planning in routine driving scenes.
Uses uncertainty-aware rollout to calibrate routing diversity to the model’s uncertainty.
Applies cross-route advantage credit assignment to learn routing from environmental rewards rather than subjective annotations.
Experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 show competitive planning quality and inference-efficiency trade-offs with state-of-the-art methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of STEER. STEER is built on an autoregressive vision-language model that takes a front-view driving image together with structured driving context as input, and generates a textual future ego trajectory as output. It formulates adaptive reasoning in autonomous driving as an explicit routing problem, where an initial decision selects either a reasoning route or a direct route before trajectory generation. The framework is trained in three stages: (1) driving-centric pretraining for domain adaptation, (2) route-balanced supervised fine-tuning to preserve support for both valid routes, and (3) route-aware policy optimization to learn the routing preference directly from task rewards, without any scene-difficulty labels.

Figure 2: Route-aware policy optimization in STEER. For each prompt, STEER first inspects the initial routing distribution to estimate routing uncertainty. When the routing decision is uncertain, the model performs route-contrastive rollout by explicitly sampling both the reasoning and direct routes under the same prompt; otherwise, it falls back to standard on-policy rollout. During optimization, STEER applies a standard content advantage to all response tokens and adds a cross-route advantage at the initial routing position, jointly optimizing response quality and route preference.

Figure 3: Prompt-level route comparison. For each prompt, we compare the trajectory produced by the route selected by STEER (blue) with the counterfactual alternative route (red). In the top case, explicit reasoning yields safer obstacle clearance. In the bottom case, STEER correctly avoids over-reasoning and selects the direct route, which better follows the road geometry compared to the perturbed reasoning alternative.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) show promise for clinical image understanding, but their computational and memory requirements hinder deployment on resource-constrained clinical hardware. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers a practical compression strategy without retraining, yet its effectiveness depends strongly on the calibration data. We propose CoreCalib, a training-free and quantizer-agnostic framework for constructing compact calibration sets that preserve the target medical VQA distribution. CoreCalib stratifies data by clinical question class, identifies representative visual modes using frozen DINOv2 features with UMAP and HDBSCAN, and expands selected images into class-balanced question-answer pairs. On Kvasir-VQA-x1, we evaluate CoreCalib with MASQuant, GPTQ, and QIG using a fixed 128-pair budget. CoreCalib achieves the best METEOR with all three quantizers and the best ROUGE-L with MASQuant and GPTQ. With W4A8 MASQuant, it improves METEOR from 0.5672 with COCO calibration to 0.6234, recovering approximately 41% of the degradation relative to BF16. These results support CoreCalib as a data-centric component for resource-efficient medical VLM deployment. Project page: https://magnusdtd.github.io/CoreCalib/ .
bullets: Addresses the challenge of deploying medical VLMs on hardware with limited compute and memory.
Constructs calibration sets by balancing clinical question classes and selecting representative visual modes with frozen DINOv2 features, UMAP, and HDBSCAN.
Is training-free and quantizer-agnostic, evaluated with MASQuant, GPTQ, and QIG using 128 question-answer pairs on Kvasir-VQA-x1.
Achieves the best METEOR for all three quantizers and the best ROUGE-L for MASQuant and GPTQ.
With W4A8 MASQuant, raises METEOR from 0.5672 using COCO calibration to 0.6234, recovering about 41% of the degradation relative to BF16.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of CoreCalib and its role in resource-efficient medical VLM deployment. (A) A medical VLM provides strong clinical VQA capability but requires substantial computational resources; PTQ converts it into a low-bit model intended to reduce the resource burden across a spectrum of computing environments. (B) CoreCalib constructs a compact calibration workload by (1) stratifying the medical VQA data by clinical question class, (2) selecting densityaware representative images using frozen DINOv2 features with UMAP and HDBSCAN, (3) expanding representative images into multiple QA pairs and balancing them across question classes, and (4) forming a small calibration set, such as 128 QA pairs from 23 images. (C) The calibration set can be used with different PTQ methods, including MASQuant, GPTQ, and QIG, to produce a quantized medical VLM with improved capability retention.

papers.abstract: Two groups of pedestrians face avoidable risk on the city sidewalk: people living with visual impairment, who reach an obstacle before anything warns them, and people walking with divided attention, who register a hazard late or not at all. A vision system can warn them only about obstacles it has learned to recognize, so its training data limits the protection it offers. No suitable training set exists: public benchmarks are recorded from vehicles, aerial platforms, or fixed rigs, general-purpose detectors omit the street furniture that causes trips, and pedestrian-focused collections are confined to single regions with incompatible class schemes. This paper introduces the Real-time Obstacle Detection (ROD) dataset: more than 24,000 images and 40,000 annotated obstacles across 25 classes, from vehicles and people to the stairs, manholes, traffic cones, and benches that general-purpose detectors overlook. Because street furniture differs between cities, ROD unifies twenty-nine public collections onto one taxonomy and adds eye-level imagery from two contrasting cities on two continents, Tehran and Toronto. Every label is human-verified, and each capture campaign is admitted only after a compact detector shows it can learn the class. Six lightweight YOLO detectors (nano and tiny variants) benchmarked on ROD all exceed 0.86 recall; YOLO12n attains the highest recall (0.889), YOLO26n the highest precision (0.925), and YOLOv9t the best mAP@0.50 (0.882) with the fewest parameters. Because the recall and mAP rankings disagree, selecting a model by mAP does not minimize missed obstacles, so per-class recall is reported for all 25 classes.
bullets: Addresses safety risks for visually impaired pedestrians and people walking while distracted.
Combines 29 public collections under one taxonomy and adds eye-level imagery from Tehran and Toronto.
Contains over 24,000 images and 40,000 human-verified obstacle annotations across 25 classes, including stairs, manholes, cones, and benches.
Benchmarks six lightweight YOLO detectors; all achieve recall above 0.86, with different models leading in recall, precision, and mAP@0.50.
Reports per-class recall because mAP rankings do not necessarily identify the model that minimizes missed obstacles.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 End-to-end construction pipeline for the ROD dataset. Track 1 downloads twenty-nine Roboflow Universe collections at pinned versions, drops out-of-taxonomy labels and unusable images, and remaps every remaining class index onto the unified 25-class schema. Track 2 normalizes fieldcaptured imagery from Tehran and Toronto, then annotates it either automatically, through the AnnotationFlow pipeline running SAM 3 inside a Roboflow Workflow, or manually in CVAT where no reliable concept prompt exists; every label from both routes is verified by a human. Each capture campaign then passes an admission gate: augmentation followed by a single-class YOLOv8n probe, admitted only if precision, recall, and mAP@0.5 all reach 0.90. papers.abstract: Subliminal learning allows AI models to inherit hidden preferences from seemingly unrelated training data, such as number sequences. Safety audits may evaluate models at standard 16-bit precision, while deployments may use compressed, quantized weights. We ask whether quantization changes the expression of a subliminal preference and what drives any resulting change. To investigate, we implant a "favourite animal: panda" preference into Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. We define its net strength as the difference in mean panda-answer probability between subliminal models and neutrally trained controls under the same quantization setting. Applying this metric across different compression levels reveals a stark contrast. While behaviour remains stable at 8 bits, 4-bit quantization triggers severe, opposing shifts depending on the quantizer. Half-Quadratic Quantization (HQQ) amplifies the preference, raising the subliminally trained model's panda probability from roughly 55% at 16 bits to 64% at 4 bits, while the controls stay near 17%. This raises the trait's net strength ~1.3 times its 16-bit value. In contrast, NormalFloat (NF4) at 4-bit suppresses it, shrinking the net strength to just ~0.3 times its 16-bit value, despite producing rounding errors of the same size to within 4%. We examine the structure of the rounding errors and find that their arrangement drives the divergence. Randomly shuffling HQQ's errors within each quantization group, without changing their magnitude, shifts the trait's net strength between 0.2 and 1.6 times its 16-bit value. Despite these opposing shifts, the underlying fine-tuning signal remains largely intact. Because a model's internal state and outward behaviour diverge so unpredictably under compression, a 16-bit audit cannot reliably bound real-world risks. Safety evaluations must test the exact quantized weights intended for deployment.
bullets: The study implants a hidden “panda” preference into Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and measures its net behavioral strength against neutral controls.
Behavior is stable at 8-bit precision but diverges sharply at 4 bits depending on the quantizer.
HQQ amplifies the preference, while NF4 suppresses it, despite producing similarly sized rounding errors.
Shuffling error arrangements changes preference strength substantially, indicating that error structure—not just magnitude—drives the effect.
The underlying fine-tuning signal remains largely intact, but compressed internal states and outputs become difficult to predict from 16-bit behavior.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview. Left: A 16-bit audit of a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct student, fine-tuned on a panda-loving teacher’s number sequences that never mention pandas, finds a “favourite animal: panda” preference at 55% against 17% for a neutrally trained control; this gap, normalized, defines the baseline net strength R = 1. Middle: Deploying these exact same weights at 4 bits using two quantizers with identical targeted layers, group sizes, and error magnitudes moves the preference in opposite directions: R ≈ 1.3 under HQQ and R ≈ 0.3 under NF4. In contrast, an explicitly trained student of matched strength remains stable at R ≈ 1. Right: Both quantizers preserve more than 99% of the fine-tuning delta. The quantized weights are nearly identical, yet the resulting behaviours are a factor of four apart; the 16-bit measurement bounds neither.

papers.abstract: Generative view synthesis aims to synthesize novel-view videos from reference observations along user-defined camera trajectories. Maintaining global scene consistency throughout this process remains challenging for camera-conditioned interactive video generators. Existing approaches typically select reference frames based solely on camera poses, overlooking whether the content remains semantically relevant or even visible. To address these limitations, we draw inspiration from semantic and episodic memory in human cognition, in which semantic memory captures generalized knowledge across experiences, whereas episodic memory preserves information tied to specific past events and contexts. Motivated by the complementary roles of semantic and episodic memory, we introduce SE-Mem, a Semantic-Episodic Memory framework that organizes historical observations in a structured 3D representation and augments its elements with semantic importance scores. A two-stage memory retrieval strategy is designed to identify the most informative frames to provide contextual guidance. Taking into account both semantic significance and geometric visibility, SE-Mem preserves semantic coherence and fine-grained visual details during novel view synthesis. Extensive evaluations show that our approach improves visual quality and achieves competitive geometric consistency across multiple benchmarks.
bullets: Addresses reference-frame selection methods that rely mainly on camera poses and may retrieve irrelevant or invisible content.
Structures historical observations in a 3D representation and assigns semantic importance scores inspired by semantic and episodic memory.
Uses a two-stage retrieval strategy to select informative frames for contextual guidance.
Combines semantic significance with geometric visibility to maintain coherent semantics and fine-grained visual details.
Evaluations report improved visual quality and competitive geometric consistency across multiple benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SE-Mem. Historical frames are processed to obtain 3D point representations and importance maps, which are integrated into a voxelized memory representation. During synthesis, a two-stage retrieval strategy selects reference frames by considering target-view visibility and voxel importance. The retrieved frames and their corresponding camera conditions are then provided to a camera-conditioned video generator to synthesize novel views, while newly generated observations are incrementally incorporated into the memory.
