papers.abstract: We introduce GateTrim, an adaptive-rank post-training quantization method for large language models that learns matrix-specific ranks through gate optimization and threshold-based rank selection. GateTrim standardizes the low-rank factors of a quantized low-rank--residual representation, learns a separate gate vector for each target weight matrix, and uses a shared threshold to automatically determine its retained rank. The resulting ranks can differ across matrices, and the compact quantized representations are subsequently reconstructed. We evaluate GateTrim under W4A8 on Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Across all five models, we observe a counterintuitive finding: increasing the threshold from $τ=0.3$ to $τ=0.7$ reduces the mean retained rank by 46.60%--67.89% while simultaneously lowering WikiText-2 perplexity by 0.59%--5.17%. Threshold 0.7 achieves the lowest mean retained rank and final perplexity among the three tested thresholds, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7, and reduces measured target-export size by 1.50%--4.25% relative to 0.3. GateTrim uses an $8\times512$-token fitting pool and a separate development pool of the same size. Its Qwen3-4B/8B/14B perplexities at $τ=0.7$ are numerically below TwinQuant's published W4A8 values, reported with a $128\times2048$-token calibration pool, in a cross-study comparison. On Qwen3-8B, the threshold-0.7 configuration already has the lowest perplexity before reconstruction under both tested initialization seeds; reconstruction improves it further without increasing retained rank or export size.
bullets: Learns matrix-specific ranks using gate vectors and a shared threshold in a quantized low-rank–residual representation.
Evaluated on five Qwen3 and Llama models under W4A8, using separate fitting and development pools.
Raising the threshold from 0.3 to 0.7 cuts mean retained rank by 46.60%–67.89% and lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 0.59%–5.17%.
At threshold 0.7, measured target-export size is reduced by 1.50%–4.25% versus threshold 0.3.
Reconstruction further improves Qwen3-8B perplexity without increasing retained rank or export size; cross-study comparisons to TwinQuant are not directly controlled.

papers.abstract: Serving and fine-tuning a large language model on the same GPUs can turn the idle capacity between inference bursts into training progress, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) makes this co-location cheap because both workloads read a single frozen copy of the base weights. The difficulty lies in the fine-tuning backward pass, which has no counterpart in inference. Current co-serving systems schedule backward work per serving iteration: each iteration carries a fixed backward budget, and requests that arrive in the meantime wait for it to finish, so fine-tuning dictates inference latency whenever load spikes. We observe that the backward pass of a LoRA microbatch decomposes into per-layer tasks over the same weights that the inference forward pass visits, which allows backward work to be scheduled at layer rather than iteration granularity. Building on this observation, LayerLoom attaches same-layer backward tasks to the inference forward pass and, at each layer, runs only as many of them as the latency slack of in-flight requests permits. To keep a ready task at every layer, LayerLoom maintains a wavefront of fine-tuning microbatches staggered across layers, and it bounds the wavefront's activation memory by offloading microbatch state to host memory and prefetching it ahead of the layer where the scheduler plans to use it. A fused kernel serves the paired forward and backward GEMMs from a single read of each base weight. Because all backward work of an iteration finishes within its forward pass, new requests join the next iteration as in continuous batching. On an RTX 4090 GPU running Llama-3.1-8B under a bursty production trace, LayerLoom raises joint SLO attainment by 13.5-21.8 points over prior works with fine-tuning throughput that is comparable or up to 12% higher, and it reaches the same training losses.
bullets: Problem: Iteration-level backward scheduling makes fine-tuning delay inference during request bursts.
Method: Attach per-layer LoRA backward tasks to inference forward passes and execute only work allowed by each layer’s latency slack.
System design: A staggered microbatch wavefront, host-memory offloading/prefetching, and fused forward-backward GEMMs maintain readiness while limiting activation memory and base-weight reads.

Results: On an RTX 4090 serving Llama-3.1-8B under a bursty production trace, joint SLO attainment improves by 13.5–21.8 points over prior work, with comparable or up to 12% higher fine-tuning throughput.
Scope: The abstract reports results for LoRA co-serving on one GPU/model and trace; broader generality is not established.

papers.abstract: Electrochemistry is central to solving many modern-day challenges, including energy storage systems for a sustainable future, and its advancement relies heavily on the data from past findings. Existing automated pipelines are limited by text-only architectures, context fragmentation, and numerical hallucinations - collectively preventing accurate, large-scale curation of property databases. We introduce ElectrochemLLM, a multimodal information extraction pipeline that jointly identifies structured electrochemical records encompassing electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations, and their measured physicochemical properties from unstructured scientific PDFs at scale. By combining hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration, the pipeline extracts verifiable, structured data across text, tables, and figures. Evaluated on the battery-electrolyte subset of our manually annotated benchmark of 232 papers, ElectrochemLLM achieves an F-1 score of 0.97, and has been applied to curate ElectroChemDB, a structured database spanning 15,000 electrochemical research articles. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by training machine learning models for electrolyte property prediction, illustrating a complete pathway from unstructured literature to predictive materials discovery.
bullets: Addresses text-only extraction, fragmented context, and numerical hallucinations in electrochemical literature curation.
Combines hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration to process text, tables, and figures.
Extracts electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations, and measured physicochemical properties.
Achieves an F1 score of 0.97 on a manually annotated battery-electrolyte benchmark of 232 papers.

papers.abstract: A robot's next action can depend on recent motion or earlier visual evidence absent from its current observation. A recurrent visual-memory architecture can retain this history in a visual state, but its usefulness depends on what the state represents and how it is updated with new observations. We introduce Prediction-Regulated Memory (PREM), a framework that uses action-conditioned future prediction to guide both memory learning and updating in vision-language-action policies. During training, predicting future visual features provides temporal supervision for memory learning. During execution, PREM compares current visual features with the prediction made at the preceding decision and uses the spatially normalized prediction discrepancy to regulate updates to the visual state at each spatial location. The updated visual state supplies temporal context for action generation alongside current observations. Built on $π_{0.5}$, PREM improves average success rate from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO dynamic manipulation tasks and from 14.4% to 83.8% on the RMBench M(1) memory-dependent setting. Further evaluations on LIBERO and LIBERO-Pro show improvements in general manipulation and robustness to spatial perturbations. PREM incurs a mean inference overhead of 7.7 ms on a single NVIDIA H800 GPU.
bullets: Addresses the need to retain motion history and earlier visual evidence missing from current observations.
Trains memory with temporal supervision from predicted future visual features.
At execution, uses spatially normalized prediction discrepancies to selectively update the visual state.
Improves success from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO and 14.4% to 83.8% on RMBench M(1).
Also improves general manipulation and spatial-perturbation robustness, with 7.7 ms mean inference overhead on an NVIDIA H800.

papers.abstract: Inference-time scaling enhances a model's reasoning by extending its chain-of-thought (CoT). However, existing approaches typically rely on a single policy trained with outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL), which often suffers from long-horizon plan failures where the implicit plan drifts from valid strategies, especially for small LMs with limited capacity. To address this, we propose Multi-Level Reasoning (MLR), which reformulates long-CoT generation as a two-level stochastic process. A high-level planner generates structured step descriptors specifying both the reasoning mode and the semantic subgoal. The low-level executor then produces detailed reasoning conditioned on these descriptors, forming an alternating plan--execute loop. To maintain scalability, we adopt a minimal design where the base model serves as the low-level policy and a lightweight LoRA module implements the high-level policy. For training, we observe that outcome-reward RL provides sparse and delayed feedback for long trajectories (e.g., several thousand tokens), hindering credit assignment. We therefore introduce iterative Step-DPO, a process-level preference optimization scheme that leverages Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo (TSMC) to provide scalable stepwise supervision. This yields more effective training, improved stability, and higher accuracy. Extensive experiments on challenging math, science, and logical reasoning benchmarks show that, under the same reduced data budget (10% SFT and 5% preference relative to the DeepSeek-R1 distillation setup), MLR outperforms both SFT-based distillation and strong RL/preference-optimization baselines across multiple base models and tasks. Moreover, MLR exhibits slower performance degradation on long-horizon reasoning, demonstrating stronger robustness under extended CoT generation.
bullets: Targets long-horizon plan drift and sparse credit assignment, particularly in small language models.
Uses a high-level planner to specify reasoning modes and semantic subgoals, while a low-level executor generates detailed reasoning in an alternating plan–execute loop.
Keeps the design lightweight: the base model acts as executor and a LoRA module serves as planner.
Introduces iterative Step-DPO with Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo for scalable, process-level step supervision.
On math, science, and logic benchmarks, it achieves higher accuracy and more stable long-CoT performance under a reduced data budget, with slower degradation on extended reasoning.

papers.abstract: The MetaFine Open Competition (RoboFineMani workshop, CoRL 2026) evaluates fine-grained manipulation beyond binary success. Its five simulated tasks, from grasping a bottle by an instructed part to inserting letter-shaped pegs with 4 mm clearance, are scored on perception under lighting and camera changes, instruction understanding, and behavior. This report presents Team Friday's solution, which got second place with an overall score of 0.947, more than twice the $π_0$ baseline. Instead of fine-tuning a large vision-language-action (VLA) model, we train one 19M-parameter policy per task with a separate instruction classifier and focus on the data, all generated in the simulator by a privileged scripted teacher, including its corrections of the student's mistakes. By analyzing failed episodes, we find that a teacher that almost always succeeds can still teach a memoryless student badly: its pauses become stalls, its fixed habits become shortcuts, and it never shows the errors the student makes. Making the teacher \emph{imitable} raised the official score on letter insertion, the hardest task, from 0.44 to 0.82 with 32\% more data and the same architecture, and finally to 0.88. We summarize practical lessons on demonstration data and evaluation, which we hope will help in imitation learning for precise manipulation.
bullets: The challenge evaluates fine-grained manipulation under visual changes, language instructions, and behavioral precision across five simulated tasks.
The solution uses one 19M-parameter policy per task, a separate instruction classifier, and simulator-generated demonstrations from a privileged scripted teacher.
Failure analysis showed that near-perfect teachers can teach memoryless students poorly through pauses, fixed habits, and missing recovery examples.
Making demonstrations more imitable improved letter insertion from 0.44 to 0.82 with 32% more data, and ultimately to 0.88 using the same architecture.
The team’s overall score was 0.947, earning second place and motivating practical lessons about demonstration design and evaluation.

papers.abstract: State of the art latent dynamics world models achieve impressive performance for robot planning. But do they actually encode the physics of the world? In this paper, we show that popular world models today achieve strong results on tasks that reduce to image similarity but forget key details about objects in the scene like mass, deformation, friction, and bounciness. We achieve this by defining precisely what ought to be encoded in such a world model and introducing two new evaluation methods that can directly tease physical properties and easily scale to new ones. Our evaluation, which we call Roz, includes 10 contrastive tasks and 3 continuous tasks, totaling 1734 individual scenarios. We validate our eval on control tasks. On our own model, AnonWM, we find that performance roughly improves with training steps, while not necessarily being correlated with reconstruction MSE. We argue current model failures are a symptom of evaluation strategies (probes and planners) that are opaque, model-specific, and high-compute. Roz requires only a model that can ingest still frames or video, a way to extract latents, and a distance function between them, and it can be run in one pass. We hope future evaluations will adopt Roz's evaluation techniques. More broadly, we hope Roz can be a case study for a future where benchmarks allow rapid iteration and comparison across models.
bullets: Current world models can perform well on image-similarity tasks while missing properties such as mass, deformation, friction, and bounciness.
Roz introduces two evaluation methods covering 10 contrastive and 3 continuous tasks across 1,734 scenarios.
The evaluation requires only frame/video input, latent extraction, and a latent distance function, avoiding opaque, model-specific, high-compute probes and planners.
On AnonWM, performance generally improves with training steps but is not necessarily correlated with reconstruction MSE.
Roz is validated on control tasks and aims to support rapid, model-agnostic comparison of world models.

papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) unlearning is often treated as an objective-design problem: given multimodal forget data, the goal is to optimize a loss that removes undesirable behavior while preserving retained capabilities. We argue that this view overlooks an equally important data-centric question: how should each forget example be represented before optimization? Existing methods typically keep image-conditioned failures in their original image-text form, implicitly assuming that pixels are the right route for unlearning whenever pixels appear in the input. We challenge this assumption by constructing modality-decomposed versions of VLM benchmarks, enabling controlled comparisons among image-only, text-only, and multimodal representations of the same examples. Our modality-mixing experiments show that unsafe instruction-following behavior is more effectively suppressed through textual representations than through images alone, while purely text-only unlearning can still weaken visual grounding when the target behavior depends on visual evidence. Motivated by this trade-off, we introduce ModRoute, a gradient-guided per-sample modality routing strategy that selectively converts high visual-pressure examples to text-only form while keeping the remaining examples multimodal. Notably, on VLGuard with LLaVA-1.5-7B, ModRoute has the strongest composite unlearning-utility score of 0.847 at $γ=0.5$, a 2.5% improvement over the best random-switching score and $\geq$46% better than pure multimodal or text unlearning. Overall, our results show that effective VLM unlearning depends not only on the objective, but also on the composition and per-sample modality routing of the unlearning data.
bullets: The work reframes VLM unlearning as both an objective-design and data-representation problem.
Modality-decomposed benchmarks enable controlled comparison of image-only, text-only, and multimodal unlearning inputs.
Textual representations better suppress unsafe instruction-following, but text-only unlearning can harm visual grounding.
ModRoute uses gradient-guided, per-sample routing to convert high visual-pressure examples to text-only form and retain multimodal inputs for others.
On VLGuard with LLaVA-1.5-7B, it achieves a composite score of 0.847, outperforming random switching by 2.5% and pure routing baselines by at least 46%.

papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recovered interpretable, causally relevant features in robot foundation models (RFMs) such as $π_{0.5}$ (arXiv:2603.19183, arXiv:2603.19233). SAE features on individual instruction tokens are less interpretable than timestep-pooled ones (arXiv:2603.19183), and whether they can redirect a robot's goal remains untested. We show that replacing the SAE features of a single goal word with those of an alternative goal word, leaving the instruction text unchanged, steers $π_{0.5}$-LIBERO into completing the alternative task. At layer 0, BatchTopK feature swaps redirect behavior in up to 20/20 rollouts in a scene where random-feature swaps redirect none, with success varying across six scenes in two LIBERO suites and across layers. The effect depends on SAE architecture: word-selected Matryoshka edits largely do not outperform random ones. SAEs are also not required. Adding a fixed difference-in-means vector at twice its natural magnitude redirects 8-10/10 rollouts. Layer-wise activation patching shows that goal-word edits remain effective up to layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity, and up to layer 13 in both cases when patching also covers camera tokens. These results are proof of existence in an RFM in simulation and an initial map of how deep goal-redirecting edits remain effective. Visit https://doubleblind-sae-pi05.github.io for video rollouts.
bullets: Per-token goal-word edits steer π₀.₅-LIBERO without changing the instruction text.
At layer 0, BatchTopK swaps redirected up to 20/20 rollouts in one scene, while random-feature swaps redirected none; results varied across scenes and layers.
Word-selected Matryoshka edits generally did not outperform random swaps, and SAEs were not necessary: a scaled difference-in-means vector also redirected behavior.
Edits remained effective through layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity; patching camera tokens extended effectiveness to layer 13.
The study is a simulated proof of existence and an initial characterization of the depth limits of goal-redirection edits.

papers.abstract: Deploying generative world models for end-to-end closed-loop evaluation and policy learning requires precise scenario control, consistent observations, and sustained generation quality during extended interactions. This report presents X-World 1.6, advancing X-World 1.0 toward a more reliable and versatile driving simulator. The upgraded base model offers finer-grained control over traffic semantics, including traffic lights and road markings, together with improved spatial consistency across cameras. Virtual City capabilities broaden scenario construction through a family of models conditioned on diverse 2D and 3D references, including support for generating multi-camera future videos from a single image. An enhanced post-training framework enables efficient causal, few-step generation with stronger temporal coherence, better quality retention over longer rollouts, and improved alignment with human preferences. We also introduce a dedicated evaluation suite to support systematic assessment and guide model iteration. Together, these upgrades expand the scenarios X-World can simulate and improve the efficiency and reliability of its generated observations, supporting broader use in autonomous-driving development.
bullets: Adds fine-grained control over traffic lights, road markings, and other traffic semantics.
Improves spatial consistency across cameras and supports multi-camera future-video generation from a single image.
Broadens virtual-city construction using diverse 2D and 3D references.
Introduces post-training for efficient few-step causal generation, stronger temporal coherence, and improved long-rollout quality.
Provides a dedicated evaluation suite for systematic assessment and model iteration.

papers.abstract: A growing body of work reports benefits from orthogonality constraints in fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). These results raise an open question: do orthogonality constraints also help LLM pre-training? We conduct a systematic empirical study of decoder-only LLM pre-training with models ranging from 360M to 3.1B parameters, trained on nearly 200B tokens. We examine fourteen variants of orthogonality training: some constrain the weight matrix itself, while others use orthogonal factors to reparameterize it. Because a strictly orthogonal square matrix loses half of its degrees of freedom, we also study block-wise orthogonality, where every $d$ rows form a row-orthonormal (Stiefel) matrix and the block size $d$ is a hyperparameter. Among block sizes ranging from 1 to the shorter side of the matrix, no $d>1$ used throughout the network reliably outperforms $d=1$, and large blocks are clearly worse; the one placement that helps, symmetric positive-definite factors on the query and key projections, loses its small gain as models grow. At $d=1$, the constraint reduces to sphere optimization, with each row direction on its own unit sphere, which by itself already improves on tuned Muon. The same two findings hold for a diffusion transformer trained on ImageNet, and after fine-tuning, downstream accuracy does not separate the parameterizations. Our conclusion is that, across the realizations we tried, orthogonality between rows does not help language-model pre-training beyond sphere optimization. Since this appears to conflict with several prior results, we re-examine five prior methods in pre-training and fine-tuning that report orthogonality improvements. In each case the reported gain is attributable to numerical precision, training horizon, optimizer realization, or per-row norm control rather than to the orthogonality the methods impose.
bullets: Systematically evaluates 14 orthogonality-based training variants on decoder-only LLMs from 360M to 3.1B parameters using nearly 200B tokens.
Block-wise orthogonality with block sizes greater than 1 does not reliably outperform row-wise constraints, and larger blocks perform worse.
A small benefit from symmetric positive-definite factors on query/key projections disappears as model size increases.
The same pattern appears in an ImageNet diffusion transformer, while downstream fine-tuning accuracy does not distinguish parameterizations.
Reanalysis of five prior methods attributes reported gains to numerical precision, training duration, optimizer details, or per-row norm control—not orthogonality itself.

papers.abstract: Activation recomputation saves accelerator memory by replaying forward segments during the backward pass, but replay is only correct if it sees the state the original forward pass saw. Mutable buffers, aliased bytes and random-generator state can change in between, so re-executing unchanged code can differentiate a different computation. We make this state explicit. A versioned replay contract specifies what replay must restore, and a joint planner chooses, per segment, between activation retention, whole-buffer snapshots and selective-region preservation, charging each option its measured memory and recovery cost. Independent derivative and byte-level checks validate the contract, and a Torch/JAX cohort retains all 5,900 execution records, including matches, rejections and divergences. On frozen sparse-write H100 workloads, each measured over fifty fresh processes, joint planning reduces paired step time by 18.16% against a correctly costed eager/whole planner at a 44 GiB budget (approximate 97.5% ratio interval $[.8172,.8195]$). At 32 GiB, where the eager/whole planner has no feasible static policy, joint planning is 4.98% faster than fixed regions at 29.94 rather than 26.20 GiB. A complete CIFAR-100 dense-queue application runs seven methods for 100 encoder and 25 probe epochs at six training seeds, with byte-identical test scores within each seed. There, joint planning uses 22.41% more allocated memory than whole snapshots, with a process-time geometric-mean ratio of 1.0080 (seed range $[.9845,1.0191]$). Together, the results map where selective preservation pays off: sparse writes with large activations benefit, while in the dense-queue workload whole snapshots use less allocated memory.
bullets: Replay can diverge when mutable buffers, aliased bytes, or RNG state change between forward and backward passes.
Versioned replay contracts specify required state restoration and support derivative and byte-level correctness checks.
A joint planner chooses activation retention, whole-buffer snapshots, or selective-region preservation using measured memory and recovery costs.
On frozen sparse-write H100 workloads, it reduced paired step time by 18.16% at 44 GiB and enabled a feasible policy at 32 GiB.
In a dense-queue CIFAR-100 workload, whole snapshots used less allocated memory, while process time was similar.],

papers.title: State-Aware Activation Recomputation with Replay Contracts and Selective Preservation
papers.tldr: A state-aware planner makes activation recomputation correct under mutable state and selectively trades memory for replay cost, improving performance on sparse-write workloads but not dense queues.

papers.abstract: Adam keeps two FP32 moments per parameter, twice the bytes of the FP32 weights, yet compressing them is risky: the update divides by the square root of the second moment, so small reconstruction errors can change the restored computation substantially. We study guarded moment compression, in which a coordinate's decoded moments are accepted only if they reproduce the native FP32 Adam update to within a tolerance $τ$, in units of the learning rate, for every gradient in a clipped domain; all other coordinates are stored exactly. The natural certificate, which ranges each update separately over gradient intervals, fails: on one million trained OPT-125M coordinates it escapes 98.9% of coordinates and the payload grows to 126.6% of raw FP32. Our key observation is that both updates consume the same gradient and parameter. Bounding their difference directly, with FP32 rounding-error allowances and a fixed mixed linear-logarithmic gradient partition, cuts escapes to 0.53% and the payload to 28.3% at $τ=0.01$. Across 120 complete-checkpoint restores of OPT-125M and ResNet-18, with four trained seeds and three training fractions per model, guarded 8-bit log codes shrink moment payloads by 69.5% and 71.9% relative to FP32, 40.8% and 45.4% relative to equally guarded BF16, and 29.3% and 37.6% relative to equally guarded blockwise 8-bit, and every restored first update stays within tolerance. Encoding and restoration together take 2.3-2.6$\times$ as long as guarded BF16 but less time than guarded blockwise 8-bit. Searching both moment codes jointly saves under 0.001% more bytes at 6% more codec time, so per-moment rounding suffices. The guarantee covers the first restored update under a pinned Torch operation model; we measure subsequent training empirically.
bullets: Naive per-update interval certificates are too loose, causing 98.9% coordinate escapes and payload growth to 126.6% of FP32.
The method directly bounds the difference between native and decoded Adam updates over a shared clipped-gradient domain, including FP32 rounding errors.
With tolerance τ=0.01, escapes fall to 0.53% and the payload reaches 28.3% of raw FP32.
Across OPT-125M and ResNet-18 restores, guarded 8-bit log codes reduce moment payloads by 69.5% and 71.9% versus FP32.
The guarantee applies to the first restored update under a pinned Torch operation model; later training behavior is evaluated empirically.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference with a drafter whose proposed tokens are verified by the target model in parallel. Under lossless speculative sampling, a draft token is accepted with probability one minus the total variation (TV) distance between the target and draft distributions, yet drafters are often trained with cross-entropy (CE) or KL. We first show that under matched and well-tuned training, TV matches or surpasses several published draft-training objectives when fine-tuning, and a fixed TV and KL mixture does the same when training from scratch. We identify two remaining problems, TV's vanishing gradients on undercovered tokens and the prefix products that starve later positions in acceptance-length objectives. To address both, we derive TVP, a loss family based on expected acceptance length, whose power parameter interpolates between coverage and acceptance oriented objectives. Annealing the power from zero to one gives the highest or tied-highest acceptance length across three drafter architectures and three target models, including longer drafts and block verification. TVP improves acceptance length over CE by 9.8% when fine-tuning, and over the public DFlash2 training recipes by 6.2 to 12.9%.
bullets: Speculative decoding accepts draft tokens according to their total variation distance from the target distribution.
TV can match or outperform existing CE/KL-based objectives, but suffers from vanishing gradients and prefix-product effects.
TVP addresses these issues with a power-parameterized expected-acceptance-length loss.
Annealing the power from zero to one performs best or ties for best across three drafter architectures and three target models.
TVP raises acceptance length by 9.8% over CE and 6.2–12.9% over public DFlash2 recipes.

papers.abstract: Structured channel pruning for convolutional neural networks (CNNs) plays an important role in pattern recognition and deep learning. Nevertheless, existing methods usually calculate channel importance scores based on the magnitudes of individual filters, making it difficult to distinguish shared redundancy from individual channel contributions. To tackle this limitation, we propose a novel structured channel pruning method termed bi-sparse matrix factorization (BSMF). Specifically, BSMF characterizes the convolutional weight matrix as output-channel coefficients over a shared basis with row-wise $\ell_{2,p}$-norm and column-wise $\ell_{2,q}$-norm regularization terms, respectively. Note that $p,q\in[0,1)$, which, to our best knowledge, has not been explored in the literature. To solve the resulting non-convex optimization problem, we develop an efficient update scheme built upon the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), in which all subproblems admit closed-form solutions. After that, a compact CNN is obtained by reconstructing the convolutional filters from the learned factors and discarding the redundant channels. Extensive experiments on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K datasets demonstrate that our proposed BSMF achieves significant network compression while maintaining high reconstruction accuracy. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/xianchaoxiu/BSMF
bullets: Addresses the limits of filter-magnitude importance scores, which may confuse shared redundancy with individual channel contributions.
Uses bi-sparse matrix factorization with row-wise and column-wise ℓ₂,p/ℓ₂,q regularization, where p,q∈[0,1).
Solves the resulting non-convex optimization with an ADMM-based update scheme whose subproblems have closed-form solutions.
Reconstructs filters from the learned factors and removes redundant channels to produce compact CNNs.
Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K report significant compression while maintaining high reconstruction accuracy.

papers.abstract: Does the level of test-time processing effort affect a language model's computational capability? A formal grammar-lens benchmark method, derived from the theory of computation, generates novel data at specified levels, each successively more computationally powerful than the levels below. Using this data, we tested GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.5-Pro-Medium, -High, and -XHigh, showing incrementally increased acceptance of test data: 16, 40, 43, and 52\%, respectively, illustrating the benchmark's ability to discern fine-grained differences among models' added test-time reasoning levels. Additionally, as test-time compute effort increases, model responses diverge from human responses to the same data. This increasing disagreement may turn out to be broadly characteristic of more capable language models, introducing the potential of a general capability-versus-alignment conflict.
bullets: The benchmark generates novel formal-language data with progressively greater computational demands.
Acceptance increased across GPT-5.5 configurations from 16% to 52% as test-time reasoning effort rose.
It differentiates fine-grained capability changes among reasoning levels.
Higher test-time compute was associated with greater disagreement between model and human responses.
The findings suggest a possible capability–alignment tension, though its broader generality remains uncertain.

papers.tldr: A grammar-based benchmark distinguishes GPT-5.5 variants by test-time reasoning effort, while revealing increasing divergence from human judgments at higher effort levels.

papers.abstract: Reasoning-oriented post-training enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex tasks via multi-step inference. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on high-quality reasoning traces is a particularly efficient approach, but its effectiveness depends critically on careful data curation. Existing pipelines rely on a costly generate-then-filter paradigm: large pools of long reasoning traces are produced by multiple teacher models and subsequently filtered for difficulty and diversity using additional LLMs, often requiring weeks of computation. In this work, we propose SFTProbe, a fundamentally different approach that bypasses this pipeline by directly predicting the quality of reasoning data. We show that a brief LoRA-based adaptation, combined with evaluating loss on only 5% of each reasoning trace, suffices to estimate both difficulty and diversity. SFTProbe is grounded in a geometric view of post-training, where pretrained LLMs lie in a low-rank, anisotropic loss basin. By probing this basin via low-rank perturbations, we construct compact loss signatures whose clustering captures diversity, while loss at curvature inflection points provides a robust proxy for difficulty. We also provide a simple criterion for teacher selection. Empirically, our approach reduces data curation time from weeks to hours while maintaining or improving performance. Remarkably, on mathematical reasoning, 5k generated examples match the highly filtered 89k-example in OpenThoughts-Math dataset, and 7.5k generated examples outperforms it by 2.5% in accuracy. We further introduce a high-quality physics reasoning dataset, and use it to train a model that outperforms an IPhO 2025 silver-medal-winning model. The code and the dataset are released at https://bigml-cs-ucla.github.io/SFTProbe-page/.
bullets: Addresses the costly generate-then-filter process for curating reasoning traces for supervised fine-tuning.
Uses brief LoRA adaptation and loss evaluation on only 5% of each trace to predict data quality.
Clusters compact loss signatures to capture diversity and uses curvature-inflection loss as a difficulty proxy.
On mathematical reasoning, 5k selected examples match an 89k-example dataset, while 7.5k outperform it by 2.5% accuracy.
Introduces a physics reasoning dataset and reports performance exceeding an IPhO 2025 silver-medal-winning model.

papers.selection_reason: Efficient SFT data generation for reasoning LLMs via loss signatures; directly relevant to LLM post-training and reasoning.
papers.title: From Weeks to Hours: Fast and Principled SFT Data Generation for Reasoning LLMs
papers.tldr: SFTProbe rapidly selects high-quality reasoning traces by estimating difficulty and diversity from brief low-rank loss probes, reducing SFT data curation from weeks to hours while preserving or improving performance.

papers.abstract: The rapid scaling of large language models (LLMs) has unlocked remarkable capabilities across various domains. However, deploying LLMs on mobile devices remains challenging because of their high computational and memory requirements. Low-bit quantization (e.g., 4-bit weights, 8-bit activations) can reduce model size while preserving accuracy, but its practical efficacy on mobile GPUs has been limited so far. In this paper, we identify that the performance gap stems primarily from frequent data type conversions between quantized and floating-point values, and dynamic and inefficient memory access patterns caused by the growing Key-Value (KV) cache during autoregressive decoding. We introduce BitLLM, a mobile inference engine that addresses type conversion overhead and suboptimal memory accesses in quantized LLMs. Our approach features an adaptive layout and packing strategy for the KV cache that ensures efficient memory access throughout LLM decoding. This is coupled with an integer-native execution pipeline that defers and overlaps type conversion outside the compute hot path, keeping the critical MatMul stages in the integer domain. Implemented on off-the-shelf mobile GPUs, BitLLM outperforms leading engines, i.e., LLAMA.CPP, MNN-LLM, LiteRT-LM, and MLC-LLM, achieving average speedups of 1.78$\times$, 1.73$\times$, 1.58$\times$, and 1.47$\times$, respectively, across various models and quantization levels. Under long-context generation, BitLLM reduces average energy consumption (per token) by up to 88.9%.
bullets: Mobile deployment is constrained by LLM computation and memory demands, while low-bit inference is hindered by conversion overhead and inefficient KV-cache access.
An adaptive KV-cache layout and packing strategy maintains efficient memory access during autoregressive decoding.
An integer-native execution pipeline moves and overlaps type conversions outside the critical MatMul path.
On off-the-shelf mobile GPUs, BitLLM achieves average speedups of 1.78×–1.47× over four leading inference engines across models and quantization levels.
For long-context generation, it reduces average energy consumption per token by up to 88.9%.

papers.abstract: Deterministic multi-agent LLM deliberation can exactly re- play a fixed transcript, yet exact replay alone does not test local resistance to controlled internal interventions. Because each response becomes context for later agents, a changed greedy token can redirect a transcript-mediated execution. We present a white-box audit of this local failure mode in a five-agent committee under greedy decoding. We prospectively select low- and high-margin token positions, require exact no-op re- play, inject norm-relative residual displacements, and measure first transcript divergence within ten generated tokens. Low- margin positions are more branch-sensitive than high-margin controls, while matched margin-reducing gradient directions branch substantially more often than margin-increasing con- trols. We then continue selected realized branches through the committee to distinguish textual persistence from preference and final-decision changes. The contribution is a controlled audit for local branch susceptibility in this specified protocol, not an estimate of deployment frequency, decision correct- ness, or a phenomenon unique to multi-agent systems.
bullets: Exact replay verifies the baseline, but does not establish resistance to local internal perturbations.
A five-agent greedy-decoding committee was tested at prospectively selected low- and high-margin token positions.
Norm-relative residual displacements were applied, with branch sensitivity measured by the first transcript divergence within ten tokens.
Margin-reducing directions branched more often than matched margin-increasing controls.
Follow-up analysis separated textual branch persistence from changes in preferences and final decisions; the findings are protocol-specific, not deployment-frequency or correctness estimates.

papers.selection_reason: Conducts a white-box audit of local robustness in multi-agent LLM deliberation by analyzing token selection and branch points under controlled interventions.
papers.title: Low-Margin Branch Points in Deterministic LLM Deliberation
papers.tldr: A controlled audit shows that low-margin token decisions in deterministic LLM deliberation are more susceptible to small residual interventions that redirect later transcript generation.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents extend their capabilities with skills, each with a name, a description, and a body. Under progressive disclosure, an LLM router selects skills by name and description alone and loads only the selected bodies. Skill libraries grow continually as users and agents add new skills. Because the router relies on this metadata, a similar new skill can displace an earlier one, breaking previously correct routing even though the earlier skill and the router are unchanged. This routing interference is aggravated for public skills, whose descriptions may not match their bodies. We formulate the problem as lifelong skill routing, a class-incremental continual learning problem. A solution must keep earlier skills selectable without suppressing new ones. Existing approaches fall short, since continually retraining the router risks catastrophic forgetting and rewriting methods either ignore similar skills or require per-skill feedback. We therefore propose Skill++, which rewrites only the name and description of each incoming skill, without router training or labeled data. The new description states what the body supports, how the skill differs from its closest predecessor, and what related work it excludes. As a library grows to 731 skills over ten sessions, Skill++ selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries, versus 36.4% under the original metadata. Across three benchmarks and five LLM routers, it outperforms all compared approaches, and its gains carry over to the Codex CLI agent harness.
bullets: Addresses routing interference, where similar new skills displace previously correct skills as libraries grow.
Rewrites only each incoming skill’s name and description to clarify capabilities, distinctions, and exclusions.
Requires no router training, labeled data, or per-skill feedback.
On a 731-skill, ten-session setting, it selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries versus 36.4% with original metadata.
Outperforms competing methods across three benchmarks and five LLM routers, with gains transferring to the Codex CLI agent harness.

figures.caption: Figure 3: This figure gives an overview of SKILL++, to show how it refines an incoming skill before the router reads it. SKILL++ first retrieves similar earlier skills from a record of their original names, descriptions, bodies and synthetic queries. Three components then refine the new skill independently. Description differentiation rewrites its description around what makes it unique, scope exclusions list related work that it does not cover, and name clarification makes an overlapping name more specific. The refined name and description enter the library that the router reads, and the original skill joins the record for future additions.

Figure 2: This figure compares three ways of handling a growing skill library, to position our problem. (a) Continuous router training follows arriving skills but retrains the router at every step, risking catastrophic forgetting of earlier skills. (b) One-shot skill optimization refines a fixed skill set once, so it ignores skills that arrive later. (c) SKILL++ keeps the router frozen and refines each new batch against similar earlier skills, so both earlier and new skills are selected for the queries that need them.

Figure 4: This figure shows FC@5 as the library grows (sizes in Tab. A2), to test whether routing stays accurate. (a) The main router, Claude Haiku 4.5 (Tab. A1). (b)–(e) Four other routers (Tab. A4). With every router, Vanilla declines while SKILL++ leads or ties at every checkpoint.

Figure 5: This figure breaks down the routing errors at S9 into two forms and seven types (defined in Appendix C.2), to show which errors SKILL++ removes. All panels draw on the eight combinations of Tab. A3. (a) The 200 Vanilla errors, by form (inner ring) and type (outer ring). (b) Errors per type under Vanilla and SKILL++, as a share of the Vanilla errors. (c) Errors per form when one component or all three are added to Vanilla, shown in the same way. SKILL++ removes most errors of both forms, and each component mainly reduces one form.

Figure 1: This figure presents an example of routing interference, to show why incoming metadata needs refinement. The router reads only skill names and descriptions. (a) For a query about an AI paper, it selects the AI paper-writing skill. (b) A biology paper-writing skill arrives with the same metadata, and the router selects it instead. (c) SKILL++ refines only the incoming skill against the earlier one, so the router selects the correct skill again.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Skill++, a method for lifelong skill routing in LLM agents that rewrites skill metadata to prevent routing interference and catastrophic forgetting as the skill library grows.
papers.title: Skill++: Towards Lifelong Agents via Routing-Aware Skill Refinement
papers.tldr: Skill++ preserves reliable skill routing in growing LLM-agent libraries by refining incoming skills’ metadata without retraining the router.

papers.abstract: Whether a policy shifts domains and, by extension, continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses previous policy is of paramount importance to the study of public policy. We propose Dual-Axis Policy Entailment (DAPE), which evaluates an ordered pair of policy directives on both dimensions at once: a binary judgment determines whether the two directives govern the same policy domain, and a five-way judgment determines whether the later directive continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses the earlier policy, or governs a different domain altogether. Read together, the two judgments form one five-category label, our primary metric. The two-axis design captures two central dimensions of policy change without conflating errors on either dimension into a generic "irrelevant" label, and it makes annotation more rigorous: a coder cannot dismiss a difficult pair as domain-irrelevant without an explicit, checkable decision. We introduce an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,000 ordered directive pairs drawn from a large corpus of Chinese government policy, together with an annotation-calibration protocol (an adjudication packet with pre/post agreement measurement) that we contribute as a methodological artifact. Fourteen open-weight models and four frontier API flagships fail the task zero-shot: even the best frontier flagship's chance-corrected agreement with expert labels is far below the human ceiling (Cohen's $κ\approx 0.29$ vs. $0.53$). A fine-tuned open-weight model (LoRA SFT of Qwen3-14B, five-fold cross-validation) closes this gap, reaching the coder-mutual human ceiling ($κ= 0.524$ vs. $0.527$). Finally, we apply our method to China's AI policy (1980-2024) and map the direction of policy change across eras.
bullets: Evaluates ordered policy-directive pairs along two axes: shared domain and policy-change relation.
Combines the judgments into five labels: continue, broaden, narrow, reverse, or different domain.
Provides an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,000 Chinese government policy pairs and an annotation-calibration protocol.
Fourteen open-weight and four frontier models perform poorly zero-shot; LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen3-14B reaches coder-level agreement.
Applies DAPE to map changes in China’s AI policy from 1980 to 2024.

papers.title: Dual-Axis Policy Entailment: A Benchmark for Policy-Change Reasoning

papers.abstract: We present WeSearch, a unified, model-centric retrieval framework for large-scale, continuously evolving content search. Prevailing methods assign documents fixed hierarchical Semantic IDs, implicitly assuming each document follows a single coherent semantic path-an assumption that often breaks down for multi-topic documents. WeSearch instead retrieves query-relevant clusters and then ranks atomic documents within the resulting query-specific candidate space, decoupling candidate pruning from fine-grained relevance modeling. Combined with relevance-aware training, compact document representations, and incremental index updates, this design enables weekly-or daily when needed-model refreshes. Deployed as the primary semantic retrieval path in WeChat Search alongside a lexical syntax tree, WeSearch shows consistent one-week A/B gains on corpora from hundreds of millions to billions of documents, and a one-month full-traffic A/B test confirms stable improvements of +0.68% CTR and +2.27% per-user article clicks, together with a 41% reduction in retrieval resource cost and a 19 ms reduction in graphic-text retrieval latency. WeSearch is now fully deployed in WeChat Search, serving 100% of production traffic.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of fixed hierarchical Semantic IDs for multi-topic documents and continuously changing content.
Uses query-relevant cluster retrieval followed by atomic-document ranking, with relevance-aware training and compact representations.
Supports weekly or on-demand daily model refreshes through incremental index updates.
Production A/B tests report +0.68% CTR, +2.27% per-user article clicks, 41% lower retrieval resource cost, and 19 ms lower graphic-text retrieval latency.
Fully deployed as WeChat Search’s primary semantic retrieval path alongside a lexical syntax tree, serving 100% of traffic.

papers.abstract: Laser doppler vibrometer (LDV) scans can be used to detect defects and cracks in manufactured parts before they are deployed. This work presents a method for reconstructing the steady-state surface wavefield of a three-dimensional part by combining automated robotic manipulation with neural rendering. A six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) robotic manipulator (UFactory xArm6) with an embedded piezoelectric transducer presented an acoustically excited test article to a stationary LDV at a sequence of known orientations, yielding a set of complex-valued 2D scans with poses derived analytically from the arm kinematics rather than from image-based pose estimation. These scans were used to train a novel complex-nerfacto model, a modified Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) pipeline that replaces the standard three-channel RGB output head with a two-channel output. Complex-nerfacto represents the real and imaginary velocity components of a wavefield, preserving the complex measurement without quantization. Reconstructions of a welded aluminum cylinder and a welded T-bracket were evaluated against measured scans using Z-normalized cross-correlation (ZNCC). The complex-valued pipeline achieved a mean ZNCC of 0.60 at held-out viewing angles, compared with 0.28 for a baseline RGB nerfacto model trained on rendered images of the same data. The resulting surface wavefield reconstructions supported defect detection and characterization on complex components. We identify geometry reconstruction from sparse LDV scans as the remaining obstacle to practical deployment.
bullets: Automated 6-DOF manipulation presents parts at known poses to a stationary LDV, producing complex-valued scans.
A modified NeRF, complex-nerfacto, predicts real and imaginary wavefield velocity components without quantization.
Evaluated on a welded aluminum cylinder and welded T-bracket using Z-normalized cross-correlation.
The complex pipeline achieved mean ZNCC 0.60 versus 0.28 for the RGB nerfacto baseline at held-out viewing angles.
Practical deployment remains limited by geometry reconstruction from sparse LDV scans.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to adapt pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs). We investigate the problem of behavioral steering: adapting a VLA's execution style to preferences such as carrying objects higher. To investigate how little trainable capacity such steering requires and how much pretrained capability can be retained, we freeze an OpenVLA-OFT 7B policy and optimize TinyLoRA adapters with 8 to 384 trainable parameters using either policy-gradient RL (GRPO) or evolutionary search (CMA-ES). With just 256 trainable parameters, we raise carry height by 120 mm on trained tasks at 92% success and by 74 mm on a held-out task at 80% success. By rescaling the learned update, we can tune the trade-off between style gains and capability retention without retraining. Increasing adapter capacity generally improves this trade-off, retaining more pretrained capability at comparable style gains. The choice of optimizer also depends on capacity, with CMA-ES being competitive at low parameter counts, while GRPO offers better trade-offs as capacity grows. These findings show that extremely low-dimensional updates can steer pretrained VLA behavior, with adapter capacity, optimizer choice, and update scaling offering practical control over adaptation and retention.
bullets: Studies behavioral steering, such as making a robot carry objects higher, without updating the full policy.
Freezes an OpenVLA-OFT 7B policy and trains TinyLoRA adapters with 8–384 parameters using GRPO or CMA-ES.
With 256 parameters, carry height increases by 120 mm on trained tasks and 74 mm on a held-out task, with 92% and 80% success respectively.
Adapter capacity, optimizer choice, and update scaling control the trade-off between behavioral change and capability retention.
CMA-ES is competitive at very low capacities, while GRPO provides better trade-offs as capacity increases.

papers.selection_reason: Steering pretrained VLA policies with tiny adapters via RL and evolutionary search, directly relevant to VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: Behavioral Steering of Vision-Language-Action Models in the Low-Parameter Regime
papers.tldr: Extremely small adapters can steer a pretrained vision-language-action model’s behavior while largely preserving its original capabilities.

papers.abstract: LLMs degrade in multi-turn conversation partly because of context pollution: the model's own earlier outputs stay in context and anchor later turns, so an early misreading of the user's intent can persist after the user corrects it. Assistant omission (AO), dropping every assistant message, removes this pollution but fails when interaction is referential: later turns refer back to drafts, decisions, and tool-call results that exist only in assistant turns. We propose Agentic Conversation Context Curation (AC3), a training-free method in which a separate analyzer (1) consolidates the task specification from the user's messages alone, (2) audits the assistant's prior outputs against it, and (3) edits the context, either appending the analysis or discarding the assistant side and rebuilding the context from the specification. A second finding: pollution is contagious. An analyzer that sees the assistant's reasoning while extracting the specification can do worse than no intervention, and instructing it to ignore them did not close the gap, so we exclude assistant turns structurally. On Lost in Conversation (replaying difficulty-selected instances), where AO is an oracle by construction, AC3 closes 55-84% of the gap between full context and AO on three of four tasks and exceeds AO on the fourth, and an LLM that faithfully summarizes the history does not reproduce the gain even with more compute. On real WildChat conversations, a GPT-5-mini judge prefers AC3's next turn over both full context and AO in every configuration of our main table, though this preference depends on the judge; on CollabLLM results are mixed. In stateful tool use (tau2-bench), AO collapses to 0% on every model; AC3 does not collapse, though it falls slightly behind full context. Detector studies show that Reset removes injected pollution but is not span-selective: the gain comes from rebuilding the specification.
bullets: Context pollution from earlier assistant outputs can preserve incorrect interpretations even after user corrections.
AC3 uses a separate analyzer to extract the user-only task specification, audit prior responses, and either append guidance or rebuild context from that specification.
On Lost in Conversation, AC3 closes 55–84% of the gap between full context and oracle assistant omission on three of four tasks and surpasses it on the fourth.
On WildChat, a GPT-5-mini judge prefers AC3 over both full context and assistant omission; results are mixed on CollabLLM.
AC3 remains functional in stateful tool use, unlike assistant omission, though it slightly trails full context; benefits depend partly on the evaluator.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Illustrative example. (a) Context pollution: an early incorrect interpretation by the assistant (a zero prepaid balance) stays in the context and re-anchors a later response even after the user has corrected it. (b) Coarse omission: AO removes the invalidated reasoning but also the state the next action needs (the restart the agent already recommended), so the agent repeats itself. The deficit is behavioral rather than a lack of capability: on LiC, the same models solve the task when it is posed in a single turn [Laban et al., 2025]. Our method (Section 3, Figure 3) supplies the missing control at the harness level by rebuilding the conversation around a specification drawn from the user’s messages and dropping the invalidated reasoning.

Figure 3: Agentic Conversation Context Curation (AC3). Before the assistant generates, a separate analyzer runs two analysis subtasks and one intervention step. Subtask 1 (specification extraction) sees only user turns, so it cannot be biased by the assistant’s prior reasoning. Subtask 2 (approach evaluation) compares that specification against the assistant’s full history. An operator (Augment, Reset, or Rewrite; the figure shows a rewritten context) then edits the context; the “retained” content in the rebuilt context is restated by the analyzer, not copied from assistant turns. Structural exclusion in Subtask 1 is essential: when the extractor sees assistant turns, accuracy falls below the full-context baseline on math and code (Table 4).

On WildChat, a GPT-5-mini judge prefers AC3-Reset’s next turn over both AO and full context (dashed line: parity). papers.selection_reason: Training-free context curation for multi-turn LLM conversations addresses context pollution and retention, relevant to LLM context and memory methods.
papers.title: Agentic Context Management for Multi-Turn Human-AI Conversations
papers.tldr: AC3 improves multi-turn LLM conversations by rebuilding context from user intent while selectively preserving useful assistant-derived information, reducing context pollution without breaking references.

papers.abstract: Most agentic robotic systems use vision-language models (VLMs) either to orchestrate predefined skills or to directly generate actions, constraints, and control programs. The former is limited by the available skill library, while the latter requires VLMs to reason about precise geometry and contact. In this paper, we propose WorldSketch, a new paradigm for agentic robotics in which a VLM constructs a world model rather than generating robot actions. The VLM acts as an agent that actively queries perception tools to build and visually validate a minimal kinematic world model, capturing only task-relevant objects, their interaction geometry, and possible motions. A geometric planner then jointly optimizes contact and whole-body motion on the resulting model. Moreover, the world model is self-improving: execution feedback verifies outcomes, updates uncertain hypotheses, and enables the agent to revise the model when its predictions are contradicted. We demonstrate the generality of this paradigm across RoboCasa, LIBERO-PRO, and R2R-CE navigation, achieving zero-shot success rates of 91%, 97%, and 76%, respectively. On RoboCasa, WorldSketch outperforms the next-best zero-shot agent baseline by 58 percentage points while using 10 times fewer VLM input tokens; on LIBERO-PRO, it exceeds CaP-X by 82 percentage points. In navigation, it matches the success rate of step-by-step VLM agents while using 6 times fewer input tokens.
bullets: Addresses the limits of skill-library orchestration and the difficulty of precise geometric reasoning by VLMs.
The VLM actively queries perception tools to construct and visually validate minimal kinematic models of relevant objects, interactions, and motions.
A geometric planner jointly optimizes contact and whole-body motion using the constructed model.
Execution feedback verifies results, updates uncertain hypotheses, and supports model revision when predictions fail.
Demonstrated across RoboCasa, LIBERO-PRO, and R2R-CE navigation, with success rates of 91%, 97%, and 76%, respectively, while using substantially fewer VLM input tokens than comparable approaches.

papers.abstract: Answering a complex question about a long video is a grounding problem: the answer turns on a few seconds of evidence, and vision-language models remain well below human accuracy at finding them. The standard way to spend extra test-time compute on this kind of video reasoning is best-of-N selection: sample several chain-of-thought answers from a fixed model, then let a second model re-watch the video and pick one. Such pipelines are reported by a single headline number, their margin over a majority vote. That number conflates two effects with opposite deployment consequences: the benefit the second model adds by selecting among candidates, and the benefit it would have supplied by solving the question itself. We separate them, measuring the Selection Increment (SI) -- selection accuracy minus the same verifier's accuracy with the candidates withheld -- alongside the margin over self-consistency, across five long-video benchmarks. The Selection Increment is largest for the weakest verifiers: a verifier that solves poorly on its own leaves the candidates the most room to help. Beating the majority vote follows the opposite profile: where the vote already sits near its ceiling no verifier we test improves on it; below that ceiling only the strongest do. On Video-Holmes, the two come apart on a single pool of candidates -- a weak verifier gains +19.3 points from the candidates yet lands 7.1 points below the vote, while the frontier verifier gains the least and beats the vote. The weakest verifier also shows a failure mode: on EgoSchema it picks by where an option sits in the list rather than by what the video shows. Read as a merit score, SI puts a verifier that fails to beat a majority vote at the top of its ranking; read as an audit, it says which of the two effects a headline number delivers. Code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/best-n-selection-video-reasoning.
bullets: Introduces Selection Increment (SI): verifier accuracy with candidates minus its accuracy when candidates are withheld.
Across five long-video benchmarks, weaker verifiers gain more from candidate answers, while stronger verifiers are more likely to beat majority vote.
On Video-Holmes, a weak verifier gained 19.3 points from candidates but remained 7.1 points below the vote; the frontier verifier gained less but surpassed it.
The weakest verifier showed positional-choice bias on EgoSchema, selecting based on option order rather than video evidence.
SI is useful as an audit of where gains come from, but is misleading as a standalone merit ranking.

figures.caption: Figure 1: What a best-of-N verifier pipeline measures. A base generator (Qwen3.5-27B) samples N=8 chain-of-thought rollouts per question, each ending in a candidate letter. Three rules score that same pool: majority voting; the verifier selecting among the candidates after re-watching K frames; and the same verifier with the candidates withheld. Their differences define our two axes, ∆maj and SI.

Figure 2: Selection Increment vs. gain over selfconsistency. Each point is a (benchmark, verifier) pair; lines link the two verifiers on one benchmark. SI>0 and beating self-consistency are dissociable. Solver policy; VRBench: first 1,000 questions (118 of 960 videos).

Figure 3: Selection Increment by benchmark and verifier. SI (selection accuracy minus the same verifier answering directly, both under the Solver policy) for the Muse holistic-48 verifier (blue) and GPT-5.6 Sol (red). GPT-5.6 Sol yields positive SI on all three benchmarks while Muse splits (negative on TempCompass)—not because GPT is the stronger selector but because its standalone accuracy typically sits below Muse’s, leaving the candidates more room, consistent with SI tracking standalone accuracy inversely (Section 4). VRBench cells use the first 1,000 questions of its split (118 of 960 videos).

SI is a column effect; beating self-consistency is set by the verifier. Cell-level tests and provenance: Appendix E.

Table 5: Position bias by response mode, weak verifier (Phi-3.5-Vision). Modes are disjoint and separated by output length. All tests are exact two-sided binomial McNemar on non-empty picks; Alift is 100(bA−cA)/n. Marker-mode A-lift magnitudes are withheld pending independent verification: no marker-mode cell reaches significance in any of the ten arms as scored here, each on its own full row set, and every marker-mode |A-lift| is below 4 points, though at these per-arm n that is a failure to distinguish the marker mode from zero rather than a demonstration that it is unbiased—the closest cell sits just above α, at p=0.0501. Accuracies are under the Solver policy.

Table 7: Answer-position bias on EgoSchema is a weak-verifier property. Per-verifier A-lift (pick-“A” rate minus gold-“A” rate, in points, under the Solver scoring policy; gold-“A” = 20.2%, gold mode E, n=500), ordered weak to strong. Only the weak cross-family verifier Phi-3.5-Vision lifts “A” above gold, at both of its compute budgets; every capable verifier stays within 1.4 points of gold.

Table 6: Base × verifier on TempCompass (full 2 × 2). Selection Increment and gain over selfconsistency (∆maj), in points, for a weak (Qwen-27B) and a strong (Muse) verifier over each of two candidate pools. SI is a column effect (large for the weak verifier, near zero for the strong one on both bases); beating self-consistency is a row effect (attainable on the harder Qwen-base pool, out of reach on the near-saturated Muse-base pool). The two axes are governed by different factors. The three small ∆maj cells (+0.9, −0.3, −0.4) are effectively at parity; the row effect is clearest in the Muse column (+7.9→−0.4). Provenance. SI is reported with both of its legs—selection and standalone—at the original 1,024-token generation cap, since re-measuring one leg alone would mix compute budgets within a single difference. Each SI cell is differenced on its verifier’s matched non-empty support. The two Qwen-27B ∆maj cells are re-measured at 8,192 tokens with a corrected answer extractor; the Muse cells never bound the cap but retain the original extractor (Appendix B). In both base-varying 2 × 2s the base axis moves the generator’s frame budget together with its identity—the Qwen-base pools read 64 frames, the Muse-base pools 32—so a row effect is a property of each pool as produced rather than of model identity alone.

Table 3: The two axes come apart on full splits. Solver-policy (prior-work convention) accuracies for the Muse holistic-48 and GPT-5.6 Sol verifiers; majority is the shared 27B majority@8 baseline. The headroom h is a per-benchmark property of the candidate pool and predicts neither delta. VRBench cells use the first 1,000 questions of its split (118 of 960 videos); deltas are McNemar-significant at α=0.05 unless marked n.s.

Table 1: Base and verifier roles. All headline best-of-N results fix Qwen3.5-27B as the base generator and vary the verifier; two base-varying 2× 2s (Video-Holmes, TempCompass; Section 4) also vary the base. The standalone solver is the same verifier answering directly from its own K frames.

Table 8: Answer-position bias is a pathology of under-capable verifiers. Per-verifier A-lift (pick-“A” rate minus gold-“A” rate, in points; under the Solver scoring policy) across benchmarks. Where a benchmark induces the bias, the weak verifier (Phi-3.5) lifts “A” above gold, whereas the capable same-family self-verifier sits below gold on both cells we re-measured without a truncating generation cap (MLVU-Test −2.2, Video-Holmes −2.8); no capable cross-family verifier lifts “A” above gold by more than 1.4 points (on Video-Holmes the frontier GPT-5.6 Sol is likewise robust, −1.2). TempCompass induces no default for any verifier. Compute budget caveat. The Qwen3.5-27B (self) column was first measured at a 1,024-token cap that truncated the verifier’s own response. Four cells were re-measured at 8,192 tokens with a corrected answer extractor. Both Qwen3.5-27B cells change sign—by −8.0 points on MLVU-Test and −5.0 on Video-Holmes—and raising the cap alone accounts for −6.4 and −4.4 of that, flipping both signs by itself; the extractor only deepens them. The other two are Phi-3.5 positive controls: its cap and extractor effects are exactly zero (its longest MLVU-Test response is five tokens, so the cap never bound), and re-measuring moved its Video-Holmes A-lift by only 0.22 points—from the +4.2 printed here to +4.0—through run-to-run sampling alone. That residual, against flips of 8.0 and 5.0 points, is what attributes the reversals to the cap rather than to the act of re-measuring. Phi-3.5 entries are the original run; the significance tests of Section 5 use the re-measured one, which changes no survivor. Every remaining entry, including the other two Qwen3.5-27B cells (−0.8, +0.6), is uncorrected: original extractor, 1,024-token cap. Phi-3.5 on EgoSchema is shown at 48 frames; dashes mark cells not run.

papers.selection_reason: Separates selection versus solving effects in best-of-N video reasoning, directly relevant to video-language understanding and VLM evaluation.
papers.title: Selecting or Solving? What Best-of-N Verification Delivers in Video Reasoning
papers.tldr: Best-of-N video reasoning gains must be split into candidate-selection benefit and the verifier’s own solving ability, because these can point to opposite conclusions.

papers.abstract: Parallel speculative drafters use a lightweight serial head to recover token dependencies within a block generated in parallel. Each head step updates only a small state, yet projects that state through the same vocabulary-sized matrix. Step-wise execution repeatedly transfers this large, immutable projection, making the head a meaningful source of latency despite its low arithmetic cost. We present Weights That Stay, an execution design that keeps projection shards on chip for the entire serial draft walk. A persistent megakernel couples weight residency with GPU-side token selection and state advancement, reusing resident weights while exchanging only compact state between steps. The design supports full or partial residency and accommodates both Markov and recurrent heads on H100 and B200. Integrated into SGLang, Weights That Stay improves throughput for Markov drafting on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, with gains of up to 12.3%. At the head level, the DSpark walk is up to 11.6$\times$ faster than the fastest measured SGLang reference path. These results show that aligning weight residency with the full draft walk translates cross-step reuse into end-to-end serving gains.
bullets: Serial heads repeatedly transfer the same large projection matrix despite updating only a small state, creating latency overhead.
A persistent GPU megakernel combines resident projection shards with token selection and state advancement, exchanging only compact state between steps.
The design supports full or partial on-chip residency and both Markov and recurrent heads on H100 and B200 GPUs.
Integrated with SGLang, it improves Markov-drafting throughput by up to 12.3% on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B.
The DSpark walk is up to 11.6× faster than the fastest measured SGLang reference path at the head level.

papers.abstract: When searching for an object, humans naturally combine semantic intuition - reasoning about where the object is likely to be stored - with geometric awareness of what parts of the space are visible, occluded, or unexplored. Effective robot object search requires the same joint reasoning, yet existing methods rely on only one: geometric methods maintain principled spatial beliefs but lack deep semantic understanding, while language-model based methods leverage commonsense knowledge but maintain no explicit belief over space. We argue that jointly reasoning over semantic and geometric evidence in an explicit 3D belief enables human-like interactive object search that outperforms either modality alone. To test this claim, we build a system that accumulates per-object VLM plausibility scores and geometric occupancy evidence via Bayesian log-odds filtering into a unified 3D voxel belief field. High-belief regions in the combined belief field drive action selection at each step: taking a closer look from a different viewpoint, navigating toward an unexplored region of the workspace, or physically interacting with a closed cabinet. We deploy this system end-to-end on a bimanual mobile humanoid and find that it outperforms geometry-only search and LLM-based planning methods. Project website - https://skymanaditya1.github.io/objsearch-website/
bullets: Addresses the gap between geometry-only methods and language-based planners that lack spatial beliefs.
Combines VLM object-likelihood scores with geometric occupancy evidence using Bayesian log-odds filtering.
Uses high-belief voxel regions to choose viewpoints, explore unseen areas, or interact with closed cabinets.
Evaluated end-to-end on a bimanual mobile humanoid, outperforming geometry-only and LLM-based search methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 6. Outcomes and failure modes. Results for SSF (left), the geometry-only baseline (middle), and the LLM planner (right), with 16 trials per method. Flows connect trial outcomes to task settings and, for failed trials, to failure categories. Flow widths represent trial counts; percentages are computed over the 16 trials shown for each method.

Fig. 3. Skill library. open cabinet and open drawer are learned via behavior cloning; explore navigates to frontier viewpoints; look at repositions the base, torso, and head to uncover occluded voxels. The four pick * skills (bottom row) retrieve objects from cabinets, drawers, shelves, and tables.

Table I. Quantitative results with a 15-minute search budget. SR is reported as successful trials over total trials; each setting comprises 2 object categories × 2 viewpoints. NA is averaged over successful trials only.
