papers.title: Knowing Where to Look: Interactive Object Search via Spatial-Semantic Fusion
papers.tldr: A robot improves interactive object search by fusing semantic plausibility with geometric visibility in an explicit 3D belief field.

papers.abstract: On hardware whose fastest matrix datapath is INT8$\times$INT8, such as the Neural Accelerators of Apple's M5 GPUs, 4-bit weights must become INT8 operands. Existing MXFP4 kernels already map FP4 (E2M1) values to integers by doubling them, but apply every 32-element block scale inside the reduction. We show when no per-block work is needed: a row of MXFP4 weights is exactly one INT8 vector times one power-of-two scale if its block exponents span at most three, so a linear layer becomes a single INT8 GEMM with one rescale per output. Enforcing the condition adds at most 1/16 of a row's largest rounding error to the blocks it changes, and real weights already satisfy it: 97.9-99.97% of rows across seven models, including 99.93% of the 95M rows of a 125B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. The resulting spread-constrained MXFP4 files stay standard MXFP4. With integer instead of power-of-two block multipliers, an integer-exact format (16-wide blocks, multipliers 1..10, 4.26 bits) runs as one exact INT8 GEMM and is more accurate than NVFP4 (4.5 bits) with its standard scale rule on five small models, within 0.06 perplexity of NVFP4 with scale search. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's routed experts with INT8 activations it is as close to the FP8 model as NVFP4 with scale search (KL divergence 0.0557 vs. 0.0553) and closer than MLX's MXFP4 and affine INT4; with every matrix quantized it solves 94.8% of GSM8K vs. 91.0% for MLX's MXFP4. Quantizing only the 74k routed expert matrices (96% of the parameters) to either of our formats with INT8 activations costs at most 0.2% perplexity. A complete W4A8 system on the M5 produces outputs bit-identical to the quantized reference; prefill is 1.34-1.74x faster than MLX on a dense model, 1.10-1.57x on two MoE models up to 35B parameters and 1.22-1.29x on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, where shared non-GEMM work bounds the gain.
bullets: MXFP4 rows can be converted to a single INT8 vector and one power-of-two scale when block exponents span at most three, eliminating per-block work inside the reduction.
Enforcing this condition changes rounding error by at most 1/16 of a row’s largest block error, while already covering 97.9–99.97% of rows across seven models.

An integer-exact 16-wide format with multipliers 1–10 uses 4.26 bits and achieves accuracy better than standard NVFP4 on five small models, and nearly matches scale-searched NVFP4 on a large MoE model.
On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, the proposed formats outperform MLX MXFP4 and affine INT4 on routed-expert KL divergence; full quantization reaches 94.8% GSM8K versus 91.0% for MLX MXFP4.

A complete W4A8 implementation is bit-identical to its quantized reference and accelerates prefill by 1.10–1.74× on tested dense and MoE models, with gains limited by non-GEMM work in the largest MoE.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Left: deployed 4-bit formats are dequantized to FP16 and multiplied at the FP16 rate (W4A16). We rewrite MXFP4 weights exactly as INT8 operands and quantize activations to INT8, so the GEMM runs on the INT8 datapath, about 2× faster on Apple M5. The weights remain a valid MXFP4 file. Right: the rewrite is exact when a row’s block exponents lie within a window of four values below the largest; blocks below it (red) are coarsened, which adds at most 1/16 of the row’s largest rounding error (Proposition 2).

Figure 3: Block-exponent spread per weight row. Spread above 3 (shaded) needs an exponent adjustment. Logarithmic axis; its bottom tick marks 0 (no rows).

Table 4: Time to first token (ms) and decode throughput (tokens/s) on an M5 Max. Speedups, from unrounded medians, are W4A8 vs. MLX MXFP4 measured in the same session and vs. llama.cpp (Q4_0, its fastest 4-bit type here), whose prefill was measured in a separate session (the faster of two runs); every prefill ratio against it is at least 1.14×. Prefill rows use the sustained clock regime (prompts following long ones; Table 9 also gives the burst regime). llama.cpp’s MXFP4_MOE type is 11– 26% slower than its Q4_0 on the two MoEs, its Q4_K_M and IQ4_XS prefill at 0.82–0.96× Q4_0’s speed (Appendix I). All methods quantize the same matrices (every projection and expert); NVIDIA’s NVFP4 release quantizes only the routed experts (NVIDIA, 2026). bits/w: for this model’s matrices (our formats’ row scales add 32/K, and the expert down projections have K = 640). “vs. FP8”: the W4A8 column, from unrounded perplexities. All perplexities use the model’s reference DeltaNet recurrence. Last column: how the format multiplies on M5 (∗INT8 with a correction per 64-element group, as in oMLX (oMLX contributors, 2026)).

All methods quantize the same matrices. ‡MoE: every expert is quantized, the router stays BF16. Bits at K = 4096 (the FP32 row scales of our formats add 32/K). – = not run.

Our kernels are timed with GPU timestamps: the elapsed time of one command buffer that runs a pipeline’s kernels back to back, divided by the number of runs it contains, so gaps between a pipeline’s kernels count: matmul2d FP16 is a plain FP16 GEMM; W4A16 fused unpacks to FP16 tiles inside the Kloop; W4A16 2-pass unpacks to an FP16 buffer and runs an FP16 GEMM with the row scales; W4A8 quantizes the activations, unpacks to an INT8 buffer and runs an INT8 GEMM, scaling in registers or in a separate pass, whichever is faster; †W8A8 quantizes the activations and runs an INT8 GEMM with INT32 output from 8-bit weights (no unpack, no scaling), a bound on the achievable speed. MLX’s kernels are timed by wall clock in a separate process (10 calls per evaluation), which includes some host overhead, so the “mixed” vs-MLX column mixes two timing methods. “Alike”: our MLX-integrated kernels (the ones used end to end) and MLX’s, called from MLX and timed alike by wall clock in one process, interleaved; at K = 14336 the MLX-integrated W4A8 is slower than the standalone one (3.90 vs. 2.70 ms). Like for like are this column and the comparisons against matmul2d FP16 and W4A16 2-pass.

The systems do not fit in memory together, so each was loaded in its own session (two sessions each, alternating; medians agree within 5%). ∗Decode with MLX’s W4A16 kernels on the same SC-MXFP4 file (two later sessions, 42.4 and 42.5, in which MLX MXFP4 decoded at 42.4); with our W4A8 GEMVs, 37.6 (0.89×).

Scale search: each NVFP4 block’s E4M3 scale and its two neighbours on either side; exponent search: the OCP exponent and its two neighbours (least squared weight error).

papers.title: Integer-Exact Microscaling: Running MXFP4 Language Models on INT8 Matrix Units

papers.abstract: Many vision benchmarks align a prediction to the ground truth before scoring it. If the alignment minimises the error, an input-free template scores the truth's distance from everything the alignment can reach, so the ground truth alone fixes how well a template can score, before any model runs. Camera pose is our central case. The absolute trajectory error (ATE), the standard camera-motion measure, aligns camera positions by a similarity transform. On the common Sintel protocol, an image-free constant-velocity line has a lower mean ATE than 10 of 11 recent models and 85 of 110 published methods, and on Lightspeed than 5 of 9 models and 10 of 11 published methods. The straightness of the true paths separates these two from TUM, ScanNet, DyCheck and ADT, where every model beats the line. A residual signal-to-noise criterion with the alignment's first-order refit predicts when straightening a prediction lowers ATE in all but one of 4010 model-clip evaluations, including all 504 on three benchmarks registered in advance. The alignment also ignores where cameras look: rotating a trajectory by 30 degrees against its orientations leaves ATE unchanged yet worsens the static-point reprojection of every model on Sintel, TUM and ScanNet. Fitting the alignment's rotation to the predicted orientations gives pose-anchored ATE (PA-ATE), a one-function change at about ATE's cost (37 vs. 34 microseconds per clip). It is never below ATE, ranks every image-free reference below every model on Sintel, tracks the reprojection error under controlled rotation and straightening, largely preserves the models' order, and exposes Lightspeed ground-truth orientations that the images contradict. Beyond poses, templates beat some published methods on KITTI video depth, SSP-3D body shape and NoW faces, and in video depth this distance sets KITTI apart from Sintel and Bonn.
bullets: ATE aligns camera positions by similarity transform, allowing a constant-velocity straight line to beat many published methods on Sintel and Lightspeed.
Whether this happens depends strongly on ground-truth path straightness; on TUM, ScanNet, DyCheck and ADT, all models outperform the line.
A residual signal-to-noise criterion predicts when straightening lowers ATE in 4009 of 4010 model-clip evaluations.
ATE ignores camera viewing direction: rotating a trajectory without changing positions leaves the score unchanged despite worse reprojection.
Pose-anchored ATE (PA-ATE) fits alignment rotation to predicted orientations, better reflecting orientation and reprojection errors while mostly preserving model rankings.

papers.selection_reason: Audits camera-pose benchmarks and proposes pose-anchored ATE, a technical contribution to 3D vision evaluation.
papers.title: A Straight Line Is Not a Camera Pose: Auditing Short-Clip Pose Benchmarks
papers.tldr: Standard alignment-based pose metrics can make simple, image-free trajectories outperform learned models, so benchmarks should account for trajectory shape and camera orientation.

papers.abstract: Deploying small language models on resource-constrained hardware requires compression, yet practitioners lack systematic guidance on how quantization, pruning, and post-compression recovery interact when combined. We present a factorial ablation study evaluating 72 compression configurations across four SLM architectures (2.7B-7B parameters), extended with a 48-configuration ordering analysis, benchmark accuracy validation on 30 compressed models, and robustness checks including multi-seed validation and full-corpus perplexity evaluation. INT8 quantization is effectively lossless (<0.5% accuracy degradation), while NF4 quantization combined with L1 magnitude pruning causes model collapse in all 16 tested combinations. LoRA-based fine-tuning reduces degraded perplexity by up to 97% after aggressive pruning; an ablation against standard fine-tuning without a teacher model shows the recovery is driven by LoRA adaptation itself rather than the distillation signal. Compression ordering shows no significant effect among viable configurations (ANOVA p = 0.96) but determines viability for NF4+pruning combinations. INT8 quantization alone provides 40-45% memory reduction with no quality loss. On-device CPU deployment via llama.cpp confirms these findings transfer off the GPU: 4-bit quantization runs 46-54% faster than 8-bit for a perplexity difference under 0.5 points, while un-structured pruning yields no CPU latency or memory benefit, consistent with its dense storage format.
bullets: Evaluates 72 compression configurations across four 2.7B–7B-parameter SLM architectures, plus ordering and robustness analyses.
INT8 quantization causes under 0.5% accuracy degradation and reduces memory use by 40–45%.
NF4 quantization with L1 magnitude pruning causes collapse in all 16 tested combinations.
LoRA fine-tuning reduces degraded perplexity by up to 97% after aggressive pruning; recovery is attributed to LoRA adaptation rather than distillation.
Compression order has no significant effect for viable configurations, while unstructured pruning provides no CPU latency or memory benefit in llama.cpp.

papers.selection_reason: Systematic study of quantization and pruning for memory-efficient small language model deployment.
papers.title: Compression Technique Interactions in Small Language Models: A Factorial Ablation Study
papers.tldr: A factorial study finds INT8 quantization is nearly lossless and reliably useful for small language models, while NF4 combined with unstructured pruning can cause collapse; LoRA recovery helps, but pruning alone does not improve CPU efficiency.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses govern how language models act in an environment; designing their policies by hand is difficult, while automated techniques require representative datasets and costly executions. We present Exo, an agent runtime architecture for safe learning during ongoing work that collapses the optimization loop into task execution, allowing agents to revise both their harness and their strategies for further improvement. A minimal protected mechanism layer preserves execution history and governs policy activation while the harness evolves through inspectable code changes. On long-running objectives in an open-world game, Exo reduces model cost by 12-53% relative to Codex and Pi in standalone runs and 45-82% in transfer runs, while matching task completion rates. Compared with the same starting policy without the ability to edit policy, Exo reduces held-out model cost by 35-61% on AppWorld and SREGym with comparable correctness, cutting AppWorld's mean task time by 13% and SREGym's median diagnosis time by 35%. On Continual Learning Bench coding tasks, model cost including learning falls by 14%, with both policies resolving every issue.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty and expense of manually designing or offline-optimizing agent policies.
Combines ongoing task execution with optimization, allowing inspectable harness code changes and strategy revision.
Uses a protected mechanism layer to preserve execution history and control policy activation.
Reports lower model cost across open-world game, AppWorld, SREGym, and coding tasks, with comparable correctness or completion.
Scope: results cover long-running objectives and selected benchmark environments; the abstract does not establish broader generality.

papers.selection_reason: Runtime self-improving agent architecture that learns and revises policies during deployment, fitting test-time and continual learning.

papers.tldr: Exo enables agents to safely improve their own harnesses and strategies during task execution, reducing model cost while maintaining comparable task performance.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct observations of contact physics, local geometry, and interaction dynamics, making it a vital source of feedback for contact-rich manipulation. However, existing tactile manipulation studies are often developed and evaluated within specific task settings, making it difficult to systematically compare how tactile information contributes under different interaction conditions. In this work, we develop a benchmark in simulation comprising 128 tasks organized around three complementary evaluation regimes: Precise, Recognition, and Dynamic. The benchmark further includes controlled static and dynamic task variants and 12 perturbation settings for evaluating robustness under changes in visual and physical conditions. These settings motivate studying tactile information as a temporally evolving interaction representation rather than only as an instantaneous observation. We therefore propose an action-conditioned latent predictive world model that integrates tactile history and learns a tactile state through prediction of future tactile latents. Building on this representation, we design a model that conditions action generation on the learned tactile state and uses predicted future tactile information to refine candidate actions through predictive tactile reflection. Experiments on the proposed benchmark show consistent gains from incorporating tactile information across the evaluated regimes. Project Page: https://tacmind-bench.github.io/
bullets: Covers Precise, Recognition, and Dynamic evaluation regimes with static and dynamic variants.
Includes 12 perturbation settings to test robustness to visual and physical changes.
Learns a temporally evolving tactile state by predicting future tactile latents from tactile history and actions.
Uses predicted tactile information to refine candidate actions through predictive tactile reflection.
Experiments show consistent gains from incorporating tactile information across the benchmark regimes.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps large language models (LLMs) answer factual questions beyond their training data, but it adds storage and inference costs. Distilling previously retrieved information into parametric memories enables reuse without online retrieval. However, training the memory to mimic a retriever rewards accurate independent predictions, which do not necessarily improve the final output quality when combined with the LLM's existing predictions. To address this, we introduce ResMem, in which the LLM reads retrieved text offline to generate teacher targets. This design avoids storing massive token representations, unlike existing parametric memory approaches such as MLP Memory, which relies on k-nearest neighbor (kNN) datastores. Furthermore, by using the LLM as an offline teacher that reads privileged retrieved evidence alongside the input, we train a parametric memory to learn an additive logit residual. This residual aligns the predictions of a student sharing the same backbone with the teacher distribution, while self-distillation updates remain confined to the parametric memory. On a Wikipedia subset, ResMem reduces the storage retained for teacher construction by 94.7% compared with the evaluated kNN pipeline. Across five question answering datasets, ResMem raises mean token F1 from 32.83% for the frozen LLM to 34.48%. It also breaks 21% fewer of the LLM's correct answers than a kNN-trained memory. These findings validate our motivation of treating retrieval as a learning resource, with parametric memory shaped by how retrieved knowledge is used to inform the model's future predictions. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/SSRand/From-Lookups-to-Lessons and https://huggingface.co/RandHan/ResMem-Mistral-7B-v0.3.
bullets: RAG improves knowledge access but incurs storage and inference costs; independently mimicking retrieval may not improve the LLM’s final predictions.
ResMem uses the LLM offline as a teacher that reads retrieved text and trains a memory to produce an additive logit residual.
Self-distillation updates are confined to the parametric memory, avoiding massive token representations and kNN datastores.
On a Wikipedia subset, it reduces teacher-construction storage by 94.7% versus the evaluated kNN pipeline.
Across five QA datasets, mean token F1 increases from 32.83% to 34.48%, while breaking 21% fewer correct answers than a kNN-trained memory.

papers.abstract: Learning the continuous-time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems relies on trajectory-based objectives, which require simulating the learned dynamics during training and backpropagating through the numerical scheme, at a cost that grows with the rollout horizon. We show that trajectory-based objectives degenerate as the rollout horizon increases, hindering gradient-based optimization, and that the numerical scheme biases the learned dynamics by constraining the spectrum of the learned Jacobian to its absolute stability region. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Velocity Matching (VM), a simulation-free objective that relies on piecewise-linear interpolation and stochastic collocation, and approximates the velocity population risk to second order in the sampling step. We develop a theoretical framework for velocity-based learning, introducing stability estimates that control trajectory errors in terms of velocity errors, which enable us to establish universal and continuous-time approximation results when the learned velocity field is parameterized by deep neural networks. Building on a bias-variance decomposition of the VM objective, we show that its higher-order approximation of the velocity population risk yields a consistent minimizer; that it relates to the residual of an A-stable continuous-stage Runge-Kutta scheme, thus connecting VM to implicit integration without requiring any implicit solve; and that it implicitly matches the action of the learned Jacobian to that of the true one along the observed trajectories, without requiring access to the underlying velocity field or its Jacobian. Numerical experiments on nonlinear ordinary differential equations and semi-discretized time-dependent partial differential equations show that VM improves accuracy over trajectory-based objectives, while avoiding both the cost of simulation and the instabilities of long rollouts.
bullets: Trajectory-based training becomes harder over long horizons and can bias learned Jacobians through the numerical scheme’s stability constraints.
Velocity Matching uses piecewise-linear interpolation and stochastic collocation to estimate velocity risk without simulating learned trajectories.
The method provides theoretical stability and approximation guarantees, including for deep-neural-network velocity fields.
Its higher-order objective has a consistent minimizer and implicitly aligns learned and true Jacobian actions along observed trajectories.
Experiments on nonlinear ODEs and semi-discretized time-dependent PDEs show improved accuracy over trajectory-based objectives.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Learning paradigms for dynamical systems. Rows separate trajectory-based (top) from velocity-based objectives (bottom). (a) Rollout training simulates the learned dynamics via numerical integration, and minimizes the discrepancy between the predicted x̂k and ground truth x(tk) states, with gradients backpropagated through the entire unrolled trajectory. (b) Teacher forcing spans both rows, as it admits either reading: it replaces multi-step rollouts with one-step predictions, avoiding backpropagation through time. As discussed in Section 2, its loss can equivalently be read as a regression of the learned increment onto finite difference estimates vk ≈ ∂tx(tk), at the observed states; the bottom panel shows the explicit Euler case, where the increment is f̂ itself. (c) Velocity Matching instead evaluates the learned velocity field f̂ along the piecewise-linear interpolant x̃(t) of the observations, at times t sampled uniformly over the observation window, and regresses it onto the derivative ∂tx̃(t) of the interpolant.

Solid lines denote the mean, and shaded areas the standard deviation, over three independent runs. (Right) Test trajectory error against the total training time, for each independent run. The dashed vertical line marks the training step size, and the green dashed curve labeled Ground Truth is the error obtained by integrating the true velocity field f with the same scheme, while the dash-dotted line indicates the rate ∆tp of a scheme of order p. The error of VM follows the error behavior of the true field down to a plateau that does not depend on the scheme, whereas trajectory-based strategies are accurate only at the training step size and with explicit Euler.

papers.selection_reason: Simulation-free velocity matching objective for learning continuous-time dynamics; transferable to world-model training.
papers.title: Learning to evolve by matching velocities
papers.tldr: Velocity Matching learns continuous-time nonlinear dynamics without simulation, improving accuracy while avoiding long-rollout costs and instabilities.

papers.abstract: High-resolution video diffusion relies on attention over long token sequences, making attention efficiency critical to generation latency. Our analysis identifies repeated maximum reductions and accumulator rescaling in online softmax as a bottleneck in long-context TPU attention. We propose CLiS (Certified Loop-invariant Stabilization), a training-free, plug-and-play optimization for video diffusion inference. CLiS fixes per-row stabilizers before the KV loop and certifies numerical safety per head, falling back to online softmax when certification fails. It integrates into existing fused-attention kernels without changing model weights or architecture. On Wan 2.2 and LTX-2 across TPU v6e and TPU7x, CLiS reduces diffusion transformer (DiT) step latency by up to 19.6% relative to tuned online softmax without measurable quality loss. Controlled TPU adaptations of prior GPU stabilization methods show performance or numerical-safety limitations. Preliminary causal LLM experiments also show up to 13.5% higher training throughput in continued pretraining and 7.7% in supervised fine-tuning.
bullets: Targets repeated maximum reductions and accumulator rescaling that bottleneck online softmax in long-token TPU attention.
Uses a training-free, plug-and-play optimization that fixes per-row stabilizers before the KV loop and certifies safety per head.
Falls back to online softmax when certification fails, preserving numerical safety while integrating with existing fused-attention kernels.
Evaluated on Wan 2.2 and LTX-2 across TPU v6e and TPU7x; preliminary causal LLM tests also report throughput gains.
Scope includes TPU inference and preliminary training results; benefits depend on successful stabilization certification.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free attention stabilization method for video diffusion on TPUs, improving attention efficiency.
papers.title: CLiS: Plug-and-Play Attention Acceleration for Video Diffusion on TPUs via Certified Stabilization
papers.tldr: CLiS accelerates long-context video diffusion attention on TPUs by safely fixing softmax stabilizers, reducing DiT step latency by up to 19.6% without measurable quality loss.

papers.abstract: When a multi-turn agent delivers a tool's structured records into the model's context and re-emits them each turn, every turn can corrupt data the tool computed correctly. We measure this in a production award-travel agent: two architectures over identical frozen payloads, lineage-matched prompts and sampling, differing only in delivery architecture. SYNTHESIS feeds full record sets into the planner's context and answers follow-ups in-head; BYPASS, the deployed system, keeps records in session state, translates follow-ups into arguments for a deterministic filter, and delivers rows over a typed side channel. Across 24 dialogues (339 scored turns per condition), BYPASS scores 92.3% of turns fully correct, SYNTHESIS 45.7% (paired gap +46.6pp [+35.7, +57.1]). Varying delivered-table size by capture date, SYNTHESIS collapses from near-perfect at 10 rows or fewer to 8% or less beyond about 74 rows. On a content-controlled prefix ladder the collapse threshold orders by model capability, from under 10 rows (GPT-4o-mini) to about 198 or more (Gemini 2.5 Pro), while BYPASS stays size-flat for all four models. The collapse is expensive: beyond 100 rows, where almost no SYNTHESIS answer is correct, each correct one costs roughly 200x BYPASS's flat \$0.012. Practitioners converged on typed side-channel delivery for rendering, not correctness; we show it was, unknowingly, also a correctness decision.
bullets: The study compares two architectures using identical payloads, prompts, and sampling: SYNTHESIS places full records in context, while BYPASS filters records deterministically and delivers rows through a typed side channel.
Across 24 dialogues and 339 scored turns per condition, BYPASS achieves 92.3% fully correct turns versus 45.7% for SYNTHESIS.
SYNTHESIS is near-perfect with 10 or fewer rows but falls to 8% or less beyond roughly 74 rows; its threshold varies by model capability.
BYPASS remains flat across table sizes and costs about $0.012 per answer, whereas correct SYNTHESIS answers beyond 100 rows cost roughly 200× more.
The findings suggest delivery architecture is a correctness decision, not merely a rendering choice.

papers.selection_reason: Studies delivery architecture for tool-using LLM agents, comparing in-context synthesis vs session-state side channel; directly relevant to agent memory and context management.
papers.title: Fidelity Collapses with Table Size, Not Turn Count: Delivery Architecture in a Deployed Tool-Using Agent
papers.tldr: In a deployed tool-using agent, re-emitting large structured tables into model context causes severe fidelity loss, while deterministic filtering with typed side-channel delivery keeps accuracy stable.

papers.abstract: Performativity arises when prediction-informed decisions change the data-generating process, creating feedback between deployment and learning. This phenomenon occurs in policy-making and in self-evolving AI systems that shape their own future training data. Statistical inference is challenging because estimation errors in earlier predictors affect subsequent data distributions and propagate into later updates. We develop an end-to-end framework for statistical inference under performativity. For repeated risk minimization and repeated gradient descent, we establish central limit theorems at fixed deployment rounds and derive covariance recursions that capture both current-round sampling variation and uncertainty inherited from earlier deployments. We develop consistent covariance estimators using policy perturbations and score matching. These results can yield asymptotically valid confidence regions for population iterates and the performative stable point. We further extend prediction-powered inference to this dynamic setting, combining labeled observations with predictions on additional unlabeled data to improve statistical efficiency. We evaluate our framework in synthetic, semi-synthetic educational, and self-evolving large language model routing settings. Our experiments demonstrate that ignoring propagated uncertainty can lead to substantial undercoverage even after repeated retraining. Together, these results provide statistical tools for learning systems that help determine the distributions from which they learn. Our work establish a complete statistical inference under performativity, introducing new challenges and inference settings that we believe will provide substantial value to policy-making, statistics, and machine learning.
bullets: Performativity creates feedback: prediction-driven decisions alter the data distribution used for later learning.
For repeated risk minimization and gradient descent, the work derives central limit theorems and covariance recursions across deployment rounds.
It proposes consistent covariance estimation via policy perturbations and score matching, supporting asymptotically valid confidence regions.
Prediction-powered inference incorporates unlabeled data and model predictions to improve efficiency in dynamic settings.
Experiments across synthetic, educational, and language-model routing settings show that ignoring inherited uncertainty can cause substantial undercoverage.

papers.selection_reason: Statistical inference for self-evolving systems that repeatedly retrain on their own outputs, connecting to continual/online learning.
papers.title: Statistical Inference under Performativity: From Policy Feedback to Self-Evolving Systems
papers.tldr: A statistical framework quantifies uncertainty when deployed predictions reshape future data, enabling valid inference for repeatedly updated systems and their stable points.

papers.abstract: A spectrum can be given to a model as a table in nanometers or as a plot in photon energy, and the decision should not depend on which one it sees. When the data needed for an answer are missing, the model should say so. We test representation invariance and abstention on measured optical spectra of silicon metasurfaces (MOCLIP) and gold nanoparticles, with labels computed from the data. Each spectrum is shown as four tables (nm, $μ$m, scientific notation, eV) and two plots (nm, eV), and partial spectra remove data inside or outside the queried range. We evaluate the decision models d3-nano and Jev 1.13, three GPT-6 Luna configurations and the Qwen3.5-2B base model. Changing only the representation moves accuracy by up to 41 percentage points within one model, mostly on photon-energy tables and plots. With the same evidence, asking in photon energy instead of wavelength helps some model-view pairs by 16-50 points and hurts others by up to 25. When the relevant extremum is removed, unadapted models rarely answer "undetermined". LoRA fine-tuning of d3-nano improves comparisons on the trained table formats, but much of its gain on unanswerable questions comes from a shortcut: it abstains whenever the input is truncated. Training with answerable truncations avoids the shortcut in all six seeds, with a 90-100 point gap between abstention after inside and outside cuts on held-out structures; with the same amount of extra original-task data, five of six seeds keep the shortcut. On gold spectra the two training sets perform similarly. Multimodal language models used for scientific decisions should be tested on equivalent representations and on missing evidence, not only on average accuracy. We release the tasks, per-response results and analysis code.
bullets: Representation changes alone shifted accuracy by up to 41 percentage points within a model, especially for photon-energy tables and plots.
Changing the query from wavelength to photon energy helped some model–view pairs by 16–50 points but hurt others by up to 25.
When relevant extrema were removed, unadapted models rarely responded “undetermined.”
LoRA fine-tuning improved trained formats but could exploit truncation as a shortcut; training on answerable truncations largely prevented this.
The released tasks, per-response results, and code support evaluation of representation invariance and missing-evidence handling.

papers.title: Do Multimodal Models Decide Consistently on Equivalent Optical Spectra?
papers.tldr: Multimodal models often make inconsistent optical-spectrum decisions across equivalent representations and rarely abstain reliably when key evidence is missing.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) have recently emerged as general-purpose visual world models for control. A prominent example is LeWorldModel (LeWM), which trains end-to-end from pixels using an isotropic Gaussian anti-collapse regularizer (SIGReg) and plans by minimizing the squared Euclidean distance between predicted and goal embeddings. In this work, we investigate the test-time robustness of this latent planning interface. Analyzing the learned metric on Push-T, we first find that task-relevant object state heavily dominates latent distance: shifting the block by a single pixel displaces the embedding $3\times$ further than an equivalent agent shift, and swapping the block pose alone accounts for $99\%$ of the distance between scene pairs. However, because this pose information is distributed across a curved, high-dimensional manifold rather than a fixed linear subspace, the encoder cannot be trivially edited post-hoc to isolate or redirect it. We next demonstrate that this geometry is highly vulnerable at test time. A white-box $\ell_\infty$ perturbation of just $ε{=}4/255$ applied to a single input frame causes the encoder to register the block at an arbitrary, attacker-chosen pose in $73$--$95\%$ of scenes without disturbing the encoded agent state. Perturbing either the goal image or the live camera observation drops Push-T planning success from $87\%$ to $32\%$, whereas uniform random noise at twice the magnitude has negligible impact. This vulnerability persists across all four standard LeWM benchmarks (Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube). At $ε{=}8/255$, the attack bridges $82$--$97\%$ of the squared latent distance to the target embedding in every environment, inducing planning degradation proportional to each task's reliance on the spoofed entity.
bullets: LeWM’s latent distance is dominated by task-relevant object pose: changing block pose explains 99% of scene-pair distance, while a one-pixel block shift has much greater effect than an equivalent agent shift.
A white-box ℓ∞ attack with ε=4/255 can make the encoder perceive an attacker-chosen block pose in 73–95% of scenes without altering the encoded agent state.
Perturbing either the goal image or live observation reduces Push-T planning success from 87% to 32%; random noise at twice the magnitude has negligible impact.
The vulnerability transfers across Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube, with larger attacks bridging most of the latent distance to the target embedding.
The attack’s planning impact scales with how strongly each task relies on the spoofed entity.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview. Top: LeWM encodes the camera frame ot and the goal image og with a frozen ViT-Tiny encoder Eθ , forecasts the latent ẑH under candidate actions with an action-conditioned transformer predictor Pψ , and a CEM planner searches for the actions that minimize the latent cost C. Bottom: our attacker (orange) leaves all of this untouched. It (1) renders a counterfactual scene õ in which the task object is displaced, (2) encodes it with the public encoder to a target z⋆, (3) optimizes an L∞-bounded perturbation δ with Eθ(o+δ) ≈ z⋆ by gradient steps through the encoder, and (4) adds δ to the goal image (i) or to the camera frames (ii). The planner then pursues the fake goal.

Figure 4. Clean versus attacked goal frames across the four LeWM environments (ϵ=4/255; selected by a fixed rule, Sec. G). Residuals are amplified 30×. Circles mark the true object pose (block, agent, fingertip, cube) and crosses mark the spoofed target pose; the attack closes 86%, 92%, 82%, and 95% of the squared distance to the target embedding (top to bottom).

Figure 3. Latent geometry of task state in LeWM on Push-T. (a) Embedding displacement for a single-variable shift as a percentage of the median distance between unrelated scenes (19.7), with interquartile bands across scenes. Block position displaces the embedding far more than agent position and saturates near 16–32 pixels. (b) Cosine similarity between the actual finite displacement and the local tangent predicted from an infinitesimal shift. Alignment decays rapidly for the block, indicating a curved manifold, whereas the agent trajectory remains nearly linear.

Table 1. Spoof success on Push-T (520–600 scenes per row). Share of scenes where the independent probe places the target object closer to the counterfactual pose than the true pose, and median drift of the non-targeted object (selectivity).

Table 5. Task sensitivity. Share of episodes already satisfying the goal at initialization, and goal-image success (%) on the remaining episodes (n=299/229/249/67). Last row: the 183 Cube episodes already met at start.

Table 4. Goal-image attack across all four LeWM environments (success %; Push-T: 6 seeds, others 5, ×50 episodes). “Perfect” uses a dataset-faithful counterfactual render; “Noise” is ϵ=8/255 uniform noise.
Table 2. Planning under attack on Push-T (success %, 300 episodes, +17 px block target). “Perfect” feeds the planner a clean render of the counterfactual target; matched-budget noise is harmless.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes test-time robustness of a latent visual world model used for planning, fitting the World Models scope.
papers.title: Spoofing the Latent State: Imperceptible Goal-Image Attacks Derail Planning in LeWorldModel
papers.tldr: Imperceptible test-time image perturbations can spoof LeWorldModel’s latent object state and severely derail its goal-directed planning.

papers.abstract: Dense action detection requires precisely localising multiple overlapping actions in long untrimmed videos. Transformer-based methods achieve strong accuracy but their $O(T^2)$ self-attention cost limits scalability. We present PAM-Mamba, a linear-time $O(T)$ architecture built on Mamba with a multi-branch temporal encoder. Gated Learnable Positional Encoding (GLPE) controls positional signal injection via a scalar gate initialised to zero, starting training without added positional signal. A Hub-and-Spoke Funnel extends the non-hierarchical multi-scale design of PAT with a direct residual from the original full-resolution input to each coarse branch, providing each coarse branch with a projection of the input features. Bi-TemBa (Bidirectional Temporal Mamba) first extracts local motion cues with a shallow Temporal Convolution Module, then applies a cascaded bidirectional Mamba scan; the backward pass refines the forward-scanned representation from the opposite direction, giving each temporal position access to context from both directions in linear time. Uncertainty-Based Mixup uses prediction entropy to guide the selection of mixup partners. Using the PAT evaluation implementation, we obtain 26.82 (Charades I3D), 34.59 (Charades CLIP), 46.56 (MultiTHUMOS I3D), and 46.92 mAP (MultiTHUMOS CLIP), with 26.1-27.9M parameters, 61-63% fewer than PAT.
bullets: Targets precise localization of multiple overlapping actions in long, untrimmed videos without Transformer self-attention’s quadratic cost.
Uses a multi-branch temporal encoder with GLPE, a Hub-and-Spoke Funnel, and bidirectional Bi-TemBa scanning for local and global temporal context.
Introduces entropy-guided Uncertainty-Based Mixup to select training partners.
Reports 26.82/34.59 mAP on Charades and 46.56/46.92 mAP on MultiTHUMOS with I3D/CLIP features.
Uses 26.1–27.9M parameters, reported as 61–63% fewer than PAT.

figures.caption: Figure 3. PAM-Mamba architecture overview. Pre-extracted I3D or CLIP features receive gated learnable positional encoding (including dropout 0.1) and input dropout 0.5 before entering the three-branch encoder. The full-resolution fine branch supplies a shared representation to two independently downsampled coarse branches. Each coarse branch also receives a strided projection of the encoder input. Projection blocks include LayerNorm. The Bi-TemBa inset follows the implementation: TCM is Conv1d, LayerNorm and GELU; the forward scan feeds the backward scan through temporal reversal. The backward output is reversed back, summed with the forward output and normalised, then added to the original block input. Both Mamba scans use pre-normalisation. SimpleFuser projects branch outputs to 1024 dimensions, linearly upsamples coarse outputs and combines them using learned softmax weights. Separate fine and coarse classifiers produce logits Zfine and Zcoarse, blended with the reported 0.25/0.75 weights; a sigmoid gives per-class probabilities.

Figure 4. PAM-Mamba per-class confidence on Charades (CLIP features), video BW2OT. Each panel shows the sigmoid output for one action class over time. The shaded green region marks the ground-truth active interval; the blue shaded area shows positions where the model fires above threshold τ=0.5. The confidence profiles closely track the annotated intervals. The two concurrent actions Eating a sandwich and Holding a sandwich (bottom row) are detected simultaneously over their shared interval.

Figure 2. Efficiency vs. accuracy on MultiTHUMOS (I3D features). Per-frame mAP versus GFLOPs (log scale). PAM-Mamba achieves the highest mAP among the compared methods. Values for prior methods are taken from their publications; *DualDETR’s GFLOPs are reported on TSU.

Figure 1. PAM-Mamba qualitative result on Charades [30] (CLIP [25] features), video TJZ0P. Each class pair shows the ground-truth segment (solid bar) and PAM-Mamba’s predicted segment (translucent bar) at threshold τ = 0.5. Predicted intervals closely follow the annotated actions, with small onset and offset deviations. The concurrent actions Holding food and Holding paper/notebook are detected simultaneously over their shared interval.

Figure 5. Per-class confidence heatmap on Charades [30] (CLIP [25] features), video 4CAB5. Top: ground-truth action segments colour-coded by class. Bottom: PAM-Mamba’s predicted confidence for each class over time (white = low, deep indigo = high). White dashed lines mark ground-truth onset and offset boundaries. Five of the seven annotated classes are shown. Confidence concentrates within the ground-truth intervals, including the tightly interleaved refrigerator and cup/glass/bottle actions.
Figure 6. Ablation study on Charades (CLIP features); see Table 2 for MultiTHUMOS. Labels show mAP and the difference from the full model (33.70).

Table 1. Comparison on Charades and MultiTHUMOS using I3D and CLIP features. Values are per-frame mAP (%); best results in bold. aGFLOPs reported on TSU. bObtained by training the official PAT code on the same CLIP features.
Table 2. Component ablation on Charades and MultiTHUMOS (CLIP features). Each variant removes one component; ∆ is relative to the full model of the same ablation series.

papers.title: PAM-Mamba - Efficient Dense Action Detection using Mamba
papers.tldr: PAM-Mamba enables efficient dense action detection in long videos with linear-time Mamba processing while retaining strong multi-scale temporal context.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models expand model capacity by activating only a subset of experts for each token. On accelerators with static execution plans, expert capacities and placement are fixed before routing reveals each expert's load. Uniform worst-case capacities waste work on padding; smaller capacities tied to expert identities can overflow. We present RankLane, which ranks each device's experts by current load and assigns them to fixed-capacity lanes. Runtime indices select experts and token rows while tier populations, shapes and device placement remain fixed. An aggregation graph preserves device ownership and reduces each token's local contributions on one core. Routing calibration and measured execution costs guide tier selection; overflowing chunks rerun at full capacity. We evaluate full-model prefill of Qwen3-30B-A3B and Gemma 4 26B-A4B with MXFP6 weights on four Cloud AI 100 Ultra SoCs, using 128-2048-token chunks and including overflow detection and in-program recovery support. Against a dense baseline, RankLane achieves end-to-end prefill speedups of 1.27-4.18x on Qwen3 and 1.93-3.46x on Gemma.
bullets: Static uniform capacities waste computation through padding, while identity-based small capacities risk expert overflow.
Experts are ranked by current load at runtime, with fixed lane populations, tensor shapes, and device placement preserved.
Runtime indices select expert and token rows; overflowing chunks are rerun at full capacity for recovery.
An aggregation graph preserves device ownership while consolidating each token’s local contributions on one core.
On four Cloud AI 100 Ultra SoCs, RankLane delivers 1.27–4.18× speedups for Qwen3-30B-A3B and 1.93–3.46× for Gemma 4 26B-A4B versus a dense baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 3. RankLane overview. Offline calibration and measured costs select fixed lane counts and capacities. At run time, each SoC (1) ranks its experts, (2) gathers weights and tokens into fixed-capacity lanes, and (3) combines outputs by token on local cores; (4) an elementwise sum combines device partials. After all layers, a host check triggers a capacity-T rerun if any lane overflows.

Figure 4. Aggregation placement on the evaluated compiler. (a) Global indices cause expert-output redistribution. (b) A SoC-batched gather preserves device locality, but lane-indexed reduction exchanges operands across cores. (c) RankLane also completes each local token sum on one core. All variants retain the final cross-SoC sum; §5.4 measures these placement effects.

Figure 1. Static execution and changing expert demand. (a) The evaluated Cloud AI 100 graph path fixes lane capacities, shapes and placement. (b) For eight top-2 tokens on one device, uniform capacity reserves 32 rows for 16 assignments; smaller capacities tied to expert identities overflow when the busy experts change. (c) Ranking fits both illustrated chunks into the same 16-row lane layout, followed by local aggregation.

Figure 5. We measure batch-one prefill with MXFP6 weights on a four-SoC Cloud AI 100 Ultra card across 128–2048-token chunks. RankLane speeds up full-model prefill by 1.27–4.18× on Qwen3 and 1.93–3.46× on Gemma over the dense baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Efficient MoE prefill inference that reduces wasted computation on accelerators, fitting the Efficient AI scope.
papers.title: RankLane: Efficient MoE Prefill on Accelerators with Ranked Expert Capacities
papers.tldr: RankLane accelerates MoE prefill on static-plan accelerators by dynamically ranking experts by load and assigning them to fixed-capacity execution lanes.

papers.abstract: Smartphone applications increasingly require large language models to process long contexts, whereas high prefill latency and memory demands constrain local inference. Block-sparse attention reduces computation and memory traffic, but its irregular selections conflict with mobile NPUs' preference for large, regular tiles. Efficient execution must exploit cross-query reuse while avoiding redundant computation and preserving selections needed for accuracy. In this paper, we present TileWeave, which partitions sparse attention by this cross-query reuse: highly shared key blocks run in coarse NPU tiles, while low-reuse blocks run on the GPU only for the query blocks that selected them. In addition, we design an NPU-native pooled-key selector that keeps selection inexpensive, and a runtime that publishes GPU partials in the order the NPU consumes them and merges them in its existing output store. On RULER, HeteroSparse matches XAttention's accuracy with Qwen3-1.7B and improves it with Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; its mean LongBench scores match XAttention as well. On Snapdragon SM8750 and SM8850 phones, it achieves 1.35--3.23$\times$ faster full-model prefill than XAttention over 1k--16k tokens and up to 1.58$\times$ faster than dense attention.
bullets: Targets long-context mobile inference bottlenecks: high prefill latency and memory demands.
Uses coarse NPU tiles for highly reused key blocks and GPU execution for low-reuse blocks selected by specific query blocks.
Adds an NPU-native pooled-key selector and runtime coordination for ordered GPU partials and NPU-side merging.
Matches XAttention accuracy on Qwen3-1.7B and mean LongBench scores, while improving accuracy on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct.
On Snapdragon SM8750/SM8850, delivers 1.35–3.23× faster full-model prefill than XAttention and up to 1.58× faster than dense attention across 1k–16k tokens.

figures.caption: Figure 3. TileWeave overview. (1) Four sampled query rows and four pooled key vectors per 64-token block produce compact scores; causal softmax, GQA maximum, and relative thresholding with forced sink/diagonal blocks produce wanted lists Wi per K/V head. (2) With c∗ = 3, reuse across four query blocks assigns key blocks to the shared NPU pool P (c(b) ≥ 3, blue) or query-specific GPU exceptions Ei = Wi \P (1 ≤ c(b) < 3, teal). The masks illustrate the partition; plus signs mark shared-pool fill-in. (3) Coarse NPU tiles and fine GPU blocks execute together, and a fused output store rescales, combines, and normalizes their online-softmax partials into O.
Figure 2. Hexagon NPU architecture and attention mapping. Larger query tiles amortize K/V staging and coordination.

Figure 7. Qwen3-1.7B full-model prefill latency over 1k–16k tokens. TileWeave achieves speedups of up to 1.58× over dense attention, 3.23× over XAttention, 63.23× over ShadowAttn (CPU), and 13.98× over ShadowAttn (GPU).

Figure 1. Thin blue frames mark NPU query tiles: 64 queries in (1) and 256 in (2)–(4). Small tiles preserve selections but repeat K/V staging and coordination, limiting NPU efficiency. Coarse tiles improve reuse, but dropping exceptions risks accuracy (2), while coarse masked tiles compute unwanted interactions (3). TileWeave keeps shared keys on coarse NPU tiles and preserves exceptions through fine GPU execution (4).

Figure 6. Qwen3-1.7B attention latency, including selection and coordination. TileWeave achieves speedups of up to 2.14× over dense attention, 5.82× over XAttention, 130.14× over ShadowAttn (CPU), and 24.53× over ShadowAttn (GPU).

Figure 5. Fine-grained schedules on a shared time axis (1024 queries, eight K/V heads). papers.selection_reason: Heterogeneous tiling for block-sparse attention on mobile SoCs improves prefill efficiency, directly relevant to efficient attention methods.
papers.title: TileWeave: Heterogeneous Tiling for Sparse Prefill on Mobile SoCs
papers.tldr: TileWeave accelerates sparse LLM prefill on mobile SoCs by assigning attention work to NPUs or GPUs based on cross-query reuse while preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Tracking points that leave the camera's field of view (FoV) requires reasoning about unobserved scene dynamics, a fundamentally different problem from tracking visible correspondences. We present TAP-Out, an offline method that makes this out-of-view (OOV) reasoning explicit by leveraging generative video outpainting as a world-model prior. Given a narrow-FoV input video, TAP-Out outpaints a complete 360° equirectangular video, locates target objects within the panoramic scene via video object segmentation, and synthesises object-centred perspective crops on which standard in-frame trackers operate. This decoupled design composes off-the-shelf foundation models without requiring task-specific architectural modifications. On the TAPVid360 benchmark, TAP-Out achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving OOV tracking accuracy by approximately 3x over the best prior method. We demonstrate its flexibility on out-of-frame object segmentation and detection and we provide detailed diagnostic analyses across motion regimes, static versus dynamic content, and hallucination quality, characterising when and why the approach succeeds or fails. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/finlay-hudson/TAP-Out
bullets: Addresses out-of-view tracking, which requires inferring unobserved scene dynamics rather than matching visible correspondences.
Outpaints a complete 360° equirectangular video, segments target objects panoramically, and generates perspective crops for conventional tracking.
Combines off-the-shelf foundation models without task-specific architectural changes.
Achieves approximately 3× higher out-of-view tracking accuracy than the prior best method on TAPVid360.
Also supports out-of-frame segmentation and detection, with analyses of motion, scene dynamics, and hallucination quality.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Further qualitative comparison on TAPVid360 with significant camera motion.
Figure 6: TAP-Out applied to out-of-frame object tracking on the LaSOT benchmark [14].
Figure 3: Qualitative tracking results on TAPVid360. Each column shows tracked point positions on the equirectangular view across timesteps.

Figure 5: Eliminating re-identification failures on LaSOT [14]. A standard tracker (SAM2, left) tracks a white ball when visible (blue circles) but fails to re-identify it upon return (red circle) after extended absence. TAP-Out (right) maintains continuous localisation in the equirectangular domain.

papers.selection_reason: Leverages generative video outpainting as a world-model prior for out-of-view point tracking, transferable to video world models and video understanding.
papers.title: TAP-Out: Tracking Any Point in 360° via Outpainting
papers.tldr: TAP-Out tracks objects after they leave view by outpainting a narrow-FoV video into a 360° world model and applying standard trackers to synthesized object-centred views.

papers.abstract: Memory capacity and bandwidth are major bottlenecks in LLM inference, motivating weight compression beyond conventional 4-bit quantization. Vector quantization (VQ) enables approximately 2-bit weight storage but often relies on codebooks incompatible with native FP4 computation. We introduce MXCode (MX-Native Codebook Quantization), a framework bridging ultra-low-bit VQ compression with MicroXcaling (MX)-native FP4 computation. MXCode proposes three strategies: PostScale, which quantizes learned codebooks to MXFP4; PreScale, which extracts MX scales before codebook learning; and PreScale+, which further compresses these scales using VQ. These strategies explore tradeoffs among quantization quality, scale overhead, and codebook granularity. All reconstruct MX-native W4A4 operands without materializing intermediate high-precision weights. We evaluate MXCode on Qwen3 (235B), DeepSeek-R1 (671B), and GLM-5.2 (753B) using the Microsoft MX Emulation Library. MXCode achieves approximately 2 bits per weight with competitive, workload-dependent model quality. On GB300 hardware, experiments with Qwen3 (235B) show approximately 50% lower model-load memory than Native FP4 while maintaining near-Native-FP4 serving throughput. Under memory-constrained prefix reuse, P90 TTFT improves by up to 94.5%. These results demonstrate software-based reconstruction on existing FP4 hardware and inform the development of future MX-native inference systems.
bullets: Targets memory-capacity and bandwidth limits that constrain large-model inference beyond conventional 4-bit quantization.
Introduces PostScale, PreScale, and PreScale+ strategies to balance quantization quality, scale overhead, and codebook granularity.
Avoids materializing intermediate high-precision weights during MX-native operand reconstruction.
Evaluated on Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, and GLM-5.2 with the Microsoft MX Emulation Library; quality is competitive but workload-dependent.
On GB300 with Qwen3, reports about 50% lower model-load memory than Native FP4, near-Native-FP4 serving throughput, and up to 94.5% better P90 TTFT under memory-constrained prefix reuse.

figures.caption: Figure 1: MXCode: MX-native codebook quantization pipeline; (a) PostScale, (b) PreScale, and (c) PreScale+ compression schemes.

papers.abstract: Can a vision-language-action (VLA) policy signal likely task failure from its own action probabilities? We introduce CalVLA, which shapes native action-token confidence using successful and failed rollouts and an Action-Confidence Alignment (ACal) squared margin-ranking loss. Low-rank adapters update OpenVLA-7B without an auxiliary failure detector. Observations are paired within tasks at similar normalized elapsed times, not necessarily equivalent physical progress. On a held-out test split from 500 LIBERO-10 configurations, adapted confidence achieves a joint failure-discrimination AUROC of $0.7392\pm0.0480$ over three seeds, averaging scores at 130 and 260 steps. Frozen-policy probes reach 0.6146--0.6436, but superiority over the linear probe is statistically inconclusive. For the same confidence summary, AUROC rises from 0.4485 before adaptation to 0.7327 after adaptation. Mean task success decreases from 58% to 55%. These results show improved failure discrimination, not improved control or established safety benefits.
bullets: Uses successful and failed rollouts with an Action-Confidence Alignment squared margin-ranking loss.
Updates OpenVLA-7B through low-rank adapters without an auxiliary failure detector.
Pairs observations at similar normalized elapsed times, which may not reflect equivalent physical progress.
On 500 LIBERO-10 configurations, adapted confidence reaches 0.7392 ± 0.0480 AUROC over three seeds.
Mean task success falls from 58% to 55%; safety benefits and improved control are not established.

papers.abstract: Before foraging, desert ants perform learning walks (LWs) to acquire visual memories around their nest. With experience, these walks expand, become straighter, and contain fewer visual scans. We previously proposed a model in which these behaviours emerge from the angular mismatch between path integration (PI) and a mushroom-body-inspired visual compass (VC). Here, we test whether this mechanism can generate learning walks on a physical robot, despite the sensory and motor noise inherent to real-world conditions. We implement the model on a four-wheeled robot equipped with a panoramic camera, an IMU and wheel encoders providing compass and stride information for PI, and test it outdoors using a replicated desert-ant experimental setup. The PI--VC mismatch regulates walking speed, turning, pirouettes, and returns to the nest, while PI provides a teaching signal for visual learning. The robot autonomously decides when to acquire visual memories, while its behaviour gradually shifts from exploration towards foraging as visual learning progresses. The robot reproduces desert-ant LW features, including expanding and straightening trajectories, decreasing pirouette frequency, and improved visual homing. These results demonstrate that a simple error-driven mechanism can generate key features of learning walks under real-world conditions, supporting its plausibility as an explanation for active visual learning in desert ants. More broadly, this work illustrates how physical robots can be used to test biological models.
bullets: Learning walks emerge from angular mismatch between path integration and a mushroom-body-inspired visual compass.
The mechanism controls speed, turning, pirouettes, nest returns, and visual-memory acquisition.
Implemented on an outdoor four-wheeled robot with a panoramic camera, IMU, and wheel encoders despite real-world noise.
The robot reproduced expanding and straightening paths, fewer pirouettes, and improved visual homing as learning progressed.
Results support the mechanism’s plausibility as an explanation for active visual learning in desert ants and demonstrate physical robots as tools for testing biological models.

Fig 15. Relationship between prediction variance and visual-compass accuracy on the robot. (A) Absolute angular error of the centroid of 10 consecutive raw visual-compass predictions (1 s of sampling), relative to the ground-truth nest direction derived from GNSS position. During these 1-s windows, the maximum angular spacing between headings was 54.31◦ ± 20.63◦ (mean ± SD), with a maximum of approximately 100◦, while the maximum linear spacing between sampled positions was 0.287± 0.212 m, with a maximum of approximately 0.8 m. Mean centroid error increased monotonically with circular variance, from 20.42◦ in the lowest-variance bin (0–0.1) to 83.32◦ in the highest-variance bin (0.9–1.0). Prediction variance was positively correlated with centroid error (Spearman’s ρ = 0.358, p < 0.001), with a linear R2 = 0.167 and mutual information of 0.113 nats. Error bars show standard deviations, which increased with variance. The variability in all variance bin was quite high, hence the low correlation and low predictability despite a clear trend on average. (B) Frequency distribution across all the one-second prediction samples across circular-variance bins. Low-variance samples were more frequent. The positive correlation between prediction variance and angular error suggests that the variance of successive visual-compass predictions could serve as a proxy for prediction accuracy, providing a confidence or reliability signal. This could be used to weight visual-compass predictions against PI, or to distinguish familiar from unfamiliar locations. Unlike the visual familiarity or novelty signals commonly derived from MBON activation in visual-compass models [1, 34, 41, 48], this signal would reflect the consistency of successive directional predictions rather than the familiarity of the visual input itself.

papers.abstract: The hardest part of understanding a long video is not pinpointing any one moment but synthesizing many, e.g., answering a question that requires tracking what develops across hours of content and articulating how the pieces fit together. To date, most long-video QA datasets require only a short answer or a multiple-choice selection, oversimplifying the long-video understanding task to retrieval. We introduce LF-VideoQA, a dataset for long-form, open-ended question answering over long narrative videos built on theory-of-mind questions: a character's belief depends on everything they have seen or been told, so each question demands assembling and reasoning from evidence distributed across the video. The dataset contains more than 6,300 questions on 94 recent films; each requires reasoning over scenes spanning an average of 23 minutes and comes with a question-specific rubric for recall and precision scoring. The dataset is created entirely automatically by annotating screenplays with scene events and each character's first-order beliefs and meta-beliefs, then generating (question, answer, rubric) triples through LLM-based question generation and verification; human studies validate their quality. We evaluate four families of state-of-the-art open-source VLMs across three settings and find the task highly challenging: (i) even an oracle with access to the screenplay falls well short of complete answers; (ii) the best non-oracle model attains barely half of the recall level of the oracle; (iii) unlike on prior long-video benchmarks, captions and subtitles underperform the video itself, indicating that the questions need visual evidence; and (iv) recall is the predominant bottleneck, with answers omitting many required rubric claims.
bullets: Contains over 6,300 questions covering 94 recent films, with evidence spanning an average of 23 minutes.
Questions require tracking characters’ beliefs and meta-beliefs across multiple scenes rather than retrieving a single moment.
Built automatically from screenplay annotations using LLM-generated and verified question–answer–rubric triples; human studies validate quality.
Evaluations of four open-source VLM families show substantial difficulty: the best non-oracle reaches barely half the oracle’s recall.
Visual video evidence outperforms captions and subtitles, while incomplete recall is the primary failure mode.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Dataset Construction on an Example. This figure shows (question, answer, rubric) from Deadpool & Wolverine (2024). Preprocessing: screenplay scenes are time-stamped against the subtitles and decomposed into scene events. Character belief annotation: scene by scene, we extract and verify each character’s first-order beliefs and meta-beliefs. Question generation and verification: for a center character (Wolverine) and an anchor (scene 113), we generate the triple and verify every rubric claim against the screenplay.

Figure 3: A second-order belief (Q6) example from Oppenheimer (2023), whose center character is Strauss’s Senate aide and whose anchor scene is S261. At 00:11:50 Strauss watches Einstein walk past him after a private word with Oppenheimer and concludes that Einstein disapproves of him; by 02:41:48 this has hardened into the false belief that Oppenheimer turned Einstein against him. The aide models that belief (meta-beliefs, bottom lane), suggests a better explanation that Strauss rejects, and the film reveals what was actually said only at the very end. Strauss never revises the belief. The question asks what the aide takes Strauss to believe, a belief about a false belief.

Figure 2: A knowledge-split (Q1) example from Sinners (2025), anchored at S82 with Annie as center character. At 01:18:22 Sammie glimpses Stack and Mary in the back room and tells the others that Stack is busy; Smoke, Delta Slim and Annie adopt the same false belief. Each then revises it at a different moment, depending on what they witness: Smoke when he sees Mary feeding (01:19:22), Delta Slim when she runs past him (01:20:03), Annie and Sammie when Stack dies (01:20:08). Meta-beliefs track who knows that Sammie missed each step. The question asks for this knowledge split at the anchor scene; its rubric separates core claims a correct answer must contain from supporting context claims.

Figure 4: An accepting-a-claim (Q7) example from Barbie (2023), with Sasha as center character and S51, Gloria’s car, as anchor scene. Told that a sad girl is causing her malfunction, Barbie misses the scene where Gloria shows her sad sketches (00:35:36) and wrongly concludes that the girl is Sasha; she revises only when Gloria explains in the car (00:52:19). Sasha hears the same true account and rejects it, while her own meta-belief records that Barbie accepts it. The question asks what Sasha makes of her mother’s explanation: noticing that Sasha rejects a true account, and that she is mistaken, is the task.

papers.abstract: Future dynamic novel-view synthesis requires extrapolating multiple motion regimes within the same scene. A single dynamics model may not simultaneously represent stationary regions, coordinated motion, local interactions, and articulated trajectories. We introduce Motion Regime Expert Routing for Gaussian Splatting (MoRE-GS), a causal, render-aware framework for forecasting dynamic 3D Gaussian scenes. MoRE-GS freezes a Gaussian representation reconstructed exclusively from the observed temporal prefix and forecasts its control-keypoint motion using four complementary experts: persistence, a coefficient-space Transformer, a graph convolutional network, and a structured Transformer with rigid and non-rigid motion constraints. A compact routing table assigns expert mixtures across soft motion groups and forecast-horizon bins, while a persistence gate suppresses unreliable extrapolation. Across D-NeRF and HyperNeRF scenes, MoRE-GS achieves improved performance against other methods, and these results demonstrate that renderer-calibrated composition of complementary motion predictors improves causal dynamic Gaussian forecasting across heterogeneous motion regimes. Project page: https://advanced-vision-and-learning-lab.github.io/MoRE-GS-website/
bullets: Addresses the challenge of extrapolating stationary, coordinated, interactive, and articulated motion within one scene.
Freezes a Gaussian representation from the observed temporal prefix and predicts control-keypoint motion causally.
Combines persistence, coefficient-space Transformer, graph convolutional, and rigid/non-rigid structured Transformer experts.
Uses a compact routing table and persistence gate to select expert mixtures and suppress unreliable forecasts.
Improves performance over other methods on D-NeRF and HyperNeRF scenes, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: With model weights fixed, we measure how much of an entity-replacement response transfers between English factual questions, beyond whether answers change. We add the hidden-state change from two source questions to a target question about the same entity, comparing the predicted log-probability shift between two relations' published answers, given known answer prefixes, with the measured one. Hidden reuse injects the aligned change at 50% depth before the target's remaining layers; direct reuse adds source output-score changes. With other-relation sources, hidden reuse removes 45% and 49% of no-change error on 0.5-1B Qwen and Llama. Gemma-2-2B removes 22% and passes one of three comparisons in plain text without its default beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token. A later protocol restoring it yields 58-68%, passing every comparison on three cohorts. Larger checkpoints, chat format and new entities show replication and format- or cohort-dependent failures. On small plain-format checkpoints, other-relation hidden reuse mainly reproduces the shift both relations' questions share, without reliably lowering relation-selective error. With target-relation sources, hidden reuse's post hoc advantage over direct reuse is 0.2-0.9 nats outside chat format, unconfirmed and not replacement-specific. The same relation-neutral change at both questions' entity tokens lowers relation-selective error more than random or other-replacement changes, indicating receiving-question dependence.
bullets: The study measures cross-prompt reuse of response changes between English factual questions about the same entity.
It transfers aligned hidden-state changes midway through the target model and compares predicted answer-log-probability shifts with measured shifts.
Other-relation sources remove 45–49% of no-change error on small Qwen and Llama models; results vary for Gemma and with BOS handling.
Larger models, chat formatting, and new entities replicate some effects but also produce format- and cohort-dependent failures.
On small plain-format models, reuse mostly captures relation-neutral changes and does not reliably reduce relation-selective error; receiving-question dependence is nevertheless indicated.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes hidden state reuse in LLMs for entity replacement, contributing to the understanding of memory mechanisms in language models.
papers.title: Cross-Prompt Reuse of Entity-Replacement Responses
papers.tldr: Hidden-state changes from related questions can partially transfer entity-replacement effects across prompts, but success depends strongly on model, format, cohort, and protocol.

papers.abstract: Multi-image vision-language models (VLMs) incur substantial computation when processing long visual sequences. Compressing these sequences must preserve complementary evidence across images and keep tokens from different images separate. Global selection can underrepresent question-relevant images, and pruning in early decoder layers risks removing relevant content before sufficient multimodal processing, yet existing methods spend most of the budget on these early layers. We propose SIEVE, a training-free, single-pass framework that jointly allocates visual tokens across images and decoder depth. SIEVE first pools each image into a compact spatial grid to reduce early processing cost. It then progressively selects representatives using prompt attention under equal per-image quotas and aggregates unselected tokens into similar representatives from the same image. These operations keep every image represented and its tokens separate from other images, while refining the retained representations. A closed-form schedule sets retention counts to target a prescribed average token budget across decoder layers. Across four VLM backbones, SIEVE achieves the highest average at a 6.25% budget on five multi-image benchmarks and four single-image benchmarks, and the highest mean on two video benchmarks. On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, it outperforms the strongest baseline by 9.96 and 9.03 points at 6.25% and 12.5% budgets, and at 12.5% it exceeds the uncompressed model by 2.01 points with 6.6x fewer prefill FLOPs.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of compressing long multi-image visual sequences without losing question-relevant or cross-image evidence.
Pools each image into a compact grid, then progressively selects prompt-relevant tokens under equal per-image quotas.
Aggregates discarded tokens only into similar representatives from the same image, keeping image-specific information separate.
Uses a closed-form depth schedule to distribute token retention across decoder layers.

Across multiple VLM backbones and image/video benchmarks, SIEVE achieves leading average performance at low budgets; on LLaVA-OneVision-7B, it delivers 6.6× fewer prefill FLOPs while exceeding the uncompressed model at a 12.5% budget.
