papers.selection_reason: Proposes SIEVE, a depth-aware token compression framework for multi-image VLMs that preserves spatial evidence, relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: SIEVE: Preserving Cross-Image Evidence via Depth-Aware Token Compression
papers.tldr: SIEVE is a training-free token-compression method that preserves evidence from every image while allocating computation across decoder layers, achieving strong accuracy with very small visual-token budgets.

papers.abstract: Self-verification and aggregation have emerged as popular approaches for bridging the gap between pass@1 and pass@N. However, increasing the number of candidates does not consistently narrow the gap between final-answer accuracy and pass@N. To understand this limitation, we use ranking error to measure how reliably models distinguish their correct generations from incorrect ones. We show that ranking error admits a bias-variance decomposition, with both components shaped by algorithmic design choices and inference compute. Across our experiments, additional compute reduces variance, while bias initially decreases before approaching a plateau. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Scorpio, a simple and general method that jointly scores randomly grouped candidates. Across math, code, and puzzle benchmarks, Scorpio improves verification, tree search, and aggregation. For verification, Scorpio improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by up to 7 percentage points while matching or exceeding that baseline's peak accuracy with 17-42% lower inference cost. For tree search, using Scorpio to score partial solutions and select the final answer improves accuracy by up to 10 percentage points over prior methods. Finally, Scorpio improves the scaling of aggregation-based methods by 11 percentage points on coding tasks.
bullets: The study analyzes why candidate generation and aggregation fail to consistently close the pass@1–pass@N gap.
Ranking error follows a bias–variance decomposition: extra compute reduces variance, but bias only falls initially before plateauing.
Scorpio jointly scores randomly grouped candidates and improves verification, tree search, and aggregation across math, code, and puzzle benchmarks.
It improves verification accuracy by up to 7 percentage points, reduces inference cost by 17–42% at comparable peak accuracy, and improves tree-search accuracy by up to 10 points.
Aggregation scaling improves by 11 percentage points on coding tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Test-time search using SCORPIO matches or outperforms prior methods without any training. Results for GPT-OSS-20B on AIME 2024 and LCBv6. We compare SCORPIO, which jointly scores partial solutions during search, with ThinkPRM-1.5B (Khalifa et al., 2025), which uses a trained process reward model, and DeepConf, which uses confidence scores derived from token probabilities. We vary the number of initial solutions: N ∈ {8, 32, 128} for SCORPIO and ThinkPRM, and N ∈ {16, 64, 256} for DeepConf to keep total costs comparable. Top-1 accuracy is plotted against total inference cost. Similar trends are observed for Qwen3.5-4B (see Fig. 20).

Figure 2: SCORPIO scales better with inference compute than prior verification methods across math (HMMT), puzzle (RG Games), and code benchmarks (LCBv6). We compare SCORPIO’s scoring with V1 (Singh et al., 2026), a recent test-time scaling algorithm that scores candidates through pairwise comparisons between similar candidates, and pointwise scoring, where LLMs evaluate candidates in isolation. SCORPIO jointly scores candidates in groups of four. Inference compute is measured as the total dollar cost of all input and output tokens, and is scaled by repeating candidate evaluations. Results are averaged over 20 seeds, with shaded regions indicating 95% confidence intervals.

Figure 1: Sampling more candidates improves the chance of a correct answer, but selecting it does not scale well with N . (a) The gap between pass@1 and pass@N exists even for frontier models on agentic tasks.1 (b) As N increases, the gap between pass@N and the selection accuracy of V1 (Singh et al., 2026), a recent self-verification method for scaling test-time compute, widens. (c) A similar trend holds for Recursive Self-Aggregation (RSA) (Venkatraman et al., 2025). For (b) and (c), we run each method until accuracy plateaus; refer Sec. E.1 for further details.

Figure 10: A judge from a different model can reduce ranking bias. Candidates generated by Qwen3.5-4B are scored with SCORPIO (K = 4) either by Qwen3.5-4B itself (the self judge) or by one of four other judges, on HMMT Feb 2025 (top) and LCBv6 (bottom). We plot bias2, variance, ranking error, and top-1 accuracy as the number of scoring rounds M increases, averaged over 20 repetitions; shaded regions show 95% confidence intervals for top-1 accuracy. At M = 20, replacing the self judge with GPT-OSS-20B reduces the ranking error from 0.17 to 0.07 on HMMT and from 0.23 to 0.13 on LCBv6, and improves top-1 accuracy from 67.6% to 75.0% and from 57.0% to 71.6%, respectively.

Figure 11: Different models have different biases. For every pair of a correct and an incorrect candidate generated by Qwen3.5-4B, we record whether the self judge and another judge rank the correct candidate higher after M = 20 scoring rounds of SCORPIO (K = 4), on HMMT Feb 2025 (top) and LCBv6 (bottom). Fractions are averaged over questions and 20 repetitions.

Figure 7: Pruning candidates with SCORPIO allows RSA to scale with pool size N . Using GPT-OSS-20B on LCBv6, we plot (a) accuracy across L = 1→ 10 aggregation rounds for different pool sizes N . Increasing N degrades RSA performance, whereas RSA + SCORPIO improves with larger pools. One failure mode contributing to this degradation is shown in (b): RSA amplifies rare incorrect responses over successive rounds on problem 120. LCBv6 requires a complete Python solution in a single turn and does not permit tool calls. However, RSA amplifies rare incorrect responses containing tool calls over successive rounds, with the effect becoming more severe as N increases (see Fig. 22). After each round, SCORPIO scores all N candidates, and only the top N/2 are used to construct aggregation sets for the next round, limiting this bad-mode amplification. Results are averaged over 8 seeds, with 95% CI.

Figure 20: Test-time search using SCORPIO matches or outperforms prior methods. Results for Qwen3.5-4B on AIME 2024 and LCBv6. Top-1 accuracy of test-time search versus total inference cost on AIME 2024 and LCBv6 for Qwen3.5-4B. We vary the number of solutions we start with: N ∈ {8, 32, 128} for SCORPIO and ThinkPRM, and N ∈ {16, 64, 256} for DeepConf to keep total costs comparable. Inference compute is measured as the total dollar cost of all input and output tokens across LLM calls; see Sec. D.2 for details.

Figure 9: Residual bias dominates ranking error as compute grows. Variance and squared bias of the ranking error of SCORPIO (K = 4) versus the number of scoring rounds M for Qwen3.5-4B (top) and GPT-OSS-20B (bottom). Black circles show the squared bias, which flattens as M grows, and teal squares the variance; curves show least-squares fits of a+ b/ √ M to the variance. The box gives the fitted a, b, and R2 for the variance, and the share of the ranking error due to squared bias at M = 20. Using the asymptotic variance a together with the squared bias at M = 20, we estimate that bias would account for 91% to 99% of the ranking error as M grows.

Figure 8: Increasing compute does not change the mean of the score distribution, but can reduce the bias in rankings. At low compute (solid curves), overlapping score distributions allow the incorrect candidate to receive a higher score than the correct one. Averaging more evaluations (dotted curves) concentrates the scores around their respective means. Since the correct candidate has a higher mean score in this example, this makes an incorrect ordering less likely, reducing the pair’s squared bias (E[Zij ]) 2.

Figure 4: Larger groups reduce variance faster but can increase bias. Results for GPT-OSS-20B on HMMT (math) and LCBv6 (code). Increasing the group size allows more evaluations within the same cost budget, reducing variance faster. However, these gains can come at the expense of increased bias: on LCBv6, K = 8 yields higher bias than smaller groups. Similar trends are observed for Qwen3.5-4B (see Fig. 18).

Figure 12: V1 (Singh et al., 2026) accuracy plateaus well below pass@N , and the gap widens as N increases. Results for GPT-OSS-20B on LCBv6. (a) Increasing the candidate pool from N = 8 to N = 128 yields modest gains in selection accuracy, while the gap to pass@N grows from roughly 5 to 11 percentage points. Points show means over 20 seeds, with error bars indicating 95% confidence intervals. (b) Accuracy plateaus as inference compute increases for each pool size, remaining below the corresponding pass@N ceiling (dashed lines). Inference compute is measured as the total cost of the input and output tokens of each LLM call; see Sec. D.2 for further details.

Figure 13: RSA’s (Venkatraman et al., 2025) final accuracy decreases as the candidate pool grows. Results for GPT-OSS-20B on LCBv6. (a) Increasing N from 8 to 128 lowers final accuracy, widening the gap to pass@N from roughly 12 to 26 percentage points. Points show means over 8 seeds, with error bars indicating 95% confidence intervals. (b) Each curve tracks accuracy over successive aggregation rounds for a fixed N . Larger pools plateau at lower accuracy despite higher compute costs. Inference compute is measured as the total cost of the input and output tokens of each LLM call; see Sec. D.2 for further details.

Figure 21: Repeated evaluation of partial solutions improves search accuracy. Top-1 accuracy of test-time search using SCORPIO versus total inference cost on AIME 2024, HMMT Feb 2025, and LCBv6. We fix the number of solutions we start with at N = 128 and vary the number of times the random grouping and scoring process is repeated, M ∈ {1, 2, 3}. Repeated evaluations improve accuracy over M = 1 across all three datasets. Inference compute is measured as the total dollar cost of all input and output tokens across LLM calls; see Sec. D.2 for details.

Figure 15: SCORPIO achieves higher accuracy on math and similar accuracy at lower cost on code compared with PPT (Kwok et al., 2026). Selection accuracy versus total inference cost for GPT-OSS-20B with N = 128 candidates. On HMMT Feb 2025, SCORPIO (K = 4) improves peak accuracy by 8 percentage points over PPT. On LCBv6, it reaches PPT’s accuracy at 1.5× lower total cost. PPT’s strategy proceeds in two phases: an initial ring phase ensures that every candidate is evaluated, followed by a tournament phase. Points labeled “ring” show accuracy after the first phase, while k = 1 and k = 2 indicate whether one or two evaluations are used per pair. Curves show mean accuracy, with shaded regions indicating 95% confidence intervals. Inference compute is measured as the total dollar cost of all input and output tokens across LLM calls; see Sec. D.2 for details.

Figure 14: V1 (Singh et al., 2026) also exhibits a widening selection gap on HMMT Feb 2025. Results for GPT-OSS20B. (a) Increasing N from 8 to 128 yields modest gains in selection accuracy, while the gap to pass@N grows from roughly 6 to 11 percentage points. (b) Selection accuracy plateaus as inference compute increases, remaining below the corresponding pass@N ceiling (dashed lines). Inference compute is measured as the total cost of the input and output tokens of each LLM call; see Sec. D.2 for further details.

Figure 22: Larger pools amplify tool-call responses in RSA, while SCORPIO limits their amplification. Proportion of responses containing tool calls across aggregation rounds for a single LCBv6 problem using GPT-OSS-20B. This is a single-turn task that requires a solution in a Python code block. Some responses attempt tool calls to test their logic, which we identify using the pattern to=[A-Za-z_]. The harness does not support tool calls, and 95% of these responses receive zero reward. Tool-call responses remain uncommon with N = 8 but become increasingly common with N = 32 and N = 128 as aggregation rounds progress. In RSA + SCORPIO, candidates are scored using SCORPIO after each round, and only the top half of candidates are used to build aggregation sets for the next round. This selection reduces the proportion of tool-call responses to nearly zero across all three pool sizes.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the limits of test-time compute for self-evaluation and introduces Scorpio, a method for joint scoring of candidates, fitting the test-time learning subtopic.
papers.title: On the Limits of Test-Time Compute for Self-Evaluation
papers.tldr: More test-time compute does not reliably improve self-evaluation because ranking bias eventually plateaus; Scorpio addresses this by jointly scoring grouped candidates.

papers.abstract: Speech language models encode audio at a much higher rate than text, causing the KV cache to dominate the memory, bandwidth, and decoding cost of long-form generation. KV retrieval can reduce per-step access by attending to only a query-dependent subset of the cache, but existing methods are designed primarily for text and do not account for the structure of audio attention. We first show that retrieval errors may compound autoregressively into generation drift. We then analyze full audio attention during long-form generation and identify three properties relevant to retrieval: unequal attention concentration across query heads, non-contiguous audio support, and temporal continuity across decoding steps. Guided by these observations, we propose $C^3$(Cluster-Compete-Compete), which organizes audio KVs in a hierarchical key-space index, lets query heads sharing a KV head compete for a common retrieval budget, and adaptively reallocates retrieval resolution through paired split-merge updates. Across long-form speech recognition, translation, and summarization on four SpeechLLMs, $C^3$ achieves the strongest overall performance among retrieval methods under comparable final-KV access budgets, with particularly large gains in the tight-budget regime, while improving long-context decoding efficiency and accelerator-memory scaling.
bullets: Audio is encoded much more densely than text, making the KV cache a major memory, bandwidth, and decoding bottleneck.
Retrieval errors can accumulate autoregressively, causing generation drift; audio attention also has unequal head concentration, non-contiguous support, and temporal continuity.
C3 uses a hierarchical key-space index, shared retrieval-budget competition among query heads, and adaptive split-merge updates to adjust retrieval resolution.
Across long-form speech recognition, translation, and summarization on four SpeechLLMs, C3 performs best among comparable retrieval methods, especially under tight KV-access budgets.
The method improves long-context decoding efficiency and accelerator-memory scaling.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of C3. Audio KVs are organized into a hierarchical key-space index. Query heads sharing a KV head compete over an active frontier for a common retrieval budget, while paired split–merge operations dynamically reallocate frontier resolution.

Figure 2: (a) C3 achieves lossless passcode recovery at substantially smaller retrieval budgets than the baselines. (b) End-to-end latency for audio contexts up to 32K tokens with a 512-KV retrieval budget; retrieval becomes more efficient than full attention as the audio context grows.

Figure 3: Retrieval-induced generation drift. The retrieval trajectory initially follows the relevant audio region but later jumps forward, causing the transcript to lose alignment and terminate prematurely. Curves are smoothed and outliers removed for visualization.

Figure 4: Attention specialization across KV and query heads. Query heads tracking task-relevant acoustic information concentrate on similar regions within each KV group, whereas heads with different preferences exhibit more diffuse attention.

Figure 5: Full audio attention during long-form decoding. (a) The dominant attention band advances with generation; red points mark top-64 positions outside the band. (b) Attention near the frontier is itself non-contiguous.
Figure 6: Needle-in-a-haystack performance on Qwen2.5-Omni-3B, Gemma-4, and Voxtral-Mini-3B. Each row reports exact-match and per-digit accuracy as a function of the audio KV retrieval budget.

Table 3: EMA strength λ (Eq. 2) and adaptation rate R (paired split–merge exchanges per decoding step). WER (↓) at a 256-KV budget with g=16. The shared default configuration (λ=0.5, R=2) is shaded; the best value per model and task block is in bold.

Table 1: Long-form speech performance under tight and large audio KV retrieval budgets. Best retrieval results within each model and budget are shown in bold. Results at intermediate budgets and additional ablations are provided in Appendix G.1.

Table 2: Long-form speech performance under different audio KV retrieval budgets. We report WER (↓) for LibriSpeech-Long (LS-Long) and multilingual long-form ASR (MLS), chrF (↑) for speech translation (ST), and ROUGE-L (↑) for summarization (Summ). Best results within each model and budget are shown in bold. Dash (–) for Quest indicates that Quest does not support the target budget.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses memory efficiency in long-context speech LLMs by proposing a hierarchical KV retrieval method (C3) tailored to the structure of audio attention.
papers.title: C3: Speech-Guided KV Retrieval for Long-Context SpeechLLM Inference
papers.tldr: C3 enables efficient long-context SpeechLLM inference by retrieving only the most relevant audio KV cache entries while preserving generation quality.

papers.abstract: We propose \emph{Déjà Vu}, a test-time decoding module for semantic correspondence. Matching semantically equivalent keypoints across images of the same object category is challenging due to variations in appearance, viewpoint, and scale. While features from large pretrained vision models carry strong zero-shot correspondence ability, existing methods reduce final matching to greedy top-$1$ nearest-neighbor selection. We show that the correct correspondence appears among the top-ranked candidates far more often than top-$1$ matching achieves: with $30$ candidates, zero-shot features exceed the top-$1$ accuracy of a supervised model. This reveals a \textit{decoding bottleneck} rather than a limit of the representation. Motivated by this observation, we formulate semantic correspondence as a \textit{recall-then-rerank} problem. Our method first nominates an adaptive candidate set, larger when the similarity distribution is ambiguous and smaller when it is confident, then re-ranks the candidates with a graded cycle-consistency score: each candidate is matched back to the source image and penalized by how far its reverse match lands from the original keypoint. The module operates entirely on the similarity matrix already computed by the base method. It consistently improves three representative baselines on SPair-71k, its geometric subset, and PF-Pascal under both unsupervised and weakly supervised settings, with gains of up to $+1.8$ PCK@0.10 on SPair-71k and $+3.4$ PCK@0.15 on PF-Pascal, and $+4.9$ under Keypoint Average Precision.
bullets: Addresses a decoding bottleneck: pretrained vision features often contain the correct match among their top candidates, even when top-1 matching fails.
Uses a recall-then-rerank strategy with candidate-set size adapted to similarity ambiguity.
Scores candidates by graded cycle consistency, penalizing reverse matches that return far from the original keypoint.
Operates entirely on the base method’s existing similarity matrix and improves three baselines across SPair-71k and PF-Pascal settings.
Reports gains of up to +1.8 PCK@0.10, +3.4 PCK@0.15, and +4.9 in Keypoint Average Precision.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method overview. Given a query source patch, we apply top-p sampling on the row of the similarity matrix to form a candidate pool (forward pass). For each candidate, we perform a reverse lookup on its column to identify the nearest source patch (backward pass). Each candidate’s final score is its forward similarity minus a penalty that grows with the distance between its reverse match and the original query.

Figure 5: Qualitative examples showing the benefit of cycle-consistent re-ranking on SPair-71k. For each pair, the left image marks the source keypoint and the right image shows three locations: ground truth (GT), the top-1 nearest-neighbor prediction, and our method’s prediction. While top-1 matching selects an incorrect target point, our cycle-consistent re-ranking successfully recovers the correct correspondence from the top-p candidate pool.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on SPair-71k. For each image pair, correspondences are shown as colored lines: green for correct matches and red for incorrect ones (PCK@0.1). We apply our cycle-consistent re-ranking to three base methods (TLR, CleanDIFT, DIY-SC). Across all three baselines and diverse object categories, our method consistently reduces incorrect matches.

Figure 3: Per-category radar plots on PF-Pascal. Each axis represents one object category, and values denote PCK@0.15 (per-keypoint). The filled area shows our method applied to TLR (left) and CleanDIFT (right); the outline shows the respective baseline. Our method consistently expands the coverage across the majority of categories.

Figure 8: Per-category radar plots on SPair-71k (per-keypoint, PCK@0.10). Each axis represents one object category. The filled area shows our method applied to TLR (left), CleanDIFT (middle), and DIY-SC (right); the outline shows the respective baseline. Our method broadly expands coverage across categories for all three base methods.

Figure 7: Additional qualitative examples showing the benefit of cycle-consistent re-ranking on SPair-71k. Each panel shows the source keypoint (left) and three predicted locations on the target (right): ground truth (GT), the top-1 nearest-neighbor prediction, and our method’s prediction. Our cycle-consistent re-ranking consistently recovers the correct correspondence that top-1 matching fails to identify.

Figure 10: Qualitative comparison on SPair-71k with TLR as the base method. Correspondences are shown as colored lines: green for correct and red for incorrect matches (PCK@0.1). Our method (TLR+Ours) consistently reduces incorrect matches across all 18 categories.

Figure 11: Qualitative comparison on SPair-71k with CleanDIFT as the base method. Correspondences are shown as colored lines: green for correct and red for incorrect matches (PCK@0.1). Our method (CleanDIFT+Ours) consistently produces fewer incorrect matches across all 18 categories.

Figure 6: Sensitivity of the cycle-consistency weight λ on SPair-71k (per-keypoint, PCK@0.05) for TLR (left), CleanDIFT (middle), and DIY-SC (right). Performance is stable across a broad range of λ values for all three base methods.

Figure 12: Qualitative comparison on SPair-71k with DIY-SC as the base method. Correspondences are shown as colored lines: green for correct and red for incorrect matches (PCK@0.1). Our method (DIY-SC+Ours) consistently improves correspondence quality across diverse object categories.

Figure 13: Qualitative comparison on PF-Pascal with TLR as the base method. Correspondences are shown as colored lines: green for correct and red for incorrect matches (PCK@0.1). Our method (TLR+Ours) yields more accurate correspondences across all 20 PF-Pascal categories.

Figure 9: Sensitivity of the cycle-consistency weight λ on PF-Pascal (per-keypoint, PCK@0.1) for TLR (left) and CleanDIFT (right). Performance remains stable across a broad range of λ values for both base methods.

Figure 14: Qualitative comparison on PF-Pascal with CleanDIFT as the base method. Correspondences are shown as colored lines: green for correct and red for incorrect matches (PCK@0.1). Our method (CleanDIFT+Ours) consistently reduces incorrect matches across all 20 PF-Pascal categories.

Figure 1: Left: Top-k zero-shot recall on SPair-71k using SD+DINO features. Right: our cycleconsistent re-ranking. The gap between top-1 accuracy and top-k recall shows that correct matches often appear among top candidates but are missed by similarity-only top-1 matching. As k increases, performance rises sharply and even surpasses the fully supervised baseline, motivating a recall-thenrerank strategy (Déjà Vu). We therefore exploit the bijective structure of semantic correspondence through cycle-consistent re-ranking of candidates (e.g., Patchi,j in the right figure).

Table 12: Composition with existing refinement components on SPair-71k (per-keypoint, full test set) with TLR as the base method. Our re-ranking adds to the pipeline in all three configurations, and adds more when window soft-argmax is disabled (+1.83) than when it is enabled (+1.37).

With the mask stripped entirely, the cycle criterion is still worth +1.06. The mask adds no new dependency: the released TLR pipeline already computes these masks for adaptive pose alignment, and we simply reuse them.

Table 3: PCK scores (per-image) across multiple thresholds on SPair-71k, SPair-71k (Geo.), and PF-Pascal. DistillDIFT was evaluated in both unsupervised (US) and weakly supervised (WS, noted with ∗) settings. DIY-SC was evaluated in both DINO (†) and SD+DINO (‡) settings. The best results are bolded and the second best underlined.

Table 2: Per-category PCK@0.1 scores (per-keypoint) on SPair-71k. DistillDIFT was evaluated in both unsupervised (US) and weakly supervised (WS, noted with ∗) [6]. DIY-SC was evaluated in both DINO (†) and SD+DINO (‡) settings. The best results are bolded and the second best underlined.

Table 1: Top-k candidate recall across feature extractors on SPair-71k. For each source keypoint we take the top-k target patches by feature similarity and count the keypoint as recovered if any of them falls within the PCK radius. The reference column is the top-1 accuracy of the supervised TLR model on the full test set; the table itself uses 100 pairs per category without sub-patch refinement, so its k=1 column differs slightly from the reference; bold marks, within each row, k⋆: the smallest k at which top-k recall exceeds that reference.

Table 14: Sensitivity to τ , Kmin and Kmax on SPair-71k (per-keypoint, full test set) with TLR as the base method. The feature grid has L = 3,600 patches, so Kmax = 3,600 removes the cutoff entirely. The total range across every setting is 0.17 PCK@0.10. Unlike λ, these three parameters do not appear in the re-ranking score of Eq. 9; they only control how many candidates are nominated.

Table 6: Comparison against standard cycle-consistency rules on SPair-71k (per-keypoint, full test set) with TLR as the base method. All variants use the same top-p candidate pool and differ only in how the cycle distance dcyc (Eq. 8) is used.

Table 7: PCK scores (per-keypoint) across multiple thresholds on SPair-71k, SPair-71k (Geo.), and PF-Pascal. DIY-SC was evaluated in both DINO (†) and SD+DINO (‡) settings. The best results are bolded and the second best underlined.
Table 4: Ablation study on SPair-71k (per-keypoint) across baselines (top to bottom: TLR, CleanDIFT, DIY-SC). The best results are highlighted in bold.

Table 5: Alternative formulation comparison on SPair-71k (per-keypoint) using TLR as the base. We compare OT-based re-ranking (Sinkhorn, Partial OT) against ours. The best results are highlighted in bold.

Table 13: How often each cycle rule fixes or breaks a prediction on SPair-71k (per-keypoint, N = 88,328) with TLR as the base method, compared against the baseline without a cycle term from Table 6. Win rate is c/(b+ c), the share of flipped keypoints that flip from wrong to right.

Table 17: Keypoint Average Precision (KAP) [21] on SPair-71k (full test set) with TLR as the base method, reported as the per-category mean AP. Unlike PCK, KAP compares the best score near the ground truth against the best score elsewhere, so it penalizes both missed matches and wrong matches to repeated or symmetric parts.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a cycle-consistent re-ranking strategy for semantic correspondence, a core task for spatial understanding in vision-language models.
papers.title: Déjà Vu: Cycle-Consistent Re-ranking for Semantic Correspondence
papers.tldr: Déjà Vu improves semantic correspondence by adaptively reranking top candidate matches using cycle consistency instead of relying on greedy top-1 selection.

papers.abstract: Audio-language models (ALMs) are evaluated on their understanding of both speech and environmental sounds. What remains underexplored is how they respond when spoken claims contradict acoustic evidence within the same recording. We introduce SAC-Bench, a benchmark of intra-audio speech--acoustic conflict comprising 616,031 unique clips from 188 sound-event classes across seven semantic, temporal, and spatial tasks. It pairs environmental recordings with compatible or contradictory synthesized spoken claims and includes audio-only controls where applicable. Across five open-weight ALMs evaluated on semantic and temporal tasks, high audio-only accuracy often coexists with large losses under conflicting claims; Event Identity accuracy is 24.8--46.5 percentage points lower in conflict than compatible conditions. Temporal Order failures persist even when speech follows the complete event sequence, so simultaneous speech--event masking cannot fully explain them. A spatial case study with Spatial-Omni finds lower motion accuracy associated with both spoken claims and the speech source's physical trajectory. Prompt interventions sometimes restore acoustic accuracy, but can also reduce claim-aligned answers without improving grounding or worsen performance. SAC-Bench thus separates acoustic competence, conflict robustness, and intervention effects.
bullets: Introduces 616,031 clips covering 188 sound-event classes and seven semantic, temporal, and spatial tasks.
Tests compatible versus contradictory spoken claims paired with environmental recordings, plus audio-only controls.
Across five open-weight models, Event Identity accuracy drops by 24.8–46.5 percentage points under conflict.
Temporal-order errors remain even when speech comes after the full event sequence, suggesting masking is not the sole cause.
Prompt interventions have inconsistent effects and may not improve acoustic grounding.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SAC-Bench. A single audio waveform contains spoken claims and environmental acoustic evidence that may imply conflicting interpretations. SAC-Bench evaluates this conflict across four task groups: event presence, event identity, temporal structure, and spatial configuration.
Figure 2: SAC-Bench construction pipeline, from environmental audio selection and spoken claim synthesis to conflict generation, audio rendering, and evaluation.

Figure 3: Taxonomic and semantic coverage of sound-event labels in AudioSet, FSD50K, and SAC-Bench. (a) Label distribution across ten ontology categories with fractional assignments. (b) UMAP projection of label-name embeddings.

Figure 6: Claim and speaker cues in Spatial-Omni’s FOA motion task. (a,b) Matched acoustic accuracy when claim C and speech trajectory S match ground truth A or an alternative B. (c) Attraction to conflicting C and S relative to audio-only controls. Error bars show 95% class-bootstrap confidence intervals; dashed lines mark 25% chance in (a,b) and zero attraction in (c).

Table 5: Prompt-policy performance on representative conflict tasks (%). Neu: neutral; AG: acousticgrounded; CA: conflict-aware. Presence uses recording-level BAcc; other tasks use accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks audio-language models under speech-acoustic conflict, contributing to evaluation of multimodal foundation models spanning non-visual modalities.
papers.title: One Waveform, Two Stories: Benchmarking Speech-Acoustic Conflict in Audio-Language Models
papers.tldr: SAC-Bench shows that audio-language models with strong audio understanding can struggle when spoken claims contradict the recording’s acoustic evidence.

papers.abstract: A child learns which words name which things from roughly 100 million words of input. Vision-language models trained at a comparable scale bind words to referents far less reliably, and we argue that part of the gap is structural: the usual next-token captioning objective has no variable standing for "this word refers to that region," so training applies no direct pressure to ground words. We add such a variable by treating each scene as a small assignment problem between the content words heard and the regions seen, solved as entropic optimal transport under two constraints. First, a word may be assigned to a special NOTHING column instead of any region, which matters because most content words in caregiver speech do not name anything visible. Second, no region may receive more than a bounded share of the assignment mass, a capacity constraint that encodes mutual exclusivity. The alignment step costs about eight Sinkhorn iterations, small next to the vision encoder. In controlled simulation, the naive version of the idea, a row-wise softmax that forces every word onto some region, collapses to 0.000 word-to-picture accuracy under realistic non-reference rates, below the 0.058 of captioning alone, while our two constraints reach 0.075 in that regime and 0.700 on clean input. A one-parameter version of the model reproduces adult cross-situational learning accuracy across three ambiguity conditions (RMSE 0.024). On the SAYCam infant video corpus, adding the alignment loss to a next-token captioning model raises word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38. A contrastive model trained on the same child's data remains stronger on its own benchmark, so our claim is that the loss improves a captioning objective under high non-reference rates, not that it sets a new best.
bullets: Motivation: Standard next-token captioning lacks an explicit variable linking words to visual regions, weakening referential grounding.
Method: Solve an entropic optimal-transport assignment between content words and regions, with a NOTHING option for non-referential words and capacity limits enforcing mutual exclusivity.
Results: On SAYCam, alignment improves word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38.

Controlled studies show the constrained formulation outperforms a row-wise softmax under realistic non-reference rates and matches adult cross-situational learning patterns across ambiguity conditions.
Scope: The method improves captioning-based grounding but does not outperform a contrastive model on that model’s benchmark.

papers.title: GAVAGAI: Referential Alignment for Infant-Scale Vision-Language Models via Balanced Optimal Transport
papers.tldr: GAVAGAI improves infant-scale vision-language grounding by adding balanced optimal-transport word–region alignment to captioning, especially when many words do not refer to visible objects.

papers.abstract: Collaborative robots (cobots) are designed to be safer and more interactive than traditional industrial robots, share the same workspace as humans, and assist them in a range of shop-floor tasks such as palletization, joint assembly, and part inspection. Many of these tasks involve repetitive workflows that may evolve with changes in production environments and task specifications. These requirements motivate the need for intuitive interfaces that allow workers to modify workflows on the shop floor and generalise these routines for future use. This work introduces the Teach-Abstract-Apply (TAA) framework, which enables human operators to (a) teach new workflows to cobots in natural language, (b) abstract the taught workflows into skills for later use, and (c) apply these skills in different settings. As a case study, we apply the TAA framework to a collaborative structure-building task and evaluate it with both open-weight (Qwen3-Coder) and closed (GPT5.2-Codex) models in self-play and cross-model configurations. Our results show that skill abstraction improves task success rates and reduces interaction cost. Beyond automated evaluation, a preliminary human-in-the-loop study suggests that the pipeline also works with human instructions.
bullets: Addresses the need for intuitive, adaptable cobot programming as shop-floor tasks and environments change.
Uses a three-stage pipeline: teach workflows, abstract them into skills, then apply those skills to new situations.
Evaluated on a collaborative structure-building task with open- and closed-model agents in self-play and cross-model setups.
Skill abstraction improved task success rates and reduced interaction cost.
A preliminary human-in-the-loop study indicates the approach can also handle human instructions.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have achieved impressive visual quality, yet they often fail to produce physically consistent dynamics due to the lack of explicit modeling of underlying physical processes. Existing approaches either rely on simulators with strong assumptions or use coarse semantic guidance, and further struggle to effectively inject physical priors into generation models. In this work, we propose Seeing the Unseen, a unified framework for physics-grounded video generation. Our approach decomposes the problem into two stages: learning physical dynamics and injecting them into video synthesis. First, we introduce a lightweight Particle-based Graph Dynamics Simulator (PGDS) that learns generalizable physical interactions from data and predicts plausible 3D motion trajectories. Second, we propose a Visible--Invisible Motion Field (VIMF) that captures both motion observable in the input frame and motion that emerges over time due to object dynamics. This representation enables more complete and structured motion guidance compared to conventional physical signals. By integrating these trajectories into a diffusion-based generator, our method produces videos that are both visually coherent and physically consistent. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved motion accuracy, interaction consistency, and reduced physical artifacts compared to strong baselines.
bullets: Addresses physically implausible dynamics in video generation caused by weak or coarse physical modeling.
Uses a lightweight Particle-based Graph Dynamics Simulator to learn interactions and predict plausible 3D trajectories.
Introduces a Visible–Invisible Motion Field that represents observed motion and motion emerging over time.
Injects the learned motion guidance into a diffusion-based video generator.
Experiments report improved motion accuracy, interaction consistency, and fewer physical artifacts than strong baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our proposed framework. Given an input image, we first lift it into a 3D scene particle representation. A particle-based graph dynamics simulator then predicts physically plausible 3D motion trajectories, which are rendered into reference-visible and future- merg nt motions to guide physically consistent video generation.

Figure 3: Architecture of the physics-guided video generation model. The visible and future visible motion fields are encoded by a frozen 3D VAE and concatenated with the noisy video latent along the channel dimension. A zero-initialized injection strategy preserves the pretrained model behavior while progressively incorporating motion guidance.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison with existing methods. Our method produces physically plausible dynamics with accurate object interactions (e.g., correct collision responses and domino chain propagation), while baseline models frequently exhibit artifacts such as object interpenetration, implausible motion trajectories, or failure to trigger expected physical events.

Figure 8: Unified motion encoding and injection pipeline. The visible tracking video Vvis and future-visible tracking video Vfv are encoded using a frozen 3D VAE to obtain two latent sequences. These are concatenated with the noisy video latent to form a multi-channel input to the diffusion transformer. To preserve pretrained behavior, the patch embedding weights corresponding to tracking channels are zero-initialized, while the original weights are copied from the pretrained model. The first frame is injected via noise replacement to provide appearance conditioning.

Figure 7: Architecture of the Particle-based Graph Dynamics Simulator (PGDS). The simulator follows an Encode–Process–Decode pipeline. Given particle states, a graph is first constructed based on spatial proximity. Node and edge features are encoded to capture material properties and geometric relations. A message-passing processor then iteratively propagates interaction effects across the graph. Finally, a decoder predicts particle velocities, which are used to update positions and roll out future dynamics.
Figure 6: Comparison with different physical prior injection methods.

Figure 5: Pairwise human evaluation comparing our method against baseline models. For each comparison, human annotators judge which method produces better results across three criteria: (a) instruction-following, measuring how faithfully the generated video adheres to the given text prompt; (b) video quality, assessing visual fidelity, temporal coherence, and artifact severity; and (c) overall preference. Results are reported as win/tie/lose rates (%).

papers.tldr: Seeing the Unseen generates more physically consistent videos by learning 3D dynamics and guiding diffusion synthesis with both visible and emerging motion.

papers.abstract: Cross-view geolocalization aims to determine the geographic location of a ground-level image by retrieving its corresponding satellite image, offering a promising alternative for localization in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-denied or degraded environments such as urban canyons, dense forests, and disaster scenarios. Despite recent progress, existing approaches remain limited by the lack of globally diverse training datasets and benchmarks that are often geographically restricted. Furthermore, most benchmarks rely on panoramic ground views, which do not reflect the limited field-of-view imagery captured by real world cameras. To address these challenges, we introduce Cross-View World 500k (CVW500k), a large-scale globally distributed dataset containing over 500,000 ground-satellite image pairs collected across diverse geographic regions and environments. Unlike previous datasets, CVW500k uses limited field-of-view ground images, providing a more realistic and challenging setting for cross-view geolocalization. In addition, we propose GeoQueryNet, a query-based cross-view fusion transformer framework designed to bridge the viewpoint gap between ground and satellite images. The model leverages a CLIP-based visual encoder with parameter-efficient LoRA adaptation and introduces a Cross-View Alignment Module that uses learnable query tokens to extract geographically consistent features across viewpoints. Our code can be found here: https://github.com/Fahim17/Cross_View_World_Dataset.git .
bullets: Cross-view geolocalization supports localization when GNSS is unavailable or degraded.
Existing datasets are geographically narrow and commonly use unrealistic panoramic ground imagery.
CVW500k provides over 500,000 globally distributed ground–satellite image pairs with limited-field-of-view observations.
GeoQueryNet combines a CLIP-based encoder, parameter-efficient LoRA adaptation, and learnable query tokens for cross-view feature alignment.
The abstract does not report quantitative results or comparisons.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory burden of large model deployment by casting the high precision trained weights to fewer bits. While this promotes memory-efficient inference, it also incurs quantization error that impairs model performance. To compensate for quantization error, the present contribution decomposes the original trained weights into a quantized matrix, a low-rank component, and a sparse matrix that accounts for outlier rows in the weights. Due to analytical intractability and the discrete structure of the decomposition, a simulated annealing search is employed to explore candidate decompositions while avoiding poor local minima. Numerical tests demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach across a broad suite of large language models, including Llama 3.2 1B, Llama 3.2 3B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen2.5 7B, evaluated on natural language generation benchmarks using 4-bit NF4 and FP4 quantizers. The novel method can markedly outperform direct quantization while incurring minimal memory overhead.
bullets: Addresses performance loss from quantization error in memory-efficient large-model deployment.
Decomposes weights into a quantized matrix, a low-rank component, and a sparse matrix for outlier rows.
Uses simulated annealing to search the discrete, analytically difficult decomposition space.
Evaluated on several Llama and Qwen models with 4-bit NF4 and FP4 quantizers on natural language generation benchmarks.
Reports marked improvements over direct quantization while adding minimal memory overhead.

papers.abstract: Held-out validation loss is the standard offline signal for choosing checkpoints and comparing models, but its relation to closed-loop success on a real robot is rarely measured. We measure it for ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and $π_{0.5}$ (action expert only), trained on nested subsets of 12 to 200 demonstrations of a pick-and-place task on an SO-101 arm. We score 82 checkpoints on 25 held-out demonstrations, with each policy's training loss and with the error of the actions it outputs, and compare the scores with 930 bench rollouts. We also score all 700 intermediate checkpoints of 70 training runs, and recover the ball positions of every training, held-out and bench episode from the front camera. Within each policy, hold-out action error correlates with bench success (Spearman $ρ$ from -0.23 to -0.88), but no more strongly than the number of training episodes alone, and not at all among seeds trained on the same data. Across policies the ranking is inverted ($ρ$ = +0.90 at 200 episodes): the policy with the lowest hold-out error succeeded in 3 of 110 rollouts. The most common failure, the arm never leaving its rest pose, ended 96% of rollouts for Diffusion Policy trained on untrimmed demonstrations and 47% for SmolVLA, and cannot occur in a hold-out set made of demonstrations. Among rollouts in which the arm moved, SmolVLA's hold-out action error predicts success well ($ρ$ = -0.81). For the diffusion and flow-matching policies, hold-out loss rises two- to five-fold during training while hold-out action error falls by up to 29%. Held-out metrics are a sound diagnostic of learning but no substitute for evaluation on the robot, and we recommend reporting initiation failure and success among started rollouts as separate bench outcomes.
bullets: Evaluated ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π₀.₅ on a pick-and-place task using 82 checkpoints, 70 training runs, and 930 real-robot rollouts.
Within individual policies, held-out action error often correlated with bench success, but not reliably across random seeds trained on the same data.
Across policies, lower held-out error could correspond to worse robot performance; one policy with the best error succeeded in only 3 of 110 rollouts.
A frequent failure— the arm never leaving its rest pose—cannot appear in demonstration-based hold-out metrics and accounted for many failed rollouts.
The authors recommend real-robot evaluation and reporting initiation failures separately from success conditional on the arm starting.

papers.abstract: We present DELBERT-2, a pretrained fingerprint language model that converts sparse molecular fingerprints into unified token sequences using a ModernBERT encoder trained with masked language modelling on 2.5M molecules from the AIRCHECK DEL corpus. We evaluate across six targets (WDR91, WDR12, SETDB1, PLCZ1, LRRK2, DCAF7) under three out-of-distribution (OOD) protocols: hierarchical cluster splits probe chemical novelty, library splits test cross-library transfer, and building-block splits assess compositional generalization. DELBERT-2 consistently improves PR-AUC and NDCG@1000 relative to LightGBM ensemble baselines and transformers trained from scratch, with the largest gains in stringent OOD regimes. DELBERT-2 achieves 13.28+/-3.72 enrichment factor at top-100 vs. 12.36+/-3.75 for no-pretraining (p=0.040), representing 7.4% improvement and 13x enrichment over random selection. These results demonstrate that fingerprint-centric self-supervised learning effectively improves hit prioritization under distribution shift, enabling practical DEL virtual screening. Code is available at \hyperlink{https://github.com/GenerativeDrugDiscovery/DELBERT-2}{DELBERT-2}.

papers.abstract: Automated theorem generation (ATG) seeks to construct new theorems rather than merely prove given conjectures. Existing approaches typically generate candidate statements that require subsequent proof or formal verification. We propose a constructive framework for ATG in first-order logic based on triangular standard contradictions. The method constructs minimally unsatisfiable clause sets from selected first-order literals, then forms theorems by retaining some clauses as premises and taking the negation of one clause, or a conjunction of clauses, as the conclusion. Minimal unsatisfiability ensures that the remaining premises are satisfiable, avoiding trivial inference by explosion, while unsatisfiability of the full set guarantees the resulting entailment. Theorems are therefore correct by construction, without a separate proof procedure for each instance. Extending the previously developed $Δ_1$ generator, we introduce seven methods, $Δ_2$--$Δ_8$, forming a unified family of eight theorem-generation methods. Four generators, $Δ_1$--$Δ_4$, have been implemented and released. We also formulate a general $Δ$-class method encompassing the family. Combinatorial analysis demonstrates the capacity to generate large numbers of distinct theorems systematically. This framework offers a principled foundation for automated theorem discovery and the construction of logically guaranteed knowledge.
bullets: Addresses automated theorem generation, which aims to create new theorems rather than only prove supplied conjectures.
Constructs triangular standard contradictions from selected first-order literals and converts subsets into premises and conclusions.
Uses minimal unsatisfiability to ensure premises remain satisfiable, while full-set unsatisfiability guarantees entailment.
Extends the Δ₁ generator with methods Δ₂–Δ₈; Δ₁–Δ₄ are implemented and released.
Combinatorial analysis shows the framework can systematically generate many distinct theorems.

papers.abstract: Computational brain imaging is constrained by a mismatch between increasingly diverse tasks and scarce, heterogeneous clinical data. Although existing brain foundation models transfer pretrained representations, their knowledge remains entangled within model-specific features and fixed architectures. This paper proposes BrainGFM, a generative foundation model that extends knowledge transfer beyond representation reuse through a reusable and reconfigurable brain-imaging prior. By pretraining on a corpus of about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices, BrainGFM supported task-aligned data synthesis for low-data predictive learning and task-adapted post-training for image reconstruction. Across 48 downstream tasks, BrainGFM improved segmentation and classification under limited supervision and achieved high-fidelity image enhancement across heterogeneous imaging conditions. Multicenter clinical validation involving 4,796 stroke patients across two internal and four external centers demonstrated its applicability to three clinically relevant tasks around stroke cohorts. Blinded reader assessments showed that BrainGFM-generated FLAIR images approached acquired FLAIR in overall diagnostic quality. In a human-AI collaboration study, BrainGFM assistance yielded a 14% relative improvement in mean radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy. These findings support generative priors as a reusable foundation for heterogeneous computational brain-imaging applications.
authors: Multi-Center Cooperative Clinical Study Group for "Lesion-Phenotype Brain Mapping in Acute Stroke"
bullets: Addresses scarce, heterogeneous clinical data and the limitations of fixed, representation-based brain foundation models.
Pretrains a reusable, reconfigurable prior on about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices.
Supports task-aligned synthesis for low-data prediction and post-training for image reconstruction.
Improved segmentation and classification across 48 downstream tasks and enabled high-fidelity enhancement across imaging conditions.
Multicenter stroke validation showed clinical applicability; radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy improved by 14% with AI assistance.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of BrainGFM for Computational brain imaging. a. Heterogeneity in brain diseases, patient populations, clinical status, acquisition protocols, and clinical centers produces heterogeneous brain imaging distributions and limits the generalization of DL models. b. Our BrainGFM-1.3M comprises about 1.3 million axial slices spanning major MRI sequences and CT, providing a large-scale dataset for brain generative pretraining. c. Our BrainGFM learns a reusable brain-imaging prior from generative pretraining on our BrainGFM-1.3M dataset. d. Task-specific conditioning controls the pretrained generator where class labels are used for class-conditioned synthesis, segmentation masks for spatially conditioned synthesis, and source images for brain image reconstruction. These conditions are combined with task-specific adaptation as detailed in Fig. 6b,c. e. Evaluation spans 48 downstream tasks, comprising 20 segmentation, 8 classification, and 20 imageenhancement tasks. f. Clinical validation in a multicenter stroke cohort assesses BrainGFM for TOAST stroke subtyping, lesion segmentation, and MRI sequence transformation, as well as its clinical utility in reader studies and radiologist-AI collaboration.

Fig. 6 BrainGFM architecture, generative pretraining and downstream adaptation. a. BrainGFM pretraining consists of brain-domain adaptation of a multi-scale visual tokenizer and next-scale autoregressive generative pretraining. A shared encoder (E) and vector quantizer (Q) map brain images and segmentation masks into multi-scale discrete tokens using a shared visual codebook. The autoregressive Transformer learns the distribution of tokens through coarse-to-fine next-scale prediction under categorical modality and sequence conditions. The pretrained decoder (D) reconstructs brain images or segmentation masks from generated tokens. b. Task-aligned data synthesis adapts BrainGFM with limited supervision using LoRA. For classification, task-specific class conditioning enables the synthesis of class-labelled images for training ResNet50. For segmentation, BrainGFM generates task-specific masks and synthesizes corresponding images, producing image-mask pairs for training UNet. c. Task-adapted post-training adapts BrainGFM for image enhancement using paired source-target images. Source-image tokens condition autoregressive prediction of target-image tokens, while LoRA is optimized using token-level prediction and image-level reconstruction losses.

Fig. 7 Data flow and study design of BrainGFM. a. Eleven public brain-imaging resources comprising 64,754 3D volumes and 1,295,080 axial slices were collected and partitioned into pretraining and held-out subsets. The pretraining subset was used for two-stage generative pretraining, including visual tokenizer training and autoregressive modeling.Heldout samples from nine shared datasets, together with 15 additional public datasets, supported downstream evaluation across 48 tasks, including segmentation (20 tasks), classification (8 tasks), and image enhancement (20 tasks). Task-specific training data were constructed through labeled image–mask pair generation, class-conditioned image synthesis, and source– target image pairing. b. Six clinical stroke cohorts comprising 4,796 patients and 4,829 cases from two internal centers (JLH and NFH) and four external centers (NJH, WXPH, NJPH, and CZSPH) were collected. Task-eligible cases were selected according to task-specific imaging and annotation criteria for lesion segmentation, TOAST subtyping, and DWI-to-FLAIR transformation. Internal-center data were used for task-specific training, including low-data settings, while separate internal and external test sets were used for clinical validation.

papers.abstract: Large generative models are commonly trained on data collected from the open web, which may contain data produced by previous generations of the same model. Previous work has shown that recursively training on model-generated data can progressively degrade model performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. Yet, generative models continue to improve dramatically over time. Existing theory suggests that this is enabled by the availability of new real data at each iteration, kept separate from generated data. However, exact separation is not realistic, and uncurated data is still commonly used. We bridge this gap by considering a more realistic setup in which real and generated data are not handled differently during training. Specifically, we present a comprehensive theoretical study of iterative estimation of the mean and covariance of a multivariate Gaussian distribution. At each iteration, samples are drawn from a mixture of the real data distribution and the estimated distribution from the previous iteration, but are used indistinguishably. We provide a single equivalent condition for consistency of the mean and covariance estimators in Euclidean norms, and convergence to zero of the expected squared 2-Wasserstein distance between the estimated and true distributions. Using this result, we show that consistency holds, i.e., model collapse is avoided, for any fixed real data fraction above zero, and even for a fraction that vanishes across iterations, provided it does not vanish too quickly. However, more real data (or data curation) remains important at practical finite times: the convergence rate of the mean estimator deteriorates as the real data fraction approaches zero. We support our results with an empirical investigation of the theoretical setup, and with experiments on iterative training of a diffusion model on CIFAR-10 that correlate with our theory.
bullets: Studies iterative estimation where real and model-generated samples are mixed and used indistinguishably.
Derives a single equivalent criterion for consistency of mean and covariance and vanishing expected squared 2-Wasserstein error.
Shows consistency for any fixed positive real-data fraction, and for fractions that vanish slowly enough across iterations.
Finds that decreasing real-data fractions still slow finite-time mean-estimation convergence.
Supports the theory with simulations and iterative diffusion-model experiments on CIFAR-10.

papers.abstract: Converting a raster image into a resolution-independent, stroke-editable vector sketch while faithfully preserving both structural contours and tonal texture remains challenging: raster-space rendering pipelines are difficult to edit at the stroke level, while generation-from-scratch vectorization methods struggle to remain faithful to an arbitrary input image. We present SketchForge, a training-free framework that converts an input raster image into a resolution-independent SVG sketch through per-instance test-time optimization of Bezier curves, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning. Strokes are seeded via a contour and attention-guided initialization, then refined by a vector-native differentiable rendering pipeline that decouples structural contour strokes from free-form texture strokes under dedicated objectives, composited via multiply-blend layering. Extensive experiments show that SketchForge consistently outperforms existing vector-based baselines in structural fidelity and generation quality. Project page: https://khangcntn123.github.io/SketchForge
bullets: Addresses the challenge of preserving contours and tonal texture while producing resolution-independent, stroke-editable vectors.
Uses per-image test-time optimization of Bezier curves, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning.
Initializes strokes with contour- and attention-guided seeds, then refines them using differentiable vector rendering.
Separately optimizes structural contour strokes and free-form texture strokes, combining them with multiply blending.
Experiments report improved structural fidelity and generation quality over existing vector-based baselines.],

papers.abstract: Dense labels of the aorta in CT are slow to draw, and the public aortic CT datasets that could stand in for them each label different structures under their own conventions. Large language model (LLM) agents can now write code and read images. We asked whether such a model labels these scans better as a free-form agent that writes its own segmentation code, or inside a harness, where an automated pass labels the scan and the model reviews the result. We built a harness, Taurus, and compared it with free-form agents by blind label recovery: we withheld the human labels of six public datasets (939 volumes) and scored every approach against each dataset's own classes. In the first version of Taurus, the model's review raised the primary metric on only two of six datasets, by less than the noise between two reviews of the same case. A free-form agent running Claude Opus 5.5 scored higher on most datasets. Moving what the free-form agents did well into the automated pass then carried most of the gain on 38 held-out cases. The final version smooths the label surfaces with a fixed rule and checks for the large errors the automated pass tends to make, such as an aneurysm drawn to half its size. Each check that fires puts a multiple-choice question to the model, with candidate corrections drawn on the scan. It matched the surface smoothness of the human references, and in the primary metric we found no difference from the free-form Opus agent, at under half its cost, $1.22 against $2.71 per case. Most of what made Taurus competitive came from the harness and its automation rather than from the language model itself. Taurus shows that this kind of annotation can be automated, so that expert time can move from drawing labels to checking them.
bullets: Dense aortic CT labeling is slow, and public datasets use inconsistent structure-labeling conventions.
Taurus combines automated segmentation with LLM review, targeted error checks, candidate corrections, and fixed surface smoothing.
It was evaluated through blind label recovery on six public datasets totaling 939 volumes, plus 38 held-out cases.
The final system matched the free-form Opus agent on the primary metric and matched human-reference surface smoothness.
The reported cost was $1.22 per case versus $2.71 for the free-form agent; most gains came from the harness and automation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Two ways to let a language model label a CT scan. papers.abstract: Outpainting sparse sketches while preserving contour coherence and stroke style remains challenging. We present SketchBloom, a training-free framework that combines pretrained raster outpainting and style-transfer guidance with per-instance vector optimization. Given a sketch, a scene prompt, and an optional reference style, it produces an editable Scalable Vector Graphic (SVG) composed of Bezier strokes. Adaptive latent blending balances content contours and reference texture without model retraining. A reference-derived stroke vocabulary initializes contour- and DINO-attention-guided strokes, which are optimized separately for structure and texture before contour-emphasizing multiply fusion. As in prior optimization-based vector sketching, no task-specific network is trained; our contribution is the synthesis design specialized to sketch outpainting. On LineArtOut-1K, comprising 1,024 input and style combinations, SketchBloom improves perceptual, semantic, and structural fidelity over the evaluated vector baselines when all methods vectorize the same outpainted raster. This protocol evaluates vector synthesis rather than end-to-end outpainting or reference-style superiority. Runtime is approximately six minutes per pair on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. Project page: https://khangcntn123.github.io/SketchBloom/
bullets: Addresses contour coherence and stroke-style preservation in sparse sketch outpainting.
Combines pretrained raster outpainting and style-transfer guidance with per-instance vector optimization.
Initializes and separately optimizes Bezier strokes for structure and texture, then fuses them with contour emphasis.
On 1,024 LineArtOut-1K input/style combinations, it improves perceptual, semantic, and structural fidelity over evaluated vector baselines under a shared-raster protocol.
Runs in approximately six minutes per pair on a single NVIDIA H200; evaluation does not establish end-to-end outpainting or reference-style superiority.

papers.abstract: LLM agents that operate over long inputs must perform context management: deciding what to retain in a fixed-size context window. A common approach is compaction, where the model replaces its history with a self-generated note. Yet off-the-shelf agentic models, including GPT-5.5 and GLM-5.3, often write ineffective notes, and reinforcement learning (RL) alone rarely discovers useful note-taking behavior. We present MEMENTO, a long-context agent built on Qwen3-8B and trained to manage its context through compaction. We first bootstrap note-taking by fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories annotated with notes generated in hindsight, then reinforce it with RL using a reward that combines answer correctness, note-quality heuristics, and confidence calibration. Although trained only to compact into a fresh window, MEMENTO extends at test time to strategies such as context folding and confidence-based backtracking. On book-level question answering across four benchmarks, with books of up to 2.5M tokens, MEMENTO raises Qwen3-8B's accuracy from 36.9% to 67.8% while never holding more than 20K tokens in context. It outperforms GPT-5.5 agent in the same harness (13.1%) and full book context (56.7%) at less than 1/50 the cost. It also nearly matches a ~100x larger GLM-5.3 agent (69.3%) at 1/9 the cost, and comes within 6.4 points of GLM-5.3 full context at 1/26 the cost.
bullets: Addresses ineffective self-generated summaries for long-context agents and the difficulty of learning note-taking with RL alone.
Bootstraps hindsight-annotated note-taking through fine-tuning, then applies RL with answer, note-quality, and confidence-calibration rewards.
Although trained for compaction, it generalizes at test time to context folding and confidence-based backtracking.
On four book-level QA benchmarks with books up to 2.5M tokens, accuracy improves from 36.9% to 67.8% while staying within a 20K-token window.
Achieves performance near the much larger GLM-5.3 agent at lower cost and exceeds the reported GPT-5.5 agent and full-book-context baselines.

papers.abstract: Dexterous robotic manipulation remains a major challenge in robotics, exemplified by piano playing, which requires coordinated control of fingers and provides a demanding testbed for reinforcement learning (RL). Although previous work established a benchmark for robotic piano playing, it is restricted to two hands and does not support unified evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce OmniPiano, a benchmark that provides one to up to five Shadow Hands and supports standard, robust, safe, and multi-agent RL within a shared piano-playing task family. OmniPiano is developed for scalable and diverse piano-playing tasks with configurable perturbations, explicit safety constraints, and decentralized cooperation settings. Particularly, to facilitate usability and extendability, OmniPiano adopts a highly modular design and provides comprehensive tasks to support RL study of task performance, robustness, safety, and cooperation in dexterous control. With at least 912 task settings and 36 baseline algorithms, OmniPiano further incorporates LLM-based agents to broaden the evaluation scope and reveal new insights. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art RL algorithms and frontier LLM-based agents still struggle on challenging piano-playing tasks, even under standard RL settings, highlighting substantial room for improvement in dexterous control. The code, dataset, tutorial, and demo are available at https://sail-research-lab.github.io/omnipiano/.
bullets: Supports one to five Shadow Hands in a unified family of scalable piano-playing tasks.
Covers task performance, robustness to configurable perturbations, explicit safety constraints, and decentralized cooperation.
Provides at least 912 task settings, 36 baseline algorithms, and LLM-based agents for broader evaluation.
Experiments show that current RL methods and frontier LLM agents still struggle with challenging piano tasks, even in standard RL settings.

papers.abstract: A deep understanding of scientific literature often relies on interpreting figures that contain key information beyond the main text. Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract insights from these figures can significantly accelerate knowledge discovery. Existing works on Scientific Visual Question Answering rely on resource-intensive training pipelines that are often inaccessible and require large computational resources. Instead of designing complex architectures, we propose RE- SciVQA, which focuses on improving the quality of retrieved context and fine-tuning small LLMs with parameter-efficient LoRA training. Using a simple query expansion step, relevant section headers are appended to the original question to improve the retrieval coverage. In addition, a simple adjustment of similarity scores is applied using figure references and caption alignment. On the SciVQA benchmark, RE-SciVQA achieves a ROUGE-1 F1 score of 73.9%, outperforming chart-focused models such as UniChart (14.7%), ChartGemma (6.9%), and Matcha-ChartQA (6.3%). Our relevance-enhanced RAG setup also improves the exact match by 11.9% and the fuzzy match by 29.5% compared with a standard RAG baseline, resulting in an overall gain of 14.3%. We also examine closed-ended infinite visual questions, a category in which chart-understanding models often struggle. Our experiments show that using plot digitization instead of synthetic captions leads to an 18.5% improvement for this question type.
bullets: Targets the high computational cost and limited accessibility of existing Scientific VQA pipelines.
Expands questions with relevant section headers and adjusts retrieval scores using figure references and caption alignment.
Uses LoRA to fine-tune smaller LLMs rather than relying on complex architectures or resource-intensive training.
On SciVQA, reports a 73.9% ROUGE-1 F1 score and improves exact and fuzzy matching over standard RAG.
For closed-ended infinite visual questions, plot digitization improves performance over synthetic captions by 18.5%.

papers.abstract: Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) is critical for medical image segmentation as it adapts a model to an unlabeled target domain without accessing source data, thereby preserving data privacy. However, its effectiveness is often limited by confirmation bias: self-training models tend to miss small polyps, hallucinate foreground, and produce imprecise contours. We propose MedRT-SFSeg, a real-time SFDA framework built on a dual-head one-to-one/one-to-many YOLO segmentation architecture. Mask-DHF fuses precision- and recall-oriented predictions into stable pseudo-instances, while DURR uses the sign of pixel-level dual-head disagreement as a directional cue to expand or shrink masks, and additionally recovers missed instances and suppresses hallucinations. Seg-MARD further regularizes feature representations through mask-guided, region-stratified sampling. Experiments on bidirectional adaptation between Kvasir-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB show that MedRT-SFSeg achieves 80.43%/80.77% Dice and 5.53/8.44 mm ASD, improving the non-adapted baseline by 7.7 and 9.8 Dice points while running at more than 62 FPS end-to-end. These results suggest that segmentation-aware dual-head supervision can improve pseudo-label quality without sacrificing real-time inference. Project page: https://danielnguyen-05.github.io/MedRT-SFSeg
bullets: Addresses confirmation bias in unlabeled target-domain adaptation, especially missed small polyps, false foreground, and inaccurate contours.
Uses a dual-head one-to-one/one-to-many YOLO segmentation architecture with Mask-DHF for stable pseudo-instances.
DURR expands or shrinks masks based on directional dual-head disagreement, while recovering missed instances and suppressing hallucinations.
Seg-MARD regularizes features through mask-guided, region-stratified sampling.
On bidirectional Kvasir-SEG/CVC-ClinicDB adaptation, it achieves 80.43%/80.77% Dice, 5.53/8.44 mm ASD, and over 62 FPS end-to-end.

Only the adapted O2O Student is used at inference.

papers.abstract: Uncontrolled hemorrhage remains a leading cause of preventable trauma mortality. Timely intervention is not always available, making autonomous systems that can aid in bleeding control a promising alternative. Given the safety-critical nature of the task, supervised autonomy, in which the system executes the technical steps while a human retains oversight, represents a necessary intermediate step toward this goal. In this work, we present a supervised autonomous bimanual robotic framework for injury cauterization (eletrosurgical coagulation) in low-grade splenic trauma. The system integrates real-time bleeding segmentation, markerless tool keypoint tracking, and deep tool-tissue contact detection to coordinate two robotic arms for synchronized suction and cauterization. Evaluated on a novel, cannulated ex vivo splenic hemorrhage model, the system achieved an average bleeding surface cauterization coverage of 82.9% across seven distinct injuries. This work demonstrates the feasibility of using a supervised autonomous bimanual system to deliver targeted coagulation across an injury site.
bullets: Addresses the need for timely hemorrhage control when immediate human intervention is unavailable.
Combines real-time bleeding segmentation, markerless tool tracking, and deep tool–tissue contact detection.
Coordinates synchronized suction and electrosurgical coagulation with human oversight.
Achieved 82.9% average cauterization coverage across seven distinct injuries.
Demonstrates feasibility in a cannulated ex vivo splenic hemorrhage model; clinical applicability remains unestablished.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning but can suffer from redundant basis directions. Constraining the basis factor to the Stiefel manifold addresses this redundancy through orthonormality. Landing methods allow temporarily infeasible iterates to explore a neighborhood of the manifold while progressively restoring orthogonality without per-step retractions. To improve optimization efficiency while retaining this flexibility, we introduce ProLand (Product-space Landing), a retraction-free optimizer that combines coordinated factor updates with Muon-style spectral directions. By designing the updates in the space of the represented weight increment, ProLand separates objective optimization from orthogonality restoration, supporting efficient feasibility recovery. This coordinated construction also enables Muon-style directions to guide objective optimization while preserving that separation. Experiments cover four GLUE validation tasks on DeBERTa-v3-base and seven language benchmarks on Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Moonlight-16B-A3B across multiple adapter ranks. Across these 11 tasks, ProLand achieves the highest average score among the compared methods in every tested encoder and decoder model-rank configuration.
bullets: LoRA can contain redundant basis directions; enforcing Stiefel-manifold orthonormality helps address this issue.
ProLand uses product-space landing to allow temporarily infeasible iterates while progressively restoring orthogonality without per-step retractions.
Its coordinated updates separate task-objective optimization from feasibility restoration in the represented weight-increment space.
Experiments span 11 GLUE and language-modeling tasks across several models and adapter ranks.
ProLand obtains the highest average score among compared methods in every tested model–rank configuration.

papers.abstract: Autonomous systems that navigate their environment need methods to quickly assess the feasibility and safety of desired trajectories. Traditional solutions that rely on numerical integration can be computationally heavy, while fast data-driven surrogates lack the formal guarantees that numerical approaches provide. This work demonstrates a framework that uses (1) a neural network with a spectral backbone to learn trajectories and quantile bands with built-in constraints (initial conditions and stability); (2) a modified conformal quantile regression to provide calibrated, joint trajectory-level coverage; and (3) interval arithmetic to extend noise-free coverage guarantees to control points. After refactoring the network for inference, the trajectory inference time for a quadrotor under a closed-loop linear quadratic regulator is 3.45~ms on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. The total pipeline time, including trajectory inference time, is 9.81~ms, or approximately 100~Hz, consistent with typical control rates.
bullets: Targets the computational cost of numerical trajectory integration while retaining formal coverage guarantees.
Learns trajectories and quantile bands with built-in initial-condition and stability constraints.
Uses modified conformal quantile regression for calibrated joint coverage over entire trajectories.
Applies interval arithmetic to extend noise-free coverage guarantees to control points.
On a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, inference takes 3.45 ms and the full pipeline runs in 9.81 ms, approximately 100 Hz.
